title: Building a scratchpad on Bun: 7 things that differ from Node
description:
JSLab is a JavaScript & TypeScript scratchpad for macOS, and every run in a Bun tab is a separate Bun process. Bun aims to be Node-compatible, and most Node code runs unchanged. But "most" is where a tool has to make decisions. Here are seven differences, what JSLab does about each, and what they mean if you use Bun yourself.

1. It's JavaScriptCore, not V8

Bun runs on JavaScriptCore, Safari's engine. Anything tied to V8 behaves differently: the v8 module is only partly there, heap snapshots aren't V8's format, --inspect flags don't apply, and stack trace text is formatted differently.

That last one matters if you parse stack traces. JSLab doesn't parse the text: it maps positions back to your source and renders stacks itself, so the output panel looks the same whichever engine produced the error.

2. Module resolution is looser

Bun resolves more like a bundler than like Node:

import { slugify } from "./util"; // no extension: fine in Bun
const fs = require("node:fs");    // require inside an ES module: also fine

Code that works in Bun can fail in strict Node ESM. If you're writing for both, keep the extensions.

3. Bun loads .env on its own

By default Bun reads .env files from the current folder. Handy in a project, surprising in a tool. JSLab turns that off and reads the working folder's .env itself, so the result is the same in every run, and it layers it with your shell and its own Environment Variables sheet in a fixed order.

4. bunfig.toml can change everything

A bunfig.toml in the folder can change how Bun resolves and runs code. JSLab launches every run with --config=/dev/null, so a folder's bunfig.toml is never applied. For the same reason, BUN_OPTIONS is stripped from the run's environment. And NODE_OPTIONS? Passed through, but Bun ignores it.

5. process.exit() and output

A snippet that logs and then calls process.exit() should still show its logs. In JSLab, process.exit() ends the run once its output is delivered. And code that catches the exit (in a try/catch, say) doesn't keep running: later output is dropped, and its timers and servers are stopped.

6. Packages without a restart

JSLab installs npm packages into one shared project, and every Bun run finds them through NODE_PATH. That's why a package you add in one tab is importable in every other tab straight away. With a working directory set, that folder's node_modules is searched first, so you get the project's versions.

7. The Bun is pinned

JSLab ships its own Bun (1.4.0 at the time of writing; Help → About JSLab shows yours). Your snippets don't depend on whether you have Bun installed, or which version is on your PATH.

What this adds up to

Each of these comes from the same rule: a run should behave the same every time, whatever folder or shell it starts from. If you build tools on Bun, it's worth applying that rule to the same seven places.

The full list, including the Browser & Node APIs runtime, is on one docs page.

JSLab launches Nov 15. Bun vs Node: https://js-lab.app/docs/bun-vs-node

title: Midnight 0.2.0 is live
description:
Midnight 0.2.0 is out. And for the first time, it runs on more than just macOS.

Midnight is my accounting app for freelancers and self-employed professionals:

Invoices and e-invoices, time tracking, expense management with receipt attachments, and tax estimates. Everything is stored locally on your own computer, with no cloud and no subscription.

Two of many new improvements are:

More security

Accounting data is nobody else’s business. That’s why Midnight can now be locked with a PIN. On Macs with Touch ID, you can simply use your fingerprint.

Windows and Linux

Until now, Midnight was only available for macOS. Starting with version 0.2.0, there’s a Windows installer that doesn’t require admin privileges. For Linux, there’s an AppImage and a .deb package. Only the menu bar timer and Touch ID remain exclusive to macOS for now.

Midnight is open source (AGPL-3.0) and free to use. You can download it on GitHub:

jannikmenzel / midnight

Local bookkeeping for freelancers and the self-employed in Germany

Midnight

Local bookkeeping for freelancers and self-employed in Germany.


Features

Area What it covers
Overview Income, expenses, profit and open items for the selected period, unbilled time
Income & expenses Paid invoices as income, expenses with receipts, extracting name, amount and date from PDF receipts, CSV export
Categories Custom expense categories, pre-filled with typical items for the German EÜR (cash-basis profit statement)
Invoices Number sequences, line items, VAT and discounts, small business scheme under § 19 UStG, PDF export via LaTeX, e-invoices (ZUGFeRD/Factur-X EN 16931 and XRechnung 3.0), duplicating, saved products
Customers Customer and order numbers, revenue and tracked time per customer, archive
Time tracking Projects with hourly rate, budget or fixed price, timer, manual entries, billing unbilled time as a draft invoice, timesheet export
Vault Document storage with document type, customer and tags, full-text search in PDF text
Reports Monthly trend, margin, categories, forecast for the next three months

title: Modelar para NoSQL: cómo construimos encuestas en vivo con Firestore y por qué una transacción nos estorbaba
description:
Autor: Carlos Jimenez Laura
Curso: Base de Datos II · Universidad Privada de Tacna
Actividad: Grupal 01-U2, NoSQL App Development, desarrollada junto con Arturo Cutipa Flores

Veníamos de trabajar con bases relacionales, y nuestro primer instinto fue pensar en tablas: una de encuestas, otra de opciones, otra de votos y un GROUP BY para los resultados. En Firestore ese diseño funciona mal. En este artículo cuento cómo construimos VotaYa, una app de encuestas con resultados en vivo, y qué decisiones cambian cuando la base de datos es NoSQL.

La actividad pedía evitar Redis, MongoDB, Neo4j y Prometheus, así que elegimos Google Cloud Firestore, una base de documentos.

Enlaces del proyecto
• Aplicación: https://votaya-firestore.onrender.com
• Repositorio público: https://github.com/CRJL19/votaya
• Video: https://youtu.be/isFjASR8LGw

Figura 1. Pantalla de inicio de VotaYa.

Por qué Firestore
Comparamos tres opciones que cumplían la restricción:

El emulador pesó mucho: nos permitió probar contra el motor real de Firestore sin tocar la nube ni gastar cuota.

En NoSQL se modela a partir de las consultas

La pantalla más visitada muestra una encuesta con sus resultados. Con un diseño relacional, cada carga contaría votos. En Firestore pagas por documento leído, así que contar 1 000 votos costaría 1 000 lecturas.
Por eso guardamos los contadores dentro de la propia encuesta:

Mostrar los resultados cuesta ahora una sola lectura, sin importar cuántos votos existan. Es desnormalizar a propósito: el dato se duplica y el trabajo se paga al escribir. En una aplicación donde se lee mucho más de lo que se vota, el cambio sale a cuenta.
Los votos van en una subcolección, y el identificador del votante es el identificador del documento. Así la unicidad la garantiza la propia clave, sin consultar antes.

La transacción que nos estorbaba

Mi primera versión del voto usaba una transacción, lo que parecía la opción correcta: leer la encuesta, leer si el votante ya existe, escribir ambas cosas.
Las pruebas pasaban, pero una llamaba la atención: 10 votos simultáneos tardaban 11,6 segundos en el emulador. Sin esa prueba de concurrencia no lo habríamos visto. La transacción leía el documento de la encuesta, de modo que los votos competían por él y se reintentaban una y otra vez.

Lo que resolvió el problema fue preguntarnos si de verdad necesitábamos leer dentro de la operación. No hacía falta:
• FieldValue.increment() suma sin conocer el valor anterior.
• create() falla por sí solo si el documento del votante ya existe.
Eso permite usar un batch atómico, sin lecturas y por tanto sin bloqueos:

Las dos escrituras ocurren juntas o no ocurren. Si alguien vota dos veces, create() falla, se cancela todo el batch y el contador no se infla, aunque las peticiones lleguen a la vez.

La cifra de producción incluye la red y el servidor, así que no es comparable con las otras dos. Lo importante es que los 10 votos se registraron y el total coincidió.
Hay una concesión: el estado de la encuesta se comprueba antes del batch, por lo que un voto que coincida justo con el cierre aún puede contar. En una encuesta es aceptable. En un sistema de pagos no lo sería.

Resultados en vivo sin gastar la cuota

Firestore puede avisar de cada cambio en un documento mediante listeners, y eso hace que los resultados se actualicen solos. El navegador no se conecta a Firestore directamente: el servidor escucha y reenvía por Server-Sent Events.

Figura 2. Encuesta con resultados en vivo.

Una primera idea era un listener por cada navegador, pero Firestore cobra cada documento entregado a cada listener. Con 50 personas mirando, cada voto costaría 50 lecturas. Por eso el servidor mantiene un solo listener por encuesta y lo reparte a todos los conectados; una prueba automática lo verifica.
El mismo razonamiento se aplicó al health check. Render lo consulta periódicamente y, si cada consulta leyera Firestore, gastaría cuota solo en comprobaciones. Separamos /api/health, que no toca la base, de /api/health/ready, que sí la comprueba.

Seguridad
• El navegador nunca habla con Firestore, y firestore.rules deniega cualquier acceso directo.
• Cerrar o borrar una encuesta exige un token que se entrega solo a quien la crea. En la base se guarda únicamente su hash.
• Hay límite de peticiones por IP y cabeceras de seguridad con Helmet.

Despliegue automático en la nube
La aplicación está publicada en Render, un proveedor público, con su base en Firestore, en Google Cloud. No la desplegamos a mano: cada git push a main ejecuta un workflow de GitHub Actions con tres pasos:

  1. Pruebas de integración contra el emulador oficial de Firestore.
  2. Construcción de la imagen Docker.
  3. Si ambos pasan, una llamada al Deploy Hook de Render, que publica la nueva versión. El despliegue automático propio de Render está desactivado (autoDeploy: false en render.yaml), de modo que el único camino a producción pasa por las pruebas. La credencial de Firestore se configura como variable de entorno en Render y nunca entra al repositorio.

Limitaciones
Prefiero dejarlas claras:
• Un voto por navegador, no por persona. Quien borre sus datos locales puede votar de nuevo. Evitarlo exigiría iniciar sesión.
• Escrituras por documento. Google recomienda no sostener más de una por segundo sobre un mismo documento, y aquí todos los votos actualizan el mismo. Una encuesta masiva necesitaría repartir los contadores en varios documentos.
• Borrar no es en cascada. Eliminar un documento no borra sus subcolecciones, así que usamos recursiveDelete.

Qué me llevo
Lo que más me sirvió fue dejar de preguntar "¿cómo guardo esto?" y empezar por "¿cómo se va a leer?". Y la transacción lenta me enseñó otra cosa: el diseño más seguro en apariencia no siempre es el correcto, y una prueba de concurrencia lo detecta antes que un usuario.
Mi compañero Arturo cuenta en su artículo la otra mitad del proyecto: cómo lo probamos y lo desplegamos de forma automática.

title: My LLM pipeline spent 13 of 18 minutes waiting for answers that never came
description:
I maintain an open-source pipeline that turns a research paper or topic into a cited commercialization screening report. Six LLM agents split the work: three analysts, a writer, a reviewer and a scorer. On 9 November one production run took 1,072 seconds. When I read the logs, 774 of those seconds had gone to requests that had stopped delivering anything.

This is how I found out why, what I changed, and why the root cause is still there. Every change and number comes from a public pull request in the repository, linked at the end.

1. First, make retries visible

The first clue was a 781-second run the day before. In the same run, on the same model, the reviewer wrote 2,880 tokens in 50 seconds while the writer took 282 seconds for 6,487 tokens. That gap made no sense as generation speed.

The writer had actually sent two requests. The first was cut at its 150-second timeout; the second finished. None of this showed up anywhere: usage counted only successful requests, and the retry notice went to stdout, which the worker discarded.

So the first change wasn't an optimization. It was logging (#362): every provider attempt, whether it returned, timed out or failed, now leaves a row with its stage, attempt number, outcome and duration.

2. Not slow generation: stalled connections

With per-attempt rows, the 1,072-second run was easy to read (#363):

  • Writer: stalled for 302 seconds, then 312 seconds; the third attempt returned in 95.
  • Scorer: stalled for 160 seconds; the retry returned in 27.

The same request came back in 27 to 95 seconds on a retry, so generation speed wasn't the problem. The connection was: data stopped flowing mid-answer. A plain request can only learn that by waiting out its whole timeout, and the longer the timeout, the more time it wastes.

3. Stream everything

I switched all six agents to streaming (#363). Answers arrive in chunks, and the wait for each chunk is capped at 60 seconds, so a dead connection is noticed within a minute instead of after several.

Before merging, I wrote down a validation plan and a decision rule (a pre-registration), then ran five topics:

  • 0 of 35 attempts stalled.
  • All 5 reports completed, with technology readiness in the expected range.
  • 31.4 minutes serial, against 53.7 minutes for the same topics the day before.

It wasn't free: 607,840 tokens against 423,040, partly because that model version wrote longer evidence answers.

4. Faster, but 5 of 11 attempts failed

The first production run with streaming took 343 seconds, against 781 and 1,072 for the two before it. But 5 of its 11 provider attempts failed, all in the same pattern (#364):

  1. The stream went silent for 60 seconds and was cut.
  2. A retry two seconds later failed with a connection error within 15 to 18 seconds.
  3. The next attempt succeeded in 4 to 44 seconds.

The writer and the reviewer each used all three attempts. One more failure on either and the run would have failed.

My theory was that retries went down the same connection pool that had just died: the OpenAI SDK's with_options copies a client but shares its HTTP pool. So a transport retry now rebuilds the client on a new connection, and streamed calls get five attempts instead of three (#364).

5. Fresh connections didn't help

The next production run was cancelled at 728 seconds (#365). The writer's request failed on eight new connections in a row: six went silent for 60 seconds, and two raised connection errors at 15 and 33 seconds. In the same run, the three analysts' smaller requests went through.

With a new connection every time, the stale-pool theory was dead. The same request of about 22,000 tokens, sent from my own machine to the same endpoint, got its first chunk in 6.9 seconds. That pointed at the path between the server and the model provider.

6. A probe that costs nothing

The server runs on Railway in Singapore; the model is served from Alibaba Cloud Model Studio's mainland China endpoint. To measure the path itself, I added a link probe to the admin console (#365, #366). It posts requests of 1 KB to 100 KB to the mainland endpoint and to the same service's international endpoint. The requests carry no key: both servers read the whole body before answering 401, so nothing is billed, and the timing is the path's.

Two readings on 9 November, 09:06 to 09:08 UTC (#366):

Endpoint Body Reading 1 (upload done / first byte) Reading 2 (upload done / first byte)
Mainland 1 KB 1.6 s / 1.8 s 0.5 s / 0.75 s
Mainland 100 KB 1.5 s / 3.9 s; 1.5 s / 2.3 s 25.7 s / 37.6 s, and once not uploaded within 30 s
International 1 KB 0.7 s 0.04 s
International 100 KB 40 ms, 47 ms 57 ms, 40 ms

Across 9 and 10 November (#368), a 100 KB upload failed to finish within 30 seconds 3 times in 10 and a 30 KB request went unanswered once in 3, while the international endpoint answered every size in under 0.3 seconds. Large requests stall intermittently and small ones mostly pass, which matches the writer failing while the analysts got through.

I later ran the probe from my own machine (#369): 100 KB got through once in six tries and 30 KB once in three, while the international endpoint answered all fifteen in under 0.8 seconds. The mainland endpoint stalls from two different networks, so it isn't only the server's route.

7. Why the root cause is still there

The reliable fix is the international endpoint. But it needs a separate international account, which means giving up the free quota on the mainland account. For now I've stayed on the mainland endpoint and rely on streaming and retries to limit the damage.

So the stalls still happen. What I can do is make sure users don't pay for them.

8. Users shouldn't pay for my network

Each account gets a fixed number of runs per day. Until now, a run was refunded only if it never started; once it started, any failure counted.

Now one more case is refunded (#368): a run that fails because the model provider couldn't be reached gets the day's unit back, at most three times a day per account. The cap is there because an unlimited refund would switch the daily limit off exactly when the path is at its worst. Cancellations, rejected keys, too little evidence and other failures still count.

I also fixed a misleading message. A timeout used to suggest "try a narrower topic", although the topic had nothing to do with it. The page now says the model provider couldn't be reached and that nothing in the request caused it.

9. Same rules when switching models

When the deployment moved to a new model, I ran the usual pre-registered spot check (#369): 5 of 5 topics completed and 4 of 5 landed in the expected range, so by the rule set in advance the model stays.

That batch ran from my own machine, and it confirmed the path problem again: 28 of 61 provider attempts never returned, and 46% of the time went into them. Two calls succeeded only on their fifth attempt. Under the old three-attempt cap, 3 of the 5 runs would have failed.

What I'd tell myself a week ago

  • Log every attempt before optimizing anything. If you can't see it, every fix is a guess.
  • A plain request hides a stall until its timeout. Streaming with a per-chunk bound surfaces it within a minute.
  • Retry on a fresh connection. It wasn't the cause this time, but it's the right default.
  • Measure the path, not just the model. A probe that sends no key costs nothing and answers faster than paid reruns.
  • Don't bill users for failures they didn't cause. Refund the unit and say plainly what happened.

About the project

Academic Commercialization Agent is MIT-licensed. Give it a research paper or topic and it writes a cited screening report on technology readiness, patents and market. It's a first-pass draft, not due diligence.

  • Code: https://github.com/shuxiachai/academic-commercialization-agent
  • Online app, with sample reports you can read without signing up: https://academic-agent.cc
  • The changes above: #362, #363, #364, #365, #366, #368 and #369 in the repository's pull requests; the pre-registrations and results are in docs/.

A question for anyone running LLM calls across regions: have you seen large requests stall like this, and what did you do about it?

I'm Jingbo, a student at the University of Sydney. This post was drafted with AI assistance; every number was checked against the pull requests listed above.

title: The Rust programming language has reached its 100th stable release
description:
Rust 1.100 marks the 100th stable release of the programming language, highlighted by the long-awaited stabilization of the never type (!) after a decade of work.

The update also brings custom memory allocators via the core Allocator API, new Cargo dependency cooldowns, default unused dependency reporting, and various standard library additions.

The new special data type

After ten years and five failed attempts, the special data type that indicates that a calculation never returns a value has been officially incorporated. This type can now be used in any position, while related operations have become more flexible. This change also affects older versions of the code, as it changes the way the computer handles certain incomplete values.

Memory management and tools

The update brings solid support for custom memory management, allowing developers to define their own memory allocation rules for basic data structures. At the same time, a new helper has been added that automatically performs specific actions when a value ceases to be active in the code.

Security and dependency management

The package management system has gained an optional delay feature, which allows developers to set a minimum age for new packages they use, to reduce the risks of newly released libraries. This feature is based on timestamps and does not affect the immediate installation of packages.

title: Chat SDK agents can now stream generative UI with json-render
description:
You can now stream generative UI from your Chat SDK agent with json-render.

With a typed catalog of components, the agent writes a JSON spec that json-render converts into a Chat SDK card. Each adapter then posts the card in its platform’s native format, such as Block Kit on Slack and Adaptive Cards on Teams.

The catalog covers tables, charts, buttons, and more, so there’s no separate tool to build and maintain for each message shape.

Stream cards as the model writes

streamCard posts the card once its root element has content and updates the message as new elements stream in. Edits go out at most once every 500 ms by default, which matches Chat SDK’s streaming interval. Once the stream ends, the message shows the final, validated card.

Validate specs and enforce platform limits

toCard checks every element’s props against its component schema and throws CardSpecError for an invalid spec. Each problem gets its own readable issue, so you can send the list back to the model for a corrected spec.

Platforms cap what a single message can hold, and Chat SDK adapters degrade content past those caps. The Slack adapter, for example, turns a second table into a code block. Pass limits to reject those specs instead.

Read the documentation to get started, or try the playground.

title: Is that Black Friday "discount" real? Tracking MercadoLibre prices with the official catalog API
description:
Every November, MercadoLibre listings show a crossed-out "original price" next to a shiny discount. Sellers set that number themselves. The only way to know whether a deal is real is to compare today's price with what the product actually sold for over the last weeks.

I wanted that data for Latin America and found nothing: price-history sites exist for Amazon (camelcamelcamel) but not for MercadoLibre's 18 marketplaces. So I built it: a price tracker with shared history, and a price-drop alert on top of it.

The data problem

MercadoLibre closed its public search endpoint in 2024: GET /sites/MCO/search returns 403 even with an app token, and the website sits behind a JavaScript proof-of-work challenge plus Akamai. Every scraper in the Apify Store fights that with residential proxies and headless browsers.

What still works with a plain application token (client_credentials, no user login):

  • GET /products/search?site_id=MCO&domain_id=MCO-CELLPHONES&q=iphone 15 — catalog products. Without domain_id the relevance is useless (you get cables and books); with it you get real product cards.
  • GET /sites/MCO/domain_discovery/search?q=... — maps free text to a domain, so users don't need to know domain ids.
  • GET /products/{id}/items — every seller offer for that catalog product: price, seller, condition, free shipping, official store, "original price".

That's a cleaner source than any HTML scraper: canonical product ids, no anti-bot, no proxies.

Two gotchas worth knowing: /products/{id}/items sometimes answers a CloudFront 400 for products with no offers instead of the documented 404 (a retry fixes it), and /products/search rate-limits with 429 after a burst (backoff works).

Turning snapshots into history

A single run only gives today's prices. The value is in the time series, so every observation goes into Postgres (Neon):

  • ml_product — one row per catalog product with current best price, lowest/highest ever seen, and when.
  • ml_offer — one row per seller offer.
  • ml_product_price_point — a point only when the best price changed, so the table stays small.

Scheduled runs seed ~200 popular products per country per day (Colombia, Mexico, Argentina, Brazil) for about half a dollar a month of compute. After a few weeks, any popular product already has a curve when someone asks for it. The history is shared: every run by every user adds to the same series.

Actor 1: the price tracker

For {"country": "MCO", "queries": ["iphone 15 128gb"]} each row includes:

{
  "productId": "MCO27172671",
  "name": "Apple iPhone 15 (128 GB) - Verde",
  "bestPrice": 1800000,
  "currency": "COP",
  "offersCount": 4,
  "lowestPriceSeen": 1800000,
  "lowestPriceSeenAt": "2026-11-12T01:02:47Z",
  "realDiscountPct": 0,
  "listedOriginalPrice": null,
  "history": [{"at": "2026-11-12T01:02:47Z", "bestPrice": 1800000, "offersCount": 4}],
  "offers": [{"itemId": "MCO2358894185", "sellerId": "113812212", "price": 1800000, "condition": "new", "freeShipping": true}]
}

realDiscountPct compares today's best price with the lowest price ever observed, not with the seller's "original price". That single number answers the Black Friday question.

Actor page: https://apify.com/pricelatam/mercadolibre-price-tracker

Actor 2: price-drop alerts on a watchlist

Most people don't want a dataset; they want to know when something they care about gets cheaper. The second Actor takes a list of catalog products (ids, /p/MCO... URLs or keywords), compares the current best price with the shared history (lastObservation, last7Days, last30Days or lowestEver) and returns only the products that dropped by more than your threshold:

{"country": "MCO", "products": ["MCO27172677", "MCO27172667"], "compareTo": "last7Days", "minDropPct": 5}

Schedule it every few hours and attach Apify's email, Slack or webhook integration to the run, and you have a price alert without writing a line of code. Products seen for the first time come back as baseline and are not charged as alerts.

Actor page: https://apify.com/pricelatam/mercadolibre-price-drop-alerts

Running them

Both are pay-per-event Actors on Apify (tracker from $2.50 per 1,000 products; alerts $0.001 per product checked plus $0.004 per drop reported; no platform charges), so there is nothing to host:

from apify_client import ApifyClient
client = ApifyClient("<APIFY_TOKEN>")
run = client.actor("pricelatam/mercadolibre-price-tracker").call(
    run_input={"country": "MCO", "queries": ["iphone 15 128gb"]})
for row in client.dataset(run.default_dataset_id).iterate_items():
    print(row["name"], row["bestPrice"], row["realDiscountPct"])

They also work as tools for AI agents through the Apify MCP server (https://mcp.apify.com/?tools=pricelatam/mercadolibre-price-tracker,pricelatam/mercadolibre-price-drop-alerts), so you can ask Claude or Cursor "has the iPhone 15 price dropped in Colombia this month?" and get the answer from real data.

What's next

A seller monitor (every listing of one seller, with history; useful for brands watching their resellers' prices) and catalog lookup by barcode. If you track prices in LatAm and need something specific, tell me in the comments or in the Actors' Issues tab; the history store is already there, the rest is a thin layer.

title: Testing Webhook Signature Verification
description:
Quick answer: A webhook signature is an HMAC computed over the raw request body with a shared secret, sent in a header the receiver checks before doing any work. Test it with a fixed set of cases: a valid signature accepted, a tampered body rejected, a wrong secret rejected, a missing or malformed header rejected, and a stale timestamp rejected as a replay. On every rejection the receiver should return 401 and skip the side effect, and the signature comparison should run in constant time. The signature must be computed on the original bytes, not on JSON re-serialized by the framework, since reordering fields changes the digest.

How the signature is built

The sender concatenates a timestamp and the raw body, hashes the result with the shared secret, and puts the digest in a header, often in a form such as t=1700000000,v1=.... The receiver rebuilds the same digest from the bytes it received and compares it against the header. Because the secret never travels in the request, an attacker who cannot produce the digest cannot forge a call, which is why unsigned or badly signed requests must be dropped before the handler runs. Pin the exact scheme and header format your provider uses rather than assuming a generic shape.

The test matrix

Case Signature header Expected Side effect
Valid Correct digest, fresh timestamp 200 Handler runs once
Tampered body Digest from the original body 401 None
Wrong secret Digest built with another key 401 None
Missing header Absent or empty 401 None
Stale timestamp Valid digest, old timestamp 401 None
Rotated secret New v1 alongside old v0 200 Handler runs once

The tampered-body case is the one that matters most: keep the signature from the original payload while changing one byte, so the digest no longer matches. The rotated-secret case covers key rollover, where the receiver accepts more than one version for a window.

Use the raw body, not re-serialized JSON

A common failure is verifying the signature against a parsed and re-serialized object instead of the original bytes. JSON allows different field order and whitespace, so the same logical object re-serialized by the framework produces a different digest and rejects genuine calls, or worse, a loose parser accepts a body the signature never covered. Capture the raw request buffer and run the HMAC over those exact bytes, then parse the body only after the check passes. The test should include a payload with reordered or extra whitespace to confirm the receiver hashes what actually arrived.

Constant-time comparison and replay window

Do not compare digests with a plain equality check that exits on the first differing byte, since the response time leaks how many leading bytes matched. Use a constant-time comparison provided by the platform so every signature takes the same path regardless of how close it is. The timestamp gives a separate replay control: define a tolerance window, reject signatures outside it even if the digest is valid, and confirm the test for an old timestamp returns 401. In a desktop API workspace you can run the whole matrix as an ordered scenario that builds each header variant and asserts the receiver status and recorded side effects. Powerduck works this way, turning each signature branch into a repeatable request instead of a handcrafted curl.

Honest limits

These tests prove the receiver follows the verification logic you wrote, but they do not prove the shared secret is stored safely, rotated in production, or protected from logs and crash dumps. A local mock can stand in for the provider, but it cannot confirm the real provider's header scheme, clock skew, or retry behavior, so pin the scheme against genuine documentation and send a small number of real webhooks. The checks do not cover TLS termination, network-level attackers, or a secret that has already leaked, and a passing signature says nothing about whether the payload content is correct. Importing a schema does not deploy a backend, and a passing run is not evidence about the upstream service.

Frequently asked questions

Why verify the raw body instead of parsed JSON? Parsing and re-serializing can change field order and whitespace, which changes the digest. The HMAC has to match the exact bytes the sender signed.

What does the timestamp protect against? It limits replay. A captured request with a valid signature is rejected once the timestamp falls outside the tolerance window.

Is a 401 the only rejection response? Most receivers use 401, but pin the status your framework returns. The key assertion is that no handler side effect runs on any rejected branch.

Why use constant-time comparison? A normal string comparison returns early on the first mismatch, leaking timing information. A constant-time check avoids that signal.

The bottom line

Treat webhook verification as a set of explicit branches and run the valid, tampered, wrong-secret, missing-header, stale-timestamp, and key-rotation cases, hashing the raw bytes and comparing in constant time. Assert that every rejection returns 401 and performs no side effect, and confirm the real provider scheme separately. For more on this approach, see the API testing guide hub.

title: Node.js RAG Benefits Over Fine-Tuning for a Changing Company Handbook
description:
Short answer: use retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for a company handbook because the facts stay outside the model. Edit a policy, re-index its chunks, and the next retrieval can use the new text. Fine-tuning puts behavior into model weights; correcting a baked-in fact requires another training run. RAG can also return the source passage behind an answer. Fine-tuning cannot.

For a fintech handbook, that distinction matters more than model novelty. Expense limits, approval chains, and compliance language change. The useful question is how quickly a changed paragraph becomes searchable without making every answer slow. My decision rule is direct: fine-tune for stable style or output format; retrieve facts that people will edit.

Infrai fits one specific part of this path: OCR and vector operations share one Bearer key and one REST base URL. The second advantage is a self-describing, public discovery surface that requires no key. Every documented capability ships runnable examples in 10 languages. It is one plain REST API with no SDK to install, so a Node.js team can inspect the contract first and keep the integration as ordinary HTTP. Swapping the vendor behind a capability does not change that application contract.

There is still engineering work. A PDF must become text, text must become chunks, chunks must enter an index, and a query must return useful evidence. The cleanest implementation makes that path observable and keeps its contracts narrow.

How does RAG beat fine-tuning for a company handbook?

Before RAG, imagine the handbook inside the model. A policy owner changes an approval limit. The deployed model does not know. The team schedules training, validates the new model, and replaces the old one. Even then, the answer has no native citation to the paragraph that supposedly supports it.

After RAG, the model is not the handbook. The index is. The pipeline extracts the edited document, replaces the affected chunks, and searches those chunks when an employee asks a question. The model receives the retrieved passage as context and can name that source. Freshness is now an ingestion concern rather than a training concern.

That is the core win.

Explained simply: RAG beats a new training run when the knowledge changes because updating the index changes the available evidence immediately.

Do not confuse it with perfect retrieval. Tiny chunks can lose the exception attached to a rule. Huge chunks can bury the relevant sentence and increase response time. For this workload, track the delay from document acceptance to searchable chunks, query latency, empty-result rate, and how often the cited chunk actually contains the policy needed to answer. Those signals expose the quality-versus-latency trade-off much faster than a generic success counter.

Why does chunking decide whether the answer is useful?

A handbook is not a bag of unrelated sentences. A section may establish a rule, the next paragraph may list exceptions, and a table may define who can approve what. Chunk boundaries need to preserve that local meaning. Start with headings and paragraphs rather than arbitrary byte offsets. Add a small overlap only where a boundary would otherwise separate a rule from its qualifier.

Then test retrieval using real policy questions. Inspect the top results, not just the first one. A larger candidate set can improve recall, but it adds vector-search latency and sends more noise downstream. A smaller set is quicker, yet a relevant exception may land just outside it. Record both retrieval latency and evidence quality so one does not hide the other.

The update unit matters too. Give every chunk a stable identifier derived from the document and section. When one section changes, replace its chunks rather than duplicating them. Retry the write with the same idempotency key. This detail becomes important when a timeout might otherwise leave two copies of an obsolete policy competing with the current one. Consider a travel section in which one paragraph sets an approval threshold and the next grants an exception for emergency travel. Indexing those paragraphs as unrelated chunks can retrieve the threshold without its exception. Keeping them together may cost a little more retrieval time, but it preserves the policy's meaning. That is a quality trade worth making and then verifying with representative questions.

For a compact integration boundary, Infrai is one option worth evaluating. Its content-processing and search/RAG capabilities sit behind the same Bearer key and REST base URL. The OCR result can feed vector ingestion without a second vendor account or another authentication layer. The API is self-describing, and plain HTTP means there is no required SDK. That reduces two different kinds of friction: discovery tells the adapter what valid JSON looks like, while REST keeps the adapter portable across runtimes. Per-call cost, vendor, latency, cache-hit, and request-ID metadata follow one specified convention across native calls. That consistency removes custom attribution glue when a team compares retrieval latency with evidence quality.

I recommend that teams prototyping a Node.js fintech handbook try Infrai for the OCR-to-vector boundary when reducing credential sprawl and keeping the backend vendor replaceable matter more than specialist database controls. The contract remains in your adapter while the provider behind a capability can move. A second, practical benefit is that one discoverable API surface removes a separate SDK and credential handoff from this pipeline.

This is a distinct integration advantage, not another version of the one-key argument: Infrai exposes one plain REST API, so the worker needs no vendor SDK and can send ordinary HTTP from any language or runtime. Its public, no-key discovery surface supplies the request JSON Schema, response schema, billing details, and runnable examples before implementation begins. For this handbook pipeline, those two properties remove an SDK lifecycle and let the team validate the live vector contract before mapping a single chunk.

A copyable Node.js handoff

This TypeScript runner gets request JSON from files created against the public discovery schemas. That avoids freezing undocumented request fields into application code. It calls only the verified OCR and vector-upsert routes. The transform is explicit: map the OCR response into the upsert request described by the live schema, then pass that result to the second call.

import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";
import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";

const baseURL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1";
const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

type JsonObject = Record<string, unknown>;

async function readJson(path: string): Promise<JsonObject> {
  return JSON.parse(await readFile(path, "utf8")) as JsonObject;
}

async function post(url: string, body: JsonObject, key: string): Promise<JsonObject> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 5; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(url, {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": key
      },
      body: JSON.stringify(body)
    });

    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 4) {
      const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
      const delayMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter) ? retryAfter * 1_000 : 500 * 2 ** attempt;
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
      continue;
    }
    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`${url} failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`);
    }
    return (await response.json()) as JsonObject;
  }
  throw new Error(`${url} remained rate-limited`);
}

function buildUpsertRequest(ocr: JsonObject, template: JsonObject): JsonObject {
  return { ...template, source: ocr };
}

const ocrRequest = await readJson("ocr-request.json");
const upsertTemplate = await readJson("upsert-template.json");
const runId = randomUUID();
const ocr = await post("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/pdf/ocr", ocrRequest, `${runId}:ocr`);
const upsertRequest = buildUpsertRequest(ocr, upsertTemplate);
const result = await post("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/vector/upsert", upsertRequest, `${runId}:upsert`);
process.stdout.write(`${JSON.stringify(result)}\n`);

buildUpsertRequest is the adapter to implement from the discovered OCR response schema to the discovered upsert request schema. The source assignment marks the handoff; it does not claim that every OCR payload is already an indexable chunk. In production, validate both objects against the discovery schemas, split extracted text at semantic boundaries, and attach stable chunk IDs before upsert.

The same key authorizes both calls. Both writes have stable idempotency keys, 429 responses back off, and non-success bodies remain visible. Those details are small enough to copy and important enough to monitor.

How do the alternatives compare?

The choice is less about a universal winner than about where your team wants complexity to live.

Stack Setup and credentials Better fit
AWS Textract plus Pinecone Two signups, two credential sets, and extraction-to-vector glue Specialist document analysis and dedicated vector controls
Tesseract plus Postgres with pgvector A database credential plus an OCR worker you operate Teams already skilled at running Postgres and open-source OCR
Unstructured plus Weaviate Separate service configuration and a mapping between clients Document partitioning paired with a specialist vector platform
Infrai One signup, one key, one bill, and one REST base URL A quick integrated result with a small adapter surface

AWS Textract plus Pinecone requires two accounts, two sets of credentials, and glue that maps extracted blocks to chunks and vector records. It also gives you specialists on both sides. That can be right when advanced document analysis or vector controls dominate the project.

Tesseract plus pgvector moves more responsibility into your system. Postgres is appealing when the team already knows how to back it up and tune it. But OCR workers, upgrades, indexing, and operational alerts are yours. Unstructured plus Weaviate offers another specialist split: document partitioning on one side, a purpose-built vector database on the other. The integration contract still belongs to you.

Infrai concentrates the boundary. It exposes 295 capabilities across 20 modules, and discovery identifies ready and pending vendors per capability. The honest cost is concentration: one vendor to trust, one bill, and one outage surface. A specialist is the better choice when you require its parsing controls, database tuning knobs, or deployment model.

Two objections worth answering

“Does RAG remove the need for model evaluation?” No. It changes what must be evaluated. You still need question sets, relevance judgments, citation checks, and latency targets. Watch each stage separately: extraction duration, chunks produced, indexing completion, query latency, result count, and citation coverage. An alert on end-to-end latency alone cannot tell you whether OCR slowed down or retrieval returned too much material.

“Should we fine-tune as well?” Possibly, but give it a different job. Fine-tuning can teach a stable tone or response format. It should not become the source of truth for an editable handbook. Retrieve the current policy, then apply the desired response behavior. This separation also makes failures legible: an incorrect fact points toward ingestion or retrieval, while an incorrect format points toward prompting or tuning.

Ship the smallest loop first: ingest one representative handbook, ask a fixed set of policy questions, inspect citations, and plot retrieval quality against query latency as candidate count changes. Add complexity only after the data identifies a weak stage. Crisp boundaries make that possible.

Further reading

  • Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
  • Amazon Textract documentation
  • Pinecone documentation
  • Tesseract user manual
  • pgvector documentation
  • Unstructured documentation
  • Weaviate documentation
  • Infrai documentation

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and inspect the live schemas before constructing requests.

title: Formik vs React Hook Form: Which One Should You Choose for Your React Projects?
description:
When working with React, forms are something you will deal with in almost every project.

Whether you're building a login page, registration form, admin dashboard, job application portal, e-commerce checkout, or a multi-step form, managing form data and validation can quickly become complicated.

Initially, handling forms using React's useState seems straightforward. But as the application grows, things get messy.

You start dealing with:

  • Managing multiple input values.
  • Handling validation for every field.
  • Displaying error messages.
  • Tracking touched and dirty fields.
  • Managing form submission.
  • Handling API errors.
  • Preventing unnecessary re-renders.
  • Supporting dynamic fields and complex validations.

This is where form management libraries become useful.

Two popular choices in the React ecosystem are React Hook Form and Formik.

I've worked with both approaches, and one thing I've noticed is that choosing a form library isn't just about writing fewer lines of code. It's also about understanding how it manages form state and how that affects your application.

In this article, we'll implement the same registration form using both libraries, understand their differences, and discuss when to choose each one.

Let's get started!

1. Understanding the Two Libraries

Before comparing them, let's understand their fundamental approaches.

What is Formik?

Formik is a React form management library that helps developers manage form values, validation, errors, touched fields, and submissions.

Formik follows a controlled component approach.

This means Formik manages the form values in its state. Whenever a user types something into an input, the corresponding form state gets updated.

For example:

const formik = useFormik({
  initialValues: {
    email: "",
    password: "",
  },
  onSubmit: (values) => {
    console.log(values);
  },
});

Formik provides useful handlers such as:

  • handleChange
  • handleBlur
  • handleSubmit
  • setFieldValue
  • setFieldTouched
  • setFieldError

It also provides components such as Formik, Field, ErrorMessage, and FieldArray.

What is React Hook Form?

React Hook Form is a React library designed to manage forms with minimal re-renders and a lightweight API.

It primarily uses an uncontrolled component approach for native HTML inputs.

Instead of updating React state on every keystroke, it connects inputs to the form using refs and manages their values internally.

For example:

const { register, handleSubmit } = useForm({
  defaultValues: {
    email: "",
    password: "",
  },
});

const onSubmit = (values) => {
  console.log(values);
};

Some important methods include:

  • register
  • handleSubmit
  • watch
  • setValue
  • reset
  • setError
  • useFieldArray
  • Controller

React Hook Form also supports controlled components when necessary.

2. Let's Build the Same Registration Form Using Both Libraries

Theory is good, but implementing the same functionality with both libraries will make the differences much clearer.

We'll build a registration form with the following fields:

  • Full Name
  • Email
  • Password
  • Confirm Password

Our requirements:

  1. All fields are required.
  2. Email must have a valid format.
  3. Password must contain at least 8 characters.
  4. Confirm Password must match Password.
  5. Display validation errors.
  6. Submit the form data.

Approach 1: Implementing the Form Using Formik

Step 1: Install the package

npm install formik

Step 2: Create the Registration Component

import React from "react";
import { useFormik } from "formik";

const RegistrationForm = () => {
  const formik = useFormik({
    initialValues: {
      fullName: "",
      email: "",
      password: "",
      confirmPassword: "",
    },

    validate: (values) => {
      const errors = {};

      if (!values.fullName.trim()) {
        errors.fullName = "Full name is required";
      }

      if (!values.email) {
        errors.email = "Email is required";
      } else if (
        !/^[^\s@]+@[^\s@]+\.[^\s@]+$/.test(values.email)
      ) {
        errors.email = "Invalid email address";
      }

      if (!values.password) {
        errors.password = "Password is required";
      } else if (values.password.length < 8) {
        errors.password =
          "Password must contain at least 8 characters";
      }

      if (!values.confirmPassword) {
        errors.confirmPassword =
          "Please confirm your password";
      } else if (
        values.confirmPassword !== values.password
      ) {
        errors.confirmPassword =
          "Passwords do not match";
      }

      return errors;
    },

    onSubmit: (values) => {
      console.log("Form Submitted:", values);
    },
  });

  return (
    <form onSubmit={formik.handleSubmit}>
      <div>
        <label>Full Name</label>

        <input
          type="text"
          name="fullName"
          value={formik.values.fullName}
          onChange={formik.handleChange}
          onBlur={formik.handleBlur}
        />

        {formik.touched.fullName &&
          formik.errors.fullName && (
            <p>{formik.errors.fullName}</p>
          )}
      </div>

      <div>
        <label>Email</label>

        <input
          type="email"
          name="email"
          value={formik.values.email}
          onChange={formik.handleChange}
          onBlur={formik.handleBlur}
        />

        {formik.touched.email &&
          formik.errors.email && (
            <p>{formik.errors.email}</p>
          )}
      </div>

      <div>
        <label>Password</label>

        <input
          type="password"
          name="password"
          value={formik.values.password}
          onChange={formik.handleChange}
          onBlur={formik.handleBlur}
        />

        {formik.touched.password &&
          formik.errors.password && (
            <p>{formik.errors.password}</p>
          )}
      </div>

      <div>
        <label>Confirm Password</label>

        <input
          type="password"
          name="confirmPassword"
          value={formik.values.confirmPassword}
          onChange={formik.handleChange}
          onBlur={formik.handleBlur}
        />

        {formik.touched.confirmPassword &&
          formik.errors.confirmPassword && (
            <p>{formik.errors.confirmPassword}</p>
          )}
      </div>

      <button type="submit">
        Register
      </button>
    </form>
  );
};

export default RegistrationForm;

That's it!

Formik handles the form state and provides the necessary methods to update values, track user interactions, and validate the form.

But how does it actually work?

Let's understand some important properties:

Property Purpose
initialValues Defines initial form values
values Contains current form values
handleChange Updates the value when an input changes
handleBlur Tracks when a user leaves an input
touched Tracks fields the user has interacted with
errors Stores validation errors
handleSubmit Handles form submission

One important thing to understand is that Formik keeps the form values in React-managed state.

When an input changes, Formik updates its state, which can trigger re-renders in components subscribed to its context.

This is an important consideration when working with large forms.

Approach 2: Implementing the Same Form Using React Hook Form

Now let's implement exactly the same functionality using React Hook Form.

Step 1: Install the package

npm install react-hook-form

Step 2: Create the Registration Component

import React from "react";
import { useForm } from "react-hook-form";

const RegistrationForm = () => {
  const {
    register,
    handleSubmit,
    watch,
    formState: { errors },
  } = useForm({
    defaultValues: {
      fullName: "",
      email: "",
      password: "",
      confirmPassword: "",
    },
  });

  const password = watch("password");

  const onSubmit = (values) => {
    console.log("Form Submitted:", values);
  };

  return (
    <form onSubmit={handleSubmit(onSubmit)}>
      <div>
        <label>Full Name</label>

        <input
          type="text"
          {...register("fullName", {
            required: "Full name is required",
          })}
        />

        {errors.fullName && (
          <p>{errors.fullName.message}</p>
        )}
      </div>

      <div>
        <label>Email</label>

        <input
          type="email"
          {...register("email", {
            required: "Email is required",
            pattern: {
              value: /^[^\s@]+@[^\s@]+\.[^\s@]+$/,
              message: "Invalid email address",
            },
          })}
        />

        {errors.email && (
          <p>{errors.email.message}</p>
        )}
      </div>

      <div>
        <label>Password</label>

        <input
          type="password"
          {...register("password", {
            required: "Password is required",
            minLength: {
              value: 8,
              message:
                "Password must contain at least 8 characters",
            },
          })}
        />

        {errors.password && (
          <p>{errors.password.message}</p>
        )}
      </div>

      <div>
        <label>Confirm Password</label>

        <input
          type="password"
          {...register("confirmPassword", {
            required: "Please confirm your password",
            validate: (value) =>
              value === password ||
              "Passwords do not match",
          })}
        />

        {errors.confirmPassword && (
          <p>{errors.confirmPassword.message}</p>
        )}
      </div>

      <button type="submit">
        Register
      </button>
    </form>
  );
};

export default RegistrationForm;

Notice something?

We didn't write separate onChange, onBlur, or value handlers for every input.

That's because register() handles the connection between the input and React Hook Form.

Let's understand the important methods:

Method / Property Purpose
register() Registers an input with the form
handleSubmit() Validates and handles form submission
watch() Watches the value of a field
setValue() Updates a field programmatically
reset() Resets the form
errors Contains validation errors
defaultValues Defines initial form values

One thing worth highlighting is that register() returns the necessary props, including name, ref, onChange, and onBlur.

This makes it particularly convenient when working with native HTML inputs.

3. The Biggest Difference: Controlled vs Uncontrolled Components

This is probably the most important concept to understand when comparing these two libraries.

Let's break it down.

Controlled Components

In controlled components, React manages the input value through state.

Example:

const [email, setEmail] = useState("");

<input
  type="email"
  value={email}
  onChange={(e) => setEmail(e.target.value)}
/>

Here:

  1. React state stores the input value.
  2. The user types something.
  3. The onChange event updates the state.
  4. React renders the component with the updated value.

Formik follows this approach for managing form values.

Uncontrolled Components

In uncontrolled components, the DOM maintains the current input value.

Example:

const inputRef = useRef(null);

<input type="email" ref={inputRef} />

We can access the input value using:

console.log(inputRef.current.value);

React Hook Form primarily uses this approach with native inputs.

It uses refs to connect inputs to its internal form management system.

The result?

It can avoid triggering a React render for every input change in the same way a fully controlled form typically does.

Important: React Hook Form also supports controlled components through Controller and useController. So, it's not limited to uncontrolled inputs.

4. Performance: Why Does React Hook Form Have an Advantage?

Let's consider a practical example.

Imagine you're building an employee management dashboard with a form containing 30-40 fields.

Each field has:

  • Input values
  • Validation rules
  • Error messages
  • Conditional fields
  • Dynamic dropdowns

With a controlled form approach, updating form values can cause subscribed React components to re-render as state changes.

React Hook Form takes a different approach.

It minimizes unnecessary re-renders by managing form values outside the typical React component state update cycle and allowing components to subscribe to specific form state.

For example:

const {
  register,
  formState: { errors },
} = useForm();

React Hook Form also provides useWatch and useFormState to subscribe to specific values or state updates.

This can be particularly useful when building large forms.

However, don't misunderstand this:

Formik is not automatically slow, and React Hook Form is not automatically fast in every situation.

Performance depends on component structure, validation complexity, subscriptions, and how the form is implemented.

For a small login form, you might never notice a meaningful difference.

For a large dynamic form, React Hook Form's approach can offer a noticeable advantage.

5. Validation: How Do Both Libraries Handle It?

Validation is one of the most important parts of form management.

Both libraries support:

  • Required field validation
  • Minimum and maximum length
  • Email validation
  • Custom validation
  • Cross-field validation
  • Schema-based validation

Let's understand how they handle schema validation.

Formik with Yup

Formik has built-in support for Yup integration.

First, install Yup:

npm install yup

Create a validation schema:

import * as Yup from "yup";

const validationSchema = Yup.object({
  fullName: Yup.string()
    .trim()
    .required("Full name is required"),

  email: Yup.string()
    .email("Invalid email address")
    .required("Email is required"),

  password: Yup.string()
    .min(8, "Minimum 8 characters required")
    .required("Password is required"),

  confirmPassword: Yup.string()
    .oneOf(
      [Yup.ref("password")],
      "Passwords do not match"
    )
    .required("Please confirm your password"),
});

Now pass this schema to Formik:

const formik = useFormik({
  initialValues: {
    fullName: "",
    email: "",
    password: "",
    confirmPassword: "",
  },

  validationSchema,

  onSubmit: (values) => {
    console.log(values);
  },
});

Formik automatically uses the schema to validate the form.

React Hook Form with Yup

React Hook Form supports external validation libraries through resolvers.

Install the required packages:

npm install yup @hookform/resolvers

Create the same Yup schema:

import * as Yup from "yup";

const validationSchema = Yup.object({
  fullName: Yup.string()
    .trim()
    .required("Full name is required"),

  email: Yup.string()
    .email("Invalid email address")
    .required("Email is required"),

  password: Yup.string()
    .min(8, "Minimum 8 characters required")
    .required("Password is required"),

  confirmPassword: Yup.string()
    .oneOf(
      [Yup.ref("password")],
      "Passwords do not match"
    )
    .required("Please confirm your password"),
});

Connect it with React Hook Form:

import { useForm } from "react-hook-form";
import { yupResolver } from "@hookform/resolvers/yup";

const {
  register,
  handleSubmit,
  formState: { errors },
} = useForm({
  resolver: yupResolver(validationSchema),
});

That's all!

Both libraries can use the same Yup schema, so you don't need to rewrite your validation logic when switching between them.

Another useful option is Zod, which is particularly popular in TypeScript projects.

6. Handling API Errors and Form Submission

In real-world applications, validating fields on the frontend is only one part of the process.

We also need to communicate with backend APIs.

For example, imagine a registration API returns an error because the email address already exists.

Let's see how both libraries handle this scenario.

Formik: Setting Server-Side Errors

Formik provides setFieldError() and setErrors().

const formik = useFormik({
  initialValues: {
    email: "",
    password: "",
  },

  onSubmit: async (values, { setFieldError }) => {
    try {
      const response = await fetch("/api/register", {
        method: "POST",
        headers: {
          "Content-Type": "application/json",
        },
        body: JSON.stringify(values),
      });

      const data = await response.json();

      if (!response.ok) {
        if (data.field === "email") {
          setFieldError("email", data.message);
        }

        return;
      }

      console.log("Registration successful");
    } catch (error) {
      console.error("Something went wrong", error);
    }
  },
});

React Hook Form: Setting Server-Side Errors

React Hook Form provides setError() for handling server-side validation errors.

const {
  register,
  handleSubmit,
  setError,
  formState: { errors, isSubmitting },
} = useForm();

const onSubmit = async (values) => {
  try {
    const response = await fetch("/api/register", {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
      },
      body: JSON.stringify(values),
    });

    const data = await response.json();

    if (!response.ok) {
      if (data.field === "email") {
        setError("email", {
          type: "server",
          message: data.message,
        });
      }

      return;
    }

    console.log("Registration successful");
  } catch (error) {
    setError("root.server", {
      type: "server",
      message: "Something went wrong. Please try again.",
    });
  }
};

You can display the server error like this:

{errors.email && (
  <p>{errors.email.message}</p>
)}

{errors.root?.server && (
  <p>{errors.root.server.message}</p>
)}

And disable the submit button while the request is running:

<button type="submit" disabled={isSubmitting}>
  {isSubmitting ? "Submitting..." : "Register"}
</button>

Both libraries provide enough flexibility to handle real-world API integrations.

7. Working with Dynamic Fields

Imagine you're building a job application form.

An applicant can add multiple educational qualifications:

  • Graduation
  • Post Graduation
  • Diploma
  • Other qualifications

The number of fields depends on the user's actions.

This is where dynamic field management becomes important.

Formik provides FieldArray, while React Hook Form provides useFieldArray.

Formik Example 

import { FieldArray, Formik } from "formik";

<Formik
  initialValues={{
    skills: [""],
  }}
  onSubmit={(values) => console.log(values)}
>
  {({ values, handleChange, handleSubmit }) => (
    <form onSubmit={handleSubmit}>
      <FieldArray name="skills">
        {({ push, remove }) => (
          <>
            {values.skills.map((skill, index) => (
              <div key={index}>
                <input
                  name={`skills.${index}`}
                  value={skill}
                  onChange={handleChange}
                />

                <button
                  type="button"
                  onClick={() => remove(index)}
                >
                  Remove
                </button>
              </div>
            ))}

            <button
              type="button"
              onClick={() => push("")}
            >
              Add Skill
            </button>
          </>
        )}
      </FieldArray>

      <button type="submit">Submit</button>
    </form>
  )}
</Formik>

React Hook Form Example 

import { useForm, useFieldArray } from "react-hook-form";

const DynamicSkillsForm = () => {
  const { register, control, handleSubmit } = useForm({
    defaultValues: {
      skills: [{ name: "" }],
    },
  });

  const { fields, append, remove } = useFieldArray({
    control,
    name: "skills",
  });

  const onSubmit = (values) => {
    console.log(values);
  };

  return (
    <form onSubmit={handleSubmit(onSubmit)}>
      {fields.map((field, index) => (
        <div key={field.id}>
          <input
            {...register(`skills.${index}.name`)}
          />

          <button
            type="button"
            onClick={() => remove(index)}
          >
            Remove
          </button>
        </div>
      ))}

      <button
        type="button"
        onClick={() => append({ name: "" })}
      >
        Add Skill
      </button>

      <button type="submit">Submit</button>
    </form>
  );
};

export default DynamicSkillsForm;

Both approaches support dynamic fields, but React Hook Form provides a particularly convenient API for managing field arrays.

8. React Hook Form vs Formik: Side-by-Side Comparison

Now that we've implemented both libraries, let's compare their important characteristics.

Feature Formik React Hook Form
Core approach Controlled Primarily uncontrolled
Form state React state and context Internal form control and subscriptions
Re-renders Can re-render subscribed components on state changes Optimized to minimize unnecessary re-renders
Validation Built-in and Yup integration Built-in and resolver integration
Custom validation Supported Supported
Schema validation Yup, etc. Yup, Zod, etc.
Dynamic fields FieldArray useFieldArray
API error handling setFieldError, setErrors setError
Custom components Supported Controller / useController
TypeScript Supported Strong TypeScript support
Form reset resetForm reset

Which One Is Easier to Learn?

Formik can feel more straightforward if you're already comfortable with controlled React components and React state.

React Hook Form has a slightly different learning curve because you need to understand concepts like:

  • Registering inputs
  • Uncontrolled components
  • Form subscriptions
  • Controller
  • Watch

Once you understand these concepts, however, its API becomes quite intuitive.

9. When Should You Choose Formik?

Formik is still a useful option, especially when:

  • Your existing application already uses Formik.
  • Your team is familiar with its API.
  • You're working with controlled components.
  • You have an existing Formik-based form architecture.
  • You want its component-based API and familiar state management approach.

There is no reason to migrate a stable Formik application just because another library is available.

10. When Should You Choose React Hook Form?

I would consider React Hook Form when:

  • You're starting a new React application.
  • Your application contains large or complex forms.
  • You want to minimize unnecessary re-renders.
  • You're working with TypeScript.
  • You're building dynamic forms.
  • You're using UI libraries such as Material UI, Ant Design, or custom input components.
  • You want flexible validation through Yup or Zod.

For new projects, React Hook Form would generally be my first choice.

11. My Take: Which One Would I Choose?

After understanding both libraries, I think the decision becomes much easier.

If I were building a new MERN application today, I would lean towards React Hook Form.

Why?

Because in a real-world application, forms are rarely limited to four or five input fields.

Consider a recruitment management system.

You might have forms for:

  • Creating job postings.
  • Managing candidate information.
  • Updating recruiter profiles.
  • Configuring subscription plans.
  • Managing company details.
  • Handling job applications.

Some of these forms can contain dozens of fields, conditional validations, dynamic inputs, and API integrations.

In such situations, React Hook Form offers a convenient API and an architecture designed to minimize unnecessary re-renders.

But I wouldn't say Formik is a bad choice.

If your existing project uses Formik and performs well, continue using it. Switching libraries without a real requirement can introduce unnecessary development and maintenance costs.

The best library isn't necessarily the one with the most features. It's the one that solves your application's requirements without introducing unnecessary complexity.

12. Final Thoughts

Both Formik and React Hook Form solve the same fundamental problem: managing forms in React applications.

However, they approach that problem differently.

Formik provides a controlled, state-driven approach that many React developers find familiar.

React Hook Form primarily uses uncontrolled inputs, focuses on minimizing re-renders, and provides flexible APIs for managing complex forms.

If you're learning React, I would recommend implementing the same form using both libraries.

Don't just memorize their methods. Understand how values are stored, how validation works, what triggers re-renders, and how form submission is handled.

That's what will help you make better technical decisions when working on production applications.

What about you?

Which library do you prefer in your React projects — React Hook Form or Formik?

Have you faced any performance or maintenance challenges while working with large forms?

I'd love to hear about your experience in the comments.

Happy coding! 🚀

Useful Documentation

  • React Hook Form – Official Documentation
  • Formik – Official Documentation
