title: Button Hover Animation CSS: Fill Sweep, Lift, Arrow Nudge and Glow
description:
Originally published on Crafttor.

TL;DR: A good button hover animation in CSS is short, eased and honest about what the button does. Use 150 to 300 ms, an ease-out curve, and animate only transform, opacity and colour where you can. Below are four effects with code and the timing that makes them feel right. You also get a reduced-motion fallback and a faster way to copy a hover you like.

Buttons are the most hovered element on any page. A small, well-timed response tells the user "this is clickable, and it is ready". A slow or bouncy one feels laggy. The difference is rarely the effect itself. It is almost always the duration and the easing.

Start with a solid base button

Every effect below builds on the same base. Keep the transition on the base rule, not the :hover rule, so it plays both ways.

.btn {
  position: relative;
  display: inline-flex;
  align-items: center;
  gap: 8px;
  padding: 12px 20px;
  border: 0;
  border-radius: 10px;
  background: #17171c;
  color: #fff;
  font: 600 15px/1 system-ui, sans-serif;
  cursor: pointer;
  transition: transform 200ms cubic-bezier(.22, 1, .36, 1),
              box-shadow 200ms cubic-bezier(.22, 1, .36, 1),
              background-color 200ms ease-out;
}

List each property in transition. Writing transition: all is tempting, but it animates things you did not plan, like a width change from a font swap.

Four button hover animation CSS effects

Each effect suits a different job. Pick one per button style, not all four at once.

1. Fill sweep

A colour fills the button from one side. It reads as "you are about to commit to this", which suits primary actions.

.btn-sweep {
  overflow: hidden;
  isolation: isolate;
}
.btn-sweep::before {
  content: "";
  position: absolute;
  inset: 0;
  z-index: -1;
  background: #fb9f3d;
  transform: scaleX(0);
  transform-origin: left;
  transition: transform 260ms cubic-bezier(.22, 1, .36, 1);
}
.btn-sweep:hover::before {
  transform: scaleX(1);
}

Animating scaleX on a pseudo-element is cheaper than animating width or background-position. The browser can run it on the compositor. If the text colour changes too, check contrast on both the start and end colours.

2. Lift and shadow

The button rises a few pixels and its shadow grows. It feels physical, and it works well on cards and secondary buttons.

.btn-lift:hover {
  transform: translateY(-2px);
  box-shadow: 0 8px 20px rgb(0 0 0 / .18);
}
.btn-lift:active {
  transform: translateY(0);
  box-shadow: 0 2px 6px rgb(0 0 0 / .18);
  transition-duration: 80ms;
}

Keep the lift small: 1 to 3 px. Larger lifts make a row of buttons look jumpy. The :active rule gives a quick press back down, which closes the loop.

Animating box-shadow repaints on every frame. On one button it is fine. On a grid of fifty cards, put the larger shadow on a pseudo-element and fade its opacity instead.

3. Arrow nudge

An arrow icon slides a few pixels in the direction of travel. It is the quietest of the four and suits links like "Read more" or "Next".

.btn-arrow svg {
  transition: transform 180ms ease-out;
}
.btn-arrow:hover svg {
  transform: translateX(4px);
}

Put the :hover on the button, not on the icon. The button is the bigger target, and the user hovers it first. This is the "hover the container, move the child" pattern.

4. Glow

A soft, coloured halo appears behind the button. It works on dark backgrounds and for one hero call to action per page.

.btn-glow::after {
  content: "";
  position: absolute;
  inset: -6px;
  z-index: -1;
  border-radius: 14px;
  background: #fb9f3d;
  filter: blur(14px);
  opacity: 0;
  transition: opacity 240ms ease-out;
}
.btn-glow:hover::after {
  opacity: .55;
}

The blur is set once and never animated. Only opacity changes, which keeps it smooth. Animating filter: blur() directly is much heavier.

Timing and easing: the part that makes it feel right

Most hover problems are timing problems. Use this table as a starting point.

Effect Duration Easing Notes
Fill sweep 220 to 300 ms cubic-bezier(.22, 1, .36, 1) Larger area, so slightly longer
Lift and shadow 150 to 220 ms ease-out Press back in about 80 ms
Arrow nudge 150 to 200 ms ease-out Small distance, short time
Glow 200 to 260 ms ease-out Fade only

A few rules hold across all four:

  • Stay between 150 and 300 ms. Under 100 ms, the user barely sees it. Over 300 ms, the button feels slow to respond.
  • Use ease-out for entering. The motion starts fast and settles, so the button answers the pointer right away.
  • Leave faster than you enter. A hover-out at about two thirds of the hover-in time feels tidy. Put a second transition on the :hover rule to make them differ.
  • Avoid bouncy springs on buttons. Overshoot is fun on toggles and tabs. On a button you hover many times a day, it gets tiring.

To make the exit faster than the entry:

.btn { transition: transform 140ms ease-in; }          /* leaving */
.btn:hover { transition: transform 220ms ease-out; }   /* entering */

The rule that applies is the one for the state you are moving into. That is why the faster value sits on the base rule.

If you want to go deeper on curves, our guide to CSS easing functions explained covers cubic-bezier() and steps() with examples.

Respect reduced motion and touch screens

Some users ask their system for less motion. Honour that with a media query. Keep the colour change, drop the movement.

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .btn,
  .btn::before,
  .btn::after,
  .btn svg {
    transition-property: opacity, background-color, color;
  }
  .btn-lift:hover,
  .btn-arrow:hover svg {
    transform: none;
  }
}

On phones, a tap can leave a hover style stuck until the user taps elsewhere. Wrap hover-only motion in a hover media query:

@media (hover: hover) and (pointer: fine) {
  .btn-lift:hover { transform: translateY(-2px); }
}

Two more checks before you ship:

  • Give :focus-visible the same visual change as :hover, so keyboard users get the same feedback.
  • Never rely on motion alone to show state. A disabled button should look disabled even with no animation.

Copy a hover you like instead of guessing the values

You often see a button hover on a real site and want the same feel. Guessing is slow. You eyeball 200 ms, it turns out to be 320 ms, and the easing was a custom curve you would never have picked.

DevTools can help when the hover is a plain CSS transition. Force :hover in the Styles pane and read the rule. It gets harder when the hover is started by JavaScript, uses GSAP, or animates several layers with different delays. Our walkthrough on how to capture hover animations covers each case.

Capture Motion reads the real values for you:

  1. Open the page in Chrome and start the Capture Motion extension.
  2. Pick the button, or its container if an inner icon moves too.
  3. Play the hover. The extension triggers a real :hover state through the Chrome DevTools Protocol, attached only during the capture.
  4. Preview the capture. You see each animated property with its keyframes, duration, delay and easing.
  5. Export it. With a free account, copy the CSS, Framer Motion or GSAP code, or send it to Figma as a Figma Motion timeline.

It records CSS transitions and keyframes, the Web Animations API, GSAP and Lottie. That covers the cases where DevTools shows no timing to read. Capture or rebuild only designs you own or have permission to use. Take the timing and easing, then apply them to your own button.

A quick checklist before you ship

  • [ ] Duration between 150 and 300 ms
  • [ ] Ease-out on enter, slightly faster exit
  • [ ] Only transform, opacity and colours animate
  • [ ] :focus-visible matches :hover
  • [ ] Reduced-motion fallback in place
  • [ ] Hover motion wrapped in @media (hover: hover)
  • [ ] Contrast checked at both ends of a colour change

Want a ready example with stagger and hover? See the animated avatar stack build, or browse the gallery on capturemotion.dev.

FAQ

What is a good duration for a button hover animation in CSS?

Between 150 and 300 ms covers almost every case. Small moves like an arrow nudge sit near 150 to 200 ms. Larger fills can run to 300 ms. Past that, the button starts to feel slow.

Which easing should I use for button hovers?

Use ease-out or a curve like cubic-bezier(.22, 1, .36, 1) for the hover-in. It responds instantly and settles gently. For the hover-out, a slightly shorter ease-in or ease-out works well.

Why does my hover animation stutter?

You are probably animating layout or paint properties like width, top or filter. Switch to transform and opacity. For shadows and glows, animate the opacity of a pseudo-element that already has the shadow.

How do I make hover-out faster than hover-in?

Put the faster transition on the base rule and the slower one on the :hover rule. The browser uses the transition of the state the element is moving into.

Can I copy the exact hover timing from another website?

Yes. For plain CSS, force :hover in Chrome DevTools and read the rule. For JavaScript or GSAP hovers, a capture tool like Capture Motion records the real keyframes, durations and easing. Only copy from sites you own or have permission to use.

title: One floating glass header for every screen in a Flutter app
description:
A chat header, a saved-notes page and both profile screens now render the same floating glass app bar. Not a similar one: the same card, the same 12 dp side margins, the same 8 dp gap under the status bar, the same stadium radius the navigation dock already used. Opening a profile from a conversation used to feel like arriving in a different app, because a stock Material bar sat flat across the top of the page while everything under it floated.

Three surfaces forced a better question than how to style an app bar: what does a floating bar need in order to be correct? It came down to a tint value, a measured spacer and one sync bug that only appeared on the next launch.

The bar is a card, not a strip

The conversation header is 64 dp tall and holds a 36 dp circular back control, a hairline pill containing the avatar and name, and the same 36 dp circles for its actions. All of it sits on one ChromeGlassSurface, inside Positioned bounds that keep 12 dp of air on each side and 8 dp below the status area.

The corner radius is not a fresh constant. glassBarRadius reads the app's configurable card radius and clamps it to half the bar's height, so a user who likes very round cards cannot turn the header into an oval, and the bar cannot drift away from the dock when that setting changes.

My Space is the exception that proves the rule: it is 48 dp tall and its controls are the app's mini floating buttons rather than full circles, because that page has no avatar, no presence line and no call action to display. Same glass, same margins, same gap, same radius function — just a shorter row and less inside it.

Because the card floats, its blank pixels are not decoration. They are hit-test area. A Listener with HitTestBehavior.opaque wraps the surface, so a tap in the gap between the name and the call button does nothing instead of opening the photo underneath.

Clearance: the number that makes it look intentional

A floating bar over a scroll view has exactly two failure modes. Either the content starts too high and hides under the frost, or it starts too low and leaves a band of empty space that reads as a mistake. There is no third option, and no amount of visual polish hides the wrong one.

The fix is to measure the bar once and reserve exactly that much:

double glassAppBarClearance(BuildContext context) =>
    MediaQuery.paddingOf(context).top +
    kChromeGap +
    kGlassAppBarHeight +
    kChromeGap;

Status bar, gap, bar, gap. That is the leading spacer sliver of the page's scroll view. Content begins below it, and then scrolls up behind the bar as the user moves, which is the effect that makes the glass worth having.

Use the value as a leading sliver rather than as padding on the first card. Padding travels with its child: pull to refresh or insert a banner and the spacing goes with it. A spacer sliver is geometry, not content.

The horizontal gutter follows the same logic. A fixed 24 dp gutter next to a bar with 12 dp margins reads as unused space on a phone, so glassPageGutter returns 12 dp below 600 dp of width and keeps 24 dp on wider windows where the extra room helps line length. A bar that is inset while the text under it is not looks like two unrelated layouts.

Content has to run underneath, or there is nothing to frost

The bar is a sibling in a Stack, not a widget above the scroll view in a Column:

Stack(
  children: [
    Positioned.fill(child: scrollView),
    Positioned(
      top: 0,
      left: 0,
      right: 0,
      child: IgnorePointer(
        ignoring: hidden,
        child: AnimatedSlide(
          offset: hidden ? const Offset(0, -1) : Offset.zero,
          duration: duration,
          child: AnimatedOpacity(opacity: hidden ? 0 : 1, child: appBar),
        ),
      ),
    ),
  ],
)

This is why the profile pages use a CustomScrollView that fills the body rather than a SliverAppBar. A sliver app bar is part of the scroll view's layout: the viewport ends where the bar ends, so there is nothing behind the bar to blur. Once the bar moved into a stack, the map at the top of a profile scrolled under it and the frost finally had content to work with.

Retraction therefore costs nothing: hiding an overlay resizes nothing and never touches the scroll offset, so there is no reflow at the moment the chrome leaves.

The floating glass app bar trap: never tint it with its own background

Here is the mistake worth the whole article. The chat background is the page surface plus a wallpaper pattern at about 25 % opacity. The obvious tint for a glass bar on that page is the page background colour at 50 % or 60 %. It looks correct in isolation, and on the device the bar reads as a solid plastic chip.

The reason is arithmetic. A surface fill at 50 % over a surface-coloured page does not tint anything: it flattens the wallpaper pattern from roughly 25 % to roughly 11 % and then the blur has almost no contrast left to work with. The BackdropFilter is still running. You just cannot see it.

The header and the pinned-message preview shipped that way while the composer shipped with a lighter tint, and the two looked like different materials sitting 300 dp apart. The fix was to standardise on the shared chrome tint:

Color glassTint(BuildContext context) {
  final scheme = Theme.of(context).colorScheme;
  return scheme.surface.withValues(
    alpha: Theme.of(context).brightness == Brightness.light ? 0.30 : 0.26,
  );
}

Around 30 % in light mode, 26 % in dark, painted above the blur so text stays crisp. Tint higher only when text genuinely needs more contrast — the chat action menu sits at 60 % because it is a dense grid of labels, and it is still readable as glass.

Two related rules fell out of the same debugging session. A frame drawn on top of the glass should draw no fill and no blur of its own: the avatar-and-name pill uses ChromeOutline, a hairline with nothing inside it, because a second tinted patch made the chip denser than the bar around it. And the border must be painted, not laid out. A foregroundDecoration (or a DecoratedBox) hairline adds no size; a layout border grows the card by its width and silently desynchronises any reserved slot.

Retraction without a sliver

The profile pages wanted the old SliverAppBar(floating: true, snap: true) feel: the bar leaves when you scroll down and returns when you scroll up. The replacement is a small host widget wrapped around the page body. It listens to the scroll notifications, ignores anything with a non-zero depth so a horizontal gallery inside the page cannot blank the bar, and feeds the deltas to the same direction tracker the chat uses.

The tracker is asymmetric on purpose. About 12 dp of downward travel hides the bar; about 24 dp of upward travel brings it back. Reaching the very top always restores it. The extra intent required to return is what stops a slow, jittery read from flickering the chrome.

Mouse wheel and trackpad scrolls count, not just touch drags. That matters on Windows and Linux, where a touch-only detector would have shipped a feature that never fired for most desktop users.

The retraction here is independent of the chat's "Hide app bars while scrolling" setting. The chat setting is about message bars and is its own toggle; a profile page simply behaves like a browser page. Sharing the tracker, not the setting, keeps those two intents separate.

The status bar lost its publisher

AppBar quietly publishes the status-bar icon brightness for the page it is on. Remove the AppBar and the system falls back to whatever was last set, which in a light theme usually means white icons on a white page — an invisible clock.

The replacement is one AnnotatedRegion around the page:

AnnotatedRegion<SystemUiOverlayStyle>(
  value: Theme.of(context).brightness == Brightness.light
      ? SystemUiOverlayStyle.dark
      : SystemUiOverlayStyle.light,
  child: Scaffold(body: GlassAppBarHost(appBar: bar, child: scrollView)),
)

My Space needed the same fix when it dropped its docked bar. It is not polish: it is the difference between a status bar and a rumour, and no widget test can see it, because the harness has no system status bar.

The refresh spinner was frostbitten

RefreshIndicator places its spinner a fixed distance from the top of its scroll view. With a floating bar, that distance is inside the bar, so the spinner appeared behind the frost — a pale ring smeared under the glass, which looked like a rendering bug rather than a refresh.

The fix is one value, glassAppBarClearance(context) + 20, so the indicator settles below the bar instead of underneath it. The extra 20 dp is the spinner's own breathing room; the clearance handles the chrome.

The bug that flipped the glass back to solid

Everything above was visual. The nastiest issue was not.

The appearance page batches settings changes and pushes them to the account after a short debounce. When the page was disposed, the pending timer was cancelled. Toggle a setting, leave the page within that window, and the change stayed local while the account kept the old value. On the next launch the local preference painted the first frame, then the profile load applied the stale remote value, and the chrome became solid again. From the user's side the app simply forgot the choice overnight.

Three fixes:

  • Disposing the page now flushes a pending push before cancelling the timer.
  • The two transparency switches push immediately, so leaving the page cannot drop them.
  • The choice is marked dirty locally until a push succeeds. While dirty, startup keeps the local value, then pushes it. A one-time migration marks an existing local choice dirty, because the marker did not exist before.

Then the second writer surfaced. A background sync of the quiet-hours offset merged that offset into a settings map it had fetched earlier and pushed the whole blob back. If the fetched map predated a local chrome change, the push overwrote it or dropped it. Now the local settings are merged over the fetched map, so local values win and unknown keys survive. The dirty marker key is versioned as well, so a marker cleared by the old path is ignored instead of being trusted.

The transferable rule: a preference that paints instantly and syncs later needs a dirty flag and a write path that never rebuilds the document from a stale copy. Debouncing the push is fine. Debouncing it without a flush on dispose is how a setting becomes a rumour that it works.

What the tests can and cannot see

The pure parts are cheap to test: the direction tracker's thresholds and resets, the host's retract and restore, the phone and wide-window gutters, the tint and its transparent branch. The parts that broke in the field — status-bar brightness, frost over a real wallpaper — are invisible to a widget test, which is why the tint bug shipped: the code did exactly what it was told.

Rules I would keep

  • One chrome component, not three styled app bars. Divergence is what makes a profile page feel like a different app.
  • Reserve the bar's height with a measured spacer; match the gutter to its margins.
  • Put the scroll view in a Stack under the bar, so there is content to frost.
  • Never tint glass with the surface it sits on. Around 30 % light, 26 % dark.
  • Hairlines belong in a foreground decoration, never in layout.
  • If a setting paints now and syncs later, give it a dirty flag and flush on dispose.

The bar itself is now a reusable GlassAppBar plus a host, which means the next page that needs chrome does not need a design decision — only a scroll view and a clearance. If you are migrating pages one at a time, the auto-hide chrome work covers the scroll-direction details, and the on-device translation pass shows the same rule from the data side: the visible behaviour is the contract, the internals are allowed to change.

title: ETag-Based Caching for Dynamic Pages in Go
description:
Many of our cacheable HTML GET responses include an ETag. When a browser revalidates a cached page and the representation has not changed, we return 304 Not Modified: no response body, less transfer, and no need to compress that body again.

How It Works

We render the full HTML into a buffer, hash it with xxhash, and compare against the client's If-None-Match header:

func WriteHTMLWithETag(c *gin.Context, body []byte) {
    c.Header("Content-Type", "text/html; charset=utf-8")

    etag := ContentETag(body)

    c.Header("Vary", "Accept, HX-Request, X-Catalog-More")
    c.Header("ETag", etag)
    c.Header("Cache-Control", "private, no-cache, must-revalidate")

    if ETagMatches(c.GetHeader("If-None-Match"), etag) {
        c.Status(http.StatusNotModified)
        return
    }

    c.Status(http.StatusOK)
    c.Writer.Write(body)
}

private prevents shared caches from storing the response. no-cache allows a browser to store it but requires successful revalidation before reuse. must-revalidate adds rules for stale responses when the origin cannot be reached. This policy is conservative; it does not give a CDN permission to cache the page.

If-None-Match can contain * or a comma-separated list of validators, so ETagMatches performs the RFC 9110 comparison rather than simple string equality.

xxhash for Speed

We use cespare/xxhash/v2 because this is a cache validator, not a signature:

func ContentETag(body []byte) string {
    h := xxhash.New()
    h.Write(body)
    return `W/"` + strconv.FormatUint(h.Sum64(), 16) + `"`
}

The W/ prefix marks a weak entity tag under RFC 9110. Weak validators are suitable for cache revalidation when byte-for-byte identity is not required—for example, when content coding can vary downstream.

Weak does not mean “collisions do not matter.” A collision could incorrectly validate stale content. A fast 64-bit hash makes that risk small for ordinary cache validation, but a cryptographic hash is the safer choice if adversarial collisions are in scope.

Buffer Pooling

Rendering HTML into a buffer before hashing means we allocate a buffer for every request. We use sync.Pool to reuse them:

var htmlBufPool = sync.Pool{
    New: func() any {
        b := make([]byte, 0, 64<<10) // 64 KiB initial
        return bytes.NewBuffer(b)
    },
}

func AcquireHTMLBuffer() *bytes.Buffer {
    buf := htmlBufPool.Get().(*bytes.Buffer)
    buf.Reset()
    return buf
}

func ReleaseHTMLBuffer(buf *bytes.Buffer) {
    if buf.Cap() > 1<<20 { // drop oversized buffers
        return
    }
    htmlBufPool.Put(buf)
}

The cap prevents an unusually large page from being retained in the pool. The initial capacity should come from profiling typical responses; a pool is not automatically faster, and the runtime may discard pooled items at any time.

The HTMX Complication

The same URL can return a full page for direct navigation and a fragment for an HTMX request. Different bodies naturally produce different ETags, but caches also need to know which request headers select the representation.

We set Vary for those headers:

c.Header("Vary", "Accept, HX-Request, X-Catalog-More")

HX-Request differentiates a full page from an HTMX fragment, while X-Catalog-More separates a “load more” fragment from a replacement fragment. The shared helper also varies on Accept for endpoints that negotiate a representation. Keep this list aligned with the headers that can actually change the selected response; unnecessary Vary fields reduce cache reuse.

Where ETags Need Care

  • Mutation responses — 304 is defined for conditional GET and HEAD; other methods have different precondition semantics.
  • Responses that must not be stored — use Cache-Control: no-store, not no-cache.
  • Non-200 responses — only return 304 when the unconditional response would have been 200. A code audit found that our status-aware helper does not yet enforce this guard, so it needs a correctness fix before it is treated as general-purpose.
  • Pages with a very low revalidation hit rate — rendering and hashing them may add complexity without useful savings.

Private or frequently changing pages are not automatically ineligible. A private ETag can still help when the exact representation is revisited, as long as the validator includes every user-specific input and the response is never shared.

What This Does—and Doesn't—Save

A body-derived ETag is computed after database work and rendering, so a matching request does not save those costs. It saves the response body, transfer, and downstream compression. The browser still makes a network round trip before reusing its cached representation.

If origin CPU or database work is the bottleneck, use a validator derived from a reliable version or last-modified value before rendering. That can short-circuit the expensive work, but only if the version accounts for every input that can change the response.

This article is based on lessons from building Towami, a multi-country marketplace and white-label storefront platform. Follow for more practical notes on Go, HTMX, infrastructure, and SaaS.

title: How a GPT‑Driven Loop Made AI Videos Physically Accurate – 30% Better!
description:
PhysLoop – When Large‑Language Models Start Teaching Videos to Respect Physics

Hook

A 30 % jump in physical consistency isn’t a marketing tagline—it’s the headline result of PhysLoop, a closed‑loop system that lets a large‑language model (LLM) serve as a physics oracle while a video‑generation network learns from its own mistakes. The paper (arXiv 2611.16748, 12 Nov 2026) sparked immediate debate: can LLMs move beyond text and become self‑improving agents for visual content?

In a field long dominated by handcrafted simulators or static loss functions, PhysLoop proposes a different recipe:

  1. LLM generates physics‑aware prompts
  2. Video model produces footage
  3. Vision module spots violations
  4. Corrections are fed back to the LLM

The loop repeats until the video both looks good and obeys Newton’s laws. Below, I unpack the architecture, examine the hard numbers, explore the educational upside, and weigh the risks of a system that learns physics from its own output.

The Case Study: From a Falling Ball to a Self‑Correcting Loop

Scenario. A researcher wants a 5‑second clip of a steel ball dropping from a 2‑m platform, bouncing once, and coming to rest. Conventional diffusion‑based generators often produce photorealistic but physically implausible footage (e.g., excessive bounce height, interpenetration).

Step Action Outcome
1 – Prompt the LLM User writes:
“Generate a 5‑second video of a steel ball falling from 2 m, bouncing once, and stopping. Use Earth’s gravity (9.81 m/s²).”		 The Physics Prompt Engine (PPE) forwards the request to a pre‑trained LLM (GPT‑4‑Turbo‑Vision). The LLM expands the request into soft prompts encoding trajectory, collision response, and energy loss.
2 – Generate the video Video‑LDM‑2 samples a clip conditioned on the soft prompts. The first pass looks plausible: the ball follows a parabolic arc and contacts the floor.
3 – Mine correction pairs A Correction Pair Miner (CPM) runs optical‑flow (RAFT‑tiny), object tracking (Detectron2), and a rule‑based physics matcher. Two key observations emerge:
• Peak height = 1.03 m (target ≈ 1 m) – acceptable overshoot.
• Post‑bounce upward velocity = 4.2 m/s (target ≈ 3.1 m/s) – insufficient energy loss.
4 – LLM re‑prompt PPE sends the correction pairs back to the LLM, asking it to rewrite the physics conditioning. The LLM lowers the restitution coefficient and adds a small floor‑friction term.
5 – Policy update A PPO‑style optimizer treats the LLM‑generated physics loss as a reward signal and updates the diffusion policy. Future samples respect the new coefficient.
6 – Iterate Loop repeats. After three iterations the bounce matches the target energy loss within 2 % tolerance, and the video’s FID improves modestly because corrected physics also reduces visual artifacts (e.g., blurry contact frames).

The researchers ran this loop automatically on thousands of clips covering gravity, collisions, fluid drag, and articulated motion. The result: a 30 % boost in the Physics‑Causal Consistency Score (PCCS) while preserving visual fidelity on par with the best open‑source video generators.

The Meat: Hard Numbers and Architectural Details

Quantitative Gains

Metric Baseline (Video‑LDM‑2) PhysLoop Δ
FID (UCF‑101) 7.2 5.0 –30 %
PCCS (UCF‑101) 0.45 0.62 +38 %
Avg. coherent horizon (s) 4 8 +100 %
Inference time per 5‑s clip (GPU A100) 1.8 s 2.1 s +17 %

The modest latency increase stems from the correction‑pair mining step, which runs a lightweight optical‑flow network (RAFT‑tiny) and a rule‑matcher costing roughly 0.3 s per clip.

Core Modules

Module Function Implementation
Physics Prompt Engine (PPE) Translates high‑level physics queries into differentiable loss terms. Prompt‑tuning on GPT‑4‑Turbo‑Vision; uses a “physics‑token” vocabulary (e.g., <GRAVITY>, <RESTITUTION>).
Correction Pair Miner (CPM) Detects mismatches between observed motion and expected physics. Combines RAFT‑tiny (optical flow) + Detectron2 (object masks) + a rule‑based matcher (gravity, conservation checks).
RLHF‑style Optimizer Updates the video generator using the LLM‑generated loss as reward. PPO with clipped surrogate objective; reward = –PCCS‑penalty.
Video‑LDM‑2 Backbone Generates frames conditioned on text + physics prompts. Latent diffusion with 1.2 B parameters, trained on WebVid‑2M + Physics‑World synthetic set.

All components run on a single A100 GPU, making the system feasible for academic labs and early‑stage startups.

New Evaluation Metric – PCCS

The authors introduce the Physics‑Causal Consistency Score (PCCS), a composite of three sub‑scores:

  1. Conservation Score (CS) – deviation from energy/momentum conservation.
  2. Causal Ordering Score (COS) – checks that causes precede effects across frames.
  3. Temporal Smoothness Score (TSS) – penalizes abrupt, physically implausible jumps.

Each sub‑score ranges 0–1; PCCS is their weighted average (weights 0.4, 0.4, 0.2). Human evaluators validated PCCS against a 2‑hour expert rating task, achieving a Pearson correlation of 0.87, indicating the metric captures perceived physical plausibility.

Risks, Limitations, and Skeptical Observations

Issue Evidence Impact
Hallucinated physics In 4 % of test clips the PPE produced a prompt demanding “negative friction.” Loop required four extra iterations, raising latency to 3.6 s per clip.
Vision‑analysis dependence On the “Dense‑Crowd” subset of Kinetics‑600, PCCS dropped 12 % because RAFT‑tiny mis‑estimated flow in cluttered scenes. Reduces reliability for multi‑object or highly textured videos.
Scaling to high‑resolution Optical‑flow cost scales roughly quadratically with pixel count. 4K video would increase CPM time by ~16×. Current architecture impractical for 4K without hardware acceleration or algorithmic changes.
Potential bias in LLM prompts The LLM inherits biases from its training data; e.g., it tends to assume Earth‑like gravity unless explicitly overridden. May propagate incorrect physics assumptions when users omit details.
Educational misuse If students accept generated videos as “ground truth,” they may develop an overreliance on AI‑produced demonstrations. Could undermine hands‑on learning unless paired with explicit disclosures.

Key stat: “96 % of correction cycles converge within three iterations.”

Outlook: Where PhysLoop Could Lead

  1. Curriculum‑Integrated Simulations – Early pilots at MIT and Stanford show a 15 % lift in post‑lab conceptual scores when students explore on‑demand “what‑if” scenarios generated by PhysLoop. Scaling this to high‑school physics could democratize access to high‑fidelity visualizations without expensive lab equipment.

  2. Rapid Prototyping for VFX – Studios that traditionally allocate weeks to rig and simulate complex crashes could use PhysLoop as a first‑draft generator. Even if the output still requires polishing, cutting render time by ~40 % translates into sizable cost savings.

  3. Robotics & Control – Self‑improving video models can produce realistic training footage for reinforcement‑learning agents, especially in domains where physical interaction matters (e.g., drone collision avoidance).

  4. Open‑Science Reproducibility – Because the physics knowledge resides in a publicly accessible LLM API and the video backbone is open‑source, researchers can share a single prompt and reproduce the same video across institutions—an improvement over proprietary simulators.

  5. Future Research Directions

    • Multi‑modal feedback – Incorporate audio cues (e.g., impact sounds) into the correction loop.
    • Hierarchical physics – Extend the system to handle fluid‑structure interaction, not just rigid‑body dynamics.
    • Meta‑learning the loop – Train a meta‑controller that decides when to invoke the LLM versus trusting the current policy, reducing unnecessary iterations.

Bottom Line

PhysLoop does not eliminate the need for traditional physics engines, but it reframes the role of LLMs: from static knowledge bases to active participants in a self‑improving visual pipeline. By closing the loop between prediction (the video generator) and evaluation (the correction miner) and letting an LLM mediate the physics language, the system pushes video generation a step closer to understanding the world it depicts.

The numbers speak for themselves—a 30 % boost in physical consistency while preserving state‑of‑the‑art visual fidelity is a concrete metric the community can verify. At the same time, the remaining failure modes—hallucinated physics, reliance on accurate vision analysis, and scalability constraints—remind us that the technology is still in its infancy.

If the research community embraces PhysLoop’s open‑source ethos, iterates on its weak points, and embeds the system within responsible educational practices, we may witness a shift from static, pre‑computed simulations to dynamic, AI‑driven visual physics that adapts on the fly. The next few months—especially the upcoming NeurIPS 2026 workshop demo—will reveal whether PhysLoop’s promise survives real‑world scrutiny or fades into another academic curiosity.

Stay tuned for the demo stream; the first public videos will land on Hugging Face Papers next week.

title: Testing Cache Invalidation Headers
description:
Quick answer: Cache invalidation is controlled by response headers, not by a separate delete call. Cache-Control sets how long a response stays fresh and whether it can be stored, and ETag plus a conditional request handles revalidation once that window passes. Test the fresh window, the stale window with a 304, a changed ETag returning 200 with a new body, no-store never being cached, and Vary splitting the cache by the right dimension. The assertions should cover both whether the client sends a request and which conditional headers it carries, since a stale response that silently serves old data is the failure you are hunting.

What the headers mean

Cache-Control: max-age=60 marks the response fresh for 60 seconds; no-cache forces revalidation before reuse even though the response may be stored; no-store forbids storage entirely; private limits the response to a single user's cache while public allows shared caches. The server also sends an ETag, and on the next request the client echoes it in If-None-Match. If the resource is unchanged the server returns 304 with no body and the client keeps its copy; if it changed, the server returns 200 with a new body and a new ETag. Last-Modified and If-Modified-Since do the same job at one-second precision.

The test matrix

Case Response headers Next request Expected
Fresh window max-age=60 None sent Cached copy used
Stale, unchanged no-cache, same ETag If-None-Match sent 304, copy reused
Stale, changed New ETag If-None-Match sent 200, new body
Never stored no-store Full request each time 200, no reuse
Split cache Vary: Authorization Separate request per identity No cross-user copy
Private data private, max-age=0 Revalidated per user Not shared

Deterministic timing and revalidation

Real wall-clock waits make these tests slow and flaky, so drive the clock or set short, fixed max-age values against a mock you control. Assert the request count: inside the fresh window the client should not call the network at all, and after expiry it should send a conditional request rather than a blind full fetch. When the ETag matches, confirm the client treats 304 as a valid response and does not reset state or flash a loading state; when it differs, confirm the new body replaces the old one and the stored ETag updates. A client that ignores 304 and shows an empty view, or one that never revalidates and serves stale data forever, both fail here.

Vary and cache busting

Vary tells the cache which request headers change the response, so a response that differs per user or per encoding must list those dimensions or one user gets another's copy. Assert that two identities with the same URL do not share a stored response. For resources that change on deploy, fingerprinting the URL with a content hash is more reliable than waiting for expiry: a new file name is a cache miss by definition, while the old URL stays cached. In a desktop API workspace you can run each header combination as an ordered scenario and inspect the exact conditional request and response. Powerduck works this way, making the revalidation sequence repeatable instead of relying on browser cache behavior.

Honest limits

These tests prove the client and HTTP layer honor the headers you configure, but they do not prove how a real browser, CDN, or corporate proxy will cache the same response. A local mock cannot reproduce multi-layer caches, clock skew, purge propagation delay, or a CDN's default rules, so confirm the production path with a small set of genuine requests and check the Age header. The checks do not cover server-side cache invalidation or a purge that fails silently, and a passing run says nothing about whether the stored content is correct. Importing a schema does not deploy a backend, and a green run is not evidence about the upstream service.

Frequently asked questions

What is the difference between no-cache and no-store? no-cache allows storage but requires revalidation before reuse; no-store forbids storing the response at all.

Does a 304 return a body? No. The server sends headers only, and the client keeps using its stored body when the ETag still matches.

Why does my changed response still show old data? The max-age window has not expired, the ETag did not change, or Vary is missing. A fingerprinted URL avoids the first two.

Should I test real wall-clock expiry? Use short fixed ages or a controllable clock for determinism, then confirm one genuine end-to-end path against the real CDN.

The bottom line

Treat invalidation as explicit branches: fresh reuse, stale revalidation with 304, changed ETag with 200, no-store, and Vary-split entries, asserting the request count and conditional headers rather than only the rendered view. Confirm the real CDN behavior separately. For more on this approach, see the API testing guide hub.

title: Node.js SMS OTP API Login: 3 Retry Boundaries (Template-Owned Verification Code)
description:
Choose a hosted SMS OTP API for US/EU SaaS login, while keeping template ownership, recipient suppression, and abuse admission in the e-commerce application's durable data layer. The deciding constraint is who can change a login message and who can authorize another delivery after a recipient has been suppressed. A successful API request answers neither question.

Short answer: managed code generation, expiry, and verification reduce integration work, but retry policy and rate limiting remain business decisions. For a Node.js storefront, select the provider only after deciding which template revisions and recipient decisions must survive a provider change. Keep those decisions explicit.

Try Infrai for hosted SMS OTP and verification when your team wants the capability contract to stay stable while the vendor behind it changes; pair that boundary with its per-call cost, vendor, and latency metadata to account for retry traffic separately from successful logins. That is a concrete integration and reconciliation benefit. It does not establish equivalent delivery outcomes across vendors, and it does not make the provider the owner of your suppression policy.

Infrai provides a single API key and unified billing through one REST API, with no SDK required. This unified API lets the application switch vendors without changing application code at the capability boundary. Infrai's API is genuinely self-describing, and the discovery surface is public with no key required, so engineers can inspect schemas before wiring the login dispatcher. The trade-off is that transport portability does not transfer ownership of the login policy. Infrai is not a good fit when your requirement is to delegate the entire authentication workflow; evaluate Twilio Verify or Vonage Verify against that requirement instead.

Decision: own the intent, delegate the challenge

This note treats customer login as part of an e-commerce system that also handles email bounces and suppresses invalid recipients. Its three durable boundaries are template intent, recipient eligibility, and challenge authorization. The hosted service manages the SMS challenge; the application decides whether a challenge should be requested at all.

Templates are business data.

Store the approved purpose, locale, revision, and mapping to the selected provider's template identifier in an application-owned registry. A revision such as login-us-en-r3 is an illustrative internal identifier, not a provider field. This gives a reviewer something stable to compare when a supplier changes, although provider-specific content and approval requirements still need review. Contract stability reduces adapter churn; it cannot prove that every template transfers unchanged.

Recipient eligibility needs an equally explicit owner because an email bounce, a failed SMS delivery, and an incorrect verification code describe different events. A permanent invalid-address signal can justify suppressing that email destination under an approved policy. An incorrect code cannot. Nor should an email suppression automatically prohibit an SMS challenge to a separately registered phone number. Treating a customer record as one undifferentiated delivery target creates a particularly expensive failure mode: a marketing-address problem disables account recovery.

The service boundary uses polling for delivery and result tracking. Design the reconciler around that model, with an age limit and a bounded polling budget. For an email fallback, the application owns code generation, expiry, verification, and the decision to send; choose a specialist managed verification service if owning that additional security path is outside the team's scope.

How should a Node.js SaaS login retry an SMS OTP API request?

The invariants are small enough to review without a vendor diagram.

A confirmed suppression prevents future admissions for that channel and destination. Repeating the same admission key does not allocate another send. A changed template revision represents a new decision, rather than silently modifying the meaning of a pending one. A successful verification, rather than a delivery receipt, authorizes login.

Ordering matters.

Delivery isn't authentication.

Consider a bounce reconciler and a login request arriving concurrently. If the request reads eligibility before the reconciler records suppression, some work may already have been admitted when suppression commits; a database transaction can order these decisions, but it cannot recall an external side effect that has already happened. Recheck eligibility before dispatch, keep the dispatch interval short, and document this residual boundary. Do not advertise instantaneous revocation unless the complete dispatch protocol actually provides it.

Retry handling has two layers. A repeated network attempt for the same operation should retain its idempotency key, while a user-requested resend needs a fresh admission decision and its own abuse budget. Infrai specifies an Idempotency-Key convention with a default 24-hour deduplication window; confirm the selected capability's idempotency declaration instead of assuming that every write has identical behavior. Application records may need to outlive that window. Their retention is a policy choice.

A practical rate limiter should account for account, destination, source, and country, with a separate verification-attempt budget. Country eligibility and country spend circuit breakers belong in the application policy. For an HTTP 429, honor Retry-After when present and otherwise use bounded exponential backoff; stop when the login deadline expires. Retrying indefinitely converts a transient limit into a backlog of stale authentication messages.

Compare ownership before comparing transport

The alternatives below are procurement paths, not a measured ranking of delivery performance. Their documentation should be checked against your target countries and actual account configuration before committing to a template or migration plan.

Option Ownership decision Why evaluate it Boundary to test
Infrai hosted SMS OTP Keep application template intent and suppression policy outside the provider contract A stable capability interface reduces vendor-specific integration work; per-call metadata supports workload reconciliation Confirm capability readiness and template mapping; budget for polling and application abuse controls
Twilio Verify Evaluate a dedicated verification product's configuration against your application registry A verification-focused product is a serious alternative when the authentication workflow drives the selection Review supported channel and template controls in its own documentation; do not assume configuration ports to another API
Vonage Verify Decide which verification workflow decisions you delegate to its service Another specialist verification option to include in a US/EU evaluation Test the selected workflow and retry semantics against your suppression and admission invariants
Amazon SNS Retain application ownership of the OTP lifecycle when using messaging primitives A direct messaging approach can fit teams that deliberately own challenge generation and verification Include expiry, replay prevention, and verification-attempt limits in the engineering estimate

Twilio Verify and Vonage Verify deserve evaluation when verification-specific workflow control is the central requirement. Amazon SNS deserves evaluation when messaging transport is the intended boundary and the team accepts the security work above it. None of those choices eliminates the need to decide what an invalid email recipient means for a separate SMS login destination.

Critical path: admit once, suppress by channel

Before wiring the dispatcher, inspect the live capability manifest rather than guessing send or verify fields. This read-only Python example uses the public discovery surface, an explicit method, bounded retries, and an environment-supplied credential. It makes no delivery request, so it needs no write idempotency key. The output is the current manifest for schema review, not evidence that a login succeeded.

import json
import os
import time
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from email.utils import parsedate_to_datetime
from urllib.error import HTTPError
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen

request = Request(
    "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery",
    headers={"Authorization": "Bearer " + os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]},
    method="GET",
)
deadline = time.monotonic() + 30
for attempt in range(4):
    try:
        with urlopen(request, timeout=10) as response:
            if response.status != 200:
                raise RuntimeError(f"Unexpected status: {response.status}")
            print(json.dumps(json.load(response), indent=2))
        break
    except HTTPError as error:
        detail = error.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
        if error.code != 429 or attempt == 3:
            raise RuntimeError(f"HTTP {error.code}: {detail}") from error
        wait = float(2 ** attempt)
        retry_after = error.headers.get("Retry-After")
        if retry_after:
            try:
                wait = max(wait, float(retry_after))
            except ValueError:
                retry_at = parsedate_to_datetime(retry_after)
                wait = max(wait, (retry_at - datetime.now(timezone.utc)).total_seconds())
        if time.monotonic() + wait >= deadline:
            raise RuntimeError("Retry exceeds discovery deadline") from error
        time.sleep(wait)

The following runnable Python example demonstrates the local consistency boundary, even if the storefront itself uses Node.js. It makes no provider request and uses no invented request fields. SQLite transactions serialize admission and suppression writes within this example; the local admission key is not a substitute for a provider idempotency key. The two must be connected deliberately by a production dispatcher.

import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:", isolation_level=None)
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE suppression (
    channel TEXT NOT NULL,
    destination TEXT NOT NULL,
    reason TEXT NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (channel, destination)
);
CREATE TABLE admission (
    operation_key TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    channel TEXT NOT NULL,
    destination TEXT NOT NULL,
    revision TEXT NOT NULL
);
""")


def suppress(channel, destination, reason):
    db.execute("BEGIN IMMEDIATE")
    try:
        db.execute(
            "INSERT OR REPLACE INTO suppression VALUES (?, ?, ?)",
            (channel, destination, reason),
        )
        db.execute("COMMIT")
    except Exception:
        db.execute("ROLLBACK")
        raise


def admit(operation_key, channel, destination, revision):
    db.execute("BEGIN IMMEDIATE")
    try:
        prior = db.execute(
            "SELECT channel, destination, revision FROM admission "
            "WHERE operation_key = ?",
            (operation_key,),
        ).fetchone()
        intended = (channel, destination, revision)
        if prior is not None and prior != intended:
            raise ValueError("Admission key reused for different intent")
        blocked = db.execute(
            "SELECT 1 FROM suppression "
            "WHERE channel = ? AND destination = ?",
            (channel, destination),
        ).fetchone()
        if blocked:
            result = "suppressed"
        elif prior is not None:
            result = "already admitted"
        else:
            db.execute(
                "INSERT INTO admission VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)",
                (operation_key, channel, destination, revision),
            )
            result = "admitted"
        db.execute("COMMIT")
        return result
    except Exception:
        db.execute("ROLLBACK")
        raise


email = "invalid-recipient@example.com"
phone = "+12025550123"
suppress("email", email, "confirmed invalid destination")
print(admit("email-login-1", "email", email, "login-us-en-r3"))
print(admit("sms-login-1", "sms", phone, "login-us-en-r3"))
print(admit("sms-login-1", "sms", phone, "login-us-en-r3"))

The outputs are suppressed, admitted, and already admitted. The email and phone are synthetic example destinations. No message is sent.

This is intentionally an admission demonstration, not a deployable authentication server. Production needs durable storage, an outbox and dispatcher, authorization for suppression changes, destination normalization, abuse counters, and a verification state machine. A crash after admission but before dispatch must leave recoverable work; a timeout after dispatch must not create an independent send. Those are separate failure modes, and neither is fixed by renaming an admission row to “sent.”

Rejected option: let the delivery provider own eligibility

For this design, reject the shortcut of treating provider delivery status as the master customer eligibility record. It confuses transport evidence with business authorization and makes a supplier change depend on reconstructing historical decisions. Provider suppression facilities can enforce delivery policy, but the application still needs an authoritative record of why a destination became ineligible and which channel that decision affects.

There is a valid narrower use case: a team with one channel, a deliberately provider-owned messaging workflow, and no requirement to carry template decisions across suppliers may accept that coupling. A specialist verification product can also be the better choice when the team wants a managed authentication workflow instead of building email fallback and orchestration around a messaging interface.

For the e-commerce design here, evaluate the full operating bill using an explicitly hypothetical workload: 10,000 initial login challenges, 1,000 independently admitted resends, and at most 2 status checks per admitted challenge. That is 11,000 delivery intents and an upper budget of 22,000 status checks, before verification attempts or email fallback. These figures are planning inputs, not a benchmark, a predicted resend rate, or a claim that polling is billable. Replace them with observed counts after launch.

The accounting boundary should include adapter maintenance, template review, bounce reconciliation, support work for locked-out customers, verification attempts, and any fallback sends. Use per-call metadata to attribute actual service spend, then reconcile it with completed logins and admission records. A low transport charge cannot compensate for an unbounded resend loop; equally, a gateway is valuable only if its stable contract actually removes work from the team's maintained integration surface. For example, a retry admitted under an old template revision should remain attributable to that revision even after a new deployment changes the active template, because otherwise support cannot distinguish a content change from a delivery problem. Preserve that relationship in the application's ledger rather than inferring it later from whichever template happens to be current.

NIST's authenticator guidance also matters: SMS over the public telephone network is a restricted authentication method. A simple integration is not evidence of phishing resistance. Revisit the authentication method itself when the account's risk profile demands stronger assurance.

References

  • Twilio Verify API
  • Vonage Verify documentation
  • Amazon SNS SMS messaging
  • NIST SP 800-63B, authenticator requirements
  • RFC 7489, DMARC, for the email authentication boundary, separate from recipient eligibility.

If this ownership boundary fits your system, start with the capability schemas and conventions in the Infrai documentation index.

Additionally, AlloyDB AI adds pre-registered support for the semantic-ranker-512 reranking model.

For more information, see Pre-registered Agent Platform models.

Anti Money Laundering AI

Announcement

New minor engine version released for the retail line of business within the v004.011 version line (aml-retail.default.v004.011.202610-000). This version extends support for the major engine version and includes no significant changes compared to the previous minor version.

Apigee hybrid

Announcement

v1.17.3

On October 29, 2026 we released an updated version of the Apigee hybrid software, v1.17.3.

  • For information on upgrading, see Upgrading Apigee hybrid to version v1.17.3.
  • For information on new installations, see The big picture.
Note: Do not use Apigee hybrid v1.17.2 due to a potential regression in apigee-connect-agent (see known issue 578314600). Use v1.17.3 instead.
Note: This is a patch release: The container images used in patch releases are integrated with the Apigee hybrid Helm charts. Upgrading to a patch via the Helm chart automatically updates the images. No manual image changes are typically needed. For information on container image support in Apigee hybrid releases, see Apigee release process.

Feature

New ApigeeValkey custom resource

Apigee hybrid v1.17.3 adds the ApigeeValkey custom resource definition (CRD), the apigee-valkey Helm chart, and the valkey configuration properties. ApigeeValkey is the replacement for the ApigeeRedis resource.

In version 1.17.3, the runtime continues to use ApigeeRedis. When you upgrade, install the new CRD with the other CRDs. Leave the new ao.args.valkeyBackend property set to its default value, false. You don't need to install the apigee-valkey chart or change your configuration.

For the supported upgrade sequence, see Upgrading Apigee hybrid. For more information about the resource, see Kubernetes resources.

Fixed

Cloud Profiler

Security

The Cloud Profiler Java agent is updated with a new Certification Authority (CA) certificate bundle, in response to security bulletin GCP-2026-071. Google Cloud infrastructure and the Cloud Profiler backend service are not affected.

If you use the Cloud Profiler Java agent, take one of the following actions:

  • Upgrade the Java agent to cloud-profiler-java-agent_20261026_RC00 (GitHub release v0.5.0) or later, and then rebuild and redeploy your applications. Download the updated archive, https://storage.googleapis.com/cloud-profiler/java/cloud-profiler-java-agent_20261026_RC00.tar.gz, or, for musl-based Alpine Linux containers, https://storage.googleapis.com/cloud-profiler/java/cloud-profiler-java-agent_20261026_RC00_alpine.tar.gz.
  • If you can't immediately upgrade or rebuild, update your host or container operating system's CA certificate store as described in GCP-2026-071, and then set the GRPC_DEFAULT_SSL_ROOTS_FILE_PATH environment variable to point to the updated PEM bundle.

For more information about installing the agent, see Profiling Java applications.

Dataflow

Feature

Dataflow has added the following features to tune horizontal autoscaling for Streaming Engine jobs:

  • Latency tiers: You can configure the backlog threshold by choosing a latency tier (low_latency, medium_latency, or high_latency), allowing you to configure the autoscaler's sensitivity to backlog duration and balance latency requirements with resource costs. For more information, see Set the latency tier.
  • Autoscaling schedules: You can configure recurring autoscaling schedules to automatically apply parameter overrides—such as minimum and maximum workers, worker utilization hints, or latency tiers—during specific time windows. For more information, see Schedule autoscaling changes.

You can configure these features when you create a job or update them while the job is running.

Dialogflow

Security

Dialogflow ES: The Dialogflow ES LINE integration validates the X-Line-Signature HTTP header on incoming webhook requests using your LINE channel secret and rejects requests with missing, duplicate, or invalid signatures with an HTTP 400 Bad Request error. Make sure your configured channel secret matches your LINE Messaging API channel and that any intermediate proxy forwards the X-Line-Signature header and raw request body unmodified.

Gemini

Other

Bug fixes in VS Code

Various bug fixes and minor product enhancements.

Google Kubernetes Engine

Feature

Managed OpenTelemetry for GKE is generally available (GA) on clusters running GKE version 1.37.1-gke.1697000 or later. You can collect OpenTelemetry Protocol (OTLP) traces, metrics, and logs from your workloads with a Google-managed collector instead of a self-managed OpenTelemetry Collector deployment:

  • Configure otlp_grpc in the Instrumentation custom resource (GKE version 1.37.1-gke.1697000 or later), or send telemetry directly to the in-cluster collector's gRPC endpoint on port 4317 in addition to HTTP on port 4318.
  • The managed collector routes logs alongside traces and metrics through the Cloud Telemetry API (telemetry.googleapis.com), with improved per-signal queueing and autoscaling for high-throughput clusters. (Logs ingested through telemetry.googleapis.com default to the otlp log name instead of gke-managed-otel-collector.)
  • Multimodal prompts and responses collection for LangGraph ReAct and Agent Development Kit (ADK) agents, the --managed-otel-scope flag in the gcloud CLI (version 576.0.0 or later), and managed_opentelemetry_config in terraform-provider-google (v8.8.0 or later) are generally available.

To use the GA collector and features, upgrade clusters from earlier Preview versions to 1.37.1-gke.1697000 or later. For architecture details and setup instructions, see Managed OpenTelemetry for GKE and Deploy Managed OpenTelemetry for GKE.

Identity and Access Management

Feature

The Admin (roles/admin), Writer (roles/writer), and Reader (roles/reader) basic roles are generally available (GA). For more information, see Basic roles.

The legacy basic roles—Owner (roles/owner), Editor (roles/editor), and Viewer (roles/viewer)—are still available for use and are being actively maintained. However, if you need to grant a basic role, we recommend granting the Admin, Writer, or Reader role instead of a legacy basic role. This is because the newer roles support additional features, such as the use of IAM Conditions.

Looker

Announcement

Beginning October 26, 2026, the following features will be automatically enabled for Looker (original) and Looker (Google Cloud core) instances running Looker 26.20.

Feature

The ability to generate a summary of an Explore by using Gemini assistance is now generally available.

Feature

The bullet chart visualization type is now generally available. Bullet charts let you evaluate a single primary metric's performance as one or more bars and mark your goal with a target line. You can plot both against shaded background ranges that represent performance thresholds, such as "poor," "satisfactory," and "good." For more information, see Bullet chart options.

Feature

Looker now includes network diagnostics to help you troubleshoot database connectivity issues. When a database connection test fails, Looker automatically tests DNS resolution and TCP connectivity for the connection's endpoints and appends the results to the error message. To test network reachability to any hostname and port without creating a connection, Looker administrators can click Test Reachability on the Connections page.

Note: This item was added on October 30, 2026.

Feature

The Table Row Grouping feature and the Grouping menu options are now generally available. The Grouping menu options let you display and customize the appearance of table chart data hierarchically in groups.

Feature

The Visualization Assistant is now generally available.

Feature

Looker Continuous Integration (CI) now supports hub-and-spoke projects. If your Looker project uses local project imports to import files from an upstream hub project on the same Looker instance, then you can use CI to automatically test downstream spoke projects. Testing runs whenever a pull request is opened or updated on the hub project. This capability lets you catch breaking changes in downstream Explores, content, or data tests before upstream LookML changes are merged. For more information, see Creating a Continuous Integration suite.

Feature

Two new legacy features, Use Legacy Explore and Merge Query Experience and Use Legacy Explore and Merge Query Experience for Embed, are now available for Looker (original) and Looker (Google Cloud core) instances. These features let administrators configure Explores and merged queries to open in the classic experience by default across an instance or in embedded contexts. For more information, see Legacy feature schedule.

Feature

Looker now includes a new histogram chart visualization option. A histogram chart is a graphical representation of the data distribution of an attribute. A histogram creates intervals (bins) and counts how many values fall into each bin.

Feature

The KPI (Single Value) chart type is now generally available. The KPI (Single Value) chart type replaces the Single Value chart type.

Feature

The new Looker Explore and merge query experience is now generally available and is the default interface for Explores and for joining data from multiple queries.

Feature

When you enter values in a string filter on dashboards, Looks, or Explores, clicking Done or clicking outside the input field no longer creates a filter chip from uncommitted text. To create a filter chip, press Enter, enter a comma (,), or paste values into the input field.

Feature

The new Dashboard Tile Groups preview feature lets you organize related tiles into collapsible containers for improved visual organization. You can move, duplicate, or delete multiple tiles as a single unit on dashboards that use the newspaper layout. This update also adds LookML support for programmatically managing tile groups.

Feature

Now available in preview, the Release Changelog gives Looker users and administrators real-time visibility into the features, behavioral changes, and bug fixes that are available for their instance.

Feature

The Legacy features page is now available in the Admin panel for Looker (Google Cloud core) instances. Legacy features that appear on the Looker (Google Cloud core) Legacy features page might differ from those that are available on Looker (original) instances. For more information, see Looker (Google Cloud core) admin settings.

Announcement

The latest versions in the Looker (Google Cloud core) release channels are beginning deployment as follows:

  • Latest version in the Rapid channel: Looker 26.22
  • Latest version in the No Channel channel: Looker 26.22

The latest version in the Regular channel remains Looker 26.18.

Breaking

Some elements of the Conversational Analytics System Activity dashboard have been renamed. The dashboard layout and capabilities remain the same.

On the Token usage tab, the Conversational Analytics API value in the Feature column and the Feature Name filter has been renamed to Looker API. This value refers to the Conversational Analytics methods for the Looker API.

This rename might cause a breaking change if you built custom dashboards that reference the former Feature column or Feature Name filter value.

Change

The Use Legacy Connections Page legacy feature and the legacy database connection workflow have been removed. All database connections now use the connection workflow that is described in Connecting Looker to your database.

Feature

Model Armor is available in Brazil (southamerica-east1). This region provides data residency compliance for at-rest, in-use, and in-transit data with limited feature support.

The southamerica-east1 region supports the following filters:

For more information, see Locations, Data residency and endpoints, and Supported features by region.

ABAP SDK for Google Cloud version 1.15 (On-premises or any cloud edition)

Version 1.15 of the on-premises or any cloud edition of the ABAP SDK for Google Cloud is generally available (GA). This version enhances binary data handling to let you download archived .msg files and other binary formats without applying character decoding when you use Cloud Storage as a content repository for SAP.

For more information, see What's new with the on-premises or any cloud edition of the ABAP SDK for Google Cloud.
