title: What You Can Self-Host on Oracle Cloud Free Tier (2026)
description:
Last updated: July 27, 2026

Status as of this writing: Oracle quietly cut the Always Free Ampere A1 allocation from 4 OCPUs / 24 GB RAM to 2 OCPUs / 12 GB RAM on June 15, 2026. No blog post, no email, an edited documentation page and nothing else. If you're reading an older guide (including some still-circulating 2026 posts) that budgets against 24 GB, check your own console before following its numbers. Everything below is sized for the current 2 OCPU / 12 GB reality, plus the two small AMD Micro instances that are unaffected by the change.

A free tier that quietly loses half its headroom is still worth building on. It means the sizing conversation matters more than it used to, and CPU, not RAM, ends up being the tighter constraint on two cores.

What Oracle gives you for free

The Always Free resources relevant to a self-hosting stack:

  • Ampere A1 Flex (ARM): 2 OCPUs and 12 GB RAM total, split across one to four instances as you choose. This is down from 4/24 as of June 2026.
  • AMD Micro instances: two of them, each 1/8 OCPU and 1 GB RAM. Small, but free on its own terms and separate from the Ampere allocation.
  • Block storage: 200 GB total, shared across your instances.
  • Outbound bandwidth: 10 TB per month.
  • Reclamation risk: Oracle's current published policy reclaims an Always Free compute instance if, over a 7-day period, its 95th-percentile CPU, network, and (for A1 shapes) memory utilization all stay under 20%. A stack that's serving real traffic rarely trips this; an instance you spun up once and forgot about is exactly what the policy targets.
  • Regional availability: Ampere A1 capacity is tightly constrained in popular regions. Frankfurt and Singapore tend to provision within minutes; US regions can sit at "out of host capacity" for hours or days. Budget for that when you're planning a migration deadline. What "2 OCPU" means on Ampere A1. On Oracle's x86 shapes, one OCPU is a full physical core with hyperthreading, billed as the equivalent of two vCPUs, so a workload can lean on simultaneous multithreading to squeeze more out of contended cores. Ampere A1 doesn't work that way: the Ampere Altra processor behind it has no hyperthreading, so one OCPU is exactly one physical core and one thread, nothing shared. Two OCPUs on this tier means two real cores and nothing more to borrow from. That's why CPU contention shows up immediately on this tier rather than being smoothed over by a hyperthreading scheduler the way it might be on an equivalent x86 box.

Two honest limitations before the stack: first, ARM64 isn't universal. Most actively maintained self-hosting images ship multi-arch builds, but some don't. Ghost's core image runs fine on ARM64; its optional ActivityPub and Traffic Analyzer add-ons are AMD64-only as of this writing, so check before assuming a feature works. Second, 2 shared OCPUs is a real ceiling once more than one service wants the CPU at the same time. RAM sizing matters, but CPU contention is what bites on this tier.

The stack: one Ampere instance, one AMD Micro

Put everything internet-facing on the single Ampere A1 instance, and use one AMD Micro purely as an external watchdog, something that checks whether the main box is reachable from outside its own failure domain. The second Micro is spare capacity for later.

Service Job Real RAM cost
Caddy TLS termination, reverse proxy Under 50 MB
Ghost + MySQL Blog/CMS (this article's own platform) Roughly 750 MB in production use
Vaultwarden Password manager, Bitwarden-compatible ~10 MB idle
Syncthing Peer-to-peer file sync, no central server needed 150–300 MB typical, spikes higher during large scans
Ollama (3B model, Q4) Lightweight local AI for personal use Roughly 3–4 GB
Uptime Kuma + Beszel agent Uptime checks plus host/container metrics 150–180 MB combined
OS + Docker overhead Everything else Roughly 500 MB

That totals somewhere around 5–6 GB of the 12 GB available, leaving real headroom rather than a stack that fits with nothing to spare. The number that won't show up in a RAM table is CPU: an AI response generating tokens, a MySQL query, and a Syncthing hash scan happening at the same moment are competing for two cores, and that's where a personal Oracle box slows down, not memory pressure.

Running Vaultwarden already and want the full hardening pass? Our dedicated Vaultwarden guide covers backup strategy, admin panel lockdown, and the HTTPS requirements the official clients enforce. Take a look at our complete Vaultwarden self-hosting guide.

If you're enjoying what you've read so far, we recommend Oracle Free Tier ARM Cutoff: What to Do Before Aug 18 as your next read.

Why each piece is on this list

Ghost runs the blog you're reading right now, so it earns a place as a real-world example rather than a theoretical pick. The official minimum is 1 GB of RAM; in production with MySQL running alongside it, a well-known self-hosting write-up clocks its own long-running instance at 214 MB for Ghost and 538 MB for MySQL, comfortably under 1 GB combined. Budget for 2 GB if you expect real traffic or plan to turn on the newsletter feature, which adds Mailgun and additional background jobs.

Vaultwarden is the easiest sizing decision in this list. It's a Rust reimplementation of the Bitwarden server, and our own Vaultwarden instance (the one covered in our dedicated guide) idles around 10 MB of RAM serving eight active users, less than a browser tab. There's no meaningful tradeoff here: it's compatible with every official Bitwarden client, and the resource cost rounds to zero next to everything else on this instance.

Syncthing covers file synchronization without needing a central server the way Nextcloud does; it syncs directly between your devices and this instance acts as one more always-on peer. That's a deliberate tradeoff for this tier: Nextcloud gets you a web UI, calendar and contacts sync, and a proper multi-user file store, all of which cost meaningfully more RAM than 12 GB comfortably supports alongside everything else here. If you have RAM to spare on a bigger box later, our productivity-stack guide covers Nextcloud, Immich, Jellyfin, and Paperless-ngx together. On this tier, Syncthing does the one job (getting files onto more than one device) for a fraction of the cost.

Idle RAM use is modest, but it's not flat: Syncthing keeps file indexes in memory, and both very large individual files and folders with hundreds of thousands of small files can push memory use well above idle during an initial scan, in some reported cases into the gigabytes on a large enough folder tree. If you're syncing a large photo library or a folder with a huge file count, set maxConcurrentWrites to 1 and sync folders sequentially rather than in parallel; both are documented tuning options that trade sync speed for a lower peak. On a 12 GB instance already running an AI model, that peak matters more than it would on a dedicated NAS.

Ollama is the one service constrained by this tier's hardware and not only its RAM budget. There's no GPU on Oracle's free tier at all, so inference runs on the Ampere A1's ARM cores. A quantized 7B model is technically possible (public benchmarks put a Q4_K_M 7B model around 5–8 tokens per second on a 4-OCPU A1 instance), but at 2 OCPUs, a smaller 3B model at Q4 quantization is the more honest fit for anything resembling a responsive personal assistant, and it leaves the other two-thirds of your CPU budget for Ghost and Syncthing to use.

Uptime Kuma paired with Beszel is the monitoring choice that matters most on a RAM-constrained tier. A combined Prometheus, Grafana, and node_exporter stack, the setup in our own monitoring guide, runs 800 MB or more at idle before it's watched a single request; Uptime Kuma plus a Beszel agent covers external uptime checks and internal host/container metrics for roughly 150–180 MB combined. On a 24 GB instance, or a paid box with RAM to spare, Prometheus and Grafana's deeper PromQL querying and alerting rules are worth the extra memory. On 12 GB shared with an AI model, Uptime Kuma is the choice between having monitoring at all and not.

Elevated

Outgrown the free tier, or tired of Oracle reclaiming idle instances? Elevated runs managed VPS hosting from SudoSecurity, with real support behind it.

See Elevated VPS plans →

The Layout

Oracle free tier architecture · SVG Oracle Free Tier: Two-Instance Layout Ampere A1 Flex -- 2 OCPU / 12 GB RAM (Always Free) Caddy (TLS, reverse proxy) -- <50 MB Ghost + MySQL -- ~750 MB Vaultwarden -- ~50 MB Syncthing -- ~150-300 MB Ollama, 3B model Q4 -- ~3-4 GB Uptime Kuma + Beszel agent -- ~150-180 MB OS + Docker overhead -- ~500 MB Remaining headroom: roughly 6-7 GB of 12 GB Shared constraint: 2 OCPU total AI inference, MySQL queries, and Syncthing hashing compete for the same 2 cores -- CPU, not RAM, is the real ceiling on this tier AMD Micro -- 1/8 OCPU 1 GB RAM (Always Free) External uptime check Watches the Ampere box from outside its own failure domain Internet-facing CPU-heaviest service

Everything internet-facing sits behind Caddy on the Ampere instance. The AMD Micro doesn't run any of the stack; its only job is checking the Ampere box from a separate failure domain, so a problem with the main instance doesn't also take down the thing telling you about the problem.

A resource-bounded Compose file 

services:
  caddy:
    image: caddy:latest
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - "443:443"
      - "80:80"
    volumes:
      - ./Caddyfile:/etc/caddy/Caddyfile
      - caddy_data:/data
    networks:
      - stack_net

  ghost:
    image: ghost:5
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      - database__client=mysql
      - database__connection__host=ghost-db
      - database__connection__user=ghost
      - database__connection__password=${GHOST_DB_PASSWORD}
      - database__connection__database=ghost
      - url=https://blog.yourdomain.com
    volumes:
      - ghost_content:/var/lib/ghost/content
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          memory: 1g
    networks:
      - stack_net

  ghost-db:
    image: mysql:8
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      - MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=${MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD}
      - MYSQL_DATABASE=ghost
      - MYSQL_USER=ghost
      - MYSQL_PASSWORD=${GHOST_DB_PASSWORD}
    volumes:
      - ghost_db:/var/lib/mysql
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          memory: 700m
    networks:
      - stack_net

  vaultwarden:
    image: vaultwarden/server:latest
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      - ADMIN_TOKEN=${VAULTWARDEN_ADMIN_TOKEN}
      - SIGNUPS_ALLOWED=false
    volumes:
      - vaultwarden_data:/data
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          memory: 128m
    networks:
      - stack_net

  syncthing:
    image: syncthing/syncthing:latest
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      - STMAXCONCURRENTWRITES=1
    volumes:
      - syncthing_data:/var/syncthing
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          memory: 768m
    networks:
      - stack_net

  ollama:
    image: ollama/ollama:latest
    restart: unless-stopped
    volumes:
      - ollama_data:/root/.ollama
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          memory: 4g
    networks:
      - stack_net

  uptime-kuma:
    image: louislam/uptime-kuma:2
    restart: unless-stopped
    volumes:
      - uptime_kuma_data:/app/data
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          memory: 150m
    networks:
      - stack_net

networks:
  stack_net:
    external: true

volumes:
  caddy_data:
  ghost_content:
  ghost_db:
  vaultwarden_data:
  syncthing_data:
  ollama_data:
  uptime_kuma_data:

Caddy stays the only exposed port on the instance. Everything else, Ghost, Vaultwarden, Syncthing's sync protocol, Ollama's API, and the Uptime Kuma dashboard, sits behind it on the internal Docker network, reachable by subdomain rather than by port number.

Still with us? We think you'll like How to Self-Host a Discord Bot: Building and Running Your Own Bot 24/7 as your next read.

Three Important Performance Fixes

The Compose file above will run. These three changes are what keep it running well once Syncthing hits a big scan or Ollama is mid-response while someone's reading the blog.

Add swap, even on a "fast enough" instance. Ampere A1 has no swap configured by default, and 12 GB with several services and an AI model loaded leaves less margin than it looks like on paper. A memory spike that would slow things down with swap available becomes an OOM-killed container without it, and Docker's OOM killer doesn't pick politely; it can take out MySQL as easily as the process that caused the spike. A modest swap file (4 GB is reasonable against 12 GB of RAM) plus a low swappiness value gives the kernel somewhere to put cold pages before it starts killing containers:

sudo fallocate -l 4G /swapfile
sudo chmod 600 /swapfile
sudo mkswap /swapfile
sudo swapon /swapfile
echo '/swapfile none swap sw 0 0' | sudo tee -a /etc/fstab
sudo sysctl vm.swappiness=10
echo 'vm.swappiness=10' | sudo tee -a /etc/sysctl.conf

Swap on a boot volume backed by network-attached block storage is slower than swap on local NVMe, so this is a safety margin for spikes, not a substitute for the RAM budget in the table above. Don't plan to run the stack out of swap day to day.

Tune MySQL down from its defaults. Out of the box, MySQL 8's innodb_buffer_pool_size defaults to 128 MB, which is conservative enough to be safe here, but the rest of its default configuration still assumes more headroom than a 12 GB shared host has to give. A small my.cnf override keeps Ghost's database from creeping past the budget in the resource table:

[mysqld]
innodb_buffer_pool_size=256M
max_connections=50
table_open_cache=200
thread_cache_size=8

Mount this as /etc/mysql/conf.d/low-memory.cnf in the ghost-db service. It won't matter for a low-traffic personal blog, and it's the difference between MySQL sitting at 700 MB and MySQL slowly climbing toward whatever's left on the box during a traffic spike.

Cap Ollama's concurrency instead of leaving it to load-balance itself. Ollama's defaults assume it can decide how many models to keep loaded and how many requests to serve in parallel, which is a reasonable default on a dedicated GPU box and a bad one on a 2-core ARM instance sharing memory with everything else here. Setting explicit limits keeps one long generation from queuing up a second one and doubling memory use:

OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=1
OLLAMA_MAX_LOADED_MODELS=1
OLLAMA_MAX_QUEUE=4

Add these as environment variables on the ollama service in the Compose file. OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=1 means the second request waits instead of doubling memory use by running alongside the first; on a personal instance where you're the only user, that queueing is invisible in practice and the memory ceiling it buys is not.

Want the general self-hosting stack playbook, beyond the free-tier version? Our shared server-prep and reverse-proxy pattern applies whether you're on a free Ampere instance or a paid box. Check out the Mailcow Guide!

Lessons from running this

Check ARM64 support before you deploy, not after. Most of the images above have solid ARM builds. A few popular self-hosting tools still don't, or only support ARM in a beta tag, and finding that out mid-migration is worse than checking before the first docker compose up:

docker manifest inspect ghost:5 | grep -A2 '"architecture"'

Look for "architecture": "arm64" in the output alongside "amd64". If it's missing, the image is x86-only and won't run on the Ampere instance at all, or will run under slow QEMU emulation if Docker's configured to allow it, which defeats the point of a free ARM box.

Watch the reclamation window if traffic is thin. A personal blog with a handful of daily visitors, a password vault only you touch, and a sync client that mostly sits idle can plausibly dip under Oracle's 20% utilization thresholds across a full week. Real, if modest, usage from an actual project protects you here better than any artificial workaround, and running an artificial load generator specifically to dodge the reclamation policy sits in a gray area against Oracle's terms of service that isn't worth the risk for a free instance.

Pin your image tags once the stack is stable. latest is fine while you're getting things running; once Ghost, Vaultwarden, and Ollama are doing real work, an unannounced upstream change landing on a routine docker compose pull is a worse failure mode than a slightly stale version.

Back up the volumes that matter. Ghost's content volume and MySQL data, Vaultwarden's data directory, and Syncthing's config and index. Model weights for Ollama are re-downloadable and not worth backing up; Uptime Kuma's history is nice to keep but not critical if it's lost.

The Compose file, ready to adapt

The full stack above, Caddy, Ghost, Vaultwarden, Syncthing, Ollama, and Uptime Kuma, is a lot to retype by hand. Grab the complete docker-compose.yml and a matching .env template below, drop in your own domain and secrets, and you're running rather than transcribing.

Get the Compose file and.env template

Enter your email and we'll send the exact configuration from this article, including the resource limits, ready to paste onto a fresh Ampere A1 instance.

If you outgrow the 12 GB ceiling, that's a genuine milestone, not a failure of the free tier. It means the stack is doing enough real work that a small paid VPS or dedicated box starts paying for itself in time saved rather than money spent, and at that point the free tier has already done its job: it got you running for the cost of an afternoon instead of a monthly bill.

title: Build a Pricing Table From Scratch: The CSS Tricks Behind It
description:
Every app that sells something has the same page: three cards side by side, a price in big numbers, a list of what you get, a button, and one card in the middle that says "Most popular". You've seen it a hundred times. Today we build that pattern from scratch, with our own plans and our own colours, and I'll show you the four small CSS tricks that make it look finished instead of almost right.

Here's the short answer first. A pricing table is a CSS grid of cards that wraps on its own with repeat(auto-fit, minmax(...)). Each card is a flex column, and the button gets margin-top: auto so every button sits on the same line. The favourite plan gets a border and a badge, not a zoom. Prices use tabular numbers and live in cents. That's the whole thing.

If you're a beginner, read it top to bottom and click every live demo, because seeing the difference is worth more than my words. If you already write CSS every day, jump to the section about the highlighted card and then to the one about subgrid. Those are the two places where people who know the basics still get it wrong. The part about prices, money and the Plan B is for anyone who has ever had to put a real price on a real page.

Why we rebuild a design everyone has already seen

This article is part of a series I call Concepts in practice. The idea is simple. Instead of learning CSS properties one by one from a list, we take a piece of a website you already know from real life, rebuild it, and look at the tricks behind it. You learn faster when you already know what the finished thing should look like.

I'll be honest about why this matters to me. When I started, I built everything from my head. No plan, no sketch, no visual reference. I just kept changing things until I liked how it looked. That works right up until it doesn't, and with a pricing table it stops working very fast, because the page has to look right with three different amounts of text, on a phone and on a big screen, and with a price that changes when someone clicks a switch.

The good news is that the people who design the big websites have already solved most of these problems. Look at enough pricing pages and you'll notice they all use the same few moves. That's what we'll steal today: the moves, not the look.

Warning: Rebuild the pattern, never the brand. The layout idea of a pricing table belongs to nobody. A company's logo, its exact wording, its illustrations and its colours do belong to someone. In this article every plan name, price and colour is made up. Do the same when you practise, and especially before anything you build goes on a public page.

Why your first pricing table always looks a little off

Let's look at the problem before we fix it. Below is the version almost everyone writes first. Three cards in a row with display: flex, and the middle card made bigger with transform: scale(1.08) so it stands out. Press "Apply the fixes" to switch to the fixed version and back again.

Live demo: Pricing cards: the first attempt and the fixed version. It runs right in the page, so try it in the original article.

Look at the first version closely and you'll see three things that feel wrong, even if you can't name them yet.

  • The buttons are at different heights. Each button sits right under its own list, and the lists have two, four and three items. Your eye expects them on one line, because they do the same job.
  • The middle card is zoomed, but the cards next to it don't know that. The gap on each side gets smaller and the card pokes out above and below the row. With a slightly bigger zoom or a smaller gap, it would cover its neighbours.
  • On a phone the row never breaks. Flexbox keeps all three cards on one line, so each one gets about a third of a small screen and the text gets squashed. Open the demo in full screen on your phone and you'll see it.

Why does this happen? Because each of those properties does exactly what it says, and nothing more. Flexbox with no wrapping puts things in one row. A card is only as tall as its content tells it to be, unless something stretches it. And a transform, by design, is a visual effect that the layout ignores. The W3C specification says it in so many words. None of this is a bug. It's us asking for the wrong thing.

The transform part surprises most people, so here's the exact line from the CSS Transforms specification: "the transform property does not affect the flow of the content surrounding the transformed element." In plain words, the browser first lays out the page as if the zoom didn't exist, and only then paints the card bigger on top of that layout.

Start with the markup, not the look

Before any CSS, decide what each piece of the card is. This sounds boring and it's the step I used to skip. It's also what makes the page readable for a screen reader and for Google, and it makes the CSS shorter, because you style real elements instead of a pile of divs.

pricing.html

<article class="card featured">
  <p class="badge">Most popular</p>
  <h3>Pro</h3>
  <p class="desc">For one person who ships every week.</p>
  <p class="price" data-monthly="1200" data-yearly="12000">
    <span class="amount">$12</span> <span class="per">/ month</span>
  </p>
  <p class="billed">Billed every month</p>
  <ul role="list">
    <li>Unlimited projects</li>
    <li>Custom domain</li>
  </ul>
  <a class="cta" href="/signup?plan=pro">Choose Pro</a>
</article>

Let's go through it line by line.

  • article: each plan is a self-contained thing that would make sense on its own, which is what article means in HTML. A div would work visually, but it tells nobody anything.
  • p class="badge": the "Most popular" label is just a short paragraph. Only the featured card has it. We'll lift it onto the card's top border later with CSS, but in the HTML it's ordinary text, so it's read out like ordinary text.
  • h3: the plan name is a heading. Someone using a screen reader can jump from heading to heading and hear Starter, Pro, Team. It's h3 because the section around the table has its own h2, like "Pick a plan". Headings go in order; don't pick a level because of its size.
  • p class="price" with two data attributes: data-monthly and data-yearly hold the price in cents, as plain numbers. The text inside, $12, is what the visitor sees when the page loads, even if JavaScript never runs. We'll come back to why cents.
  • span class="amount" and span class="per": the number and the "/ month" are separate, because they look different. The number is big, the "/ month" is small and grey.
  • ul role="list": the features are a real list. The role="list" looks redundant, and I'll explain later why it's there.
  • a class="cta": the button is a link, not a button element. It takes you to another page, the sign-up page with the plan in the address. That's a link's job. A button element is for things that happen on the same page, like the monthly and yearly switch.

Tip: Quick rule for links and buttons: if it goes somewhere, it's a link. If it does something here, it's a button. Get this right and keyboard users, screen readers and the browser's back button all behave the way people expect, without extra code.

Trick one: a grid that wraps itself

Now the layout. We want three cards side by side when there's room, two when there's a bit less, and one on a phone. The old way was three media queries. The modern way is one line. If grid itself is new to you, my visual guide to CSS Grid covers the basics, and Flexbox vs Grid on real layouts explains why this job belongs to grid and not to flexbox.

pricing.css

.plans {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(100%, 13rem), 1fr));
  gap: 1.25rem;
}

That middle line looks scary, so let's read it from the inside out.

  • 13rem is the narrowest a card is allowed to be. With the default font size that's 208 pixels. Below that, the text inside a card starts to feel cramped.
  • min(100%, 13rem) picks the smaller of the two. On a normal screen that's 13rem. On a very narrow phone, where 13rem would be wider than the screen, it becomes 100%, so the card never sticks out sideways. Without this little min(), a 13rem card on a tiny screen causes a horizontal scrollbar.
  • minmax(that, 1fr) means: each column is at least that wide, and at most one equal share of the free space. So the cards grow to fill the row, all the same width.
  • repeat(auto-fit, ...) tells the browser: you count how many columns fit. Three fit on a laptop, two on a tablet, one on a phone. You never write a breakpoint.
  • gap: 1.25rem is the space between cards, both between columns and between rows when they wrap. No margins on the cards, so nothing doubles up at the edges.

Think of a long bench where people only sit if they have at least shoulder width. When the bench is long, three people sit and spread out a bit. When it's shorter, only two fit, and the third person starts a new row behind them. Nobody has to tell them where to sit; the rule does it.

You'll also see auto-fill instead of auto-fit, and the difference matters with only three cards. MDN puts it like this: auto-fit "behaves as auto-fill, except that after placing grid items, any empty repeated tracks are collapsed." On a very wide screen, auto-fill keeps empty columns as ghosts, so your three cards stay narrow and huddle on the left. auto-fit throws the empty columns away, and the three cards stretch across the row. For a pricing table you want auto-fit. You'll also want a max-width on the section, so the cards don't stretch into pancakes on a huge monitor.

Trick two: push every button to the same line

Grid already gives us one gift for free. By default, every card in a grid row is stretched to the height of the tallest one. So the white boxes are already the same height. The problem is what's inside them: the button still sits right under the list. We need the button to fall to the bottom of its card.

pricing.css

.card {
  display: flex;
  flex-direction: column;
}

.cta {
  margin-top: auto;
}
  • display: flex with flex-direction: column turns the inside of each card into a vertical stack. Badge, name, description, price, list, button, one under the other, like before.
  • margin-top: auto on the button is the trick. In a flex container, an auto margin takes all the free space it can. So all the empty space in the card ends up above the button, and the button lands at the bottom.

Picture a compressed spring placed right above the button. The spring pushes out until it hits the content above it, and whatever space is left, it fills. Every card has its own spring, so every button ends up at the bottom of its card, and because grid made the cards the same height, the buttons line up. MDN's page on aligning items in a flex container explains it with a row instead of a column: the auto margin "consumes all the space it can in its axis". Same idea, turned 90 degrees.

What breaks if you remove it? Take away margin-top: auto and the buttons jump back under their lists. Take away display: flex on the card and the auto margin does nothing, because in normal block layout an auto top margin is just zero. You need both lines.

You'll find people doing this with a fixed height on every card, something like height: 420px. Please don't. The day someone adds a fifth feature to the Pro plan, or a visitor makes the text bigger in their browser, the text spills out of the card. The spring adapts. A fixed height doesn't.

Trick three: highlight the favourite without zooming it

Every pricing page wants one plan to stand out. The zoom we saw in the first demo is the most common way, and now you know why it fights the layout. Here's the version that works with the layout instead.

pricing.css

.featured {
  position: relative;
  border: 2px solid #0b6e4f;
}

.badge {
  position: absolute;
  top: 0;
  left: 50%;
  translate: -50% -50%;
  white-space: nowrap;
}
  • .featured gets a thicker border in our accent colour. That alone makes it stand out, and it takes up real space, so the layout knows about it. The cards next to it make room.
  • position: relative on the card doesn't move the card at all. It only says: anything inside me with position: absolute should measure from my corners, not from the page.
  • position: absolute on the badge takes it out of the stack, so it doesn't push the plan name down. Then top: 0 and left: 50% put the badge's top-left corner at the middle of the card's top edge.
  • translate: -50% -50% moves the badge back by half of its own width and half of its own height. Now its centre sits exactly on the card's border, half outside and half inside. That's the classic "label sitting on the edge" look.
  • white-space: nowrap keeps "Most popular" on one line, even when the card gets narrow.

Wait, didn't I just say transforms are bad here? Look closely: translate on the badge is fine, because we want the badge to float over the border, and it's out of the layout anyway. The problem was never transforms. The problem was using a transform on something that the rest of the layout should make room for.

If you want the favourite to look bigger as well, give it more padding at the top and bottom, or a slightly larger price. Those are real sizes, so the grid adapts. Just remember that grid stretches every card in the row, so a taller featured card makes the others taller too. That's usually fine, and it keeps the buttons in line.

Trick four: prices that don't wobble

This one is small and almost nobody notices it consciously, which is the point. When you switch from monthly to yearly, the numbers change. In most fonts, the digit 1 is narrower than the digit 0, so $12 and $10 are different widths and the price jumps sideways a little when it changes.

pricing.css

.price { font-size: 2.25rem; font-weight: 700; line-height: 1; }
.amount { font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums; }
.per { font-size: 0.9rem; font-weight: 400; color: #52606d; }
  • .price makes the number big and bold, and line-height: 1 stops a big font from adding a lot of empty space above and below the line.
  • .amount uses font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums. That asks the font for its table digits, which are all the same width. Same idea as numbers in a bank statement lining up in a column.
  • .per makes "/ month" small, normal weight and grey, so the eye reads the number first and the period second.

MDN describes tabular-nums as the set of figures "where numbers are all of the same size, allowing them to be easily aligned like in tables." It depends on the font having those figures; the system fonts on the common operating systems do, and most good web fonts do. If a font doesn't have them, nothing breaks, you just get the normal digits.

The monthly and yearly switch is a radio group in disguise

Most pricing pages have a pill-shaped switch on top: Monthly or Yearly. It looks like a custom widget, and a lot of people build it from divs and click handlers. But think about what it really is. You pick one option out of two, and exactly one is always selected. HTML has had an element for that since forever: radio buttons.

pricing.html

<fieldset class="billing">
  <legend class="visually-hidden">Billing period</legend>
  <input type="radio" id="monthly" name="billing" value="monthly" checked>
  <label for="monthly">Monthly</label>
  <input type="radio" id="yearly" name="billing" value="yearly">
  <label for="yearly">Yearly, 2 months free</label>
</fieldset>
  • fieldset groups the two options, and legend gives the group a name, "Billing period". A screen reader announces it when you enter the group. We hide the legend visually because the pills explain themselves to sighted visitors, but we don't remove it.
  • Both inputs share name="billing", and that's what makes them one group: choosing one automatically un-chooses the other. You get that for free.
  • checked on the monthly input makes it the starting choice, and it matches the prices written in the HTML.
  • Each label is tied to its input with for and id. Clicking the label selects the radio, so the whole pill is clickable. The arrow keys move between the two options, again for free.

pricing.css

.billing input { position: absolute; opacity: 0; width: 1px; height: 1px; }
.billing label { padding: 0.5rem 1rem; border: 1px solid #1f2933; border-radius: 999px; }
.billing input:checked + label { background: #1f2933; color: #fff; }
.billing input:focus-visible + label { outline: 3px solid #0b6e4f; outline-offset: 2px; }
  • The first line hides the round radio circles, but not with display: none. That's important. display: none would remove the inputs completely, and the keyboard couldn't reach them anymore. opacity: 0 and a 1-pixel size keep them in the page, just invisible.
  • The labels become the pills: some padding, a border, and a border-radius so big that the ends are fully round.
  • input:checked + label means: the label that comes right after a checked input. That's why each label sits directly after its input in the HTML. The selected pill gets the dark background.
  • input:focus-visible + label draws a clear outline on the pill when someone reaches it with the keyboard. Since the real input is invisible, the focus ring has to show on the label, otherwise a keyboard user can't see where they are.

If you'd rather build it with two buttons, that's fine too, but then you need aria-pressed on each button and you have to keep exactly one pressed yourself. The first demo above uses aria-pressed on its single "Apply the fixes" button, which is the right tool for one on/off switch. For one choice out of two, the radio group does that work for you.

Prices live in cents, and the page only displays them

Now the JavaScript. It has one job: when the switch changes, show the right numbers. Before the code, one rule that will save you real trouble one day. Never do arithmetic with prices as decimals.

money-check.js

console.log(0.1 + 0.2);      // 0.30000000000000004
console.log(119.99 / 12);    // 9.999166666666666

I ran both lines under Node 26, and that's the real output. Computers store most decimal fractions as tiny approximations, so sums and divisions of dollars drift. That's why the HTML stores 1200 instead of 12.00. Whole cents are whole numbers, and whole numbers stay exact. We only turn them into dollars at the very last moment, when we print them.

pricing.js

const money = new Intl.NumberFormat("en-US", {
  style: "currency",
  currency: "USD",
  minimumFractionDigits: 0,
  maximumFractionDigits: 0,
});

function showPrices(period) {
  for (const price of document.querySelectorAll(".price")) {
    const cents = Number(price.dataset[period]);
    if (cents === 0) continue;
    const perMonth = period === "yearly" ? cents / 12 : cents;
    price.querySelector(".amount").textContent = money.format(perMonth / 100);
    price.nextElementSibling.textContent =
      period === "yearly" ? `${money.format(cents / 100)} billed once a year` : "Billed every month";
  }
}

document.querySelector(".billing").addEventListener("change", (event) => {
  showPrices(event.target.value);
  document.querySelector("#status").textContent = `Showing ${event.target.value} prices`;
});

Line by line, because this is where beginners usually start copying without reading.

  • new Intl.NumberFormat("en-US", {...}) creates a formatter once. Give it a number, it gives you back a properly written price, with the dollar sign in the right place for that language. We create it once at the top instead of inside the loop, because it never changes.
  • minimumFractionDigits: 0 and maximumFractionDigits: 0 say: no cents after the point. Our prices are whole dollars, so $10 looks cleaner than $10.00. Set both. Dollars come with default digit settings, and MDN warns that these defaults can clash with a value you set yourself and throw a RangeError, even if you only set one of the two.
  • showPrices(period) receives "monthly" or "yearly", the value of the radio that was picked.
  • document.querySelectorAll(".price") finds every price paragraph, and the for...of loop visits them one by one. Same pattern as rendering a list of cards: one piece of code, many items.
  • price.dataset[period] reads data-monthly or data-yearly, depending on the period. dataset gives you every data- attribute of an element, and they always come back as text, so Number() turns "1200" into 1200.
  • if (cents === 0) continue skips the free plan. Its text, "$0" and "Free forever", is already correct in the HTML for both periods, so we leave it alone.
  • perMonth: for yearly billing we show the monthly equivalent, because that's the number people compare. 12000 cents a year divided by 12 is 1000 cents a month.
  • money.format(perMonth / 100) turns cents into dollars only now, at the moment of printing, and writes the result into the .amount span with textContent. textContent sets plain text, never HTML, so nothing in there can turn into markup.
  • price.nextElementSibling is the paragraph right after the price, the "billed" line. It changes to "$120 billed once a year" or back to "Billed every month", so nobody is surprised at checkout by a bigger number than the one they saw.
  • The change listener sits on the fieldset, not on each radio. A change event from either radio bubbles up to the fieldset, so one listener covers both. event.target is the radio that was just picked.

Every option of the formatter, including that warning about digit defaults, is on MDN's Intl.NumberFormat page. Keep it open the first few times you format money.

If the loop over every .price feels familiar, it should. It's the same idea as rendering many cards without repeating code: one function, a list of items, and the data decides what each one shows. In a real project you'd go one step further and build the three cards from an array of plans too.

Warning: Rounding hides cents. With maximumFractionDigits: 0, a yearly price of 9900 cents shows as $8 a month, because 825 cents gets rounded. I ran it: the zero-decimals formatter prints $8, the normal one prints $8.25. Pick prices that divide evenly by 12, or show cents. Either way, the number on the page is only a display. The amount the customer actually pays must come from your server or your payment provider, never from a number the browser sent back.

One quiet line for screen reader users

The last line of the listener writes "Showing yearly prices" into a paragraph with aria-live="polite". That paragraph is visually hidden. When its text changes, a screen reader reads it out after it finishes what it's saying. Without it, a blind visitor presses the switch and hears nothing, while every price on the page has changed. We announce one short sentence instead of reading all three prices, because hearing three numbers at once is noise.

Here is everything together: the markup, the grid, the spring, the badge, the switch and the script. Switch to Yearly and watch the Pro and Team prices change while their width stays the same. Then press Tab to walk through the page with the keyboard.

Live demo: Finished pricing table with a monthly and yearly switch. It runs right in the page, so try it in the original article.

For the advanced reader: line up every row with subgrid

Our buttons line up, but look at the lists. If one plan has a longer description, its list starts lower than the lists next to it, and so does its price. On a pricing page people compare across the row, Starter's price next to Pro's price, so rows that don't line up make comparing harder. The demo below has one long description on purpose. Press "Use subgrid" and watch the prices and lists snap into line.

Live demo: Lining up rows across cards with subgrid. It runs right in the page, so try it in the original article.

pricing.css

.plans .card {
  display: grid;
  grid-row: span 5;
  grid-template-rows: subgrid;
}
  • display: grid turns the card into a grid instead of a flex column.
  • grid-row: span 5 makes each card occupy five rows of the outer grid, one row for each of its five children: name, description, price, list and button.
  • grid-template-rows: subgrid is the key line. Instead of having its own rows, the card borrows the five rows of the outer grid. Since all three cards share the same five rows, each row is as tall as the tallest piece in it, across all cards. The long description makes row two taller for everyone, and every price lands on the same line.

This used to be impossible without JavaScript measuring heights. MDN marks subgrid as widely available and says it has worked across browsers since September 2023. Two things to watch. First, the number in span 5 must match the number of children in the card; if one plan has a badge as a sixth child, either take the badge out of the flow with position: absolute like we did, or count it. Second, the subgrid inherits the outer grid's gap between its rows, so the spacing inside the card is the same as the spacing between cards unless you set your own row-gap. In our demo that's fine. In a real design you may want to tune it.

Is it overkill for a beginner? Yes, a bit. The flex version with the auto margin is perfectly fine for most pages. Reach for subgrid when the rows really need to line up, like a pricing table with long feature lists that people read across.

Checkmarks that a screen reader still reads as a list

Feature lists on pricing pages almost never show bullets. They show checkmarks. The usual move is list-style: none and a little icon. Here's a version that draws the check with plain CSS, no image, no icon font.

pricing.css

.card ul { list-style: none; padding: 0; }
.card li { position: relative; padding-left: 1.5rem; }
.card li::before {
  content: "";
  position: absolute;
  left: 0.3rem;
  top: 0.2em;
  width: 0.4rem;
  height: 0.75rem;
  border: solid #0b6e4f;
  border-width: 0 2px 2px 0;
  rotate: 45deg;
}
  • list-style: none removes the bullets, and padding: 0 removes the space the browser kept for them.
  • Each li gets position: relative, so the checkmark can be placed against its own corner, and padding-left makes room for it.
  • ::before creates an extra, empty box in front of the text. content: "" is required; without content, the box doesn't exist at all.
  • The box is narrow and tall, with only a right and a bottom border. That's an L shape. rotate: 45deg turns the L into a check. It's the same trick as drawing a tick with two strokes of a pen.
  • Because content is empty, there's no character for a screen reader to read out. A checkmark character in content would be read aloud in some screen readers, on every single line.

Now the role="list" from earlier. Safari with VoiceOver stops treating a list as a list when CSS removes its bullets. Scott O'Hara has written up this behaviour, including that WebKit does it on purpose. Adding role="list" to the ul puts the list back for that combination, and it changes nothing anywhere else. On a pricing table, "list, 4 items" is useful to hear, because it tells you how much a plan includes before you listen to all of it.

One more thing about colour. I checked our colours with the standard WCAG contrast formula: white text on the green #0b6e4f comes out at 6.25 to 1, and the grey #52606d on white at 6.46 to 1. Both pass the 4.5 to 1 that normal text needs. Pricing pages love pale grey for the small print, and the small print is exactly the text people need to read.

So that's all a pricing table is

Look back at what we built. A grid that decides on its own how many cards fit in a row. Cards that are flex columns, with a spring above the button. One card with a thicker border and a label sitting on its edge. Numbers that keep their width. A switch that is really two radio buttons, and ten lines of JavaScript that read cents from the HTML and print dollars.

That's it. No framework, no library, nothing you couldn't type in a plain HTML file today. Every pricing page you admire is some version of these moves, plus good colours and good words. When you can see the moves, you stop seeing a design you could never make, and start seeing a few decisions you can make yourself.

Where this goes wrong, and the Plan B

  • The zoomed card. If you inherit a design with transform: scale on the featured plan, swap it for a border and extra padding. If the designer insists on the bigger look, give the featured card real extra padding so the layout makes room, rather than a zoom that the layout ignores.
  • Fixed heights. Any height: 400px on a card breaks the day the text changes, or the day a visitor zooms their browser to 200%. Let content decide the height; use the auto margin or subgrid to line things up.
  • Prices that exist only in JavaScript. If the cards are empty until a script fills them, a visitor on a slow connection sees blank boxes, and a search engine may see no prices at all. Write the default prices in the HTML and let JavaScript only change them.
  • Trusting the page's price. The price on the page is a label. If your checkout takes the amount from the browser, someone will send a smaller one. The server looks up the plan and its price itself. This is the same rule as checking a login form twice, once in the browser for comfort and once on the server for real.
  • Hiding the yearly total. Showing $10 a month without saying it's $120 paid at once is how people end up feeling tricked at checkout. The "billed" line costs one sentence and buys trust.
  • Too many plans. Three columns fit the layout and the head. If you need five, the grid still works, but ask whether a visitor can really compare five things at once. That's a product question, not a CSS one, and it's worth asking.
  • Copying a real company's page. Rebuilding the pattern to learn is fine. Shipping their logo, their wording, their illustrations or their exact colour scheme is not, and it also makes your product look like a copy.

The "check twice" idea is the core of why you validate a login form on the client and the server, and when you get to real payments, the Stripe setup guide for Next.js shows where the real price comes from.

Note: If an AI assistant wrote your pricing table, check exactly the things in this article. Is the favourite card zoomed with a transform? Are there fixed heights? Is the switch a pile of divs that the keyboard can't reach? Are prices calculated with decimals? I use AI for a lot of my work, and I check what it writes as far as I can, because it can make these mistakes without meaning to. A pricing table is a good place to practise that kind of review, because every mistake is visible.

And for motion: the finished demo lifts a card by 4 pixels when you hover it, but only inside @media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference). People who asked their system for less motion get a still page. It's one wrapper around two lines, and it's the polite default for every hover effect you add.

What to build next

Take this exact pattern and make it yours without looking at the demo code. Change it to four plans, add a long description to one of them, and check it on your phone. Then pick another piece of a website you use every day, a sign-up form, a product card, a page header that stays on top while you scroll, and rebuild it with your own text and colours. Write down the tricks you had to look up. That list is how you learn CSS for real. If you're starting from zero, build your first web page with HTML and CSS first, and if you want the bigger picture of where this fits, what web development is, from scratch connects HTML, CSS and JavaScript into one whole.

A real pricing page connected to real payments, accounts and plans is exactly the kind of thing a course builds step by step. For the blog, this is the concept: once you can see the four tricks, you can rebuild the page yourself.

You can do this, and you have to. If you weren't capable, I wouldn't spend my time on you. Just don't give up, and you'll always have me on your side.

This article first appeared on CodeFromScratch, where the live demos run right in the page. If you want the next one in your inbox, join the newsletter.

title: SOC 2 vs SecNumCloud: What French Enterprise Buyers Are Actually Looking For
description:
You have a clean SOC 2 report, your US and UK deals close without friction, and then a French procurement team asks: “is your infrastructure SecNumCloud qualified?”

Why SOC 2 is not the final answer. A SOC 2 Type 2 report shows an independent CPA firm found your controls operating effectively over a real review period. France adds a second concern: sovereignty, meaning whether a foreign government can compel access to your data wherever your servers sit. That concern comes from the US CLOUD Act. SOC 2 says your controls work, but nothing about which country’s courts can reach your data.

What SecNumCloud is. It is a qualification, not a certification in the SOC 2 sense, issued by ANSSI, France’s national cybersecurity agency. Four things set it apart:

Sovereignty is built in. Capital and voting rights must be majority-controlled within the EU, generally no more than 24% individually or 39% collectively held by non-EU entities.

Fixed term. Qualification lasts three years with a surveillance audit roughly every eighteen months.

Key sovereignty. Encryption keys must be managed by the provider or customer, never by a third party subject to non-EU law.

Personnel vetting. Staff with access to sensitive systems must be vetted.

They are not competing frameworks. SOC 2 asks whether your controls work. SecNumCloud asks whether data can be protected from foreign government access given who owns and operates the infrastructure. Many providers hold both or partner with a SecNumCloud-qualified host.

Who needs it. Mostly French government, OIV and OES operators, and buyers in sensitive-data sectors with a sovereignty-first posture. Many commercial French buyers are fine with a strong SOC 2 Type 2 report. Ask your prospect what their criteria actually require.

If SecNumCloud is out of reach, be specific. Separate what your SOC 2 covers (operational controls) from how sovereignty and data residency are handled, for example through EU-based hosting with contractual commitments.

Full guide with the FAQs:
https://accorppartners.com/blogs/soc-2/soc-2-vs-secnumcloud-what-french-enterprise-buyers-are-actually-looking-for

title: Decompiling generic constraints and variance: reconstructing where-clauses and out/in from metadata
description:
Most C# features a decompiler recovers are compiler sugar: the compiler lowered a foreach into a try/finally around an enumerator, or an iterator into a state machine, and the decompiler recognises the shape of the emitted code and folds it back. Generic constraints and variance are not like that. There is no code to recognise, because a constraint is not executable. where T : class, IComparable<T>, new() and the out in IProducer<out T> compile to metadata — rows in a couple of side tables and a handful of flag bits — and nothing in any method body mentions them. A decompiler that only reconstructs IL into statements will emit a generic type that is missing its variance, missing its constraints, or carrying them in an order that does not compile.

That matters because constraints and variance are part of a type's public contract. The constraints decide what a caller is allowed to substitute for T; the variance decides which assignments between constructed types are legal. Get them wrong and the regenerated type either rejects code that used to work or, worse, silently loosens a guarantee callers relied on. This post walks exactly where the data lives in metadata, how Glass reads it back, and how it sorts the constraints into the one order C# will accept.

Variance and constraints in source

Here are the three shapes this post reconstructs. First a covariant interface — T appears only in output position, so it can be marked out:

public interface IProducer<out T>
{
    T Produce();
}

Covariance is what lets an IProducer<string> be handed to code expecting an IProducer<object>: every string the producer yields is an object, so the assignment is safe and the compiler allows it. The mirror image is contravariance — T appears only in input position, so it can be marked in:

public interface ISink<in T>
{
    void Accept(T value);
}

An ISink<object> can stand in for an ISink<string>, because anything that accepts any object certainly accepts a string. Finally a method with a full set of constraints:

public static T CreateAndRank<T>(IEnumerable<T> items)
    where T : class, IComparable<T>, new()
{
    var seed = new T();
    foreach (var item in items)
        if (item.CompareTo(seed) < 0)
            seed = item;
    return seed;
}

T must be a reference type (class), must be comparable to itself (IComparable<T>), and must have a public parameterless constructor (new()). All three facts are recorded in metadata, in a specific order-free form that the decompiler has to turn back into a legal, ordered where clause.

Where the data actually lives

Two metadata tables and one bitmask carry everything.

The GenericParam table has one row per type parameter, for both types and methods. Each row stores the parameter's zero-based position, its name, its owner, and a Flags column with two independent bit groups:

  • The VarianceMask (low two bits): 0x0 non-variant, 0x1 covariant (out), 0x2 contravariant (in). Only ever non-zero on interface and delegate parameters.
  • The SpecialConstraintMask: 0x04 reference-type constraint (class), 0x08 value-type / non-nullable constraint (struct), 0x10 default-constructor constraint (new()).

The GenericParamConstraint table has one row per type constraint, each pairing a GenericParam row with a TypeDefOrRef — the base class or interface the parameter is bound to. where T : SomeBase, IComparable<T> produces two rows for the same parameter: one pointing at SomeBase, one at IComparable<T>.

Rendered the way ILDasm shows it, the covariant interface puts +T right in the class header:

.class interface public abstract auto ansi IProducer`1<+T>
{
    .method public hidebysig newslot abstract virtual
        instance !T Produce() cil managed
    {
    }
}

The +T is the VarianceMask covariant bit; a contravariant parameter renders as -T, and a non-variant one as plain T. The 1 is arity. For the constrained method, ILDasm prints the base-type constraint in parentheses before the parameter name and the special constraints as keywords on the parameter:

.method public hidebysig static !!T CreateAndRank<class .ctor
    ([mscorlib]System.IComparable`1<!!T>) T>
    (class [mscorlib]System.Collections.Generic.IEnumerable`1<!!T> items)
    cil managed
{
}

Read that header carefully: class and .ctor are the SpecialConstraintMask bits (class + new()), the parenthesised ([mscorlib]System.IComparable1<!!T>)is the singleGenericParamConstraintrow, andT` is the parameter name. None of this appears in any instruction — it is pure declarative metadata attached to the method's signature.

The notnull and unmanaged subtlety

The three classic special constraints each own a SpecialConstraintMask bit. The two modern ones do not, because the bitmask was frozen before they existed, and they are encoded indirectly:

  • notnull is carried by a System.Runtime.CompilerServices attribute on the GenericParam, with no special-constraint flag set. A reader that only consults SpecialConstraintMask sees nothing and emits an unconstrained parameter, dropping the constraint entirely.
  • unmanaged is encoded as the struct flag (0x08) plus a GenericParamConstraint row whose type carries a required modifier — a modreq of System.Runtime.CompilerServices.IsUnmanagedAttribute — on a System.ValueType constraint. A reader that sees only the struct bit emits where T : struct, which is a strictly weaker constraint than unmanaged and silently lets managed value types through.

In IL the unmanaged case looks like a struct-flagged parameter with a modreq'd ValueType constraint:

plaintext
.method ... static void Blit<valuetype .ctor
(class [System.Runtime]System.ValueType modreq(
[System.Runtime]System.Runtime.CompilerServices.IsUnmanagedAttribute)) T>
(...) cil managed

The presence of the modreq(...IsUnmanagedAttribute) is the entire difference between unmanaged and struct. Glass checks for it explicitly, and for the notnull attribute, so neither modern constraint is lost or widened.

What a naive decompiler produces

A decompiler built around method bodies has nothing to anchor on here, because none of this is in a method body. Two failure modes dominate, and both are quiet.

Dropped variance. The interface comes back invariant:

csharp
// WRONG — the out is gone
public interface IProducer<T>
{
T Produce();
}

This compiles. Its single member is identical. But it is no longer covariant, so every IProducer<string>-to-IProducer<object> assignment that callers wrote against the original now fails to compile against the regenerated interface. Nothing in IProducer itself looks wrong; the breakage shows up only at the assignment sites, frequently in other assemblies.

Wrong constraint order. A decompiler that walks the metadata and appends keywords as it encounters them emits something like:

csharp
// WRONG — does not compile
public static T CreateAndRank<T>(IEnumerable<T> items)
where T : IComparable<T>, class, new(), struct
{ ... }

C# rejects this outright. The class constraint must come first, new() must come last, class and struct are mutually exclusive, and interface constraints sit in the middle. The metadata preserves none of this ordering — the GenericParamConstraint rows are in an arbitrary order and the flag bits have no order at all — so the decompiler has to impose the correct order rather than echo what it read.

The figure below shows the two metadata sources feeding Glass's constraint sorter, which buckets each constraint by category and emits the buckets in the fixed C# order:


GenericParam.Flags (parameter T)

SpecialConstraint: class | .ctor

VarianceMask: 0x0 (non-variant)
GenericParamConstraint rows

T -> IComparable`1<!T>

Glass
constraint sorter





Fixed C# order the sorter emits

class

IComparable<T>

new()
class/struct first, then base type, then interfaces, then new() last.
where T : class, IComparable<T>, new()
Order is imposed by language rule, not read from the table — the rows carry no order.

How Glass reconstructs it

Glass treats generic parameters as a first-class metadata concern, separate from method decompilation. For each parameter — type or method — it runs an explicit pipeline:

  1. Read the VarianceMask from GenericParam.Flags. Covariant becomes out, contravariant becomes in, and the keyword is placed in the declaration (IProducer<out T>), not the where clause. Variance is only read for interface and delegate parameters, where it is legal.
  2. Read the SpecialConstraintMask for the class, struct, and new() bits — but before trusting a bare struct bit, check whether the ValueType constraint carries the IsUnmanagedAttribute modreq, in which case the constraint is unmanaged, not struct. Check the GenericParam attributes for the notnull marker too.
  3. Read every GenericParamConstraint row for the parameter and resolve each TypeDefOrRef to a base class or interface. A class type goes in the base-type bucket; interfaces go in the interface bucket.
  4. Sort into the fixed C# order and emit: the class / struct / unmanaged / notnull constraint first, then the base type, then the interfaces, then new() last. Buckets that are empty are skipped, and a parameter with no constraints at all gets no where clause.

The result is the source you started with, contract-for-contract equivalent:

public static T CreateAndRank<T>(IEnumerable<T> items)
    where T : class, IComparable<T>, new()
{
    var seed = new T();
    foreach (var item in items)
        if (item.CompareTo(seed) < 0)
            seed = item;
    return seed;
}

Because the class and new() keywords came from the SpecialConstraintMask and IComparable<T> came from the GenericParamConstraint row, and because the sorter placed them in the order C# demands, the method recompiles with exactly the constraints the original declared — no stronger, no weaker, and in an order the compiler accepts.

A covariant interface, round-tripped

The interface reconstruction is shorter but shows the variance path end to end. Glass reads the +T covariant bit from the single GenericParam row and re-emits the out:

public interface IProducer<out T>
{
    T Produce();
}

The out is back in the declaration, so IProducer<string> is once again assignable to IProducer<object>. Had Glass read only the member signatures and skipped the VarianceMask, the interface would have come back invariant and every variant assignment downstream would have broken — the kind of loss that is invisible in the type itself and only surfaces at the call sites.

Running it

Point Glass at the assembly and ask for the one type. Note the backtick-arity in the type name:

glass decompile MyApp.dll --type MyApp.Abstractions.IProducer`1

The output is the out-annotated interface above. To decompile the constrained method's declaring type and confirm the constraints round-trip:

glass decompile MyApp.dll --type MyApp.Ranking.Ranker --members

To sweep a whole namespace and verify every generic parameter's variance and constraints survive reconstruction:

glass decompile MyApp.dll --namespace MyApp.Abstractions --constraint-check

--constraint-check re-reads the GenericParam and GenericParamConstraint tables after reconstruction and verifies that the emitted variance keywords, special constraints, and where-clause type bindings match the metadata exactly — so you get a guarantee, not a hope, that the regenerated signatures carry the same contract as the original. Glass is a free, open decompiler; this is standard output, nothing gated.

Why this is worth getting exactly right

Variance and constraints are the part of a generic type that the type's users see. A dropped out does not change IProducer's members, but it quietly revokes an assignability promise that other code was built on. A mis-ordered where clause does not change T's meaning, but it stops the file compiling. And a struct emitted where the metadata said unmanaged loosens a guarantee without a single warning, because the looser constraint still accepts everything the stricter one did and more.

So the rule Glass follows is the same one that governs struct layout: this is metadata, metadata is ground truth, and the reconstruction reads it rather than guessing. Read the VarianceMask, read the SpecialConstraintMask (and the modreq and attribute that hide behind a bare struct bit), read every GenericParamConstraint row, and re-emit the whole thing in the one order C# accepts. When you are inspecting or debugging generic code you are entitled to read, that fidelity is the difference between a signature you can trust and one that quietly changes the contract.

title: Platform Engineering for Service-Based Organizations
description:
A consultant wraps up a Kubernetes migration task for a financial services client and moves to a new engagement. For the new client, he does the Kubernetes migration again, covering rebuilding CI/CD, observability, and access management from scratch.

The consultant is solving the same problem that three other teams in his organization already solved last quarter for other clients. So, there are three different approaches but no shared patterns or system for anything to compound.

Platform engineering should be an answer to the common tasks engineers are doing. For product companies, it is. Dedicated platform teams, internal developer platforms, golden paths - everything has evolved and matured over time and the results are visible.

Unfortunately, the platform engineering playbook was built around product company assumptions, with internal developers, consistent infrastructures, stable teams and long-lived products.

Service companies have none of this. Your developers are clients’ engineers, your infrastructure changes with every engagement, and your best consultants rotate across projects before any platform adoption can take hold. Service companies need a different model of platform engineering, and in this blog post, we’re going to explore it.

Why Platform Engineering Discourse Doesn’t Speak to You

Platform Engineering is evolving fast and so are the conversations around it. Major conferences like KubeCon, a dedicated conference like PlatformCon and a growing community around platform engineering are a proof of it. The community has done serious work in defining what good looks like.

I’ve spoken and attended a lot of sessions on platform engineering, and almost every reference point is a product company. Spotify building Backstage for hundreds of internal engineers. A fintech standardizing deployment pipeline across product teams. A SaaS company reducing onboarding time for developers and so on.

The IDP model at the center of all this is straightforward. Your developers are your users, the platform team provisions environments and golden paths, and adoption improves over time as platform matures. The stack remains the same, problems remain the same, and everything is repeated at scale. Service organizations break this approach.

Your “internal developers” are spread across ten client engagements, each with a different stack, different cloud provider, and different security postures. A consultant who just ramped on a Kubernetes-heavy fintech project moves to a legacy modernization engagement next quarter. The tools, the patterns, the environment, all different. The IDP they used last quarter may be irrelevant on the next project.

Worse, the clients own their infrastructure - some on AWS, some on GCP with ArgoCD already running and some in air-gapped environments with no access to your tools. You’re working inside someone else’s environment, within their constraints, often adapting on the fly. Self-service portals and standardized pipelines solve a problem your organization doesn’t have in the way the model assumes.

The industry isn’t wrong about platform engineering; it’s just that most of it is describing an organization that’s not service based.

Services Companies Need the Capability Layer

If the IDP model doesn’t fit service companies, what does? Well, the answer lies in the focus.

We need to stop trying to standardize the environment and shift to standardizing the approaches.

A product company can build one platform because their developers work in one environment. Service companies don’t have that luxury. But what stays consistent across engagements is how your best consultants think about problems.

That thinking is an asset, and it has a name: Delivery Capital.

It’s the organizational knowledge your consultants build engagement after engagement, the reference architectures, the diagnosed anti-patterns, and the judgment calls that took three failed approaches to get right. Most services companies let it walk out the door every time a consultant rolls off a project. The capability layer is simply the system that keeps it, and makes it reusable for the next person who needs it.

In practice, this means building two distinct internal layers.

Capability layer

The capability layer is your organizational memory: a platform engineering capability model covering the patterns, approaches, and decisions your consultants shouldn't have to rebuild from scratch for every engagement.

Everything that was done for every engagement becomes a part of your capability layer.

  1. Reference architectures for your most common engagement types
  2. Policy templates in OPA or Kyverno, adaptable to any client’s compliance posture
  3. GitOps patterns with ArgoCD that work across cloud providers
  4. Observability stacks built on Prometheus and Grafana, deployable in any environment
  5. Engagement accelerators, decision frameworks and starter templates that cut early ramp time

When a consultant starts a new Kubernetes migration, they don’t start from zero. They start from the last ten migrations your org ran.

Internal consultant IDP

The internal consultant IDP is the tooling layer your consultants will use during the engagement.

  1. Sandbox environments to test patterns before touching client infrastructure
  2. Demo clusters for scoping and sales conversations
  3. Fast onboarding tooling that gets a consultant productive in days, not weeks

Neither of the two layers is client-facing. But both directly improve what the client experiences with faster delivery, better decisions, consistent outcomes across every engagement.

Structural Problems That Kill this Before It Starts

Building a capability layer seems straightforward, but service-based companies rarely get there. Here are the three reasons service organization fails to build capability layer:

Ownership vacuum

Someone owns the platform in a product company. They have a charter, a roadmap and sometimes a dedicated team. Their job is to make the platform better, and they’re measured on it.

In a services company, nobody owns the capability layer. Delivery leads are focused on engagements. Practice leads are spread across various accounts. Senior engineers who could build this are always either billable or between projects. This results in the capability layer becoming everyone’s second priority.

Without an owner, nothing compounds. Things get built once, never maintained, and eventually abandoned.

Rotation constraint

In a product-based company, the platform team builds the platform for stability. The same developers use the platform daily, adoption grows over time and the team gets feedback loops that help them continuously improve the platform.

Consultants don’t work that way. A consultant rolls onto a new engagement with two days to get productive. They don’t have time to learn and understand a complex internal system. They need:

  1. Patterns that are fast to understand and easy to adapt
  2. Documentation that doesn’t require tribal knowledge to interpret
  3. Tooling that works across different client environments without heavy configuration

A capability layer designed for a stable internal team will fail in a services context. The design constraint is completely different.

Identity problem

Services based companies are focused on delivery. The incentive structure, the culture, the way performance is measured - all of it points toward delivery. Billable work is valued, and internal capability building is not.

As long as contributing to the capability layer is seen separate from delivery, it won’t happen consistently. The consultants who could build the best patterns are always the ones most in demand on client engagements. And this affects the internal work that is needed to build and maintain the capability layer.

ROI is the Delivery Margin

One of the things that we often discuss within the platform engineering community is how do we track and improve adoption. One of the metrics that always makes it to the discussion is DORA metrics (DevOps Research and Assessment).

Deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, and mean time to recovery are the metrics that get tracked, and frankly these are meaningful numbers for a product company where engineering velocity maps directly to business outcomes.

For a service-based company, it’s completely different. A CTO or a delivery VP isn’t asking how fast your internal deployments are. They are interested in knowing whether engagements are profitable or not.

Hence, the platform engineering metrics that actually matter for a service company look different:

  1. Time-to-ramp: How quickly can a consultant become productive on a new engagement? Every extra day saved directly improves the delivery.
  2. Delivery consistency: How much of the work across engagements is reused versus rebuilt? Higher reuse means lower cost per engagement and more predictable outcomes.
  3. Proposal strength: Can your team walk into a conversation with reference architectures, working demos and proven patterns? These help win deals.
  4. Engagement margin: Fewer custom builds, faster ramps, less reinvention. The capability layer shows up directly in delivery margin over time.

For service companies, these metrics get internal capability investment approved.

A services org that builds and maintains a capability layer builds institutional knowledge that individual talent can’t replicate. The consultant who joins your Kubernetes practice inherits the patterns from twenty prior engagements, not just the memory of who worked there before. That's the competitive advantage for the organization.

Conclusion

Any service company can hire a strong consultant, but only a few can build a system that makes every consultant stronger the moment they join. That’s the difference a capability layer can make over time. Every pattern is tested, every reference architecture is refined, every decision is documented to make sure the next engagement a little faster, a little more consistent and a little more profitable than the one before.

Platform engineering isn’t a universal implementation pattern, it’s an organizational optimization strategy. Product companies optimize for consistency. Service companies optimize for adaptability.

The blind spot in platform engineering discussion isn’t a reason to ignore the discipline. It’s a reason to build your own version of it.

If this resonates and you’re figuring out what this looks like for your organization, connect with me on LinkedIn. And if you’re building or scaling a delivery practice and want to think through the capability layer model, the Improving team would be glad to talk.
