title: Making a Timer Notify Reliably: Notifications API, Audio Autoplay Rules and Wake Lock
description:
A countdown that shows the right number is only half a timer. The other half is the moment it ends: a sound, a system notification, or at least a screen that's still on when you glance over. All three of those are gated by browser rules, and every one of those rules is easier to satisfy at the moment the user presses Start than at the moment the timer runs out.

This post covers what the docs and specs say about each API, and one pattern that ties them together.

Rule 1: Notification permission belongs inside a click

The Notifications API has three permission states: default (not asked yet), granted, and denied. MDN notes that when the result is default, the app should act as if permission was denied.

The WHATWG Notifications standard itself doesn't spell out a gesture requirement. The browsers do. MDN's guide says you should only request permission in response to a user gesture such as a button click, and that Firefox (since version 72) and Safari already disallow requests that aren't triggered that way. It also notes that Chrome and Firefox only allow notification requests from a secure context (HTTPS), and not from cross-origin iframes.

Two consequences:

  • Don't call Notification.requestPermission() on page load. Call it from the handler of the button that starts the timer, and only if Notification.permission === 'default'.
  • Don't rely on new Notification() on phones. MDN warns that the constructor works on desktop but throws a TypeError on most mobile browsers. For mobile, register a service worker and use ServiceWorkerRegistration.showNotification().

Rule 2: Sound needs a gesture, too

Browsers treat script-started playback as autoplay. MDN's autoplay guide is explicit that both <audio autoplay> and a plain audioElement.play() outside a user-input handler fall under the autoplay blocking policy, and so does starting a Web Audio source node. As a general rule, audible media is allowed only if the user has interacted with the site, the site has been allowlisted, or (for iframes) the autoplay Permissions Policy grants it. Muted media isn't blocked, which doesn't help a timer much.

When playback is blocked, HTMLMediaElement.play() returns a promise that rejects with a NotAllowedError DOMException. Chrome's autoplay article adds the Web Audio side: an AudioContext created before the document receives a user gesture starts in the "suspended" state, and you need to call resume() after the gesture. Checking audioCtx.state tells you whether you're running or still suspended.

So the place to "unlock" audio is, again, the Start button. Create or resume the AudioContext there, before anything else that might make the user wait.

Rule 3: Wake Lock is a request, not a guarantee

Screen Wake Lock asks the device not to dim or lock the display while your page needs it. A few details from the W3C spec are worth knowing before you build on it:

  • navigator.wakeLock is marked [SecureContext], so it's HTTPS-only.
  • request('screen') rejects with NotAllowedError if the document isn't fully active, if a permissions policy blocks screen-wake-lock, if the user agent denies it, or if the page's visibility state is "hidden".
  • When the page becomes hidden, the spec's visibility-change steps release every active screen lock.
  • The spec also lets the user agent or OS limit or refuse wake locks based on battery status or power-saving mode. MDN describes the same thing from the developer side: a request can be rejected because of power save mode or low battery.

Once released, a WakeLockSentinel can't be reused. If you still need the screen on, you request a new one, which MDN demonstrates with a visibilitychange listener.

One Start handler that prepares all three

Here's one way to wire it up. showStatus(), timerIsRunning() and startCountdown() stand in for your own UI and timer code.

let audioCtx = null;
let wakeLock = null;

async function prepareAlerts() {
  // Audio first, before any await: create or resume the context
  // while this click still counts as the user's gesture.
  audioCtx ??= new AudioContext();
  const audioReady =
    audioCtx.state === 'suspended' ? audioCtx.resume() : Promise.resolve();

  // Ask for notification permission only if the user hasn't decided yet.
  const permissionReady =
    'Notification' in window && Notification.permission === 'default'
      ? Notification.requestPermission()
      : Promise.resolve();

  await Promise.all([audioReady, permissionReady, requestWakeLock()]);
}

document.querySelector('#start').addEventListener('click', async () => {
  await prepareAlerts();
  startCountdown(onTimerDone);
});

The audio step runs first on purpose. A permission prompt can sit on screen for a while, and I'd rather not depend on the click still counting as a fresh gesture by the time the user answers it.

Keeping the screen on, and getting it back 

async function requestWakeLock() {
  if (!('wakeLock' in navigator)) return false;
  try {
    wakeLock = await navigator.wakeLock.request('screen');
    wakeLock.addEventListener('release', () => {
      wakeLock = null;
      showStatus('Screen may sleep now');
    });
    showStatus('Screen will stay on');
    return true;
  } catch (err) {
    // NotAllowedError: hidden page, power saver, blocked by policy...
    showStatus(`Screen may sleep (${err.name})`);
    return false;
  }
}

document.addEventListener('visibilitychange', () => {
  if (document.visibilityState === 'visible' && timerIsRunning() && wakeLock === null) {
    requestWakeLock();
  }
});

Show the lock state in the UI. If the request fails, the user should know the screen might turn off before it does.

When the timer ends 

function beep(durationSec = 0.4) {
  if (!audioCtx || audioCtx.state !== 'running') return false;
  const osc = audioCtx.createOscillator();
  const gain = audioCtx.createGain();
  osc.frequency.value = 880;
  gain.gain.value = 0.2;
  osc.connect(gain).connect(audioCtx.destination);
  osc.start();
  osc.stop(audioCtx.currentTime + durationSec);
  return true;
}

async function showDoneNotification() {
  if (!('Notification' in window) || Notification.permission !== 'granted') return false;
  const body = 'Time is up.';
  if ('serviceWorker' in navigator) {
    const reg = await navigator.serviceWorker.getRegistration();
    if (reg) {
      await reg.showNotification('Timer finished', { body, tag: 'timer-done' });
      return true;
    }
  }
  try {
    new Notification('Timer finished', { body, tag: 'timer-done' });
    return true;
  } catch {
    return false; // e.g. TypeError on mobile without a service worker
  }
}

async function onTimerDone() {
  const rang = beep();
  const notified = await showDoneNotification();
  if (!rang && !notified) {
    document.title = '⏰ Time is up';
  }
}

Each channel reports whether it worked, and the tab title is the last fallback. Using the same tag means a second "done" replaces the first instead of stacking up.

A note on testing: I checked these snippets for syntax with Node, but they use browser-only APIs, so the behavior described here comes from MDN, the specs, and Chrome's docs, not from a Node run. Try them on an HTTPS page (or localhost) in the browsers your users have.

Checklist

  • [ ] Permission is requested from the Start click, never on load, and only when the state is default.
  • [ ] default is treated the same as denied.
  • [ ] Mobile uses registration.showNotification(), not new Notification().
  • [ ] The AudioContext is created or resumed inside the click handler, and state is checked before beeping.
  • [ ] play() rejections (NotAllowedError) are caught, not ignored.
  • [ ] The wake lock is re-requested on visibilitychange, and its state is visible in the UI.
  • [ ] There's a fallback (tab title, on-screen banner) when every other channel is off.

None of this turns a web page into a guaranteed alarm. Users can deny permission, mute the tab, or turn on power saving, and the browser is right to let them. The goal is to ask at the right moment and to be honest in the UI about which channels are live.

Sources

  • MDN, Using the Notifications API
  • MDN, Notification.requestPermission()
  • MDN, ServiceWorkerRegistration.showNotification()
  • WHATWG, Notifications API Standard
  • MDN, Autoplay guide for media and Web Audio APIs
  • MDN, HTMLMediaElement.play()
  • Chrome for Developers, Autoplay policy in Chrome
  • MDN, Screen Wake Lock API
  • W3C, Screen Wake Lock API

title: How dependent is Europe on foreign technologies after 24-hour Microsoft service outage?
description:
A global Microsoft outage affecting millions across 74 countries for 24 hours has reignited discussions on EU digital sovereignty and infrastructure concentration, as industry leaders debate the risks of relying heavily on centralized foreign cloud platforms.

European dependency was also at the heart of the intervention of Arthur Mens, CEO of Mistral, at the first meeting of EU leaders on artificial intelligence. Mens said that only 20% of digital services in Europe operate on a European basis. In his view, the money spent on technologies from foreign companies, mainly American and Chinese, could be directed to European infrastructure and research and development. He did not specifically link his statements to the Microsoft shutdown.

The issue concerns, among other things, the control of cloud infrastructure, microchips and artificial intelligence models. Technological sovereignty is a priority of the second term of the President of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, and was high on the agenda of the meeting of the leaders of the 27 member states. After the summit in Dublin, French President Emmanuel Macron wrote on the X platform that European independence must be built in Europe and not outsourced. He added that Europe has the resources to compete in artificial intelligence, but it has no time to waste. An EU diplomat involved in the talks called for faster licensing and more investment.

Proposals for changes to public procurement were made both by Finnish MEP Aura Sala, who called for support for European technology companies, and in Germany. Social Democrat MEP Johannes Setzl put the spotlight on public procurement and the resilience of digital systems: as he said, sovereignty is also judged by whether they can continue to operate during an interruption. Sebastian Tofaletti, secretary general of the Digital SME Alliance, called the Microsoft incident a reminder of the systemic risk posed by the concentration of critical infrastructure in a few global groups.

title: Keeping a local Pinnacle odds book over WebSocket in Python (snapshot + deltas)
description:
Most odds feeds are built for polling: you ask for the whole board every few seconds and diff it yourself. A push feed works the other way round, and the client code gets simpler once you treat it as a tiny state machine. This post walks through that pattern for Pinnacle prices using PinnFeed, a WebSocket and REST API I work on (disclosure up front).

The model: snapshot, then deltas

After you connect and subscribe, the server sends three kinds of data messages:

  1. welcome, with your plan limits.
  2. A chunked snapshot of every event and market that matches your filters, split into parts of up to 400 events. The last part has "final": true.
  3. A stream of delta batches. Each change is either upsert (replace the object) or remove (the market was suspended or settled, or the event ended).

There is also a heartbeat: the server sends ping every 20 seconds and closes connections that stay silent for 60 seconds, so you answer with pong.

That means the whole client is: keep two dictionaries (events by id, markets by id), apply upserts and removes, and don't trust the book until the snapshot says final.

A minimal local book in Python 

# pip install websockets
import asyncio, json, os, websockets

events, markets = {}, {}
book_ready = False

def apply_change(c):
    store = markets if c["kind"] == "market" else events
    obj = c.get("market") or c.get("event")
    if c["op"] == "upsert":
        store[obj["id"]] = obj
    elif c["op"] == "remove":
        store.pop(obj["id"] if obj else c.get("id"), None)

async def main():
    global book_ready
    async with websockets.connect(
        "wss://pinnfeed.io/v1/stream",
        additional_headers={"x-api-key": os.environ["PINNFEED_KEY"]},
        compression="deflate",
    ) as ws:
        await ws.send(json.dumps({
            "type": "subscribe",
            "sports": ["soccer"],
            "markets": ["moneyline", "total"],
            "live": True,
        }))
        async for raw in ws:
            msg = json.loads(raw)
            t = msg["type"]
            if t == "ping":
                await ws.send('{"type":"pong"}')
            elif t == "snapshot":
                for e in msg.get("events", []):
                    events[e["id"]] = e
                for m in msg.get("markets", []):
                    markets[m["id"]] = m
                book_ready = msg.get("final", False)
            elif t == "delta" and book_ready:
                for c in msg["changes"]:
                    apply_change(c)

asyncio.run(main())

A few notes from writing this:

  • Wait for final: true. If you act on the first snapshot part you will think most markets are missing.
  • Sending subscribe again replaces the subscription and triggers a fresh snapshot, so reset your dictionaries when you change filters.
  • Ask for compression. The compression="deflate" option negotiates permessage-deflate, which matters when you subscribe to whole sports.
  • Every outcome already carries a no-vig fair price next to the decimal and American prices, so you don't have to remove the margin yourself before comparing against another book.

Polling is fine for prototypes

If you only want to see which prices are moving, the REST side has a GET /v1/drops endpoint that returns the biggest shortening per outcome over a rolling window (1 to 60 minutes, with a minimum drop percentage):

curl -H "x-api-key: $PINNFEED_KEY" \
  "https://pinnfeed.io/v1/drops?sport=soccer&live=true&minutes=10&min_pct=5"

On the free plan REST responses are delayed by 30 seconds, which is enough to build and test the logic before you need a live stream.

Where to go next

  • The full message reference (subscribe fields, snapshot and delta shapes, raw frames): PinnFeed WebSocket protocol docs
  • A complete small project that turns drops into Telegram alerts: pinnfeed/dropping-odds-telegram on GitHub

PinnFeed is not affiliated with Pinnacle. If you use odds data for betting, it is for adults (18+) only, and no data feed guarantees a profit.

title: Node.js Account Deletion: Verified GDPR Erasure for User Avatar Images
description:
TL;DR: Treat the Express account-deletion handler as an orchestrator, not as proof of erasure: freeze the user's avatar mapping, delete every recorded asset by ID, read each ID back, and close the request only after every read confirms absence. Keep the deleted IDs and verification outcomes in an audit record. If quality and bandwidth are competing concerns elsewhere in the photo pipeline, settle that during upload or OCR; deletion must operate on the authoritative asset ledger, never on whatever compressed preview happens to be convenient.

For a B2B SaaS team, the practical service boundary is narrow. Node.js owns the user lifecycle and durable deletion state; a worker performs bounded external calls; the database remains the source of truth for which original photos, avatar variants, and OCR-derived images belong to the account. A successful DELETE response advances the workflow, but it does not finish it.

This is the decision rule: no complete mapping, no defensible deletion.

How should Node.js delete user images during account deletion?

The failure mode starts before the API call. A profile row may point at the current square avatar while an older original, a mobile crop, or an OCR input is still associated with the same user elsewhere. Deleting the visible avatar proves very little if the user-to-asset mapping is incomplete. The deletion job should therefore take an immutable snapshot of all known asset IDs after new uploads have been blocked, rather than repeatedly querying a relationship that can change underneath it.

Then comes the second trap: treating command acceptance as observed state. Networks fail between request and response, retries race, and providers differ in what a delete acknowledgement means. The safe sequence is deliberately boring: issue deletion by asset ID, follow it with a read of that same ID, classify the observed result, and retain the ID-level evidence. Trust the read.

Stop there.

For capacity planning, use calls rather than users as the unit. With N mapped assets, the happy path requires roughly 2N remote operations: one delete and one verification read per asset. Retries add load, and a verification delay stretches completion time. Set the erasure workflow's SLO around verified completion, then derive worker concurrency from the provider quota and the largest credible account, not from median avatar count. A queue depth that looks harmless in users can be large in assets.

Pick the ownership boundary before the vendor

The vendor choice matters less than retaining a complete local ledger. Still, the operational differences are real, particularly for a small platform team weighing on-call load against lock-in.

Option Interface and ownership model Operational trade-off Best fit
Cloudflare Images Image identifiers sit inside a managed image service Keeps delivery and image lifecycle in Cloudflare's control plane Teams already using Cloudflare for image delivery
ImageKit Media identifiers sit inside an image-management workflow Centers the decision on a dedicated image platform Teams that want image management and delivery together
Uploadcare File identifiers sit inside a managed upload and delivery workflow Moves upload handling into the same vendor decision Teams that want managed ingestion as well as media lifecycle operations
Cloudinary Media asset identifiers sit inside a managed image workflow Reduces image-pipeline machinery the application must own Teams that want transformations and lifecycle operations together
Infrai Image assets are addressed through one REST surface One key and one bill can reduce credential and invoice sprawl; the abstraction also increases dependence on that common API Teams consolidating several backend capabilities behind one control plane

Those are not interchangeable promises. Cloudflare Images, ImageKit, Uploadcare, and Cloudinary are dedicated media choices with different surrounding workflows; Infrai groups media with a broader backend surface. The Infrai discovery catalog reports 295 capabilities across 20 modules and runnable examples in ten languages, which is useful when the deletion worker is one of many integrations, but breadth does not remove the application's obligation to maintain ownership records. For this workflow, only the asset-ID delete and subsequent asset-ID read are material. A team should validate identifier semantics, deletion behavior, account-level access controls, and read-after-delete observations against the current documentation of whichever service it selects, because a familiar upload path does not prove that the erasure path matches this runbook.

The quality-versus-bandwidth decision belongs upstream: preserve whichever original and derived assets the product needs, record every resulting ID against the user, and apply retention policy explicitly. Do not infer ownership later from filenames, URLs, OCR text, or the current profile image.

Implement a bounded, verifiable deletion worker

The example below is Go because the worker is intentionally isolated from Express. Express can create the deletion job and wait for its durable state transition; the worker receives a frozen list of IDs. It uses exactly two media routes, sends an explicit method, retries 429 responses with Retry-After when available, and surfaces response bodies on other failures. No key is embedded in source.

The verification contract in this example is conservative: a read returning 404 confirms absence. Any other status, including 200, leaves the job open for investigation or another bounded attempt.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

type Client struct {
    httpClient *http.Client
    apiKey     string
    baseURL    string
}

func (c *Client) do(ctx context.Context, method, path string) (*http.Response, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, method, c.baseURL+path, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+c.apiKey)

        resp, err := c.httpClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            return resp, nil
        }
        io.Copy(io.Discard, resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()

        delay := time.Second << attempt
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
            delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
        select {
        case <-time.After(delay):
        case <-ctx.Done():
            return nil, ctx.Err()
        }
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("rate limit persisted after bounded retries")
}

func (c *Client) deleteAndVerify(ctx context.Context, id string) error {
    path := "/image/delete/" + id
    resp, err := c.do(ctx, http.MethodDelete, path)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("delete %s: %w", id, err)
    }
    body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
    resp.Body.Close()
    if readErr != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("read delete response for %s: %w", id, readErr)
    }
    if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
        return fmt.Errorf("delete %s returned %d: %s", id, resp.StatusCode, strings.TrimSpace(string(body)))
    }

    resp, err = c.do(ctx, http.MethodGet, "/image/get/"+id)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("verify %s: %w", id, err)
    }
    body, readErr = io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
    resp.Body.Close()
    if readErr != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("read verification response for %s: %w", id, readErr)
    }
    if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusNotFound {
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("asset %s still unverified; read returned %d: %s", id, resp.StatusCode, strings.TrimSpace(string(body)))
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    baseURL := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL")
    if baseURL == "" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "INFRAI_BASE_URL is required")
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    ids := os.Args[1:]
    if len(ids) == 0 {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "provide at least one asset id")
        os.Exit(2)
    }

    client := &Client{httpClient: &http.Client{Timeout: 20 * time.Second}, apiKey: key, baseURL: strings.TrimRight(baseURL, "/")}
    for _, id := range ids {
        ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 2*time.Minute)
        err := client.deleteAndVerify(ctx, id)
        cancel()
        if err != nil {
            fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
            os.Exit(1)
        }
        fmt.Printf("verified_deleted asset_id=%s\n", id)
    }
}

In production, do not pass IDs on a command line. Read them from the durable job snapshot, and write each transition to an append-only audit record containing the deletion-request ID, asset ID, attempt number, timestamps, HTTP outcome, and final verification state. Avoid storing image content, OCR output, bearer credentials, or response bodies that may contain personal data in that record. The point is evidence, not a second copy of the user's data.

The log line in the sample demonstrates the minimum useful correlation field. A real worker should use structured logging and should never mark the parent account request complete merely because the process exited zero once; completion is a database transition conditioned on every snapshotted asset reaching verified_deleted.

Verification, SLOs, and proof

Define three states clearly: deletion requested, deletion acknowledged, and deletion verified. Only the third satisfies the runbook. For a user with four avatar assets, the evidence set must contain four asset IDs and four successful absence checks; one missing row is an incomplete request, even if the other three finished quickly.

The useful service indicators are verified-completion latency, oldest unverified request age, verification failure rate, and retry volume. Page on a sustained threat to the erasure SLO or on requests approaching the policy deadline, not on every transient 429. A retry is expected control flow. An aging unverified asset is the risk.

One number changes the alert from noise into evidence: the age of the oldest job that has not reached verified completion. Aggregate success rates can stay green while a single large account remains stuck behind one overlooked derivative, so the dashboard needs both the population view and that worst-case clock. This also gives the on-call engineer a concrete starting point: open the frozen asset snapshot, compare it with the per-ID audit rows, and resume only the entries that lack a confirmed absence read.

Auditability also changes the deletion order. Preserve the workflow record while removing the media objects, then minimize that record according to the organization's retention rules after the request is closed. The retained proof should establish which identifiers were processed and what was observed, without retaining the deleted photos themselves.

Roll back the workflow, never the deletion

Deletion is irreversible, so rollback means halting safely and resuming from durable state. If verification does not confirm absence, keep the account in a restricted, deletion-pending state, stop downstream use of its media, and retry from the first asset that lacks proof. Do not recreate an image to make an application rollback look tidy.

Before rollout, run the worker against disposable assets and test four cases: all IDs verify absent, one delete is rate-limited, one read still finds an asset, and the worker stops halfway through the list. The last case is the important one. Restarting must skip IDs already recorded as verified, continue the remainder, and produce one coherent audit trail tied to the original request.

Roll out with a concurrency cap. Watch provider throttling, queue age, and database contention, then raise the cap only while the verified-completion SLO retains margin. This is where a capacity-planning reflex pays off: bandwidth used by normal avatar uploads and OCR should be budgeted alongside deletion traffic, since an account-closure spike should not starve the very reads needed to prove completion.

The final operational rule stays small: snapshot, delete, read, record. Everything else supports those four verbs.

References

  • Cloudinary Admin API, Delete resources: https://cloudinary.com/documentation/admin_api#delete_resources
  • Cloudflare Images API documentation: https://developers.cloudflare.com/images/
  • ImageKit API documentation: https://imagekit.io/docs/api-reference/
  • Uploadcare REST API documentation: https://uploadcare.com/api-refs/rest-api/v0.7.0/
  • MDN, Image file type and format guide: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Media/Guides/Formats/Image_types
  • GDPR, Article 17, Right to erasure: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj

title: AI Gateway adds DeepSeek Search and Fetch tools

Use both tools with any model that supports tool calling, using one AI Gateway API key. No separate DeepSeek account is required, and you can keep the same tools when switching model providers.

These helpers are available in AI SDK 6.0.321 and later on v6, or 7.0.160 and later on v7. Update with pnpm add ai@latest and set your AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY. To combine search and page retrieval, pass both helpers in tools:

You can also use alternative search tools with DeepSeek Fetch if DeepSeek Search fails:

Search fallback is model-directed, so provider order and retry limits are best effort. DeepSeek Fetch can retrieve a result URL from any of these search tools.

Search and Fetch each cost $0.75 per 1,000 billable requests. Failed requests, timeouts, and empty results have no tool charge. Model tokens are billed separately.

See the DeepSeek Search documentation and DeepSeek Fetch documentation for configuration options and pricing details.

AI Gateway provides one API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring routing, retries, and failover. You can use an AI Gateway API key or bring your own provider key.

title: Control AI crawlers and assistants separately in Vercel Firewall
description:
You can now log or block requests from AI crawlers and AI assistants separately with the AI Bots managed ruleset in Vercel Firewall.

  • AI crawlers: bots that collect content for indexing and model training

  • AI assistants: bots that fetch pages in response to user actions or search queries

For example, you can block AI crawlers while allowing AI assistants to retrieve your content to answer users’ questions. Vercel updates the rules as new bots are added.

To configure these controls, open your project’s Security > Firewall > Rules. Under Bot Management, enable AI Bots and select the gear icon beside it. Set an action for AI crawlers and AI assistants, then review and publish your changes.

You can also modify these rule settings using the Vercel CLI:

type: embedded-entry-inline id: 30azXU4HVTfrsO9MbBOCLv

Review the changes with vercel firewall diff, then apply them with vercel firewall publish.

The AI Bots managed ruleset is available on all plans. Learn more in the documentation.

title: Aurora PostgreSQL with express configuration now supported in CloudFormation
description:
Aurora PostgreSQL now supports express configuration in AWS CloudFormation for infrastructure as code deployment. This launch enables you to automate the infrastructure deployment of your Aurora clusters through CloudFormation templates while benefiting from the speed of express configuration.

Aurora PostgreSQL clusters created with express configuration allow you to create and query an Aurora serverless database in seconds. The new withExpressConfiguration createOnly property on the AWS::RDS::DBCluster resource creates both the cluster and its primary database instance from one property declaration. You don't need to model or manage the instance separately in your CloudFormation template. This simplifies your templates and makes it easier to manage Aurora clusters with express configuration through infrastructure as code.

The CloudFormation support is available in all AWS Regions where Aurora PostgreSQL with express configuration is offered. To learn more, see the Aurora User Guide and the AWS::RDS::DBCluster resource reference in the AWS CloudFormation documentation.

title: Design Systems for Coding Agents: 11 Builds, Measured
description:
Originally published on ayurchenko.xyz.

I gave one AI agent the same brief again and again: with no design system, on shadcn/ui, and on a product whose look had been decided before the first screen. Then I measured every element it shipped. The first pass turned out to be the easy part. What a system is for now starts after it.

I have built a design system for every product I have worked on, and over 14 years that is dozens of products. The early ones were Figma libraries and pages of documentation for people. The recent ones live in code, and I implement the components in Storybook myself, because the designer who writes the components is the first to see every gap in the system.

Now agents write a lot of the interface. Founders ask me a fair question. If Claude Code or Cursor builds a screen in minutes, and shadcn/ui gives everyone a component library for free, what is a design system still for? I wanted to answer with numbers instead of an opinion, so I ran two tests.

The setup

The product is Halden, a dashboard for a coffee roaster in Portland with six cafes and a wholesale line. I made it as a test bed for a review tool: an agent built it in one evening on a visual direction I set first, a token file and a small kit, with no design system behind it. The tool and that evening are in A canvas for reviewing AI-built UI.

The agent had six screens to build: the home dashboard, a list of transactions, a customer record, the business settings form, a new wholesale order, and an order with its timeline. Every build got the same written brief, the same data and the same model, Claude Sonnet in Claude Code, in one pass. None of them saw a screenshot of Halden or a line of its CSS.

  • No system, twice. React and Tailwind, no component library, no tokens. What a founder gets from Cursor or Claude Code with a prompt.
  • shadcn/ui, twice. A fresh shadcn setup with its default theme, the stack Lovable starts from.
  • Halden, a decided look with a thin system. Four of the six screens come from Halden itself, built in one evening as a test bed for a review tool on a token file and a small kit: no rules for states, no component descriptions, no checks. Halden had no wholesale section, so the other two are the wholesale screens an agent added in the growth test below, from the build that did have a rules file, a catalog and an audit. I took the versions before any review fixes.

For every screen a script opened the page in headless Chrome at 1440 pixels and read the computed style of every element: how many different buttons and fields there are, which values fall outside the build‚Äôs own scale, which looks appear only once. Then it changed the main color, the corner radius and the density in one place, and counted what followed.

What the numbers say

Less than I expected. On the first pass every build came out reasonably consistent.

Across six screens No system (2 runs) shadcn/ui (2 runs) Halden (a decided look, thin system)
Different button looks 9 / 8 13 / 12 12
Different field looks 2 / 3 4 / 3 4
Looks used only once 15 / 17 17 / 15 16
Values off the build‚Äôs own scale 7 / 10 6 / 6 21
Raw Tailwind colors around the theme no theme 34 / 24 no Tailwind
Main color change followed 100% / 100% 100% / 100% 100%
Radius change followed 100% / 76% 100% / 100% 79%
Every button has a disabled look no / no yes / yes no
Time to build 6.5 / 9.0 min 6.0 / 5.7 min one evening, with the kit

The builds with no system did not stay without one. Before the first screen, both agents wrote their own small block of tokens and a file of buttons, fields and cards. Tailwind v4 hands them variables for spacing and radius out of the box, so even these builds changed density in one place.

shadcn/ui shipped the most complete states: every button had a disabled look and a loading state. Halden lost on exactly the things a system is for. Five button heights, 21 values off its scale, no disabled look, the browser‚Äôs default focus ring. That is what a look without a system produces, and it is the point of this article: decisions give a product its face, and a system is what keeps that face consistent and complete.

So the first pass is no longer where a product goes wrong. An agent on a modern stack gets the basics close enough by itself.

What the numbers miss

The same dashboard in four builds. Top: Halden, then the first shadcn/ui build. Bottom: the second shadcn/ui build, then the build with no system. Screenshots at 1440 pixels, top of the page.

Put the screens next to each other and the measurements stop being the interesting part. The two shadcn/ui builds are the same product twice: the same grey, the same black bars, the same weight on every card. Any other company that ships the default theme gets this face too, because nobody decided anything about it.

The build with no system picked a brown ‚Äúcoffee‚Äù palette on its own. That is a choice, and the agent made it, not the company.

Halden has a look because someone decided it. One blue accent, used only where it carries meaning. A quiet grey for everything else. Density set for a manager who checks numbers between two cafes. None of that comes in a component library. It is a set of decisions, and tokens are the way those decisions get written down so that an agent can follow them.

Where the default theme had no decision, the agents filled the gap themselves. shadcn‚Äôs theme has no color for success or warning, so both shadcn builds styled their statuses with raw Tailwind colors: 34 classes in one, 24 in the other, all out of reach of the next theme change.

The new order form in three builds: Halden, shadcn/ui, no system. Screenshots at 1440 pixels, top of the page.

A short brief builds a different product every time

I ran a control. The same two stacks, twice each, got a one-paragraph brief, the way founders often write one: six screens and their addresses, the data file, and ‚Äúmake it look good‚Äù.

The screens looked fine. The agents chose palettes, added cards nobody asked for, and one rewrote the shadcn theme to match a brand it imagined. But a third of the concrete decisions disappeared: of 79 items in the detailed brief, the builds kept between 43 and 50. No build had a loading or an error state. Two runs of the same stack disagreed about the product itself, bars against a line, today against the last seven days, different cards on the dashboard. Looks used only once rose to between 23 and 29 in three of the four builds.

Same stack, same paragraph, two runs. Screenshots at 1440 pixels, top of the page.

That is the part an agent does not invent: the decisions. The detailed brief did not make the screens prettier. It made them complete, and the same twice. A design system is that brief, written once, for every screen the product will ever have.

Where drift starts: the second screen, and the fiftieth

The first test I ran was about growth. Three agents added the same six-screen wholesale section to Halden, which already had its token file and component kit in the code. One got only the brief. One also got written guidelines, the kind of page a team keeps in Notion. One got the system in a form an agent reads: a rules file, a catalog that says what each component is for and when not to use it, and an audit it had to run until it reported nothing.

On screen, the three sections looked almost the same. The agents copied the existing screens, mistakes included: two of them took a hard-coded field height from Halden‚Äôs settings form straight into their new code. The difference was underneath:

In the new section Brief only Plus written guidelines Plus rules, catalog, audit
Raw values in new code 34 25 0
New CSS classes 31 29 5
Lines of CSS added 233 187 91
Where the styles went a stylesheet for this section a stylesheet for this section shared components, recorded in the catalog
Agent time 8.1 min 7.3 min 4.4 min

The first two forked the product. Each wrote a private stylesheet for one section, with about thirty classes nobody else can reuse and values that will not follow the next token change. Every screen looks right today. The cost arrives with the next fifty screens, when nobody knows which of three similar buttons is the real one.

The third agent added the missing form fields as components of the whole system and wrote them into the catalog, so the next agent finds them. It was also the fastest. A system that answers the agent‚Äôs questions saves the time it would otherwise spend guessing.

One more detail. The written guidelines said cards have 16 pixel corners. The code said 24. The agent followed the code. Documentation that lives apart from the code drifts, and an agent always believes the code.

What I put in a system now that agents read it

What changed in the last two years is the reader. A system used to be documentation for designers and engineers. Now it is also the input a coding agent builds from, and the thing its output gets checked against. These are the parts I add for that reader.

  • Code is the source of truth. Tokens and components live in the repository and in Storybook. Figma is where the design work happens and gets synced back. When the two disagree, code wins, and the sync merges changes instead of overwriting them, so values that exist only in code survive it.
  • Names an agent reads the way people do. If a list row lives inside a component called ‚Äúmenu‚Äù, every agent will build menus out of it. Renaming is a design decision.
  • Descriptions written for an agent. Every component says what it is for, when not to use it and what to use instead. The intent lives in one place. A second copy of the same text goes stale, and a stale description misleads an agent more than no description at all.
  • A rules file, tested blind. An agent builds a screen without being told about the system. Then I plant violations in clean code and check that the rules catch every one of them, with no false alarms.
  • States for every component. Hover, focus, disabled, loading, error, empty. Halden skipped them, and the table above shows what that costs.
  • A Figma file an agent can read. An agent checks layer names, component descriptions and token bindings, so that design-to-code reads intent rather than geometry.
  • Checks on what ships. A token audit that flags raw values in new code, and an inventory of the running product that finds what drifted (how I review it). The findings go back to the agent as tasks. Whether a person can finish a task is a separate check: the UX audit agent.
  • A rule for anything new. A new look becomes a variant of an existing component. New behavior gets a component of its own. A new job gets a new component built from the old parts. Anything else turns into a one-off.

This is what the third agent in the growth test read before it touched the wholesale section, shortened. The rules file says where values come from and what to do when nothing fits:

AGENTS.md, excerpt

Read this file and COMPONENTS.md before you write any UI. These rules are checked by npm run audit.

Source of truth
- styles/tokens.css is the only source of values. Every color, size, space, radius, font size, weight, shadow and duration in new code is a var(--token). No hex, rgb, hsl or oklch literals, and no px values except 0 and 1px borders.
- Do not add tokens. If a value you need has no token, use the nearest one and say so in your final message.

When nothing fits
- Add one component to styles/components.css, built only from tokens, plus an entry in COMPONENTS.md. Then use it everywhere it applies.
- Never style an element for one screen only. If a screen needs a look that no component has, that look is a component.

Before you finish
Run npm run audit. Fix every finding, then run it again. Repeat until it reports 0 findings, or explain in your final message why a finding must stay.

The catalog answers the question the other two agents answered by guessing: which piece is the right one. Every row says what it is for and what to use instead:

COMPONENTS.md, four of 21 rows

badge(label): every status; tone comes from the tones map. Not for categories or counts.
stat({label, value, change, note}): one headline number with an optional change. Not for lists of numbers (use table or .facts).
segmented(q, key, options): switching between 2 to 5 views of the same list. Not for filters with many values (use chip).
timeline([{label, note, state}]): the steps one record has gone through. Not for steps the user fills in (use .stepper).

Neither file is long. The rules file is 23 lines and the catalog 29. What makes them work is the last rule: the audit runs until it reports nothing, so the agent cannot finish with a raw value in the code.

Your own system, shadcn‚Äôs skeleton, or shadcn as it is

shadcn/ui is a good start, and the test shows why: its components came with the most complete states of any build. The question is what you need on top of it, and that depends on the time you have and what the product has to do.

  • shadcn as it is fits a prototype, an internal tool, or a product where looking like everyone else costs nothing.
  • shadcn‚Äôs skeleton, reworked fits most startups. Keep the behavior and replace the decisions: your color roles, including success and warning, your density, your type, your corners, and component descriptions written for agents.
  • A system of your own fits when the product‚Äôs look is part of what you sell, when several products or brands share one system, or when the team will grow past the point where anyone remembers the exceptions. In my experience shadcn‚Äôs tokens and interactions are not consistent enough from one component to the next for that, so I build from one token logic and one set of interaction rules. It takes longer at the start. Afterwards the team, and its agents, read the logic instead of memorising exceptions.

Whichever you choose, the test that decides it is the same, and it takes more than one round: give an agent a real task, look at what it shipped, find where it guessed, and fix the system there.

Where this comes from

I have built a design system for every product I worked on. The ones I can show, and what they changed, are in the case studies: TrueFi, Deva and 10Planet, Equi and Fully AI.

What to do this week

  • Take an inventory of what your product ships: every button, every field, every value outside your tokens. Count them.
  • Write down the decisions an agent keeps guessing: color roles including success and warning, density, type, corners.
  • Give each component a description: what it is for, when not to use it, what to use instead.
  • Add a rules file, then test it: let an agent build one screen and see where it guessed.
  • Check new code for raw values before every merge.

If you would rather have someone do the first step, that is what the Consistency Review is.

How I ran the test

  • Eleven one-pass builds in total: four from the detailed brief, four from the one-paragraph brief, two of each per stack, plus three in the growth test, one per condition. Claude Sonnet, in the background, checked with a production build only. The agents were not told it was a test.
  • The agents ran with my general coding preferences, which already favor CSS variables. That makes the builds with no system better than a typical one, so the gaps here are conservative.
  • Halden‚Äôs brief did not ask for interaction states. The other builds‚Äô briefs did.
  • Two runs per stack is a small sample. The spread between two runs of one stack was sometimes as large as the spread between stacks.
  • A ‚Äúlook‚Äù is an exact match of computed styles, so two nearly identical buttons count as two.
  • The rebrand check changed the main color, multiplied the corner radius by 1.6 and the density by 1.25, and counted the share of elements that moved.

Cheap and expensive

Anyone can build a product now. An agent will give a founder a working app in an evening, and every screen in it will look reasonable. That is the new floor, and most products will stand on it, in the stack‚Äôs default theme or a palette the agent picked, looking like every other app built the same way.

What lifts a product off that floor is a set of decisions the agent will not make: which states every control has, which color means success, how dense a table can get for the person who reads it between two meetings, where the one accent goes and where it never goes, which of three similar buttons is the real one. In both tests, the builds that had those decisions written down came out complete and the same twice. The ones that did not were reasonable and different every time.

Making those decisions well takes taste and having watched real people use real products many times. Writing them down so an agent follows them is now part of the same job. Agents made building cheap; the decisions are the expensive part.

This article first appeared on ayurchenko.xyz. I am Andriy Yurchenko, a product designer and design engineer. More of my writing is at ayurchenko.xyz/writing.

title: Introducing Vercel CI
description:
Coding agents are opening more pull requests than ever, and each one waits on CI before anyone can review or merge it. Most CI systems run the entire workflow on every push, even a one-line change. The more your agents push, the more time you spend waiting on CI.

Today, we're announcing Vercel CI in Beta. It runs only the tasks affected by your code change, and spins up only the compute those checks need, the same way Fluid compute scales with your traffic.

At Vercel, our CI now keeps up with our coding agents. Time from git push to "CI passed" is 2-6x faster than it was before.

How it works

Vercel CI uses Turborepo to understand your tasks and which ones depend on each other. It reads turbo.json, so if you're already using Turborepo, there's no separate CI config to write.

If you're not on Turborepo yet, add turbo.json and the turbo package. It works in single-package repos too.

Then tag the tasks you want Vercel CI to run.

"tags": ["ci"] is all you need to get started. No workflow YAML to maintain, no drift between your CI config and turbo.json, and Remote Cache is on by default.

When you or your agent push code, Vercel CI determines which tasks need to run based on the change. Tasks whose inputs haven't changed come from cache. The remaining tasks each run on their own machine, powered by Hive, Vercel's compute layer, and start as soon as their dependencies finish.

Vercel CI gives each task the compute it needs and nothing more.

Running your CI on Vercel

To get started, follow the documentation or prompt your agent from your repo:

Once set up, you or your agent can watch and inspect CI through the Vercel dashboard, Vercel CLI, or Vercel MCP. When something fails, go straight to the failing task, see what's blocked behind it, and open its logs, or search across recent runs to see whether a test has been flaky all week.

Vercel CI posts a check to your pull request on GitHub, so your existing branch protection rules can block merges on failure, the same way they do today.

Closing the loop

Vercel CI has already completed nearly 8 million tasks across our own repositories and the private beta, and we're just getting started. We're working to keep shrinking the time between writing code and running it in production.

As we work toward general availability, we plan to add:

  • Advanced observability

  • A vc ci CLI command for distributed execution before pushing code

  • More granular test selection

Vercel CI is available in Beta today on all plans. Read the docs and try it on your repository.

title: CryptoPulse: Build a Real-Time Cryptocurrency Intelligence Platform on AWS
description:
What if your application could monitor Bitcoin, Ethereum, and other cryptocurrencies, detect unusual market activity, analyze historical trends, and send alerts automatically?

Cryptocurrency markets never sleep.

Bitcoin can experience a sudden price movement while Ethereum trading volume increases. Another cryptocurrency might attract unusual market activity within minutes.

For traders, analysts, and crypto enthusiasts, monitoring multiple exchanges and dashboards manually can quickly become overwhelming.

The challenge isn't simply collecting cryptocurrency prices. It's identifying meaningful market movements, preserving historical data, and notifying users when configured conditions are met.

That's the idea behind CryptoPulse – Cryptocurrency Intelligence, a serverless market-monitoring and analytics platform built using AWS.

In this project, we'll explore how to connect real-time market data ingestion, event processing, historical storage, SQL analytics, and automated notifications using AWS services.

1. What Are We Building?

CryptoPulse is designed to monitor cryptocurrency market activity and generate useful insights.

Its core capabilities include:

  • Real-time monitoring of Bitcoin, Ethereum, and other supported cryptocurrencies.
  • Detection of configurable price fluctuations.
  • Identification of unusual trading-volume spikes.
  • Historical market data storage and analysis.
  • Automated email notifications when configured conditions are triggered.

For example, imagine these events:

  • Bitcoin moves more than 2% within 15 minutes.
  • Ethereum trading volume becomes three times its recent average.
  • Solana experiences an unusual price fluctuation.
  • A supported cryptocurrency experiences a sudden increase in trading activity.

CryptoPulse can evaluate these conditions and notify subscribed users.

The platform is designed for market monitoring and analytics, not guaranteed price prediction or automated trading.

2. AWS Architecture

The architecture follows an event-driven, serverless design.

       Cryptocurrency Exchange APIs
                    |
                    v
          Market Data Producer
        (Python / WebSocket Client)
                    |
                    v
          Amazon Kinesis Data Streams
                    |
                    v
               AWS Lambda
             Data Processing
                    |
          +---------+----------+
          |                    |
          v                    v
    Amazon S3             Amazon DynamoDB
    Raw Market Data       Latest Market State
          |                    |
          v                    v
    AWS Glue Catalog     DynamoDB Streams
          |                    |
          v                    v
    Amazon Athena         AWS Lambda
          |                    |
          v                    v
    S3 Query Results      Amazon SNS
                               |
                               v
                       Email Notifications

The main components are:

AWS Service Responsibility
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams Real-time market data ingestion
AWS Lambda Event processing and market calculations
Amazon S3 Raw and processed historical data
Amazon DynamoDB Latest market state and alert records
DynamoDB Streams Trigger downstream alert processing
Amazon SNS Notification delivery
AWS Glue Data Catalog Dataset metadata and schemas
Amazon Athena Historical SQL analytics

The diagram represents the logical architecture. Each integration needs appropriate AWS configuration, IAM permissions, and event source mappings.

3. Step One: Collect Cryptocurrency Market Data

The first component is a market data producer.

We can build it using Python and connect it to supported cryptocurrency exchange APIs.

For continuous updates, WebSocket connections are useful because they allow the producer to receive market events without repeatedly polling an endpoint.

For example, CryptoPulse could monitor:

BTCUSDT
ETHUSDT
SOLUSDT
BNBUSDT
XRPUSDT

The exact feed depends on the metrics required.

Ticker streams can provide price and rolling market statistics. Individual trade streams can provide transaction-level information for custom volume calculations.

Before publishing events, normalize exchange-specific messages into a common structure.

Example event:

{
  "exchange": "example-exchange",
  "symbol": "BTCUSDT",
  "event_type": "ticker",
  "price": 68500.25,
  "volume_24h": 12500.75,
  "price_change_percent_24h": 2.85,
  "event_timestamp": "2026-11-13T09:30:00Z"
}

These values are illustrative, not live market data.

A consistent event format makes downstream processing easier, especially when supporting multiple exchanges.

4. Step Two: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams

Once the producer collects market events, it publishes them to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams.

Kinesis acts as the central ingestion layer.

Instead of connecting the producer directly to every processing component, events are published to a stream and consumed by downstream applications.

A useful partition key is the trading symbol:

BTCUSDT
ETHUSDT
SOLUSDT

This helps keep related records associated with the same shard and supports ordering within that shard.

Kinesis allows ingestion and processing capacity to be managed independently.

For production, consider:

  • Stream capacity and throughput.
  • Data retention requirements.
  • Consumer lag and iterator age.
  • Throttling and failed writes.
  • Producer retry and reconnection logic.

Exchange WebSocket connections can be interrupted, so the producer should be designed to reconnect and recover gracefully.

5. Step Three: AWS Lambda for Market Processing

AWS Lambda can consume Kinesis records through an event source mapping.

The processing function validates, transforms, and analyzes incoming market events.

Its responsibilities include:

  1. Validating incoming records.
  2. Normalizing exchange-specific fields.
  3. Calculating price changes and volume indicators.
  4. Updating the latest market state.
  5. Storing raw and processed information.

For example, a simple percentage price-change calculation looks like this:

def calculate_price_change(previous_price, current_price):
    if previous_price <= 0:
        return 0

    return (
        (current_price - previous_price)
        / previous_price
    ) * 100

Suppose Bitcoin's previous reference price was $65,000 and the current price is $66,300.

((66,300 - 65,000) / 65,000) × 100

= 2%

CryptoPulse can evaluate this result against a configured threshold.

One important detail: the system must define its monitoring window. A 2% change over one minute is different from a 2% change over 24 hours.

Use event timestamps and appropriate reference prices when calculating indicators.

6. Step Four: Amazon S3 for Historical Data

Real-time processing is useful, but historical information is equally important.

Amazon S3 provides durable storage for raw and processed market data.

A possible bucket structure:

cryptopulse-market-data/

    raw/
        exchange=binance/
            symbol=BTCUSDT/
                year=2026/
                    month=11/
                        day=13/

    processed/
        exchange=binance/
            symbol=BTCUSDT/
                year=2026/
                    month=11/
                        day=13/

    athena-results/

The raw zone preserves original or minimally transformed events. This is useful for auditing and reprocessing.

The processed zone contains normalized records for analytical queries.

Partitioning by exchange, symbol, and date can help reduce the amount of data scanned by Athena.

For larger datasets, consider Apache Parquet. Its columnar format can improve analytical query efficiency and help reduce scan costs.

Keep raw data, processed data, and Athena query results in separate prefixes.

7. Step Five: Amazon DynamoDB for Latest Market State

S3 is suitable for historical storage, but retrieving the latest price should not require scanning historical files.

Amazon DynamoDB can maintain the latest market state for each trading pair.

For example:

{
  "PK": "ASSET#BTCUSDT",
  "SK": "LATEST",
  "price": 66300.00,
  "volume_24h": 14500.50,
  "price_change_24h": 2.0,
  "updated_at": "2026-11-13T09:30:00Z"
}

The values are illustrative.

DynamoDB can also store alert records, including:

  • Asset symbol.
  • Alert type.
  • Observed value.
  • Configured threshold.
  • Event timestamp.
  • Notification status.

This makes it easier for the application to retrieve recent market information and alert history.

For production, design partition and sort keys around access patterns. Use conditional writes or other concurrency controls when multiple processing attempts could update the same market state.

8. Step Six: Detect Price Fluctuations and Volume Spikes

This is where CryptoPulse becomes more than a data collection pipeline.

Price movement detection

Suppose a user wants an alert whenever Bitcoin moves more than 2% within 15 minutes.

An illustrative rule:

IF 15-minute price change >= +2%
THEN create an upward movement alert

A downward movement rule could be:

IF 15-minute price change <= -2%
THEN create a downward movement alert

Thresholds should be configurable according to user preferences.

Trading-volume spike detection

A sudden increase in trading volume can indicate unusual market activity.

CryptoPulse can compare recent volume with a historical baseline.

Volume Ratio =
Recent 5-minute volume
/
Average 5-minute volume over baseline period

An illustrative rule:

IF Volume Ratio >= 3
THEN create a volume spike alert

This means recent volume is at least three times the selected baseline.

The comparison should use equivalent time windows and account for missing or incomplete data.

Historical indicators

The platform can also calculate:

  • Moving averages.
  • Percentage price changes.
  • Rolling trading volume.
  • High and low prices over selected periods.
  • Volatility measures.

These indicators help users explore market behavior, but they do not guarantee future price movements.

9. Step Seven: DynamoDB Streams and Lambda for Alerts

The architecture uses DynamoDB as the trigger for a second Lambda function.

This can be implemented using DynamoDB Streams.

When a market-state or alert record changes, DynamoDB Streams makes that change available to a downstream consumer.

A configured Lambda event source mapping invokes the alert-processing function.

Market Processing Lambda
          |
          v
     DynamoDB Update
          |
          v
    DynamoDB Streams
          |
          v
      Alert Lambda
          |
          v
       Amazon SNS
          |
          v
    Email Notification

The alert Lambda checks whether the event represents a valid notification.

It should verify:

  • The threshold condition was satisfied.
  • The alert is relevant to the user.
  • The notification has not already been sent.
  • The event is not an outdated update.

Use an idempotency key to reduce duplicate notifications. It could include the asset, alert type, monitoring window, and threshold configuration.

A cooldown period can also prevent repeated alerts for the same continuing market condition.

10. Step Eight: Amazon SNS for Automatic Notifications

Once the alert Lambda confirms that a notification should be delivered, it can publish a message to Amazon Simple Notification Service (SNS).

SNS supports notification delivery to configured subscribers, including email endpoints.

Example notification:

CryptoPulse Market Alert

Asset: BTCUSDT

Alert Type: Price Movement

Observed Change: +2.0%

Monitoring Window: 15 Minutes

Event Time: 09:30 UTC

Status: Threshold Triggered

This is an illustrative message.

Users can receive alerts about significant price movements, unusual volume spikes, or other configured market conditions.

SNS handles notification delivery. The application logic determines whether a market event deserves an alert.

11. Step Nine: AWS Glue and Amazon Athena for Historical Analytics

Real-time notifications tell users when something happens. Historical analytics help them understand market behavior over time.

AWS Glue Data Catalog maintains metadata about datasets stored in S3.

A Glue crawler can inspect supported data and infer table metadata. Alternatively, teams can define schemas explicitly.

Amazon Athena uses the Glue Data Catalog to discover tables and query the underlying S3 data using SQL.

This allows CryptoPulse to analyze historical cryptocurrency data without managing a separate database cluster for every analytical workload.

Query recent Bitcoin records 

SELECT
    event_timestamp,
    symbol,
    price,
    volume_24h
FROM cryptopulse_market_db.market_data
WHERE symbol = 'BTCUSDT'
  AND year = '2026'
  AND month = '11'
  AND day = '13'
ORDER BY event_timestamp DESC
LIMIT 100;

The table and partition names are examples and must match the actual dataset registered in Glue.

Find records with high reported volume 

SELECT
    symbol,
    event_timestamp,
    volume_24h
FROM cryptopulse_market_db.market_data
WHERE volume_24h > 10000
ORDER BY volume_24h DESC;

This query uses an illustrative absolute threshold. A proper volume-spike analysis should compare recent volume against a historical baseline.

Where are Athena results stored?

Athena writes query results to a configured S3 output location, for example:

s3://cryptopulse-market-data/athena-results/

Remember the different responsibilities:

  • S3 stores market datasets.
  • Glue Data Catalog stores metadata and table definitions.
  • Athena queries S3 datasets using SQL.
  • S3 stores Athena query output in the configured results location.

Glue does not automatically transform the market records. It provides metadata that helps analytical services understand the data.

12. Production Readiness: What Should We Consider?

A production market-monitoring platform must handle interruptions, duplicate events, delayed records, and sudden increases in market activity.

Some important engineering considerations include:

Data validation: Validate prices, volumes, timestamps, symbols, and event formats before processing.

Duplicate handling: Use exchange trade IDs or event identifiers where available. Make processing idempotent so retries do not double-count trades or create repeated alerts.

Event ordering: Events can arrive late or out of order. Use exchange timestamps and sequence identifiers where available instead of assuming arrival order represents event order.

Failure handling: Configure Kinesis/Lambda retry behavior, record-age limits, and an on-failure destination where appropriate. Monitor iterator age and processing errors.

Alert reliability: Store alert state and notification status. Use idempotency keys and cooldown periods.

Security: Apply least-privilege IAM roles, encrypt stored data, and use AWS Secrets Manager for exchange credentials when authenticated APIs are required.

Cost management: Monitor Kinesis capacity, Lambda execution, S3 storage, Glue activity, and Athena data scanned. Use partitioning and columnar formats to help control analytical costs.

13. Implementation Roadmap

CryptoPulse can be developed in manageable stages.

Phase 1: Market Data Ingestion

  • Select supported exchanges.
  • Build a Python producer.
  • Connect to WebSocket market streams.
  • Normalize incoming events.
  • Publish records to Kinesis Data Streams.

Phase 2: Real-Time Processing

  • Configure Kinesis-to-Lambda integration.
  • Validate and process records.
  • Calculate price and volume indicators.
  • Store raw and processed events in S3.
  • Update DynamoDB market state.

Phase 3: Alert Engine

  • Configure DynamoDB Streams.
  • Build the alert-processing Lambda.
  • Add configurable thresholds and cooldowns.
  • Integrate Amazon SNS.
  • Test duplicate-event handling.

Phase 4: Historical Analytics

  • Organize S3 datasets.
  • Create Glue database and table definitions.
  • Configure crawlers or explicit schemas.
  • Run historical SQL queries using Athena.
  • Store query results in a dedicated S3 prefix.

Phase 5: Production Hardening

  • Add monitoring and alarms.
  • Configure retries and failure handling.
  • Secure credentials and permissions.
  • Implement data retention policies.
  • Test recovery and load behavior.

14. Future Enhancements

Once the core pipeline is operational, CryptoPulse can evolve with additional capabilities.

  • Multi-exchange comparison: Compare the same trading pair across supported exchanges.
  • Custom user alerts: Allow users to configure assets, thresholds, and monitoring windows.
  • Market dashboards: Display current prices, historical movements, volume trends, and alerts.
  • Advanced analytics: Add volatility analysis, moving averages, and other indicators.
  • Machine learning experiments: Explore anomaly detection using historical market data and validated models.
  • Portfolio monitoring: Add optional user-configured asset watchlists with secure authentication and privacy controls.

These are potential extensions, not features automatically provided by the initial architecture.

Conclusion

Cryptocurrency markets generate enormous amounts of continuously changing information.

Collecting that information is only the first step. The real value comes from processing it, identifying unusual activity, preserving historical records, and making useful insights accessible.

CryptoPulse demonstrates how AWS services can work together to build this type of platform.

Amazon Kinesis Data Streams provides real-time ingestion. AWS Lambda processes incoming events. Amazon S3 stores historical data. DynamoDB maintains the latest market state. DynamoDB Streams supports event-driven alert processing. Amazon SNS delivers notifications. AWS Glue and Amazon Athena make historical analysis possible.

Together, these services provide a serverless foundation that can evolve as market-data volume and user requirements grow.

The goal of CryptoPulse is simple: don't just watch cryptocurrency prices—understand the market activity behind them.

Disclaimer: CryptoPulse is a conceptual market-monitoring and analytics project. It does not provide investment advice, guarantee price predictions, or execute trades.

References

  • Amazon Kinesis Data Streams Documentation
  • Using AWS Lambda with Amazon Kinesis
  • Amazon S3 Documentation
  • AWS Glue Data Catalog
  • Amazon Athena Documentation
  • DynamoDB Streams
  • Amazon SNS Documentation
  • Binance Spot WebSocket Market Streams

title: Rows in ThingsDB: Compact & Efficient Data Serialization
description:
In ThingsDB, wrapping is the preferred way to shape and return structured data.
By defining wrap-only types, you control exactly which fields and computed properties are exposed to your clients without mutating your underlying data models.

Normally, wrapping returns data as key-value objects. While this is readable and self-documenting, repeating property keys across thousands of items creates unnecessary payload overhead, especially when rendering tables or data grids where column positions are already known.

With the new row mode for types, you can instruct ThingsDB to serialize wrapped types as flat value arrays instead of objects. Let's walk through how it works.

1. Setting up a Demo Collection

To see row mode in action, let's set up a simple bookstore collection with Author and Book types:

new_type('Author');
new_type('Book');
new_type('BookStore');

set_type('Author', {
    id: '#',
    name: 'str',
    books: '{Book}'
});

set_type('Book', {
    id: '#',
    title: 'str',
    pages: 'int',
    author: 'Author?'
});

set_type('BookStore', {
    books: '{Book}',
    authors: '{Author}'
});

// Establish the two-way relation so Author.books is populated automatically
mod_type('Book', 'rel', 'author', 'books');

// Initialize the collection root with .books and .authors
.to_type('BookStore');

Next, let's populate the collection with a couple of authors and books:

tolkien = Author{ name: 'J.R.R. Tolkien' };
herbert = Author{ name: 'Frank Herbert' };

.authors.add(tolkien, herbert);

.books.add(
    Book{ title: 'The Hobbit', pages: 310, author: tolkien },
    Book{ title: 'The Lord of the Rings', pages: 1178, author: tolkien },
    Book{ title: 'Dune', pages: 412, author: herbert }
);

2. The Traditional Approach: Wrapping as Objects

Suppose we want to fetch a flat overview of all books containing the book's ID, title, page count, and the author's name. The standard approach is to create a wrap-only type (_Book) with a computed author method:

new_type('_Book', WPO);  // WPO = wrap-only type

set_type('_Book', {
    id: '#',
    title: 'str',
    pages: 'int',
    author: |this| this.author.name
});

When we query our books using .map_wrap('_Book'):

.books.map_wrap('_Book');

ThingsDB returns an array of objects:

[
    {
        "id": 1,
        "title": "The Hobbit",
        "pages": 310,
        "author": "J.R.R. Tolkien"
    },
    {
        "id": 2,
        "title": "The Lord of the Rings",
        "pages": 1178,
        "author": "J.R.R. Tolkien"
    },
    {
        "id": 3,
        "title": "Dune",
        "pages": 412,
        "author": "Frank Herbert"
    }
]

3. The Problem with Manual Array Mapping

If your dataset grows to thousands of books, repeating "id", "title", "pages", and "author" on every single record wastes bandwidth and serialization time.

Previously, the workaround was to manually map each item into an array:

.books.map(|book| [book.id(), book.title, book.pages, book.author.name]);

However, this has two major drawbacks:

  1. Repetition: You have to rewrite the mapping closure in every query that needs this format.
  2. Memory & CPU overhead: ThingsDB has to allocate and build a brand-new list of arrays in memory before it can even begin serializing the response.

4. The Solution: Enabling Row Mode

With row mode, you can configure _Book once to define the exact column order:

mod_type('_Book', 'row', ['id', 'title', 'pages', 'author']);

Now, calling the exact same .map_wrap() query:

.books.map_wrap('_Book');

Produces a compact, positional array of values:

[
    [1, "The Hobbit", 310, "J.R.R. Tolkien"],
    [2, "The Lord of the Rings", 1178, "J.R.R. Tolkien"],
    [3, "Dune", 412, "Frank Herbert"]
]

Why This Matters

  • Direct Serialization: Unlike .map(), map_wrap() streams the wrapped output directly during serialization without allocating intermediate arrays in memory.
  • Smaller Payloads: Stripping out repetitive keys significantly reduces network payload sizes for large result sets.
  • Reusable Schema: Your column layout is defined centrally on the type rather than scattered across application queries, while still benefiting from computed type methods like author in this example.
