title: Moving a desktop app from PostgreSQL to SQLite without losing a cent
description:
Why PostgreSQL had to go

Personal Finance Intelligence (PFI) is a local-first budgeting app for Windows: a WinUI 3 shell, a FastAPI backend and Next.js screens, with no account and no cloud. Up to version 0.3 it ran its own private PostgreSQL server inside the user's data folder.

That worked, but it was the wrong tool for a single-user desktop app. The Microsoft Store build tripped over PostgreSQL's files, PostgreSQL could not run from the Store's read-only install folder without copying its binaries elsewhere first, and the app carried a whole database server for one user. Version 0.4 moved everyone to a single SQLite file; 0.5 removed PostgreSQL, which made the app about a third smaller to download and 155 MB smaller on disk.

The hard part was not SQLite. It was moving real people's money records from one database to another on their own PCs, with nobody there to fix it if it went wrong.

The rules

Three rules decided every design choice:

  1. Never lose a cent. Every amount must arrive exactly, and the app must prove it, not assume it.
  2. Never touch the original until the copy is proven. If anything fails, the user keeps running on their old data as if nothing happened.
  3. Never delete on the user's behalf. The old database is kept after the move and only removed when the user asks, one release later.

Exact money in SQLite

PostgreSQL has a real NUMERIC type; SQLite does not, and storing amounts as floats would make 0.10 + 0.20 drift. PFI stores every amount as an integer scaled by 10², so CHF 12.34 is 1234. A small SQLAlchemy TypeDecorator does the conversion in both directions:

class ExactDecimal(TypeDecorator):
    """A decimal stored as an integer scaled by 10 ** scale."""
    impl = BigInteger
    cache_ok = True

    def __init__(self, scale: int) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.scale = scale
        self._factor = Decimal(10) ** scale
        self._quantum = Decimal(1).scaleb(-scale)

    def process_bind_param(self, value, dialect):
        if value is None:
            return None
        return int((Decimal(str(value)) * self._factor)
                   .to_integral_value(ROUND_HALF_EVEN))

    def process_result_value(self, value, dialect):
        if value is None:
            return None
        return (Decimal(int(value)) / self._factor).quantize(self._quantum)

Money = ExactDecimal(2)

Because the database only ever sees integers, SUM() and comparisons are exact, and they run inside SQLite rather than in Python. Rounding is half-to-even, as a NUMERIC(p, 2) column would do. A test adds ten amounts of 0.10 and one of −1,234,567.89 and checks the total is exactly −1,234,566.89.

The copy: prove it, then switch

On the first start of 0.4, if the data folder still held a PostgreSQL cluster, the app moved it before opening anything else:

  1. Start the old PostgreSQL one last time and bring its schema up to the newest 0.3 version.
  2. Create the new database as pfi.sqlite.part, never as the real file name, and run the SQLite schema migrations on it.
  3. Copy every table in foreign-key order, 2,000 rows at a time, with foreign keys switched off during the copy. Timestamps with a time zone are converted to UTC, because SQLite keeps no time zones.
  4. Check the copy: the same row count in every table, the same SUM(amount) over all transactions (exact, thanks to the integer cents), and PRAGMA foreign_key_check returning nothing.
  5. Only then rename pfi.sqlite.part to pfi.sqlite with os.replace, which is atomic on the same disk.
  6. Rename the old pgdata folder to pgdata-0.3. Nothing is deleted.

If any check fails, the .part file is removed and the user sees a plain message: nothing was changed, the old data is still in use, and the log file to send. The core of the check:

src_sum = sconn.scalar(select(func.coalesce(
    func.sum(source.tables["transactions"].c.amount), 0)))
dest_sum = dconn.scalar(select(func.sum(Transaction.amount)))
if Decimal(str(src_sum)) != (dest_sum or Decimal("0.00")):
    raise LegacyError("The transaction total differs after copying ...")
broken = dconn.execute(text("PRAGMA foreign_key_check")).fetchall()
if broken:
    raise LegacyError(f"{len(broken)} broken references after copying ...")

While 0.4 was current, the build tested this path on every build: its smoke test created a 0.3-style PostgreSQL cluster with sample data, started the new app on it and compared the totals.

What if it stops halfway?

A reader asked the right question: what happens if the PC loses power in the middle of the copy?

Nothing breaks, by construction. Until step 5 the real pfi.sqlite does not exist and pgdata has not been renamed, so on the next start the app sees exactly what it saw the first time: an old cluster and no SQLite file. It deletes any leftover pfi.sqlite.part (and its -wal and -shm files) and starts the copy again from scratch. There is no “resume” to get wrong, because the copy is all or nothing.

Old backups needed the same care. Version 0.3 wrote backups with pg_dump, and a user might restore one months later. Version 0.4 could still read them: it restored the .dump into a throw-away PostgreSQL cluster in a temporary folder, then ran the same checked copy into SQLite. Since 0.5, which no longer ships PostgreSQL, the app explains that a .dump file needs 0.4.0 and links to that installer.

Retiring PostgreSQL, one release later

Version 0.4 still shipped PostgreSQL, but only to perform the move once. Version 0.5 removed it completely:

  • Settings shows an “Old data from PFI 0.3” row with the size of what is left (pgdata-0.3, the copied binaries, old server logs) and deletes it only when the user clicks. Old .dump backups are deleted only if the user ticks a separate box.
  • If someone jumps straight from 0.3 to 0.5, the app does not guess. It refuses to open the old data and shows a page explaining that 0.4.0 must run once first, with a link to that installer.

The result: one SQLite file instead of a database server, no background service, backups that are a single zip of that file, and an app about a third smaller to download. My own data went from 0.3 to 0.4 to 0.5 this way, and I checked each step in the logs.

What I'd do again

  • Write to a temporary name, verify, then rename. It turns “what if it crashes halfway” into a non-question.
  • Check totals, not just row counts. A row count can match while an amount was rounded; an exact sum cannot.
  • Keep the old data for a release. Disk space is cheap; a user's ten years of transactions are not.
  • Make the error messages say what to do. Every failure above tells the user that nothing changed and what to try next.

The same idea now runs the other way: version 0.5.1 adds a “Test this backup” button that opens a backup in a temporary folder and compares balances, counts and a random sample of transactions with the live data, without restoring anything.

PFI is free and open source (MIT). I built it with Claude as a coding assistant; the design decisions, testing on my own data and the releases are mine.

title: The progress bar that made typing lag: debugging a 331 ms INP in a React game
description:
TL;DR: A friend told me that typing felt laggy in Museek, my free multiplayer music quiz. I was sure the culprit was my autocomplete filtering. The profiler disagreed. The real problem was a progress bar animating its width once per second, plus a full-screen backdrop-filter: blur(). Switching the bar to transform cut background Rendering time by roughly 7x and took keystrokes out of the slow interactions list.

The bug report

Museek is a browser-based "blind test": up to 12 players each bring a Spotify, Deezer or Apple Music playlist, a song snippet plays, and everyone types the artist and title as fast as they can. It's built with Next.js 16, React 19 and Tailwind 4, with a Node/Socket.io backend.

A friend playing a game sent me this: "There's a delay between what I type and what shows up in the answer field."

In a game where you're racing a 30-second timer, that's not a cosmetic issue.

My first guess (and why it was wrong)

Each answer field has an autocomplete. On every render, my Game component filtered the whole song and artist database, and called a fairly expensive normalizeString() (Unicode NFD normalization plus two regexes) twice per item. Worse, it normalized the user's input again for every single item, inside the loop:

const filteredArtists = (database_artists || [])
  .filter((a) => {
    if (!artistQuery || artistQuery.length < 3) return false;
    const search = normalizeString(artistQuery); // once per item!
    return normalizeString(a.artist).includes(search)
      || normalizeString(a.internationalArtist).includes(search);
  })
  .slice(0, 5);

A quick benchmark gave about 18 ms per render with 2,000 artists and 2,000 tracks on my PC. That's enough to hurt on a phone, so I fixed the cheap part straight away: normalize the input once per render, and skip the loop entirely below 3 characters.

const artistSearch = normalizeString(artistQuery);

const filteredArtists =
  artistQuery.length < 3
    ? []
    : (database_artists || []).filter(/* ...uses artistSearch... */).slice(0, 5);

But one detail didn't fit. With the CPU throttled in DevTools, the lag started from the very first letter, and the filter does nothing below 3 characters. Something else was going on, so I stopped guessing and opened the Performance panel.

Step 1: measure properly (and beware of your extensions)

My setup: Chrome DevTools → Performance, CPU throttling at 4x (roughly a mid-range phone), record, type about ten letters, stop.

First result: INP 510 ms. Terrible. But the call stack under the slow keystroke looked odd: onCommitFiberRoot, handleCommitFiberRoot, then a long chain of updateFiberRecursively. And the "Forced reflow" insight pointed at measureHostInstance @ installHook.js.

installHook.js is injected by the React Developer Tools extension. After every React commit, it walks the component tree and measures elements on screen, which forces a layout. On that keystroke, Museek's own code accounted for 12.8 ms. The extension was responsible for most of the 191 ms of reflow.

Lesson #1: profile in an incognito window, where extensions are disabled by default. Your users don't run React DevTools.

Step 2: the real numbers

Same test, incognito window, 4x CPU, on the live site:

  • INP: 331 ms
  • INP breakdown: input delay 3 ms, processing 297 ms, presentation delay 31 ms
  • Inside that processing time: a single purple Layout of ~290 ms, triggered by Event: textInput
  • Scripting for the whole interaction: about 30 ms

So JavaScript wasn't the bottleneck. Layout was. And the summary showed the page was busy even when nobody typed: 2,217 ms of Rendering and 954 ms of Painting over an 11.6-second recording. That's more than a quarter of the time spent laying out and painting.

Then the Animations track: a continuous chain of width segments, one per second.

Step 3: find the pattern

Zooming in on the slow keystroke, the timing was suspicious. It landed exactly at the start of a new width segment, right after a tick of the game clock.

The animated element was my timer bar:

<div
  className="h-full rounded-full transition-all duration-1000 ease-linear ..."
  style={{ width: `${((totalPhaseTime - timeLeft) / totalPhaseTime) * 100}%` }}
/>

Every second, timeLeft changes. That one state update does three things at once:

  1. it updates the "Time left" text under the bar,
  2. it updates the same text in the header of the open answer field,
  3. it starts a new 1-second width transition on the bar.

All three invalidate layout. Animating width is especially bad: the browser has to recompute layout on every frame of the transition. If a keystroke arrives right at that moment, the browser has to finish all that layout work before it can paint the new letter. Keystrokes between two ticks stayed fast, which matches what my friend felt: not constant lag, but stutters.

One surprise: only 10 of 83 nodes needed layout, and it still took 262 ms on one capture. The node count wasn't the issue. The keystroke simply had to pay for the layout that the clock tick had just invalidated.

The fix: transform instead of width

transform and opacity are the two properties browsers can animate on the compositor (the GPU), without running layout. So the bar now always has full width and slides in from the left with translateX, inside a container that has overflow: hidden:

<div className="h-2 w-full overflow-hidden rounded-full bg-(--white)/20">
  <div
    className="h-full w-full rounded-full transition-transform duration-1000 ease-linear will-change-transform ..."
    style={{ transform: `translateX(-${(timeLeft / totalPhaseTime) * 100}%)` }}
  />
</div>

A few details:

  • Why translateX and not scaleX? scaleX would squash the rounded ends when the bar is short. Translating a full-width bar inside a clipped container looks identical and keeps the corners round.
  • transition-all → transition-transform. transition-all watches every property, so any change can trigger an expensive transition. Only transition what you actually animate. (Small trade-off: the bar's color now switches instantly between phases instead of fading.)
  • will-change-transform promotes the bar to its own compositor layer.
  • tabular-nums on the countdown text. With proportional digits, "10s" and "9s" have different widths, so the text shifts every second. Tabular digits all have the same width, so nothing around them moves.

Result

Same test, production build (run locally this time), incognito, 4x CPU. The Animations track now says transform instead of width.

Over the recording Before (11.6 s) After (7.8 s)
Rendering 2,217 ms (19%) 213 ms (2.7%)
Painting 954 ms (8.2%) 71 ms (0.9%)

Relative to recording length, that's about 7x less Rendering and 9x less Painting. Most importantly, keystrokes disappeared from the slow interactions. The INP was still 368 ms, but the worst interaction was now a click, not a keystroke.

Bonus round: the full-screen blur

That slow click was the one that opens the answer field. Its breakdown was very different:

  • processing: 13 ms
  • presentation delay: 353 ms

My code reacted instantly. The browser took 353 ms to show the result. When the field opens, a full-screen overlay appears behind it with backdrop-blur-sm. Blurring the whole viewport (including an animated timer bar and an SVG noise background) is expensive GPU work, and it doesn't show up as JavaScript or Layout on the main thread.

I removed the blur and made the background slightly more opaque to keep the dimming effect (/60 → /80). The click's presentation delay dropped to 237 ms, with 1 ms of processing.

One last tweak: the overlay was mounted conditionally ({isActive && <div ... />}), so every opening forced the browser to create and paint a brand new full-screen layer. Now it's always in the DOM, and only its opacity changes:

<div
  aria-hidden="true"
  className={`fixed inset-0 z-40 bg-(--background)/80 transition-opacity duration-250 ease-out ${
    isActive ? "opacity-100" : "pointer-events-none opacity-0"
  }`}
/>

After that, only the very first opening of the field is still slow (about 270 ms at 4x, a one-time cost to create the layer). Later openings no longer show up as long interactions, and you get a fade-out on close for free.

What I'm taking away from this

  1. Profile in incognito. React DevTools alone turned a 331 ms problem into a 510 ms one and pointed me at the wrong function.
  2. Read the INP breakdown before touching code. High processing means your code (or forced layout). High presentation delay means rendering and GPU work. They need completely different fixes.
  3. A timer running while the user types can cost more than your JavaScript. Animate transform and opacity, never width, and avoid transition-all.
  4. Full-screen backdrop-filter isn't free, especially on low-end phones and on top of other animations.
  5. Your first hypothesis is just a hypothesis. My autocomplete fix was still worth keeping, but it wasn't the bug my friend was hitting.

The changes are in two small commits in the Museek repository: dfddfd7 and 02a0f42.

If you want to check that typing is smooth now, start a game on Museek: it's free, there's no account, and you can play with friends using your own playlists. You can also read the full case study on my portfolio.

title: Enhanced integrations and local data management in Relay
description:
Generated by AI for testing my app Relay

I have worked on significantly improving how Relay connects to external services and securing local data across multiple platforms. The app now feels more complete, with deeper integration capabilities for publishing content, managing notes, and running complex terminals locally.

Core Application Stability and Deployment

The foundational structure of the application has undergone several updates. I scaffolded Relay from the Wails3 React template and upgraded to various versions of Wails and Go. This included establishing CI builds that support macOS, Windows, and Linux simultaneously. The app can now run in the background with a tray icon and proper app naming conventions across installers and bundles.

For development experience, I added features like version checking for the status page and improved release handling so that publishing happens directly from CI rather than relying on drafts. I also ensured better backward compatibility by addressing multiple system-specific bugs, such as those related to SmartScreen warnings on Windows setup or incorrect behavior in settings menus.

Content Creation and Integration

I focused heavily on making content creation more streamlined through key integrations:

  • Buffer: Added comprehensive support for Buffer, allowing sign-in using OAuth (Authorization Code + PKCE). I implemented a full workflow that includes the ability to create, list, edit, and draft ideas directly within Relay. Users can now see scheduled posts in a dedicated queue panel, and the composer reviews drafts before sending them.
  • Dev.to: The system can now handle publishing articles and syncing existing content with Dev.to. I also addressed how links are handled for posts that have not been published yet.
  • Plane Kanban & Notes: I rebuilt the Plane integration to include a full cross-project inbox, enhanced kanban boards with drag capabilities and filters, module lanes view, and item drawers that now support comments and activity tracking. Quick capture is available via ⌘K for immediate note saving.

Local Vault and Security

To improve data security and user experience across different operating systems, I built out the following features:

  • Encrypted Storage: Implemented a dedicated vault using AES-256-GCM storage, which requires a keychain key for access. This ensures sensitive project and module data is locally secured.
  • Biometric Locking: On macOS, I added functionality to lock projects and modules behind Touch ID authentication.
  • Secrets Management: I moved secrets out of plaintext configuration files (config.toml) and now require them to be stored in the OS keychain or local file systems for maximum security.

Advanced Terminal Capabilities

The terminal experience received a major overhaul, providing a much more robust development environment:

  • Session Management: I implemented Go-owned PTY sessions that support detaching and reattaching, similar to tmux.
  • Enhanced UI: The xterm integration now includes panes, tabs, and splits, with functionality for zooming and dragging between windows. A quick terminal view (⌘/) is available over all other application views. I also added logic to detect installed shells so the app can automatically pick one on startup, even if standard shells like zsh or bash are unavailable.

AI Providers Layer

I introduced a dedicated provider layer in Go to manage multiple local and cloud-based generative AI services. This now supports:

  • Cloud Services: OpenAI, Anthropic, and OpenRouter providers.
  • Local Services: Automatic detection for Ollama and LM Studio local providers.
  • The settings section is updated to allow testing a model before saving it, and includes mechanisms to block locked data from being sent to cloud AI services.

What's next
I plan on updating the documentation with the latest changes and addressing remaining minor UI/UX touch-ups across different views.

title: Port 1433 Exposed: How Weak SQL Server Passwords Led to a Miner and a RAT
description:
Port 1433 is the door many website databases still leave on the public internet. A campaign described by FortiGuard Labs this week is about something more basic than stopping injection in the application: a Microsoft SQL Server left reachable from outside, with a weak administrator password.

In research published on 12 November 2026, FortiGuard researcher Xiaopeng Zhang says the lab found the campaign in early October. The malware scans for SQL Servers open on the SQL Server default port, 1433, then tries to log in. After a successful login it uses built-in SQL Server features to run commands on the Windows server, and installs a Monero miner and a remote-access trojan. Infosecurity Magazine notes that the report does not say how many servers were compromised or who is behind the campaign.

If your site or app sits on SQL Server, the useful question is not whether you are in the unnamed victim list. It is whether that SQL Server port is reachable from the internet, and whether the sa or admin password would survive a long password list.

What Fortinet reported

FortiGuard says the initial payload is a Go-based program that embeds the open-source Naabu port scanner. It retrieves a target address range from an attacker-controlled server, then looks for hosts with TCP port 1433 open. A companion brute-force tool then tries usernames such as sa and admin against a list of more than 2,700 passwords. CSO Online, reporting on the same research, uses the same figures.

After a login, the malware runs Transact-SQL (T-SQL) commands on the server. Those commands enable xp_cmdshell, a SQL Server feature that runs operating-system commands, then download or unpack a loader. Fortinet and Infosecurity both describe the loader pulling further malware from the attackers' infrastructure.

One payload, named to look like a Microsoft Edge update, is an XMRig-based Monero miner that uses the compromised server's CPU. Another, named after a Windows system process, was identified as a Gh0st RAT variant. Fortinet says its features include keylogging and data theft, with more than 30 control commands, and plugins for screen capture and remote desktop. The C2 server had already shut down before Fortinet's analysis, so that part of the work was static.

The malware also tries to stay. Fortinet says the first payload creates a scheduled task that runs every 30 minutes, with a name that imitates a Microsoft Edge update. The downloader sets another task; the Gh0st RAT uses a registry Run key, a Windows service and a further scheduled task. Infosecurity also reports a copy placed in the Startup folder so it ran at boot, and says each compromised server was registered with the attackers' backend.

Why an exposed port 1433 matters to site owners

Many websites and web apps sit on SQL Server databases. Some of those databases end up on a host or a cloud virtual machine with port 1433 open to the world, often because of a leftover firewall rule, a development shortcut or a "temporary" remote-admin path that was never closed. A weak or reused sa password then turns that exposure into a full server compromise. That is a database security failure as much as a firewall one. CSO quotes Sectigo's Jason Soroko on the same point: remove direct internet access to SQL Server, restrict connections to approved systems, and enforce strong, unique credentials.

This is the same class of failure as an open login form that never rate-limits guesses, only the target is the database instead of the site. Our brute-force login protection guide is about closing that pattern on a website. If you later find a miner or a remote-access tool on the box, telling a brute-force technique from an infection helps you decide what to rebuild and what to rotate. And if the database lives with a host, be clear about what your host handles and what you still need to check, including which ports are public.

What to check this week

  1. Keep port 1433 off the public internet. SQL Server should accept connections from the application server or a private network, not from every address on the internet. Ask your host or cloud provider which public ports are open, and close 1433 if it is among them.
  2. Lock down or disable the sa account. Do not leave a default or shared administrator password in place. If you do not need sa, disable it and use named accounts with only the rights they need.
  3. Use strong, unique passwords. The password list in this campaign had more than 2,700 entries. A reused or obvious admin password is enough.
  4. Leave xp_cmdshell disabled. Fortinet says the attackers turned it on after they logged in so they could run operating-system commands. Unless you have a documented reason to use it, keep it off, and watch for attempts to enable it.
  5. Look for leftover persistence if the server was ever exposed. Unexpected scheduled tasks that imitate a Microsoft Edge update, unfamiliar programs in the Startup folder, or a new Windows service deserve a closer look, and usually a restore from a clean backup.

A public look from an outside-in website security scanner can show what your website exposes from the outside, on a domain you own or have permission to test. It is not a substitute for a database-port and credential review, and it should not be used as a brute-force test against anyone else's server. We build HackerMe.

FAQ

How do I know if SQL Server is reachable from the internet?

Ask your host or cloud firewall which public ports are open. Port 1433 is the SQL Server default port. If that port is reachable from addresses you do not trust, close it and allow only the application servers that need it.

Should I disable the sa account?

If you do not need it, yes. If you do, give it a strong unique password, restrict where it can log in from, and do not use it as the application's everyday account.

What is xp_cmdshell, and why does it matter?

It is a built-in SQL Server feature that runs operating-system commands. Fortinet says this campaign enabled it after a successful login, then used it to drop a miner and a remote-access trojan. Keep it disabled unless you have a clear, temporary reason to turn it on.

Originally published on the HackerMe security blog.

title: I built a finance engine that reconciles bank emails, SMS and PDF statements into one ledger
description:
Every month I had the same problem: my money lives in three places — HBL, ABL and NayaPay — and no single app shows the whole picture. Transfers arrive as emails, card spends arrive as SMS, and the "official" record only shows up weeks later in a PDF statement.

So I built FinSync: a personal finance engine that pulls transactions from every channel, collapses duplicates, reconciles them against bank statements, and turns it all into one clean ledger with analytics and a forecast.

👉 Live demo (no signup): https://finsync-green.vercel.app — click "View live demo"
👉 Source: https://github.com/danishzulfiqar/FinSync

The problem: no bank APIs in Pakistan

In the US or Europe, a budgeting app connects to your bank in two clicks through Plaid, TrueLayer or a PSD2 open-banking API. In Pakistan, none of that exists for everyday users:

  • No public APIs. Banks don't offer developer APIs to read your own account data.
  • No aggregators. There's no Plaid-style service that supports local banks, so global apps like YNAB or Mint simply can't connect.
  • No clean exports. Most banks give you a PDF statement — not a CSV — and only for past months.

So your own financial data is locked inside three separate apps, and the only things the banks do hand you are the notifications they already send: SMS alerts, emails and PDF statements. FinSync is built entirely on those — the data you already legitimately receive — without scraping banking apps, reverse-engineering private APIs or ever asking for a password or OTP.

The real problem: one payment, three copies

A single card payment can reach me as:

  1. a real-time SMS (merchant, exact time, no balance),
  2. a notification email (reference number, sender name), and
  3. a statement line a month later (running balance, generic description, posting date — not the transaction time).

Naively importing all three triples your spending. Naively deduplicating on amount + date merges two genuinely different ₨1,500 payments on the same day. The interesting engineering is everything in between.

Architecture

Five tiers, one direction of flow: the signals banks already send → read-only ingestion → a deterministic reconciliation engine → a ledger where every real event is exactly one row → analytics on top.

  • Backend: Python 3.12, FastAPI, SQLAlchemy 2, Alembic, PostgreSQL, pdfplumber
  • Frontend: React 18, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind, Recharts
  • Infra: Render (API), Neon (Postgres), Vercel (dashboard)

1. One transaction, many sources

The key modelling decision: a financial event and the evidence for it are different things.

There's one transactions table and a separate transaction_sources table. When the same payment arrives via email and SMS and statement, those become three sources attached to one transaction — never three transactions. Each extra source raises the record's confidence and can fill in blank fields.

2. Deterministic fingerprints

Every parsed event gets a SHA-256 fingerprint built from:

provider + type + amount + currency + account_last4 + reference + rounded time bucket

Ingestion then resolves to one of four outcomes:

Outcome Action
unique create a new transaction
exact_duplicate same fingerprint → attach the source only
probable_duplicate same money, close in time → attach, raise confidence, enrich fields
needs_review similar but conflicting reference → keep both and flag

That last rule matters: when in doubt, FinSync never silently deletes money. Re-processing the same email or SMS is a no-op, guarded by unique source IDs and content hashes — so every sync is idempotent.

3. Reconciling alerts with statements

Fingerprints can't catch the alert-vs-statement case, because the statement has a different date and often no reference. A separate reconciliation pass handles it:

  • match by reference when both sides have one (strong signal),
  • otherwise the nearest time within a few days, same direction and amount,
  • keep the statement row (it carries the authoritative running balance),
  • enrich it with the alert's merchant and exact time, repoint the alert's source onto it, and drop the duplicate.

The result: balances that reconcile to the rupee, with the rich details from the real-time alerts.

4. Analytics and forecasting

Once the ledger is clean, the fun part is easy:

  • per-account balances anchored on the newest statement running balance,
  • income/expense flows that exclude internal transfers between my own accounts,
  • "learn-once" categorization — re-categorize one merchant and every matching row follows,
  • a Monte-Carlo balance forecast for the next few months.

Security: read-only by design

Handling bank data means being strict about what not to do:

  • Gmail access is read-only OAuth (gmail.readonly), nothing else.
  • No scraping of banking apps, no private APIs, never stores passwords, OTPs, PINs or card numbers.
  • Raw SMS text isn't persisted — only normalized fields plus a one-way hash for dedup.
  • The SMS webhook is authenticated with HMAC-SHA256 and timestamp anti-replay.

What I learned

  • Model evidence separately from facts. The transaction_sources split made every later feature simpler.
  • Make ingestion idempotent from day one. Being able to re-run any sync safely is what makes debugging bearable.
  • Prefer "keep both and flag" over clever merging. A false merge is far worse than a visible duplicate.
  • Test parsers with real (redacted) samples. The test suite (71 tests) is mostly parser, dedup and reconciliation cases.

Try the demo at https://finsync-green.vercel.app and have a look at the code on GitHub. I'd love feedback — especially on the reconciliation strategy. How do you deal with the same transaction showing up in multiple places?

title: Byg en tilgængelig informationsside med HTML og CSS
description:
Forestil dig, at en boligforening skal have fjernet et stort træ fra et fællesareal.

Beboerne skal vide, hvornår arbejdet finder sted, hvilke områder der bliver berørt, og hvem de kan kontakte.

Det er en lille kommunikationsopgave, men den er oplagt til at lære noget om moderne HTML.

For hvordan bygger man en informationsside, som er nem at læse på mobil, fungerer med tastatur og giver mening for en skærmlæser?

I denne tutorial bygger vi en enkel side med semantisk HTML og almindelig CSS.

Ingen JavaScript-frameworks. Ingen eksterne komponentbiblioteker.

Og faktisk behøver vi slet ikke JavaScript.

Eksemplet handler om formidling af planlagt arbejde. Det er ikke et system til at vurdere træers stabilitet, godkende afspærringer eller planlægge sikkerheden ved træfældning.

1. Hvad skal siden kunne?

Vi tager udgangspunkt i et tænkt eksempel.

En boligforening i Kolding har planlagt professionel træfældning af et træ på et fællesareal.

Beboerne skal kunne finde fire oplysninger:

  • Hvad arbejdet handler om
  • Hvornår det forventes at foregå
  • Hvilke praktiske ændringer der er planlagt
  • Hvem de kan kontakte ved spørgsmål

Derudover ønsker vi, at siden fungerer godt på små skærme.

Indholdet skal være let at læse, og besøgende skal kunne åbne supplerende information med tastaturet.

Vi bygger det hele i én HTML-fil, så eksemplet er let at teste.

2. Start med semantisk HTML

En webside kan bygges med mange div-elementer.

Men HTML har allerede elementer, der beskriver indholdets funktion.

Vi bruger blandt andet:

  • header til sidens introduktion
  • main til hovedindholdet
  • section til selvstændige afsnit
  • time til tidsoplysninger
  • details og summary til supplerende information
  • footer til afsluttende oplysninger

Det gør dokumentet mere forståeligt for både udviklere og hjælpemidler.

Opret en fil med navnet index.html.

<!doctype html>
<html lang="da">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport"
        content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">

  <title>Information om planlagt træarbejde</title>
  <meta name="description"
        content="Praktisk information om planlagt træarbejde på et fællesareal.">

  <link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">
</head>

<body>
  <header class="site-header">
    <div class="container">
      <p class="eyebrow">Beboerinformation</p>
      <h1>Planlagt træarbejde på fællesarealet</h1>
      <p>
        Her finder du den praktiske information
        om det kommende arbejde.
      </p>
    </div>
  </header>

  <main id="main-content" class="container">
    <section aria-labelledby="overview-title">
      <h2 id="overview-title">Overblik</h2>
      <p>
        Der er planlagt arbejde med et træ
        på ejendommens fællesareal.
      </p>
    </section>
  </main>

  <footer class="site-footer">
    <div class="container">
      <p>Eksempel på en informationsside.</p>
    </div>
  </footer>
</body>
</html>

Bemærk, at lang="da" står på html-elementet.

Det fortæller browseren og relevante hjælpemidler, at sidens primære sprog er dansk.

Vi bruger også kun ét h1-element og en naturlig rækkefølge af overskrifter.

Det er et godt udgangspunkt for en tydelig dokumentstruktur.

3. Vis tidspunktet med det rigtige HTML-element

En dato kan selvfølgelig skrives som almindelig tekst.

Men HTML har også elementet time.

Det gør det muligt at angive datoen i et maskinlæsbart format.

Tilføj denne sektion inde i main:

<section class="notice" aria-labelledby="when-title">
  <h2 id="when-title">Hvornår foregår arbejdet?</h2>

  <p>
    Forventet arbejdsdag:
    <time datetime="2027-04-15">
      15. april 2027
    </time>
  </p>

  <p>
    Forventet tidsrum:
    <time datetime="09:00">09.00</time>
    til
    <time datetime="14:00">14.00</time>
  </p>

  <p class="notice-note">
    Tidspunktet er foreløbigt og skal bekræftes
    af den ansvarlige for ejendommen.
  </p>
</section>

Datoen er kun eksempeldata, ikke en virkelig aftale.

I et rigtigt projekt skal den ansvarlige person bekræfte både dato og tidspunkt, før siden bliver offentliggjort.

En vigtig detalje er, at maskinlæsbar HTML ikke gør oplysningerne korrekte.

datetime beskriver datoens format.

Det kontrollerer ikke, om arbejdet faktisk er planlagt.

4. Beskriv praktiske ændringer tydeligt

En informationsside bør ikke gøre det svært for læseren at finde det vigtigste.

Forestil dig, at en parkeringsplads eller en sti bliver påvirket af arbejdet.

Så skal oplysningerne stå tydeligt.

Vi kan bruge en almindelig liste.

<section aria-labelledby="access-title">
  <h2 id="access-title">Praktiske forhold</h2>

  <p>
    Følgende forhold forventes at gælde,
    hvis arbejdsplanen godkendes:
  </p>

  <ul class="info-list">
    <li>
      En del af fællesarealet kan være afspærret.
    </li>
    <li>
      Enkelte adgangsveje kan blive påvirket.
    </li>
    <li>
      Beboerne får besked om eventuelle
      ændringer i parkeringen.
    </li>
    <li>
      Afspærringer skal respekteres.
    </li>
  </ul>

  <p>
    Den endelige afspærring og adgangsløsning
    fastlægges af de ansvarlige fagfolk
    og relevante parter.
  </p>
</section>

Det er vigtigt ikke at lade denne type eksempeltekst fremstå som en godkendt sikkerhedsplan.

En hjemmeside kan informere om en plan.

Den kan ikke erstatte den konkrete vurdering af arbejdsområdet.

Hvis en adgangsvej bliver ændret, skal informationen stemme med den faktiske, godkendte løsning.

5. Brug details og summary uden JavaScript

Nogle oplysninger behøver ikke være synlige hele tiden.

Det kan eksempelvis være en forklaring af, hvad beboerne skal gøre, hvis arbejdsdatoen ændrer sig.

Her er details og summary nyttige.

<section aria-labelledby="faq-title">
  <h2 id="faq-title">Ofte stillede spørgsmål</h2>

  <details>
    <summary>Kan tidspunktet blive ændret?</summary>
    <p>
      Ja. Hvis planen ændres, skal informationen
      på siden opdateres.
    </p>
  </details>

  <details>
    <summary>Må beboerne bruge fællesarealet?</summary>
    <p>
      Følg de konkrete oplysninger fra
      ejendommens ansvarlige og respekter
      eventuelle afspærringer.
    </p>
  </details>

  <details>
    <summary>Hvem kan svare på spørgsmål?</summary>
    <p>
      Kontakt ejendommens administrator
      via de officielle kontaktoplysninger.
    </p>
  </details>
</section>

Browseren håndterer selv åbning og lukning.

Det betyder, at vi ikke behøver skrive JavaScript til en almindelig informationsboks.

De indbyggede elementer giver også en tastaturbetjent kontrol.

Det er ofte bedre end at opfinde en klikbar div og derefter forsøge at tilføje alle de manglende funktioner.

6. Tilføj et synligt kontaktområde

Når noget ændrer sig på en ejendom, kan beboerne have spørgsmål.

Derfor bør kontaktoplysninger være lette at finde.

Vi laver en enkel kontaktsektion.

<section class="contact-box"
         aria-labelledby="contact-title">

  <h2 id="contact-title">Spørgsmål om arbejdet?</h2>

  <p>
    Kontakt ejendommens administrator
    for oplysninger om den planlagte opgave.
  </p>

  <p>
    <strong>Kontakt:</strong>
    Ejendommens administration
  </p>

  <p>
    De officielle kontaktoplysninger
    indsættes, når de er bekræftet.
  </p>
</section>

I dette eksempel indsætter vi ikke et opdigtet telefonnummer eller en e-mailadresse.

Det er bedre at vise tydeligt, at oplysningerne mangler, end at opfinde en kontaktperson.

I et rigtigt system bør siden ikke publiceres som færdig beboerinformation, før de nødvendige kontaktoplysninger er bekræftet.

7. Gør designet responsivt med CSS

Nu har vi en grundlæggende HTML-struktur.

Næste skridt er at gøre siden behagelig at læse på både mobil og computer.

Opret filen style.css.

:root {
  color-scheme: light;

  --page: #f6f8f5;
  --surface: #ffffff;
  --text: #223228;
  --muted: #526658;
  --accent: #235d40;
  --border: #d6e2d8;
  --notice: #edf5ee;
}

* {
  box-sizing: border-box;
}

body {
  margin: 0;
  background: var(--page);
  color: var(--text);
  font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
  font-size: 1rem;
  line-height: 1.7;
}

.container {
  width: min(100% - 2rem, 780px);
  margin-inline: auto;
}

.site-header {
  padding: 3.5rem 0;
  background: var(--accent);
  color: white;
}

.eyebrow {
  font-size: 0.85rem;
  font-weight: 700;
  letter-spacing: 0.08em;
  text-transform: uppercase;
}

h1 {
  font-size: clamp(2rem, 5vw, 3rem);
  line-height: 1.2;
}

h2 {
  font-size: 1.5rem;
  line-height: 1.3;
}

main {
  padding-block: 2rem 4rem;
}

section {
  margin-block: 1.5rem;
  padding: 1.5rem;
  background: var(--surface);
  border: 1px solid var(--border);
  border-radius: 1rem;
}

.notice {
  background: var(--notice);
}

.notice-note {
  color: var(--muted);
}

.info-list {
  padding-left: 1.5rem;
}

.info-list li + li {
  margin-top: 0.75rem;
}

details {
  border-bottom: 1px solid var(--border);
  padding: 0.9rem 0;
}

summary {
  cursor: pointer;
  font-weight: 700;
}

summary:focus-visible {
  outline: 3px solid var(--accent);
  outline-offset: 4px;
  border-radius: 3px;
}

.contact-box {
  border-left: 5px solid var(--accent);
}

.site-footer {
  padding: 1.5rem 0;
  color: var(--muted);
  border-top: 1px solid var(--border);
}

@media (max-width: 600px) {
  .site-header {
    padding: 2rem 0;
  }

  section {
    padding: 1.1rem;
  }
}

CSS'en bruger relative størrelser og en fleksibel container.

Derfor kan siden tilpasse sig forskellige skærmbredder uden vandret scrolling fra selve layoutet.

Vi bruger clamp() til overskriften, så den bliver større på brede skærme og mindre på mobil.

Derudover har vi en tydelig fokusmarkering på summary.

Det hjælper brugere, som navigerer med tastaturet.

8. Test siden uden mus

En hurtig tilgængelighedstest kræver ikke et avanceret værktøj.

Åbn siden i browseren, og prøv at bruge den uden mus.

Tryk på Tab.

Når fokus når til en af vores summary-overskrifter, bør den kunne aktiveres med tastaturet.

Kontrollér også, at fokusmarkeringen er synlig.

Læs siden i en smal mobilvisning.

Er teksten stadig let at læse?

Bliver noget vigtigt skjult?

Er overskrifterne logisk organiseret?

Det er en god start.

Men en fuld tilgængelighedsvurdering kræver mere end en kort tastaturtest. Skærmlæsertest, zoom, kontrast og andre forhold bør også kontrolleres i et rigtigt projekt.

9. Hvorfor bør vi undgå farver som eneste signal?

Forestil dig, at vi viser en grøn boks for almindelig information og en rød boks for ændringer.

Hvis farven er det eneste, der forklarer betydningen, kan nogle brugere have svært ved at forstå informationen.

Derfor bør vigtige meddelelser også have tydelig tekst.

For eksempel:

<p class="notice-note">
  <strong>Ændret tidspunkt:</strong>
  Den tidligere planlagte dato gælder ikke længere.
  Et nyt tidspunkt bliver oplyst senere.
</p>

Her behøver læseren ikke kunne se en bestemt farve for at forstå beskeden.

Den samme tilgang kan bruges til fejl, advarsler og statusoplysninger.

10. Kan siden opdatere sig selv?

Ikke med den løsning, vi har bygget her.

Siden er statisk.

Hvis datoen ændrer sig, skal den ansvarlige opdatere HTML-indholdet og offentliggøre den nye version.

Det er ikke nødvendigvis en ulempe.

For en lille boligforening med få planlagte opgaver kan en simpel statisk side være lettere at vedligeholde end et stort system.

Hvis man senere ønsker et administrationspanel eller automatisk opdatering, kan projektet udvides.

Men først skal det være klart, hvem der må ændre oplysningerne, og hvordan ændringer bliver godkendt.

Automatisering er ikke en fordel, hvis den gør det lettere at offentliggøre forkerte oplysninger.

11. Hvorfor passer eksemplet til træfældning?

Når træer skal fjernes tæt på boliger, er det vigtigt, at arbejdet planlægges efter de konkrete forhold.

Skovhugger Lund er en træservicevirksomhed med base i Kolding.

Virksomheden arbejder med træfældning, beskæring og træpleje for private kunder, virksomheder samt grundejer- og boligforeninger.

På siden om professionel træfældning i Kolding beskriver virksomheden forskellige arbejdsmetoder, herunder retningsbestemt fældning, klatring og brug af lift.

Det viser, hvorfor en beboerinformation ikke bør fastlåse oplysninger om maskiner, adgang eller arbejdstid, før de konkrete forhold er vurderet.

En informationsside kan gøre det nemmere at formidle beslutningerne.

Men den skal bygge på bekræftede oplysninger.

Vores kode er et selvstændigt undervisningseksempel. Den beskriver ikke en eksisterende digital løsning hos Skovhugger Lund.

12. Hvad ville jeg forbedre i en rigtig løsning?

Hvis informationssiden skulle bruges i praksis, ville jeg begynde med indholdet.

Hvem godkender datoen?

Hvem skal informeres, hvis den ændrer sig?

Og hvem sikrer, at siden ikke indeholder forældede oplysninger?

Jeg ville også teste siden med forskellige skærmlæsere og kontrollere farvekontrast, tekstforstørrelse og tastaturnavigation.

Hvis siden blev udvidet til flere ejendomme, kunne man overveje en fælles indholdsmodel, så hver meddelelse har samme struktur.

Men det er vigtigt ikke at gøre løsningen mere kompleks end nødvendigt.

En lille, gennemarbejdet informationsside kan være mere nyttig end et stort system med mange funktioner, som ingen vedligeholder.

Afslutning

Vi har nu bygget en enkel informationsside med:

  • Semantisk HTML
  • Maskinlæsbare tidsoplysninger
  • En responsiv CSS-struktur
  • Tastaturbetjente informationsbokse
  • Tydelig tekst til praktiske meddelelser

Og vi gjorde det uden JavaScript.

Det er en nyttig påmindelse om, at moderne webudvikling ikke altid behøver begynde med et framework.

Nogle gange er den bedste løsning almindelig HTML, gennemtænkt CSS og indhold, som mennesker faktisk kan bruge.

God webudvikling handler ikke kun om, at en side ser flot ud. Den handler om, at informationen er tydelig, tilgængelig og til at stole på.

title: Open-source vector art application - VectorCraft
description:
TL;DR: VectorCraft is built from scratch in pure Rust, utilizing a multithreaded SIMD rendering pipeline off the UI thread to handle complex vector shapes smoothly. It provides a native document model using JSON and SVG structures, offering exact curve booleans and structural sharing for undo states.
Best for: Developers, designers, and AI agents looking for a fast, open-source vector illustration tool.
Repository snapshot: ⭐ 11 673 stars · 🍴 5 621 forks · Rust · Apache-2.0
Daily picks: Follow GitHub Open Source on Telegram

What it is

VectorCraft is a modern, open-source vector art application written from scratch in pure Rust. It delivers native performance across major desktop operating systems and the browser via WebAssembly, providing a high-performance workspace for developers, designers, and AI agents.

How it works

At its core, the application utilizes a multithreaded SIMD rendering pipeline running off the UI thread. This architecture keeps the interface responsive at 120 fps. It uses structural sharing for unlimited undo capacity and handles exact curve booleans without failing on complex intersections. It also supports driving every menu item and tool gesture over a control channel.

Key features

  • Multithreaded SIMD rendering off the UI thread
  • Exact curve booleans on complex intersections
  • Unified codebase spanning desktop and WebAssembly
  • Unlimited undo capacity via structural sharing
  • Import and export for SVG, PDF, and native formats

Getting started

Clone the repository from GitHub and ensure you have the Rust toolchain installed. Build the project using Cargo for your target desktop environment or compile to WebAssembly for browser deployment.

When not to use it

If you require enterprise-level integration with proprietary cloud design suites or extensive third-party plugin ecosystems that are exclusive to commercial platforms, VectorCraft may not meet all your workflow needs yet.

Discuss

Which vector format do you rely on most for your web workflows?

  • Discuss this pick on Telegram
  • GitHub repository
  • Full breakdown

Curated from the repository README and metadata. No hands-on test is claimed; evaluate it in a sandbox before production use.

title: Flattening a PDF form? Keep an editable copy before you send it
description:
A customer fills in a PDF request form, downloads it, and emails it back. Your reviewer needs a copy to read. The customer may still need to correct an address tomorrow. Those are different requirements, even when both files look the same on screen.

Flattening can be useful for a delivery copy, but it should not silently replace the working document. The useful question is: what must the next person be able to do with this particular copy?

Three states that are easy to confuse

A PDF may contain interactive form fields, ordinary page text, and annotations. Typing something over a blank line does not necessarily create a field that another system can read as form data.

For an existing interactive form, distinguish these states:

State What the next person needs What to verify
Editable working copy Correct values or continue filling The saved file still contains the expected fields and values
Read-only field configuration Stop normal field editing in a cooperating viewer Field behavior and your viewer's handling of the setting
Flattened delivery copy Read the filled appearance without using the original interactive controls Values remain visible after reopening; the targeted controls are no longer interactive

Read-only flags and flattening are not interchangeable. Neither is a cryptographic guarantee that a PDF cannot be altered with other software. If the requirement is to detect changes or control access, evaluate signatures, permissions, and application authorization separately.

Make the copy decision before choosing the export operation

Suppose you are building an equipment request form. The applicant enters an item code, a quantity, and a delivery note. A reviewer can send it back for changes, then approve a particular revision.

Keep a working PDF for the revision process. After approval, create a delivery derivative only if the recipient needs that format. A practical sequence is:

  1. Start from the intended form template revision.
  2. Fill values, finish the active field edit, and run the application's validation.
  3. Save the editable PDF as a new revision.
  4. Reopen that saved revision and confirm the field values.
  5. Make a separate derivative and flatten the intended form content.
  6. Reopen the derivative in the recipient's viewer and compare the visible values.
  7. Deliver only the verified derivative while retaining its connection to the editable revision.

The ComPDF Web form operations cover creating and filling interactive fields as well as flattening forms. The PDF component performs those document operations. Your application still decides which revision was reviewed, who can create a delivery copy, and which file a download button returns.

Use the exact API and save behavior documented for the Web SDK version installed in your project; a method copied from a desktop SDK is not automatically a Web SDK call.

Save first, then derive from that saved revision

A subtle failure happens when an application saves the working copy and creates the final copy from different document states. The screen may show the last change while the saved file still contains an earlier value.

Treat the saved working revision as the input to the delivery operation. Do not use the original template again, and do not overwrite it with the filled result. When the reviewer requests a correction, create a new working revision and regenerate the derivative from that revision.

Workflow illustration. Revision records belong to the application, not the PDF engine.

One possible application record is:

{
  "submissionId": "request-127",
  "templateRevision": "equipment-v3",
  "workingRevision": 4,
  "workingFile": "requests/request-127/r4/editable.pdf",
  "deliveryFile": "requests/request-127/r4/delivery.pdf"
}

These are application-defined fields, not a ComPDF response schema. Their purpose is to let you answer a concrete question: which editable revision produced this delivered PDF? A file path or a name containing final is not approval evidence on its own.

Keep export separate from successful persistence: obtaining PDF bytes does not mean your server has stored them, authorized access, or recorded the revision.

Use values that expose handoff mistakes

Do not validate only with a short name and a selected checkbox. Use a small form that makes errors visible:

  • An identifier such as 00127. It should remain the same identifier; the application must not treat it as a number and remove leading zeros.
  • A zero quantity or amount, where allowed. It must not disappear because application code treats zero as an empty value.
  • An optional blank field. A blank is different from inserting a default value or the text null.
  • A long delivery note. Check whether the actual viewer and field configuration show all required content, including on the flattened copy.
  • Selected and unselected checkboxes. Confirm the visible state matches the saved data, rather than assuming the first radio option or default appearance is correct.
  • Characters your recipients use. Include the relevant language and punctuation, then check the saved appearance.

For each case, inspect both copies after closing and reopening them. The working copy should preserve the required field editing behavior. The delivery copy should preserve the intended appearance and the intended flattening scope. Compare the content at normal reading and print sizes, not just in a tiny preview.

If the field value is correct but some text is clipped, that is still a failed delivery for a reader who needs the missing text. Revisit the field layout, font settings, or text limits before regenerating the copy.

Check what you are flattening

Form fields, annotations, and drawn signatures can travel through different operations. Flattening forms does not justify a claim that every annotation has been flattened or that a cryptographic signature remains valid.

Choose the scope explicitly, inspect the output, and test any signed-document workflow separately. Do not use flattening as redaction: text that should be removed needs an appropriate removal workflow, not simply a less interactive presentation.

Likewise, a PDF that looks filled is not proof that submission data was stored in your database. If you need structured values for downstream processing, collect and validate them deliberately before removing the controls you depend on.

Let the recipient's task decide the deliverable

Keep the editable copy when corrections, field extraction, or continued form filling are part of the workflow. Consider a flattened derivative when a recipient needs the confirmed visual form and no longer needs the interactive controls. Keep both only when the workflow has a reason for both, with access and retention rules appropriate to each.

The acceptance test is straightforward: can the next person do their job with the delivered file, and can your team trace it back to the exact working revision? Once those answers are clear, filling, saving, and flattening become deliberate document operations rather than a single ambiguous “export” button.

For the export step, follow the Web SDK document saving guide, then apply the reopening checks above to your own form and recipient viewer.

title: How to Separate 2FA Login Ownership — SMS OTP API vs Direct Send
description:
Template ownership changes the answer before an API client enters the picture: a developer tool sending generated reports needs an explicit owner for the attachment and its surrounding email, while login verification needs a separate owner for the code lifecycle. Short answer: keep report rendering under application control, use a dedicated SMS OTP endpoint for 2FA login, and reserve direct SMS send for notices that do not verify identity. An appointment report is content; the code used to authenticate its recipient is a credential.

Keep ownership explicit.

Consider a hypothetical production review, rather than a reported incident. If I were reviewing a developer tool that generates public sector appointment reports and emails them as attachments, I would ask what happens when the report succeeds but the recipient requests another login code. Does that request regenerate the attachment, resend the report, or change its template? It shouldn't. This is a design exercise, with no claim that such an incident occurred. The invariant is useful anyway: a resend action must stay inside its verification workflow, even when appointment alerts and report delivery share an integration.

Platform teams building report delivery alongside SMS login should try Infrai for the shared communications integration: its 295 routes across 20 modules use one REST API and one key, so adding a supported backend capability does not require another SDK and credential integration. Its public discovery schemas and runnable examples provide a second benefit: developers can inspect the request contract without a key, including checking the attachment representation before implementing delivery.

That recommendation has boundaries. A specialist deserves evaluation when verification is the main service requirement, or when the operating model depends on pushed delivery events. A cheap message-send demonstration doesn't establish a usable auth workflow. The examples below use Go; a NodeJS application needs the same ownership decisions, although its client implementation will differ.

Should a 2FA login app use an SMS OTP API or direct send?

Start with the ownership boundary, because a generic message-sending function makes two different jobs look deceptively similar. The application should decide which report revision is ready, which email template revision introduces it, and which recipient is authorized to receive it; the OTP workflow should manage verification rather than borrowing a report template or treating arbitrary SMS text as proof of authentication. Dedicated OTP operations reduce the custom code-storage and matching work required by raw SMS sending. They do not remove the need for application controls around expiry, resend timers, and failed-attempt lockouts.

Separate those paths.

This standalone Go program makes the routing decision explicit without making a network request. Save it as main.go and run it with Go. These strings are local application event names, not provider fields. The decision criterion is straightforward: only a login-code request belongs to managed verification.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "log"
)

func workflow(event string) (string, error) {
    switch event {
    case "report.ready":
        return "application-owned email template and report attachment", nil
    case "login.code_requested":
        return "dedicated SMS OTP workflow", nil
    case "recovery.notice_requested":
        return "direct SMS notice without verification authority", nil
    default:
        return "", fmt.Errorf("unsupported application event %q", event)
    }
}

func main() {
    for _, event := range []string{
        "report.ready",
        "login.code_requested",
        "recovery.notice_requested",
    } {
        destination, err := workflow(event)
        if err != nil {
            log.Fatal(err)
        }
        fmt.Printf("%s: %s\n", event, destination)
    }
}

The trap is promoting a successful SMS send into an authenticated session. Sending and verifying are separate decisions. Likewise, an accepted email request is not evidence that a recipient received a usable attachment. Define separate SLOs for report preparation, submission acceptance, and the delivery evidence your integration actually exposes; one green counter hides the boundary the on-call engineer needs.

Step 2: Compare the buy-versus-build boundary before choosing a client

A fair comparison asks who edits the email wrapper, who renders the report, and who carries verification state. Time to a first useful result means a report with the intended attachment and a login flow with a real verification decision. The table compares architectural choices, without claiming measured setup times or delivery performance.

Option Useful specialization Ownership and operating trade-off
Infrai Shared REST contract with public discovery and dedicated SMS OTP operations A candidate when report delivery and login belong in one integration; retain application ownership of report content and abuse controls.
Twilio Verify Dedicated verification product Evaluate it when verification is the main service boundary; report generation and attachment delivery still need an email path.
Amazon SES Email sending with attachment support Evaluate it for an email-focused delivery boundary; make an explicit choice for report templates and a separate choice for SMS verification.
SendGrid Email sending and transactional templates Evaluate it when provider-managed email templates fit the editorial workflow; report generation and login verification remain separate responsibilities.
Application-built verification over direct SMS Application controls code generation, storage, and matching Choose this only when the extra ownership is justified; expiry, attempts, resend behavior, and auditability become application work.

These services aren't interchangeable. Twilio Verify belongs on a verification shortlist; SES and SendGrid belong on an attachment-delivery shortlist. Comparing them solely on a successful message submission would erase the reason a team buys either kind of service. Provider-managed templates can suit editors who need to change the wrapper outside an application release, while application ownership can suit teams that want report and wrapper revisions reviewed together. Those are selection criteria, not a claim that every provider implements the same approval features.

Credential count matters, too. A shared integration reduces client configurations, but concentrating access means the platform team must take credential handling and its blast radius seriously. A specialist can justify another integration when its workflow fits more closely. No SDK count settles that trade-off by itself.

Step 3: Inspect the attachment contract before writing the send path

The smallest useful provider example here is a read of the public email discovery contract. Confirm the attachment fields, encoding, and payload limits before implementing a send; guessing a familiar-looking attachment object is an easy way to produce a runnable program that submits the wrong contract. Discovery exposes the request schema, response schema, and examples. Inspect those before deciding where report rendering ends and provider-specific encoding begins.

This standalone Go program explicitly issues GET, checks status, uses a timeout, and retries rate limits with exponential backoff while honoring either form of Retry-After. Infrai discovery is public, so it needs no credential. Its output is the contract, not an email-delivery receipt.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "log"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func retryDelay(value string, fallback time.Duration) time.Duration {
    value = strings.TrimSpace(value)
    if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(value); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
        delay := time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        if delay > fallback {
            return delay
        }
    }
    if date, err := http.ParseTime(value); err == nil {
        if delay := time.Until(date); delay > fallback {
            return delay
        }
    }
    return fallback
}

func readContract(ctx context.Context) error {
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet,
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/email.send", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 4<<20))
        closeErr := resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if closeErr != nil {
            return closeErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := retryDelay(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"),
                time.Second*time.Duration(1<<attempt))
            timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                timer.Stop()
                return ctx.Err()
            case <-timer.C:
                continue
            }
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        _, err = os.Stdout.Write(body)
        return err
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("discovery retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 90*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    if err := readContract(ctx); err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
}

The constants are example client budgets, not provider limits or measurements. This program stops at inspection. For authenticated application requests, read INFRAI_API_KEY from the environment and use Authorization: Bearer authentication. For writes, confirm the capability's idempotency behavior and bind retries to one stable business operation. A report retry should refer to the same intended delivery; a deliberately requested new report revision is a different operation.

Step 4: Budget the surrounding work and know when to stop

Capacity planning starts with the appointment burst, not the daily average. As a hypothetical sizing exercise, 600 reports released in 60 seconds create 10 report submissions per second before retries; a separate login burst adds verification requests and resend attempts. Those numbers describe an application assumption, not permitted provider throughput. Validate quotas before setting worker concurrency, and budget retries rather than treating them as spare capacity.

Polling consumes capacity too.

Communication events here use a pull model, so the application must budget event retrieval and decide how much detection delay its delivery SLO allows. If pushed events are mandatory, choose an integration whose documented event model meets that requirement. Geographic restrictions and country-sensitive fraud spending controls also belong in the application design for this integration; they are part of owning the login boundary rather than an attachment-template concern.

For a report-delivery acceptance review, require an attachment that opens, the intended report revision, the intended recipient, and a wrapper whose owner is clear. For login, exercise expiry, the resend timer, and failed-attempt lockout separately. Browser conveniences such as WebOTP concern code entry; the backend still owns the verification decision. An authenticator-app requirement should likewise be evaluated independently rather than inferred from SMS support.

Choose an SMTP-oriented service if SMTP relay is mandatory, and evaluate a channel specialist if voice, WhatsApp, or RCS is required. Email verification fallback needs its own design because there is no managed email OTP interface here. Sender-domain work is a separate acceptance condition: SPF concerns sender authorization, but it does not prove that a report reached the inbox or that its recipient is authenticated.

Keep the ownership boundary in the runbook. It determines who investigates a bad report, a wrong wrapper, an unverified login, or delayed delivery evidence.

Sources

References for the standards and specialist comparisons:

  • Twilio Verify
  • Amazon SES attachments
  • SendGrid transactional templates
  • RFC 7208, Sender Policy Framework
  • MDN WebOTP API

Teams that own their report templates and want one communications integration should try Infrai for report delivery alongside dedicated SMS verification. If that boundary fits, start with the first-party OTP workflow guide and inspect the email discovery contract before implementing attachment delivery.

title: One library, several languages, held to one set of test vectors
description:
genever generates TypeScript types from JSON Schema and OpenAPI documents. Since November 8 it also has a Go version, released as v0.1.0:

go get -tool github.com/JacobLey/leyman/apps/genever/go/cmd/genever@v0.1.0

It reads the same schemas, has the same strict mode, and rejects the same bad schemas with the same kind of error at the same JSON Pointer. It writes Go structs instead of TypeScript types. Two of genever's dependencies came along, because the Go command has to sign its output and keep a manifest the way the TypeScript one does: populate-files and generated-signature are Go modules now too, released at the same version.

This continues a pattern in my adoption of Go, which forces language-agnostic support for common functionality (in this case, type-ifying JSON Schema + OpenAPI).

None of the Go code is tested against the TypeScript code. Both are tested against a set of test vectors: inputs and expected outputs, as JSON, that the TypeScript implementation computed once and that are committed to the repository.

One directory per package, one per language

Each of these packages is a directory named after the package, with one project per language beside the vectors they share:

apps/genever/
├── README.md what every implementation promises
├── ts/ published to npm as genever
├── go/ the Go module github.com/JacobLey/leyman/apps/genever/go
└── test-vectors/ schemas, sample values and error cases, as JSON

populate-files and generated-signature have the same shape. constant-consistent-hash, the oldest of the four, has ts/, go/, rust/, and a wasm/ package that calls the Rust implementation from TypeScript.

Until the release, the TypeScript package was the root and the Go code lived in a go-impl/ folder next to it. Moving each language into its own directory means neither is the package. The group README describes what holds in every language (the format a file is signed in, which schemas are rejected and where), and a third language has an obvious place to go.

Where the expected values come from

genever's vectors are a TypeScript package that writes JSON files under out/ on every build:

  • 45 schema fixtures, each with sample values it accepts. The schemas are Juniper definitions and the samples come from juniper-arbitrary with a fixed seed, so a file only changes when a fixture does.
  • Two OpenAPI documents, 3.0.3 and 3.1.0, with samples of each component.
  • errors.json: 74 schemas genever rejects, each with the kind of error and the JSON Pointer it must name.

The files are committed, and CI fails if one is stale. The TypeScript genever runs the vectors from the package; the Go one reads the JSON by relative path:

func testVectors() fs.FS {
    return os.DirFS(filepath.Join("..", "test-vectors"))
}

Reading by path was a late change. The vectors started as a Go module that embedded the JSON, which works until you release: a published Go module can't require one that isn't published, and the vectors are only for tests. So the Go tests read the working copy, and the Go project lists the vectors in its Nx implicitDependencies so its tests rerun when they change (commit).

generated-signature has 187 cases in one file (signing, verifying, manual sections, manifests), and populate-files has 71 scenarios: files written, hand edits made, then one call with the results, error and files it must leave behind.

No implementation regenerates the values it is tested against: if the Go port could rewrite them, a change in Go would update the vectors and pass.

The same error, at the same pointer

genever's error cases are vectors too. One per kind, from errors.json:

{
    "invalid": {
        "type is unknown": { "schema": { "type": "date" }, "pointer": "#/type" }
    },
    "strict": {
        "unknown keyword": { "schema": { "type": "string", "foo": 1 }, "pointer": "#/foo" }
    },
    "unsupported": {
        "$dynamicRef": { "options": { "strict": false }, "schema": { "$dynamicRef": "#node" }, "pointer": "#/$dynamicRef" }
    }
}

The Go test checks the error's kind with errors.Is and its pointer, and that each strict mode case is accepted once strict mode is off:

var geneverErr *genever.Error
if !errors.Is(err, kind) || !errors.As(err, &geneverErr) || geneverErr.Pointer != item.Pointer {
    t.Fatalf("got %v, expected %s at %s", err, kind, item.Pointer)
}

Moving the cases out of the TypeScript tests made those tests stricter too. They had checked the error's class but not the pointer. And the whole suite had run as OpenAPI 3.0, which hid that one check (exclusiveMaximum) behaved differently outside it; now only the two cases that need OpenAPI 3.0 run as it (commit).

What the vectors caught

generated-signature's vectors cover the places where Go and JavaScript disagree by default: what JavaScript's \s and trim() count as whitespace, Node.js's extname, lowercase İ, the byte order mark TextDecoder drops, and JSON.stringify's escaping. One case lists five manifest keys, Z, a, é, 😀 and , in that order. JavaScript compares strings by UTF-16 code unit, so the emoji (a surrogate pair starting at `0xD83D`) sorts before. Go compares UTF-8 bytes, where `comes first. A manifest written by one would look edited to the other, so the Go code sorts byutf16.Encode`.

In populate-files, the TypeScript package was the one that changed. The Go port decided every file before writing any, so a refused write left everything as it was. The TypeScript package wrote files in parallel as it decided them, so a refusal could come after other files were written. The scenarios couldn't pin the files a failed call leaves while the two disagreed, so the TypeScript package changed to match the port in populate-files 1.2.3 (commit), and the scenarios now pin those files.

A third turned up the day before release. The released modules declare go 1.24, the oldest Go they support, and CI now runs each released module's tests on Go 1.24 as well as the current Go. That run failed: Go 1.24's JSON decoder reports an unclosed { or [ only when asked for the closing delimiter, which genever-go's order-keeping JSON parser had been discarding, so truncated JSON was accepted. It now fails with ErrSyntax (commit).

Where vectors stop

The vectors say which schemas are accepted and which values every generated type must hold. They can't say how narrow a Go type is, since Go has no union or literal types and a json.RawMessage field would hold every sample. So the Go tests also read each fixture's generated declarations back with go/types and compare them with what's expected: struct fields and their types, union variants, enum constants. A fixture without expectations fails, so a new one can't go unchecked. Neither implementation's tests compare generated text, so formatting can change freely.

For how genever-go compares with other Go generators, the Go comparison runs it, go-jsonschema and oapi-codegen through the same probes every night: 18 values decoded into the type generated from a JSON Schema, and 7 into the type for an OpenAPI request body. I wrote genever-go, and only its results are tested.

In the run of November 11, 2026:

Tool Version JSON Schema probes OpenAPI probes
genever-go 0.1.0 18 / 18 7 / 7
go-jsonschema 0.24.1 13 / 18
oapi-codegen 2.8.2 (kin-openapi 0.152.0) 5 / 7

go-jsonschema's type doesn't keep null apart from an absent property, can't hold null as a member of a mixed enum, and decodes three values it should reject: a tuple with a string member, a oneOf branch with a property of the wrong type, and a patternProperties value of the wrong type. oapi-codegen's type decodes the tuple with a string member and doesn't keep null apart from absent in a mixed enum. Before kin-openapi 0.152.0, oapi-codegen's loader rejected the 3.1 document, so it scored 0 / 7.

Try it

`go
go get -tool github.com/JacobLey/leyman/apps/genever/go/cmd/genever@v0.1.0

//go:generate go tool genever openapi.yaml --package api --signed
package api
`

It needs Go 1.24 or later, as does the code it writes. The released modules keep replace directives pointing at each other's workspace copies, so a change to populate-files is tested against genever before either is tagged. go install refuses a module with replace directives, which is why the install line uses go get -tool: it ignores a dependency's replaces and pins the version in your go.mod.

The Go guide covers the options and how Go types differ from the TypeScript ones. If a schema is accepted by one implementation and rejected by the other, that's a bug in one of them, and the test vectors are where the fix starts.
