title: A daily list of new building permits from 12 US cities, with the contractor named
description:
A building permit is a public notice that work is about to start, often with the address, the value of the job and the contractor's company. That makes permits one of the best lead sources in construction: a roofing supplier wants every re-roof permit, a solar installer wants to know which ZIP codes are busy, a materials rep wants the contractors pulling the most permits this month. The catch is that every city publishes them differently, in its own portal with its own column names.

This post pulls permits from 12 US cities in one format, keeps only new or changed ones on a daily schedule, and ranks contractors by recent work.

Disclosure: I'm Aurelix, and I built the New York Building Permits Scraper, which despite the name covers all 12 cities below. It's a paid tool (prices below).

Where the data comes from

The cities' own open-data permit records: Seattle, Chicago, New York City (DOB NOW work permits), Los Angeles, San Francisco, Austin, Baton Rouge, Cincinnati, Mesa, New Orleans, Norfolk and Orlando. Every row has the same 30 fields:

  • permit_key (stable, for joins and dedupe), city, state, permit_number, permit_type, permit_subtype, description.
  • address, zip_code, neighborhood, latitude, longitude.
  • valuation (the value declared by the applicant), status, and applied_date, issued_date, expires_date, completed_date where the city publishes them.
  • contractor_company in nine of the cities, contractor_phone in Austin, Mesa and Orlando, contractor_email in Mesa, and contractor_name and contractor_address where published.
  • owner_name and applicant_name in five cities, and Chicago's full contacts list.

Names are returned as each city publishes them; Los Angeles records carry none, because its portal terms bar collecting personal information.

A daily contractor lead feed 

pip install apify-client

import csv
import os
from collections import Counter

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient(os.environ["APIFY_TOKEN"])
run = client.actor("aurelix/building-permits-scraper").call(
    run_input={
        "cities": ["austin", "chicago", "mesa", "orlando"],
        "daysBack": 7,
        "contractorOnly": True,
        "minValuation": 50000,
        "maxResultsPerCity": 200,
        "incremental": True,
        "stateKey": "contractor-leads",
    }
)
permits = list(client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items())

fields = ["city", "issued_date", "permit_type", "description", "address", "zip_code",
          "valuation", "status", "contractor_company", "contractor_phone", "url"]
with open("new_permits.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    w = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=fields, extrasaction="ignore")
    w.writeheader()
    w.writerows(sorted(permits, key=lambda p: p["valuation"] or 0, reverse=True))

busy = Counter((p["contractor_company"], p["city"]) for p in permits)
value = Counter()
for p in permits:
    value[(p["contractor_company"], p["city"])] += p["valuation"] or 0
print(f"{len(permits)} new or changed permits")
for (company, city), n in busy.most_common(10):
    print(f"  {company} ({city}): {n} permits, ${value[(company, city)]:,.0f} declared")

With incremental on, the first run returns everything that matches; each later run with the same stateKey returns only permits that are new or whose status changed, so a daily schedule pays only for fresh rows. To run it without a script, save the input as a task in the Apify Console and schedule it daily; a Slack webhook URL in slackWebhookUrl posts the count and the top 10 with links, and nothing when there is nothing new.

Other ways to cut the same data:

  • Solar, roofing, ADUs: "keywords": ["solar", "roof", "ADU"] matches the description of work or the address. Group by zip_code to see where the work is.
  • Large projects: "permitTypes": ["new"] with "minValuation": 1000000 across NYC, Chicago and Los Angeles, then follow status and completed_date on later runs.
  • Find the contractor's website and phone: search the contractor_company names with the Google Maps Phone Scraper.

Working in Canada? The Canada Building Permits tool does the same for Toronto and six other Canadian cities.

Why this tool

  • $1.50 per 1,000 permits ($1.05 on paid plans) plus $0.006 per run, cheaper than the leading tools.
  • All twelve cities in one run, in one schema.
  • Built for a daily feed: new-or-changed mode, a contractor-only filter, keyword and minimum value filters, and a Slack or webhook digest.
  • What it doesn't cover: cities outside the twelve above.

Limits

  • Twelve cities. Open an issue on the Store page to ask for another.
  • Publishing lag (as measured in our checks): New York City runs about 2 to 5 days behind, Los Angeles refreshes weekly and can be up to about 10 days behind; the other ten were 0 to 2 days behind. A look-back shorter than the lag returns nothing for that city, and the run status says so.
  • Contractor names are published by nine cities; Los Angeles, San Francisco and Norfolk publish none. Phones only in Austin, Mesa and Orlando.
  • Issued permits only, filtered by issue date; applications not yet issued are not included.
  • Valuation is what the applicant declared; some permits carry none.
  • Up to 90 days back and 50,000 rows per city per run; by default 1,000 per city, newest first.

Cost

You pay per permit returned. Cities that return nothing are free, and in new-or-changed mode, permits already returned are not charged again. The current price per permit is on the Store page; Apify's free plan includes $5 of credit a month, about 3,300 permits.

Links

  • New York Building Permits Scraper on the Apify Store
  • Canada Building Permits on the Apify Store

title: OpenAI's ChatGPT Wallet Lets Agents Buy Things. One Bought a Potato
description:
A guy on r/wallstreetbets put $200 into an AI shopping agent and let it buy his groceries. It ordered two of something. It picked the wrong variation of something else.

And once, with no explanation, it bought a single potato.

i read that comment three times. Not because it was funny, though it is funny. Because one potato is the clearest summary of this whole product category i have seen so far.

The agent did not fail in a dramatic way. It did not empty his account or buy a boat. It just quietly decided that one potato was the right amount of potato.

That comment landed hours after OpenAI announced ChatGPT Wallet on November 13. The wallet lets agents in dots, ChatGPT Work, and Codex pay for things on your behalf. It was built with American Express, Mastercard, and Visa.

Right now it only runs in dots, for ChatGPT Pro subscribers in the US, 18 and up, with a US-issued card and a US billing address.

OpenAI is selling this as trust infrastructure. The card gets tokenized. You approve every purchase with Face ID or a fingerprint.

The agent never sees your number.

All of that is true, and none of it is the interesting part. The plumbing works. The question is whether the agent knows what you actually want.

How the token thing actually works

here's a question people always ask when a card gets involved: where does my number go?

It doesn't go anywhere. The flow is short:

  1. You save a card once.
  2. Your dot finds the item and shows you the merchant, items, total, and card.
  3. You approve with Face ID or a fingerprint.
  4. The network issues a token with its own number, code, and expiry.

That token is what the store sees. Your real card stays hidden from both the merchant and the agent.

Your rewards still apply. Your dispute protections still apply. If the sweater shows up with one sleeve, you call the merchant, not OpenAI.

But here's the line from OpenAI's own release notes that made me stop scrolling:

approval alone doesn't confirm an order. check the merchant's confirmation after checkout.

So the agent can take your Face ID, get a token, and still not have bought anything. The approval is a permission slip, not a receipt.

The stores are the real story

what actually happens is that half the internet does not want your agent there.

United Airlines changed its contract of carriage on November 11 and blocked third-party AI agents from booking flights. Amazon has been blocking outside shopping agents, including Meta's Muse and Perplexity. eBay blocks them too.

OpenAI admits this in the announcement. Some sites "may unintentionally block purchases."

That word is doing a lot of work. Much of it looks intentional.

So OpenAI shipped a playbook for merchants. Claim your business in ChatGPT. Allow signed requests through Web Bot Auth.

Then ask your fraud vendor to stop flagging agent traffic. They name Forter, Riskified, Sardine, Signifyd, Adyen, Checkout.com, and Stripe as partners already working on it.

Read that list again. OpenAI is asking retailers to reconfigure their fraud stack so a robot can check out.

That is a big ask, and it is the actual bottleneck. Not the card. The permission.

Who What they want
OpenAI Agents to complete checkouts everywhere
Merchants Traffic they can see, price, and control
Networks Transactions that do not look like fraud

Follow the money

most coverage skipped the fee question. CNBC reported OpenAI takes no cut of Wallet transactions at launch.

No cut, for now. That phrasing is doing work too.

OpenAI already charges merchants a 4% fee on sales through its Instant Checkout flow, which has been live since early 2026. Wallet is a different pipe, but it feeds the same machine. Free at launch usually means free until the habit forms.

And the incentive is obvious once you see it. If OpenAI owns the checkout, it owns the last step before money moves. That is the most valuable square on the board.

Reddit noticed faster than the press did.

"This is just a way for them to take a cut isn't it?"

That was the top-voted take in r/technology. It got there in about an hour.

What it costs

Wallet itself is free. Getting access is not.

ChatGPT Pro now comes in three tiers: $100, $200, and $500 a month. Wallet rolls out to Pro subscribers first. So the real entry price for letting your dot buy groceries is a hundred dollars a month.

And dots are the only place it works right now. Not the regular ChatGPT chat. Not Codex yet, even though OpenAI's own marketing copy mentions Work and Codex in the same breath.

The blog post says dots. The tagline says more. Trust the blog post.

Approval is not the hard part

The obvious criticism is the one i keep seeing. Who is this for?

If you can buy something in two taps on your phone, why would you ask an agent to do it and then approve it with your face anyway?

The answer is that per-purchase approval is training wheels. OpenAI says the quiet part in the announcement. Over time, they expect users to hand over purchases entirely, with spending limits, categories, and time windows set in advance.

That is the product. Not "approve every purchase." Approve the rules once and stop looking.

Which brings back the potato. An agent with a spending limit and a grocery category does not need your face to buy one potato. It needs judgment.

And judgment is the thing that failed.

A short detour about onions

i once ordered twelve kilos of onions because i misread a recipe that said two. My fridge smelled like a crime scene for a week. i made soup for six days and still threw half of it out.

So i have no room to judge a machine that buys one potato. We are both bad at this in different directions.

Every grocery store near me also replaced six humans with four machines that yell at me about bananas. You put a banana on the scale. The machine says unexpected item in bagging area.

You move the banana. It says the same thing. A teenager with a keycard walks over, sighs, and fixes it.

We spent a decade teaching machines to take payments and we still cannot weigh a banana correctly. Now we are handing those same machines a credit card and a shopping list.

Real talk

Most people should not touch this yet.

If you live outside the US, you cannot. If you are on Plus, you cannot. If you buy things the normal way and it takes thirty seconds, you are not the customer.

This is for people who already pay for Pro, already run dots, and already lose an hour a week on repetitive purchases. Maybe restocking the same five items. Maybe rebooking the same flight.

And even for them, i would wait a month. The blocklist problem is real.

A wallet that works on six sites is not a wallet. It is a demo with a Visa logo on it.

The ending

The part i keep thinking about is not the partnership or the token architecture. Those are solved problems. Payments people have been doing this for forty years.

It is the potato.

Somewhere a model looked at a household, a list, and a budget, and concluded that the correct number of potatoes was one. Nobody wrote a rule against it. There was no error message.

The system worked exactly as designed.

That is the thing about handing your card to something that thinks. It will not always be wrong in ways you can predict. Sometimes it will just be wrong in a way that is small, cheap, and completely inexplicable.

i would still try it. But i would check the bag.

title: Can JVM caches speed up Spring Boot on Kubernetes? A JDK 21 and JDK 25 study
description:
Can JVM caches speed up Spring Boot on Kubernetes? A JDK 21 and JDK 25 study

A study of one Spring Boot workload found that mnemo-warmup reduced the application's reported startup time with both JDK 21 AppCDS and the JDK 25 AOT cache. With a 1 CPU and 1 GiB application limit, the median fell from 3.14 to 1.90 seconds on JDK 21 and from 3.23 to 1.47 seconds on JDK 25. In both cases, the median Kubernetes pod start-to-Ready remained 5 seconds.

That distinction matters. A JVM can start the application faster while container setup, archive fetching, readiness probes, and timestamp resolution leave the observed pod readiness time unchanged. Measure both before deciding whether a startup cache is useful for your service.

This article describes a benchmark of mnemo-warmup, an open-source tool for training and distributing Java startup caches in Kubernetes. It is based on the study report and raw results. The results are measurements from one workload and environment, not a prediction for every Java application.

What is mnemo-warmup?

mnemo-warmup trains a JVM startup cache using an application's container image in a Kubernetes cluster. It stores the archive in an OCI registry and arranges for later pods to fetch a compatible archive at startup. A fingerprint of inputs such as the JDK, application JARs, and JVM options helps decide whether an archive fits the launch.

The tool supports AppCDS, which shares prepared class metadata, and the JDK's AOT cache. In this study, its automatic selection used AppCDS with JDK 21 and AOT with JDK 25. The application remains a JVM application; this is a different deployment choice from compiling it to a GraalVM native executable.

Training runs a real instance of the application. That means startup actions, such as connecting to services or applying migrations, can also happen during training. Operators need to review the trainer configuration and measure the deployment overhead as well as the JVM saving. The project describes itself as alpha in its README.

The experiment

The benchmark used the same Spring Boot application, containing 70 JARs and about 59 MiB of application files, on Temurin JDK 21.0.13 and JDK 25.0.5. It ran on an Apple M5 laptop using Docker Desktop and a single-node, ARM64 kind cluster. The cache registry was local to the Docker network.

There were four configurations: each JDK with no application resource limits, and each JDK with application requests and limits of 1 CPU and 1 GiB. For each configuration, the harness discarded a warm-up round and measured 12 rounds of three interleaved variants:

  1. A pod without mnemo-warmup.
  2. A pod with mnemo-warmup but no archive in its store.
  3. A pod with mnemo-warmup and a trained archive.

The cached variant reported a successful fetch and archive use in all 12 measured pods in each configuration. The measurements below compare the first and third variants. The full study report includes the no-cache variant, ranges, environment, training records, registry samples, and links to raw pod data and logs.

Results: application startup and pod readiness

All values are medians. Application startup is taken from the Spring startup log. Pod start-to-Ready uses Kubernetes timestamps, which have whole-second resolution in this setup.

Configuration Application start without tool Application start with archive Pod start-to-Ready without / with archive
JDK 21 AppCDS, no application limits 1,328 ms 693 ms 3.0 / 3.0 s
JDK 25 AOT, no application limits 1,352 ms 523 ms 2.5 / 3.0 s
JDK 21 AppCDS, 1 CPU / 1 GiB 3,142 ms 1,901 ms 5.0 / 5.0 s
JDK 25 AOT, 1 CPU / 1 GiB 3,234 ms 1,471 ms 5.0 / 5.0 s

Under the application limit, the measured median JVM startup saving was 1,242 ms for JDK 21 AppCDS and 1,763 ms for JDK 25 AOT, each compared with the no-tool baseline on the same JDK. Those are approximately 40% and 55% reductions in the application's reported startup time, respectively. They are not reductions in pod start-to-Ready: both limited cached and uncached deployments had a median of 5 seconds.

The no-limits JDK 25 comparison also shows why a faster application alone is not enough to establish a faster pod: its median cached pod start-to-Ready was 3.0 seconds, compared with 2.5 seconds without the tool. The timestamps and readiness probe in this experiment have approximately one-second resolution, so treat small differences with care.

What did the caches cost?

The AppCDS archive was about 87 MB in both JDK 21 runs. The JDK 25 AOT archive was about 109 MB. Five direct downloads from the kind node to the local registry had median times of roughly 24 ms for AppCDS and 30 ms for AOT. These are local-network results, not remote-registry performance measurements.

The trainer container ran for 4 seconds in each JDK 21 run and for 5 and 6 seconds in the two JDK 25 runs. Those are single observations, measured from container start to finish. They include work beyond producing the archive. The trainer had no CPU or memory limits, even when the application pods were limited.

When might mnemo-warmup be worth evaluating?

Consider a measured trial if you run Java services on Kubernetes, want to retain JVM deployment, and application startup is a meaningful part of rollout or scale-out time. A cluster-trained cache may be useful when the cluster's actual JDK and launch options differ from assumptions made during an image build. Compare against any cache already in the image; another training step and archive download may add cost without enough benefit.

Use caution when a workload already supplies JVM cache flags. In a separate local OpenJDK 25.0.1 check, combining -XX:AOTCache in JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS with -XX:SharedArchiveFile on the command line stopped JVM initialization. The project's operations guide describes that limit. Preview warnings identify possible cache markers; they do not establish which flags a Kubernetes workload will ultimately use or guarantee compatibility.

If pod setup, network downloads, readiness checks, or application work outside class loading dominate startup, a faster JVM start may not improve the time users wait for a ready pod. Teams already satisfied with an image-baked cache or a native executable should benchmark those choices against the cluster-trained approach on their own workload.

What this study does and does not establish

  • It measures one Spring Boot application, one ARM64 laptop and one local kind cluster. Results may differ on other applications, processors and production nodes.
  • JDK version and cache mechanism changed together. The experiment does not isolate AppCDS versus AOT on the same JDK.
  • The three variants were interleaved within each configuration, but JDK configurations were run sequentially. Machine conditions can drift between them.
  • The registry was local, images were already available, and pods started one at a time. The study does not measure remote registry latency, image pulls, or concurrent scale-out.
  • One limited JDK 21 no-cache application start took 21.3 seconds. It remains in the raw data and reported ranges.

How to evaluate it on your application

Start with the mnemo-warmup README, then read the benchmark method and results and operations guide. Compare repeated deployments with and without the tool under representative CPU and memory limits. Record application startup, pod start-to-Ready, archive size, download time, training cost, and failure behavior. Include any existing image-baked cache as its own baseline.

For this workload, mnemo-warmup made the Java application report startup sooner. The experiment did not show a lower median pod readiness time in the limited configuration.

title: How to structure a full-stack React + Motoko dApp on the Internet Computer
description:
Hey builders,

When you first start building on the Internet Computer Protocol (ICP), getting a basic "Hello World" canister running is pretty straightforward. The real headache starts when you try to scale that into a full-stack SaaS application with a multi-tool React frontend, user state tracking, and clean file handling.

While building VaultyPDF (a 15-tool on-chain PDF utility suite), I had to reorganize my project several times before finding a structure that didn't turn into spaghetti code. Here is the clean folder architecture I landed on for pairing React with Motoko.

1. Keep Backend Canisters Modular

Instead of stuffing thousands of lines of logic into a single main.mo file, separate your data types and helper functions early on:

src/
├── backend/
│   ├── main.mo          # Main entry point & public actor methods
│   ├── types.mo         # Custom user & document metadata types
│   └── storage.mo       # Stable memory & state management helpers

Using a dedicated types.mo file makes it much easier to keep your Motoko records aligned with your frontend JavaScript/TypeScript interfaces.

2. Isolate Frontend Canister Calls

Never call your backend actor directly inside your UI components. Create a dedicated service or hook layer in your React folder so your UI stays focused purely on rendering:

src/
├── frontend/
│   ├── src/
│   │   ├── components/  # Reusable dark-mode UI cards & modals
│   │   ├── hooks/       # Custom hooks for auth & canister queries
│   │   ├── pages/       # Individual tool views (Merge, Split, Redact)
│   │   └── App.jsx      # Main dashboard layout & routing

3. Handle Heavy Client-Side Processing Locally

On-chain storage and compute are great for user profiles, audit logs, and document metadata. However, for heavy PDF manipulation (like merging pages or applying visual redactions), run the heavy lifting directly in the user's browser via JavaScript, and only send the verified metadata or final state hashes to your Motoko canister. This keeps your cycle burn rate low and makes the UI feel instant.

Want to skip the boilerplate setup?

Setting up the React routing, dark-mode SaaS dashboard UI, and Motoko canister bindings from scratch easily eats up a couple of weeks.

If you want a ready-to-deploy foundation for your own ICP project, I packaged my entire 15-tool codebase into a clean starter template:

👉 Check out the VaultyPDF React + Motoko Boilerplate on Gumroad

How do you guys usually organize your Motoko projects when the codebase starts growing? Drop your folder tips below!

title: Google Custom Search API is closing. Here's a drop-in replacement
description:
I'm part of the team behind Serpbit, so this post is about what we built. I've tried to keep the comparison fair.

Google is shutting down the Custom Search JSON API. New sign-ups are already closed, and on January 1, 2027 it stops working for everyone else too.

Google's suggested replacement, Vertex AI Search, is built for searching your own websites, not the whole web. Microsoft shut down the Bing Search API back in 2025. So if your app, script or AI agent needs real web search results, you have to move somewhere, and soon.

We built Serpbit so that this move takes minutes rather than a sprint.

Same request, same answer, new address

Serpbit answers the exact same requests as Google's Custom Search, in the exact same format, with results straight from Google. Your parsing code doesn't change. Your tests don't change. You swap the address and the key:

https://www.googleapis.com/customsearch/v1  →  https://api.serpbit.com/customsearch/v1

Google's own client libraries for Python and Node keep working, and so do LangChain and LlamaIndex with a small tweak. We tested all of them against the live API before writing this.

A few honest differences:

  • Results come from the whole web, so your search engine's site settings (cx) no longer apply. To limit a search to one site, pass siteSearch.
  • The pagemap block isn't there.
  • It's a bit slower: about 2 seconds per search instead of under one.

More than a replacement

The same key also gives you the rest of Google:

  • Search, with the AI Overview included at no extra cost
  • AI Mode, Shopping, Maps, News, Images and Autocomplete
  • An MCP server, so Claude, ChatGPT or Cursor can search Google. You connect by signing in, with no key to copy.
  • Answers in JSON or Markdown
  • You only pay for answers. A failed search costs nothing.

How it compares

What 100,000 searches a month costs, from each provider's public pricing:

Results Works with your Custom Search code Free tier 100k searches/month
Serpbit Google Yes, change the URL 1,000/month, no card $75
Serper Google No, new integration 2,500 to start ~$75
SerpApi Google No, new integration 250/month $725
Brave Search API Brave's own index No, new integration $5 credit/month, card required ~$500
Google Custom Search (until Jan 1) Google — 100/day $485

In plain words:

  • Serper costs about the same as us. If you're starting from scratch and only need web results, it's a fine choice. Serpbit makes more sense if you already have Custom Search code, or want AI Mode, Maps and the rest on one key.
  • SerpApi covers many search engines beyond Google, and you pay for that breadth.
  • Brave has its own independent index. It's great for feeding an AI agent relevant pages, but its results won't match what people see on Google. That matters for SEO and rank tracking.

Try it

The first 1,000 searches every month are free, and you don't need a card. Get a key, point one of your existing Custom Search calls at us, and compare the results with what you get today.

If anything in your setup doesn't work the way it did with Google, tell me in the comments or at support@serpbit.com. We'd like to fix it before January, not after.

title: How to Find Exposed API Keys in Your Vibe Coded App (a 5 Minute Check)
description:
If you built your app with Lovable, Bolt, Replit, Cursor or v0, there's a real chance something secret ended up in the code your browser downloads. Not because you did anything dumb. The AI just put the key where it made the feature work.

Short answer: to find exposed API keys in a vibe coded app, open your live site, open DevTools, press Ctrl+Shift+F (Cmd+Option+F on Mac) and search every loaded file for strings like sk_, sk-, service_role and secret. If a secret key shows up, it's public. Move it to the server and rotate it today.

That's the whole idea. Below is how I actually do it, what the results mean, and what to do if you find something.

Why vibe coded apps leak API keys

When you ask an AI builder to "add Stripe" or "call OpenAI", the fastest working version often calls the API straight from the frontend. It works on the first try, so nobody looks again.

The problem is that anything in your frontend is shipped to every visitor. Minified, sure. Hidden, no. Anyone can open DevTools and read it.

Build tools make this easy to miss. In Vite, any env variable that starts with VITE_ gets bundled into the client code (Vite docs). In Next.js it's the NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix (Next.js docs). So VITE_OPENAI_KEY in your .env file isn't private. It's in the bundle.

The 5 minute exposed API keys check

You don't need any tool for this. Just Chrome or any Chromium browser.

  1. Open your live site, not localhost. Log in if most of the app sits behind a login, because some code only loads after that.
  2. Open DevTools (F12, or right click and Inspect).
  3. Press Ctrl+Shift+F on Windows/Linux or Cmd+Option+F on Mac. This opens a search across every file the page loaded.
  4. Search these one at a time:
    • service_role
    • sk_live and sk_test
    • sk- (OpenAI style keys start like this)
    • secret
    • apikey and api_key
    • Bearer
  5. Click around the app a bit, open the main pages, then search again. Lazy loaded chunks only show up after you visit them.
  6. Open the Network tab, reload, and click a couple of requests to your own API or to third party APIs. Look at the request headers. If an Authorization header carries a secret key from the browser, that key is public too.

Most of the time you'll get matches. Don't panic yet. Some keys are supposed to be there.

Which keys are fine to be public (and which aren't)

Usually fine in the browser:

  • The Supabase anon (publishable) key. Supabase built it to be public, and your Row Level Security policies are what protect the data (Supabase docs on API keys). Fine, as long as RLS is actually on.
  • Stripe publishable keys that start with pk_. Those are made for the frontend (Stripe docs).
  • The Firebase web config object. It identifies your project, and Firebase Security Rules do the protecting.

Never in the browser:

  • The Supabase service_role (secret) key. It skips RLS completely. Anyone with it can read and write every table.
  • Stripe secret keys, sk_live_ or sk_test_. Stripe's own docs say to keep them on the server.
  • OpenAI, Anthropic or any other AI API key. Someone copies it, and you pay for their usage.
  • Email provider keys (Resend, SendGrid, etc). These can send mail as your domain.

What to do if you find an exposed key

I'd do it in this order:

  1. Rotate the key first. Make a new one in the provider dashboard and delete the old one. Removing it from the code is not enough, because the old bundle may still be cached, and the key may already be in your git history.
  2. Move the call to the server. A Supabase Edge Function, a Next.js API route, a Replit backend route, whatever your stack has. The browser calls your endpoint, your endpoint holds the key.
  3. Check usage. Look at the provider dashboard for calls you don't recognize. For AI keys, set a hard monthly spend limit if the provider has one.
  4. Search again. Redeploy, hard refresh, run the Ctrl+Shift+F check one more time.

A prompt that usually works in Lovable, Bolt or Cursor:

Move every call that uses a secret API key out of the frontend into a server side function. The frontend should call that function instead. Read the key from a server only environment variable, not one with a VITE_ or NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix. Show me which files you changed.

Then check what it did. Don't just trust the "done!" message.

Exposed API keys checklist (copy this)

  • [ ] Ran Ctrl+Shift+F on the live site for service_role, sk_, sk-, secret, apikey, Bearer
  • [ ] Logged in and visited the main pages, then searched again
  • [ ] Checked Network tab request headers for secret keys
  • [ ] No secret keys in env variables that start with VITE_ or NEXT_PUBLIC_
  • [ ] Any exposed key was rotated, not just deleted from code
  • [ ] Secret calls now go through a server function
  • [ ] Spend limits set on AI and email providers
  • [ ] RLS is on for every Supabase table (since the anon key is public anyway)

FAQ

Is the Supabase anon key safe to expose?

Yes, it's designed to be public. But it's only safe if Row Level Security is enabled with real policies on every table. With RLS off, the anon key can read your tables.

Can someone really find my API key in minified JavaScript?

Yes. Minifying shortens variable names, it doesn't hide strings. A key stays a plain string, and the DevTools search finds it in seconds.

I deleted the key from my code. Am I safe?

Not yet. Rotate it. Old builds, caches and git history can still have the old key.

Does this check cover everything?

No. It catches keys sitting in the frontend. It won't tell you if your database rules let user A read user B's data, which is the other big one in vibe coded apps.

A free self-check for the rest

I built ShipShield after seeing the same handful of problems over and over in AI-built apps. The free self-check is 10 yes/no questions, takes about two minutes, and needs no signup. It covers exposed keys plus the things this post doesn't, like RLS and who can see whose data.

You can run it here: shipshield.app

If you run the Ctrl+Shift+F check and find something weird, tell me in the comments. I'm curious what people actually find.

title: Declare your color schemes before the first paint (Web HIG tip #17)
description:
You open example.com on a phone that prefers dark mode. The page was authored as light, with no color-scheme in the head or the first CSS. In the Safari 27.3 beta, with Adaptive Dark Mode turned on, Safari can repaint that light page as dark: colors and light gradients change, some SVG images and simple logos recolor, and some masks or blend effects can be turned off. Scripts that read the page's colors still get the authored values. The page never told the browser which schemes it supports.

Web HIG tip #17 (Quick #64): Dark mode must re-verify contrast for every semantic token combination used. Declare supported color schemes in the document head or the initial CSS, before JavaScript. light dark is the usual declaration when both schemes are supported. light only is a narrow opt-out, not the default.

Why it matters

A missing declaration leaves the browser free to invent an appearance you did not author:

  • Safari Adaptive Dark Mode may transform a light page that does not declare schemes. Canvas stays as authored; CSS colors, gradients, and some images may not
  • Script and computed styles keep the authored values, so the repaint is invisible to ordinary CSS checks and many automated contrast tools
  • Text, focus, hover, SVG logos, transparent images, and canvas can look wrong while a lab check still reports the authored contrast
  • A declaration added by JavaScript later still takes effect, but the first render may already have used the browser's default light canvas and controls. That is the flash you're trying to avoid. WebKit advises against waiting to inject it with script

The full HIG covers this in §3.1, Supported color schemes: pages that support light and dark appearances MUST declare those schemes in the initial document, before any JavaScript runs. In practice, that means the browser knows the schemes before it first renders the page. Quick #64 is Quick-only guidance (no rule ID of its own). The same section states that Safari's contrast aim after a transformation is not a substitute for checking the authored interface in each supported scheme, including focus, hover, and non-text UI.

Before and after

This page has light and dark styles in /styles.css but never declares its schemes. The browser keeps its own canvas, form controls and scrollbars on light defaults, and Safari's Adaptive Dark Mode has to analyse the page instead of being told:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <title>Orders — example.com</title>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="/styles.css">
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Orders</h1>
</body>
</html>

Declare both schemes up front, in markup, in first-paint CSS, or both:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta name="color-scheme" content="light dark">
  <title>Orders — example.com</title>
  <style>
    :root { color-scheme: light dark; }
  </style>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="/styles.css">
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Orders</h1>
</body>
</html>

light dark tells supporting browsers, including Safari Adaptive Dark Mode, that both appearances are intentional. Only declare dark when you ship an authored dark appearance (prefers-color-scheme, light-dark() or an explicit theme). Otherwise the browser's dark canvas, form controls and system colors can clash with colors you authored for light. Then re-check contrast in that appearance. This snippet does not ship a theme switcher, token files, or a full dark palette.

Do this instead

  • Put <meta name="color-scheme" content="light dark"> in the document head, and/or color-scheme: light dark on :root (WebKit also accepts body) in CSS that applies on first paint, such as a <style> in the head, so the browser has it before the first render and before any theme script runs. Only the root element's scheme sets the page canvas, so prefer :root
  • Use light dark when you support both. Use light only (and the matching meta value) only when a surface must stay light; it is a narrow opt-out, not the default
  • Do not rely on light only as an opt-out until you've confirmed it works in each browser in your matrix. Browsers have parsed only for years, and MDN notes Chrome's Auto Dark Theme respects it. But WebKit says Safari 27.3 beta 1's Adaptive Dark Mode did not support it, so it wasn't a working opt-out there
  • Re-check contrast for text, focus, hover, and non-text UI in every scheme you declare. Measure authored colors; a browser repaint that computed styles cannot see is not that measurement
  • When Safari is in your matrix, keep a visual record (screenshot or equivalent) of Adaptive Dark Mode cases. The HIG requires reviewers to capture these. Automated contrast on computed styles can stay green while the painted page fails
  • If the product adds a theme control later, keep the document-level declaration honest about the schemes you actually support

Quick check for your app

Open example.com and a second key page at a phone width. View source or the Accessibility/Elements panel and confirm a color-scheme meta tag or first-paint CSS declaration before any theme script. Toggle the OS appearance and, where you support Safari Adaptive Dark Mode, capture light pages with and without the declaration. Compare authored computed colors with what you see painted. Suitable automated checks can catch a missing declaration and authored contrast regressions; they do not prove how Adaptive Dark Mode paints. Pair them with a visual check on the browsers your audience uses.

The Web HIG is an open set of guidelines for how the web should behave, not a component library. Design systems define how it looks. The Web HIG defines how it behaves.

  • GitHub: https://github.com/frozonfreak/webhig/discussions/35

title: AWS Secrets Manager now supports cross-account replication
description:
AWS Secrets Manager now supports cross-account replication, enabling you to maintain a synchronized copy of a primary secret in a secondary AWS account for cross-account access, backup, and disaster recovery. Cross-account replication extends the existing multi-Region replication capability across account boundaries.

With cross-account replication, platform or security teams can own and rotate a secret centrally, and each consuming account gets a local, always-current copy without any shared KMS keys or cross-account secret policies. The replica secret is a full, independent resource, encrypted with a customer managed KMS key owned by the replica account. Secrets Manager updates it automatically whenever the primary secret's value changes, including rotations.

You can keep a live copy of critical secrets in a dedicated recovery or failover account, isolated from ransomware or a compromised primary account. If needed, the replica can be promoted to a standalone secret.

Cross-account replication is available in all AWS Regions where Secrets Manager is available. For a list of regions where Secrets Manager is available, see the AWS Region table.

To learn more, see Replicate secrets across AWS accounts in the Secrets Manager User Guide and the AssociateCrossAccountReplica API reference. For pricing details, see AWS Secrets Manager pricing.

title: How Java Exceptions Work: A Quick Walkthrough
description:
You write try/catch every day. But when a throw runs, what does the JVM actually do? There is no magic: there is a table lookup, a stack unwinding procedure written down in the JVM specification, and - in one genuinely surprising case - a hardware trap and a kernel signal. Let's take it apart with real bytecode and real runs on JDK 21.

What an exception is, per the spec

The JVM spec (JVMS 2.11.9) says: "An exception is thrown programmatically using the athrow instruction. Exceptions can also be thrown by various Java Virtual Machine instructions if they detect an abnormal condition."

So two sources: your explicit throw (compiled to one bytecode instruction, athrow), and the JVM itself (a bad cast, an array index out of range, a null dereference). Either way, the exception is an ordinary object - allocated on the heap like any other - whose class extends Throwable. What makes it special is what the constructor records. From the Throwable JavaDoc: "Fills in the execution stack trace. This method records within this Throwable object information about the current state of the stack frames for the current thread."

That recording happens at construction time, before anything is thrown. The stack trace you print later is a snapshot taken the moment the object was born.

Here is the whole throw-and-catch journey, animated:

The catch block is a table entry

Here is the part most people never see. A simple try/catch:

public class ExTable {
    static int parse(String s) {
        try {
            return Integer.parseInt(s);
        } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
            return -1;
        }
    }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(parse("42"));
        System.out.println(parse("oops"));
    }
}

Running it prints 42 and -1. Now javap -c on the compiled class - this is the real output:

  static int parse(java.lang.String);
    Code:
       0: aload_0
       1: invokestatic  #7        // Method java/lang/Integer.parseInt:(Ljava/lang/String;)I
       4: ireturn
       5: astore_1
       6: iconst_m1
       7: ireturn
    Exception table:
       from    to  target type
           0     4     5   Class java/lang/NumberFormatException

Notice what is not there: any instruction for try. The try block compiles to nothing. All that exists is:

  • the normal code path (offsets 0-4: call parseInt, return its result),
  • the handler code (offsets 5-7: store the exception, push -1, return), and
  • one exception table row: "if an exception of type NumberFormatException (or a subclass) is raised by any instruction at offsets 0 up to 4, jump to offset 5."

That is exactly the rule the spec states (JVMS 2.10): "An exception matches an exception handler if the offset of the instruction that caused the exception is in the range of offsets of the exception handler and the exception type is the same class as or a subclass of the class of exception that the exception handler handles." A catch clause is data, not code that runs on the happy path.

Unwinding: what happens when nobody catches

What if the current method has no matching handler? The spec describes the cascade (JVMS 2.10): "If no such exception handler is found in the current method, the current method invocation completes abruptly. On abrupt completion, the operand stack and local variables of the current method invocation are discarded, and its frame is popped, reinstating the frame of the invoking method. The exception is then rethrown in the context of the invoker's frame and so on, continuing up the method invocation chain."

One honest caveat, as always with the JVMS: this is the conceptual model. The spec's own Chapter 2 says it "specifies an abstract machine", and frames/operand stacks are its vocabulary. A JIT-compiled HotSpot method may have inlined these calls and keep values in registers, so no physical frame literally pops. The observable behavior - which handlers run, in what order, what state survives - is what the spec guarantees.

Watch the observable behavior for real:

public class Unwind {
    static void level3() { throw new IllegalStateException("boom from level3"); }
    static void level2() { level3(); System.out.println("level2 after level3 - never prints"); }
    static void level1() { level2(); System.out.println("level1 after level2 - never prints"); }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try {
            level1();
        } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
            System.out.println("caught in main: " + e.getMessage());
            StackTraceElement[] st = e.getStackTrace();
            System.out.println("recorded stack depth: " + st.length);
            for (int i = 0; i < st.length; i++)
                System.out.println("  frame " + i + ": " + st[i].getMethodName());
        }
        System.out.println("main continues after catch");
    }
}

Real output:

caught in main: boom from level3
recorded stack depth: 4
  frame 0: level3
  frame 1: level2
  frame 2: level1
  frame 3: main
main continues after catch

Three things to read there. The two "never prints" lines indeed never printed - each frame was abandoned the moment the exception passed through, mid-method. The recorded stack depth is 4 even though the catch is in main: the snapshot was taken at construction inside level3, when all four frames were live. And after the catch, main simply continues - unwinding is a transfer of control, not a crash.

What a throw costs

The unwinding itself is cheap. The expensive part is that snapshot: fillInStackTrace has to walk the current thread's frames and record them. One small benchmark, one machine, one run - real numbers from this JDK 21 (Temurin 21.0.13) sandbox, nothing more:

plain return x1M: 8,655,307 ns
throw+catch x1M:  473,695,890 ns
ratio: 54.7x slower (this machine, this run)

Fifty times slower here - your number will differ with stack depth, JIT state and hardware, so treat the exact figure as a single sample. The direction is the point: creating and throwing an exception costs orders of magnitude more than returning a value. That is why the classic advice exists: exceptions are for exceptional situations, not for ordinary flow control.

Where the kernel genuinely appears

An ordinary throw is pure user-space JVM work: allocate an object, record frames, consult the exception table, branch. No system call, no kernel involvement at all.

But remember the spec's second source: "exceptions... thrown by various Java Virtual Machine instructions if they detect an abnormal condition." Some of those detections go through real hardware. When JIT-compiled code dereferences a reference that is null, many JVMs on Linux deliberately let the bad memory access happen: the CPU traps, and the kernel delivers a signal to the faulting thread. From signal(7): "A signal may be thread-directed because it was generated as a consequence of executing a specific machine-language instruction that triggered a hardware exception (e.g., SIGSEGV for an invalid memory access...)." HotSpot installs a handler for that signal, recognizes that the fault came from code where it omitted an explicit null check on purpose, and converts it into the NullPointerException your catch block sees. The kernel was genuinely in the loop - hardware trap, signal delivery, handler - between your bad dereference and your NPE.

Two cautions, both worth more than the trick. That mechanism is a HotSpot-on-Linux implementation detail, not a language guarantee - a JVM may instead emit explicit null checks and never touch a signal, and the JLS promises only that you get an NPE, never how. And most exceptions you will ever write (throw new ...) travel nowhere near the kernel. The honest picture is: user space by default, hardware and signals as an optimization path a particular JVM may choose for a particular check.

Habits worth keeping

  • Catch the specific type. The table matches by class-or-subclass; catching Exception everywhere hides bugs you meant to see.
  • Return values for expected outcomes, exceptions for exceptional ones. The 54x sample above is why.
  • Don't swallow. An empty catch discards the snapshot the constructor paid to record.
  • Read stack traces top-down. Frame 0 is where the object was constructed, which is where the problem started - exactly what the Unwind output shows.

Sources

  • JVMS 2.10: Exceptions
  • JVMS 2.11.9: Throwing Exceptions
  • Java 21 API: java.lang.Throwable
  • Linux man-pages: signal(7)

Written with AI assistance; every bytecode listing, stack trace and timing above comes from real compiles and runs on JDK 21 (Temurin 21.0.13), and the timing ratio is one machine's single run, not a general bound. The animation is an illustration of the spec's conceptual model - JIT-compiled execution may inline calls and keep values in registers rather than literal frames.

title: How to Build Versioned Retrieval Architecture for Engineering Docs in Go — Citations
description:
Use a staged retrieval design with explicit collections, bounded queries, and traceable source context. For internal engineering documentation, document versioning is part of retrieval correctness: an answer that cites a superseded runbook is operationally wrong even when the wording looks perfect.

The design below treats every page revision as a deliberate record, carries its source and revision in the result, and measures the behavior before production. It also keeps the integration surface small enough to replace a vector backend without rewriting the application.

Start with the retrieval contract

Write the user-visible answer contract before picking a database. In this media example, a watcher collects a web page, detects a change, and asks an internal documentation assistant to explain the diff. The retrieval contract says:

  • return chunks from the requested document version (or the explicitly selected current version);
  • return source_url, document_id, revision, and an effective timestamp with every chunk;
  • bound candidate count, query time, and downstream generation time;
  • make an empty or stale result visible to the caller instead of silently blending revisions.

That contract is the boundary between ingestion and answer generation. A collection can then be named for a stable scope, such as eng-docs-prod, while metadata filters carry document identity and revision. Keep old revisions available for audit, but mark one revision as current in your catalog. Deleting a page means deleting its records from the active collection, not merely hiding the link in a UI.

For this workflow, Infrai is a practical candidate when the watcher, indexer, and assistant should share one plain REST surface. The contract stays in your code while the backend behind it can move, so a provider swap does not force a rewrite of every client.

Short answer: stage lexical or metadata narrowing first, run bounded vector retrieval second, and attach citation context before generation.

How should a versioned retrieval architecture handle changed documentation?

Treat a page update as a small transaction in the index pipeline:

  1. Fetch and normalize the new page, preserving the canonical URL and a content hash.
  2. Split it into deterministic chunks. Include document_id, revision, source_url, and is_current metadata in each record.
  3. Upsert the new revision into the explicit collection.
  4. Flip the catalog pointer only after the upsert succeeds.
  5. Remove records for deleted pages, and remove superseded records from the current-only view if that is the query policy.

The ordering matters. If the pointer moves first, a failed indexing run can advertise a revision that retrieval cannot find. If deletion is skipped, a page removed from the site can still be cited by a nearest-neighbor search weeks later.

Do not make the query unbounded. Set a small top-k, a deadline, and a total byte limit for context passed to the model. A slow source must not block the page-change alert; the watcher can emit “no grounded match” and queue a retry for later.

Here is a Go runner that keeps the HTTP boundary explicit. It reads request bodies from files because the exact JSON schema is discoverable per capability and should be generated from the live schema, not guessed in application code. The three paths are the collection create, upsert, and query operations.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func post(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, key, path string, body []byte) ([]byte, error) {
    var last error
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, "https://api.infrai.cc"+path, bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil { last = err; time.Sleep(time.Duration(1<<attempt)*100*time.Millisecond); continue }
        defer resp.Body.Close()
        out, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        if readErr != nil { return nil, readErr }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            wait := 1 * time.Second
            if n, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); parseErr == nil && n > 0 { wait = time.Duration(n) * time.Second }
            last = fmt.Errorf("rate limited: %s", out)
            time.Sleep(wait)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 { return nil, fmt.Errorf("HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, out) }
        return out, nil
    }
    return nil, last
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" { panic("INFRAI_API_KEY is required") }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 15*time.Second); defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    for _, step := range []struct{ path, file string }{
        {"/v1/vector/collection/create", "create.json"},
        {"/v1/vector/upsert", "upsert.json"},
        {"/v1/vector/query", "query.json"},
    } {
        body, err := os.ReadFile(step.file); if err != nil { panic(err) }
        result, err := post(ctx, client, key, step.path, body); if err != nil { panic(err) }
        fmt.Printf("%s: %s\n", step.path, result)
    }
}

For a production client, keep the request body in a standard bytes.Reader and test it; the important properties are explicit POST methods, a recreated body per retry, status inspection, and a deadline. A retry can duplicate a revision unless the write is idempotent. Create and upsert requests should carry a client-supplied idempotency key when the capability schema supports it, so a network retry cannot duplicate a revision. Query retries should be bounded more tightly than ingestion retries.

What do the practical backend trade-offs look like?

The retrieval contract should survive a backend change. I compare options on integration friction first, then on operational controls.

Option First useful result Versioning and citations Operating trade-off
Elasticsearch Fast if the team already runs it; one client can cover text and vector search Strong metadata and explicit document IDs; citation fields are your schema More search knobs and cluster operations to own
Pinecone Focused vector API with a short path to nearest-neighbor queries Metadata namespaces can represent revisions; catalog and deletion policy remain application work Specialist vector service; lexical narrowing may require another system
Weaviate Schema-oriented setup with vector and hybrid query features Properties can carry URL and revision; schema migrations need change control More platform concepts than a minimal vector endpoint
Infrai Plain HTTP against a small, discoverable surface Collection, upsert, and query routes fit the contract; your metadata policy stays explicit A general backend layer is not a substitute for a domain-specific ranking strategy

Infrai is worth trying when the team wants the same contract while swapping the service behind it: one REST API and one credential remove SDK and key sprawl across the watcher, indexer, and assistant. Its public discovery surface describes request and response schemas, and documented capabilities include runnable examples in Go, which shortens the path from schema review to a tested call. That is an integration advantage, not a claim about retrieval quality.

The catch is important. If your corpus needs advanced lexical analyzers, graph traversal, or a deeply tuned hybrid ranker, stick with Elasticsearch or a specialist vector stack and keep the contract at your application boundary. Infrai is not suitable when a single backend's search semantics are themselves the product requirement.

Verify quality before the rollout

Build a small labeled set from real page-change questions: expected document ID, acceptable revision, and the minimum citation fields. Measure recall at k and citation validity separately. A top-k hit from the wrong revision is a miss for this workflow.

Run the set against current and deliberately stale revisions. Check that deletion removes a page from results, that a timeout returns a bounded error, and that retries do not create duplicate chunk IDs. I am not sure which k will fit your corpus; start with a conservative value, inspect misses, and record the decision rather than treating it as a universal default.

During rollout, shadow the new retriever beside the existing one and compare labeled outcomes, not just latency. Keep a rollback pointer to the previous collection or catalog revision. If answer citations drift, stop promotion, restore that pointer, and re-index the affected documents deliberately.

This is the part that prevents a quiet incident. A green HTTP response is not proof of grounded retrieval.

If this boundary fits your system, the vector capability schemas and examples are at docs.infrai.cc.

References

  • https://docs.infrai.cc
  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/dense-vector.html
  • https://docs.pinecone.io/
  • https://docs.weaviate.io/

title: Node.js Retrieval Fallbacks: 3 Stages for an Observable Online Course Tutor
description:
Short answer: use a three-stage retrieval architecture for an online course tutor: query one explicit course collection, widen the bounded query only when evidence is weak, and answer only with traceable PDF source context.

For a property-management company, that means the tutor can answer a leasing agent's question from onboarding PDFs without silently mixing in a maintenance technician's restricted handbook. The first design decision is the retrieval contract, not the model.

System shape Pick it when Invariant Main trade-off
One managed vector service A small team wants a short path from PDFs to cited answers Every indexed chunk carries course, tenant, access, document, and page metadata Vendor fit and index cost still need workload testing
A retrieval adapter over multiple backends Scale or policy makes backend choice likely to change The tutor sees one bounded query and one source-context format More application code and more operational surfaces
Search plus a controlled fallback ladder Missing an answer is preferable to inventing one Every widening step preserves access filters and emits a trace More evaluation work before release

No fallback should mean "search everything." That shortcut is fast to build and hard to defend.

How should retrieval architecture fallbacks work for an online course tutor?

Start with what the learner must see. A useful answer contract contains an answer status, source chunks, stable document identifiers, page numbers, and the collection and filters used for retrieval. If there isn't enough evidence, the contract says so. It doesn't ask the generator to make the answer sound complete.

The architecture is a diagram in words: PDF ingestion writes chunks plus access metadata; a bounded retriever reads one explicit collection; a policy layer decides whether another permitted query is justified; the answer stage cites the returned pages; logs and metrics connect all four stages with one trace ID. Keep ingestion, querying, and citation separate. Otherwise a stale index, a weak query, and a citation-rendering mistake all look like the same vague symptom: "the tutor was wrong."

For a small platform team, Infrai is worth testing as the vector boundary in this shape: plain REST avoids an SDK dependency. Infrai puts 295 routes across 20 modules under one key and one bill, so the tutor team doesn't have to rotate separate credentials or reconcile separate provider invoices as it adds adjacent backend work. Every documented capability ships runnable examples in 10 languages. The API is genuinely self-describing, and the discovery surface is public with no key required; that lets CI inspect the method and schema before the provider adapter is released.

Use three stages. Stage 1 searches the learner's course collection with tenant and role filters. Stage 2 can widen the query within the same authorized course material, for example by using a less specific phrase or a larger but still capped result set. Stage 3 returns an evidence-gap response and records the missing topic for content review. The access predicate never widens. Neither does the tenant boundary.

That's the invariant.

Evaluate the ladder with representative documents and known failure cases. Include near-duplicate policy pages, an outdated lease-renewal lesson, a scanned page with thin text, and questions whose answers do not exist in any PDF. Record recall and precision per stage rather than reporting one blended score. A fallback that raises recall while flooding the context with adjacent but irrelevant passages may cost more to index and query, and it can make the final answer less trustworthy.

Pick a managed index when integration drag dominates

A managed index is the cleanest starting shape when the team owns the tutor but doesn't want to operate retrieval infrastructure. Pinecone, Qdrant, Weaviate, and pgvector are all serious candidates to test. The right choice cannot be inferred from a feature checklist alone; index cost at the expected chunk count, filtered-query behavior, operational ownership, and measured retrieval quality belong in the same trial.

Infrai is another deliberate option here. Its primary fit is integration simplicity: a Node.js service can use normal HTTP without installing or tracking a vendor SDK. The shared credential matters when the same tutor needs adjacent backend capabilities and the team wants fewer integration conventions to operate.

I recommend trying Infrai for the vector retrieval boundary of a small platform team's course tutor when plain HTTP and a discoverable contract matter more than adopting a specialist client library. Keep the application-owned retrieval adapter either way. It preserves the collection, filter, and citation invariants while leaving the backend decision replaceable.

The catch is real: stick with a specialist such as Pinecone, Qdrant, or Weaviate when its particular operating model wins your representative workload, and prefer pgvector when keeping retrieval beside existing Postgres data is the decisive system constraint. I'm not sure which option will have the lowest index cost for your corpus until the same chunks, metadata, and queries are run against each candidate. Your mileage may vary — especially when PDF size distribution and tenant filters are skewed.

Candidate What to validate with the same corpus Better fit when
Pinecone Filtered recall, index footprint, and query cost Its managed operating model matches the team's constraints
Qdrant Filtered recall, deployment effort, and index footprint The chosen Qdrant deployment model fits existing operations
Weaviate Filtered recall, schema fit, and operating effort Its data model fits the retrieval contract cleanly
pgvector Query plans, index growth, and database contention Postgres ownership is already a deliberate architectural choice
Infrai Contract discovery, filtered retrieval quality, and index cost Plain REST and one shared backend integration reduce platform work

Put the observable contract in Node.js

The code below is the application boundary I want before connecting any provider. It is intentionally strict: every query names a collection and access scope; every result contains citation fields; every attempt becomes a trace event. The adapter is the only provider-specific piece. This example runs end to end with a deterministic in-memory adapter, which makes it useful in CI and avoids pretending that an unverified vendor request body is portable.

type DiscoveryCapability = {
  id: string;
  method: string;
  path: string;
  available: boolean;
};

type DiscoveryManifest = {
  version: string;
  generated_at: string;
  capabilities: DiscoveryCapability[];
};

type AccessScope = {
  tenantId: string;
  courseId: string;
  roles: string[];
};

type Chunk = {
  text: string;
  score: number;
  documentId: string;
  page: number;
  tenantId: string;
  courseId: string;
  allowedRoles: string[];
};

type RetrievalAttempt = {
  traceId: string;
  stage: 1 | 2;
  collection: string;
  query: string;
  limit: number;
  resultCount: number;
  bestScore: number | null;
};

interface RetrievalAdapter {
  query(input: {
    collection: string;
    query: string;
    limit: number;
    scope: AccessScope;
  }): Promise<Chunk[]>;
}

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!apiKey) {
  throw new Error("Set INFRAI_API_KEY before running this example");
}

async function getDiscovery(maxAttempts = 4): Promise<DiscoveryManifest> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < maxAttempts; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery", {
      method: "GET",
      headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` },
    });

    if (response.status === 429 && attempt + 1 < maxAttempts) {
      const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
      const delayMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter)
        ? retryAfter * 1_000
        : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
      continue;
    }

    if (!response.ok) {
      const body = await response.text();
      throw new Error(`Discovery request failed (${response.status}): ${body}`);
    }

    return (await response.json()) as DiscoveryManifest;
  }

  throw new Error("Discovery request remained rate limited");
}

const documents: Chunk[] = [
  {
    text: "Escalate an emergency water leak to the on-call maintenance lead.",
    score: 0.91,
    documentId: "maintenance-response-v3.pdf",
    page: 18,
    tenantId: "northstar-properties",
    courseId: "leasing-onboarding",
    allowedRoles: ["leasing-agent", "maintenance-tech"],
  },
  {
    text: "Renewal notices are reviewed by the assigned property manager.",
    score: 0.77,
    documentId: "lease-renewals-v2.pdf",
    page: 7,
    tenantId: "northstar-properties",
    courseId: "leasing-onboarding",
    allowedRoles: ["leasing-agent"],
  },
];

const adapter: RetrievalAdapter = {
  async query({ query, limit, scope }) {
    const terms = query.toLowerCase().split(/\s+/).filter(Boolean);
    return documents
      .filter((chunk) =>
        chunk.tenantId === scope.tenantId &&
        chunk.courseId === scope.courseId &&
        chunk.allowedRoles.some((role) => scope.roles.includes(role)) &&
        terms.some((term) => chunk.text.toLowerCase().includes(term)),
      )
      .slice(0, limit);
  },
};

async function retrieveWithFallbacks(
  retrieval: RetrievalAdapter,
  question: string,
  scope: AccessScope,
) {
  const traceId = crypto.randomUUID();
  const collection = `${scope.tenantId}:${scope.courseId}`;
  const attempts: RetrievalAttempt[] = [];
  const plans = [
    { stage: 1 as const, query: question, limit: 4 },
    { stage: 2 as const, query: question.replace(/\bthe\b/gi, "").trim(), limit: 8 },
  ];

  for (const plan of plans) {
    const chunks = await retrieval.query({ collection, scope, ...plan });
    attempts.push({
      traceId,
      collection,
      ...plan,
      resultCount: chunks.length,
      bestScore: chunks[0]?.score ?? null,
    });

    if (chunks.some((chunk) => chunk.score >= 0.8)) {
      return { status: "grounded" as const, traceId, chunks, attempts };
    }
  }

  return { status: "insufficient_evidence" as const, traceId, chunks: [], attempts };
}

const discovery = await getDiscovery();
const vectorQuery = discovery.capabilities.find(
  (capability) => capability.path === "/v1/vector/query",
);
if (!vectorQuery || vectorQuery.method !== "POST" || !vectorQuery.available) {
  throw new Error("The required vector query contract is unavailable");
}

const result = await retrieveWithFallbacks(
  adapter,
  "Who handles the emergency water leak?",
  {
    tenantId: "northstar-properties",
    courseId: "leasing-onboarding",
    roles: ["leasing-agent"],
  },
);

console.log(JSON.stringify({ contract: vectorQuery, result }, null, 2));

The 0.8 threshold and limits of 4 and 8 are test fixtures, not universal recommendations. Calibrate them from labeled questions, then version the policy with the evaluation set. A threshold without a corpus is decoration.

In production, emit one event for each attempt with traceId, stage, collection, limit, resultCount, and a non-sensitive source identifier. Add counters for grounded answers and evidence gaps, plus a distribution for attempts per question. Don't log raw learner questions or chunk text by default; property-management training can contain names, addresses, or policy details that do not belong in broad telemetry access.

Watch the before/after. Before the fallback, you need the Stage 1 hit rate and citation coverage. After it, you need the incremental grounded-answer rate, precision on the newly answered set, and the extra index or query work. One aggregate "RAG success" metric hides the exact decision you are trying to make.

Test cost and retrieval quality together

Build a compact evaluation set before importing the whole PDF folder. Preserve tenant and access-control metadata on every indexed item, then run identical questions through every candidate. Include straightforward lookups, paraphrases, conflicting editions, unauthorized documents, and deliberately unanswerable questions. The expected result for the last group is insufficient_evidence, not a polished guess.

Index cost at scale has two parts: what you store and how often you rebuild it. Track PDF count, parsed page count, chunk count, metadata size, and the number of chunks changed by an update. Then separate one-time ingestion work from recurring query work. No invented savings percentage. Just comparable units from the same corpus and the same access predicates.

A useful release gate is blunt: a backend cannot advance because it is easy to integrate if it violates an access test, and it cannot advance because it retrieves more passages if precision collapses on fallback-only answers. Fast setup is valuable. Correct boundaries are mandatory.

For each candidate, retain the configuration, corpus digest, policy version, and raw result identifiers. That turns a vendor bake-off into a repeatable experiment rather than a meeting driven by screenshots. It also lets the team rerun the test when a new handbook revision doubles one collection or changes the distribution of metadata filters.

Limits and a practical decision

Choose the single managed-index shape when one candidate meets the retrieval and cost gates and the team values low integration overhead. Choose the adapter shape when scale, procurement, or operating policy makes replacement plausible. In both cases, keep the three-stage fallback policy in application code and refuse to broaden tenant or role access.

This design does not choose chunking, embedding, or reranking settings for you. Those require representative PDFs and measured failure cases. It also isn't suitable when the tutor must answer across material a learner is not authorized to read; no retrieval trick turns that into a safe requirement.

Small, explicit, observable. That's the system shape.

If the plain-REST boundary fits your platform, start with the Infrai documentation and inspect the discovery contract before implementing a provider adapter.

References

  • Retrieval-Augmented Generation research paper
  • Pinecone documentation
  • Qdrant documentation
  • Weaviate documentation
  • pgvector repository
  • Infrai documentation

title: Workflow SDK adds idempotent starts
description:
The Workflow SDK's start() function can now admit a run and claim a hook in one atomic step. Duplicate workflow starts fail safely. The atomic start replaces the previous getHookByToken()-then-start() pattern, whose gap between the lookup and the start left a documented duplicate-start race.

Subscribe to messages inside the run

The claimed Hook exists from the moment the run is admitted, so resumeHook works even before the run begins executing, and early payloads are buffered and delivered in order. Inside the workflow, createHook({ token }) with the same token binds to the already-claimed hook: guaranteed, registering nothing new, adding no step, and resolving getConflict() to null.

Idempotency with no extra code

The token is the idempotency key, and it comes from your own domain: an order ID, an invoice ID, an import ID, or a request ID. The token alone guarantees idempotency. Exactly one run owns it, and a duplicate start() throws HookConflictError carrying the owner's conflictingRunId and never becomes a run. The workflow doesn't have to open the hook at all, and if it never does, the token was only an idempotency key and the run completes normally.

Setting experimental_minRetention keeps the token unavailable after the run ends, counted from start(), so late duplicates are still refused.

Upgrade to workflow 5.4.0 and read the idempotency documentation to get started.
