title: DeepSeek API Expansions, Local 284B MoE Runs, and New Developer Tooling
description:
TL;DR This digest covers local execution of the 284-billion parameter DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 via llama-modchip, new developer endpoints for DeepSeek, and updates to harnesses like Claude Code 2.1.323 and Qwen Code 1.0. We also examine Anthropic's multi-turn safety evaluations and a novel clustering algorithm from Meta FAIR.

What actually moved today

The landscape of local inference and developer tooling shifted this week with major updates to quantization techniques, API capabilities, and agent harnesses. Developers can now run massive mixture-of-experts models on modest hardware configurations previously thought impossible for such parameter counts. Meanwhile, production-facing APIs are expanding to include native multi-modal and file-handling features directly within backend endpoints, reducing the need for custom middleware.

At the same time, coding agent environments are iterating rapidly. New experimental modes allow agents to execute structured code to invoke external tools, changing how we think about tool-use reliability in CLI environments. These changes collectively lower the barrier for deploying sophisticated workflows both locally and in production architectures.

The model watch

Running DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 locally with llama-modchip

The open-source llama-modchip project released patches enabling the execution of the 284-billion parameter DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 model on a standard developer machine with 64GB of RAM and no dedicated GPU. By compressing attention weights down to 3.75 bits and pushing the expert weights further to an average of 1.72 bits, the resulting file size drops to a manageable 56.9 GiB. On a Ryzen 9 9955HX, the implementation generates approximately 8.66 tokens per second while processing input prompts at speeds between 36 and 44 tokens per second. This development makes it feasible to test massive mixture-of-experts architectures locally without renting cloud accelerators, though memory bandwidth remains the primary bottleneck for token generation throughput.

DeepSeek expands developer API

DeepSeek expanded its developer-facing API to expose capabilities previously locked inside the proprietary user interface. Developers can now programmatically integrate web search, native file and link handling, built-in safety mechanisms, and voice processing functions directly into their applications. Alongside these endpoints, new options for optical character recognition, automatic speech recognition, and text-to-speech were demonstrated alongside an open-source chat interface reference implementation. This structural update allows engineering teams to construct feature-complete assistant applications that leverage DeepSeek's backend parsing and search infrastructure without spinning up auxiliary microservices for document parsing or transcription.

Claude Code and Cursor harness updates

Coding assistants saw significant feature drops across multiple platforms. Claude Code 2.1.323 introduced an experimental Code Mode where the model writes raw JavaScript to invoke tools directly, minimizing intermediate parsing overhead. Cursor integrated voice chat capabilities across its IDE, web interfaces, and iOS clients using Grok Voice for lower-latency conversational loops. Additionally, Qwen Code 1.0 launched in preview as a unified package combining features from Qoder and previous iteration lineages, simplifying the local installation footprint for developers managing multiple command-line coding agents alongside tools like Codex CLI 0.168.0 and OpenCode 2.2.6.

Anthropic details multi-turn safety evaluations

Anthropic published a technical report detailing how they evaluate AI safety across extended dialogues using a separate instance of Claude acting as a simulated user. Instead of evaluating individual prompts in isolation, an automated judge model inspects the entire transcript, failing the candidate model if any single turn breaches established safety boundaries. This methodology captures behavioral degradation, prompt drift, and compliance erosion that typically manifest only after twenty or thirty turns of context accumulation, providing a more realistic benchmark for production deployment.

Meta FAIR proposes a new clustering algorithm

Researchers at Meta FAIR published work on a novel clustering algorithm engineered to surpass traditional k-means across core machine learning workloads. The algorithm targets foundational bottlenecks in vector search, retrieval-augmented generation pipeline construction, embedding space organization, dataset balancing, and weight quantization routines. By improving centroid assignment efficiency, the approach aims to accelerate large-scale vector operations without sacrificing cluster purity.

Rumours, clearly labelled

It is important to separate verified software releases from unconfirmed reports circulating in developer forums and community channels. None of the items in this section have official confirmation from the respective engineering teams:

Item Status Basis Notes
Microsoft 365 global outage Unconfirmed User reports Alleged 12-hour disruption across Outlook, Teams, and Copilot
Gemini 4 Hydrogen indexing Unconfirmed Platform metrics Rumoured appearance on third-party tracking benchmarks
Claude Code secret persistence Unconfirmed Social media claims Alleged saving of command secrets in .claude/settings.local.json

These claims lack reproducible artifacts, official changelogs, or verifiable repository commits. Treat them with skepticism until primary sources or official patches provide concrete verification.

Odd finds and small tools

Quietly tucked away in repository commits and community discussions are utility scripts that solve mundane engineering frictions. A lightweight utility for parsing messy markdown headers in local documentation pipelines gained traction among static site maintainers. Another script helps automate the pruning of stale Docker build caches based on active branch references rather than simple time-to-live thresholds. These tools rarely make headline announcements, but they frequently save hours of brittle bash scripting in CI pipelines.

What I would try this weekend

If you have a free afternoon, grab the latest llama-modchip repository and attempt to spin up DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 on your local 64GB RAM machine to measure actual token generation latency against your daily workflow notes. Compare the prompt ingestion speeds with a smaller model like Nemotron-30B to see where memory bandwidth constraints begin to degrade response times. Afterward, experiment with Claude Code 2.1.323's experimental Code Mode by writing a custom JavaScript tool wrapper to observe how reliably the model generates execution scripts compared to standard JSON-schema tool definitions.

Where this leaves us

We are witnessing a fascinating convergence where massive, highly quantized mixture-of-experts models are becoming accessible on consumer hardware, while agent harnesses become increasingly autonomous through direct code execution. However, running 284 billion parameters locally at single-digit token rates remains more of an exploratory exercise than a viable production strategy for latency-sensitive applications. API expansions like those from DeepSeek reduce boilerplate code for search and voice, but engineering teams must still weigh the trade-offs of third-party backend dependencies against self-hosted alternatives. As multi-turn evaluation frameworks mature, our understanding of long-context safety will improve, yet many deployment edge cases remain unresolved.

What debugging strategy do you rely on most when local quantization artifacts produce subtle output drift in your pipelines?

💬 Questions, corrections or a better way to run these evals? Feedback and discussion are in the channel: https://t.me/GitHub_Open_Source

title: Node.js Marketplace Images: Strip EXIF Location Data Before 2 Publishing Gates
description:
Short answer: re-encode every public image derivative at the marketplace boundary, then read the derivative back and refuse publication if EXIF location data remains. Keep the uploaded original, metadata included, only when a documented business or legal reason justifies it, and keep that original under access control. For a Node.js Express pipeline that turns seller uploads into short promo videos, I would put both checks on the upload path unless request latency is the product; on-demand processing is viable, but it moves privacy enforcement into every render and preview path.

The failure I plan around is narrow and serious: an upload is copied into a public derivative, a promo-video job consumes it, and the seller's location travels with the image because the bytes were copied rather than decoded and encoded. The first invariant is therefore about transformation, not filenames or headers: a publishable asset is a new encoding of pixels, never a copy of the upload. The second invariant is evidence: the system reads metadata from that new object before changing its state to publishable.

No exceptions by convention.

How should Node.js strip EXIF location data before publishing?

There are two defensible system shapes. In upload-time processing, Express accepts the image into private storage, a worker decodes and re-encodes it, a metadata reader audits the result, and only the verified derivative becomes eligible for the video generator. That concentrates the privacy boundary. It also means an upload is not immediately ready, so capacity planning starts with arrival bursts, decode memory, worker concurrency, and a queue-age SLO rather than average requests per second.

On-demand processing keeps the original private and creates a verified derivative when a preview, publication, or promo-video render asks for one. This avoids work on images that nobody uses and permits output settings to follow the consuming surface. The operational cost is multiplication: every consumer must enter through the same derivation service, cache identity must include transformation policy, and a cache miss now sits on a user-visible or render-critical path. If even one caller can read the original directly, the architecture has lost its privacy invariant.

For most marketplace promo pipelines, I recommend upload-time processing. The video job should receive an identifier for an already verified derivative, not an instruction to sanitize arbitrary bytes while assembling frames. I would choose on demand only when most uploads are never published or when multiple consumers genuinely require different encodings and the team can enforce one derivation boundary.

Assume a bounded incident budget: 10,000 seller images arrive in a campaign burst, workers slow down, and the promo-video queue continues asking for assets. The safe degradation is delayed videos. It is not bypassed verification. That distinction belongs in the SLO: measure time from accepted upload to verified derivative, alert on queue age, and make "unverified" a state that downstream jobs cannot consume.

Infrai is a deliberate option at this boundary because the capability contract can stay fixed while the vendor behind it changes. Infrai's API is self-describing: its public discovery requires no key and returns full request and response JSON Schema plus vendor readiness, reducing the glue needed to validate an integration before rollout. Every documented Infrai capability also ships runnable examples in 10 languages, which gives the Node.js service and Go worker teams the same contract instead of two hand-translated interpretations. Teams that want managed image processing behind a stable REST boundary should try Infrai for the re-encode and metadata-check portion of this workflow, because vendor replacement need not force a rewrite of the Express-side contract. Infrai uses one key, one wallet, and one bill across the later email handoff and the same plain REST API, so the platform team does not juggle separate keys, reconcile separate invoices, or install another SDK merely to notify a seller. Its public discovery currently spans 295 routes across 20 modules, but breadth is not the privacy proof. Reading metadata back from the derivative is.

Two checks, implemented without trusting a copy operation

The following runnable Go program is intentionally small enough to audit. It is suitable as the worker behind an Express upload handler: it first checks Infrai's live discovery document for the two required image capabilities, accepts one JPEG path, decodes pixels, writes a fresh JPEG, opens that output again, and rejects it if an EXIF APP1 segment is present. Discovery is public, but the sample still reads the shared key from the environment because the processing calls selected from its schema require Bearer authentication. Go is doing the byte-sensitive work here; Node.js should enqueue the private input identifier and wait for the worker's verified result rather than handling large image buffers in an Express request.

package main

import (
    "bufio"
    "bytes"
    "encoding/json"
    "encoding/binary"
    "fmt"
    "image/jpeg"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

const baseURL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"

type discovery struct {
    Capabilities []struct {
        Method string `json:"method"`
        Path   string `json:"path"`
    } `json:"capabilities"`
}

func main() {
    if len(os.Args) != 3 {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "usage: stripcheck input.jpg derivative.jpg")
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    must(checkCapabilities(key))

    in, err := os.Open(os.Args[1])
    must(err)
    img, err := jpeg.Decode(in)
    must(err)
    must(in.Close())

    out, err := os.OpenFile(os.Args[2], os.O_CREATE|os.O_WRONLY|os.O_TRUNC, 0600)
    must(err)
    must(jpeg.Encode(out, img, &jpeg.Options{Quality: 90}))
    must(out.Close())

    clean, err := os.Open(os.Args[2])
    must(err)
    hasEXIF, err := containsEXIF(clean)
    must(clean.Close())
    must(err)
    if hasEXIF {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "verification failed: derivative contains EXIF")
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    fmt.Println("verified: derivative contains no EXIF segment")
}

func checkCapabilities(key string) error {
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, baseURL+"/discovery", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            resp.Body.Close()
            delay := time.Second << attempt
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            body, _ := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 4096))
            resp.Body.Close()
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery returned %s: %s", resp.Status, body)
        }

        var doc discovery
        err = json.NewDecoder(resp.Body).Decode(&doc)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        needed := map[string]bool{
            "POST /v1/image/process":  false,
            "POST /v1/image/metadata": false,
        }
        for _, capability := range doc.Capabilities {
            key := capability.Method + " " + capability.Path
            if _, ok := needed[key]; ok {
                needed[key] = true
            }
        }
        for capability, found := range needed {
            if !found {
                return fmt.Errorf("required capability unavailable: %s", capability)
            }
        }
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("discovery remained rate-limited after 4 attempts")
}

func containsEXIF(r io.Reader) (bool, error) {
    b := bufio.NewReader(r)
    soi := make([]byte, 2)
    if _, err := io.ReadFull(b, soi); err != nil {
        return false, err
    }
    if !bytes.Equal(soi, []byte{0xff, 0xd8}) {
        return false, fmt.Errorf("not a JPEG")
    }

    for {
        prefix, err := b.ReadByte()
        if err != nil {
            return false, err
        }
        if prefix != 0xff {
            return false, fmt.Errorf("invalid JPEG marker")
        }
        marker, err := b.ReadByte()
        if err != nil {
            return false, err
        }
        for marker == 0xff {
            marker, err = b.ReadByte()
            if err != nil {
                return false, err
            }
        }
        if marker == 0xd9 || marker == 0xda {
            return false, nil
        }

        var size uint16
        if err := binary.Read(b, binary.BigEndian, &size); err != nil {
            return false, err
        }
        if size < 2 {
            return false, fmt.Errorf("invalid JPEG segment length")
        }
        payload := make([]byte, int(size)-2)
        if _, err := io.ReadFull(b, payload); err != nil {
            return false, err
        }
        if marker == 0xe1 && bytes.HasPrefix(payload, []byte("Exif\x00\x00")) {
            return true, nil
        }
    }
}

func must(err error) {
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

This is deliberately JPEG-specific. A production service must select a decoder, encoder, and verifier for every accepted file type; changing the suffix is not conversion, and a successful decode alone says nothing about the metadata on the encoded output. The MDN image-format guide is a useful inventory of formats, but the accepted-format policy still belongs to the application.

The state transition should be equally plain: private_original -> processing -> verified_derivative -> publishable. Failure to decode, encode, or verify ends in quarantine or rejection. It never falls through to a copied original. Retries must address the same asset and transformation policy so that a worker retry cannot create competing publication records.

Buy, build, or keep a specialist?

The decision is not "managed good, library bad." It is where the team wants to own codecs, patching, queue behavior, vendor credentials, transformation semantics, and evidence.

Option Boundary the team owns Useful fit Limitation to budget for
Sharp with libvips Express/worker code through storage and verification Teams wanting local control and a compact Node.js image stack The team owns deployment, memory limits, codec updates, retries, and metadata-audit behavior
ImageMagick CLI or service wrapper through storage and verification Broad format and policy work where operators already maintain the toolchain A larger operational and security-patching surface, plus wrapper discipline
Cloudinary Upload and managed transformation contract Media-heavy products that want a specialist asset platform and its transformation model More coupling to a media-specific asset model and vendor workflow
Imgix Source integration and delivery transformations Delivery-led systems centered on image rendering and CDN behavior The source and delivery model may be more machinery than a private-to-public audit gate needs
AWS S3 plus Lambda Object events, function runtime, IAM, and audit state AWS-standardized teams that want infrastructure-level control At least two service surfaces, IAM design, event retries, and verification state remain yours
Infrai One REST contract for processing and metadata inspection Teams prioritizing a replaceable capability boundary and public schema discovery One platform becomes a shared trust, billing, and outage surface

Sharp is my default build choice when a team already operates Node workers and accepts codec ownership. Cloudinary or Imgix is the better choice when the requirement is a mature, specialist media lifecycle rather than this narrow sanitation gate. S3 plus Lambda fits organizations whose controls and on-call practice are already built around AWS. The managed REST option fits when contract stability across underlying vendors matters more than direct specialist integration; its runnable examples in 10 languages reduce integration interpretation, although the production SLO and the derivative audit remain the marketplace's responsibility.

There is another seam worth resisting. If a notification must follow a verified asset, a self-managed stack using Puppeteer plus Resend or SES generally introduces two signups, two credential sets, and application glue for handoff, retries, and correlation. A single Infrai key can cover content-processing and email capabilities under one base API, avoiding a temporary bucket used only to move an attachment between vendors. That consolidation has a cost: one vendor now carries a wider blast radius. Also, do not assume an email attachment shape from a marketing page; generate the client from the discovery schema and test the exact contract before adopting the combined path.

What should the publication SLO actually say?

"Metadata was stripped" is not an SLO. It is an assertion without a measurement point.

Use a numerator that counts derivatives whose post-encode metadata read contains no EXIF location data, and a denominator of derivatives admitted to publication. The target can be strict because a failed check does not require risky availability behavior: it can block the asset while the rest of the marketplace remains available. Track latency separately. Otherwise a team under queue pressure will be tempted to treat privacy verification as optional work.

Capacity planning follows the same separation. I start with a CPU model, then revise it as soon as the largest accepted dimensions expose the memory ceiling; that correction matters because an apparently idle core does not make another concurrent decode safe. Benchmark decode and encode memory, cap concurrent workers from memory rather than CPU alone, and load-test the upload burst that matters to the marketplace. Those values are workload measurements, so I would not borrow someone else's numbers. The useful test produces a service curve: arrival rate, worker count, queue age, verification failures, and time to recover after the burst.

Keep originals only under a retention rule with an owner and a reason. Private originals may be necessary for disputes, seller editing, or later transformations, but "we might need them" is not a control. If the reason expires, so should the original.

Where does this architecture stop fitting?

Upload-time re-encoding is a poor fit when an image must retain provenance metadata, when the original itself is the regulated record, or when users explicitly download originals. In those systems, preserve the record privately and create a separate disclosure policy for derivatives; never describe destructive metadata removal as archival integrity.

On-demand processing can also be the right call for a marketplace with a very low publication ratio and a well-enforced central delivery service. The condition is architectural, not financial: no preview, video renderer, emailer, or CDN origin may bypass that service. If the team cannot demonstrate that invariant, it should pay the upload-time processing cost and simplify the security argument.

The decision rule is compact. Re-encode once at upload when many consumers need the same safe derivative. Re-encode on demand when few uploads are consumed or outputs materially differ, but force every consumer through one verified transformation boundary. In either design, copying is not sanitation and encoding success is not proof; the metadata read-back is the second gate.

If that managed boundary fits your system, start with the platform documentation and inspect the live discovery schema before writing the adapter.

References

  • MDN: Image file type and format guide
  • Sharp documentation
  • ImageMagick documentation
  • Cloudinary image transformations
  • Imgix rendering API
  • AWS Lambda with Amazon S3
  • Infrai documentation

title: Build an LLM Gateway with hikyaku: One Endpoint, AI-Picked Models and Failover Across Providers
description:
Introduction

Look at how your app calls a model today. There is an SDK, an API key and a model name, all in the code. That works until one of three things happens:

  • The provider has a bad hour, and your feature is down with it.
  • A cheaper or better model ships, and moving to it is a code change in every service.
  • You pay for the strongest model on every request, including "say hi".

An LLM gateway fixes this. It is one endpoint that sits between your apps and the model providers. The apps call the gateway. The gateway picks the model, retries, and fails over to another provider.

hikyaku (飛脚) is an open-source message relay written in Go. Its launch article builds a webhook relay with AI routing. This article uses the same binary for a different job. A chat request is a message. A model is a destination. So the relay you already know is also a gateway.

Why Calling Providers Directly Hurts

Each app calls a provider Apps call a hikyaku gateway
Model choice A model name in the code of every service fast, smart or auto, mapped in one YAML file
A provider is down Your feature is down The request falls back to another provider
Easy and hard requests The same expensive model for both A decision model sends each one to the right model
Provider keys In every service Only in the gateway; apps hold one gateway key
A new model A deploy per service One line in the spec, and a reload
Token usage A dashboard per provider One Prometheus metric, per destination

How a Request Travels

Three parts of the spec do the work:

  • An openai source is the endpoint. It speaks the OpenAI HTTP API, so any OpenAI SDK can call it.
  • model destinations are the models. Each one runs the request on one model and answers in the OpenAI format.
  • A route picks a destination for each request. Rules handle the names fast and smart. For auto, a decision model picks.

Every model destination has the delivery features of any hikyaku destination: a timeout, retries, a circuit breaker and a fallback.

What You Will Build

A gateway over three providers:

  1. fast is Gemini. smart is Claude. backup is an OpenAI model that only serves when the others fail.
  2. auto lets a decision model choose between fast and smart for each request.
  3. Streaming, function calling and JSON output pass through.
  4. When Claude fails, Gemini answers the same request.

What You Need

  • hikyaku 1.6.1 or newer: brew install xavidop/tap/hikyaku, or go install github.com/xavidop/hikyaku/cmd/hikyaku@latest.
  • curl.
  • API keys for the providers you want to use. This guide uses GEMINI_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and OPENAI_API_KEY.
  • A TypeSafe API key in TYPESAFE_API_KEY, for the decision model behind auto.

Step 1: Write the Gateway Spec

Create a folder and add this hikyaku.yaml:

# yaml-language-server: $schema=https://xavidop.github.io/hikyaku/schema/hikyaku.schema.json
version: 1
name: llm-gateway

secrets:
  PROXY_KEY: env:PROXY_KEY                    # the key your apps send to the gateway
  GEMINI_API_KEY: env:GEMINI_API_KEY          # the provider keys stay here
  ANTHROPIC_API_KEY: env:ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
  OPENAI_API_KEY: env:OPENAI_API_KEY
  TYPESAFE_API_KEY: env:TYPESAFE_API_KEY

genkit:
  plugins: [systemone, googlegenai, anthropic, openai]

sources:
  - name: api
    type: openai
    listen: ":8080"
    models: [auto, fast, smart]               # what GET /v1/models lists
    auth: { bearer: { tokens: ["{{secrets.PROXY_KEY}}"] } }

defaults:
  timeout: 60s
  retry: { attempts: 2, backoff: 500ms }

destinations:
  - name: fast
    type: model
    model: googleai/gemini-3.8-flash
    fallback: [backup]
  - name: smart
    type: model
    model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5
    fallback: [fast]
  - name: backup
    type: model
    model: openai/gpt-5.4-mini

routes:
  - name: chat
    from: [api]
    router:
      type: rules
      rules:
        - { when: 'msg.json.model == "fast"', to: [fast] }
        - { when: 'msg.json.model == "smart"', to: [smart] }
      fallback:
        - type: ai
          when: msg.json.model == "auto"      # only "auto" pays for a decision
          model: typesafe/jev-1.13.0
          instructions: Pick the model for this chat request.
          state: "{{ .json.messages }}"
          candidates:
            - { name: fast, description: "A short or simple request: a greeting, a lookup, a rewrite, small talk" }
            - { name: smart, description: "A hard request: multi-step reasoning, math, code, analysis" }
          min_confidence: 0.6
          on_low_confidence: [smart]
          fallback:
            - { type: static, to: [fast] }

server:
  admin: { listen: ":9090" }

Read it from top to bottom:

  • secrets are references, not values. The provider keys stay on the gateway. PROXY_KEY is the one key your apps send.
  • genkit.plugins loads the model providers. hikyaku calls models through Genkit Go.
  • The source lists the model names your clients may ask for. These are your names, not the providers' names.
  • The destinations map each name to a real model. smart falls back to fast. fast falls back to backup.
  • The route has a chain of routers: rules first, then the AI router, then a static catch-all.

Check it 

export PROXY_KEY=local-dev-key
hikyaku validate
hikyaku doctor

✓ spec hikyaku.yaml: 1 sources, 3 destinations, 1 routes
✓ secrets 5 resolved
✓ plugins
✓ destination backup
✓ destination fast
✓ destination smart
✓ dead_letter
✓ store default (default)
✓ model anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5
✓ model googleai/gemini-3.8-flash
✓ model openai/gpt-5.4-mini
✓ model typesafe/jev-1.13.0

doctor resolves every secret and checks that each model answers. Fix what it reports before you go on.

hikyaku graph draws the spec. The dashed lines are the fallbacks:

Start the gateway:

hikyaku run

Step 2: Call It Like the OpenAI API

List the models 

curl -s localhost:8080/v1/models -H 'Authorization: Bearer local-dev-key'

{"data":[{"id":"auto","object":"model","created":0,"owned_by":"hikyaku"},{"id":"fast","object":"model","created":0,"owned_by":"hikyaku"},{"id":"smart","object":"model","created":0,"owned_by":"hikyaku"}],"object":"list"}

Ask for a model by name 

curl -s localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer local-dev-key' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"fast","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Say hi in five words."}]}'

{"id":"chatcmpl-01M7A7SNT3ZMV41Y8T56EQ9G9W","object":"chat.completion","created":1794566313,"model":"googleai/gemini-3.8-flash","choices":[{"index":0,"message":{"role":"assistant","content":"Hi! Hope you are well."},"finish_reason":"stop"}],"usage":{"prompt_tokens":7,"completion_tokens":7,"total_tokens":408}}

The answer has the shape of an OpenAI chat completion. The model field tells you which real model served it. Now smart:

curl -s localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer local-dev-key' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"smart","max_tokens":60,"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"In one sentence, why is a mutex needed around a shared map in Go?"}]}'

{"id":"chatcmpl-01M7A7STYGDEXJFNTPZHQVH3JS","object":"chat.completion","created":1794566319,"model":"anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5","choices":[{"index":0,"message":{"role":"assistant","content":"A mutex is needed because Go's built-in maps aren't safe for concurrent use, so simultaneous reads and writes (or multiple writes) from different goroutines cause data races that can cor"},"finish_reason":"length"}],"usage":{"prompt_tokens":31,"completion_tokens":60,"total_tokens":91}}

Same endpoint, same request shape, a different provider. The answer stops at 60 tokens, as the request asked.

Use an SDK

Because the endpoint speaks the OpenAI API, an OpenAI SDK only needs a new base URL and the gateway key:

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="http://localhost:8080/v1", api_key="local-dev-key")

Good to know:

  • A request without the key gets a 401 in OpenAI's error format: {"error":{"code":"invalid_api_key","message":"unauthorized: missing or wrong bearer token","param":null,"type":"invalid_request_error"}}.
  • The caller's Authorization header is never copied into the message. A provider never sees your gateway key, and a client never sees a provider key.

Step 3: Let a Decision Model Pick

Most requests are easy. A few are hard. With "model": "auto", the gateway decides.

The AI router does not use a chat model for this. It uses a decision model: a model that answers typed questions about a piece of data and gives each answer a calibrated probability. Here the question is "which of these two models should take this request?" The model is jev, served by TypeSafe through the System One plugin of Genkit.

See the decision before you spend a token

Save two requests:

echo '{"model":"auto","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"What is the capital of France?"}]}' > easy.json
echo '{"model":"auto","max_tokens":300,"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Write a Go function that merges two sorted linked lists and prove its time complexity step by step."}]}' > hard.json

hikyaku route --dry-run shows what the router would do, without calling any chat model:

hikyaku route --dry-run --source api --data @easy.json
hikyaku route --dry-run --source api --data @hard.json

route chat: ai (typesafe/jev-1.13.0) → fast
    fell back from rules: no rule matched
    * fast                 p=1.00
      smart                p=0.00
    reason: fast (p=1.00, margin 1.00)
    plan: fast → backup
route chat: ai (typesafe/jev-1.13.0) → smart
    fell back from rules: no rule matched
      fast                 p=0.00
    * smart                p=1.00
    reason: smart (p=1.00, margin 1.00)
    plan: smart → fast → backup

The rules did not match auto, so the AI router decided. The last line of each block is the delivery plan, fallbacks included.

Send them for real 

curl -s localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer local-dev-key' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @easy.json

{"id":"chatcmpl-01M7A7SWTN5XQ304FJYZDKWZ3T","object":"chat.completion","created":1794566321,"model":"googleai/gemini-3.8-flash","choices":[{"index":0,"message":{"role":"assistant","content":"The capital of France is **Paris**."},"finish_reason":"stop"}],"usage":{"prompt_tokens":8,"completion_tokens":8,"total_tokens":69}}

The same call with hard.json comes back from anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5, with 37 prompt tokens and 300 completion tokens.

Request with "model": "auto" Answered by
"What is the capital of France?" googleai/gemini-3.8-flash
"Write a Go function that merges two sorted linked lists and prove its time complexity step by step." anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5

Good to know:

  • Only auto pays for a decision. The AI router has when: msg.json.model == "auto", so fast and smart never reach it.
  • When the decision model is unsure, on_low_confidence: [smart] sends the request to the stronger model. A wrong guess costs money, not quality.
  • A model name that no rule knows, such as gpt-9, skips the AI router and lands on the static catch-all. In this spec that is fast.

Step 4: Score the Router on Labeled Cases

"It picked right twice" is not a test. Write down what you expect in cases.yaml:

cases:
  - name: greeting
    data: { model: auto, messages: [{ role: user, content: "Hi there, how are you today?" }] }
    expect: [fast]
  - name: lookup
    data: { model: auto, messages: [{ role: user, content: "What is the capital of France?" }] }
    expect: [fast]
  - name: rewrite
    data: { model: auto, messages: [{ role: user, content: "Rewrite this sentence in a friendlier tone: send me the report now." }] }
    expect: [fast]
  - name: code
    data: { model: auto, messages: [{ role: user, content: "Write a Go function that merges two sorted linked lists and prove its time complexity step by step." }] }
    expect: [smart]
  - name: math
    data: { model: auto, messages: [{ role: user, content: "A train leaves at 9:40 at 80 km/h and another at 10:10 at 110 km/h from the same station. When does the second catch the first? Show the steps." }] }
    expect: [smart]
  - name: analysis
    data: { model: auto, messages: [{ role: user, content: "Compare optimistic and pessimistic locking for a ticket booking system and recommend one, with trade-offs." }] }
    expect: [smart]

Then score the route:

hikyaku ai test --route chat --cases cases.yaml

route chat: 6 cases
accuracy  100.0% (6/6)
latency   p50 147ms  p95 307ms  max 307ms

per destination   precision  recall
  fast                 1.00    1.00
  smart                1.00    1.00

confusion (rows: expected, columns: got)
                         fast      smart
  fast                      3          0
  smart                     0          3

calibration (confidence → accuracy) ECE 0.000
  0.9-1.0  n=6   confidence 1.00  accuracy 1.00

Six of six, and a decision takes about 150 ms. That is the price of auto on top of the model call.

Good to know:

  • --min-accuracy 0.9 makes the command exit with 1 below that accuracy. Run it in CI when you change a candidate description.
  • Pin the decision model version (jev-1.13.0). Thresholds are tuned per version.
  • Use your own traffic for the cases. Six made-up prompts prove the idea; fifty real ones prove your gateway.

Step 5: Stream the Answer

Add "stream": true, and the answer arrives as server-sent events while the model writes it:

curl -sN localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer local-dev-key' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"fast","stream":true,"stream_options":{"include_usage":true},"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Count from one to five in words."}]}'

data: {"id":"chatcmpl-01M7A7T1J7RJHDPAV4SHVJF55F","object":"chat.completion.chunk","created":1794566325,"model":"googleai/gemini-3.8-flash","choices":[{"index":0,"delta":{"role":"assistant","content":"One, two, three, four, five."},"finish_reason":null}]}

data: {"id":"chatcmpl-01M7A7T1J7RJHDPAV4SHVJF55F","object":"chat.completion.chunk","created":1794566325,"model":"googleai/gemini-3.8-flash","choices":[{"index":0,"delta":{},"finish_reason":"stop"}]}

data: {"id":"chatcmpl-01M7A7T1J7RJHDPAV4SHVJF55F","object":"chat.completion.chunk","created":1794566325,"model":"googleai/gemini-3.8-flash","choices":[],"usage":{"prompt_tokens":9,"completion_tokens":10,"total_tokens":122}}

data: [DONE]

stream_options.include_usage adds a last chunk with the token usage, as on OpenAI.

One rule to remember about failures:

  • Before the first chunk, a failure is retried or falls back to another model, like any delivery.
  • After the first chunk, a failure ends the stream with an error event. No other model takes over half an answer.

Step 6: Function Calling and JSON Output

Function calling

Function calling lets a model ask your app to run a function. The gateway passes your function definitions to the model and passes the model's calls back to you. It runs no tool itself.

Save this as tools.json:

{"model":"fast",
 "tools":[{"type":"function","function":{"name":"get_weather","description":"Current weather for a city",
   "parameters":{"type":"object","properties":{"city":{"type":"string"}},"required":["city"]}}}],
 "messages":[{"role":"user","content":"What is the weather in Madrid right now?"}]}

curl -s localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer local-dev-key' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @tools.json

The answer holds the call. This is its choices part, with the long signature cut short:

{"index":0,
 "message":{"role":"assistant","content":null,
   "tool_calls":[{"id":"call_S46HHVWPVMN5J67WWXEFO76SV5","type":"function",
     "function":{"name":"get_weather","arguments":"{\"city\":\"Madrid\"}"},
     "extra_content":{"google":{"thought_signature":"EogCCoUCAWkUfRMk..."}}}]},
 "finish_reason":"tool_calls"}

Your app runs the function. Then it sends the conversation back, with the assistant message and one tool message that carries the call's id:

{"role":"tool","tool_call_id":"call_S46HHVWPVMN5J67WWXEFO76SV5","content":"{\"temp_c\": 14, \"sky\": \"clear\"}"}

The model reads the result and answers:

{"id":"chatcmpl-01M7A7TQMRCP7FJ39NZYCG09KZ","object":"chat.completion","created":1794566348,"model":"googleai/gemini-3.8-flash","choices":[{"index":0,"message":{"role":"assistant","content":"The current weather in Madrid is clear with a temperature of 14°C (57°F)."},"finish_reason":"stop"}],"usage":{"prompt_tokens":129,"completion_tokens":22,"total_tokens":182}}

Good to know:

  • Gemini adds a thought_signature to its calls. Send the assistant message back as you got it, signature included. Gemini 3 requires it.
  • Gemini gives no call id of its own, so the gateway makes one (call_...). Claude and OpenAI ids pass through.

JSON that follows a schema

response_format works too. Pass a JSON Schema, and the model must answer in that shape:

curl -s localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer local-dev-key' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"fast","response_format":{"type":"json_schema","json_schema":{"name":"ticket","schema":{"type":"object","properties":{"team":{"type":"string","enum":["billing","support"]},"urgent":{"type":"boolean"}},"required":["team","urgent"]}}},"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Classify: I was charged twice and I am furious."}]}'

{"id":"chatcmpl-01M7A7TSD6A3MQ4NVRKAZ2THAF","object":"chat.completion","created":1794566350,"model":"googleai/gemini-3.8-flash","choices":[{"index":0,"message":{"role":"assistant","content":"{\"team\":\"billing\",\"urgent\":true}"},"finish_reason":"stop"}],"usage":{"prompt_tokens":13,"completion_tokens":9,"total_tokens":326}}

Step 7: Fail Over Between Providers

This is the reason to run a gateway. Take Claude away and see what the client notices.

You do not need a real outage. hikyaku chaos runs the relay with one destination wrapped in a fault injector. Stop the gateway, and start it this way:

hikyaku chaos --destination smart --fail 100%

Every call to smart now fails. Ask for smart:

curl -s localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer local-dev-key' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"smart","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"In one sentence, why is a mutex needed around a shared map in Go?"}]}'

{"id":"chatcmpl-01M7A83P7XXZPKSSEZ8JTFDVHT","object":"chat.completion","created":1794566642,"model":"googleai/gemini-3.8-flash","choices":[{"index":0,"message":{"role":"assistant","content":"A mutex is needed because Go maps are not safe for concurrent use, and simultaneous reads and writes by multiple goroutines will cause a fatal runtime crash."},"finish_reason":"stop"}],"usage":{"prompt_tokens":17,"completion_tokens":30,"total_tokens":379}}

The client asked for smart and got an answer in 4.3 seconds. The model field is the only sign that Gemini wrote it. The gateway's log and metrics tell the full story:

{"time":"2026-11-13T11:44:02.029817+01:00","level":"INFO","msg":"destination fallback","from":"smart","to":"fast","reason":"exhausted"}

curl -s localhost:9090/metrics | grep -E "^hikyaku_(fallback_total|delivery_attempts_total)"

hikyaku_delivery_attempts_total{destination="fast",endpoint="fast",outcome="ok"} 1
hikyaku_delivery_attempts_total{destination="smart",endpoint="smart",outcome="transient"} 2
hikyaku_fallback_total{from="smart",reason="exhausted",to="fast"} 1

Two attempts on smart, as retry.attempts: 2 says. Then one on fast, which answered.

In a real outage, the circuit breaker helps too. After enough failures on a destination, hikyaku stops calling it for a while and sends requests straight to the fallback. Clients do not wait for retries that cannot succeed.

Good to know:

  • Put fallbacks on a different provider. smart to fast crosses from Anthropic to Google. fast to backup crosses from Google to OpenAI.
  • Providers accept different parameters. Some OpenAI models refuse stop, for example. A fallback can only answer a request that its model accepts.

Step 8: Watch Tokens per Model

The admin API on :9090 serves Prometheus metrics. After the requests of steps 2 to 6:

curl -s localhost:9090/metrics | grep -E "^hikyaku_(model_tokens_total|ai_decisions_total|router_skipped_total|delivery_attempts_total)"

hikyaku_ai_decisions_total{outcome="chosen",route="chat"} 2
hikyaku_delivery_attempts_total{destination="fast",endpoint="fast",outcome="ok"} 7
hikyaku_delivery_attempts_total{destination="smart",endpoint="smart",outcome="ok"} 2
hikyaku_model_tokens_total{destination="fast",type="input"} 220
hikyaku_model_tokens_total{destination="fast",type="output"} 81
hikyaku_model_tokens_total{destination="smart",type="input"} 68
hikyaku_model_tokens_total{destination="smart",type="output"} 360
hikyaku_router_skipped_total{route="chat",router="ai"} 1

Read it as a bill:

  • Seven requests went to the cheap model, two to the strong one.
  • The decision model was asked twice, for the two auto requests.
  • One request skipped the AI router: the unknown name gpt-9 from step 3.

Input and output tokens per destination are what you need to compare providers, or to see what auto saves.

Conclusion

A gateway turns the model into configuration. Your apps ask for fast, smart or auto. Which provider serves each name, and what happens when it fails, is one YAML file that you can review, test and reload.

Three things make hikyaku a good fit for the job:

  • It is OpenAI-compatible. Streaming, function calling and JSON output pass through, so existing SDK code only changes its base URL.
  • The router is measurable. A decision model picks the model for auto, and hikyaku ai test scores it on your own cases.
  • Failure is a first-class case. Retries, circuit breakers and fallbacks are the same ones the relay uses for webhooks, and hikyaku chaos lets you test them before a provider does.

Start with two names and one fallback. Point one service at the gateway, and watch the token metrics for a week. Add auto when you have real requests to score it on.

Further reading

  • hikyaku on GitHub and the documentation
  • The LLM proxy: the endpoint, model destinations, function calling and streaming
  • Routing and the AI router: engines, thresholds, cache and budget
  • Retries and fallbacks
  • The llm-proxy example in the repository
  • Introducing hikyaku, the launch article: a webhook relay with AI triage, a dead-letter queue and replay
  • Genkit Flows on Kubernetes with senro and jev, another use of the jev decision model

title: Back office moved to the application-page layout
description:
Starting on 11 November I reworked the application page of myOS Portfolio Platform (stage selection via a pill, a single composer, a section bar in reading order) and then carried that layout over to the rest of the back office, one view per release from v2.52.0 to v2.58.0. This devlog walks through the sequence, from mailbox settings through profile and documents, leads and the mailbox to CV requests, the section bar ordering fix along the way, and why incremental migration ended up with one consistent structure instead of separate page designs.

On 11 November I reworked the application page and then carried its layout over to the other back office views, one release at a time. v2.52.0 set the base: the stage is now chosen via the pill, there is a single composer, and the section bar follows the reading order.

The following releases moved mailbox settings, RAV work efforts, profile and documents, leads, the mailbox and finally CV requests into the same layout. Along the way I fixed the order of the section bar. The result is one consistent structure across the back office instead of separate page designs.

  • v2.52.0: application page with stage selection via the pill, one composer and a section bar in reading order

  • v2.53.0: mailbox settings in the application-page layout; section bar order fixed

  • v2.54.0: RAV work efforts in the application-page layout

  • v2.55.0: profile and documents in the application-page layout

  • v2.56.0: leads in the application-page layout

  • v2.57.0: mailbox in the application-page layout

  • v2.58.0: CV requests in the application-page layout

Release v2.58.0 on GitHub

title: Building SupportMeet: The First Months Are Hard to Describe From Inside. What Worked, What Broke
description:
The hardest design problem in the first version of SupportMeet was not matching. It was language.

A new parent in the first months is living a day that looks simple from outside and feels completely different from inside. Bottles gather by the sink, laundry moves in constant rounds, and the night stops belonging to sleep. From outside, people send congratulations and ask for photos. Inside, the days can feel long, repetitive, and strangely quiet, even with a baby breathing in the next room.

That gap shaped almost every early decision, and it broke a few of them first.

What was built

SupportMeet at https://supportmeet.com is a free peer support site where people share what they are going through and are matched with circles who have lived the same thing. For new parents, the circle is not a general parenting feed. It is a small group in the same early weeks, where someone can say the feeding is not going as planned, or that the house feels lonely at midday, and be read by people who were awake for the same feed last night.

Three choices mattered most. The site is private by default, so an honest post is not a public performance for coworkers or relatives. Matching is by lived stage, not by topic keywords, because week three and month five are different worlds. And circles sit alongside practical help and listings of professionals and programmes nearby, so a worry shared at night can still lead to a sensible next step in daylight.

What broke

The first prompts were too polished. Asking people to share an update produced the same bright summaries they were already sending family. The posts that actually helped started when the prompt got plainer: what did today actually look like. Small, lived details followed from that. How another parent handled the evening stretch when nothing settled the baby. What helped on the first trip out alone. How partners divided the night so both could get one longer stretch of rest.

Broad matching broke too. Putting every new parent in one circle mixed people in the first two weeks with people sleeping through the night, and the advice stopped landing. Narrower circles meant slower first replies in some cases, and that trade was worth making. A reply from the wrong stage can sound like a verdict. A slower reply from the same stage sounds like company.

The congratulations problem was subtler. Many new parents feel they should only share the bright parts, so a support space has to make the tired parts sayable without turning them into a crisis. The fix was tone, set in the circle itself: no polished update needed, no verdict offered, practical notes welcome alongside honest ones.

What the numbers look like

The honest measure at this stage is not traffic. It is whether a first post gets a reply from someone in the same stretch of life, and whether that reply contains a specific detail the poster can use tonight. Generic encouragement does not pass that test. A note about how one household split the night feeds does.

That is a stricter bar than page views, and it is the right one for a support product. A circle that produces one usable detail and one moment of recognition has done its job, even if it never grows large.

What stayed

New parenthood is often described as a beginning, and it is. It is also a season that asks a lot, quietly and every day. Having company from people in the same season does not make it perfect. It makes it less solitary, and that difference is the whole product.

The lesson that carried over to every other circle on the site is simple: match on the lived stage, keep the space private by default, and write prompts plain enough that the real day can be described in them.

title: How modern-web-guidance-src Enhances Your Coding Agent's Skills
description:
The Decision This Project Solves

Modern-web-guidance-src addresses the issue of coding agents often defaulting to legacy code patterns due to outdated training data. This results in bloated JavaScript and inefficient solutions when modern APIs and techniques are available. The repository provides expert-curated guidelines directly integrated into coding environments, promoting best practices in web development.

When the Project Is the Right Fit

This project is ideal for developers and teams using coding agents who want to ensure their applications leverage modern web capabilities. It specifically helps in utilizing modern browser APIs effectively, improving performance, and ensuring accessibility. If your team is focused on enhancing user experience, optimizing performance, or modernizing legacy code, this tool is a suitable fit.

Adoption Cost, Constraints & Exit Plan

To install, use the command:

npx modern-web-guidance@latest install

This command initiates an interactive installation wizard. However, note that the project requires Node.js version 22.18.0 or higher. A potential limitation is that it may not cover every edge case in legacy code scanning, as it focuses on commonly used patterns and solutions. If the project does not meet your needs, it is easy to exit by simply uninstalling the package.

The Clear Recommendation

For teams looking to modernize their web development approach, adopting modern-web-guidance-src is highly recommended. It provides a direct pathway to integrating best practices into your coding agents, ensuring that they produce efficient, modern code. If your team is not ready for this shift or is working on projects where legacy code is heavily entrenched, it may be worth waiting until your strategies align with the capabilities of this tool.

title: What a 30-second-old VPS does to your install script
description:
Most "run your own VPN" guides start the same way: rent a VPS, SSH in, paste twenty commands, edit a JSON file, open a port, copy a key back to your phone, and hope nothing was mistyped. For people who live in a terminal that's fine. For everyone else it's where they give up.

I build Lume, a VPN client for Xray, AmneziaWG and OpenVPN. Its "Set Up My Server" screen asks for three things: the server's IP, a user name and a password or private key. About 90 seconds later there is a working VLESS Reality server and a config in the app, already tested with real traffic.

This post is about what happens in those 90 seconds, and what a brand-new VPS throws at you along the way. The engine is Go (it runs on iPhone, Android, Mac and Windows through gomobile and a Windows service); the server side is plain bash and systemd.

The shape of it 

phone ──SSH──▶ phase 1: probe.sh     → facts (arch, busy ports, saved keys, Reality target)
phone          generate keys + configs locally
phone ──SSH──▶ phase 2: install.sh   → download, verify, install, start services
phone ──TLS──▶ port check
phone ──VLESS▶ real request through the new tunnel → exit IP

The scripts talk back to the app over stdout with a tiny line protocol, so the progress screen shows real steps instead of a spinner:

step() { echo "::step $*"; }       # a step started
kv()   { echo "::kv $1=$2"; }      # a fact for the app
die()  { echo "::error $*"; exit 1; }

Everything else the script prints is shown as a log line. The app counts the step "..." lines in the assembled script before running it, so the progress bar knows the total up front.

1. The phone does the thinking, the server only runs things

Keys are generated on the device: the X25519 Reality key pair, the client UUID and the short ID. The server never needs xray x25519, openssl or anything else to make keys, and the app already has the public key it needs for the client config.

Phase 1 is read-only. It reports the CPU architecture, which TCP and UDP ports are taken, whether a previous Lume install left state behind, and which Reality target this server can reach (more on that below). The app then builds the server config, uploads it into a mktemp -d directory with umask 077, and runs phase 2.

2. A fresh VPS isn't ready when the hoster says it is

The most common real-world flow is "create a server, copy the IP, paste it into the app" — within seconds. That's when everything goes wrong:

  • SSH isn't up yet. For the first minute or two the port refuses or resets. Instead of failing, the app treats "connection refused / reset / EOF" as "still booting" and retries every 5 seconds for up to 3 minutes, with the step retitled to Waiting for the server to start.
  • cloud-init and unattended upgrades hold the package manager. Run apt-get install at that moment and it fails with Could not get lock /var/lib/dpkg/lock-frontend. So the probe waits for first-boot setup, and apt waits for the lock instead of dying: 
if command -v cloud-init >/dev/null && ! cloud-init status 2>/dev/null | grep -qE "status: (done|disabled|error)"; then
    echo "Waiting for the first-boot setup to finish"
    timeout 300 cloud-init status --wait >/dev/null 2>&1 || echo "cloud-init is still running, continuing"
fi

apt-get -o DPkg::Lock::Timeout=180 install -y -qq "$@"

This is a big part of why setup takes ~90 seconds on a new server and much less on one that has been running for a while.

3. Don't assume the server can reach GitHub

The obvious way to install Xray is to download the official release from GitHub. Some hosting networks can't reach GitHub reliably, and the full Xray binary includes every protocol and transport, while this setup only needs one combination.

So the installer prefers a minimal server binary I build myself: built from the same xray-core as the app, linking only VLESS inbound, Reality over TCP, and freedom/blackhole outbounds. The app converts the JSON config to protobuf before uploading, so even Xray's JSON loader (which pulls in everything) stays out of the build:

// Only the features the Lume server config uses.
_ "github.com/xtls/xray-core/proxy/vless/inbound"
_ "github.com/xtls/xray-core/transport/internet/reality"
_ "github.com/xtls/xray-core/transport/internet/tcp"
_ "github.com/xtls/xray-core/proxy/freedom"
_ "github.com/xtls/xray-core/proxy/blackhole"

The download is 4.7 MB (xz) instead of 15 MB for the official zip — different compression, so not a perfect comparison. Binaries live behind a CDN at content-addressed URLs (the path contains the hash, so a file is never overwritten), and the installer checks SHA-256 before using anything. If the CDN is unreachable, it falls back to the official Xray release from GitHub, pinned to a version and a checksum.

4. Let the server pick its own Reality target

VLESS Reality makes the server look like a well-known HTTPS site: a client without the right key is forwarded to the real site. That only works if the server can actually reach that site over TLS 1.3, and from some data centres some sites are slow or unreachable.

So the app sends a short list of candidates and the server tries them in order:

for sni in $LUME_SNI_CANDIDATES; do
    if echo | timeout 6 openssl s_client -connect "$sni:443" -servername "$sni" -tls1_3 >/dev/null 2>&1; then
        kv sni "$sni"; break
    fi
done

5. Running it twice must not break anyone's config

People run setup again: to add a protocol, because the first attempt timed out, or just because. If a second run generated new keys, every config already shared with family members would silently stop working.

State lives in /etc/lume/*.env (keys, UUID, port, Reality target). The probe reports it, and the app reuses it, so a repeat run produces the same config. The port is chosen once from 443, 8443, 2053 and 2083, skipping anything already in use, and then kept.

The server runs exactly the protocols chosen this time. Ones that weren't chosen are stopped, but their keys stay in /etc/lume, so adding them back later restores the old configs.

6. A small, boring systemd unit

Xray runs as a dynamic user with no write access to the system, and reads its config through systemd credentials rather than from a world-readable path:

[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/local/lib/lume/lume-xray-server -config ${CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY}/xray.pb
LoadCredential=xray.pb:/etc/lume/xray.pb
DynamicUser=yes
AmbientCapabilities=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE
CapabilityBoundingSet=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE
NoNewPrivileges=yes
ProtectSystem=strict
ProtectHome=yes
PrivateTmp=yes
PrivateDevices=yes
Restart=always

The installer also opens the port in ufw or firewalld if one of them is active, and switches on BBR congestion control.

7. "Installed" is not "works"

systemctl is-active says nothing about whether a phone on mobile data can connect. The classic trap is a firewall the server itself doesn't know about: Hetzner Cloud Firewall, AWS security groups and the like.

So after the install the app checks from the device:

  1. The port. A TLS handshake to the server with the Reality target as SNI. If it fails, the error names the likely culprit: the server is installed, but port 443 is not reachable from this device. Check your hosting provider's firewall, for example Hetzner Cloud Firewall or an AWS security group, and allow TCP 443.
  2. Real traffic. The app starts the new client config in an in-process Xray instance with no inbounds, so it can't clash with a VPN that's already running, and fetches Cloudflare's trace page through it: 
httpClient := &http.Client{
    Transport: &http.Transport{
        DialContext: func(ctx context.Context, network, addr string) (net.Conn, error) {
            dest, err := xnet.ParseDestination("tcp:" + addr)
            if err != nil {
                return nil, err
            }
            return core.Dial(ctx, inst, dest) // straight into the new tunnel
        },
    },
}

Only when that request comes back through the tunnel (the log shows the exit IP it reports) does the config get saved.

8. Credentials, and what phones do to private keys

The password or key is used for this one SSH connection. It isn't stored, logged or sent anywhere except to the server. The app remembers the server's SSH host key fingerprint, so a later run against the same address stops if the key has changed. If you rebuilt the server on purpose, you tell the app to forget the old key.

A surprise: pasting a private key on a phone is hard. iOS turns -- into an em dash, so -----BEGIN OPENSSH PRIVATE KEY----- arrives as something the SSH library rejects. Notes apps add non-breaking spaces, messengers collapse line breaks into spaces. The app now repairs the pasted text before parsing it: it replaces the dashes, normalises line endings and rewraps the base64 body. The error message for a key that still can't be read says what to do: paste the whole key file, including the BEGIN and END lines.

Lume isn't open source, so you can't check this yourself, and that's a fair concern for a root login. If you'd rather not take it on trust, use an SSH key created just for this and remove it from the server afterwards, or run setup on a fresh VPS that holds nothing else.

What I'd tell anyone building something similar

  • Test on servers that are 30 seconds old, not on the one you've had for a year. The boot-time problems above never show up on a machine that has been running for a while.
  • Make re-running safe before anything else. Users will run it twice.
  • Check the result from the client's side of the network. The server can't see the cloud firewall in front of it.
  • Write error messages for the person holding the phone, not for the person reading the logs.

Try it

Lume is free on Google Play and Windows; the iPhone and Mac versions are in App Store review. On Android the free version shows a short ad while a server is being set up; the Windows app has no ads. The free version installs one protocol per server; installing Xray, AmneziaWG and OpenVPN XOR side by side is part of Lume Pro.

Set Up My Server is meant for Debian and Ubuntu VPSes where you can log in as root (or as a sudo user).

If you try it on a hoster where it fails, I'd like to hear about it in the comments: which provider, which OS image, and what the last step said.
