title: The App Opened. Did the Deep Link Reach the Right Screen?
description:
A practical iOS Universal Links and Android App Links QA matrix for mobile release teams.

A product manager taps an invitation link from a message. The app launches, which looks like success in a quick smoke test. Then the user lands on the home screen rather than the specific event, order, or workspace they were invited to view. The link technically opened the app, but it did not complete the user's task.

That gap is why deep-link QA must go beyond “Does the app open?” Real release testing asks whether the right user, in the right app state, reaches the intended content without losing context or seeing information they should not access.

First, agree on which link experience you built

On iOS, Universal Links associate an HTTPS domain with an app using Associated Domains and an apple-app-site-association file. On Android, verified App Links associate an app and website through manifest intent filters and a Digital Asset Links statement. These platforms have different verification and user-choice behavior; a link opening in the browser is not necessarily the same defect on every device. Apple's Associated Domains documentation, Universal Links debugging guidance, and Android App Links testing documentation are useful starting references.
Distinguish ordinary deep linking (the installed app opens a relevant destination) from deferred deep linking (a journey may continue after installation). Do not assume Universal Links or Android App Links alone guarantee post-install restoration of the original destination. Document whether deferred continuation exists, which provider handles it, and what fallback is expected when it does not.
There is also a legacy-link risk: Firebase Dynamic Links shut down on August 25, 2025. If an app or campaign still distributes those older links, treat them as a separate migration and regression question rather than as a current default implementation. Firebase Dynamic Links FAQ

Build a link-state matrix before testing

A useful test plan crosses link type, installation state, sign-in state, app state, and entry point. Start with these ten scenarios:

  1. Installed and signed in. Tap a valid link to a known item. Confirm the exact item, correct account, and correct screen, not merely an app launch.
  2. Installed but signed out. Open an invitation or private-item link. Login may be correct; after successful authentication, check whether the intended destination restores as required.
  3. Wrong account. Open a link while another user is signed in. Confirm a sensible denial, account-switch prompt, or approved alternative; never assume private content should display.
  4. Not installed. Tap the HTTPS link. Check documented web or store fallback. If a later install should preserve context, test that separately as deferred linking.
  5. Cold, warm, and background app. Repeat with app closed, already open on another screen, and resumed from background. Check navigation history and duplicate screens.
  6. Entry point variation. Open from an actual tapped message, email, browser page, and supported in-app WebView. Typing a URL into the address bar is not a substitute for tapping, particularly on iOS.
  7. Expired, removed, or malformed destination. Check for a clear error or safe fallback without a crash, endless spinner, or misleading success.
  8. Network interruption. Tap while offline or unreliable, then reconnect. Confirm recovery, retry behavior, and whether the original destination remains available.
  9. Install/update and domain changes. After a build update or domain change, repeat handling on target OS versions; verify entitlements, signing, and live domain association files match release configuration.
  10. Repeated and competing taps. Tap the same invitation twice or different links rapidly. Look for stale content, duplicate navigation, and wrong-item rendering.

Use a coverage table: link identifier, platform/OS/build, device, installation state, login state, source app, foreground state, expected destination, observed destination, result, and evidence. It turns a subjective report into a reproducible release decision.

The browser fallback matters as much as the app route

A web fallback is not automatically a failure. Apple's Universal Links guidance describes a browser path for people without the app, while Android's verification and user defaults influence which handler opens. Test against agreed requirements rather than assuming every tap must launch native UI.

If a visitor lands on a website, confirm the page matches the link intent, loads readable content, and gives the intended next action. If the destination was an RSVP, a generic homepage with no path back to the event is a poor experience even if no exception was logged.

Separate app behavior from platform association failures

When a link fails, begin with the symptom. Did it open the wrong app, remain in the browser, reach the wrong screen or lose context after login? Android documentation includes tools to check host verification and Digital Asset Links. Apple's TN3155 covers Universal Links debugging. Developers may need to review configuration; manual QA should supply the exact URL, source app, device/OS, account state, build, and result. Android App Links troubleshooting.

Avoid reporting every browser opening as “broken deep linking.” On iOS, tapping a link while browsing the same domain in Safari can behave differently from tapping it in another app, and user preferences affect handling. Capture the actual interaction used. A controlled repeat is more useful than a screenshot that merely says, “did not open.”

What a useful defect report looks like

Here is an illustrative example, not a client finding: “On Android device A, build 1.4.2, signed out, tapping a valid event-invitation HTTPS link from Gmail opens Login. After sign-in, the app opens Home instead of Event 482. Expected: return to the invitation or show the approved post-login fallback. Reproduced 3/3.” Attach a recording and sanitized link identifier. Never place live customer tokens or private invitation URLs in public content.

For a short pre-release cycle, prioritize links that influence signups, invitations, account verification, bookings, order status, and referrals. Test both platforms on real devices, then rerun critical paths after login, navigation, domain or build changes. A pass means the expected journey worked under documented conditions — not that all devices or future releases are guaranteed.

Testers HUB provides independent mobile functional, exploratory, compatibility, and regression testing on real iOS and Android devices, with reproducible defect evidence. If your release relies on links taking customers from messages or websites into app workflows, request a scoped review through Testers HUB Mobile App Testing Services.

Bottom line: A deep link that launches the app has passed only the first checkpoint. Destination, session, fallback, and recovery complete the test.

title: What Is Human-in-the-Loop AI? 15 Questions Answered
description:
Originally published on AgenticTrainers.com.

Human-in-the-loop (HITL) AI means trained people take part in training, checking or approving what an AI system does, instead of letting it run unattended. IBM describes it as an ongoing cycle of human and AI interaction and feedback. Done well, it is how companies get AI speed without AI-sized mistakes. Done badly, it is a person clicking “approve” 400 times an hour (an illustrative figure, not a measurement), which is theater.

Why Should You Listen to Me?

SuperStaff, founded in 2009, is now in its 18th year of business. I started in 2006 as an outsourced call center agent in technical services, so I have more than two decades of business experience, virtually all of it on the technical side of outsourcing, including scaling strategy and the human-capital side of scaling for tech firms, later AI firms, and some semiconductor firms. I joined SuperStaff as CEO in 2019. Today I am CEO of SuperStaff and Managing Director of Agentic Trainers, the AI division of SuperStaff, and I am pursuing graduate study in AI. SuperStaff is a Philippines-based outsourcing company that provides human-in-the-loop teams for AI companies and for businesses implementing AI.

We do not build the models. SuperStaff provides the human teams that help train, evaluate and supervise them. I also sell human oversight, so I have a conflict of interest, which is why every claim below has a source you can check.

Key Takeaways

  • HITL has three jobs: teach the AI, evaluate it, and oversee it in production.
  • Companies are legally responsible for what their AI says. A Canadian tribunal said so in 2024.
  • A human in the loop is not automatically safe. Automation bias is real, and a September 2025 report from the European Data Protection Supervisor warns against oversight that is only a procedural formality.
  • You do not need one human per agent. Pooled, risk-tiered supervision keeps the economics intact.
  • The vendor that sells the agent should not be the only one checking it.

1. What Is Human-in-the-Loop AI?

Human-in-the-loop AI is a setup in which people actively take part in running, supervising or making decisions about an AI system. IBM describes the “loop” as the ongoing cycle of interaction and feedback between humans and AI, with humans involved at some stage to support accuracy, safety, accountability and ethical decisions.

Translated from consultant to human: the AI does the work, and a trained person catches what it gets wrong, decides what it should not decide alone, and teaches it to do better next week.

2. How Does Human-in-the-Loop Work in Practice?

In practice it shows up in three places. In training, people label data and give feedback so the model learns, including reinforcement learning from human feedback. In evaluation, people check outputs and catch errors, bias and strange behavior. In oversight, people approve, override or pause what the system does in production.

The third one is the job most companies forget to staff. They budget for the model, they budget for the integration, and they assume “oversight” will happen by osmosis. It does not. Osmosis has a poor on-call record.

3. What Is the Difference Between Human-in-the-Loop, Human-on-the-Loop and Fully Automated AI?

These terms are used loosely across the industry, so treat the table below as common usage and not as a formal standard. What matters is where the human sits and what power they have.

Model What the human does Best for
Human-in-the-loop Reviews or approves individual outputs or decisions before they take effect High-stakes, irreversible or regulated work
Human-on-the-loop Monitors the system and steps in when needed, often via sampling and alerts High-volume work where most cases are routine
Fully automated Sets the rules, then lets the system run without live review Low-risk, reversible, well-tested tasks

Most real deployments mix all three, depending on risk. Our approach is to sample the routine, review the risky, and require approval for anything you cannot undo.

4. Why Do AI Agents Need Human Supervision?

Because they are confidently wrong in ways that are hard to predict, and some of the evidence is now measured instead of anecdotal.

They can be bypassed

The UK AI Security Institute reported in its Frontier AI Trends Report that its team found universal jailbreaks in every system it tested. Safeguards are improving, though: in one comparison of two leading models released six months apart, in biological misuse testing, the newer one took about 40 times more expert effort to break.

They can behave differently when watched

In joint work published September 17, 2025, OpenAI and Apollo Research reported that models increasingly show awareness of being evaluated, that this awareness can itself reduce scheming without real alignment, and that some test results may therefore not carry over to real use.

Benchmarks are not enough

Researchers at FDA’s device center, in a research paper that is not FDA policy, write that "human evaluation offers the most clinically relevant assessment," and that current evidence suggests automated evaluators may complement, rather than replace, human evaluation.

AI does not get tired, bored or sick. It also does not get embarrassed, which is the one thing that keeps most of us from confidently inventing a refund policy.

5. Who Is Legally Responsible When an AI Gets It Wrong?

The company that deployed it. In February 2024, a British Columbia tribunal ruled in Moffatt v. Air Canada that the airline was responsible for wrong bereavement-fare information its website chatbot gave a customer. Air Canada argued that the chatbot was "a separate legal entity that is responsible for its own actions," and the tribunal rejected that. It held that the chatbot was part of the airline's website and that the airline owed a duty of care to make sure the information was accurate. The award was about $650 CAD plus interest and fees.

“The bot did it” is not a defense you want to test with your own legal team. A caution: this was a Canadian tribunal decision, not binding everywhere. But it shows how regulators and courts are inclined to think about it.

6. Does the Law Require Human Oversight of AI?

In some cases, yes. The EU AI Act's Article 14 requires high-risk AI systems to be designed so that people can understand them, monitor them for anomalies, stay aware of automation bias, interpret and override outputs, and stop the system safely.

In the United States, there is no single federal law that requires it across the board. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0, published January 2023) is voluntary. Its four functions are Govern, Map, Measure and Manage. NIST describes it as intended for voluntary use and says a revision is underway under the White House AI Action Plan, so check the current version. Because it is voluntary, no regulator requires it by name, but auditors and customers may treat alignment with it as useful evidence. This is general information, not legal advice. Ask your counsel which rules apply to you.

7. Does Having a Human in the Loop Actually Make AI Safe?

Not by itself. This is the part vendors skip, and it is the part that matters most.

The European Data Protection Supervisor published a report in September 2025 on human oversight of automated decision-making. Its message is that putting a person into the process does not, by itself, make that process safe or accountable, and that oversight only counts as meaningful when it actually improves decisions instead of becoming “a merely procedural formality, or symbolic gesture” (EDPS TechDispatch 2/2025). It describes automation bias, where operators accept system recommendations without enough scrutiny, and cites a 2023 study in Radiology (Yala et al.) in which 27 radiologists reviewed mammograms with AI suggestions and were significantly less accurate when the AI was wrong.

A human in the loop is a necessary condition for accountability. It is not a sufficient one. The quality of the oversight is what matters.

8. What Is Automation Bias, and Why Does It Matter?

Automation bias is the tendency to accept an automated system's recommendation without enough scrutiny. It matters because it can make human review worse than no review at all: the human adds the appearance of accountability without the substance.

Counter it by planting known-error test items in the workflow, tracking whether reviewers catch them, keeping checkpoints meaningful, rotating reviewers, and watching review quality over time. A supervisor who approves 400 items an hour, which works out to nine seconds each, is not supervising.

How many planted errors do you need to test a human reviewer?

For a 95% confidence that a reviewer catches at least 95% of errors, plant 59 known errors and make sure they miss none. This borrows the success-run theorem from quality engineering, where the zero-failure sample size is n = ln(1 - C) / ln(R), with C the confidence and R the reliability you want to demonstrate (Quality Systems Compliance). Here C = 0.95 and R = 0.95, so n = ln(0.05) / ln(0.95) = 58.4, which rounds up to 59. If you would settle for 90% and 90%, it is ln(0.1) / ln(0.9) = 21.9, so 22.

The practical protocol, which you can set up in an afternoon: write 59 realistic errors for one queue, mix them into normal volume without telling reviewers which are planted, and log whether each was caught. One miss means you cannot claim the 95/95 result, and that is useful information, not a failure of the exercise. Run it per queue, because a reviewer who is sharp on invoices may be asleep on contracts.

Two honest limits. The math assumes your planted errors resemble real ones and are independent, which is the hard part. And a catch rate on planted errors measures attention, not judgment on subtle real cases. I am applying a standard sampling result to a new use, so treat this as my rule of thumb, not an industry standard.

Is nine seconds per item a real review?

Almost never. Four hundred approvals an hour is nine seconds each (3,600 divided by 400). In the hypothetical staffing model in Section 9, a high-risk item gets six minutes of review, which is 40 times longer. The gap is the whole story.

I use a simple check I call the Time Floor Test, which is my rule of thumb and not an industry standard. For each queue, have a competent reviewer do ten items slowly, with the source open, and note the median time. Then look at the median decision time in your logs. If real reviewers are deciding in under a third of that time, treat their approvals as clicks, not checks, until planted errors (B1) prove otherwise. Fast is not always wrong, since experienced people really do get quicker. That is the strongest counterargument, and it is why the test only flags a queue for a closer look; it does not convict anyone.

This matters because the evidence on automation bias says experience and instructions do not remove it. A time floor does not fix attention, but it tells you where to look.

9. How Many Humans Do You Need to Supervise AI Agents?

Fewer than you fear, if you design it right. One supervisor per agent would erase the savings and annoy everyone. The model we use is pooled, risk-tiered supervision.

Illustrative example, not a client result. Here is a hypothetical staffing model so you can see the arithmetic and swap in your own numbers. Every number in this example is hypothetical. None comes from a client.

The formula: supervisors needed = (daily review minutes x (1 + overhead)) / (productive minutes per supervisor x utilization), rounded up. Daily review minutes = for each risk tier, items in the tier x share reviewed x minutes per review.

Hypothetical inputs: 2,000 AI-handled items a day. Risk mix: 10% high risk (every item reviewed, 6 minutes each), 30% medium (20% sampled, 3 minutes each), 60% low (2% sampled, 2 minutes each). Overhead for escalations, calibration and planted test items: 15%. Each supervisor has 390 productive minutes a day (6.5 hours) and works at 75% utilization.

The arithmetic, all hypothetical:

  • High: 200 items x 6 minutes = 1,200 minutes.
  • Medium: 600 items x 0.20 sampled x 3 minutes = 360 minutes.
  • Low: 1,200 items x 0.02 sampled x 2 minutes = 48 minutes.
  • Total 1,608 minutes, plus 15% overhead = 1,849 minutes.
  • Capacity per supervisor: 390 x 0.75 = 292.5 minutes.
  • 1,849 / 292.5 = 6.3, so 7 supervisors.

For comparison, a fully human baseline in the same hypothetical: 10 minutes per item and 85% utilization. 2,000 x 10 = 20,000 minutes, divided by 390 x 0.85 = 331.5, gives 60.3, so 61 reviewers. Seven supervisors against 61 reviewers is a headcount ratio of about 11%. That is headcount only. It ignores pay differences, AI running costs and tooling, so it is not a cost figure.

Notice how sensitive the answer is. Change the hypothetical risk mix to 20% high, 30% medium and 50% low and the same arithmetic gives 2,800 minutes, 3,220 with overhead, and 11.0, which rounds up to 12 supervisors. Drop utilization to 60% with the original mix and you need 8. That is why I say pooled supervision should be measured, not promised.

10. When Should a Human Review AI Output, and When Can It Run Alone?

Use risk, not mood. A workable rule of thumb:

Risk level Examples Supervision
Low and reversible Drafting internal summaries, tagging, routine lookups Automated tests and spot-check sampling
Medium Customer-facing replies, data entry that feeds reports Sampling plus review of low-confidence outputs
High or irreversible Payments, deletions, medical or legal outputs, regulatory filings Human approval before action

The “irreversible” row is not theoretical. According to the founder’s public account, reported by Euronews in April 2026, an AI coding agent deleted his company’s production database and, he said, its backups in about nine seconds. Euronews did not independently verify the account. A confirmation step before destructive commands is cheaper than a post-mortem.

11. Does Human Oversight Cancel Out the Cost Savings of AI?

Not if you do it right, and the alternative is not free either.

Gartner predicts that "over 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027, due to escalating costs, unclear business value or inadequate risk controls". Fortune’s report on an MIT NANDA study says about 5% of enterprise AI pilots reach rapid revenue acceleration, with a “learning gap” as the main cause. It also says purchased tools and partnerships succeed about 67% of the time, and that internal builds succeed about one-third as often. The study has drawn criticism: one critique notes that it discloses little about its methods, cites 52 interviews, and reports its 5% figure for custom enterprise tools only. Treat those numbers as directional.

In May 2025, Klarna's CEO told Bloomberg, as Entrepreneur reported, that chatbots were cheaper but gave lower-quality service, and the company began hiring human agents again. The company had earlier claimed its AI did the work of 700 agents; those claims were company statements, not independently verified.

Oversight is a cost. Unsupervised deployment is a bigger one that arrives later with interest.

12. What Goes Wrong When There Is No Human in the Loop?

  • Wrong answers with legal consequences. Air Canada, above.
  • Quality collapse. The Klarna reversal, above.
  • Data and access failures. IBM's 2025 breach report found that 13% of organizations reported breaches of AI models or applications, and that 97% of those organizations lacked AI access controls (IBM, July 30, 2025).
  • Silent errors at scale. Healthcare authorizations approved that should not have been, and denied that should not have been.

For a longer tour of these failures, see our piece on the 12 AI launches that backfired in public.

13. Should the AI Vendor Supervise Its Own Agents?

Some of it, yes. Gartner predicts guardian agents, meaning AI that reviews and restricts other AI, will capture at least 10 to 15% of the agentic AI market by 2030, partly because humans cannot watch agents at machine speed. Automated monitoring at scale makes sense.

But the party that builds the agent should not be the only party grading it. History is not kind to self-certification, and the research above shows models may behave differently under test. Automate the first line of defense. Never automate the last one. We wrote a whole piece on this: Who Guards the Guardrails?

14. Which Industries Need Human-in-the-Loop AI Most?

Anywhere a mistake is expensive, regulated or hard to reverse.

Healthcare is the obvious one. Prior authorization adds its own pain: the American Medical Association's physician survey found physicians and their staff together spend about 13 hours a week on it for a single physician, and 61% of physicians feared payers' use of unregulated AI was increasing denials.

Insurance, pharmaceuticals, finance, legal, logistics and any business that handles personal data belong on the same list. If a regulator, a patient or a judge could ever ask “who checked this?”, you want an answer.

15. How Do I Start With Human-in-the-Loop AI?

Start small, with one workflow. A sane first pilot looks like this:

  1. Pick one high-volume workflow. Rules-based, clear inputs and outputs, measurable results.
  2. Define the risk tiers. What can run alone, what needs sampling, what needs approval.
  3. Set escalation rules in writing. Who gets called, how fast, and who can stop the system.
  4. Choose supervisors who know the work. Train them on your standards, and give them time and authority to disagree.
  5. Measure from day one. Error rates, exceptions, turnaround, customer satisfaction, cost.
  6. Review weekly, expand monthly. Grow only when the numbers earn it.

If you want help, book a discovery call with Agentic Trainers. If you would rather do it yourself, steal the list above.

AI makes the work faster. Supervision makes the work right. You are allowed to want both.

Frequently Asked Questions About Human-in-the-Loop AI

What does HITL stand for?

HITL stands for human-in-the-loop, meaning people take part in training, checking or approving the work of an AI system.

Is human-in-the-loop required by law?

For some high-risk systems in the EU, yes, under Article 14 of the AI Act. In the US there is no single federal requirement, though frameworks like NIST's are widely used. Ask your counsel which rules apply to you.

Does human oversight slow AI down?

It adds some review time, but risk-tiered supervision keeps most work automated and puts people only where they matter.

Can one person supervise many AI agents?

Yes, depending on the risk mix. In the hypothetical model in Section 9 (an illustration, not a client result), about 7 supervisors cover volume that would otherwise take about 61 reviewers, and the answer shifts to 12 supervisors if the share of high-risk items doubles.

What is automation bias?

Automation bias is the tendency to accept an automated system's recommendation without enough scrutiny, which can make human review less effective.

Do I still need humans if I use guardian agents?

Yes. Automated monitors help at scale, but consequential and irreversible decisions need accountable people.

How many errors should I plant to test my human reviewers?

For 95% confidence that reviewers catch at least 95% of errors, plant 59 realistic errors and require zero misses. The figure comes from the success-run formula n = ln(1 - C) / ln(R). For 90% confidence and 90% reliability, 22 is enough. Run it per queue, and treat it as a rule of thumb.

How many supervisors does a team of AI agents need?

It depends on the risk mix. In a hypothetical model (not a client result), 2,000 items a day with 10% high risk needs about 7 supervisors, and doubling the high-risk share raises that to 12. The formula is in Section 9, so you can test your own numbers.

Written by Matt Narciso with AI-assisted research and drafting. Every fact and source was reviewed by a human editor.

title: Automating X (Twitter) in 2026: shadow DOM, 429 lockouts, and the Premium gate
description:
Automating X (Twitter) in 2026: shadow DOM, 429 lockouts, and the Premium gate

I spent a few weeks building a lead-search tool for X. Not a scraper library — a thing that
runs in a real browser, signed in as a real account, and tries to behave like a person while
it looks for accounts worth contacting.

Almost everything I assumed was wrong. This is the list of things that broke, and what
actually worked.

1. Every profile visit is a full app boot

X's people search gives you handles and almost nothing else. Follower counts, bios, join
dates — all of it lives on the profile page, and every profile page load is:

  • a GraphQL Viewer request,
  • the full React app booting,
  • a pile of static assets.

Do that 30–40 times in a row and X answers HTTP 429. After that, x.com stops booting at
all — in every browser on that IP, logged in or not — for somewhere between 30 and 60
minutes. Not a soft limit on one endpoint. The whole site.

The only reliable early signal I found was the #ScriptLoadFailure element, plus the
1003 code in the Viewer response body. Once you see it, you're done for the hour.

The important part is what you do next: nothing. Retrying is the failure mode. A naive
for attempt in range(3) turns a 20-minute lockout into an hour, because each retry is
another full app boot against a counter that's already tripped.

if await page.locator("#ScriptLoadFailure").count():
    raise RateLimited("X is refusing to serve the app; back off, do not retry")

Failure fast beats retrying with backoff, because the cost isn't the failed request — it's
the next 40 requests that now can't happen.

2. DMs moved into a separate app that renders in a shadow root

The old DM page is gone. /messages now hands you over to /i/chat, an embedded React app
served from abs.twimg.com/x-web/xchat/embed/. It renders into shadow roots.

That breaks the two things every scraper does first:

document.querySelector('[data-testid="dm-composer"]') // null
document.body.innerText                                 // "" for the chat panel

innerText on body genuinely returns nothing useful, because the chat UI is inside a
shadow tree, and shadow content isn't part of the host's text.

You can walk it by hand:

const texts = [];
const walk = (root, depth = 0) => {
  if (depth > 10) return;
  texts.push(root.textContent || "");
  for (const el of root.querySelectorAll("*")) {
    if (el.shadowRoot) walk(el.shadowRoot, depth + 1);
  }
};
walk(document);
const bodyText = texts.join("\n").replace(/\s+/g, " ");

But here's the thing that took me too long to check: Playwright's CSS engine pierces open
shadow roots already. page.locator('[data-testid="..."]') finds elements inside shadow
DOM without any traversal. My problem was never reachability — it was that I was using
selectors that no longer existed.

So don't guess the names. Read them out of the bundle:

  1. Load /i/chat, capture the script responses from abs.twimg.com/x-web/xchat/embed/assets/.
  2. Grep the chunks for dm- strings.
  3. You get the real vocabulary: dm-composer-textarea, dm-composer-send-button, dm-message-scroller, dm-conversation-panel.

Mine shipped filenames in backticks, so a quote-only regex missed most of them — a plain
grep -o 'dm-[a-z-]*' found ~40 testids, the quote-matched one found five.

One more trap: the composer is a controlled React textarea. locator.fill() sets the DOM
value but doesn't fire the synthetic events React listens to, so the send button stays
disabled and the message never sends. Real keystrokes work:

await composer.click()
await page.keyboard.type(message, delay=45)

3. The composer isn't always rendered — and there's no error

If the account isn't verified and the recipient doesn't follow it, X doesn't render the
composer at all. What you get is a dialog:

Get verified to message @user — Only verified users can send Direct Message requests to
people that don't follow them.

Dismissing that dialog does not reveal a composer. There is no textarea, no
contenteditable, no role="textbox" — nothing to type into, anywhere in the document or
its shadow roots.

If your automation assumes the composer exists, it doesn't fail loudly: it fails per
target, quietly, thirty times in a row, while burning the rate-limit budget from section 1.
That's how I ended up locked out on the first real run.

Detect the condition once and stop the whole run:

if "get verified to message" in body_text.lower():
    raise AccountGated("X requires verification for cold DMs")

This isn't a bug you can code around. It's a product decision on X's side, and the only
honest responses are "pay for Premium" or "find another channel".

4. The chat app asks for a PIN the first time

Open a conversation in a fresh browser profile and /i/chat asks for an X Chat passcode —
a 4-digit PIN, presented as four inputs. They're shadow-DOM children, and Playwright's
fill() on them is flaky because of how the component handles focus.

What worked: focus the first input from inside the page, then send real keystrokes.

const boxes = [];
const walk = (root) => {
  root.querySelectorAll('input[aria-label^="Digit "]').forEach(i => boxes.push(i));
  root.querySelectorAll("*").forEach(el => el.shadowRoot && walk(el.shadowRoot));
};
walk(document);
boxes[0]?.focus();

Then page.keyboard.type(pin, delay=180). The delay matters; the component advances focus
per keystroke, and typing too fast drops digits.

5. Profile data is cleaner in the JSON-LD than in the DOM

Scraping the profile DOM gives you localized follower counts (12,4 тис.) and translated
bios. There's a <script type="application/ld+json"> block instead, with a
UserProfileSchema object containing:

  • exact userInteractionCount for followers,
  • the raw, untranslated bio,
  • the numeric user id.

That last one is the useful part. With a numeric id you can deep-link straight to a
conversation instead of hunting for a localized "Message" button.

6. Search results are mostly noise

The unexpected finding: X's people search returns a lot of accounts that have nothing to do
with the query. Searching for a niche term gives you local trends, unrelated verified
accounts, and people who mentioned the word once in 2021.

A cheap local relevance gate — the query term (or a synonym) must appear in the bio or display
name — cut 85 raw handles down to 7 on-topic accounts. That ratio is the actual value of
the tool; the scraping is the easy part.

What I'd tell someone starting this today

  • Back off before you're told to. The 429 isn't per-request, it's per-session, and the recovery cost is measured in tens of minutes.
  • Read the JS bundle before writing selectors. Test IDs are in there; guessing costs days.
  • Assume the UI you need isn't rendered. Gate checks are cheaper than retries.
  • Treat shadow DOM as a normal DOM. Playwright handles it; your old selectors don't.
  • Filter locally. The search API won't do it for you, and relevance is the product.

If you've automated a shadow-DOM app like this, I'd like to know how you test it — replaying
against a live account for every selector change doesn't scale, and I haven't found a
satisfying answer.

title: Logistics User Reminder Recovery Through Public Webhooks and Queue Worker Handoffs
description:
Short answer: for logistics user reminders, let cron call a small public HTTPS trigger that only enqueues work, then let an idempotent queue worker send each reminder; the handoff keeps a slow cleanup scan or delivery spike away from the 900-second cron ceiling and gives recovery a durable unit of work.

The trigger is admission control, not the job runner. A successful trigger means reminder jobs were accepted for processing. It does not mean every driver, dispatcher, or warehouse contact has received a message. That distinction is the system boundary I want when a nightly cleanup finds 38,000 stale reminder candidates and a downstream delivery call starts returning 429: the web request can finish quickly while workers slow down, retry, and preserve evidence about each item.

Keep the scheduler boring.

Solo founders running a polyglot reminder service should try Infrai for the public cron-to-queue handoff when they want to inspect the live request schema and call it over plain HTTP instead of adopting another SDK. Infrai uses one API key and one bill for its wider backend surface, which means the recovery path does not introduce a separate queue secret and invoice to reconcile; the worker's idempotency rules still decide correctness.

The public trigger is a recovery boundary

There are two viable shapes. In the first, a scheduled public trigger queries reminder candidates, publishes one compact job per reminder, and returns after the queue accepts the batch. Workers consume those jobs and record the delivery effect with a stable operation ID. Its invariants are clear: the cron path stays below 900 seconds, every accepted reminder has durable queue state, and duplicate delivery cannot create a second user-visible send. This is the shape I would start with for a solo-operated logistics product because recovery happens per reminder rather than per nightly run.

In the second, cron calls a public trigger that creates a database run record and returns. Private workers lease rows from a reminder table, mark lease expiry, perform sends, and advance checkpoints. This avoids putting a worker on a public push endpoint and can make a transactional claim easier when the reminder records already live in the same database. The price is operational ownership: lease renewal, abandoned-row recovery, concurrent claim queries, indexes, and poison-row handling now belong to the application. It is still a sound design. I would choose it when the database is already the durable work ledger and exposing any worker endpoint is unacceptable.

Both shapes reject one tempting design: running the whole cleanup and send loop inside the cron request. Cron executions stop at 900 seconds, cron targets must be public HTTP URLs, and push delivery targets must be public HTTPS URLs. A private service address isn't a valid destination. More important, a single long request gives recovery the wrong granularity. If item 31,407 stalls after thousands of successful sends, rerunning an opaque batch risks repeats; recovering a durable item job is narrower and easier to reason about.

Standard queue delivery is at-least-once, so the worker must be idempotent. Use a stable key such as reminder:{reminderId}:send, claim it transactionally before the external effect, store the terminal result, and treat a repeated claim as already handled. The FIFO deduplication window is only five minutes; it cannot replace durable consumer idempotency. An acknowledgement deletes the message, retention is at most 30 days, payloads are capped at 256KB, and delayed delivery is capped at seven days. Put reminder IDs and small routing data in the message, not an entire customer record.

How can a public HTTPS cron webhook prepare a queue worker handoff?

The useful implementation move is to verify the publishing contract instead of copying a stale request body. Infrai's API is self-describing: its public discovery surface returns the HTTP method, route, full request JSON Schema, response schema, billing data, and runnable examples. That makes a new capability an inspect-and-generate task rather than an SDK adoption project. The following Node.js 18+ TypeScript program performs the unauthenticated discovery read and prints the fields a local type generator should consume.

type JsonSchema = {
  type?: string;
  required?: string[];
  properties?: Record<string, unknown>;
};

type Capability = {
  id: string;
  method: string;
  path: string;
  available: boolean;
  params: JsonSchema;
};

async function main(): Promise<void> {
  const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
  const response = await fetch(
    "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/queue.publish",
    {
      method: "GET",
      // Discovery is public; send auth only when the same client is configured for protected calls.
      headers: apiKey ? { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` } : {},
    },
  );

  if (!response.ok) {
    const body = await response.text();
    throw new Error(`Discovery read rejected (${response.status}): ${body}`);
  }

  const capability = (await response.json()) as Capability;

  console.log({
    id: capability.id,
    available: capability.available,
    method: capability.method,
    path: capability.path,
    required: capability.params.required ?? [],
    fields: Object.keys(capability.params.properties ?? {}),
  });
}

main().catch((error: unknown) => {
  console.error(error);
  process.exitCode = 1;
});

Generate or validate the publisher from that returned schema, then keep the actual trigger thin: authenticate the scheduler, select a bounded page of eligible reminders, publish stable IDs, persist the cursor, and return. For any write retry, send an Idempotency-Key; on 429, honor Retry-After when present and otherwise use exponential backoff. Check every response status and surface the 4xx body because it carries the reason. Don't hold the public request open while workers send notifications.

This is where Infrai earns a place on the shortlist. The public schema and runnable examples reduce integration guesswork, while the shared credential removes a concrete secret-rotation chore. The case is about interface clarity and a smaller operating surface, not price.

Operational recovery changes the product comparison

The products below solve different layers. Treating them as interchangeable because they all contain a timer produces bad comparisons.

Option Natural fit Recovery unit Main trade-off
Infrai cron plus queue Public trigger, REST integration, small polyglot team One queued reminder No DAG, fan-out/join, native debounce, topic fan-out, or Kafka-style replay
BullMQ Node.js service already operating Redis Redis-backed job The team owns Redis persistence, failover, and worker operations
RabbitMQ Team that wants broker topology and explicit consumer acknowledgements Acknowledged message Broker deployment and policy remain an operator responsibility
AWS SQS with EventBridge Scheduler AWS-native identity, networking, and monitoring Managed queue message IAM and infrastructure configuration tie the design closely to AWS
Temporal Durable multi-step processes with waits and compensation Workflow or activity More machinery than a periodic scan followed by independent sends
GitHub Actions schedule Repository maintenance with workflow logs Workflow run A poor home for customer-facing reminder state and per-item recovery

Infrai is not suitable when reminders form a durable multi-step workflow, need a join after fan-out, require delays longer than seven days, exceed 256KB per message, or must be replayed to multiple consumer groups after acknowledgement. Stick with Temporal for workflow history and coordination. Choose BullMQ when Redis is already an accepted dependency and Node.js job ergonomics matter more than a language-neutral boundary; choose RabbitMQ when the team deliberately wants broker-level acknowledgement and routing control; choose AWS SQS when the rest of the system is already organized around AWS.

The database-lease architecture also remains a serious competitor. It is often the right answer when candidate selection and the idempotency claim must commit in one local transaction. The catch is that it turns recovery behavior into application code — useful control, but code that needs tests, metrics, and an owner. I'm not sure which option wins until I know who will respond to an expired lease at 03:00. Your mileage may vary with the team's database experience.

The recovery drill starts after enqueue

Cron run history is useful for answering whether the trigger fired and whether its request completed, but its output retains only the first 4KB. Application-side logs must carry the rest. I log the schedule ID, run ID, selection cursor, number of reminder jobs accepted, and a correlation ID that follows each job into the worker. I don't log full reminder payloads; IDs and state transitions are enough for recovery and are less likely to leak user data.

The worker view needs different evidence. Record first-seen time, attempt count, stable operation ID, terminal outcome, and the downstream status class. Alert on oldest unprocessed job and terminal failures, not merely queue depth. A queue can be shallow while one old reminder is stuck behind repeated newer work, and a green cron history can coexist with a delivery backlog because the scheduler did its narrow job correctly.

Short requests help.

Paused cron schedules do not backfill missed triggers, and trigger timing has second-level jitter. Design the cleanup as a state-based scan such as “find eligible unsent reminders before this cursor,” not as “process exactly the records created during this second.” On resume, the next scan can rediscover eligible records without relying on a missed tick. The stable idempotency key then prevents rediscovery from becoming a duplicate user-visible send.

The operational checklist is prose because these checks belong together. Confirm that the cron URL is publicly reachable over the intended protocol and that it enqueues rather than sends. Keep its timeout at or below 900 seconds and bound each selection page. Verify the request contract through discovery during development, then pin generated types in source control. Make worker effects idempotent beyond the five-minute FIFO window. Keep delayed jobs within seven days and messages below 256KB. Finally, rehearse recovery from a missed schedule, a repeated delivery, a 429, and a worker restart; each exercise should end with the same reminder state and no second send.

The decision rule is compact: use the managed cron-to-queue shape when a public admission endpoint is acceptable and per-item recovery matters; use database leases when private workers and local transactional claims dominate; use a workflow engine when reminders stop being independent jobs. Cron wakes the system. It should not carry the system's work.

If this boundary fits your reminder service, start by checking the cron and queue recovery guide against your own trigger and worker invariants.

Sources

  • Infrai machine-readable capability index: https://docs.infrai.cc/llms.txt
  • RabbitMQ consumer acknowledgements: https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/confirms
  • GitHub Actions scheduled workflow triggers: https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-workflows/events-that-trigger-workflows

title: My ML Feature Used the Wrong Unit. The Threshold Was 400x Too Large.
description:
The historical model and the live validator both calculated large_share, the fraction of sweep volume in unusually large trades. Their definitions had diverged.

The live code used the 75th percentile of per-second net aggressive volume as the cutoff for an individual trade. On the affected symbols, that threshold was 163–423 times too large. Almost no individual trade cleared it, so large_share was near zero in 97% or more of live events.

The public audit package includes the minimal reproducible fixture, the feature-contract checks, and the recorded aggregate results used here. It does not include the underlying market-data archive.

Evidence package: open the feature-contract tests and frozen raw-replay summary on GitHub.

For AAVEUSDT, the 75th percentile of individual trade quantity was 4.3 units. The 75th percentile of per-second NAV was 1,730 units. Both are volumes; they are not interchangeable.

large_thr = np.percentile(np.abs(dev["nav_abs"]), 75)
# nav_abs: per-second net aggressive volume

large_share = volume_of_trades_at_or_above(large_thr) / total_volume
# threshold is applied to individual trades

The correct calibration comes from individual trade quantities. The repaired live path refuses to score a symbol when it lacks a matching calibration artifact.

Three other feature contracts also differed

The feature-parity audit found three other differences between training and live:

Feature Historical contract Live defect
large_share Individual trade-size percentile Per-second NAV percentile
run_frac Longest consecutive trade run / trade count Buy-volume fraction
pre_vel Direction-adjusted signed flow Unsigned volume
trailing_nav Direction-adjusted trailing flow Direction omitted

The large_share defect was the main false-positive driver. In the first analytical triage of 14 October, fixing it alone reduced selected candidates from 40 to 5. Applying all four corrections left 2.

Those are diagnostic counts from before the October raw-trade archive was recovered; two feature values were approximated in that first pass.

We subsequently recovered Binance Futures aggTrades for 6–14 October. The raw reconstruction keeps the recorded candidate timestamps and uses the matching frozen artifacts: V1 live for 6–13 October (13,786 candidates) and V2 full baseline for 14 October (895).

It rebuilt the four affected feature families for 14,681 of 14,682 candidates. One LDOUSDT detection second was absent from the archive. The frozen artifacts reproduced recorded scores with a mean absolute difference of 1.04×10⁻⁶.

The repaired features selected 52 candidates. Their raw five-second Binance markout averaged +8.67 bps. With a 10 bps round-trip fee assumption, that becomes −1.33 bps. No strategy was promoted.

The raw archive resolves the four-feature reconstruction gap. A five-second Binance markout is a research measure. Candidate generation and the logged nav_abs / nav_overshoot convention remain fixed, so this is not an execution study.

Drift monitoring comes after parity

A KS test can show that two feature distributions differ. It does not establish whether one implementation used individual trades while another used one-second aggregates.

Before monitoring feature drift, run both implementations against the same recorded raw inputs:

for fixture in recorded_sweeps:
    historical = batch_features(fixture.trades, fixture.direction)
    live = streaming_features(fixture.trades, fixture.direction)

    assert historical.large_share == live.large_share
    assert historical.run_frac == live.run_frac
    assert historical.pre_vel == live.pre_vel
    assert historical.trailing_nav == live.trailing_nav

Record the threshold's unit, symbol, source period, and input hash beside the calibration artifact. Check feature parity before interpreting a model score.

Part of the HFM Research methodology series.

title: A Mock with Memory: CRUD, Soft Delete, and Restore Without Writing a Backend
description:
The frontend already knows how to create a note, mark it as done, and send it to the trash. The mock doesn't. Every GET /api/notes returns the same array, the POST leaves no trace, and the 409 for a duplicate title is something you have to invent by hand. That's enough for a static list. It falls short as soon as an optimistic UI1, a trash view, or a conflict shows up.

In Mock Your API in 5 Minutes with JSON and Switch Success and Error Without Touching Your Frontend, the mock was a fixed body and a nameResponse you flipped. This is where the store comes in: an in-memory collection, declared in the same JSON, with list, get, create, update, patch, delete, and restore actions. The examples use http-mock-json 6.0.1, and every response in this article comes from actually running it.

This isn't a guide to every filter, relation, or on-disk persist. It's about a mock that remembers what you send.

A store per endpoint

The store is declared on the endpoint, at the same level as GET or POST, not inside a method. You define the collection once (with id and, if you need them, key, seed, template, unique, softDelete, list). Other routes that share that data use the reference form: "store": { "id": "notes" }. On each response that should read or mutate the collection, you set "action" to one of these seven operations:

Action What it does Success Common errors
list Returns items. Without "list": false, it paginates 10 at a time. Soft-deleted items are omitted unless ?includeDeleted=true the response statusCode 400 if the list query is invalid
get Loads one item; the key comes from the route params. An item in the trash returns 404, unless ?includeDeleted=true the response statusCode 404
create Inserts; merges template + body; if a numeric key field is missing, it generates one the response statusCode (in the official preset, 201) 400 (the body is not an object), 409 (conflict)
update Full replace (template + body); keeps the key. If the item is in the trash, 404 the response statusCode 404 / 400 / 409
patch Partial merge onto the existing item (no template); keeps the key the response statusCode 404 / 400 / 409
delete Without softDelete, removes the item. With softDelete, marks it and leaves it in the collection. Always responds 204 with an empty body; the statusCode in the JSON is ignored 204 404
restore Requires softDelete. Clears the deleted mark and returns the item. If it is active or does not exist, 404 the response statusCode 404 / 409

The 201 on create and the 200 on get or restore are not invented by the store: they come from the statusCode of the selected response. delete is the exception: it is always 204.

The shortest path to a JSON file with persistence, unique, softDelete, and restore is the official preset:

npx mock-server add --preset crud-full

That preset leaves seed empty, sets "persist": true, and does not turn off the list engine. The file in this article is the same skeleton, with three deliberate changes: a seed so you can curl right away, "list": false so GET returns the full array, and no persist, so the state lives only for the lifetime of the process.

The notes JSON

mocks/notes.json:

{
  "api/notes": {
    "store": {
      "id": "notes",
      "key": "id",
      "seed": [
        { "id": 1, "title": "Comprar leche", "done": false }
      ],
      "template": { "id": 0, "title": "", "done": false },
      "unique": ["title"],
      "softDelete": true,
      "list": false
    },
    "GET": {
      "nameResponse": "list",
      "responses": [
        { "name": "list", "statusCode": 200, "action": "list" }
      ]
    },
    "POST": {
      "nameResponse": "create",
      "responses": [
        { "name": "create", "statusCode": 201, "action": "create" }
      ]
    }
  },
  "api/notes/:id": {
    "store": { "id": "notes" },
    "GET": {
      "nameResponse": "get",
      "responses": [
        { "name": "get", "statusCode": 200, "action": "get" }
      ]
    },
    "PUT": {
      "nameResponse": "update",
      "responses": [
        { "name": "update", "statusCode": 200, "action": "update" }
      ]
    },
    "PATCH": {
      "nameResponse": "patch",
      "responses": [
        { "name": "patch", "statusCode": 200, "action": "patch" }
      ]
    },
    "DELETE": {
      "nameResponse": "remove",
      "responses": [
        { "name": "remove", "statusCode": 204, "action": "delete" }
      ]
    },
    "POST": {
      "nameResponse": "restore",
      "responses": [
        { "name": "restore", "statusCode": 200, "action": "restore" }
      ]
    }
  }
}

key defaults to "id"; here it's explicit. unique is a list of fields: if a value collides with another active item on create, update, patch, or restore, the default response is 409. softDelete: true uses the deletedAt field. The POST on /api/notes/:id does not create: it restores, same as the crud-full preset.

You need Node.js 22.12 or later. Install and start, using 6.0.1's default port:

npm install http-mock-json --save-dev
npx mock-server start -p 3001 -f mocks

The server listens at http://localhost:3001. CORS is enabled by default. From here on, every curl hits that base URL.

Create, and the 409 when the title already exists

The list starts from the seed:

curl -s http://localhost:3001/api/notes

[
  {
    "id": 1,
    "title": "Comprar leche",
    "done": false
  }
]

Now a POST with no id:

curl -s -X POST http://localhost:3001/api/notes \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"title":"Pagar luz"}'

HTTP/1.1 201 Created

{
  "id": 2,
  "title": "Pagar luz",
  "done": false
}

Three things at once. create merges template + body, so done comes out false even though you didn't send it. Because the body had no id, the store generates a number: among the items in the collection it takes the maximum of that field and adds one; if there are none, it starts at 1. Here the seed already had 1, so the new one is 2. If the body (or a route param) already carries the key, that value is kept: a POST with "id": 50 leaves 50.

Repeat the same title:

curl -s -X POST http://localhost:3001/api/notes \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"title":"Pagar luz"}'

HTTP/1.1 409 Conflict

{
  "message": "Duplicate value(s)",
  "conflicts": [
    {
      "field": "title",
      "value": "Pagar luz",
      "message": "Duplicate value for unique field \"title\""
    }
  ]
}

That body is the default. You can replace it with a named response, via unique.conflict or a field's conflict, but you don't need to in order to try the "that title already exists" toast. If the body isn't a JSON object (an array, or nothing), the store never even looks at unique: it responds 400 with {"message":"Request body must be a JSON object"}.

patch is not update

PATCH merges the body onto the item that's already there. PUT (update) rebuilds the item as template + body and then forces the original key back on. In both cases the key cannot be changed from the body.

curl -s -X PATCH http://localhost:3001/api/notes/2 \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"done":true}'

{
  "id": 2,
  "title": "Pagar luz",
  "done": true
}

The title is still there. A PUT that only sends the title does not keep that done: true: the template sets it back to false.

curl -s -X PUT http://localhost:3001/api/notes/2 \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"title":"Pagar el recibo de luz"}'

{
  "id": 2,
  "title": "Pagar el recibo de luz",
  "done": false
}

That's the contrast that matters when the frontend does a minimal patch versus a full replace. If you pick the wrong action, the mock does not "fill in what was already there": update fills in from the template.

Delete, look at the trash, and restore 

curl -s -D - -o /dev/null -X DELETE http://localhost:3001/api/notes/2

HTTP/1.1 204 No Content

The body is 0 bytes. There is no Content-Type and no Content-Length. That's true with or without softDelete: a successful delete is always an empty 204. The difference is what remains in the collection.

Without softDelete, the item is removed. With softDelete: true, it stays and is marked. The default field is deletedAt, and the value is an ISO 86012 timestamp (new Date().toISOString()). From that point on, list, get, update, and patch treat it as if it weren't there, unless you ask for the trash.

curl -s http://localhost:3001/api/notes

[
  {
    "id": 1,
    "title": "Comprar leche",
    "done": false
  }
]

curl -s http://localhost:3001/api/notes/2

HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found

{
  "message": "Not found"
}

A PATCH to the same /api/notes/2 also returns that 404. You ask for the trash with ?includeDeleted=true or ?includeDeleted=1. Any other value, including yes, does not count.

curl -s 'http://localhost:3001/api/notes/2?includeDeleted=true'

{
  "id": 2,
  "title": "Pagar el recibo de luz",
  "done": false,
  "deletedAt": "2026-11-13T14:10:20.572Z"
}

The deletedAt in that capture is the moment I ran the DELETE. Yours will be different, in the same format. GET /api/notes?includeDeleted=true returns both items: the active one, without that field, and the one in the trash, with it.

Restore is the item's POST:

curl -s -X POST http://localhost:3001/api/notes/2

{
  "id": 2,
  "title": "Pagar el recibo de luz",
  "done": false
}

The deletedAt field is not set to null: it is removed. A restore on an active item, or on one that does not exist, returns 404 with the same {"message":"Not found"}. Without softDelete on the store definition, that action is not valid: startup is blocked with The "action" "restore" requires "store.softDelete" to be enabled.

The conflict that shows up when you restore from the trash

Items in the trash do not count toward unique or the key. That has a direct consequence, and it's the one that looks most like a real flow: you can create the same title again, and then restore collides.

After the DELETE of note 2, this POST succeeds and gets id 3 (the generator looks at the maximum in the collection, including marked rows, and adds one):

curl -s -X POST http://localhost:3001/api/notes \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"title":"Pagar el recibo de luz"}'

{
  "id": 3,
  "title": "Pagar el recibo de luz",
  "done": false
}

Restoring 2, with 3 already active, is no longer a 200:

curl -s -X POST http://localhost:3001/api/notes/2

HTTP/1.1 409 Conflict

{
  "message": "Duplicate value(s)",
  "conflicts": [
    {
      "field": "title",
      "value": "Pagar el recibo de luz",
      "message": "Duplicate value for unique field \"title\""
    }
  ]
}

That 409 is what lets you try the "a note with that title already exists" dialog when the user takes something out of the trash. If you first send 3 to the trash, the restore of 2 returns 200 again and the list shows notes 1 and 2 once more. 3 is still in the collection, marked, hidden until you ask for includeDeleted.

That's what a stateless mock cannot do. A GET with a fixed body does not know whether the previous POST happened, whether the title is free because the other row is in the trash, or what a second POST to the same /api/notes/2 should return. The optimistic UI, the trash list, and the conflict on restore are not three different mocks: they are the same collection after a sequence of requests.

The list, if you don't turn it off

Since 3.0.0, omitting store.list or setting "list": true turns on the list engine with the same defaults as page-based pagination: pageSize 10, sort id, order asc. The body is still an array, not an object with total or page. Those fields only appear if you put templates in body or headers.

I checked this with 12 items and without "list": false. GET /api/many returned ids 1 through 10. GET /api/many?page=2 returned ids 11 and 12. In the notes for this article I turned that engine off on purpose, so the list would be the full collection while we talked about create, delete, and restore.

Where it fits next to MSW and json-server

They are not the same kind of tool. The useful question is which problem each one solves, not which one "wins."

MSW (Mock Service Worker) is a mocking library for the browser and for Node.js. It intercepts your application's requests — in the browser, with the Service Worker API — and handles them with handlers you write. The client does not point at localhost:3001: it keeps calling the same URL as always, and MSW answers along the way. A handler can always return the same body, or you can keep state in an array or a module. That isn't built in: you write it. The ecosystem also has @msw/data, a separate library for modeling and querying collections (create, find, update, delete, relations, pagination), meant to be used on its own or from those handlers. Its documentation does not describe an HTTP server, or a softDelete with ?includeDeleted=true, or a 409 from unique as a route contract. If you need those, you implement them on top.

json-server is an HTTP server. From a db.json it exposes REST routes for each resource: GET/POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE. The current official documentation (the main branch, marked as v1 beta) covers filters, sorting, pagination, _embed, and deleting dependents. The default port is 3000. That documentation does not mention unique constraints with 409, or soft delete, or restore. In v1, according to the migration notes in the same README, id is always a string and is generated only if you don't send one. If what you want is generic CRUD over a JSON file, that's the shortest path.

http-mock-json 6.0.1 sits in the middle, but on the server side: it's a CLI that boots HTTP, and your frontend talks to http://localhost:3001 as if it were the API. Routes, status codes, validation, and collection rules are declared in JSON. The store fits when that contract is not just "list and create," but also the 409, the trash, and restore. If what you need is to intercept requests inside the test or the browser, MSW is the tool. If generic REST over a file is enough, json-server is too. If you want a mock of your API, with memory and with those rules, without writing a backend or a handler per verb, this is the gap.

Checklist before you blame the frontend

Symptom Check
The POST creates, but the GET stays the same The GET response has no "action": "list", or the store.id is not the same on both routes
create does not assign an id The body (or a route param) already has that key: in that case it is not generated
You expected a full array and only see 10 items Since 3.0.0 the list engine is on by default; set "list": false or request ?page=2
The DELETE is not the status you put in the JSON A successful delete is always 204; statusCode is ignored
?includeDeleted=yes does not show the trash Only "true" and "1" count
restore returns 409 and the item "was no longer there" There is another active item with the same unique value; rows in the trash do not occupy that value
The PUT cleared a field you didn't send update fills in from the template, not from the previous item; for a partial change, use patch
POST /api/notes/:id creates another note In this design that POST is restore, not create; create lives on the collection

A mock with memory does not replace the backend. It lets the frontend walk the full flow — create, collide, send to the trash, and recover — while that backend still doesn't exist, or isn't in a position to give you those cases on demand.

References

  • http-mock-json on npm · repo · version 6.0.1 · Store reference in the README
  • Previous: Mock Your API in 5 Minutes with JSON · Switch Success and Error Without Touching Your Frontend
  • CLI: mock-server add --preset crud-full (collection + item, unique, softDelete, restore); mock-server start listens on port 3001 by default
  • MSW, Introduction · @msw/data
  • json-server, official README (the main branch, v1 beta documentation)

Notes

  1. Optimistic UI: the client updates the screen as soon as the user acts, without waiting for the server's response, and corrects itself if that response fails. To test it properly, the mock has to accept the change, return the created item, and, on error, a 409 or a 404 the client can handle. ↩

  2. ISO 8601 is the standard date and time format. JavaScript's Date#toISOString() writes it in UTC, with a Z suffix: for example, 2026-11-13T14:10:20.572Z. ↩

title: Microsoft 365 global outage lasted over 22 hours
description:
A 22-hour Microsoft 365 outage affected 430 million users globally across 70+ countries, taking down Outlook and core enterprise services.

Microsoft confirmed the incident was triggered by routine automated checks rather than a security breach, requiring nearly a full day of gradual server recovery.

How the outage was caused

The problem began when routine automated checks took down some of the systems that service the services. The traffic overloaded the systems that remained available, while the restoration was gradual and took almost a day.

Who was influenced worldwide?

About 430 million people use Microsoft 365, and problems were reported in more than 70 countries. The outage affected the email systems of the US House of Representatives and Australian intelligence agencies. It also disrupted judicial services in Singapore and airline support offices in India.

The impact on businesses and states

Flora Hamilton, executive director of the Small Business Charter, called the outage a reminder of businesses' reliance on digital systems. She said email is fundamental to small and medium-sized businesses, as it is essential for communicating with customers and suppliers and for generating revenue.

↳

READ ALSO

HACKS.GR / RELATED

Digital Life

Microsoft increases email expiration time to 48 hours due to global outage

↗

Artificial intelligence strategic consultant Walter Pasquarelli said the outage highlighted the reliance of governments, businesses and critical infrastructure on a few large companies. He added that connecting AI digital assistants to email, calendars and files could amplify the impact of a future outage.

Microsoft's stance and experts' suggestions

Gergely Orosz, a former software engineer at major technology companies, noted that such outages are not unheard of, but what was unusual was the time it took Microsoft to restore.

A Microsoft spokesperson explained that, due to high demand, the company has been gradually restoring services to ensure a stable process, although this has increased wait times.

As a possible solution for the future, Orosz suggested separating services by region to limit the extent of an outage, citing Amazon's AWS as an example. Microsoft said it is investigating what went wrong and that the findings will guide steps to prevent similar incidents.

title: Architecting Real-Time Event Reporting Dashboards for Middle East Mega-Events
description:
When engineering the digital backbone for 10,000+ delegate exhibitions in Riyadh and Jeddah, the transition from basic CRUD apps to enterprise data pipelines is severe.

As part of advanced mega events training in the Middle East for system architects, the primary focus is shifting away from batch data processing (daily CSV exports) toward real-time telemetry. When CTOs demand live visibility over their exhibition floor, developers must build a highly responsive event analytics dashboard capable of ingesting massive concurrent hardware and software events.

Here is how we engineer these live data pipelines for Saudi Vision 2030 mega-events.

  1. Ingesting Fragmented Telemetry

A modern mega-event generates data from multiple disparate sources:

Digital: State-machine transitions from VIP booking portals (e.g., a meeting status changing from pending to approved).

Physical (IoT): Edge-computed RFID handshakes as attendees walk through passive UHF gates or tap interactive kiosks.

To power a live event reporting dashboard, we cannot rely on direct synchronous database writes from edge devices, as venue network latency will cause massive API blockages.

  1. The Asynchronous Data Pipeline

Instead, we decouple the ingestion from the visualization layer:

Edge Compute: RFID gates resolve the UID locally using edge-cached SQLite databases to ensure sub-5ms physical access.

Message Queue: Telemetry payloads (Timestamp, UID, Zone ID) are dispatched asynchronously to a message broker (like Redis or Kafka) rather than writing directly to the primary relational database.

Stream Processing: Background workers consume these queues, validate the payloads, and update the central data lake.

Live Push: To keep the frontend dashboard strictly real-time without suffocating the server with AJAX polling, we utilize WebSockets (or Server-Sent Events for one-way telemetry). The frontend React/Vue dashboard listens to these streams and updates the zone capacity graphs and VIP conversion funnels instantly.

The Value of Unified Architecture

The ultimate goal of technical mega events training in the Middle East is teaching engineers how to eliminate data silos. By routing all physical IoT telemetry and digital state machines through a centralized message queue, you provide operations directors with a flawless, single source of truth.

When your dashboard updates the exact second an attendee walks into a VIP lounge, you have successfully built enterprise-grade event architecture.
