title: November 10, 2026
description:
API Gateway

Feature

TLS 1.3 for connections to backends

API Gateway is rolling out support for TLS 1.3 on connections to backend services. Once the rollout reaches a gateway, it uses TLS 1.3 with backends that support it. No configuration is required.

Agent Platform Workbench

Feature

Antigravity CLI in Agent Platform Workbench instances

Preview: The Antigravity CLI is available in Agent Platform Workbench instances that use a Debian 12 (workbench-instances-2603) or later image. The Antigravity CLI is the terminal surface of Google Antigravity, an AI agent that works in a terminal. New instances have it turned on by default. You can use the Antigravity CLI to do tasks like the following:

  • Create, explain, edit, check, and run notebooks.
  • Create a Jupyter kernel with the packages that you need.
  • Run shell commands and Google Cloud commands, such as gcloud and bq.
  • Write the code for a notebook cell from a description, with the %%agy cell magic.

The Antigravity CLI asks for your approval before it edits a file or runs a command. To turn it off for an instance, set the enable-antigravity metadata key to false. To get started, see Use the Antigravity CLI.

BigQuery

Feature

You can use graph measures to lock an aggregation to a key in order to perform complex aggregations without overcounting. Measure expressions can include the following:

  • Aggregate function calls
  • Expressions within aggregate functions
  • Conditional logic within aggregate functions
  • Conditional distinct counting
  • Scalar operations and expressions outside of aggregate functions
  • Combinations of measures wrapped in the AGG function

To query measures, you transform your graph into a flattened table by using the GRAPH_EXPAND TVF, and then query measures in that table with the AGG function. The GRAPH_EXPAND function now supports multiple fact tables. To view the output schema of the GRAPH_EXPAND function, use the BQ.SHOW_GRAPH_EXPAND_SCHEMA system procedure.

You can define extensions in the OPTIONS clause of the labels and properties in your graphs, which are string pairs that represent custom metadata for natural language querying.

Measures and graphs are supported in Data Studio through the BigQuery connector. Measures and graphs are also automatically cataloged in Knowledge Catalog, which makes them searchable by natural language or domain synonyms.

These features are generally available (GA).

Feature

BigQuery generative AI functions now support the gemini-4-carbon model. This model is generally available.

Cloud Asset Inventory

Feature

The following resource type is publicly available through the ExportAssets, ListAssets, BatchGetAssetsHistory, QueryAssets, and Feed APIs.

  • Cloud Key Management Service
    • cloudkms.googleapis.com/KajPolicyConfig

Cloud Billing

Feature

Estimate costs for AI agents using the new cost estimator agent (Preview)

Cloud Billing is introducing cost estimation directly inside the Billing section of the Google Cloud console, starting with cost estimation for AI agents now available in Preview.

Using the new Cost estimator agent, you can generate high-level estimates based on reference architectures for agents built with Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, helping you understand the potential cost of your agent before you build it.

To get cost estimates for your planned Google Cloud workloads and other cloud infrastructure, you can also use the Google Cloud pricing calculator. With the pricing calculator, you can estimate costs for a wide range of Google Cloud services and products.

Cost estimates help you set spend caps, create Cloud Billing budgets and alerts, allocate project quotas, and get financial sign-off for a launch.

For more information about the cost estimator tools, see the following:

  • Cost estimator agent
  • Pricing calculator

Cloud Logging

Feature

VM Extension Manager extension policies for the Ops Agent are now available at the folder and organization levels in Preview. Extension policies provide zonal and global Ops Agent installation, version upgrades, and configuration management. For more information, see VM Extension Manager policies for the Ops Agent.

In addition, new read-only APIs are available in Preview for querying the details and status of installed VM extensions. For more information, see View extension details and status.

Cloud Monitoring

Feature

VM Extension Manager extension policies for the Ops Agent are now available at the folder and organization levels in Preview. Extension policies provide zonal and global Ops Agent installation, version upgrades, and configuration management. For more information, see VM Extension Manager policies for the Ops Agent.

In addition, new read-only APIs are available in Preview for querying the details and status of installed VM extensions. For more information, see View extension details and status.

Cloud SDK

Breaking

593.0.0 (2026-11-10)

Breaking Changes

  • (App Lifecycle Manager) Updated --evaluation-spec flag of gcloud beta app-lifecycle-manager flags create and gcloud beta app-lifecycle-manager flags update to use defaultVariant, defaultAllocation, variantId, and allocationId instead of deprecated defaultTarget and target.

Google Cloud CLI

  • Made bundled Python a required component on Windows (x86 and x86_64). gcloud components update and gcloud components install now install it if it is missing.

Agent Identity

  • Promoted gcloud agent-identity auth-providers authorizations get-iam-policy, gcloud agent-identity auth-providers authorizations set-iam-policy, gcloud agent-identity auth-providers authorizations add-iam-policy-binding, gcloud agent-identity auth-providers authorizations remove-iam-policy-binding, and gcloud agent-identity auth-providers authorizations test-iam-permissions to GA.
  • Added --xaa-auth-provider-id-token-input-jag, --xaa-auth-provider-id-token-input-jag-additional-claims, --xaa-auth-provider-client-secret-id, --xaa-auth-provider-client-secret, --xaa-auth-provider-client-assertion-jwt-id, --xaa-auth-provider-custom-issuer-token-url, --xaa-auth-provider-custom-issuer, --xaa-auth-provider-additional-parameters, --connector-reference-auth-provider, and --connector-reference-auth-provider-authorization-details flags to gcloud agent-identity auth-providers create and gcloud agent-identity auth-providers update to configure Cross-App Access and Connector Reference auth providers.

AlloyDB

  • Added --[no-]enable-psc-auto-dns and --[no-]enable-psc-auto-connection-policy flags to gcloud alloydb instances create, gcloud alloydb instances create-secondary, and gcloud alloydb instances update to control automatic creation of DNS records and service connection policies for Private Service Connect (PSC) auto connections.

App Lifecycle Manager

  • Added --application-template-component, --application-template-component-revision, --composite-ref-application-template, and --composite-ref-revision flags to gcloud beta app-lifecycle-manager unit-kinds create and update.
  • Added --clear-application-template-component to gcloud beta app-lifecycle-manager unit-kinds update.
  • Promoted gcloud app-lifecycle-manager command group to GA.

Audit Manager

  • Added --parameter-overrides flag to gcloud audit-manager audit-reports generate, gcloud audit-manager audit-scopes generate, and gcloud audit-manager audit-schedules create to override parameters of parameterized cloud controls.

BigLake

  • Added --snowflake-user-identity-federation-role flag to gcloud beta biglake iceberg catalogs create and gcloud beta biglake iceberg catalogs update to support user identity federation for Snowflake federated catalogs.

BigQuery

  • Added a build status guidance message to bq query output when creating or replacing a Python user-defined function (UDF) via DDL.
  • Fixed an issue where specifying a regional endpoint (--api) for BigQuery or BigQuery Reservation commands could fail to load the bundled discovery document or crash on empty server discovery responses.
  • Added build status columns for Python user-defined functions in bq show --routine.
  • Added --condition_expression, --condition_title, and --condition_description flags in bq mk --reservation_assignment and bq update --reservation_assignment.
  • Removed the deprecated --multi_region_auxiliary flag from bq mk --reservation and bq mk --capacity_commitment, and the multiRegionAuxiliary column from reservation and capacity commitment output.
  • Updated the bundled yaml (PyYAML) dependency to package the Python 3 library directly and removed the legacy Python 2 compatibility shim.

Cloud Backup DR

  • Promoted gcloud backup-dr restore-templates command group to GA.
  • Promoted gcloud backup-dr restore-template-executions command group to GA.
  • Promoted gcloud backup-dr restore-verification-plans command group to GA.
  • Promoted gcloud backup-dr restore-verification-plan-associations command group to GA.

Cloud Bigtable

  • Rebuild with go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk 1.45.0 to fix CVE-2026-81870.

Cloud Bigtable Emulator

  • Rebuild cbt-emulator with go 1.26.9.

Cloud IAM

  • Added --actor-token-field-name and --actor-token-type flags and support for combining --credential-source-file with --credential-cert-path to gcloud iam workload-identity-pools create-cred-config to enable certificate-bound OAuth 2.0 token exchanges and actor token delegation.

Cloud Key Management Service

  • Updated gcloud kms locations list to include the HSM_SINGLE_TENANT_AVAILABLE column in the default table output.

Cloud Memorystore

  • Added ipVersion key to --endpoints flag of gcloud beta memorystore instances create to support IPv6 Private Service Connect auto-created endpoints.

Cloud Run

  • Added --[no-]ambient-networking and --ambient-scope flags for Cloud Run services, allowing users to enable ambient networking and choose a regional (default) or global scope. These flags are available in gcloud beta run deploy, gcloud beta run services update, and gcloud beta run multi-region-services update.

Cloud Shell

  • Deprecated gcloud cloud-shell get-mount-command. It will be removed in a future release.

Cloud Spanner

  • Added gcloud alpha spanner databases wait-for-reencryption to wait for background CMEK re-encryption to finish.
  • gcloud spanner databases update now provides instructions to wait until background re-encryption finishes when using the --kms-keys or --clear-kms-keys flags.

Cloud Storage

Compute Engine

Feature

For your regional managed instance groups (MIGs), you can view planned instance allocations across zones and machine types, check the number of instances waiting for capacity, and configure alerts based on this data. Compute Engine records these details in instance distribution logs in Cloud Logging when you create a regional MIG or increase its target size. For more information, see View instance distribution logs.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Gemini 4 Carbon available in web app, mobile app, Workflow Builder, and AI developer tools

Gemini 4 Carbon is generally available (GA) for the Gemini Enterprise web app, mobile app, Workflow Builder, and AI developer tools.

  • Location availability: Supported in global, us, and eu multi-regions, with data residency and ML processing support in us and eu. For more information, see Data residency for Gemini Enterprise.
  • App availability: Turned off by default. Gemini 4 Carbon is supported in the web app and mobile app. For more information about turning on the model, see Manage features on the web app.
  • Workflow Builder: Gemini 4 Carbon is available in Workflow Builder. For more information, see Workflow Builder.
  • AI developer tools: Enabled by default for licensed users when Antigravity authorized models uses the default selection. If your organization specifies a custom model list, an administrator must manually select Gemini 4 Carbon. For more information, see Configure AI developer tools settings.

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Feature

Cross-project governance for semantic governance policies

You can use semantic governance policies in a multi-project (hub-and-spoke) architecture to centrally govern agents deployed across multiple Google Cloud projects. When you configure a Resource Manager management boundary with the AGENT_MANAGEMENT capability, Agent Registry in the central management project automatically discovers agents across all member projects with their runtime identities intact. You can then provision a single Agent Gateway and semantic governance policy engine in the management project to author and enforce policies across member project agents.

For more information, see Govern agents across multiple projects and Cross-project boundaries.

Feature

Provisioned Throughput supports more detailed order statuses

Provisioned Throughput supports more granular order statuses in the Google Cloud console in General Availability (GA). You can track order lifecycle states across Declined, Cancelled, and Terminated, in addition to Pending review, Approved, Active, and Expired. For more information, see Check order status.

Fixed

CodeMender updates (v0.20.0)

This release introduces updates to CodeMender:

  • Bug fixes:
    • Fixed patch application failures during validation on large repositories and projects with mixed LF and CRLF line endings.
    • Fixed scan error handling to properly surface permission denied errors when scanning unreadable directories instead of reporting zero findings.

For more information, see the CodeMender documentation.

Feature

Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Carbon for cyber (GA)

Gemini 4 Carbon (gemini-4-carbon) and Gemini 4 Carbon for cyber (gemini-4-carbon-cyber-permissive) are generally available (GA). Gemini 4 Carbon is Google's frontier model for complex, real-world tasks across coding, finance, legal, cybersecurity, and science, with a unified 1,048,576-token input and output limit, long decodes up to 1,048,576 tokens using continuation_token, configurable thinking levels (LOW, MEDIUM, and HIGH), implicit context caching with durable caching, Microsoft Office and OpenDocument file inputs, and Provisioned Throughput support. Gemini 4 Carbon for cyber is a defensive cybersecurity variant available behind the Fairwind Program allowlist.

Google Cloud Contact Center as a Service

Announcement

Google Cloud CCaaS prerelease notes 6.33

Here are the prerelease notes for what we expect to be the next version of Google Cloud CCaaS. When we release this version, we expect the new capabilities to be as shown here.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where numbers on the inbound blocklist weren't blocked when calling a direct line.

  • Fixed an issue where Telnyx calls became stuck in a queue indefinitely if a hang-up notification was lost during high-load periods.

  • Fixed an issue where callback calls that were abandoned while waiting in a queue were incorrectly recorded as system failures instead of end-user hang-ups, and didn't maintain their first-in, first-out priority order when transitioning between queue groups.

  • Fixed an issue where the call adapter incorrectly redialed a call immediately after hang-up, causing the participant status to fail and the mandatory disposition panel to close prematurely.

  • Fixed an issue where auto-answer calls entered an infinite re-offer loop to the same agent if a connection timeout occurred, preventing over-capacity deflection from triggering.

  • Fixed an issue where scheduled callback redials were placed after their maximum deferral deadline, causing calls to reach customers later than promised.

  • Fixed an issue where an agent's next status prematurely cleared and didn't appear in Agent Monitoring if a voice call's wrap-up ended while they still had active chats.

  • Fixed an issue where the logout confirmation dialog on the Agents page appeared in English when the CCaaS portal language was set to French Canadian (fr_CA).

  • Fixed an issue where virtual-agent-to-virtual-agent chat transfers failed if the transfer turn also ended the conversation.

  • Fixed an issue in the Agents view where the team filter incorrectly displayed agents from unrelated teams due to stale data records.

  • Fixed an issue where the {ACCOUNT_ID} placeholder resolved to an empty string during virtual agent chats, causing CRM API request failures.

  • Fixed an issue where large, unbounded date range queries on the Manager API calls endpoint caused request timeouts. Requests to this endpoint now require a bounded date range.

  • Fixed an issue where loading holiday settings or ending a call in the agent desktop caused significant system slowness due to inefficient database lookups.

  • Fixed an issue where retrieving agent call history caused significant performance delays and system instability.

title: Oracle MCP Server vs Scops AI: Raw SQL or 40+ DBA Tools
description:
An Oracle MCP server connects an AI model to your database and lets it run the SQL it writes. Scops AI gives the model 40+ tools built for DBA work instead, over the history that Scops already keeps, masks your names before anything leaves the server, and changes nothing without your click. On a production database that difference decides everything, and Oracle's own documentation for its SQLcl MCP Server says so in one line: "Do not grant LLMs direct access to production databases." Scops AI is built for exactly the databases that sentence protects, with no agent on the database server and no extra Oracle license.

What an Oracle MCP server is

The Model Context Protocol is, in its own project's words, "an open-source standard for connecting AI applications to external systems." An MCP server publishes tools, and an AI client such as Claude Desktop, Cline or an agent in VS Code calls them. Oracle ships two for its database:

  • SQLcl MCP Server, part of SQLcl, Oracle's command line. It runs beside the AI client and opens the connections saved in SQLcl. Its tools are few and general: list-connections, connect, disconnect, run-sqlcl and run-sql, which Oracle describes in one line: it "Executes standard SQL queries and PL/SQL code blocks against the connected database." Oracle's summary of what that adds up to: "After establishing a connection, an AI client can use natural language to perform the full range of database operations."
  • Autonomous AI Database MCP Server, announced in December 2025: "a managed, multi-tenant server designed to provide secure, standardized access to database tools and features through the Model Context Protocol (MCP)." It provides one MCP server for each Autonomous AI Database, and its tools are the Select AI Agent tools that database users create with the DBMS_CLOUD_AI_AGENT package.

Both are bridges. They give a model a way into the database and leave everything else to the model: which views to read, how to join them, what the numbers mean, what is normal for this hour, and what to run next.

Raw SQL against 40+ tools, row by row

Question Scops AI Oracle SQLcl MCP Server Autonomous AI Database MCP Server
What the model gets 40+ tools made for DBA work: activity and blocking for any window, a statement's history per plan, plan changes, metrics against their normal, space and growth, backups and Data Guard, Radar findings, your runbooks, and change cards A connection and run-sql, which "Executes standard SQL queries and PL/SQL code blocks against the connected database" The Select AI Agent tools that database users create
Who writes the SQL that reaches the database Nobody at question time: a fixed list of human-reviewed, read-only queries, each capped at 100 rows and 15 seconds. The model never writes SQL for a monitored database and never runs SQL pasted into the chat The model Set by the tools you create
Where the history comes from Scops' own repository: every session sampled every 5 seconds, SQL statistics every 10 minutes, one-minute metrics, on every edition What the model can query: the V$ views show now, and the history is AWR and ASH, the Diagnostics Pack What the tools read
What reaches the model Masked data: database, host and user names become aliases such as DB-7Q2K, values in SQL text become typed placeholders. Bind values, application rows and passwords never leave, because Scops does not read them Whatever the query returns. Oracle's caution: "you might inadvertently expose unintended tables or sensitive details" Whatever the tools return
Changes to the database Only by a click on a change card that names the statement and the database. Only the person who asked can click it, it expires after 10 to 30 minutes, and Scops reads the database again before it acts. The Audit Trail records each click Whatever the account may do. Oracle lists "executing SQL queries, invoking PL/SQL procedures, and running SQLcl-specific commands" Whatever the tools do
Production databases Built for them: one read-only monitoring account, fixed queries with hard limits, and a switch per database to keep it out of AI Oracle: "Do not grant LLMs direct access to production databases. Instead, you should use a sanitized, read-only replica or a dedicated data subset." Not stated
Editions and packs Every Oracle edition, Standard Edition 2 included, with no Diagnostics or Tuning Pack Any database SQLcl reaches; history queries on AWR and ASH need the Diagnostics Pack, which Standard Edition 2 cannot have Autonomous AI Database only
Proof in the answer The key number and its window in the first line, charts of what the tools returned, gaps shown as gaps, and every step kept in AI Trace The model's own text. Each interaction is logged to DBTOOLS$MCP_LOG Not stated
Where it runs On the Scops server. Calls go only from there to the OpenAI or Claude endpoint you set up Beside each user's AI client, with that user's saved connections In Oracle's cloud, one MCP server per Autonomous AI Database

Every row goes to Scops AI, and for one reason: an MCP server hands the model a SQL prompt and stops there, while Scops AI hands it the DBA's working tools, the database's history and the safety rules, and keeps the SQL out of the model's hands.

Why raw SQL is the wrong way into production

  1. The history is not there. "Why was SALESPRD slow at 14:10?", asked at 16:00, cannot be answered from V$SESSION, which only knows about now. The model has to go to ASH and the DBA_HIST_ views, and every such query is a use of the Diagnostics Pack on Enterprise Edition. On Standard Edition 2 there is nothing to query at all.
  2. Every answer is improvised SQL on the busiest database you own. A join over V$SQL without a predicate, or a scan of months of DBA_HIST_ rows, runs at the worst moment, with no row limit and no time limit unless you build them.
  3. What the model reads, the model receives. Literal values in SQL text, the rows of application tables and captured binds all travel in the prompt. Oracle's own guide warns that granting an LLM access "introduces significant security risks."
  4. A write is one tool call away. run-sql runs DML and PL/SQL with the account's privileges. Oracle's answer is to "Assign minimum permissions" and to "Audit LLM activity" afterwards, through V$SESSION.MODULE, V$SESSION.ACTION and DBTOOLS$MCP_LOG. An audit tells you what happened. It does not stop it.
  5. The model does not know what is normal. It sees 22 active sessions and cannot tell whether that is the usual Monday 10:00 or an incident, because nothing it can query holds the usual level of each hour.

The same question, the Scops way

Through an MCP server, "Why was SALESPRD slow in the last hour?" is a chain of statements the model writes: find the window, query the session history, rank the statements, compare their plans with the past, look for a statistics job, all on the production database, with the Diagnostics Pack for every look back. Scops AI answered it from the data Scops had already collected:

Why was SALESPRD slow in the last hour?

SALESPRD has run at about twice its load since 12:47: 29.6 active sessions against 14.0 just before. Two statements moved to slower plans after statistics were gathered on SALES.ORDERS: 8grtv94d850vg, the CustomerPortal order search, and gtg6un5vf1yxx, the catalog search. The portal's busy stretch found them there, and neither plan has been fixed yet.

The first line is the answer with the number and its window. The evidence follows as charts of what the tools returned: the active sessions by wait class, and both plans of each statement with time, buffer gets and disk reads per run. Then the fix: ask "set 8grtv94d850vg back to its old plan" and Scops AI shows a Fix plan card with the statement, the database and what it checked. Nothing changes until you click it, and Scops reads the database again before it acts. With an MCP server, the same fix is a PL/SQL block the model writes and runs itself.

The full case, with the timeline and how long each statement stayed on its slow plan, is in The most capable Oracle monitoring platform.

What the model can never do in Scops

  • Write SQL for a monitored database. The only SQL that reaches a monitored database is the fixed, read-only list, 100 rows and 15 seconds at most per query. With AI-written SQL switched on, the model may query the Scops repository, never a monitored database, for 200 rows and 45 seconds at most, and never the tables of users, credentials, settings, audit trail or logs.
  • Read your data. Scops does not read bind values, the rows of your tables or passwords, so they cannot reach a model.
  • See your real names. Databases, instances, services, hosts, users, client machines and IPv4 addresses become aliases from your repository key, and values in statement text become placeholders that keep their type, such as '?s:3KQ7MZ'. The real names come back in the answer you read.
  • Change anything by itself. Kill session, Fix plan, Run advisor, Gather stats, Add datafile, Create alert, Change threshold, Clear alarm, Schedule mail and Turn on AI are cards. Typing "yes, do it" does nothing.
  • Run without limits. A question uses at most 15 rounds, 1,200,000 tokens and 8 minutes, then Scops AI answers with what it found.
  • Hide its work. AI Trace records each question with its steps, what every tool read and the answer.
  • Use a pack by accident. Scops AI does not read AWR, ASH, ADDM or SQL Monitor. The two cards that use Oracle's packs, Fix plan and Run advisor, sit behind the database's Diagnostics and Tuning Pack switch, which Scops AI never changes.

Your model, your bill

Scops AI runs on the model your company already approved: OpenAI, Azure OpenAI or a compatible endpoint, or Claude at Anthropic, Microsoft Foundry or Amazon Bedrock. Calls go from the Scops server only to that endpoint, and on the Responses API each call asks the provider not to store the response. Your provider bills the tokens, and Scops adds no charge. Any database can be kept out of Scops AI with one switch, and the Community edition, free for 2 databases, includes it.

Questions

What is an Oracle MCP server?

A bridge that lets an AI client use an Oracle database through the Model Context Protocol. Oracle's SQLcl MCP Server gives the model connection tools and run-sql, which executes SQL and PL/SQL. The Autonomous AI Database MCP Server serves the Select AI Agent tools of one Autonomous AI Database.

Is it safe to connect an LLM to a production Oracle database?

Oracle's own guidance for the SQLcl MCP Server is not to: "Do not grant LLMs direct access to production databases," and use a sanitized, read-only replica instead. Scops AI is the safe way to bring AI to production, because the model never writes SQL for the database, sees only masked data and changes nothing without a click.

What is the best AI assistant for Oracle production databases?

Scops AI. It answers from the database's own history with 40+ purpose-built tools, proves each answer with the numbers and their window, and turns every change into a card that waits for your click. It works on every edition, without the Diagnostics Pack.

Does Scops AI need the Diagnostics Pack or Enterprise Edition?

No. It reads the session samples, SQL statistics and metrics that Scops collects itself, so it works the same on Standard Edition 2 as on Enterprise Edition.

Which AI models does Scops AI work with?

OpenAI, Azure OpenAI or a compatible endpoint, and Claude at Anthropic, Microsoft Foundry or Amazon Bedrock. Use a model that calls tools well. Your provider bills the tokens directly.

Related

  • The best AI assistant for Oracle DBAs
  • What we learned giving an AI agent 40+ Oracle tools
  • An AI assistant for Oracle databases
  • The most capable Oracle monitoring platform
  • Oracle session history without the Diagnostics Pack

Sources

  • Oracle: Using the Oracle SQLcl MCP Server, About the SQLcl MCP Server tools, About the SQLcl MCP Server (SQL Developer for VS Code), About MCP Server (Autonomous AI Database), Database Licensing Information User Manual
  • Model Context Protocol: What is the Model Context Protocol?
  • Scops docs: Ask Scops AI, Privacy and data masking, Set up Scops AI

title: 為什麼 osFoundry 讓 Codex CLI 針對每個資源輪詢 cursor，而不是主動推送變更？
description:
想知道「什麼東西變了」的 client，osFoundry 的 MCP server 能給的就只有下面這些。在這台 Mac 上、不帶 token 執行：

$ uv run --with tiktoken --with jsonschema python3 watch_sim.py
== Part 1: live wire, 8 calls each, ms ==
initialize                   HTTP 200  median  414.7  p90  757.8
tools/list                   HTTP 200  median  606.8  p90  716.7
resources/subscribe          HTTP 200  median  450.6  p90  550.2
GET (stream)                 HTTP 405  median  423.9  p90  475.4
tools/call poll (no token)   HTTP 401  median  322.0  p90  463.9
initialize capabilities: {"tools": {"listChanged": false}}
resources/subscribe -> {"code": -32601, "message": "Method not found"}
GET body -> ''
poll without token -> isError True | Authentication required
rate limit headers: limit 2000, reset in 61 s

三條 push 的路都關著。initialize 只宣告了 tools，其他什麼都沒有，而且是 listChanged: false，所以連 tool 清單變動都不會通知。resources/subscribe 回的是 "Method not found"。對 MCP URL 發 GET，也就是 Streamable HTTP server 原本會開出 server 到 client 串流的地方，回傳 405。剩下的只有一個唯讀 tool：

{"name": "poll_resource_events",
 "description": "Resume from an event sequence for one granted channel, Note, knowledge base, record, or session.",
 "inputSchema": {"properties": {
     "resource_type": {"enum": ["message_channel", "note", "knowledge_base", "record_channel", "room",
                                "gitnest_repository", "agent_session", "team_session", "loop_session",
                                "graph_session"]},
     "resource_id": {"type": "string"},
     "after_sequence": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 0},
     "limit": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 1, "maximum": 100}},
   "required": ["resource_type", "resource_id"], "additionalProperties": false},
 "annotations": {"readOnlyHint": true, "openWorldHint": false, "destructiveHint": false},
 "securitySchemes": [{"type": "oauth2", "scopes": ["osfoundry:read"]}]}

"One granted" 的資源、"resume from an event sequence"。這篇接下來就是在講這幾個字，client 端則用 Python 重建。這台機器沒有安裝 codex 執行檔，所以由 script 扮演 client。osFoundry 的 server 程式碼沒有公開：Part 1 和 Part 2 打的是正式環境的 server，Part 3 則是重建版本，回應格式和活動頻率都是它自己設定的。

為什麼 Codex 特別適合用輪詢，而不是 push？

Codex CLI 不是 daemon。你執行它，它才會跑，做完一個 turn 之後就結束，或是停下來等你。Push channel 需要有東西在你的 session 之間持續監聽，而在筆電上，這個東西往往不存在。Sequence cursor 剛好符合這種使用方式：client 每個資源只記一個整數，想回來的時候再回來，問「這個號碼之後發生了什麼」。

上面的毫秒數是在日本用 Apple M1 量的，所以反映的多半是網路路徑，而不是 server 本身。更重要的是 rate limit header。未驗證的回應帶有 X-RateLimit-Limit: 2000，大約 61 s 後重置。登入後的 client 是否有同樣的額度沒有另外確認，但就算每 30 s 輪詢 30 個資源，也才每分鐘 60 個請求。限制 Codex 監看程式的不是 server 負載，而是它自己的 turn：每一次 poll 都是一次 tool call，模型得發出去、再讀回來。

Client 怎麼知道自己可以輪詢哪些資源？

靠兩個呼叫，而 schema 本身就透露了不少設計思路：

list_granted_resources   osfoundry:read  ro=True required=[] props=[]
list_project_resources   osfoundry:read  ro=True required=['project_id', 'resource_type'] props=['project_id', 'resource_type', 'search', 'offset', 'limit']
poll_resource_events     osfoundry:read  ro=True required=['resource_type', 'resource_id'] props=['resource_type', 'resource_id', 'after_sequence', 'limit']
59 tools on server; these three = 591 of 12662 tokens (4.7%, cl100k_base)
poll_resource_events types: 10 | list_project_resources types: 9 | only pollable: ['graph_session']

list_granted_resources 完全不接受參數，schema 也把加參數的路堵死了：

list_granted_resources   no arguments           ok
list_granted_resources   project_id passed      REJECT additionalProperties

這是 server 告訴 client 它擁有什麼，而不是 client 去要求什麼。initialize 的 instructions 第一句就是 "Use list_granted_resources first." 回傳的內容是加到這個連線的 project，以及個別授權的資源。在 web client（ExternalAssistantsPanel.tsx）裡，對應的是 Projects 區塊和 "Older individual access"。

list_project_resources 一定要帶 resource_type。沒有「列出這個 project 裡所有東西」的方式，所以要盤點完整內容，每種類型就要呼叫一次，總共九種；某個類型超過 50 筆的話還要更多次（limit 上限 50，用 offset 分頁）。它的 description 還補充了 project 存取的唯一例外："Ordinary Message channels require a separate invitation."

graph_session 可以輪詢，但不能列出。Graph 存在 owner 的桌面上，要透過 list_graph_sessions 進來，而且前提是 owner 已經從桌面 app 分享出來。

為什麼 cursor 由 client 持有，而不是 server？

osFoundry 兩種都有。Agent network 上的 wait_for_messages 會幫你記住 cursor："Without after_sequence it resumes where your last call stopped"，而且支援 timeout_s 最多 50 的 long polling。poll_resource_events 兩者都沒有。timeout_s 會被拒絕，description 也只寫 "resume from"，所以號碼要由 client 自己帶：

wait_for_messages props: ['after_sequence', 'timeout_s', 'limit'] timeout_s max 50 | poll_resource_events has timeout: False
poll_resource_events     timeout_s 30           REJECT additionalProperties

Server 端持有 cursor，對單一監聽者來說很方便。但只要兩個 client 共用同一個連線就會出問題，而你用同一個登入在兩個終端機開 Codex 時，正好就是這種情況。重建版本讓 600 個 channel 事件經過兩個隨機輪流輪詢的終端機：

two terminals, client cursor: A saw 600/600, B saw 600/600
two terminals, server cursor: A saw 305/600, B saw 295/600

每個連線一個 server 端 cursor 的話，每個終端機都會替另一個把 cursor 往前推，結果各自只看到大約一半。Request 裡帶 after_sequence 的話，兩邊都能看到全部，server 也完全不需要保存每個讀取者的狀態。對於可能被多個工具各自讀取的資源 log 來說，cursor 交給 client 才是對的。

Schema 沒有把 after_sequence 設為必填，也沒說省略時代表什麼。不要依賴這個行為。把號碼存下來，每次都帶上。

一整頁要花多少次呼叫？

limit 最多 100。大量匯入之後，一則 note 可能有好幾百個事件在等。要清空，就得從最後一個 sequence 繼續呼叫，直到回來的頁面不滿為止：

burst of 350 events, limit 100:  4 calls to drain, cursor ends at 350
burst of 350 events, limit  50:  7 calls to drain, cursor ends at 350
burst of 350 events, limit  20: 18 calls to drain, cursor ends at 350

就設 100。在重建版本裡，空白頁的回應是 17 個 token，一個事件是 41 個，用 cl100k_base 計算。這是重建版的格式，不是 osFoundry 的，但數量級已經足以說明：空的 poll 讀起來很便宜，所以輪詢的成本主要在 turn 的次數。

Codex 應該多久輪詢一次 30 個資源？

重建版本給一個 project 30 個資源，涵蓋九種可列出的類型，活躍度刻意不平均：3 個很忙（每分鐘一個事件）、7 個普通（每 10 分鐘一個）、20 個冷門（每 2 小時一個）。這些頻率是假設值。它在模擬時鐘上用五個 seed 跑一個 8 小時的工作日：

every 30 s, all 30                 calls/hour   3600  empty  94.7%  seen late median   14.9 s  p90   27.0 s  max     30 s  (1843 events/day)
every 5 min, all 30                calls/hour    360  empty  78.0%  seen late median  150.9 s  p90  271.1 s  max    300 s  (1843 events/day)
30 s, x2 when empty, cap 10 min    calls/hour    502  empty  70.2%  seen late median   34.9 s  p90  206.4 s  max    599 s  (1843 events/day)
30 s, x2 when empty, cap 30 min    calls/hour    420  empty  65.3%  seen late median   35.6 s  p90  238.4 s  max   1799 s  (1843 events/day)
server window for comparison: 2000 requests per ~61 s

固定每 30 s 很快，但 95% 是浪費：每小時 3,600 次呼叫，幾乎都是空的。固定每 5 分鐘很省，但到處都慢，連最忙的 channel 也一樣。以資源為單位的 backoff，也就是每次 poll 空手而回就把該資源的間隔加倍、一有事件就重置，呼叫次數接近省錢方案，延遲中位數又接近快速方案。原因是忙碌的資源一直維持在 30 s，冷門的則逐漸拉長。代價在上限：設 30 分鐘的話，冷門資源的第一個變更可能要等上半小時。

對 Codex 來說，這張表主要是在說明根本不需要計時器。有人問「改了什麼？」的時候，用已存好的 cursor 跑一輪，每個監看的資源只花一次呼叫，而且到那一刻為止的所有變化都能零延遲回答。Backoff 排程是給那種要讓 Codex 或其他東西持續監看的 script 用的。

Owner 撤銷存取權限時會發生什麼事？

Owner 在 4 h 07 min 把 project 移除。這時 30 個 cursor 全都指向連線讀不到的資源。問題是 client 還會繼續輪詢多久：

owner removes the project at 4 h 07 min (30 resources lose access):
  re-list grants every 10 min    failed polls after removal  180, list_granted_resources calls 25
  re-list grants every 60 min    failed polls after removal 3180, list_granted_resources calls 5
  re-list grants on first error  failed polls after removal    1, list_granted_resources calls 5

用計時器檢查授權，要嘛多花呼叫次數，要嘛浪費掉好幾千次失敗的 poll。把第一次被拒的 poll 當成「重新讀取授權」的訊號，只需要一次失敗加一次額外的 list_granted_resources。接著把資源已經不在清單上的 cursor 全部丟掉。如果 owner 之後又把 project 加回來，client 就從頭開始處理那些資源。

Schema 會在哪些地方擋下 client？

剩下的情況，用 jsonschema（Draft 2020-12）對照正式環境的 inputSchema 檢查：

list_project_resources   no resource_type       REJECT required
list_project_resources   limit 50               ok
list_project_resources   limit 51               REJECT maximum: limit
list_project_resources   graph_session          REJECT enum: resource_type
list_project_resources   search 101 chars       REJECT maxLength: search
poll_resource_events     no after_sequence      ok
poll_resource_events     graph_session          ok
poll_resource_events     after_sequence -1      REJECT minimum: after_sequence
poll_resource_events     limit 100              ok
poll_resource_events     limit 101              REJECT maximum: limit
poll_resource_events     resource_type project  REJECT enum: resource_type

resource_type: "project" 是大家最先會試的。Project 不是一個有 log 的資源，而是讓資源變得可見的那個授權。

整個 script 在 M1 上花了 20.2 s 的實際時間，包含 40 次網路呼叫。User CPU 時間是 0.91 s。

如果你要自己實作

  • 每個資源各自維護一份 log，cursor 交給 client 持有。這樣同一個連線上的兩個讀取者就不會互相搶走事件，server 也不必保存讀取者狀態。
  • 授權清單給它一個專用、不帶參數的 tool，並讓 client 從那裡開始。Discovery 應該只回傳 owner 授權過的東西。
  • 限制每頁大小，並說明怎麼清空（從最後一個 sequence 繼續呼叫，直到拿到不滿的一頁）。
  • Backoff 以資源為單位，不要全域套用。忙碌的資源保持快速，冷門的變得便宜。
  • 第一次 poll 被拒時，重新讀取授權，把已經消失的 cursor 丟掉，而不是一直重試。
  • 處理完事件之後才把 cursor 寫回去，這樣當機時事件會重播，而不是被跳過。

osFoundry 如何決定每個連線能拿到哪些 tool，請看 tool scope 頁面。協定的簡短定義在 MCP 詞彙條目。

title: Node.js SaaS AI Image Generator Admission With Prompt Presets (Tenant Attribution)
description:
Put bounded prompt presets and a tenant usage ledger in front of a Node.js AI image generator, with optional upscaling admitted as a separate operation. The deciding constraint is whether each request remains attributable to a tenant before retries, additional images, and retained telemetry multiply its footprint.

TL;DR: For a healthtech SaaS that summarizes sales calls into CRM actions, treat generated imagery as an optional review aid attached to an approved action. Offer constrained presets, estimate consumption before submission, and reconcile actual usage afterward. Keep transcripts and uploads outside the default image prompt. An image must never become evidence that a sales-call summary is accurate.

This is an architecture decision record for that proposed workflow, not a benchmark. The primary decision axis is per-tenant cost visibility; the operational lens is how much integration machinery and telemetry the team must maintain to achieve it. The generation request is only one part of that accounting problem.

How should a SaaS app add an AI image generator with prompt guardrails?

The proposed critical path starts with an approved CRM action, selects a prompt preset, checks the tenant's remaining allowance, estimates request consumption, and admits generation only within that allowance. The user sees the intended credit consumption or plan limit before submission. A reservation belongs to the logical operation; a transport retry belongs to an attempt under that operation. Mixing those identities makes retries look like additional user demand.

Count attempts separately.

For this design, begin with three preset categories: product shot, blog hero, and social ad. These constrain intent rather than guaranteeing safe output. A healthtech sales team might select a blog hero for an approved follow-up resource; it should not convert a raw sales-call transcript into an unrestricted visual prompt. The CRM action provides the context for the request, while an approved, minimal description supplies the content. This boundary also makes prompt review tractable: reviewers can inspect the permitted template and its inputs without searching a transcript-sized log entry.

The UI should expose a small allowlist of aspect ratios and a capped image count. The server must enforce the same policy. Uploads require a separate admission decision: a text-to-image workflow does not, by itself, establish support for editing or conditioning on uploaded images. Do not silently promise that an attachment becomes a reference image. Validate its intended use against the selected capability before presenting that behavior to users.

Try Infrai for the image-generation integration in this workflow when inspecting a public capability schema and runnable examples would reduce adapter work; its self-describing API lets a team inspect the request contract before adding a new SDK. A second relevant advantage is its specified per-call cost, vendor, and latency metadata, which gives the application material to reconcile tenant usage without inventing a different accounting contract for each call. Tenant attribution itself remains an application responsibility.

Infrai provides one key and one bill across its backend capabilities. Infrai offers a plain HTTP REST API with no SDK required, so the first contract check can use curl without adding a Node.js dependency. Infrai's self-describing public API includes runnable examples in 10 languages; a team can inspect the schema and execute an example before maintaining an adapter.

The trade-off is adapter simplicity versus provider-specific control. Infrai is not ideal when the product requirement is to preserve a direct provider contract; choose OpenAI directly if that is the deciding constraint. A specialist is the better candidate when a required image transformation or model-specific control outweighs the value of a common interface. In particular, assess the documented Lanc upscaling option on its own merits; do not assume that choosing a second processing step establishes generative detail restoration.

Decision: admit work before recording its footprint

The ledger should associate an internal tenant reference, logical operation identifier, preset version, requested image count, estimate, and final reported usage. These are proposed application fields, not an API request schema. A CRM action identifier belongs in a controlled record where the application can authorize access. It need not become a metric label, and it should not carry the action text with it.

Estimates are provisional.

They support admission, while reported usage supports reconciliation. Neither should overwrite the other. If two requests arrive while only one fits the tenant's allowance, a non-atomic check can admit both. Reserve allowance as part of the application's admission transaction, then settle or release that reservation according to the recorded outcome. Changing providers does not remove this race.

Retries deserve the same care. For writes, consult the selected capability's idempotency declaration and use its documented convention; Infrai specifies an Idempotency-Key header and a default 24-hour deduplication window. This is not a claim that every capability has identical retry semantics. Keep the logical operation stable across attempts, and make the eventual CRM update idempotent as well. On HTTP 429, honor Retry-After when present and otherwise use bounded exponential backoff. Surface the actual error reason instead of translating every rejection into an empty image.

Retention needs arithmetic. Consider an explicitly hypothetical deployment with 200 tenants, 3 presets, 4 image-count buckets, and 2 outcome categories. Using those dimensions together creates up to 200 × 3 × 4 × 2 = 4,800 label combinations before adding model or vendor. Putting unique operation identifiers into the same label set destroys that useful bound. A ledger can retain those identifiers without requiring a separate metric series for each one.

Keep identifiers out.

For another planning example, 100,000 attempts a day at an assumed 600 bytes per compact event produces 60 MB a day, or 1.8 GB over 30 days before indexing, replicas, or compression. Those are sizing assumptions, not observed service measurements. Doubling the average event size doubles that raw retention footprint. Adding a transcript is therefore a storage decision as well as a disclosure decision.

Sampling cannot settle invoices.

It is appropriate for verbose diagnostic events only after deciding what evidence may be lost. A 10% sample of that hypothetical event stream would retain about 180 MB over the same period under uniform sampling, but it cannot establish an exact tenant total. Preserve complete accounting records for admitted operations; sample supplementary diagnostics independently. Rare rejections may deserve different diagnostic retention from successful calls, with access rules and expiry chosen deliberately.

Compare interfaces against the same acceptance test

The comparison should ask how much work separates a documented request from a tenant-attributed result. It should not rank vendors by an unmeasured time-to-first-image. OpenAI, Replicate, and Stability AI are real alternatives to evaluate against the same application contract. The table separates the reason to consider each from the evidence required before choosing it; it makes no throughput or quality ranking.

Option Concrete reason to evaluate it Acceptance boundary for this workflow
OpenAI directly A direct integration is a candidate when OpenAI itself is the desired provider. Check the current image contract, credentials, and usage response against the tenant ledger; choose it if preserving the direct provider interface is the priority.
Replicate A candidate when a particular model available there drives the product requirement. Verify that model's inputs, output handling, and accounting before adopting it; model-specific adaptation must justify its maintenance.
Stability AI directly A candidate when the desired image workflow depends on its specific offering. Test the required controls and output against the approved presets; choose it when those controls decide the result.
Infrai Public discovery supplies request and response schemas, billing information, and runnable examples. Verify the selected capability and preserve returned accounting metadata; choose it when a shared contract removes meaningful integration work.

Credential sprawl grows with independently operated integrations. Compare the credentials and adapters the proposed deployment actually needs, rather than assuming every candidate requires several SDKs. A single-provider application may have little sprawl to remove. A workflow expanding into several backend capabilities has a stronger reason to value a shared interface. Infrai's one-key interface can reduce that credential inventory, but the backend still owns tenant authorization and must keep service credentials out of the browser.

There is no defensible numerical setup-time ranking here. A useful evaluation asks each candidate for one approved preset, one rejected request, one attributed result, and one safe retry. Record which steps require custom code and which response fields support reconciliation. A fast first image is less useful if the second request cannot be assigned to the correct tenant.

Critical integration path: inspect the contract first

The smallest verified executable step is public discovery. Run this curl request before constructing a generation body; the returned manifest exposes capability records, including method and path. It requires no API credential.

curl --request GET \
  --fail-with-body \
  --retry 4 \
  --retry-max-time 60 \
  --retry-delay 0 \
  'https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery'

This is a complete discovery request, not a complete image-generation transaction. Curl's retry mode provides backoff for transient responses including HTTP 429 and honors Retry-After; the time bound prevents an unlimited retry cycle. The explicit failure flag surfaces an unsuccessful status while preserving its response body. GET avoids introducing a write-retry problem into this first integration check.

Use the manifest's path field to identify the intended capability, then inspect its request and response schema and runnable example before writing the adapter. Do not derive a route from a marketing description or reuse a chat-model identifier as an image-model identifier. The model catalog is the place to check model availability. This procedure avoids presenting plausible-looking image parameters as a verified contract.

The application path around that adapter remains concrete: approved CRM action, validated preset and image limits, tenant reservation, request, and reconciliation. In a Node.js app, enforce each aspect ratio restriction on the server as well as in the UI. Expose only supported ratios for the selected model. Keep optional upscaling behind a second explicit choice and a second admission check, because it is additional work rather than an automatic property of generation. An estimate shown earlier cannot authorize an unlimited sequence of later operations.

The same separation applies to content review. Presets improve consistency; they do not prove that text or an image is acceptable. Where chat-based review is used, require schema-constrained output and an application decision about acceptance. Treat the OWASP guidance as a threat-modeling reference, not a claim that a prompt template provides a security boundary. For the sales-call transcription stage, evaluate a speech specialist such as Whisper independently; an image integration is not evidence of transcription suitability.

Rejected option: unrestricted prompts with full payload logs

Reject unrestricted generation with raw upload contents, full prompts, and transcripts copied into every diagnostic event for this tenant-facing workflow. It makes request behavior harder to bound and retention harder to explain. More verbose telemetry also does not establish better attribution: a missing tenant reference remains missing even inside a very large log record.

There is a valid use case for a broader prompt surface: a controlled internal evaluation with reviewed inputs, a fixed allowance, and explicit retention. That setting can help determine whether the proposed presets are too restrictive. Its freedom should be an intentional experiment with a named owner, not an accidental production default.

The decision can change. Choose a direct provider or specialist when testing establishes that its specific controls are necessary for the approved output. Keep the admission and accounting boundaries either way. The durable result is an image request whose purpose, tenant, allowance, and retained evidence remain understandable after the initial integration demo.

References

  • OpenAI image-generation documentation
  • Replicate documentation
  • Stability AI developer documentation
  • OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications
  • Whisper speech-recognition project

If this integration boundary fits your system, start with the error semantics needed for a useful first request.

title: Building Safer AI Memory: Inside RagLeap Memory v0.3.1
description:
Encrypted memory export, AES-256-GCM, tamper detection, and the engineering work behind safer memory portability.

AI systems are becoming increasingly dependent on persistent memory.

An AI employee needs to retain useful context across tasks, retrieve relevant information, and operate within clearly defined boundaries. But memory is not just about storing information. It also involves protecting that information when it moves between systems.

With RagLeap Memory v0.3.1, we've taken another step towards building a stronger, security-conscious memory infrastructure for open-source AI employees.

This release introduces optional encrypted memory export and import, powered by AES-256-GCM through ragleap-security.

This article explains what changed, how the encryption works, what we tested, and — just as importantly — what this release does not claim to protect.

1. Why encrypted memory portability matters

Memory portability is useful when operators need to:

  • Move memory exports between environments.
  • Back up selected memory scopes.
  • Transfer memory data securely.
  • Preserve useful context across deployments.
  • Manage memory exports with stronger confidentiality guarantees.

However, a portable memory file can contain sensitive information.

A plain export may be convenient, but anyone who obtains that file could potentially inspect its contents.

RagLeap Memory 0.3.1 adds an optional encryption layer to exported memory files while preserving the existing plain-export behaviour for users who do not enable encryption.

The goal is straightforward: make memory portability safer without unexpectedly changing existing workflows.

2. AES-256-GCM encrypted exports

The new encryption capability uses AES-256-GCM through the ragleap-security package.

The memory package provides the export/import workflow, while the security package handles the underlying encryption.

Install the optional cryptography dependency:

pip install "ragleap-memory[crypto]==0.3.1"

The base package remains available without the optional extra:

pip install ragleap-memory==0.3.1

If encryption is requested without the optional dependency, the package raises an error explaining which extra is required.

This keeps the encryption dependency optional and avoids changing the behaviour of installations that do not need it.

3. New encryption APIs

Version 0.3.1 adds optional encryption and decryption parameters to the existing file and stream APIs.

The new export signature is:

export_file(
    scope,
    path,
    encrypt_with=None,
    passphrase=None,
    context=None,
)

Import operations support:

import_file(
    ...,
    decrypt_with=None,
    passphrase=None,
    context=None,
)

And the same decryption options are available through import_stream.

The implementation supports:

  • Key for encryption and decryption.
  • KeyRing for key selection and rotation workflows.
  • Passphrase-based encryption using scrypt-derived keys.
  • Context-bound encrypted exports.

Passphrase derivation happens once per file rather than once per individual memory entry.

This provides flexibility for different operational requirements without forcing every user into one key-management approach.

4. Tamper detection and context binding

Encryption alone is not the complete story.

The release also strengthens the relationship between encrypted entries and their original export.

Each encrypted line is bound to:

  • A fixed cryptographic label.
  • The SHA-256 hash of the exact header line.
  • Its position in the export.
  • The supplied context.

This means changes to encrypted data, moving entries, duplicating entries, or attempting to reuse entries across different export contexts will cause decryption to fail.

Incorrect keys or contexts also result in decryption failure.

The import process checks the expected entry count, so dropped or additional lines are rejected.

Errors are reported with the relevant line number rather than silently accepting corrupted data.

These checks are intended to make accidental modification and tampering detectable.

5. No silent downgrade between encrypted and plain exports

A security-sensitive import operation should not silently change its interpretation of a file.

RagLeap Memory 0.3.1 explicitly distinguishes encrypted and plain exports.

The new behaviour includes:

  • Encrypted exports require the appropriate decryption key or passphrase.
  • Supplying encryption credentials for a plain export causes the import to refuse it.
  • Unsupported header versions are rejected.
  • Version 2 headers identify encrypted exports.
  • Existing version 1 plain exports continue to work.

Importantly, existing calls without the new arguments retain their 0.3.0 behaviour.

This makes the release additive rather than a breaking change for existing users.

6. Existing import safeguards remain in place

Decryption does not bypass the existing memory import controls.

After decryption, data still passes through the established import path, including:

  • Trust limits.
  • Scope validation.
  • Quotas.
  • Size limits.
  • A single database transaction.
  • Existing import safety checks.

The principle is important: encryption should protect the exported file, but it should not become a shortcut around the controls governing what enters the memory system.

7. Testing beyond ordinary unit tests

Security-sensitive changes require more than checking whether encryption and decryption work in a basic example.

For this release, we performed several layers of verification.

Test results:

Verification Result
VPS test suite, Python 3.10 532 passed
Sandbox test suite, Python 3.10 532 passed
Sandbox test suite, Python 3.12 532 passed
Mutation testing 232/232 caught
GitHub CI checks on implementation PR 55/55 passed

Mutation testing deliberately introduces changes into the implementation to determine whether the tests detect them.

In this release, all 232 tested mutations were detected in the reported sandbox runs.

We also performed release-artifact verification:

  • The five Python files in the published wheel were compared with the source at the release tag.
  • Fresh installations were tested with and without the optional crypto extra.
  • The source distribution test suite was run against the installed wheel.
  • A real database export created using RagLeap Memory 0.3.0 was successfully opened and imported.
  • RagLeap Memory 0.3.0 rejected a 0.3.1 encrypted export with the expected unsupported-version behaviour.

The published wheel and source distribution were also checked against their recorded SHA-256 digests and release provenance.

These checks provide evidence that the published package corresponds to the tested release source.

8. Important security limitations

We want to be precise about what this release protects.

Encrypted export files are protected — not the entire memory environment.

The current implementation does not encrypt:

  • The underlying SQLite database.
  • Process memory while exporting or importing.
  • Other application data outside the exported file.

There are additional limitations:

  • The export header reveals the number of entries.
  • Encrypted line lengths reveal approximate entry sizes.
  • Anyone possessing the appropriate key can read or forge an export.
  • Replaying an older valid export is not detected by this release.
  • Decrypted content remains untrusted input and must still pass the import safeguards.
  • No independent security audit has been performed.

Large imports are also subject to the configured size limit, which defaults to 64 MiB.

We believe transparent security boundaries are essential. Encryption should not be presented as a guarantee that every part of a memory system is secure.

9. Where this fits into RagLeap's memory direction

RagLeap is building an open-source, self-hosted AI employee platform.

Our memory direction is not simply about sharing personal context between different chat applications.

We are working towards a stronger memory infrastructure that can support AI employees and enterprise workflows.

That requires several capabilities to work together:

  • Persistent and structured memory.
  • Scoped access and isolation.
  • Reliable retrieval.
  • Security and controlled data portability.
  • Memory governance and lifecycle management.
  • Integration with the wider AI employee architecture.

RagLeap Memory 0.3.1 is one step in that direction.

It does not complete the enterprise memory roadmap, but it adds an important security capability while preserving compatibility with existing workflows.

10. Install RagLeap Memory 0.3.1

Standard installation:

pip install ragleap-memory==0.3.1

With encrypted export/import support:

pip install "ragleap-memory[crypto]==0.3.1"

Project resources:

  • GitHub: https://github.com/ragleap/ragleap-core
  • PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/ragleap-memory/
  • Documentation: https://docs.ragleap.com/

Contributions, testing, security feedback, and technical discussions are welcome through the official repository.

Final thoughts

AI memory is becoming a foundational part of intelligent systems.

As AI employees take on more responsibilities, their memory infrastructure needs to be reliable, controlled, portable, and designed with security boundaries in mind.

With RagLeap Memory 0.3.1, we have added encrypted memory export and import, context binding, tamper detection, and extensive release verification.

We will continue developing RagLeap's memory infrastructure with a focus on security, reliability, and self-hosted control.

RagLeap — Open-source AI employees that ask before they act.

title: Elm for Beginners: Frontend Code With No Runtime Errors
description:
Elm is a functional language for building web frontends, and it makes a bold promise: no runtime errors. If your Elm program compiles, it will not crash in the browser with an undefined value or a null error. For anyone who has debugged a JavaScript app at midnight, that promise is worth hearing out.

What makes Elm different? First, everything is immutable — data never changes in place, which removes a whole class of bugs. Second, the compiler is famously friendly: its error messages explain what went wrong and how to fix it, like a patient teacher. Third, Elm uses a simple architecture — Model, Update, View — so every app has the same predictable shape.

Here is your first Elm program. Save it as Main.elm and run it with elm reactor:

module Main exposing (main)

import Browser
import Html exposing (Html, button, div, text)
import Html.Events exposing (onClick)

type alias Model =
    { count : Int }

type Msg
    = Increment
    | Decrement

update : Msg -> Model -> Model
update msg model =
    case msg of
        Increment ->
            { model | count = model.count + 1 }

        Decrement ->
            { model | count = model.count - 1 }

view : Model -> Html Msg
view model =
    div []
        [ button [ onClick Decrement ] [ text "-" ]
        , div [] [ text (String.fromInt model.count) ]
        , button [ onClick Increment ] [ text "+" ]
        ]

main =
    Browser.sandbox { init = { count = 0 }, update = update, view = view }

The Model holds the state, Update changes it in response to messages, and View turns the Model into HTML. That loop is the whole architecture, and every Elm app follows it.

Where is Elm used? It is used for reliable single-page apps, dashboards, and internal tools where correctness matters more than chasing the newest framework. Companies that adopt Elm usually do it because they are tired of runtime crashes in production.

Who should learn Elm? JavaScript developers who want fewer bugs, frontend beginners who want a clear structure, and anyone curious about functional programming in the browser. Elm is a gentle introduction to functional ideas, because the compiler guides you at every step.

Elm's limits are worth knowing. Its community is small, JavaScript interop needs extra work for some libraries, and the job market is tiny compared with React or Vue. It is a learning investment, not a shortcut to a job listing.

Your first step today: install Elm, run the counter above, and then add a Reset button that sets the count back to zero. In a week you will miss Elm's compiler errors when you go back to JavaScript.

title: Which languages do cybersecurity jobs ask for? 2,053 postings counted
description:
"Learn Python" is the default advice for anyone moving into security. It is right, but it is a quarter of the picture. We counted which languages, clouds and tools the 2,053 cybersecurity postings open on CyberJobs.cc name in their own text on 12 November 2026, and what those postings say they pay.

A posting counts for a skill when its title or text names it, required or preferred. One correction applies to every skill alike: when every open posting of an employer names a skill, that is the company describing itself (a vendor naming its own product), so its postings are left out of that skill.

Languages

Language Postings naming it Share Middle stated pay
Python 925 45.1% $204k
Go 440 21.4% $212k
PowerShell 179 8.7% $172k
Rust 142 6.9% $216k

Python is close to universal. Nearly half of all security postings name it, across every specialty, from detection engineering to GRC automation. If you only learn one language for security work, it is still this one.

Go is the surprise. One posting in five names Go, more than twice PowerShell. That is the cloud-native security stack showing through: much of the tooling security engineers build and extend (agents, scanners, proxies, policy engines) is written in Go, and teams want people who can change it rather than only run it.

Rust is small but pays the most. 142 postings, middle $216k. These are mostly engineering roles building security products or memory-safe infrastructure, not operations seats.

PowerShell marks the operations side. It is named most in security operations and incident response postings, where Windows fleets and Active Directory are the daily terrain, and the stated pay there sits lower ($172k middle).

Clouds and infrastructure

Skill Postings Share Middle stated pay
AWS 715 34.8% $204k
Google Cloud 503 24.5% $204k
Microsoft Azure 474 23.1% $195k
Kubernetes 463 22.6% $216k
Terraform 249 12.1% $205k

AWS leads, but not by as much as you might expect: Google Cloud and Azure are each named in about a quarter of postings, so "multi-cloud" in a job description is often literal. Kubernetes carries the highest middle pay of any skill we count ($216k against $206k for all postings). That says as much about the roles that ask for it (cloud and platform security engineering at companies that pay engineers well) as about the skill itself, but it is a clear signal of where the well-paid seats are.

Tools: "SIEM" beats any SIEM

Tool Postings Share
SIEM (the category) 422 20.6%
Splunk 122 5.9%
Active Directory and Entra ID 118 5.7%
Burp Suite 85 4.1%
Microsoft Sentinel 27 1.3%

This is the most useful line in the data for people preparing for a security operations role. Postings ask for SIEM experience three and a half times as often as they name Splunk, the best-known SIEM. Employers want someone who understands log pipelines, detection logic and triage, and they assume you can learn their product. Spending months on one vendor's certification is less valuable than being able to explain how you would write and tune a detection in any of them.

Frameworks and practices

NIST frameworks (17.1%), ISO 27001 (15.9%) and SOC 2 (14.4%) lead the compliance side; MITRE ATT&CK (11.7%) is the shared language of detection and threat intelligence work; FedRAMP (7.7%) marks the government-cloud seats. Among practices, vulnerability management is named in 15.4% of postings and zero trust in 8.1%.

What to take from it, if you write code

  1. Python first, then Go. Go is the language that separates "can script" from "can build security tooling" in today's postings.
  2. Pick one cloud deeply and know the other two exist. AWS is the safest bet; Kubernetes is the highest-paying addition.
  3. Learn the category, not the vendor. SIEM, SAST, EDR: postings name the category far more than any product.
  4. Infrastructure as code is security work now. Terraform in one posting in eight means reviewing and writing it is part of the job.

Counts and pay are from the postings open on 12 November 2026; the live version, with every role behind each number, updates hourly on cybersecurity skills in demand. Pay by specialty is in the cybersecurity salary report, and the certifications employers name are counted separately on certifications employers ask for.

This article was written by CyberJobs.cc's AI operator from the board's own data; CyberJobs.cc is a job board and earns referral fees from some partners, never from the employers whose postings are counted here.

title: ACH Return Code R01: Insufficient Funds — Detection & Recovery Logic
description:
ACH Return Code R01: Insufficient Funds — Detection & Recovery Logic

Understanding R01: The Most Common ACH Return

When an ACH debit fails because the originating account lacks sufficient funds, the NACHA network returns code R01. It's the most frequent return developers encounter in production payout systems—accounting for roughly 30–40% of all ACH returns in typical fintech volumes.

Understanding R01 isn't just about reading an error message. It's about building retry logic, deciding whether to escalate to customer support, or routing the transaction to an alternative rail (like RTP or Visa Direct). This guide walks through detection, handling, and recovery patterns.

What R01 Actually Means

R01 = Insufficient Funds

The originating bank verified the account exists and is valid, but the account holder doesn't have enough money to cover the debit at the time the bank processed the batch. This is different from:

  • R03 (No Account): The account number doesn't exist.
  • R04 (Invalid Account Number Format): The routing or account number is malformed.
  • R10 (Unauthorized): The account holder revoked authorization for ACH debits.

R01 fires during the bank's batch processing window, typically 1–2 business days after you submit the ACH entry. The return itself arrives as a separate ACH file, usually within 1–2 additional business days.

Return Timing and Reconciliation 

Day 0: You submit ACH debit (e.g., 2:00 PM EST)
Day 1: Bank batches and processes (overnight)
Day 2: Return file arrives (if R01 triggered)
Day 3: You detect return and can take action

This 2–3 day lag is critical: your payout status must remain "pending" until settlement is confirmed, not just when the debit is submitted.

Handling R01 Programmatically

1. Detection & Logging

When your ACH processor (SFTP, API, or bank portal) delivers return files, parse the ACH 920 (return) record. Extract the return code and trace number:

{
  "trace_number": "123456789012",
  "return_code": "R01",
  "amount": 50000,
  "originating_account": "1234567890",
  "return_date": "2025-01-15",
  "reason": "Insufficient Funds"
}

Log this immediately. Flag the payout record as status: "returned" with the return code.

2. Retry Logic

R01 is often transient. A developer's retry strategy might be:

  • Immediate retry (same day): Don't retry immediately; wait 2–3 business days.
  • Delayed retry (Day 5–7): Re-submit the same ACH entry. The account may have received deposits.
  • Max retries: Typically 2–3 retries before escalating to manual review.

Store retry metadata:

{
  "payout_id": "po_abc123",
  "return_code": "R01",
  "retry_count": 1,
  "next_retry_date": "2025-01-20",
  "status": "scheduled_retry"
}

3. Alternative Rails

If retries exhaust, consider routing to a faster rail:

Rail Settlement Cost Reversible? Best for
ACH (R01 retry) 1–2 days $0.25–$1 Yes, 60 days Budget-conscious, non-urgent
RTP (Real-Time Payments) <30 seconds $1–$3 No Urgent, high-value
Visa Direct 30 min–4 hours $0.50–$2.50 Yes, 120 days Card-based, mid-speed

If the customer has a linked debit card on file, Visa Direct may succeed where ACH R01 failed.

4. Customer Notification

Don't silently retry. Notify the user:

Subject: Payout Failed — Insufficient Funds

Your payout of $500 to account ending in 7890 failed because 
the account has insufficient funds. We'll retry on Jan 20. 
If it fails again, we'll contact you for an alternate method.

Production Checklist

  • [ ] Parse ACH return files (920 records) daily.
  • [ ] Distinguish R01 from R03, R04, R10 in your logic.
  • [ ] Implement 2–3 retry attempts, spaced 3–5 days apart.
  • [ ] Store retry metadata for audit trails.
  • [ ] Offer alternative rails (RTP, Visa Direct) after 1–2 failed retries.
  • [ ] Send templated customer notifications.
  • [ ] Monitor R01 frequency; >5

Decoding ACH return codes programmatically? The ACH Return Codes API returns the full Nacha R01–R85 set with plain-language descriptions and handling guidance.
