title: Why Kubernetes GPU Scheduling Keeps Breaking Your Golden Path
description:
A platform team gets a request to enable GPU support. They provision a node pool, wire up a self-service request flow, and add it to the internal developer portal (IDP). The problem looks solved as the developers got what they needed, and platform team successfully closed the ticket.

Then an ML engineer submits a four-node training job. Three pods come up while the fourth sits pending. Nobody gets paged, and nothing crashes. The node just sits there, quietly burning time, capacity, and the training run's deadline, while the platform team tries to figure out whether this is a quota issue, a scheduling issue, or something they didn't know they needed to design for.

Good abstractions remove complexity, but only after the underlying problem is stable. GPU platform engineering isn't there yet. Scheduling, tenant isolation, and driver coordination are all still moving. If you abstract over something that's still moving, then you're hiding a decision your team hasn't actually made.

Platform Engineering for GPUs

Platform engineering for GPUs is the discipline of building self-service infrastructure, most of it running on Kubernetes today, that lets application teams request and run GPU-backed workloads (training jobs, inference services, batch ML pipelines) without needing to understand the underlying scheduling, driver, and hardware layers themselves. It's the same golden-path model platform teams already use for CPU and memory, applied to a resource that behaves nothing like CPU and memory.

The difference between CPU and GPU platform engineering is:

  • CPU scheduling, isolation, and quota management were solved by the time platform engineering became a discipline.
  • GPU scheduling and isolation are still being actively rebuilt inside Kubernetes itself, which means the golden path is still robust.

Kubernetes GPU Scheduling is Changing

What the old model couldn't see

Since 2017, Kubernetes has scheduled GPUs through the device plugin model, and that model has one job: tell the scheduler nvidia.com/gpu: 1. This was just a number and nothing more.

VRAM capacity, NVLink topology, and MIG profiles don't exist as far as the scheduler is concerned. Platform teams compensated for this with node labels for GPU type, tolerations to keep the wrong workloads off the wrong nodes, and affinity rules to nudge scheduling toward hardware that actually fits. It worked mostly. That compensation is now baked into golden paths as tribal knowledge disguised as YAML.

What's changing right now

Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) or Kubernetes DRA graduated to general availability in Kubernetes 1.34, and it changes what the scheduler is allowed to know. Instead of a bare count, DRA lets the scheduler reason for real device attributes like GPU, topology, MIG profile, etc.

This is not an additive upgrade. The device plugin and Kubernetes DRA are mutually exclusive on the same node because they expose GPU resources through conflicting allocation paths. Kubernetes 1.34 does add a compatibility shim, the DRAExtendedResource feature gate, that lets the scheduler translate old-style extended resource requests into DRA claims automatically. That softens the migration but every golden path built on the device plugin model still faces an architectural decision..

Scheduling isn't finished moving, either. Native gang scheduling, the ability to schedule a multi-pod training job as an all-or-nothing unit instead of pod by pod, is alpha in Kubernetes 1.35 and disabled by default, with beta targeted for 1.37. Until then, production gang scheduling means reaching for Volcano or NVIDIA's KAI Scheduler, a second scheduler your platform team now owns, patches, and upgrades, sitting alongside the one that ships with the cluster.

⚠️ Common mistake: Gang scheduling is not a nice-to-have to add later. Without it, the pending-pod failure mode from the introduction is the expected outcome. You have to fill the gap of as Kubernetes' default scheduler has no concept of "these four pods are one unit."

Nobody could have waited for DRA to stabilize before shipping GPU support to their ML teams. If your GPU platform predates 2026, you built it on a model mid-migration and didn't know it.

Every GPU Platform Has Already Made a Tenant Isolation Decision

Even if your team never sat down and discussed tenant isolation for GPUs, your platform has already made a decision. It's just not written anywhere.

Compare the three Kubernetes GPU sharing strategies and their costs

Three strategies dominate GPU sharing in Kubernetes, and each one trades isolation for flexibility differently:

  • Time-slicing: This approach gives every workload a turn on the full GPU. It's flexible and works on any GPU, but delivers zero memory isolation. VRAM isn't cleared between pods sharing the device, so one tenant's data and another tenant's model weights can end up occupying the same physical memory space at different points in time.

  • Cost: It looks cheap on a dashboard right up until one overallocated pod runs out of memory and takes down every other workload sharing that GPU.

  • MIG (Multi-Instance GPU): It carves a physical GPU into up to seven isolated hardware partitions, the right call for production multi-tenant workloads. It only runs on Ampere, Hopper, and Blackwell-class hardware (A30, A100, H100, H200, and B200), and it's a node-level policy, not a per-request dial: changing a profile means draining every workload on that node first.

  • Cost: GPU MIG is efficient when profile sizes match workload sizes, wasteful when they don't, since profiles are fixed at the node level.

  • Whole GPU exclusive: This model hands one tenant the entire device. Maximum isolation, correct for large training runs, wasteful for a small inference model that needs a fraction of that capacity.

  • Cost: It is easiest to bill and justify to finance, until someone asks why a model that needs 4GB of VRAM is sitting on an 80GB device.

All three are legitimate in the right context. The problem is that the golden path doesn't surface which strategy is used by the platform team.

MIG Reconfiguration cost in practice

NVIDIA's GPU Operator takes roughly 30 to 60 seconds per GPU to drain, reconfigure, and uncordon a node when a MIG profile changes.On a shared inference node with eight GPUs, a single profile change costs 4 to 8 minutes of node-wide drain time, during which every workload scheduled on that node is unavailable.

Most teams don't budget the operational cost when they pick MIG because it "does isolation properly." The isolation is per-GPU, but the reconfiguration cost is per-node.

What isolation alone doesn't cover

Hardware and workload isolation aren't the only layers in play. GPUs typically sit on a shared interconnect fabric (NVLink, PCIe, or similar), and by default that fabric lets GPUs talk to each other across the whole node.

A scheduler that respects MIG or whole-GPU boundaries can still place two tenants' workloads on GPUs that share the same NVLink domain, which reintroduces a data-exposure risk that looks, from the scheduler's perspective, like a correctly isolated placement.

Fabric-level isolation, restricting which GPUs can communicate with which, is a fourth decision layered on top of the sharing strategy, and it's the one platform teams are least likely to know they need to make.

A developer requesting "a GPU" for a multi-tenant inference service, with no visibility into which sharing strategy sits underneath the request, is making a security assumption without knowing they're making it.

  • On CPU workloads, tenant boundaries are close to automatic: cgroups isolate memory, namespaces isolate process visibility, and a developer requesting compute doesn't think about what's sharing the underlying core.
  • On GPUs, tenant boundary requires an explicit architectural decision, and most teams haven't made it consciously.They've made it by default, usually time-slicing, because it's the fastest strategy to work on whatever hardware is already in the cluster. The default is fine for a proof of concept or internal experimentation. But it stops being fine the moment a second business unit, or a second client in a multi-tenant SaaS product, starts sharing that node pool. At that point, "we enabled GPU support" quietly became "we made a data isolation decision for regulated or sensitive workloads," and nobody signed off on that framing because nobody stated it that way to begin with.

Chargeback breaks for the same reason. If the platform can't tell you which sharing strategy a workload landed on, it can't tell you why one team's GPU bill is three times another team's for what looks, on paper, like the same workload.

Driver and Firmware Lifecycle is its Own Isolation Layer

In a shared cluster, a driver upgrade affects every tenant on that node simultaneously, because tenants share the host kernel. If one team needs a newer driver version for a feature and another team's workload was validated against the older version, there's no way to give them different versions on the same node without containerized driver stacks (the NVIDIA GPU Operator for Kubernetes supports this) or per-tenant node isolation. If that decision is skipped, the first driver upgrade can quickly become an incident when a workload that worked yesterday breaks today, leaving the platform team to discover that “upgrade the driver” was never a documented or owned process.

💡 Counterintuitively: The fix here is treating the driver version as part of the workload class taxonomy from the start, the same way sharing strategy is, so a driver mismatch shows up as a scheduling constraint instead of a production outage.

What a Durable GPU Golden Path Actually Looks Like

Platform teams fail whenever they abstract a decision before it's actually stable, GPUs just make the failure mode more expensive and harder to reverse. The fix is to be deliberate about which layers are stable enough to hide.

  • Abstract fully: Container packaging, CI pipelines, observability, access controls. These problems are solved. Hide them completely, because the complexity here is genuinely accidental, not load-bearing.
  • Keep visible, because each cost strategy is an active architectural decision.
  • Workload class: Training, inference, or development. Each carries different scheduling, isolation, and storage requirements. Collapsing them into one "GPU workload" category throws away information the scheduler and the platform both need.
  • Sharing strategy: An explicit, documented decision per workload class.
  • Driver and firmware lifecycle: A coordination policy the platform team owns on purpose.

Build the Request Flow Around Workload Class

The self-service question has to change. Instead of "request a GPU," the intake flow should ask what kind of GPU workload this is: training or inference, multi-tenant or dedicated, latency-sensitive or batch.

Each answer routes to a different sharing strategy and a different set of guardrails, and the developer making the request understands what they're getting.

  • A training job answers "training, dedicated, batch" and routes to whole-GPU exclusive automatically.
  • A latency-sensitive inference endpoint serving a small model answers "inference, multi-tenant, latency-sensitive" and routes to MIG.

The developer never sees the word "MIG" or “whole-GPU.” They see a request that got the right hardware behavior because the platform asked the right question up front.

We worked with a services organization navigating exactly this shift, and one advantage came up repeatedly that platform teams often underestimate: services organizations see this failure mode across clients before any single product team hits it independently.

A training job stalling on pending pods, a time-sliced GPU getting OOM-killed by a noisy neighbor, and a MIG profile that doesn't match the workload it's serving show up as pattern when you're looking across multiple GPU platforms instead of just your own.

A platform team inside a single organization usually discovers a given failure mode the hard way, once, in production. A team that's rebuilt this same golden path for a dozen different clients has typically already seen it before the client asking for help has.

Teams With Less GPU Platform Debt Aren't the Ones Abstracting Most

Eighteen months from now, the platform teams with the least AI infrastructure debt won't be the ones who hid the most complexity behind the nicest developer portal. They'll be the ones who knew, specifically, which layer underneath their golden path was still moving, and refused to paper over it.

Abstraction built on an unstable foundation amplifies the instability, because the instability becomes invisible until it fails in production. Right now, GPU platforms are sitting on two unstable foundations at once:

  1. A scheduling model mid-migration between the device plugin and DRA
  2. A tenant isolation model that requires an explicit choice most teams haven't gotten around to making

You don't need to solve both before you ship anything. You need to know, and be honest with your team about, which decisions you've actually made and which ones you've inherited by default.

This isn't the first time we've written about golden paths hiding decisions teams haven't made consciously. If this resonated, Everyone Talks About Golden Paths. Nobody Talks About Building Them and What Nobody Tells You About Golden Paths at Scale cover the same failure pattern outside the GPU context.

I'm always looking to compare notes on how teams are handling GPU platform decisions. Connect with me on LinkedIn if you're working through this. If your organization needs help figuring out where the debt actually lives in your AI platform, reach out to our team.

title: My Error-Handling Mock Broke pytest's Own File Operations
description:
An error-handling test was supposed to make a file operation fail and check the application's response. Its mock also affected pytest's own file operations.

This happened in agent-cost, a CLI I maintain. The test checked that an OSError from operations such as os.fstat became the application's BillingPlanError while loading a billing-plan file.

PR #24 records the failure with pytest 9.2.0: its capture machinery called os.fstat on pytest's own file descriptors, and the test's unconditional fake raised before load_billing_plan was reached.

The fix changed the tests. The application's file-loading implementation stayed as it was.

A module-qualified patch can still change a shared object

Before the fix, the relevant test looked like this:

def failing_fstat(fd):
    raise _oserror_on(path)

monkeypatch.setattr(bp.os, "fstat", failing_fstat)
with pytest.raises(bp.BillingPlanError):
    bp.load_billing_plan(path)

This is an excerpt from the project test, not a standalone reproducer. bp is the agent_cost.billing_plan module; path and _oserror_on come from its test setup.

Writing bp.os does not confine the change to billing_plan.py. That module imports os, so under normal import behavior it refers to the same module object:

import os
from agent_cost import billing_plan as bp

assert bp.os is os

Python resolves previously imported modules through sys.modules; the module-cache documentation describes this behavior.

Replacing the fstat attribute on that shared object is visible to other users of the object, including pytest.

The original fake did not inspect its argument. Every file descriptor received the same failure. A descriptor is an integer handle for an open file or another resource. The billing-plan descriptor and pytest's capture descriptors were all treated alike.

Restoring a patch at the end of a test does not isolate its effects while the test is running.

Fail only for the target file descriptor

The replacement checks whether the descriptor refers to the plan file. Other calls delegate to the real function.

The central pieces are:

_REAL_FSTAT = os.fstat

def _is_fd_of(fd, path):
    try:
        st = _REAL_FSTAT(fd)
    except OSError:
        return False
    target = os.stat(path)
    return (st.st_dev, st.st_ino) == (target.st_dev, target.st_ino)

def failing_fstat(fd):
    if _is_fd_of(fd, path):
        raise _oserror_on(path)
    return _REAL_FSTAT(fd)

The helper compares the device and inode returned for the open descriptor with those returned for the target path.

It uses _REAL_FSTAT, captured before patching, so the identity check does not call the fake recursively.

The plan file still encounters the error under test. Calls involving pytest's own descriptors use the real function. The patch target has not changed; the set of calls that fail has.

This helper identifies the test's target file. It was not introduced as a general solution for file identity or concurrent filesystem changes.

Apply the boundary to read and close, too

The patch also narrows the os.read and os.close fakes:

Operation Target plan-file descriptor Other descriptors
fstat Raise the synthetic error Call the real function
read Raise the synthetic error Call the real function
close Close it, then raise the synthetic error Perform the real close only

For close, the order matters. The test must decide whether the descriptor is its own before closing it:

mine = _is_fd_of(fd, path)
real_close(fd)
if mine:
    raise _oserror_on(path)

Closing successfully and then raising is the behavior this particular test models. It is not a model of every possible close failure.

What the recorded checks show

GitHub Actions retains the before-and-after runs:

Run Recorded result
Before the test fix The Test step failed on Python 3.10–3.14; Python 3.9 and the packaged-install smoke test passed
After the test fix All seven jobs passed

Those outcomes belong to that CI matrix. They do not establish that Python 3.9 itself prevents the problem.

The PR and fix commit also report 549 passing tests with both pytest 9.1.1 and 9.2.0. Those are recorded verification results, not a new run performed for this article.

The full PR changes only the test file and adds workflow_dispatch to let CI run manually. No production loading code changed in this fix.

A shorter patch lifetime is only one boundary

The pytest monkeypatch guide already warns that patching standard-library functions can break pytest itself. It also describes MonkeyPatch.context() for limiting a patch to a block.

A smaller block limits lifetime. It does not stop pytest from using the shared function while that block is active.

This fix limits which file operations receive the synthetic failure. It does not add context(), and it does not claim a new discovery about monkeypatching in general.

For this test, the missing boundary was the descriptor the call operated on. The fake needed to fail the application's operation while letting the test runner continue doing its own work.

  • agent-cost PR #24
  • The test-fix diff

AI assistance was used to draft and edit this article.

title: Lost updates in four MCP servers: GitHub, Grafana, PostHog and Kubernetes
description:
Two agents changed different fields of the same GitHub issue at the same moment, through GitHub's official MCP server. Both were told the write succeeded. In 19 of 30 pairs, one of the two changes was gone. GitHub's own per-field API, given the same two changes, lost none in 28.

I run IsoKron, which sells MCP audits. This is self-funded research, AI-assisted, and not commissioned or endorsed by GitHub, Grafana Labs, PostHog, the kubernetes-mcp-server maintainers or Red Hat. It was first published on isokron.ai.

We audited the MCP servers that GitHub, Grafana and PostHog publish for their own products, and the open-source containers/kubernetes-mcp-server. In the first three, two writes sent at the same moment to the same object could lose one of the changes, and both callers were told their write had succeeded. In the Kubernetes server, a full copy of an object re-applied through the tool without its resourceVersion, after another writer had changed a field, set that field back. This page puts the four results side by side. Each row links to the full audit.

The reason to look at this class of bug now is that it was rare when one person used one client. It stops being rare when several agents work on the same backlog, dashboard or project at once.

The four results

Server What was tested Lost through the MCP server Through the platform's own API Where the defect is
GitHub MCP server v2.1.0 Two updates to different issue fields of one issue 19 of 30 pairs 0 of 28 pairs, using GitHub's per-field update In the MCP tool
Grafana MCP server v2.2.0 Two patches to different panels of one dashboard 30 of 30 pairs, on Grafana 13 and on Grafana 11 Legacy save endpoint: 30 of 30 on Grafana 13; 20 of 30 on Grafana 11, one save rejected in the other 10. Kubernetes-style API on Grafana 13: 0 of 30, one save rejected in every pair In the MCP tool and in the legacy save endpoint
PostHog MCP server Two updates to different fields of one insight 7 of 11 pairs, through the hosted server 6 of 11 pairs In PostHog's API; the MCP server passes it through
Kubernetes MCP server v0.1.2 A full copy re-applied through the tool after another writer changed a field Without resourceVersion, the other writer's change lost: replicas 10 of 10, a ConfigMap key 10 of 10. With the stale resourceVersion kept: refused with 409 in 10 of 10 The same body without force, straight to the API: 409 conflict, 3 of 3 Not filed as a bug: the tool applies with force: true, which upstream chose on purpose

Figure 1: Two simultaneous writes to one object, through three of the MCP servers and through each vendor’s own API

Group Arm Pairs that lost a change Pairs with one call rejected (conflict) Pairs
GitHub MCP server v2.1.0 Through the MCP server 19 0 30
GitHub MCP server v2.1.0 GitHub’s per-field update 0 0 28
Grafana MCP server v2.2.0, on Grafana 13 Through the MCP server 30 0 30
Grafana MCP server v2.2.0, on Grafana 13 Legacy save endpoint 30 0 30
Grafana MCP server v2.2.0, on Grafana 13 Kubernetes-style API 0 30 30
Grafana MCP server v2.2.0, on Grafana 11 Through the MCP server 30 0 30
Grafana MCP server v2.2.0, on Grafana 11 Legacy save endpoint 20 10 30
PostHog MCP server Through the hosted MCP server 7 0 11
PostHog MCP server PostHog’s API 6 0 11

Source: the table above, from the three linked audits.

A pair counts as lost when both calls returned success and one of the two changes was missing afterwards. All pairs were deliberately simultaneous. The figure covers the three servers tested with simultaneous pairs; the Kubernetes trials were a stale copy re-applied after another writer's change, so they are in the table only. None of these numbers says how often this happens in normal use.

Four different causes

GitHub: the MCP tool rewrites more than it was asked to change. To set one issue field, the tool reads every field value, merges in the change and writes the whole set back, with no version check. Two agents changing different fields overwrite each other. GitHub's own per-field update does not have the problem, which is why the control lost nothing. The MCP layer introduced the loss.

Grafana: the MCP tool switches off a check, and the endpoint behind it has a gap of its own. Patch mode reads the dashboard, applies the patch and saves the whole dashboard with overwrite forced on, so Grafana's version check never runs. Grafana rejected a stale save in 10 of 10 trials when the check was allowed to run. But two saves that arrive at exactly the same moment through the legacy save endpoint were both accepted even with the check on. Grafana 13's Kubernetes-style API did not have that gap: it rejected one of two simultaneous saves in 30 of 30 pairs.

PostHog: the loss is in the product's API. The same two requests sent straight to PostHog's API lost a write about as often as they did through the MCP server. The MCP server added nothing and removed nothing. An agent hits it more easily than a person does, because agents work in parallel.

Kubernetes: forced apply is upstream's choice, measured, not filed. resources_create_or_update applies with server-side apply and force: true. Upstream chose this on purpose (issue 799). The API has two protections for this edit: server-side apply without force refuses to take over fields another manager owns, and a resourceVersion in the body makes a stale write fail. Forcing switches off the first, so only the second remains, and only if the client keeps the resourceVersion it read. Neither native session in that audit ever sent a resourceVersion: in the concurrent-edit job, another writer changed MAX_CONNECTIONS from 100 to 200 about half a second after the agent read the ConfigMap, the agent's forced apply set it back to 100 four seconds later, and the agent told the user that the other keys were unchanged. Where the server does use optimistic concurrency, it held: resources_scale sends the resourceVersion it read, an injected conflict came back as an error with nothing changed (3 of 3), and real contention surfaced 10 of 10 times. A related design gap, K8S-04, is that resources_delete sends no uid or resourceVersion precondition, so it deleted an object recreated after the agent's read (10 of 10; kubectl has no uid precondition either).

The distinction matters when you read an audit of any MCP server. "The MCP server loses writes" can mean the server is wrong, that it faithfully exposes a backend that is, or that it made a deliberate trade-off. The control against the platform's own API is what tells them apart, and it should be in the report.

What happened next

Server Reported Status on 12 November 2026
GitHub Issue 3751 Our fix is open as pull request 3781, with no maintainer review as of 12 November 2026. In our test of that approach a patched build lost 0 of 12 pairs
Grafana Pull request 1518 Open; as of 12 November 2026 it was awaiting maintainer review, rebased onto the current main branch and mergeable. The proposed fix saves through the Kubernetes-style API where it exists and lost 0 of 60 pairs on Grafana 13. Grafana 11 has only the legacy endpoint; there the restored version check reports stale saves but still lost 14 of 30 simultaneous pairs
PostHog Pull request 131519 Fixed for insights. A maintainer re-created the change as pull request 131620, with IsoKron as co-author, and merged it about 17 hours after we opened ours. Cohorts and dashboards lost writes in the same tests and, as of 12 November 2026, are not yet fixed
Kubernetes Not filed Forced apply is a deliberate upstream decision, and K8S-04 is a design gap; neither was filed. The research build adds resources_patch with an optional resourceVersion precondition, in the shape of upstream's open proposal 1352, and makes apply without force the default. That reverses a deliberate upstream decision, so it is a proposal, not a fix

PostHog's response is the one to copy: a small fix, reviewed and merged the next morning.

What this does not show

  • The counts are small: 11 to 30 pairs per cell for GitHub, Grafana and PostHog, with the two calls released together on purpose, and 10 trials per arm for Kubernetes (3 for the API control and for the injected scale conflict), on one machine, one cluster or one test account.
  • Real agents did task work through the server in all four audits. The lost-update counts did not come from those sessions: they come from scripted pairs and trials, so they show that a collision or a stale copy loses a write, not how often agents collide on their own.
  • Four servers is not a survey. We chose them because they are widely used and open source, not at random.
  • In the three simultaneous-pair cases the lost change can be put back by writing it again, and at Grafana it stays in the dashboard's version history. The harm is that nothing tells the agent or the user that it needs to.
  • The findings were found with AI assistance and checked as each audit describes. We sell audits of this kind, so read the method sections with that in mind.

How to check a server you run

  1. Pick a tool that updates part of an object: one field, one panel, one tag.
  2. Send two calls that change different parts of the same object at the same moment, from two separate server processes. Repeat at least ten times.
  3. Read the object back. If both calls said success and one change is missing, you have a lost update.
  4. Repeat with the same two changes sent straight to the product's API. If the API loses nothing, the MCP tool is the cause. If the API loses them too, the fix belongs in the API, and the tool should at least surface a conflict where the API offers one.

The full method, including the controls and the ways we got it wrong before getting it right, is in How to test an MCP server without fooling yourself.

Reproduce it

  • The method, with the controls and the mistakes we made first: How to test an MCP server without fooling yourself.
  • GitHub: isokron-ai/github-mcp-writepath-experiment is v2.1.0 plus the fixes as separate commits; go test ./... runs the upstream tests plus the ones added for each fix. Its concurrent-pair harness is tied to a private test repository and isn't published yet.
  • PostHog: isokron-ai/posthog-mcp-writepath-experiment, with the benchmark harness in harness/.
  • Kubernetes: isokron-ai/kubernetes-mcp-writepath-experiment, with the frozen harness; for b in baseline fixed research; do harness/build/build.sh $b; done builds all three binaries.
  • Grafana: the fix is pull request 1518 upstream.

If your numbers differ from ours, open an issue on the matching repository. Reproductions that disagree are the most useful feedback.

How this was tested. AI agents run much of the testing: scripted checks, attempts to disprove each finding, and real tasks that use the server the way an agent would. I also test every server myself on a separate machine and check each finding against the AI results. A finding appears here only if it holds up in both. — Joshua Bryan

For this piece: Every figure is taken from the four linked audits, which give the method, the controls and the limits for each.

Over to you

Have you seen a write tool report success and lose data? Which MCP server should we test next? Tell me in the comments.

title: The Stanley Cup Champion Ranks 9th: A Year of Social Data on All 32 NHL Clubs
description:
Every hockey fan has a theory about attention: win, and the internet follows. We tested it on a full year of data.

We pulled 365 days of public social conversation about all 32 NHL clubs and the league itself with the LunarCrush CLI, 12 November 2025 to 11 November 2026, across X, Reddit, TikTok, YouTube, Instagram and 10K+ news sources. That is 27.20B interactions (views included) on the 32 club series and 21.93B on the NHL topic.

The full study, with interactive charts and a free dataset, is at lunarcrush.com/research/nhl-fan-attention-2026.

Winning barely moves attention

For each club we took its win share in the window (completed regular-season and playoff games; overtime and shootout losses counted as losses; the window covers the end of 2025-26 and the start of 2026-27) and its total interactions for the year. We measured attention two ways: the main keyword collection, and a stricter one that counts full club names only.

The correlation between win share and log annual interactions is 0.00 on the main measure, 0.27 counting full club names only, across 32 clubs. Swap in NHL points percentage (regular-season games, a point for an overtime or shootout loss) and it is 0.02 and 0.25. With 32 clubs, all of those are weak.

Two clubs show it on both measures:

  • Carolina won the Stanley Cup and ranks 9th on the main measure (991.8M), 6th counting full club names only.
  • Toronto won 32 of 86 games in the window and ranks 2nd on the main measure (2.05B), 3rd on full names.

The ranking

Montreal leads on the main measure; San Jose leads on full names. Montreal drew 2.26B interactions, ahead of Toronto (2.05B) and San Jose (1.83B). Nashville is 32nd at 275.9M. Counting full club names only, San Jose leads at 1.55B.

Each club series is a keyword collection: the full club name, its one-word form and its nickname. Ordinary-word nicknames (Hurricanes, Jets, Rangers, Kings, Stars, Lightning and the rest) only count with league, hockey or home-city context, and relevance on each club's 25 top posts ran 80% to 100%. Unique nicknames like "Canadiens" and "Canucks" match alone, which can lift those clubs; Vancouver is 5th on the main measure and 21st on full names. That is why the dataset carries both ranks. 8 of the top 10 hold their place within 3 ranks.

The top three clubs' largest days

The top three got there through very different days.

Montreal. Its three largest days were playoff nights: Game 7 in Buffalo (57.9M on 19 May UTC), Game 7 against Tampa Bay (42.7M on 4 May UTC) and the next round's opener (38.5M on 22 May UTC). French-language posts are visible in its top posts, including the club's own bilingual publishing.

Toronto. Its two largest days were lottery night (36.9M on 6 May UTC, after the 5 May ET draw) and the draft's first round (34.9M on 27 June UTC; the first pick was made on 26 June ET). Neither was a game night.

San Jose. Its largest day was 19.6M. Most of its total is a steady daily floor of posts from the club's own accounts and a large fan-edit community around Macklin Celebrini and Sharks forward Will Smith.

The league year, day by day

The largest day in NHL conversation followed the Olympic men's final: 23 February 2026 UTC, 147.2M interactions. The ten largest days were four Olympic days around the men's final, a league-news and Ovechkin milestone day, Utah's Zammoth day (a Mammoth-themed ice resurfacing machine), the draft's first round (125.4M), the draft lottery (111.2M) and two trade-deadline days.

No Stanley Cup Final game makes the list. The Cup-clinching date, 15 June UTC, drew 81.7M, less than the draft's first round ten days into the offseason by our calendar.

The season still matters in aggregate. In-season days average 70.5M interactions and offseason days (16 June to 28 September) 34.3M, a ratio of 2.05x.

Attention is concentrated

The top five clubs draw 33.0% of the 32 clubs' combined 27.20B interactions (views included; a post naming two clubs counts for both). The bottom five draw 5.7%. Montreal alone draws 8.2 times Nashville's total.

In interactions per home-market resident, with all 32 clubs normalized, Buffalo leads at 869, then Edmonton (742), Winnipeg (516) and Montreal (491). Interactions come from anywhere, so this is a scale index, not a count of local fans. New York's three clubs share one market, as do Los Angeles and Anaheim, which puts them at the bottom of that view.

Reproduce one number

Every series on the page is a public LunarCrush topic or collection. Here is how to get the largest league day yourself:

curl -fsSL https://lunarcrush.ai/install.sh | bash
lunarcrush login

# a year of daily metrics for the NHL topic
lunarcrush topic nhl time-series --interval 1y --start 2025-11-12 --end 2026-11-12 --json > nhl.json

import json
from datetime import datetime, timezone

rows = json.load(open("nhl.json"))["data"]
day = lambda r: datetime.fromtimestamp(r["time"], timezone.utc).strftime("%Y-%m-%d")
year = [r for r in rows if "2025-11-12" <= day(r) <= "2026-11-11"]
peak = max(year, key=lambda r: r["interactions"])
print(day(peak), peak["interactions"])
# 2026-02-23, about 147.2M; totals move slightly as late engagement lands

Each club works the same way with its collection id, for example Montreal:

lunarcrush topic lc1sQWOkyy time-series --interval 1y --start 2025-11-12 --end 2026-11-12 --json

Public topic pages follow the same pattern: lunarcrush.com/topic/lc1sQWOkyy. All 32 collection ids, plus the full-name-only ids, are columns in the team table download.

The shipped club series remove two items you will see in a raw pull: activity credited to an older post beyond its lifetime interactions (4.0% of the combined club total), and a recurring non-hockey weather video matched by Tampa Bay's collection (302.1M interactions).

How the data works

  • Interactions include views alongside likes, comments and shares, so they are not unique people. They are summable across days.
  • Active contributors and active posts are unique counts per day. We report them as daily means and never sum them.
  • Sentiment is the daily 0 to 100 score, weighted by each day's interactions for the annual figure.
  • A post naming two clubs counts for both, so the 32 club series sum to more than the league topic. Every share uses the 32 clubs' combined total.
  • Correlations are across the 32 clubs, not across games. All dates are UTC; an evening game in North America often lands on the next UTC date.

Take the data

The dataset is free on the study page: the 32-club table with both ranks, win share and points percentage, every club by day (11,680 rows), the league by day, in CSV and Parquet, plus an AI guide with the schema and validation anchors so an assistant reproducing the numbers gets ours.

The same read works for any club and its rivals, a sponsor, a player, or any brand or ticker, hourly, through the API, the CLI, bulk files or the LunarCrush MCP server for Claude, ChatGPT and other assistants.

Social data: LunarCrush daily series, 12 November 2025 to 11 November 2026, pulled 12 and 13 November 2026. Results: ESPN completed regular-season and playoff games. Population: 2025 U.S. Census CSA and Statistics Canada CMA.

Independent research by LunarCrush. Not affiliated with or endorsed by the NHL or any club.

title: Track Indian startup funding with Python (stdlib RSS)
description:
"How much did Indian startups raise this week?" sounds like a question with one answer. It has at least three. The main Indian startup publications each publish a weekly funding roundup, and for the same week their totals disagree — because each uses a different date window, a different deal list, and a different way of handling currency.

Rather than pick one roundup and trust it, you can track Indian startup funding with Python: we built a small script that pulls funding headlines straight from the publications' RSS feeds and writes them to a CSV. Every row keeps its source and link, so any figure can be traced back to the headline it came from. The columns are: date, source, company_guess, amount_as_reported, title, link.

The feeds

We probed a handful of feed URLs. Four returned HTTP 200 on 14 Nov 2026:

  • Indian Startup News — indianstartupnews.com/rss (note: /rss, not /feed)
  • YourStory — yourstory.com/feed
  • ETtech Funding — economictimes.indiatimes.com/tech/funding/rssfeeds/78570540.cms
  • Inc42 — inc42.com/feed/

Two returned 404: entrackr.com/feed and indianstartupnews.com/feed. Feed URLs rot, so check them before assuming a source went quiet.

Feeds are also short-lived. At fetch time, ETtech and ISN held 50 items each, Inc42 24, YourStory 20, and the oldest matching row in our run was dated 3 Nov 2026. A feed is a rolling window, not an archive — run the script on a schedule and append, or history falls off the back.

The script: track Indian startup funding with Python

The whole thing is about 60 lines, standard library only — urllib, xml.etree, csv, re, email.utils — so there is nothing to pip install.

"""Pull Indian startup funding headlines from public RSS feeds into one CSV.

Standard library only. Usage: python3 funding_feed.py > rounds.csv
"""
import csv, re, sys, urllib.request
import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET
from email.utils import parsedate_to_datetime

FEEDS = {
    "Indian Startup News": "https://indianstartupnews.com/rss",
    "YourStory": "https://yourstory.com/feed",
    "ETtech Funding": "https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/tech/funding/rssfeeds/78570540.cms",
    "Inc42": "https://inc42.com/feed/",
}
ROUND = re.compile(r"\b(raises?|raised|bags|secures|nets|funding)\b", re.I)
# skip VC funds, results, rumours and weekly roundups (they would double count)
NOT_A_STARTUP_ROUND = re.compile(
    r"\b(fund|ipo|q[1-4]|loss|profit|revenue|in talks|looks to|plans to|weekly|digest|startups raised)\b",
    re.I)
AMOUNT = re.compile(
    r"(\$\s?[\d.]+\s?(?:million|mn|m|billion|bn|b)\b"
    r"|(?:rs\.?|inr|₹)\s?[\d.,]+\s?(?:crore|cr|lakh)\b)", re.I)


def fetch(url):
    req = urllib.request.Request(url, headers={"User-Agent": "funding-feed/0.1"})
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=20) as r:
        return ET.fromstring(r.read())


def rows():
    for source, url in FEEDS.items():
        try:
            root = fetch(url)
        except Exception as e:  # one dead feed should not kill the run
            print(f"skip {source}: {e}", file=sys.stderr)
            continue
        for item in root.iter("item"):
            title = " ".join((item.findtext("title") or "").split())
            if not ROUND.search(title) or NOT_A_STARTUP_ROUND.search(title):
                continue
            amount = AMOUNT.search(title)
            company = re.split(ROUND, title, maxsplit=1)[0].strip(" ,:-")
            pub = item.findtext("pubDate")
            yield {
                "date": parsedate_to_datetime(pub).date().isoformat() if pub else "",
                "source": source,
                "company_guess": company[-60:],
                "amount_as_reported": amount.group(0) if amount else "",
                "title": title,
                "link": (item.findtext("link") or "").strip(),
            }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    out = csv.DictWriter(sys.stdout, fieldnames=[
        "date", "source", "company_guess", "amount_as_reported", "title", "link"])
    out.writeheader()
    for row in sorted(rows(), key=lambda r: r["date"], reverse=True):
        out.writerow(row)

Run it with python3 funding_feed.py > rounds.csv.

The filtering is three regexes:

  • Keep titles matching raise, raised, bags, secures, nets, or funding.
  • Drop titles containing fund, IPO, Q1-Q4, loss, profit, revenue, "in talks", "looks to", "plans to", weekly, digest, or "startups raised".
  • Extract the amount exactly as written in the headline — a dollar figure or a rupee figure — and store it as text. No currency conversion.

The exclusion list exists because the first run without it also pulled weekly digests — one ETtech digest headline read "weekly funding falls to $12 million" — and rumour headlines using "in talks" or "looks to". A digest restates rounds that can also appear as single-deal headlines, so keeping both risks double counting.

Amounts stay as text because publications convert currencies differently (more below). Storing amount_as_reported verbatim, plus the link, keeps the row faithful to the source; conversion happens later, under a rule we choose ourselves.

What one run returned

An excerpt (first four columns; title and link trimmed for width):

date,source,company_guess,amount_as_reported
2026-11-13,Indian Startup News,Can an AI agent run a factory? Morsa,$1.5 million
2026-11-13,Indian Startup News,Jaipur menswear brand QB MEN,
2026-11-12,Indian Startup News,Kerala startup mistEO,Rs 18 crore
2026-11-12,Inc42,NHRC Member Flags Meta-UNICEF,
2026-11-07,Indian Startup News,Jewellery brand GIVA,Rs 975 crore
2026-11-04,Indian Startup News,bay to 9 countries: Cleaning robot maker Peppermint Robotics,Rs 100 crore
2026-11-04,ETtech Funding,Peppermint Robotics,Rs 100 crore
2026-11-03,Indian Startup News,Karnataka tech,$4.6 billion

The run on 14 Nov 2026 produced 20 rows, exit code 0. Reading them closely:

  • 3 of the 20 rows were not startup rounds: a Karnataka policy story, an NHRC story about "funding ties", and a state-level $4.6 billion figure. Keyword filters produce false positives, so treat each row as a lead to check, not as data.
  • Some genuine round headlines carry no amount — for example QB MEN "raises pre-seed funding". Those rows get an empty amount_as_reported.
  • False negatives happen too: YourStory's Kutlerri.ai headline ("raises $4M to help US restaurants grow revenue...") was dropped because the word "revenue" appears in the title. The exclusion list trades recall for precision.
  • The same round shows up in more than one feed: Peppermint Robotics' Rs 100 crore appeared in both ISN and ETtech, and altM's $10.3 million and Cosmoserve's $6 million likewise. Summing the column as-is double counts. Note that company_guess is a raw headline fragment clipped to the last 60 characters before the verb, so the same round reads "bay to 9 countries: Cleaning robot maker Peppermint Robotics" in one feed and "Peppermint Robotics" in another. Dedupe on a normalized company name plus amount, after checking the link.

Why your total won't match Inc42, YourStory or ISN

For the same week in early November 2026, the three publications printed three different totals. Inc42 said 20 startups raised $255 Mn for Nov 2-6. YourStory said $263 million across 23 deals for Oct 31-Nov 6. Indian Startup News said over $290.55 million across 22 startups for Nov 2-7.

Three reasons:

Windows. Nov 2-6, Oct 31-Nov 6, and Nov 2-7 are different windows, so a round announced on 31 October or 7 November lands in some totals and not others.

Deal lists. ISN counted Braid, a $38M round for a company headquartered in The Hague, which Inc42 did not list. What counts as an "Indian startup" is itself an editorial decision.

Conversions. ISN's weekly roundup put GIVA at "about Rs 955 crore", while ISN's own deal story said "about Rs 975 crore". Peppermint was Rs 100 crore in YourStory but Rs 101.4 crore in ISN's weekly. Only ISN printed a method: "Amounts in USD as reported; rupee rounds converted at announcement rates."

Hence the design choice: store the amount as reported, keep the source link, and apply your own window, inclusion and conversion rules later — written down, so the total is reproducible.

Next steps

  • Put the script on cron and append to a CSV or SQLite table; feeds only hold recent items, so a gap in the schedule becomes a gap in the data.
  • Dedupe on a normalized company name plus amount, after checking the link, before computing any total.
  • Open the link before trusting a row — keyword matches are leads, not verified rounds.
  • Add your own window and conversion rule, and print both in the output header so anyone reading the CSV knows exactly what the numbers mean.

FAQ

Why not feedparser? It works fine, but the standard library covers these four RSS 2.0 feeds, so the script has no dependency to install.

Why is Entrackr missing? Its /feed URL returned 404 when we checked, as did indianstartupnews.com/feed; ISN's working feed is /rss.

Why keep amounts as text? The same round is converted differently even within one publication: GIVA was "about Rs 955 crore" in ISN's weekly and "about Rs 975 crore" in ISN's deal story. Converting at ingest would hide that.

If you try it, put it on a daily cron first and look at a week of rows before you trust any total you compute from them.

Disclosure: posted from the Mantis team account under the LazyFounder organization; LazyFounder is founded by Tarun Kumar (lazyfounder.in). Drafted with AI from the run log and sources above, checked against them before posting.
