title: AWS Security Hub CSPM now supports centralized configuration with AWS Organizations declarative policies
description:
AWS Security Hub CSPM now supports AWS Organizations declarative policies. You can use them to enable Security Hub CSPM across all accounts and Regions in your organization and to define which security standards and controls are enabled.

Policies can apply broadly to every account and Region, or target specific account and Region combinations. Declarative policies help keep each account's configuration aligned with its attached policy, which helps prevent configuration drift. You can also apply them automatically to new accounts, so each account starts with a baseline configuration as soon as it's created.

Declarative policies are now the recommended way to manage Security Hub CSPM across an organization. They align with how other security services, such as Amazon GuardDuty, Amazon Inspector, and AWS Security Hub allow customers to manage configuration of the service. They also provide more flexibility, such as configuring Region-specific settings. You can continue to use central configuration until you're ready to migrate. When you are, use the migration process in the Security Hub CSPM console. It converts your existing central configuration policies into declarative policies and applies them to the appropriate accounts and regions.

Declarative policies for Security Hub CSPM are available in all commercial, AWS GovCloud (US), and China Regions. To get started, see Migrating central configuration policies. To learn more, see Declarative policies in the AWS Security Hub CSPM User Guide and Security Hub CSPM policies in the AWS Organizations User Guide. To receive notifications about new Security Hub CSPM features and controls, subscribe to the Security Hub SNS topic. You can also try Security Hub CSPM at no cost for 30 days with the AWS Free Tier offering.

title: Embedded Java: 20x Smaller Than Chrome, Faster Than Rust, Royalty Free
description:
Embedded software has the hardest job description in our industry. It has to run for years without a reboot. It has to fit in whatever RAM and flash the bill of materials allowed, because every chip you add is paid for again on every unit you ship. It has to respond instantly on a CPU slower than a phone from five years ago. And now it also has to look like the phone app, talk to the phone app, and report to a cloud service, because that's what customers expect from anything with a power cord.

What is Codename One? Codename One is an open-source framework for building native iOS, Android, desktop, and web apps from a single Java or Kotlin codebase. Learn more at codenameone.com.

Most teams solve that with three or four stacks. C or C++ on the device for size and control, a browser or Qt for the screen, Swift and Kotlin for the companion app, something else on the server. Every boundary between them is a protocol written twice and a bug waiting to happen.

Codename One now runs on embedded Linux, and it covers every one of those pieces with one Java or Kotlin codebase. On our benchmark, the UI drew an animated gauge in 18 MB of memory with no GPU, about a twentieth of what a Chromium kiosk needed to draw the same thing. The headless backend served 379,900 requests per second on two cores, 1.3 times Rust's axum. And we don't charge royalties.

Coming This Week

Today is the embedded story. Then one post a day:

  • Saturday, November 7: Dash: An Endless Runner That Races Through Your City. A game template that turns from 2D into 3D mid-run, builds levels from real streets, and lets friends race with voice chat.
  • Sunday, November 8: Pulse: Heart Rate Zones From the Watch to the Trainer's Screen. A gym and studio template built around HealthKit, Health Connect and Bluetooth heart rate straps.
  • Monday, November 9: Real-Time Java: Control Loops the Garbage Collector Never Stops. What real time means, why it's hard for a managed language, and how we do it.
  • Tuesday, November 10: Packaging Java Apps for Xbox Developer Mode, and Why Consoles Need Help. One build hint today. Shipping to consoles needs help we can't get alone.
  • Wednesday, November 11: Port Your Spring Code With Fewer Edits, and Libraries That Bring Their Own Server. Logging, typed JSON, CORS, content negotiation and more of the JDK in the backend, plus cn1libs with a server half.
  • Thursday, November 12: Debug Your Dart in a Java Debugger, and JFX Central on a Phone. Dart call stacks, Flutter fixes from a real port, a faster web port and a real JavaFX app on an iPhone.

Dash, mid-run in 3D.
Pulse's live class view.
JFX Central on an iPhone.

Two flavors, two kinds of product

The port comes in two flavors. The easiest way to explain them is with two products.

A point of sale terminal: the UI flavor

A POS terminal lives or dies on price. It needs a responsive touch screen, a receipt printer on a serial port, a card reader, and it has to sync with the store's back office. The merchant buys a hundred of them, so ten dollars of hardware is a thousand dollars on the order and the difference between winning and losing the deal.

A GPU is one of the first things you'd like to cut. Android won't let you: AOSP needs a board support package with a GPU driver. Flutter can limp along without one, if Mesa emulates OpenGL on the CPU, and on our gauge that took 1.4 CPU cores and 112 MB. A Chromium kiosk runs in 400 MB of RAM. Codename One draws in software by default, through DRM/KMS or the Linux frame buffer, with no X11 or Wayland. It needs nothing from the board but a frame buffer, so the cheapest SoC that drives your screen is enough.

When the board does have a GPU, set one build hint (or let the board profile choose it) and the same renderer composites through GBM, EGL and GLES 2. The frames are identical to the software output; the CPU time per frame drops. If the GPU driver turns out to be broken, the app logs why and falls back to software instead of showing a black screen.

The screen code is the code you'd write for a phone. Your POS app, the manager's phone app and the back office share the same entity classes, so a change to the receipt format breaks the build rather than a store.

A robot vacuum: the headless flavor

A robot vacuum needs a brain but no screen. The UI is the phone app. The device has to read its sensors, drive its motors, expose an API the app can find on the local network, accept only the owner's phone, take updates and keep working when the Wi-Fi drops. Every component inside it is multiplied by every unit sold, so memory and CPU headroom cost real money for the life of the product.

That's the backend flavor: the same Codename One backend that runs your cloud server, compiled to a native executable for the board. REST endpoints, WebSockets, the ORM, MQTT, Bonjour discovery and mutual TLS for device identity are all there, next to the hardware API.

A controller on the vacuum is a Spring-style class that reads the hardware directly:

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/robot")
public class RobotController {
    private final I2cDevice fuelGauge;

    public RobotController() throws HardwareException {
        fuelGauge = Hardware.getInstance().openI2c(1, 0x36);
    }

    @GetMapping("/battery")
    public BatteryDto battery() throws HardwareException {
        return new BatteryDto(fuelGauge.readRegister(0x04));
    }
}

The phone app compiles against the same BatteryDto. It finds the vacuum with Bonjour when it's on the same network and goes through the cloud backend when it isn't, and the API is the same either way.

Competitors that need a GPU, gigabytes and a prayer

We ran the same workload in five toolkits: an 800 by 480 gauge with a sweeping arc, a needle and a bold percentage, redrawn every frame and capped at 60 frames per second, in software. Same Debian arm64 container, three runs each, median shown.


Toolkit First frame, cold Frames per second Memory (PSS) On disk (files mapped)
Codename One 46 ms 57 18 MB 15 MB
Slint 1.8 45 ms 51 23 MB 4.3 MB
Qt 6.4 Widgets 73 ms 62 23 MB 73 MB
JavaFX 26 327 ms 62 116 MB 102 MB
Chromium kiosk 717 ms 60 398 MB 378 MB
flutter-pi, GPU emulated on the CPU 767 ms 59 112 MB 233 MB
Android (AOSP) needs a GPU and a BSP

Read that table as a hardware budget. The kiosk browser, the stack most teams reach for when they want "modern UX", needs 22 times our memory and 25 times our disk to draw one gauge, and takes three quarters of a second to show it. JavaFX, the other way to put Java on a board, needs six times our memory. Flutter does run without a GPU, but only by emulating one: it held its frame rate on 1.4 CPU cores, where we used 6% of one, in six times our memory and fifteen times our disk. Android can't run without a GPU at all. We're the only Java option in the table that fits on the board you'd actually want to pay for.

The container ran on an Apple Silicon Mac, not a board, so a real board will be slower. Compare the rows against each other, not against your hardware. Slint needs less disk than we do, and Qt pushes a few more frames. Our form also draws more than the others: a title bar, a button, a slider and a label around the gauge. The flutter-pi row is a release build of the same gauge drawing to the kernel's virtual display, because flutter-pi needs a display device; the others drew to memory. LVGL isn't in the table either. It's a low-level C graphics library: its widgets are drawn objects you wire up by hand, with no component model, data binding, navigation, networking or storage around them. Comparing it with a full application toolkit wouldn't be a fair test of either.

The headless flavor ran its own benchmark: a small JSON service pinned to two cores.

Runtime Start Idle memory Peak requests/s p99 at peak
Codename One backend 40 ms 9.2 MB 379,900 0.22 ms
Rust, axum 35 ms 1.6 MB 290,200 0.25 ms
Go, net/http 48 ms 5.2 MB 178,900 0.59 ms
Node.js 147 ms 48 MB 63,500 1.1 ms
Spring Boot 3.5 1,340 ms 164 MB 33,300 3.3 ms
Python, FastAPI 270 ms 42 MB 6,700 11 ms

Rust and Go use less memory. But a Java backend that serves 1.3 times Rust's peak at a lower p99, and starts 33 times faster than Spring Boot in an eighteenth of its memory, changes what you can put in a vacuum. Like Rust, our server makes two system calls per request and allocates nothing but the object the handler returns. CI reruns this on arm64 with every change to the backend runtime and fails the build if we fall below Rust. The harness is public, so check our Rust setup.

The only stack that goes from the vacuum to the browser

Here's what I think matters more than any single number. Look at what each option covers:

Device UI Headless device Real-time loop iOS and Android Desktop Web Cloud backend
Codename One yes yes yes yes yes yes yes
Qt yes Qt Core no yes yes WebAssembly HTTP server module
Slint yes no no Android, iOS preview yes WebAssembly no
Flutter (flutter-pi) GPU, or emulated on the CPU no no yes yes yes no
Chromium kiosk yes no no as a web app as a web app yes no
Android (AOSP) GPU only no no Android only no no no

Nobody else gives you a device UI, a headless device, a real-time control loop, the phone app, the desktop app, the web app and the cloud server from one language, one build and one set of classes. That's the "super full stack": the entities, the DTOs and the API contract live in a shared module that every target compiles against. A field renamed on the vacuum is a compile error in the phone app, not a support ticket. One team can own the whole product, and one security fix lands everywhere at once.

The rest of the ecosystem comes along: Bluetooth LE, NFC, MQTT, Bonjour, the ORM, push, crash reporting and the build tools you already use for mobile.

What it looks like in code

Hardware access is in the core API. GPIO, I2C, SPI, serial, PWM, CAN, the watchdog and the backlight go through the kernel's own interfaces, with no extra library:

Hardware hw = Hardware.getInstance();
try {
    if (hw.isSupported(Hardware.FEATURE_GPIO)) {
        GpioPin led = hw.openGpioOutput("gpiochip0", 17, false);
        GpioPin button = hw.openGpioInput("gpiochip0", 27,
                GpioPin.BIAS_PULL_UP, GpioPin.EDGE_FALLING);
        button.setListener((pin, rising, nanos) -> {
            try {
                led.setHigh(!led.isHigh());
            } catch (HardwareException e) {
                Log.e(e);
            }
        });
    }
    if (hw.isSupported(Hardware.FEATURE_I2C)) {
        I2cDevice sensor = hw.openI2c(1, 0x48);
        Log.p("Sensor reads " + sensor.readRegister(0));
    }
} catch (HardwareException e) {
    Log.e(e);
}

On a phone, isSupported answers false, so the same class is safe everywhere. In the simulator it runs against a virtual board with 32 GPIO lines, a TMP102 temperature sensor, an EEPROM and loopback SPI, serial, and CAN. You can write and unit test the hardware code before the board arrives.

Getting it onto the board is one command. It builds, copies the executable over SSH, installs it as a systemd service and follows the log:

mvn cn1:runOnDevice -Dcn1.board=rpi5 -Dcn1.device.host=pi.local -Dcn1.device.user=pi

Board profiles cover the Raspberry Pi family, i.MX 8 and i.MX 6, RK3588, Jetson, BeaglePlay and generic arm64, armv7, x64 and RISC-V. There's a Yocto layer for production images, and a cross build can point at a Yocto or Buildroot SDK sysroot.

No royalties, and the support embedded actually needs

Embedded UI is usually sold per unit. You ship ten thousand terminals and pay a royalty on each one, which is fine until the product succeeds and the toolkit becomes a line item on every unit you ship.

Codename One doesn't charge royalties. It's open source under GPL 2 with the Classpath exception, on devices like everywhere else.

What embedded teams need from a vendor is different. A device ships once and stays in the field for ten years or more. It runs the exact framework version it was certified with, and the team needs a security fix in that version five years from now, not an upgrade to whatever master looks like then. That's long-term support: a maintained branch for your product, backports of the fixes that matter to you, and someone who answers when the board vendor's new kernel breaks something.

That runs far past the timeline we normally support, and it's work we're happy to do with you directly. It's a better deal for both sides than a royalty: you pay for the support you use, and the price doesn't grow with your success. If you're planning a product, talk to us early so the branch matches your release.

Linux today, other systems and RTOS on request

We only support embedded Linux right now. If your product runs on Zephyr, QNX, VxWorks, FreeRTOS or a vendor OS, tell us. The renderer needs a frame buffer and the backend needs sockets, and ParparVM already emits portable C, so a new OS means porting two layers. Real demand decides which one comes next, and that includes a proper hard real-time RTOS.

More This Week

Real-time threads

A vacuum's motor loop, or a POS card reader's timing, has deadlines, and a garbage collector that stops the world is the usual reason people say Java can't meet them. Codename One now has real-time threads on PREEMPT_RT Linux that the collector never stops:


class MotorLoop extends RealtimeTask {
    private final double[] gains = new double[64];   // allocate up front
    private PwmChannel pwm;

    public void setup() {                            // may allocate
        try {
            pwm = Hardware.getInstance().openPwm(0, 0);
        } catch (HardwareException e) {
            Log.e(e);
        }
    }

    public void cycle() {                            // must not allocate
        // read sensors, compute gains, then pwm.setDutyCycle(...)
    }
}

Realtime.getInstance().start("motor",
        new RealtimeParameters().setPeriodNanos(1000000).setPriority(80).setCpu(3),
        new MotorLoop());

If cycle() allocates, the build fails and names the method and the line. Every thread keeps latency statistics so you can prove the deadline on your own board. Monday's real-time article explains the terms, what makes this hard for a managed language and how we handle each part.

Dash: race through your city

Dash gameplay on a neon track.

Dash is our second game template: an endless runner whose levels can start as a 2D side-scroller and swing into 3D mid-run. Pick two points on a real street map and the route becomes a level, street names and landmarks included:

CityRoute route = new CityRoute("Old Harbour")
        .leg(420, CityRoute.STRAIGHT, "Quay Street")
        .leg(310, CityRoute.LEFT, "Rope Walk");
LevelDef level = route.level();

The server replays every run to keep the leaderboards clean, and friends race the same track with voice chat. Saturday's Dash article has the details.

Pulse: heart rates from the wrist to the trainer

Download the trainer video.

Pulse is a gym and studio template built around health data. A member's watch or Bluetooth chest strap feeds a workout session, the readings go to the studio's backend, and the trainer sees every member's heart rate zone live. Past workouts come in from HealthKit or Health Connect through one API. Sunday's Pulse article walks through the health code.

Xbox, and help with consoles

codename1.arg.windows.xbox=true builds the native Windows port as a UWP app for Xbox Developer Mode:

Your game keeps reading Display.getGameAction() as it does on a phone. We haven't run it on a real Xbox yet, and Developer Mode can't sell a game. Shipping on consoles needs SDKs behind NDAs, so Tuesday's Xbox article is also a request: if you can open that door, talk to us.

Port your Spring code with fewer edits

Porting real services to the Codename One backend keeps finding the small things a Spring developer expects. This round closed a batch of them, so code like this now moves over unchanged:

@RestController
@CrossOrigin(origins = "https://shop.example.com")
public class OrderController {
    private static final Logger LOG = Logger.getLogger(OrderController.class);

    @PostMapping(value = "/orders", consumes = "application/json", produces = "application/json")
    public Order place(@RequestBody Order order) {
        if (order.lines.isEmpty()) {
            throw new ResponseStatusException(400, "An order needs at least one line");
        }
        MDC.put("customer", order.customer);
        LOG.info("Placing order with {} lines", order.lines.size());
        return orders.save(order);
    }
}

Json.read(body, Order.class) and Json.write(order) work through codecs generated at build time, String.matches and java.util.regex work, and BigDecimal, YearMonth, Semaphore and ConcurrentLinkedQueue are there. A cn1lib can now also ship its own controllers, entities, and migrations. Wednesday's backend article has the full list.

Dart debugging, a faster web port and JFX Central

Download the JFX Central video.

That's JFX Central, a real JavaFX application written by JavaFX experts, running on an iPhone through our JavaFX layer. It isn't as polished as an app written for Codename One, but bindings, cells, CSS and remote images all work.

Flutter apps now debug in Dart: the build rewrites the class files' line tables and adds a JSR-45 source map, so stack traces name your .dart files and the standard Java debugger steps through Dart. The JavaScript port got faster too. It inlines getters and setters, fuses StringBuilder chains into plain string operations and keeps every array packed. String building in our compute suite went from 99 to 68 ms, and every checksum still matches the JVM. Integer division by zero now throws ArithmeticException in the browser, as Java says it should. Thursday's article covers all three.

Try it

The embedded Linux chapter covers displays, the GPU path, board profiles, deployment, hardware access, the five connected-product shapes and the full benchmark with its method. The harness is in scripts/embedded/bench in the repository if you want to rerun it on your own board. I'd love to see those numbers.

If you're building a device, tell me what board it runs on and what you're using today. And if your product needs an OS we don't support yet, that's exactly the conversation I want to have.

title: IP geolocation now covers more visitors at higher resolution
description:
IP geolocation on Vercel now resolves visitor locations with finer network granularity, delivering city-level data for nearly all requests and postal-code data for 90% of traffic.

Geolocation data is now refreshed more often, so locations keep up as IP ranges are reassigned and routing changes. This is enabled for all projects with no code or configuration changes required. Existing geolocation headers along with the geolocation() helper in @vercel/functions, return the same fields for Vercel Functions and Routing Middleware.

If you use geolocation for access controls, localization, or compliance, some visitors will now resolve to a different city or country, most often traffic from VPNs, hosting providers, and leased IP ranges:

  • Physical termination location:

    Subnets announced from a hosting provider in a different country than their regional internet registry (RIR) record now resolve to the data center where the traffic actually terminates.

  • Testing geo-dependent routes:

    Verify access rules against an IP's active network location rather than its static registry allocation.

Read the request headers documentation for all available geolocation headers and fields.

Read more

title: Spy on your competitors' Google ads (Search, YouTube, Display) and get alerted when they launch new ones
description:
Disclosure: I'm Lindenbyte, the small studio that built the Apify Actor used below, and this post was
drafted with AI assistance. Google's own Ads Transparency Center is free and works fine for a quick look;
the Actor adds bulk export, filters you can script, and daily runs.

Every advertiser on Google has a public page in the Ads Transparency Center:
every Search, YouTube and Display ad they run, with first-shown and last-shown dates. That is free
competitive intelligence, but the UI has no export, no "what's new since yesterday" and no alerts.
Here is how to get it as data, find a competitor's likely winners, and get pinged when they launch something new.

1. Pick the competitor: use the domain, not the name

Open the Google Ads Transparency Center Scraper
and give it domains:

{
  "queries": ["notion.com", "hubspot.com", "shopify.com"],
  "region": "US",
  "format": "all",
  "maxAdsPerAdvertiser": 300
}

A domain query returns ads that point to that domain, from all advertiser entities. A name query has to
guess which legal entity you mean, and it can guess wrong. When I ran "Notion", the log said:

"Notion" -> Notion Limited (AR01024198173649797121, ~80 ads). Other matches (pass the ID or a domain
to target them): Notion OU AR03733763719230914561; Notionmind AR08497814192110174209; ...

That picked a different company: 17 image ads, none shown since July. The notion.com query returned
125 ads, all from Notion Labs, Inc. So use the domain; if you do use a name, read that log line and pass
the right AR... ID (or raise maxAdvertisersPerQuery).

The domain query has a bonus: it also catches partners and resellers advertising your competitor.
For hubspot.com, 78 of the 300 ads came from 49 other advertisers (agencies, app vendors) pointing to hubspot.com.

Each row looks like this (trimmed):

{
  "advertiserName": "Hubspot, Inc.",
  "creativeId": "CR01111966079451660289",
  "format": "video",
  "firstShown": "2026-02-17T21:36:11.000Z",
  "lastShown": "2026-11-13T06:27:26.000Z",
  "daysActive": 269,
  "landingDomain": "hubspot.com",
  "transparencyUrl": "https://adstransparency.google.com/advertiser/AR10072600183532683265/creative/CR01111966079451660289"
}

Image ads carry an imageUrl, video and some text ads a previewUrl, and every row links to the ad on Google's own page.

2. Narrow it: region and format

region takes a country code (US, GB, DE, BG ...) or anywhere; format is all, text, image or video,
the same filters as Google's UI. Results come newest-first (by last shown), so maxAdsPerAdvertiser gives you
the most recently active ads and caps your cost.

Watch the cap with big advertisers. With "maxAdsPerAdvertiser": 1000 and "onlyNewSince": "2026-11-12",
shopify.com in the US hit the cap: 1,000 ads, all last shown in the previous ~10 hours. If a competitor is
that large, split the job by format or region so you are not looking at an arbitrary slice.

3. Analyze: what's new, what's working, what mix

Export as JSON and a few lines of pandas give you the picture:

import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_json("ads.json", convert_dates=["firstShown", "lastShown"])
now = pd.Timestamp.now(tz="UTC")
for q, g in df.groupby("query"):
    new30 = (g.firstShown >= now - pd.Timedelta(days=30)).sum()
    print(q, len(g), "ads |", new30, "first shown in last 30 days |", g.format.value_counts().to_dict())
    print(g.sort_values("daysActive", ascending=False)
           [["advertiserName", "format", "daysActive", "transparencyUrl"]].head(5).to_string(index=False))

What my run on 13 Nov 2026 (US) showed:

Domain Ads returned First shown in last 30 days Format mix (text / video / image) Running 180+ days
notion.com 125 (all) 7 79 / 32 / 14 22
hubspot.com 300 (cap) 22 216 / 74 / 10 196
shopify.com 300 (cap) 62 185 / 76 / 39 178

How to read it:

  • Long-running ads are probably winners. Nobody pays to keep a losing ad live for months. HubSpot's oldest still-active creatives were first shown in October 2021 (daysActive 1,846) and were still showing this week. Open those transparencyUrls first: that is the messaging they keep betting on.
  • Fresh ads show what they're testing now. Notion launched 3 new ads on 9 Nov; HubSpot's 22 new ads this month split 12 text, 9 video, 1 image, so they are pushing video harder than their overall mix.
  • Format mix shows where the budget goes. Roughly a quarter of HubSpot's and Shopify's recent ads are YouTube/video.

4. Get alerted when they launch something new

Set newAdsLastDays and the Actor returns only ads first shown in that window. Ads that are older but
still running are skipped, and you aren't charged for them. With HubSpot in the US and
"newAdsLastDays": 30, it returned 32 ads (all first shown on or after 15 Oct). That's more complete than
the 22 from step 3, which only looked at the 300 most recently shown ads.

Because the window is relative ("last N days"), the input never changes, so a plain Apify Schedule works:

{
  "queries": ["notion.com", "hubspot.com", "shopify.com"],
  "region": "US",
  "newAdsLastDays": 1,
  "maxAdsPerAdvertiser": 500
}

Save that as a task, add a daily Schedule, and attach a Slack or email integration (or a webhook) to
"run succeeded". If you'd rather handle the results in your own code:

# pip install apify-client
from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient("YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN")
run = client.actor("lindenbyte/google-ads-transparency-scraper").call(run_input={
    "queries": ["notion.com", "hubspot.com"],
    "region": "US",
    "newAdsLastDays": 1,
})
for ad in client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items():
    print(f'{ad["advertiserName"]} launched a {ad["format"]} ad: {ad["transparencyUrl"]}')

(onlyNewSince is different: it keeps ads last shown after a date, i.e. everything still running. Use
it for "what is live right now", not for alerts.)

Limits (honest ones)

  • Google's text format bucket also contains image-rendered ads: in my HubSpot sample, 210 of 216 "text" ads had an imageUrl. Treat format as Google's filter label, not a strict ad type.
  • No ad copy extraction yet: you get the image/preview link and Google's page, not the headline text as a field.
  • No per-region impression stats or audience targeting details; firstShown/lastShown are the dates Google publishes.
  • Very large advertisers (Shopify) can have more live ads than a sensible cap; filter by format/region.

Cost: $0.001 per ad plus $0.003 per run, so the 125-ad Notion pull is about $0.13. A daily
newAdsLastDays: 1 check only pays for the few ads launched that day: HubSpot's 32 new US ads in 30 days
come to about $0.12 a month, plus $0.09 for the 30 run fees.

Not affiliated with Google. Data comes from Google's public Ads Transparency Center; it is advertiser
business data, not personal data.

title: One Vite build, two runtimes: shipping a browser game to the open web and into an offline WebView
description:
I shipped ApexDrawn as a plain static site: you draw a closed loop, it becomes a racetrack, and then you drive it. Later I needed a second build target - a mobile shell that loads the same game from local assets with no network at all.

The interesting part wasn't the game logic. It was that the whole app assumed a server: accounts, /api/* for purchases and garage state, a WebSocket relay for races, analytics, payments. None of that can exist in an offline WebView. I didn't want a fork, so the split is one build-time flag and everything else follows from it.

One flag, two bundles 

// src/appMode.ts
export const OFFLINE_APP = import.meta.env.VITE_OFFLINE_APP === "true";

Because this is a compile-time constant, Rollup tree-shakes the unreachable branch. The offline bundle genuinely contains no auth SDK, no analytics and no checkout code - not "code that checks a boolean at runtime and returns early". That distinction matters when your CSP forbids all network egress: the easiest network call to forget is the one hidden behind a feature flag.

The web build emits absolute /assets/... URLs. The offline build is emitted with relative paths and copied under assets/web/ in the Flutter project, so its HTML references ./i18n.js and assets/index-*.js instead.

Replace the session at the boundary, not in every component

Components ask a context for authLoaded, signedIn, getToken() and user. The web provider wires that to an auth SDK. The offline provider is deliberately boring:

export function OfflineSessionProvider({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) {
  const session: AppSession = {
    authLoaded: true,
    signedIn: true,
    getToken: async () => "local-only",
    userLoaded: true,
    user: /* a local profile */ null,
  };
  return <SessionContext.Provider value={session}>{children}</SessionContext.Provider>;
}

No component needs if (offline). That's the whole point: one boundary, two implementations. The same trick covers state. Web state lives behind /api/*; offline state is a localStorage record with a schema version in the key (apexdrawn.offline-profile.v1) holding the balance, a ledger, owned items and tuning. Every read is defensive:

const raw = window.localStorage.getItem(STORAGE_KEY);
const parsed = JSON.parse(raw);
return {
  ...fallback,
  ...parsed,
  balance: Number.isFinite(Number(parsed.balance)) ? Math.max(0, Number(parsed.balance)) : 0,
  ledger: Array.isArray(parsed.ledger) ? parsed.ledger : [],
};

If storage is unavailable or contains garbage, it falls back to an in-memory copy. A WebView can and will hand you a corrupted profile; treating local storage as a trusted typed object is how you get a crash on launch.

Relative paths are the actual hard part

The site uses directory-style routes (/garage/, /free-racing-games/, /es/...). On a normal host the server resolves those. Inside a WebView loading assets/web/garage/index.html, a relative asset URL resolves relative to that file, so the correct prefix depends on how deep the current page is.

The fix is a small path helper that strips the assets/web/ prefix, counts the remaining segments, and builds the prefix from that depth:

const marker = "/assets/web/";
const markerIndex = pathname.lastIndexOf(marker);
const suffix = markerIndex >= 0 ? pathname.slice(markerIndex + marker.length) : pathname;
const segments = suffix.split("/").filter(Boolean);
if (segments.at(-1) === "index.html") segments.pop();
const rootPrefix = "../".repeat(segments.length);

Extensionless routes get normalized to index.html, query strings are preserved, and publicAsset() passes through data:, blob: and https?: URLs untouched. Routing itself uses the same logic: appPathParts() removes the WebView mount prefix so the app sees /garage whether it's hosted at a domain root or six directories deep in an APK.

Language selection had the same shape. On the web, the language is the first path segment:

const pathLanguage = window.location.pathname.split("/").filter(Boolean)[0]?.toLowerCase();
if (pathLanguage in localeByLanguage) return pathLanguage;

Offline there is no meaningful path segment, so it reads a stored preference (apexLang) and finally falls back to document.documentElement.lang. Same public API, different source of truth.

Enforce offline with the platform, not with discipline

The offline HTML injects a strict CSP before anything else:

default-src 'self' data: blob:; connect-src 'self'; object-src 'none';
base-uri 'self'; form-action 'self'; navigate-to 'self'

It also short-circuits fetch, XMLHttpRequest and sendBeacon for cross-origin or /api|auth|oauth URLs, neuters window.open, and cancels clicks on external links in the capture phase. This is belt-and-braces: even if a component accidentally tries to phone home, it can't.

Native purchases go through an explicit bridge instead. The JS side posts a message to the host, listens for a CustomEvent, and matches on a request id:

window.addEventListener("apexdrawn:purchase-result", onResult);
bridge.postMessage(JSON.stringify({ type: "purchase", requestId, packageId }));

A 180-second timeout, a matching requestId, and validation of packageId plus transactionId before resolving. An async bridge without those checks is a race condition waiting for a referee.

A third shape, almost free

There are also ~49 static landing pages generated by a Node script from a template. For those, the script strips the main module bundle and modulepreload links and replaces them with a tiny /info-page.js plus a stylesheet:

html = html.replace(/\s*<script defer src="\/i18n\.js"><\/script>/,
                    '<script defer src="/info-page.js"></script>');
html = html.replace(/\s*<script type="module"[^>]*src="\/assets\/[^\"]+\.js"[^>]*><\/script>/, "");

Those pages are content, not an app. Shipping a full SPA bundle to them would be pure cost. It's the same lesson as the offline build in miniature: decide what a page actually needs, then remove the rest.

What this costs

  • Every networked feature needs two implementations. That's a real ongoing tax, not a one-time setup.
  • The build matrix is easy to get wrong. I once nearly deployed the offline dist/ to the live site; the analytics code had been tree-shaken out, so the site would have quietly stopped reporting. Build flags belong in CI, not in someone's memory.
  • Offline state doesn't sync. Local coins, unlocks and tuning are device-local by definition. That's a product decision, not a technical bug.
  • Store rules differ. An offline in-app purchase goes through the platform's billing, with its own review and receipt semantics.

The upside is one set of game logic and one place to fix a bug. Keep the differences at a handful of explicit boundaries (session, state, asset paths, network), and the rest of the codebase never learns that there are two runtimes.

The playable web build is at https://apexdrawn.org/ - no download or account needed. If you've shipped a Vite app inside a WebView, I'd like to hear which boundary caused you the most trouble.

title: 10 PCB faults that pass DRC and still cause a respin
description:
Your PCB passed DRC with zero errors. The Gerbers look clean in the viewer. So the board is ready for fab, right?

Not quite. DRC checks the rules you gave the tool. It has no idea what the board is meant to do. In design reviews we keep finding the same small group of faults on boards that passed every automated check. Each one is cheap to fix on screen and expensive to fix after the boards come back.

Here are ten of them, with the quick check that catches each one.

1. The right part with the wrong suffix

A regulator, an LDO or a MOSFET can come in fixed and adjustable versions, or in two packages, under nearly the same part number. The schematic symbol is drawn for one variant and the BOM orders the other. DRC can't see it because the footprint is fine.

Check: read the full ordering code in the BOM against the datasheet ordering table. Every character, including the suffix.

2. Strap pins that float at power-up

Many processors and wireless SoCs read a few pins at reset to choose the boot mode. If one of those pins also drives an LED or goes to a header, the boot mode depends on whatever else is on that net. The board boots on the bench and fails in the field.

Check: list every strap pin from the datasheet. Confirm its level at reset with everything else on the net taken into account.

3. Land patterns copied from the wrong package

A QFN from one vendor and a "compatible" part from another can differ in exposed pad size and pin 1 position. A generic library footprint looks right in 3D and still solders badly.

Check: compare pad size, pitch, pin 1 and the thermal pad against the recommended land pattern in the datasheet of the exact part you are ordering.

4. A fast signal crossing a plane split

The trace is fine. The return current is not. When a clock or a high-speed line crosses a gap in its reference plane, the return path takes a long detour. That shows up as emissions and noise that are very hard to debug later.

Check: turn on the reference plane under each fast net and follow the trace. Any crossing of a split, slot or void needs a stitching capacitor or a reroute.

5. A switching regulator hot loop that grew during routing

The layout guide shows the input capacitor right next to the switch. Then a connector moved, the capacitor moved with it and the loop doubled in area. Nothing fails DRC. The rail rings and the EMI scan fails.

Check: highlight the input capacitor, the switch node and the ground return. Compare the loop area to the reference layout in the datasheet.

6. Impedance traces that don't match the fab's stackup

The trace width was set from a calculator using a generic stackup. The fab builds with different prepreg and the impedance lands outside tolerance.

Check: get the stackup from your fab first and size controlled-impedance traces from their numbers. Put the targets and tolerance on the fab drawing.

7. DRC run with tool defaults

The default rule set in most EDA tools is not your fab's capability. Minimum annular ring, drill to copper and mask expansion all vary by fab and by price tier.

Check: load the fab's published rules into the tool before the final DRC. Keep the rule file in the project.

8. MLCC capacitance measured at 0 V

A 10 uF 0603 capacitor at 5 V DC bias can deliver a fraction of its rated value. The regulator loop was designed around the full 10 uF.

Check: look up the DC bias curve for each bulk MLCC at the real working voltage. Size up the case or add parts if needed.

9. Connector orientation that only works in 2D

The connector is placed correctly on the board. In the enclosure the cable has to bend 180 degrees to reach it, or the latch faces a wall.

Check: check mating side, latch direction and cable exit against the enclosure model or the mechanical drawing, not only the PCB view.

10. Output files that don't match the design of record

A late ECO changed the schematic. The netlist and BOM in the release folder are from the day before. The fab builds what you sent, not what you meant.

Check: regenerate every output from the same revision. Confirm the revision text on copper or silkscreen matches the file names and release notes.

Use a checklist, at three gates

None of these checks is hard. They get skipped because they happen at the end, under time pressure, by the same person who drew the board. Two things help.

First, run reviews at three gates instead of one: schematic freeze, after placement and before release. Most of the items above are much cheaper to catch at the first two gates.

Second, rank findings. A Critical finding means the board won't work or can't be built. A Major finding means it might work on the bench but will likely need a respin. A Minor finding is documentation or style. Release only with zero open Critical and Major items.

We published our full 42-point list as a free, open checklist on GitHub so you can copy it into your own release process: PCB design review checklist on GitHub. It comes as Markdown and CSV under CC BY 4.0. The longer write-up with the reasoning behind each check is on our blog: PCB design review checklist: the checks we run before fab.

If your board is part of a product moving from prototype to production, the review gates map well onto EVT, DVT and PVT builds. This guide explains what each build should prove: EVT, DVT and PVT explained.

Circuit Board Design is the PCB design division of Electuni LLC, a US company founded in 2016. We have delivered 500+ PCB designs and our lead designer is IPC CID+ certified. If you want a second set of eyes before fab, we offer a free quick design check.

title: How Does Discord Work?
description:
TL;DR

  • Discord runs text and voice as separate systems, because messages must never be lost but audio can’t wait.
  • Text goes through an HTTPS API and a Gateway WebSocket. Messages are stored in ScyllaDB, which replaced Cassandra in 2022.
  • Voice setup uses a WebSocket, and the audio travels over UDP through a selective forwarding unit (SFU) that copies packets to everyone in the call.
  • Since March 2026, calls are end-to-end encrypted with the DAVE protocol. Text is not.

Before Discord, talking to friends while you played a game took real effort. Like, being in the same room as them! Or you could use voice chat services like TeamSpeak, Ventrilo, or Mumble. But that meant someone in the group had to rent or run a server and hand out an IP address and port. Yes, Skype existed, but it could expose your IP address to the people on the call, and getting knocked offline mid-match by a sore loser was a real thing.

And you needed an entirely different setup for chat, on a forum or in IRC.

Discord blew all that away. One app for all your pwning. You join a server from an invite link, the text channels keep every message anyone has ever sent, and the voice channels are always there. Just join and enjoy.

How? Today Discord stores trillions of messages. Single servers have had more than a million people online at once, and since 2025, voice traffic has moved to an edge network with locations in over 300 cities. Discord's engineers have written about it in detail, but here we’re going to go over what is known about how Discord works, how it stores and serves text and voice from millions of users, and what you can learn if you’re looking to build your own platform for the world’s gamers.

How Discord Is Put Together

Text and voice are completely different mediums, and need opposite things from a network.

A chat message must never be lost, but nobody minds if it takes half a second to appear. Audio can't wait that 500 milliseconds, but you can drop the packet and move on.

Understandably, then, Discord runs the two as separate systems and the client (web, mobile, or desktop) holds connections to both.

Text and State Voice and Video
Client connections HTTPS API and the Gateway WebSocket A second "voice" WebSocket and a UDP socket
What travels over them Messages, reactions, presence, permissions, who's in which voice channel Opus audio and video frames in RTP packets
Transport TCP UDP for media, TCP for the voice WebSocket
What's on the backend API servers, Elixir guild and session processes, Rust data services, ScyllaDB Voice servers, each running a signaling component and an SFU

What the app calls a server is called a guild inside Discord (engineers keep the word "server" for actual machines. A guild records members, roles, channels, and permissions. One Elixir process per guild routes events to whichever members are connected.

Channels are different, again. A voice channel exists whether or not anyone's in it, the opposite of a Zoom meeting. Nobody schedules anything or sends a link. People join, talk, and leave, and the channel stays put.

The only link between the chat and voice systems is the moment you join a voice channel. The request goes out over the Gateway WebSocket on the chat side, the guild picks a voice server, and your client gets its address back. From then on, the audio never goes near the chat system.

The two systems also live in different places. The Gateway and the guild processes run in Google Cloud. Voice servers are spread around the world so that one is near you, because distance adds latency to every packet.

How Your Client Stays Connected

A chat client can't keep asking the server whether anything's new. With millions of people online, polling would swamp the API, and messages would still show up late. So the client talks to Discord in two ways:

  • The HTTPS API is for doing things. Sending a message, adding a reaction, changing a setting, and loading older history are all ordinary REST calls.
  • The Gateway is for hearing about things. It's a WebSocket that the client opens at startup and keeps open, and Discord pushes events down it as they happen.

Setting up the Gateway goes like this:

  1. The client connects, and Discord sends a Hello message containing a heartbeat_interval.
  2. The client sends an Identify message with its token. Discord answers with a Ready event, which includes a session_id and the guilds the user belongs to.
  3. Events start arriving. Each one has a type (t), a payload (d), and a sequence number (s).
  4. Every heartbeat_interval milliseconds, the client sends a heartbeat containing the last sequence number it received.

A new message arriving looks like this:

{
  "op": 0,
  "t": "MESSAGE_CREATE",
  "s": 1042,
  "d": {
    "id": "1551636673593475079",
    "channel_id": "613425648685547541",
    "author": { "id": "268473310986240001", "username": "Potatoaim", "global_name": "PotatoAim" },
    "content": "hello",
    "timestamp": "2026-09-21T16:50:11.000000+00:00"
  }
}

The sequence number is what lets a shaky connection recover. If your laptop drops off Wi-Fi for a few seconds, the client reconnects and sends a Resume message with its session_id and the last sequence number it saw, and Discord replays the events it missed. If the gap was too long, Discord rejects the resume. The client then sends an Identify message again and starts a new session. Nothing is replayed that time, so the client loads the current state from scratch.

On Discord's side, the other end of that WebSocket is an Elixir process. Every connected client gets its own session process, and every guild gets a guild process. Elixir runs on the Erlang VM, the same runtime WhatsApp uses, and for the same reason. It was built to run millions of small processes that send messages to each other.

How a Message Gets to Everyone in the Channel

Say PotatoAim types “hello” in #general, in a server he shares with Lagw1zard and CtrlAltDefeat.

  1. PotatoAim's client sends a POST to /channels/{channel.id}/messages over HTTPS.
  2. The API checks his token, checks that his roles allow him to post in #general, and checks that he isn't over the rate limit.
  3. The message gets an ID. Every ID on Discord is a Snowflake. It's a 64-bit number, and the top 42 bits are a millisecond timestamp counted from the first second of 2015, so sorting by ID also sorts by time.
  4. The message is written to the messages database.
  5. The guild process for that server picks up the new message and fans it out to the session process of every member who's online and allowed to see #general.
  6. Each session process pushes a MESSAGE_CREATE event down its client's Gateway connection, and hello appears on Lagw1zard's and CtrlAltDefeat's screens.

So when does Lagw1zard see it? If she has Discord open, at step 6. If her connection blipped, the Resume replay delivers it a moment later. If she's been offline for a week, nothing was held for her. When she opens #general, her client asks the API for the channel's recent messages, which is the same call it makes when you scroll back.

WhatsApp handles this the other way round. It queues messages for offline users and deletes them once they're delivered. Discord keeps everything, so the stored history does the queue's job.

How the Same Fanout Works With a Million People Online

Fanout is easy for three friends. For Midjourney's server, which pushed Discord past a million people online at once in a single guild, it's a serious problem. A guild process is a single Elixir process, so it runs on one core, and the fanout work grows with both the number of members and how much they post.

Discord made two changes:

  • Passive sessions. If you're in a server but haven't opened it, Discord marks your session as passive. The guild skips the permission checks for you and sends your client far less until you click in. About 90% of the connections to large servers turned out to be passive, which made the fanout 90% cheaper.
  • Relays. A relay processing layer sits between the guild and the sessions. Each relay handles permission checks and fanout for its own slice of sessions, spreading the work across many cores.

A five-person server works the way it always did, with one guild process sending to five sessions.

How Discord Stores Trillions of Messages

Discord decided early on to keep all chat history forever. This means the message table only ever grows. By January 2017, it was taking in more than 120 million messages a day, and Discord found that reads were about as frequent as writes. And because of the way Discord is set up, servers behave differently from each other:

  • A server that's mostly used for voice might send a message or two every few days, fewer than 1,000 a year. Loading its last 50 messages means random disk seeks, and those push other data out of the disk cache.
  • A small private server that's mostly text sends between 100,000 and a million messages a year. Its members only want recent messages, but there are fewer than 100 of them, so they don't ask often enough to keep those messages in cache.
  • A large public server sends millions of messages a year, and thousands of members read the last hour of chat all day long. That data stays in cache.

Discord initially kept messages in one MongoDB collection with a compound index on channel_id and created_at. That lasted until about 100 million messages in late 2015, when the data and the index stopped fitting in RAM and latency became unpredictable. They then moved to Cassandra.

How the Messages Table Is Laid Out

Discord describes Cassandra as a KKV store, where the two Ks make up the primary key:

  • The first K is the partition key, which decides which node a row lives on and where it sits on disk.
  • The second K is the clustering key, which identifies a row within its partition and sets the order in which rows are stored.

Every message query is only about one channel, so channel_id became the partition key. created_at couldn't be the clustering key, because two messages can be created at the same time. The message ID could, because it's a Snowflake and already sorts by time. That gave a primary key of (channel_id, message_id).

A channel can run for years, so a partition keyed on the channel alone would keep growing, and Cassandra handles very large partitions badly. Discord added a bucket to the partition key, a number for the ten-day window a message falls in, and the 2023 version of the table still uses the same key:

CREATE TABLE messages (
  channel_id bigint,
  bucket int,
  message_id bigint,
  author_id bigint,
  content text,
  PRIMARY KEY ((channel_id, bucket), message_id)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (message_id DESC);

The bucket comes straight out of the message ID. Take the millisecond timestamp in its top 42 bits, divide by the number of milliseconds in ten days, and round down. PotatoAim’s “hello” from earlier lands in bucket 428.

To load a channel's recent messages:

  1. The API works out the current bucket and the bucket the channel was created in. A channel ID is a Snowflake too, so the creation time is already in the ID, and no message can be older than the channel.
  2. It reads the newest bucket's partition. Rows are stored newest first, so this is the top of the partition.
  3. If that doesn't return enough messages, it moves to the bucket before and keeps going until it has enough or reaches the channel's first bucket.

A busy channel gets everything it needs from the first partition. A channel that's been silent for three months makes the API walk back through nine empty buckets before it finds anything. Discord accepted that because active servers are the majority, and the query code remembers which buckets came back empty for a channel and skips them the next time.

How Discord Got From Cassandra to ScyllaDB

By early 2022, the cluster had grown from 12 nodes in 2017 to 177, held trillions of messages, and was paging the on-call team regularly. Latency was unpredictable, compactions kept falling behind, and JVM garbage collection pauses sometimes got bad enough that an operator had to reboot a node by hand.

Hot partitions were a big part of it. Take an @everyone announcement in a server with hundreds of thousands of members. They all open the same channel within seconds and ask for the same rows, which all sit in one partition on three nodes. Reads cost more than writes in Cassandra, so those nodes fell behind. Discord reads and writes at quorum, so every other query that touched those nodes slowed down with them.

Discord fixed it in two places:

  • The first fix sits in front of the database. Rust “data services” run between the API and the database. If a thousand requests for the same row arrive at once, the first one starts a query, and the other 999 subscribe to its result, so the database is asked once. Discord calls this request coalescing. Requests are routed by channel ID, so everything for one channel reaches the same instance, and more duplicates get caught.
  • The second was the database itself. In May 2022, Discord moved the messages cluster to ScyllaDB, which had been on its list to explore since 2017. ScyllaDB speaks the same query language as Cassandra but is written in C++, so there's no JVM garbage collector to pause it.
Cassandra ScyllaDB
Nodes 177 72
p99 latency, fetching history 40 to 125 ms 15 ms
p99 latency, inserting a message 5 to 70 ms 5 ms

The off-the-shelf migration tool estimated three months to move the data. The team wrote its own migrator in Rust, which peaked at 3.2 million messages a second and finished in nine days. Seven months later, during the 2022 World Cup final, every goal showed up as a spike in Discord's message graphs. The cluster took the load without trouble.

How Joining a Voice Channel Works

Audio can't go through the Gateway. A WebSocket runs over TCP, and when TCP loses a packet, it holds back everything behind it until the retransmission arrives. Nobody notices that in a text chat. In a conversation, it's a half-second freeze followed by a burst of stale audio. So Discord sends audio over UDP and uses WebSockets only to set up the call.

When PotatoAim clicks a voice channel:

  1. His client sends a Voice State Update over the main Gateway, naming the guild and the channel.
  2. The guild picks a voice server. All the voice channels in a guild share one voice server, so if people are already talking, PotatoAim is sent to theirs. If he's first in, the guild assigns the least loaded voice server in the region. That's the "Awaiting Endpoint" status you sometimes catch in the client.
  3. The Gateway sends back two events. One contains a session_id. The other, Voice Server Update, contains a token and the voice server's address.
  4. The client opens a second WebSocket to that address and identifies itself with the session ID and token. The voice server replies with an IP address, a UDP port, an SSRC that will label PotatoAim's audio stream, and the encryption modes it supports.
  5. The client opens a UDP socket to that IP and port. PotatoAim is probably behind a home router doing NAT, so the client first sends a small IP discovery packet, and the voice server replies with the public IP and port it saw. The client reports those back over the voice WebSocket, along with the encryption mode it picked.
  6. The voice server replies with a 32-byte secret key. The client sends a Speaking message, and audio starts flowing.

From there, PotatoAim's microphone audio is encoded with Opus at 48 kHz, wrapped in RTP packets, encrypted with that key, and sent over UDP. The voice WebSocket stays open for the small stuff, such as who's speaking, who joined, and heartbeats.

Discord's desktop and mobile apps cut a lot out of standard WebRTC to make this quick. WebRTC normally describes a call with SDP, which can run to ten kilobytes, and hunts for a network path with ICE. The native apps skip both. Every client connects to a Discord server with a public address, so there's no peer-to-peer path to find, and the whole exchange above comes to about a kilobyte. The browser client has no such freedom, since it has to use the browser's own WebRTC stack.

How Audio and Video Get From One Person to Everyone Else

With six people in a voice channel, PotatoAim's audio has to reach five other people. If his laptop sent five copies, his upload would grow with the channel size, and everyone in it would learn everyone else's IP address.

Discord puts a server in the middle. Each voice server runs a selective forwarding unit, or SFU. PotatoAim uploads one stream, and the SFU copies his packets to the other five by reading each packet's header and forwarding it, without decoding or mixing any audio. Each receiving client holds packets briefly in a jitter buffer, decrypts them, decodes them, and mixes the voices itself.

Camera video and Go Live screen shares take the same route, as RTP packets over UDP to an SFU that forwards them without decoding. A Go Live stream has to be watchable for every viewer, so the streamer won't send more than the slowest viewer's connection can take. Conferencing tools such as Zoom avoid that with simulcast, where the sender uploads several qualities, and the server picks one for each viewer.

Routing every call through a server also means:

  • Nobody on the call sees your IP address. Only Discord does, which ends the DDoS problem that came with peer-to-peer calls.
  • Moderation happens in the SFU. When a moderator server-mutes someone, the SFU drops that person's packets.
  • Nothing is sent while you're quiet. The native apps stop sending packets when you stop talking. In a big channel, only a few people talk at once, so that's a large saving, and sequence numbers are rewritten so the gap doesn't look like packet loss.

Voice servers fail, and since they're the only part of the backend exposed directly to the internet, they get DDoSed as well. Recovery is the same in both cases. The dead server drops out of service discovery, the guild picks a new one and pushes the channel's state to it, and every client receives a new Voice Server Update and reconnects. You hear a short dropout and the call carries on.

Discord picks one SFU to host an entire call, and every participant stays connected to that machine for the duration of the call. Calls aren't split across regions the way Zoom does it with cascaded media servers. So a call's quality depends heavily on where that one host is.

In 2018, the host was one of about 850 voice servers in 13 regions. Since 2025, Discord has been moving voice and video onto Cloudflare's edge network, which has locations in over 300 cities, and by June 2026 more than 80% of that traffic ran there. Discord has also been rolling out a new SFU written in Rust to replace the original C++ one. Each host runs eight worker threads, and each thread has its own UDP socket.

How Calls Are Encrypted End to End

Every call goes through Discord's servers, so for years the honest answer to “can Discord hear this?” was yes. Audio was encrypted between your client and the voice server, using the secret key from the handshake, and the server had that key too.

That changed with DAVE, Discord's end-to-end encryption protocol for audio and video. The rollout started in September 2024, and since early March 2026 every call is end-to-end encrypted by default, across DMs, group DMs, voice channels, and Go Live streams. Clients that don't support DAVE can no longer join calls.

In a DAVE call:

  1. Everyone in the call joins a Messaging Layer Security (MLS) group. MLS is an IETF standard for agreeing on keys in a group whose membership keeps changing.
  2. Each participant derives their own sender key from the group's secret, and encrypts every audio and video frame with AES-128-GCM before it's split into packets.
  3. When someone joins or leaves, the group moves to a new epoch and everyone's keys change. A newcomer can't decrypt what was said before they arrived, and someone who left can't decrypt what comes after.

The voice server is still involved. It acts as the MLS group's external sender, which lets it propose adding and removing members as people connect and disconnect, and it never holds the group's keys. The transport encryption from the handshake is still there, wrapped around the already encrypted frames. The SFU can read the RTP headers it needs for routing and can't decode the media inside.

The protocol and the implementation are both public, and Trail of Bits audited them.

Stage channels are the exception. They're built for broadcasting to large audiences, and Discord doesn't end-to-end encrypt them. Text isn't end-to-end encrypted either, and Discord says it has no plans to change that because many of its features rely on the server being able to read messages. Search, AutoMod, and every bot that reads message content work that way.

How Discord Got Here

The first version of Discord was built in under two months in early 2015, with everything stored in a single MongoDB replica set. There was no ScyllaDB cluster, no relays, and no edge network. Each piece arrived when the last one stopped coping.

If you're building a Discord-like app yourself, that's the encouraging part. You can start with the tools that exist today for chat, voice, and video, and worry about a million people in one server when you have them.

title: Architecting Full-Stack React & Django Web Applications: Zero-Bloat REST APIs, Edge Caching, and Sub-Second Core Web Vitals
description:
Architecting Full-Stack React & Django Web Applications: Zero-Bloat REST APIs, Edge Caching, and Sub-Second Core Web Vitals

When modern businesses scale beyond static websites or monolithic templates, they frequently choose a decoupled architecture: a reactive React / Next.js frontend paired with a resilient, security-hardened Python / Django REST Framework (DRF) backend.

However, many decoupled implementations suffer from severe architectural anti-patterns:

  1. Network Cascades & N+1 Database Queries: Serial API requests and unindexed database queries causing Time to First Byte (TTFB) to surge past 1,200ms.
  2. Client-Side Bundle Bloat: Oversized JavaScript bundles (>2.5MB) blocking the main thread, resulting in catastrophic Interaction to Next Paint (INP > 400ms) and slow Largest Contentful Paint (LCP > 3.5s).
  3. State Management Friction: Overly complex global state stores causing unnecessary full-tree re-renders and memory leaks.

At UCDREAMS, our senior engineering team builds bespoke, enterprise-grade custom web applications, SaaS platforms, and high-performance business portals. In this engineering guide, we break down our battle-tested production blueprint for deploying React + Django web apps that guarantee sub-second TTFB, 95+ PageSpeed scores, and flawless Core Web Vitals.

1. Architectural Topology: Decoupled & High-Speed

To deliver enterprise reliability and sub-second user interactions, we decouple concerns across three tiers:

[ Client Browser / Mobile WebView ]
               │
               ▼  (HTTP/3 + Brotli Compression)
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Edge Proxy & CDN (Caddy / Cloudflare)       │
│  • Edge TLS Termination & Automated Certs    │
│  • Micro-Caching Static Assets & GET Payloads│
└──────────────────────┬───────────────────────┘
                       │
       ┌───────────────┴───────────────┐
       ▼                               ▼
┌───────────────────────────┐   ┌───────────────────────────┐
│ React / Next.js Frontend  │   │ Django REST Framework API │
│ • Tree-shaken bundle      │   │ • Gunicorn + Uvicorn Async│
│ • Code-split chunks       │   │ • Redis Cache Layer       │
│ • Web Workers Offloading  │   │ • Celery Task Queue       │
└───────────────────────────┘   └─────────────┬─────────────┘
                                              │
                                              ▼
                                ┌───────────────────────────┐
                                │ PostgreSQL 16 + PgBouncer │
                                │ • Indexed Foreign Keys    │
                                │ • Read/Write Pooling      │
                                └───────────────────────────┘

2. Eliminating Database Bottlenecks in Django REST Framework

The most frequent culprit behind slow API endpoints is the infamous N+1 query problem in Django ORM serializations.

When serializing relational data (e.g., an order with customer profile, items, and billing address), naive querysets execute an additional SQL SELECT for every single relational child row.

The Solution: Strategic select_related and prefetch_related 

# views.py - Optimized Queryset Pipeline
from rest_framework import generics
from rest_framework.permissions import IsAuthenticated
from .models import EnterpriseProject
from .serializers import EnterpriseProjectSerializer

class EnterpriseProjectListView(generics.ListAPIView):
    serializer_class = EnterpriseProjectSerializer
    permission_classes = [IsAuthenticated]

    def get_queryset(self):
        return (
            EnterpriseProject.objects
            .filter(organization=self.request.user.organization)
            .select_related('client', 'lead_architect', 'billing_profile')
            .prefetch_related('milestones__tasks', 'deliverables', 'technology_stack')
            .only(
                'id', 'title', 'status', 'created_at', 'budget_estimate',
                'client__name', 'client__email', 'lead_architect__username'
            )
        )

Architectural Gains:

  • Reduces database roundtrips from 150+ individual queries down to 2 unified SQL queries.
  • Reduces database latency from 850ms to 18ms.
  • Drops memory overhead during serialization by fetching only designated fields via .only().

3. High-Concurrency Connection Pooling with PgBouncer

Django establishes a new database connection per thread/process by default. Under traffic spikes or concurrent API bursts, PostgreSQL connection limits are rapidly exhausted, leading to FATAL: remaining connection slots are reserved for non-superuser connections.

We enforce connection pooling via PgBouncer in transaction pooling mode:

; pgbouncer.ini
[databases]
enterprise_db = host=127.0.0.1 port=5432 dbname=enterprise_db pool_mode=transaction

[pgbouncer]
listen_addr = 0.0.0.0
listen_port = 6432
auth_type = scram-sha-256
auth_file = /etc/pgbouncer/userlist.txt
max_client_conn = 2000
default_pool_size = 30
min_pool_size = 10
reserve_pool_size = 5
reserve_pool_timeout = 3
server_idle_timeout = 60

4. Sub-Second React Architecture: Zero-Bloat Bundle & INP Under 50ms

To guarantee 95+ PageSpeed scores on desktop and mobile, the React client must minimize main-thread execution time.

Route-Level Dynamic Splitting & Idle Hydration 

// AppRoutes.tsx
import React, { Suspense, lazy } from 'react';
import SkeletonLoader from './components/SkeletonLoader';

const DashboardAnalytics = lazy(() => 
  import(/* webpackChunkName: "dashboard-analytics" */ './views/DashboardAnalytics')
);
const ProjectIntakeForm = lazy(() => 
  import(/* webpackChunkName: "project-intake" */ './views/ProjectIntakeForm')
);

export const AppRoutes: React.FC = () => (
  <Suspense fallback={<SkeletonLoader count={4} />}>
    <Routes>
      <Route path="/dashboard" element={<DashboardAnalytics />} />
      <Route path="/intake" element={<ProjectIntakeForm />} />
    </Routes>
  </Suspense>
);

Offloading Heavy Computations to Web Workers

Any client-side data parsing, PDF rendering, or file processing must run off the main UI thread. We showcase this zero-lag principle across all our free utilities in the UCDREAMS Tools Hub, including our zero-server FileShareOnline WebRTC 50GB Transfer and client-side Free Online DOCX Editor.

5. Production Docker Compose & Caddy Reverse Proxy

Here is our production deployment configuration utilizing Caddy 2 for automated Let's Encrypt TLS and Zstandard/Brotli compression:

# Caddyfile
api.yourdomain.com {
    encode zstd gzip

    # Reverse proxy to Django Gunicorn socket
    reverse_proxy django_api:8000 {
        header_up Host {host}
        header_up X-Real-IP {remote}
        header_up X-Forwarded-For {remote}
        header_up X-Forwarded-Proto {scheme}
    }

    # Security headers
    header {
        Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains; preload"
        X-Content-Type-Options "nosniff"
        X-Frame-Options "DENY"
        Referrer-Policy "strict-origin-when-cross-origin"
    }
}

Summary & Benchmark Results

By systematically engineering both the backend query pipeline and client-side asset delivery:

  • Server Response Time (TTFB): Reduced from 920ms to 140ms.
  • First Contentful Paint (FCP): Under 0.8 seconds.
  • Interaction to Next Paint (INP): Under 45 milliseconds.
  • Core Web Vitals: 100% Passed across mobile and desktop.

Need Custom Full-Stack Web Development or Performance Optimization?

If your company requires bespoke full-stack web applications, React/Next.js platforms, Python/Django architectures, or custom WordPress engineering with guaranteed 95+ PageSpeed scores:

title: Welvet: a Go AI engine that trains and runs on your hardware, from Raspberry Pi to CUDA, Metal, Vulkan, ROCm, MLX, and Qualcomm NPU
description:
Round 1 demos on Linux, Windows, macOS, iOS, and Android. These are working paths on real hardware, not a claim that anything is fastest or best.

I built Welvet because I wanted a Go engine that can actually train and run neural nets on my own machines, not just ship tensors off to somewhere else.

Source is at github.com/openfluke/welvet. There's a product page at openfluke.com/welvet and a feature book at openfluke.github.io/welvet.

This is a walkthrough of v1.7: backends, training modes, storage, and some of the messier runs (Macs, cheap VMs, ~1GB Raspberry Pi 3Bs).

What it does

Roughly four jobs:

  • Run: load weights, compute, get an answer
  • Train: update those weights from experience
  • Store: keep dtypes and quants as they are (no fake float32 master copy)
  • Measure: check what the chosen hardware actually did

Defaults are portable Go: CPU tiling, Plan 9 SIMD, and WebGPU. Extra accelerators are opt-in mounts. No silent "Prefer" path that pretends GPU/NPU work happened when it didn't.

Snapshot (v1.7)

Area What you get
Language Open-source Go AI / ML engine
Core Train + local inference
Numbers 34 storage dtypes, 20 quant formats, storage-truth (no QAT morph)
Training 29 named training modes, including cameral / multi-branch
Defaults Go CPU tiled, Plan 9 SIMD, WebGPU
Optional CPU NativeCPU via welvet.cpp C ABI
NVIDIA CUDA sessions (train + SyncToGo)
AMD ROCm sessions (library validated; GPU compute needs HSA)
Apple Metal train/run, MLX forward-only
Vulkan Linux x86_64 train + SyncToGo
Qualcomm Hexagon HTP on Windows ARM64 (Snapdragon X)
Other Layer packages, spatial grids, MoE / cameral parallelism
Platforms Linux, Windows, macOS (app also targets iOS and Android)
Docs Book chapters, examples, w2a validation

Paragon and Loom were earlier engines in the same project line. Welvet is the rewrite. They're history, not competing products.

Where it can run

Unsupported hosts soft-SKIP. Caps reject unsupported layer×dtype instead of lying.

Defaults

  1. Go CPU tiled (BackendCPUTiled): full layer set, 34 dtypes, 20 quants, train modes
  2. Plan 9 SIMD (BackendSIMD): Dense + Softmax/SiLU fused paths on amd64/arm64
  3. WebGPU (BackendWebGPU): Dense/MHA/CNN/norms and friends on compatible GPUs

NativeCPU

BackendNativeCPU + SyncToNative can push FormatNone forward, NormalBP, and TrainMode updates through sibling welvet.cpp on linux/amd64. Sync pending weights before writing .entity.

Optional accelerators

Backend Sibling Hosts Forward Train Notes
Apple Metal welvet.metal / nativemetal.Mount Apple silicon macOS Yes Yes Explicit SyncToGo. Not Apple Neural Engine. Book §82–88
Apple MLX welvet.mlx / nativemlx Apple silicon macOS Yes No Forward-only. Book §110–113
NVIDIA CUDA welvet.cuda / nativecuda.Mount Linux x86_64, Windows amd64 Yes Yes Two weight copies until SyncToGo(). Book §89–95
AMD ROCm welvet.rocm / nativerocm.Mount Linux x86_64, Windows amd64 Yes (API) Yes (API) Library validated; GPU compute untested until HSA. Book §96–102
Vulkan welvet.vulkan / nativevulkan.Mount Linux x86_64 Yes Yes No silent host fallback labeled as Vulkan. Book §103–109
Qualcomm Hexagon HTP welvet.qnn / BackendQNN Windows ARM64 (Snapdragon X) Yes n/a Explicit sync/prepare. Never Prefer default. Book §79–81

Mixed Go/C++/GPU JSON routing exists on the mount backends. Automatic routing is Linux amd64 today. You own sync and placement.

Dtypes and quants stay real in storage. Not a QAT morph that quietly becomes float32 underneath.

Some published timings

Same shapes, honest timers from the book / matrices. Not "peak marketing" numbers.

Metal, Mamba forwards (book §88):

dtype Go Metal Metal/Go
float64 89.3ms 29.0ms 3.1×
float32 69.0ms 29.0ms 2.4×
float16 190.5ms 28.9ms 6.6×
bfloat16 149.4ms 29.0ms 5.1×
fp8e4m3 265.9ms 29.2ms 9.1×

Qualcomm NPU, large shapes (go_v_qnn on Snapdragon X; DLL graphExecute vs Go f32 CPU):

Layer dtype Go f32 NPU DLL vs Go
Dense u8 3.05ms 164µs ~95% faster
Dense f32 3.05ms 201µs ~93% faster
CNN2 i8 12.56ms 763µs ~94% faster
MHA f16 4.51ms 372µs ~92% faster

Online layers still pay compose cost on the full Go→NPU call. The book calls that out on purpose.

Where it can train

Training lives in the Go runtime (forward, backward, step, TrainMode). You're not exporting to another framework to learn.

29 training modes

Not just SGD/backprop. See §67 TrainMode.

Modes include StepBP, Tween*, TweenSplit, HeadProxy, Linear, FastProxy, Sparse, Alt, cameral BranchModes, and more. On the big Tide boards, non-SGD modes beat matched SGD on Acc about 97–98% of the time. SGD still wins some individual boards. It's a baseline, not the religion.

Cameral

Cameral stacks sibling branches that share an input, merge, and can train under different rules. CamSync averages cam weights (and same-shape cross-layer pairs). Useful when you want learn / keep / share jobs running together under load.

Lucy

Lucy scores whether a net can keep serving while it learns:

Lucy Score ≈ Throughput × Availability × Acc (scaled)

That's what drove the Tide/Ocean runs: cameral×LR sweeps, Test53 mode farms, volatile cloud soaks, Pi 1GB layer farms.

Train support by backend

Path Train?
Go CPU / SIMD / WebGPU Yes
NativeCPU (welvet.cpp) Yes
Metal Yes (TrainMSE, then SyncToGo)
CUDA Yes (train on GPU, SyncToGo before save)
Vulkan Yes
ROCm API yes; GPU compute pending HSA
MLX No (forward-only)
QNN Forward / prepare-exec; see book caps

Layers and the Dense core

Most transformer/CNN FLOPs are weights × activations, so Welvet keeps one Dense stack as the shared MatVec kernel (FormatNone×34 + 20 quants × CPU/SIMD/WebGPU). Layers that are mostly GEMV reuse it.

Layers include Dense, MHA (RoPE / GQA), SwiGLU, RMSNorm, LayerNorm, Embedding, Softmax, Sequential, Residual, CNN1–3, RNN/LSTM, SeqMix, GDN, Mamba, ConvT 1–3, Soft K-Means, Parallel, Metacognition.

Also: volumetric grids, ENTITY save/reload, HF helpers, tokenizer/sampling, DNA/evolution/tween, telemetry.

Runs on ugly hardware

Catalogue: openfluke.com/welvet/experiments

Four experiment waves (cameral LR, Test53 modes, volatile Linode soak, Pi 3B ~1GB farm) finished 90,334 Tide model cells.

  1. Cameral × LR: does width and LR matter under Lucy live-fit?
  2. Test53: dense × all 29 modes × storage types × aggressive LRs; Ocean compares cam1 vs cam3
  3. Volatile online: cheap VMs, restarts, crowded dashboards. Checkpoint resume mattered. Cells stayed storage-truth (no silent float32 "rescue")
  4. Pi 3B / 1GB: 22 layer sprints. Dense/CNN/norms were fast; MHA/LSTM/Mamba still finished. One dense champ hit Lucy Score ~16344 on fp4 tween_chain with >100k outputs/sec. CNN1 hit ~94% hard Acc on a Lucy champ. Mode-vs-SGD Acc beat-rates ~97–98%

I'm not claiming SOTA. The point is live-fit on honest storage, from Macs to $5 VMs to 1GB Pis, with artefacts you can open.

Welvet app (separate, still early)

The library is the Go engine. The Welvet app (0.1.0+1) is a different thing: run and serve models on Linux, Windows, macOS, iOS, and Android.

  • openfluke.com/welvet/app
  • openfluke.com/welvet/models
  • Round 1 demos on CUDA/Metal/Vulkan-class stacks
  • 15 models in the public matrix right now
  • "Working" means it runs. Not that it's fast or best yet.

Not language-only. Detection, tracking, classification, depth, segmentation, pose, audio, etc. are in the mix.

Validation / family repos

Engine code stays in welvet/. Proof and wrappers live elsewhere, mainly w2a (Go↔native parity for cpp/cuda/metal/vulkan/rocm/mlx/qnn), plus C ABI, Python ctypes, and TypeScript/WASM.

Sibling engines: welvet.cpp, welvet.cuda, welvet.metal, welvet.vulkan, welvet.rocm, welvet.mlx, welvet.qnn.

Hard rules: no silent fallbacks, no hardcoded float32 tensors, storage-truth train, fail closed if a sibling binary is missing.

Links

Resource Link
Product page openfluke.com/welvet
Feature book openfluke.github.io/welvet
Book on site openfluke.com/book
Examples openfluke.com/examples
Experiments openfluke.com/welvet/experiments
Source github.com/openfluke/welvet
Architecture dashboard files.openfluke.com/.../dashboard
Research PDF Welvet 1.7 Technical Research
Feature book PDF v1.7.0 PDF
Slides PDF / PPTX
Home openfluke.com

If you write Go and want train+infer in-process, or you care about dtype honesty and learn-while-serve on edge boxes, give it a look.

  1. openfluke.com/welvet
  2. Feature book
  3. github.com/openfluke/welvet
  4. Experiments

I'm Samuel Watson / OpenFluke, Australia. Forks and harsh readings of the scorecard are welcome. The docs try to keep implemented features, recorded measurements, and stubs clearly separated.
