title: Can One Failed Hard Drive Bring Down Your Entire Business?
description:
Hello, I'm Arthur. Imagine opening your business website one morning and finding that nothing is working. Customers cannot log in, orders are not processing, and your team cannot access important files.

You check the server and discover something unexpected: one hard drive has failed.

It sounds like a small hardware problem, but it can create a serious business disaster.

A single drive failure can cause downtime, data loss, interrupted services, and unhappy customers. The real damage depends on how your server is configured and whether you have a recovery plan.

Let's understand how this happens and what you can do to prevent it.

1. Why Is a Hard Drive So Important?

A server uses storage to keep important information, including:

  • Website files and applications
  • Customer records
  • Database information
  • Business documents
  • Emails and backups
  • Operating system files

When a storage device stops working, the server may lose access to some or all of this information.

For example, imagine an online store that keeps product information, customer accounts, and order records on its server. If its storage fails and there is no reliable backup, the business may struggle to continue operating.

2. What Happens When a Server Drive Suddenly Fails?

A drive failure doesn't always mean the entire server immediately shuts down.

The impact depends on the storage configuration.

Here are some possible situations:

Scenario 1: The operating system drive fails

The server may become unable to boot. Even if other data is safe, the operating system and applications may need to be restored.

Scenario 2: The database drive fails

Websites and applications that depend on that database may stop working. Customers might receive errors when trying to log in or place orders.

Scenario 3: The storage drive containing business files fails

Employees may lose access to important documents, project files, and other business information.

The biggest problem is not always the failed hardware. It's how much the business depends on that single device.

3. RAID Can Help Prevent Storage Downtime

One way to reduce the risk of a single drive failure is RAID (Redundant Array of Independent Disks).

RAID combines multiple drives to improve performance, provide redundancy, or both.

Some common RAID configurations include:

RAID 0: Combines multiple drives for performance, but provides no redundancy. If one drive fails, the entire array can become unavailable.

RAID 1: Mirrors data across two drives. If one drive fails, the other can continue providing access to the mirrored data.

RAID 5: Distributes data and parity across at least three drives. It can tolerate one drive failure.

RAID 10: Combines mirroring and striping. It offers good performance and redundancy but requires at least four drives.

Choosing the right RAID level depends on your workload, storage requirements, and budget.

4. RAID Is Not a Replacement for Backups

This is one of the most important things every server owner should understand.

RAID can help keep a system running when a drive fails, but it cannot protect against every type of data loss.

For example:

  • Someone accidentally deletes important files.
  • Malware encrypts business data.
  • A software error damages a database.
  • Multiple drives fail before recovery.
  • A fire or other disaster damages the entire server.

This is why regular backups are essential.

A useful approach is the 3-2-1 backup rule:

  • Keep three copies of important data.
  • Store them on two different types of storage.
  • Keep one copy off-site.

Also, test your backups regularly. A backup that cannot be restored is not much help during an emergency.

5. Monitor Your Drives Before They Fail

Hard drives and SSDs can show warning signs before complete failure.

For example, you may notice:

  • Increasing read or write errors
  • Unusual disk activity
  • Unexpected system slowdowns
  • SMART health warnings
  • High storage temperatures

SMART (Self-Monitoring, Analysis and Reporting Technology) can provide useful information about drive health.

Tools such as smartmontools can help administrators inspect supported storage devices.

However, monitoring cannot predict every failure. A drive can stop working without giving a clear warning.

That is why monitoring, redundancy, and backups should work together.

6. Choose Server Storage Based on Your Workload

Different businesses have different storage requirements.

A small website may work comfortably with a single SSD and reliable external backups.

However, a database server, virtualization environment, or business application handling large amounts of data may need faster storage and additional redundancy.

When comparing server infrastructure, consider:

  • SSD or NVMe storage
  • Storage capacity
  • RAID configuration
  • Backup options
  • Drive replacement support
  • Expected read and write performance

You can explore dedicated server infrastructure and hosting solutions at Seimaxim when evaluating hardware options for your business workloads.

The right configuration should balance performance, reliability, and recovery requirements.

7. Create a Recovery Plan Before Something Goes Wrong

Many businesses think about recovery only after experiencing downtime.

That is a risky approach.

A simple disaster recovery plan should explain:

  1. Where important data is stored.
  2. How frequently backups are created.
  3. Who is responsible for restoring services.
  4. How replacement hardware will be arranged.
  5. How long the business can operate without its systems.

Two useful terms to understand are:

RPO (Recovery Point Objective): How much recent data your business can afford to lose.

RTO (Recovery Time Objective): How quickly your business needs its systems restored.

For example, an online business processing orders throughout the day may need frequent backups and a short recovery time.

Testing your recovery plan is just as important as creating it.

Final Thoughts

A failed hard drive may look like a small technical issue, but its impact can reach every part of a business.

Websites can go offline, databases can become unavailable, and employees may lose access to important information.

The good news is that these risks can be reduced with proper planning.

Use suitable storage configurations, monitor drive health, maintain reliable backups, and test your recovery process regularly.

One question for server administrators and developers:

If one drive failed on your production server today, would your system continue running, or would your business experience downtime?

I'd love to hear how you handle storage failures and data protection in your infrastructure.

title: Game Feel in Jetpack Compose Without a Game Engine
description:
Cubbles is a block-placing puzzle with cute faces on the blocks, and almost all of its charm is feedback: a piece that settles with a bounce, a row that melts away in a wave, a sound and a buzz that grow with your streak. None of it needs a game engine. This post walks through how it is done in plain Jetpack Compose, what the numbers are, where the shortcuts are, and how two other games of ours solve the same problem differently.

Why a puzzle does not need an engine

An 8 by 8 board, three pieces in a tray and a drag gesture do not need physics, a scene graph or a game loop framework. What they need is a clock and a way to draw. Compose gives you both: a Canvas to paint on, and a frame callback to read time from. Everything below sits on those two things.

One Canvas, one clock

The game screen draws the board, the tray, the effects and the floating text in a single Canvas. A coroutine started with a launched effect loops forever: it waits for the next frame with withFrameNanos, ignores the frame time it is given, writes the current uptime in milliseconds into a state variable called now, and drops any finished effects from a list.

The important detail is where now is read. It is read inside the Canvas draw lambda, so each frame invalidates the drawing only, not the composition of the whole screen. The score text and the buttons around the board do not recompose sixty times a second. The board itself is a plain mutable object rather than observable state, so a small counter is bumped after each move to make the Canvas redraw. The cost of this design is honest: the loop never stops, even when no effect is running, because blinking eyes and the gently bobbing tray pieces also need a clock.

Effects are data, not animations

Instead of one Animatable per block, the game keeps a list of small effect objects. There is a sealed class with a start time and a duration, and subclasses for a placement pop, a line clear, a floating text, a screen shake, a particle burst, a color flash and a sweeping light. They are created at the instant a piece is dropped and appended to the list.

The drawing code turns each one into a progress value between zero and one, by subtracting the start time from now and dividing by the duration, and derives everything from that number. There is no coroutine per effect, nothing to cancel, and nothing that can drift out of sync with the board. Layering is free: a big clear simply adds several effects to the list.

Squash, stretch and the wave

A placed piece pops for 480 milliseconds. Its scale is one plus 0.28 times a sine over the first part of the animation, multiplied by one minus the progress, so it swells and settles with a fading amplitude. To be accurate, this is a damped swell rather than a volume-preserving squash and stretch: the blocks are rounded squares scaled uniformly, which is cheap and reads clearly at phone size.

The clear animation is where the personality is. Each cleared cell waits a delay of 28 milliseconds per step of Manhattan distance from the center of the piece you placed, so the clear spreads outward like a ripple and tells your eye where it began. Then the cell swells to 1.4 times its size during the first 30 percent of 380 milliseconds, shrinks to nothing, mixes toward white and fades its alpha, and wears a happy face until 70 percent of the way through. One smoothstep function, the classic three t squared minus two t cubed, is the only easing curve used anywhere in the file.

Faces are just a few arcs

Every block has a face drawn from circles, lines and arcs, with a mood chosen per frame: normal, happy, excited or sad. Blinking needs no state. The eyes close when the current time plus the cell index times 911, taken modulo 3700 milliseconds, is under 130, so each block blinks on its own schedule. The eyes also shift by four percent of the block size toward the finger while you drag, which is a small thing that makes the board feel alive.

Particles without a particle system

A particle here is an immutable object with a start position, a velocity, a size, a color and a spin. Nothing is updated per frame. The draw code computes the position in closed form from the elapsed time: start plus velocity times t, with a gravity term of half g times t squared added to the vertical axis, where g is sixteen cell heights per second squared. There is no pool and no per-particle state to maintain.

Counts are bounded by design. Each cleared cell emits 2 plus the hype level, capped at 4, particles, where hype is lines cleared plus the combo minus one. A board has 64 cells, so a single burst cannot exceed 384 particles. A perfect clear adds 90 pieces of confetti and a new record adds 70. A burst lives 1.1 seconds, shrinks to 40 percent of its size and fades out. Squares spin and circles do not. All randomness comes from a generator seeded with the event time, so effects are reproducible while debugging.

Floating text that stays readable

Floating text such as the score, the combo and the praise words rises with the same smoothstep, pops in with a quick overshoot and stays for 1.9 seconds. It used to vanish in one second and players missed it. The words are drawn with a dark outline made of eight shifted copies, because white text on a light bathroom-tile background is unreadable without one. A real bug lives here too: on very small screens a long praise word was wider than the space available, and a clamp call with an inverted range crashed the app. The fix was a small helper that never inverts the range, plus shrinking the text to fit.

Sound without sound files

There are no audio assets. At first use, a sound is synthesized into a short array of 16-bit samples at 22,050 Hz mono: a sine at the note frequency plus a second harmonic at 20 percent, multiplied by an exponential decay, with a 60-sample attack ramp, about three milliseconds, to avoid the click you get from starting at full amplitude. The arrays are cached by name, and each playback builds a static-mode AudioTrack with that array, tagged as game usage, and releases it from a position marker when it finishes.

Haptics that you can actually feel

The vibration class drives the vibrator directly. A comment in the code explains why: the standard view haptic call follows the user's touch feedback setting and was barely perceptible on many phones in the first release. Instead the game builds waveforms, with amplitude control where the hardware reports it and plain timings where it does not, and wraps the call so a missing vibrator never crashes anything.

The rule that keeps it honest

Feedback is cheap to add and easy to overdo, so the project notes set a rule: no effect for its own sake. The puzzle must stay readable and a bad moment must never feel like a punishment. In code that looks like this. A ghost of the piece and a highlight on the rows it would clear appear before you drop. The dragged piece is lifted 1.6 cells above your finger so that your hand does not hide it. Trays are generated so that a legal move always exists. And the game over screen only says how close you were to your best score when you are within 60 percent of it; otherwise it simply shows the best, so a poor run is not followed by a scolding.

One gap, stated plainly: Cubbles has no reduced-motion switch yet. Our bingo game does, and it shows the pattern. A setting is exposed through a composition local, and the confetti and the looping home screen animations check it and stand down.

The same ideas in two other games

Where the screen is made of widgets rather than one Canvas, the standard animation API fits better. In the bingo game, a drawn ball pops in with an Animatable and a bouncy spring, scaling from 0.2 to 1 while it rotates. The daub on a bingo card uses an animate-as-state call with a spring of damping 0.42 so it lands with a wobble. A rejected tap increments an integer key, and a launched effect on that key snaps a shake value to one and springs it back to zero, read inside a graphics layer so nothing recomposes.

In a space puzzle of ours, the frame loop moves each gate a fixed 38 percent of the remaining distance toward its target cell on every frame. It is the simplest possible smoothing and it feels good, with the caveat that the speed depends on the frame rate. A rule of thumb from all three: use the animation API for widgets, and time-derived drawing for free-form scenes.

What to take away

Keep effects as small data objects with a start time and a duration, derive everything from progress, read your clock inside the draw lambda, cap every effect, and let the game rules run ahead of the animation. You get a surprising amount of life from a few hundred lines of Canvas code and a sine function. If you want to see these numbers at work, Cubbles is the game they were tuned for.

FAQ

Can you build game feel in Jetpack Compose without a game engine?

Yes, for puzzle and casual games. One Canvas, a frame loop with withFrameNanos and time-derived drawing cover squash, particles and screen shake.

How do you avoid recomposing the whole screen every frame?

Read the clock state only inside the Canvas draw lambda. Then each frame invalidates drawing, not composition.

How are the sounds made without audio files?

They are synthesized once into short arrays of samples, cached, and played with a static-mode AudioTrack that is released when playback ends.

Why drive the vibrator directly?

The standard haptic call depends on the user's touch feedback setting and was hardly felt on many phones, so the game builds its own waveforms.

Does more feedback always make a game better?

No. Effects should never hide the puzzle or punish the player, so each one here has a cap and the game over screen avoids discouraging messages.

If you want to see this in action, Cubbles is free on Google Play and needs no account. More notes like this one live on my site.

title: Will Quantum Computers Make the Internet Unsafe?
description:
How much of a threat are quantum computers to our encrypted data — and where are their mathematical limits?

256 Bits — How Secure Is That?When we visit a website, send a message, or access our online banking, we rely on encryption to protect our data during transmission.

Yet quantum computers are often described as machines that will one day break encryption systems that would take classical computers an almost unimaginable amount of time to defeat.

How serious is this threat?

To find out, let’s consider a specific example: An attacker has recorded the encrypted traffic of an internet connection. The data was encrypted using AES-256. The attacker does not know the encryption key and wants to recover it using a quantum computer.

256 Bits — How Secure Is That?

AES stands for Advanced Encryption Standard and is one of the most widely used encryption algorithms in the world.

With AES-256, the secret key consists of 256 bits. Each bit can have one of two values: 0 or 1.

This gives us a total of:

2 ²⁵⁶ possible keys.

That is a number containing 78 digits.

If our attacker does not know the correct key, one possible approach is to try different keys and check whether they correctly decrypt the recorded data.

For a randomly generated key, a classical brute-force search requires, on average, approximately half of all possible attempts.

That would mean roughly 2 ²⁵⁵ key tests.

To put this into perspective, imagine a hypothetical supercomputer capable of testing one quintillion keys every second.

One quintillion is 10 ¹⁸, or one billion billion.

Even at that speed, an exhaustive search would take approximately 3.7 × 10 ⁵¹ years.

For comparison, our universe has existed for approximately 13.8 billion years.

The search would not merely be time-consuming. With classical computing technology, it would be practically impossible.

But our attacker has a quantum computer.

What Changes With a Quantum Computer?

A quantum computer processes information differently from a classical computer.

While a classical bit has a definite value of either 0 or 1, a quantum bit, or qubit, can exist in a superposition of both states.

Multiple qubits can form a quantum state whose mathematical description includes many possible combinations simultaneously.

This often leads to the simplified claim that a quantum computer can try every possible key at once.

But that is misleading.

When we measure such a quantum state, we obtain only one result.

Measuring an equal superposition of all possible keys would simply return a randomly selected key.

The probability of finding the correct AES-256 key this way would be just as small as making a single random guess on a classical computer.

The real advantage comes from using an appropriate quantum algorithm.

And for our example, such an algorithm exists.

Grover’s Algorithm

In 1996, computer scientist Lov Grover developed an algorithm that allows a quantum computer to search an unstructured set of possibilities significantly faster than a classical computer.

In a classical search, the amount of work grows in proportion to the number of possible solutions.

Grover’s algorithm reduces this to approximately the square root of that number.

If we had one million possible keys, a classical computer might have to examine all one million in the worst case.

A quantum computer using Grover’s algorithm would need only around a thousand search iterations, apart from a constant factor.

That is already an impressive improvement.

The difference becomes even more striking with our AES-256 key.

The classical search space contains 2 ²⁵⁶ possibilities.

Grover’s algorithm reduces the theoretical search complexity to:

√(2 ²⁵⁶) = 2 ¹²⁸

This reduces the theoretical security strength from 256 bits to 128 bits.

In cryptography, we therefore often say that Grover’s algorithm halves the security strength.

But there is an important distinction: The number of search steps is not simply cut in half. It is reduced to approximately its square root.

And 2 ¹²⁸ is still an enormous number.

How Does Grover Find the Correct Key?

Our attacker first needs a quantum computation capable of checking whether a particular key matches the recorded encrypted data.

This verification is implemented as part of a quantum operation called an oracle.

The oracle does not simply reveal the correct key. Instead, it changes the phase of the quantum state representing the desired solution.

Grover’s algorithm then applies another operation known as diffusion.

This changes the probability amplitudes of the possible solutions by reflecting them about their mean.

Together, these two operations form a Grover iteration.

We can think of the process as a system of overlapping waves.

Through repeated operations, quantum interference occurs: The amplitude associated with the correct solution increases, while the amplitudes of the other possibilities collectively decrease.

After a sufficient number of iterations, measuring the quantum state has a high probability of revealing the correct key.

The quantum computer is therefore not reading out all possible keys simultaneously.

Instead, it gradually transforms the quantum state so that measuring the correct key becomes increasingly likely.

That is the fundamental advantage of Grover’s algorithm.

However, this process still requires an enormous number of consecutive iterations.

How Long Would the Attack Take?

For our AES-256 key, the theoretical search complexity is on the order of ²¹²⁸ Grover iterations.

Written out, that number is:

340,282,366,920,938,463,463,374,607,431,768,211,456

A number containing 39 digits.

Now imagine that our attacker possesses a quantum computer capable of performing one trillion complete Grover iterations every second.

At that speed, performing 2 ¹²⁸ iterations would take approximately 10.8 quintillion years.

Taking into account the more precise iteration count required by Grover’s algorithm, approximately π/4 × 2 ¹²⁸ for a single marked solution, the calculation time would be reduced to around 8.5 quintillion years.

For comparison, the universe has existed for approximately 13.8 billion years.

The calculation would therefore take more than 600 million times the entire age of the universe so far.

And remember: We have already granted our attacker a hypothetical quantum computer operating at a speed far beyond today’s technological capabilities.

Why an Iteration Is Not a Simple Operation

Our calculation assumes that one complete Grover iteration can be performed in one trillionth of a second.

This is a purely hypothetical assumption.

In reality, each iteration requires a sequence of complex quantum circuits.

In particular, testing an AES key must be implemented as a reversible quantum computation.

This involves numerous quantum gates that must be executed in a specific order.

Furthermore, qubits are highly sensitive to disturbances. A quantum computer capable of performing such a long calculation reliably would require quantum error correction.

The additional qubits and operations needed for error correction significantly increase the hardware requirements.

Researchers have already investigated the resources required to implement Grover-based attacks against AES.

Their studies show that there is a substantial difference between the theoretical speedup of a quantum algorithm and its practical implementation on quantum hardware.

Our assumed rate of one trillion iterations per second is therefore not a realistic performance prediction. It serves only to illustrate the mathematical scale of the problem.

Could the Attack Be Parallelized?

Our attacker might try to use multiple quantum computers searching for the key simultaneously.

This is possible in principle.

However, Grover’s algorithm cannot be parallelized arbitrarily without sacrificing part of its quantum advantage.

The iterations within an individual Grover search depend on one another. They cannot simply be executed independently.

If the search space is divided among multiple quantum computers, each machine can examine a separate subset.

With P equally sized subsets, however, the number of iterations required per quantum computer decreases by only approximately a factor of √P.

By contrast, a classical brute-force search can distribute its workload almost linearly across independent processors.

Additional quantum computers can therefore accelerate an attack, but the relationship between additional hardware and reduced execution time is less favorable than one might initially expect.

There are also the substantial hardware requirements of every individual quantum computer.

Simply adding more machines does not make the astronomical scale of our AES-256 example disappear.

Does That Mean Internet Encryption Is Safe?

For our specific example, the answer is clear: A direct attack against a correctly generated AES-256 key remains practically out of reach, even with Grover’s algorithm.

The theoretical quadratic speedup is remarkable, but it is not sufficient to overcome the enormous size of the remaining search space.

However, this does not mean quantum computers pose no threat to internet security.

In a real internet connection, an AES key is not used in isolation.

The communicating parties must first securely establish shared secrets and verify the identity of the server.

These tasks rely on additional cryptographic mechanisms, some of which are vulnerable to sufficiently powerful quantum computers.

If an attacker can compromise the key establishment process of an internet connection, they may not need to attack AES directly.

The security of a connection therefore depends on more than the strength of its data encryption alone.

Our example answers one specific question: How resistant is AES-256 to a direct quantum-assisted key search?

It does not establish whether every component of today’s internet connections is already quantum-safe.

That is precisely why new quantum-resistant cryptographic methods for key establishment and digital signatures are being introduced.

Conclusion

Quantum computers are changing the security requirements of the internet. But they do not automatically make every encryption algorithm insecure.

AES-256 demonstrates that even a mathematically impressive speedup does not necessarily translate into a practically feasible attack.

Grover’s algorithm reduces the theoretical search complexity dramatically, yet the remaining task is still enormous.

The future security of the internet will depend not only on the capabilities of quantum computers, but also on our ability to distinguish which cryptographic systems actually need to change.

Sources and Further Reading

NIST — Post-Quantum Cryptography FAQ
https://csrc.nist.gov/projects/post-quantum-cryptography/faqs

Grassl et al. — Applying Grover’s Algorithm to AES: Quantum Resource Estimates (2016)
https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.04965

NIST — Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards
https://csrc.nist.gov/projects/post-quantum-cryptography

NASA — What Is the Universe?
https://science.nasa.gov/exoplanets/what-is-the-universe/

Can Quantum Computers Break 256-Bit AES? Grover’s Algorithm Explained

title: Wiring the Keyright SDK into ASP.NET Core DI as a typed HttpClient with resilience
description:
Most Keyright integrations start the same way: someone needs to validate a license against the self-hosted issuing service, so they write new HttpClient(), point it at the ServiceUrl, and ship it. It works in development and on the demo. Then it goes to production and one of two things happens.

Either the client is created per call — a fresh HttpClient inside the method that checks the license — and under real traffic the process runs out of sockets. Each disposed client leaves connections in TIME_WAIT, the ephemeral port range fills, and you start seeing SocketException: Only one usage of each socket address is normally permitted. Or someone reads the "reuse one HttpClient" advice, makes a single static instance, and holds it for the life of the process — which fixes sockets but freezes DNS. The day you move or scale your issuing service, that static client keeps dialing the address it resolved at startup, long after it is gone.

Both failures come from managing the HttpMessageHandler by hand. The right answer in ASP.NET Core is to stop doing that and register the Keyright client as a typed client through IHttpClientFactory, which pools and rotates the handler for you, and then to layer a resilience pipeline so a brief issuing-service blip degrades gracefully instead of hard-failing a paying customer.

Key takeaway: Register the Keyright client with AddHttpClient<IKeyrightClient, KeyrightClient>() so the factory pools and rotates the underlying handler — no socket exhaustion, no stale DNS. Inject IKeyrightClient as you would any service (the wrapper is singleton-safe; the HttpClient is not held forever). Attach AddStandardResilienceHandler() with a timeout, retry-with-jitter, and a circuit breaker tuned for a licensing call — retry the idempotent ValidateAsync/RefreshAsync, be careful with activation — and fall back to cached validation when the service is briefly unreachable.

The two anti-patterns, concretely

Here is the socket-exhaustion version. It looks harmless because every client is disposed.

// ANTI-PATTERN 1: a new HttpClient per license check.
public async Task<bool> IsLicensedAsync(string key, CancellationToken ct)
{
    using var http = new HttpClient { BaseAddress = new Uri("https://keyright.example.com") };
    var client = new KeyrightClient(http, _options);     // new handler every call
    var info = await client.ValidateAsync(key, ct);
    return info.IsValid;
}

using disposes the client, but the TCP connection it opened lingers in TIME_WAIT for a couple of minutes. A few hundred checks a second and you are out of ports. The second anti-pattern inverts the problem:

// ANTI-PATTERN 2: one static HttpClient for the life of the process.
static readonly HttpClient Http = new() { BaseAddress = new Uri("https://keyright.example.com") };
static readonly KeyrightClient Client = new(Http, Options);
// Reuses connections — but the handler never rotates, so DNS is cached forever.

This one survives load, then fails silently on the next infrastructure change. Neither is wrong about HttpClient being expensive to create or cheap to reuse — they are each half right, and the half they are missing is handler rotation.

Registering Keyright as a typed client

The fix is one registration at startup. AddHttpClient<IKeyrightClient, KeyrightClient>() tells the factory to construct KeyrightClient with an HttpClient whose handler comes from the pool. You configure the client — base address, timeout, default headers — in the callback, and the SDK-level options (product, public key) through the usual KeyrightOptions.

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

builder.Services.Configure<KeyrightOptions>(o =>
{
    o.Product         = "acme-suite";
    o.PublicKeyBase64 = builder.Configuration["Keyright:PublicKey"]!;  // ships in your binary; not a secret
    o.ServiceUrl      = builder.Configuration["Keyright:ServiceUrl"]!; // your self-hosted instance
});

builder.Services
    .AddHttpClient<IKeyrightClient, KeyrightClient>((sp, http) =>
    {
        var opts = sp.GetRequiredService<IOptions<KeyrightOptions>>().Value;
        http.BaseAddress = new Uri(opts.ServiceUrl);
        http.Timeout     = Timeout.InfiniteTimeSpan;   // let the resilience pipeline own timeouts
        http.DefaultRequestHeaders.Add("X-Keyright-Product", opts.Product);
    })
    .AddStandardResilienceHandler();                    // Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience

Two details matter here. First, KeyrightClient takes an HttpClient in its constructor — the typed-client overload resolves the rest of its dependencies from DI, so the public key and product flow in through KeyrightOptions. Second, the client's own HttpClient.Timeout is set to infinite on purpose: when a resilience pipeline is attached, you want it to own the per-attempt timeout, not the blunt whole-request timeout baked into HttpClient, which cannot distinguish a slow first attempt from a retry.

If you prefer a single call site, wrap the registration in an extension method so applications just say AddKeyright(...):

public static IServiceCollection AddKeyright(
    this IServiceCollection services, Action<KeyrightOptions> configure)
{
    services.Configure(configure);
    services.AddHttpClient<IKeyrightClient, KeyrightClient>((sp, http) =>
            {
                var o = sp.GetRequiredService<IOptions<KeyrightOptions>>().Value;
                http.BaseAddress = new Uri(o.ServiceUrl);
                http.Timeout     = Timeout.InfiniteTimeSpan;
            })
            .AddStandardResilienceHandler();
    return services;
}

Now the whole thing is builder.Services.AddKeyright(o => { o.Product = "acme-suite"; /* … */ });, and consumers inject IKeyrightClient without ever seeing an HttpClient.

Lifetimes: why the wrapper is singleton-safe but the handler is not

AddHttpClient<TClient>() registers the typed client as transient by default, and that is deliberate. The client object itself is cheap — it is a thin wrapper — and each instance it hands you is bound to an HttpClient the factory produced. The expensive, long-lived thing is the HttpMessageHandler underneath, and the factory keeps a pool of those, rotating each out after its handler lifetime (two minutes by default) so connections are reused but DNS does not go stale.

The practical rule: resolve IKeyrightClient wherever you need it and use it; do not capture the HttpClient it wraps in a field of your own singleton. The Keyright wrapper's state — the embedded public key, the cached lease, the last-known license edition — is process-wide and safe to treat as a singleton, which is why KeyrightClient.Initialize(...) returns a long-lived object in non-DI apps. In ASP.NET Core you get the same ergonomics through the factory without freezing a handler, because the cached lease lives in the SDK, not in the HttpClient.

public sealed class LicensedFeature(IKeyrightClient license)
{
    public async Task<IResult> RunAsync(CancellationToken ct)
    {
        // Pure, offline check against the embedded public key — no network, never throws.
        var info = license.Validate();
        if (!info.IsEnabled("acme.export"))
            return Results.StatusCode(StatusCodes.Status402PaymentRequired);

        return Results.Ok(await DoExportAsync(ct));
    }
}

Validate() serves the gate decision from the cached lease, so it is fine on the hot path. The network call lives only in RefreshAsync, which you run on a timer — not on every request.

The resilience pipeline, tuned for a licensing call

AddStandardResilienceHandler() gives you a sensible default stack: a total request timeout, a retry strategy, a circuit breaker, and a per-attempt timeout, in that order. The defaults are tuned for a generic downstream API; for a licensing call you want to adjust a few knobs.

builder.Services
    .AddHttpClient<IKeyrightClient, KeyrightClient>(ConfigureClient)
    .AddStandardResilienceHandler(o =>
    {
        // Per-attempt timeout: the issuing service answers a validate in well under a second.
        o.AttemptTimeout.Timeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(3);

        // Retry: idempotent validate/refresh is safe to repeat. Exponential + jitter so a
        // fleet recovering from a blip does not stampede the service in lockstep.
        o.Retry.MaxRetryAttempts = 3;
        o.Retry.BackoffType      = DelayBackoffType.Exponential;
        o.Retry.UseJitter        = true;
        o.Retry.Delay            = TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(200);

        // Circuit breaker: once the service is clearly down, stop hammering it and fail fast,
        // letting the SDK's cached-lease path take over instead of queueing doomed requests.
        o.CircuitBreaker.FailureRatio      = 0.5;
        o.CircuitBreaker.MinimumThroughput = 10;
        o.CircuitBreaker.SamplingDuration  = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30);
        o.CircuitBreaker.BreakDuration     = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(15);

        // Total timeout must exceed AttemptTimeout × attempts, or retries get cut off.
        o.TotalRequestTimeout.Timeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(15);
    });

The standard handler retries only on transient conditions — connection failures, HttpRequestException, timeouts, 5xx, and 408 — and never on a 4xx. That default is exactly right for licensing: a 403 or a 409 from the issuing service is a definitive answer (revoked, seat withdrawn, product mismatch) and must not be retried, while a 503 during a rolling deploy is transient and should be.

If you would rather build the pipeline by hand — for example to vary the strategy per operation — Polly's ResiliencePipelineBuilder drops in the same way:

var pipeline = new ResiliencePipelineBuilder<HttpResponseMessage>()
    .AddRetry(new HttpRetryStrategyOptions
    {
        MaxRetryAttempts = 3,
        BackoffType      = DelayBackoffType.Exponential,
        UseJitter        = true,
        ShouldHandle     = static args => ValueTask.FromResult(
            args.Outcome.Result is { StatusCode: >= HttpStatusCode.InternalServerError }
            || args.Outcome.Exception is HttpRequestException or TimeoutException),
    })
    .AddCircuitBreaker(new HttpCircuitBreakerStrategyOptions())
    .AddTimeout(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(3))
    .Build();

Validate is retry-safe; activation is not

This is the one place where a single policy for every call gets you in trouble. ValidateAsync and RefreshAsync are idempotent reads — they ask for the current state and change nothing — so retrying a timed-out one is always safe. Activation is different. It can consume a seat or bind a machine, so a blind retry risks double-counting: if the first attempt actually reached the service and succeeded but the response was lost on the way back, a retry activates a second time.

Register activation on its own named client with a more conservative policy, and lean on an idempotency key the service de-duplicates on:

// A separate, named client for the non-idempotent activation call.
builder.Services.AddHttpClient("keyright-activate", ConfigureClient)
    .AddResilienceHandler("activate", b => b
        .AddRetry(new HttpRetryStrategyOptions { MaxRetryAttempts = 1, UseJitter = true })
        .AddTimeout(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(10)));

// …and pass an idempotency key so a retried activation is coalesced server-side.
var result = await license.ActivateAsync(
    key, new ActivationRequest { IdempotencyKey = deviceInstallId }, ct);

With the idempotency key, even the one permitted retry cannot double-consume a seat: the service recognises the repeated key and returns the original result rather than activating again.

Degrading gracefully instead of hard-failing

The reason all of this matters is that the network call to the issuing service should never be the thing that takes your customer down. A validate that times out once, retries, and succeeds is invisible. A service that is genuinely down for a minute trips the circuit breaker, and instead of every request queueing behind a doomed connection, the breaker fails fast and your gate decisions fall back to the SDK's cached lease — the same cached-validation path that keeps a brief outage from locking anyone out. When the service returns, the breaker half-opens, a probe succeeds, and traffic resumes with no restart and no intervention.

Testing the wiring

You can test the registration and the resilience behaviour without a live issuing service by swapping the primary handler for a stub. ConfigurePrimaryHttpMessageHandler replaces the innermost handler while leaving the resilience handlers in place, so you are exercising the real pipeline.

var services = new ServiceCollection();
services.AddKeyright(o => { o.Product = "acme-suite"; o.ServiceUrl = "https://keyright.test"; });

// Fail twice, then succeed — proves the retry strategy is wired and bounded.
var attempts = 0;
services.ConfigureHttpClientDefaults(b => b.ConfigurePrimaryHttpMessageHandler(() =>
    new StubHandler(_ =>
        ++attempts < 3
            ? new HttpResponseMessage(HttpStatusCode.ServiceUnavailable)
            : new HttpResponseMessage(HttpStatusCode.OK) { Content = ValidLeaseJson() })));

var client = services.BuildServiceProvider().GetRequiredService<IKeyrightClient>();
var info = await client.RefreshAsync(CancellationToken.None);

Assert.Equal(3, attempts);                 // two transient failures were retried
Assert.Equal(RefreshStatus.Confirmed, info.Status);

A second test points the stub at a 403 and asserts the call is not retried and surfaces as a definitive rejection — that is your guard against someone loosening the ShouldHandle predicate until revocations start getting retried.

That is the whole shape of a correct Keyright integration in ASP.NET Core: one typed-client registration so handlers are pooled and rotated, a resilience pipeline that retries the idempotent calls and respects the definitive ones, and a cached lease underneath so a blip in your issuing service costs a retry — never a customer.

title: Why I Built My Portfolio with Vanilla Stack (Instead of Reaching for Heavy Frameworks)
description:
When you decide to build a developer portfolio today, the default advice is almost always the same: spin up a modern JavaScript framework, install a heavy UI component library, configure a bundler, and deploy.

For complex, state-heavy web applications, that stack makes complete sense. For a portfolio website? Often, it is overkill.

When I set out to build CyberNova, my web and AI solutions portfolio, I made a deliberate engineering choice: skip the heavy frameworks and build the entire frontend using a pure Vanilla Stack (HTML5, CSS3, and Vanilla JavaScript).

Here is why going lightweight was the right call—and what it taught me about frontend performance.

1. Eliminating Unnecessary Bloat

Modern frameworks ship with significant runtime overhead before a single line of your own content renders. For a site whose primary job is to showcase projects, technical skills, and services clearly, loading hundreds of kilobytes of JavaScript just to render static sections slows down the user experience.

By sticking to semantic HTML5, modern CSS, and lightweight vanilla scripts, the site stays fast even on slower mobile connections.

2. Total Control Over Layout & Styling

Using pure CSS3 gave me direct, unobstructed control over the design system without fighting framework-specific overrides or bloated utility dependencies:

  • CSS Custom Properties (:root): Made managing a consistent dark-mode color palette, spacing scale, and typography effortless.
  • CSS Grid & Flexbox: Handled responsive multi-column project cards and navigation layouts natively.
  • Zero Specificity Wars: Every style rule was written intentionally, keeping the stylesheet clean, readable, and easy to maintain.

3. Clean, Purposeful JavaScript

Instead of importing third-party packages for simple UI interactions, writing clean vanilla JavaScript kept the logic transparent and dependency-free:

  • Smooth mobile menu toggles and active navigation states
  • Lightweight scroll animations using the native IntersectionObserver API
  • Form handling and interactive UI transitions in just a few dozen lines of code 
// Example: Lightweight scroll reveal with IntersectionObserver
const observer = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => {
  entries.forEach((entry) => {
    if (entry.isIntersecting) {
      entry.target.classList.add('visible');
    }
  });
}, { threshold: 0.15 });

document.querySelectorAll('.reveal').forEach((el) => observer.observe(el));

4. Better SEO & Technical Foundations

Static semantic HTML is naturally crawler-friendly. Pairing clean markup with structured JSON-LD Schema (WebSite and ProfessionalService), proper canonical URLs, and Open Graph metadata ensured search engines could parse the site structure cleanly without relying on client-side rendering workarounds.

When Frameworks Still Win

Choosing vanilla for a portfolio doesn't mean avoiding frameworks everywhere. When I am building full-stack backend systems, authentication flows, or dynamic data-driven platforms (like PHP/Laravel applications or complex dashboards), frameworks provide structure, security patterns, and scalability that plain scripts shouldn't replicate from scratch.

The key is matching the tool to the problem rather than reaching for the heaviest stack out of habit.

Final Thought

Sometimes the strongest engineering decision isn't adding another tool to your package.json—it's knowing how much you can build cleanly without one.

What stack did you use for your latest portfolio, and why? Let me know in the comments!

title: Managed Services Partners: A Buyer's Guide to Choosing the Right Fit
description:
Choosing a managed services partner means handing over responsibility for the systems your business runs on every day, so the wrong fit shows up fast in downtime, security gaps, and frustrated internal teams. The global managed services market is projected to grow from USD 437.3 billion in 2026 to USD 847.4 billion by 2033, according to Grand View Research, as organizations shift routine IT operations to specialized partners. This guide profiles ten leading managed services companies and breaks down exactly what to evaluate before signing a contract.

Executive Summary

Managed services shift the day-to-day burden of running IT, from monitoring and patching to security operations and cloud licensing, onto a specialized partner operating under defined service levels. Done well, this frees internal teams from constant firefighting and gives leadership predictable costs, measurable uptime, and a partner accountable for outcomes.

This guide profiles 10 leading managed services companies and outlines how to assess partners based on service level commitments, security maturity, delivery model, and reporting transparency. It also covers how managed IT, managed security, and cloud licensing services differ from adjacent models like staff augmentation and traditional break-fix support. The goal is a repeatable framework for choosing a partner who stabilizes your environment today and scales with you tomorrow.

Who Is This Guide For?

  • CIOs and CTOs evaluating whether to outsource IT operations, security monitoring, or cloud administration to free internal teams for strategic work.
  • VPs of IT Operations who need a partner capable of meeting defined SLAs across infrastructure, endpoints, and applications.
  • IT Directors and Managers comparing managed services providers against the cost and risk of building an equivalent capability in-house.
  • Security and Compliance Leads assessing a provider's ability to strengthen threat monitoring and maintain regulatory alignment.
  • Procurement and Sourcing Leads building a shortlist and needing a consistent framework to compare vendors on cost, coverage, and delivery model.

Each of these roles shares the same underlying goal: reducing operational risk while making IT spend more predictable.

What Is Managed Services & How Does It Work?

Managed services is an arrangement where an external provider takes ongoing, contractual responsibility for specific IT functions, such as infrastructure monitoring, endpoint management, cybersecurity operations, or cloud licensing, in exchange for a recurring fee tied to defined service levels. Organizations get continuous monitoring, proactive maintenance, and a documented escalation path when issues occur, so support no longer waits for something to break first. The provider typically supplies the tooling, staffing, and processes, while the client retains oversight through regular reporting and governance meetings. This model shifts IT from a reactive cost center to a managed, measurable function.

Common delivery models include:

  • Fully managed IT operations, where the provider owns end-to-end monitoring, patching, and helpdesk support for an environment.
  • Managed security services (MSSP/MDR), focused on continuous threat monitoring, detection, and incident response.
  • Cloud Solution Provider (CSP) and licensing management, where the partner manages Microsoft 365 or Azure subscriptions, cost optimization, and configuration.
  • Co-managed IT, where the provider supplements an existing internal IT team without replacing it.
  • Application and platform production support, where the provider maintains uptime and performance for one specific system, narrower in scope than whole-estate IT operations.

Managed Services vs. Staff Augmentation vs. Break-Fix IT Support

These three models are often confused, but they carry very different accountability structures. Staff augmentation adds individual contractors or engineers under the client's own management and processes, useful for filling a skills gap but offering no service-level guarantee. Break-fix support means paying for help only when something fails, with no proactive monitoring and unpredictable costs. Managed services sits apart from both by combining ongoing, proactive operation of an environment with contractual SLAs the provider is accountable for meeting.

The bottom line: if predictable costs and proactive coverage matter more than direct day-to-day control, managed services is the model built for that trade-off.

How To Choose the Best Managed Services Partner?

  1. Defined SLAs and escalation paths: Insist on specific, written commitments on response and resolution times; vague language like "prompt support" should be a red flag. Ask how missed SLAs are tracked and remediated.
  2. 24/7 monitoring and incident response coverage: Confirm whether monitoring is truly around-the-clock or only during business hours, and who actually responds when an alert fires at 2 a.m.
  3. Security maturity and compliance alignment: A partner should be able to show how its monitoring and incident response practices map to frameworks relevant to your industry, and this matters more every year as the managed security services market grows at a 16.4% CAGR, according to Research and Markets.
  4. Onboarding and discovery process: A rigorous onboarding phase that documents your environment, priorities, and risks reduces the chance of blind spots once the contract starts.
  5. Reporting transparency and governance cadence: The best partners provide regular, readable reporting and scheduled governance meetings that give real strategic context, beyond a raw support ticket log.
  6. Licensing and cloud cost optimization: For organizations running Microsoft 365 or Azure, ask whether the partner actively audits and rightsizes licensing on an ongoing basis, beyond simply processing renewals.
  7. Delivery model and cultural fit: Understand whether support is onshore, nearshore, offshore, or blended, and whether that model matches your internal team's working hours and communication style.
  8. SLA accountability: Ask what happens if the partner misses an SLA, and expect a specific, contractual answer with defined remedies.
  9. After-hours incident handling: Ask how the partner handles a security incident outside business hours, since the answer reveals whether "24/7 coverage" is real or marketing language.

The bottom line: judge the right managed services partner on documented SLAs and a proven incident track record.

Managed Services Companies Compared

Accenture delivers managed IT, security, and cloud operations at global scale, spanning infrastructure monitoring, cybersecurity operations, and application support for large, complex environments. Building a Managed Services Partnership That Scales With You

If you are ready to evaluate what a Managed Services partnership could look like for your organization, explore Improving's Managed Services offerings and talk to our experts through your environment.

Frequently Asked Questions

1) What is the difference between managed services and outsourcing?

Managed services is a specific type of outsourcing focused on ongoing, proactive operation of defined IT functions under service level agreements. Broader outsourcing can include one-time projects or staff augmentation, which carry no continuous, SLA-bound structure.

2) How much do managed services typically cost?

Pricing ranges from per-user or per-device monthly fees for managed IT support to larger fixed contracts for enterprise-wide infrastructure and security operations. Look closely at what each pricing tier actually includes; the headline price alone rarely tells the full story.

3) Can a managed services provider work alongside our existing internal IT team?

Yes. Co-managed IT is a common model where the provider takes on specific functions, such as security monitoring or after-hours support, while the internal team retains ownership of the rest.

4) How do I know if a provider's security coverage is strong enough?

Ask for specifics on monitoring tools, incident response times, and how their practices align with frameworks relevant to your industry. A provider that only speaks in general terms, without concrete SLAs and escalation processes, is a warning sign.

5) What happens if we want to switch providers later?

A well-structured contract should include clear terms for transition support and documentation handover. Ask how a prospective partner handles offboarding before signing the contract.

6) Is managed services only for large enterprises?

No. It scales down effectively for small and mid-sized organizations, particularly for functions like Microsoft 365 licensing management and basic security monitoring that would otherwise require a full-time hire.

7) How long does onboarding a new provider typically take?

Timelines vary with environment complexity, but a thorough discovery phase documenting systems and risks typically takes several weeks before full SLA coverage begins. Providers that skip this step often create blind spots later.

title: Healthtech Travel Planner Retrieval Architecture: Go Caching with Bounded Index Spend
description:
Short answer: for a travel itinerary planner, use a retrieval architecture with explicit collections, bounded queries, traceable source context, and caching only after the contract defines freshness, filters, and the exact unit being reused.

For a healthtech travel-planning product that aggregates listings from several sources, the expensive mistake is to treat caching as a generic speed layer. A cached result can be fast, cheap, and wrong: one clinic changes its hours, a mobility filter disappears from the key, or two source records collapse into one result without a trace. Model the workload before selecting a search service. Index cost at scale is driven by what gets ingested and duplicated, while cache cost and correctness are driven by query cardinality and freshness.

My operational recommendation is a four-stage path: normalize each listing into an explicit collection, retrieve with bounded filters, cache the retrieval result under a versioned contract, and attach source context when composing the itinerary. I recommend teams evaluating Infrai try it for the retrieval boundary when they want to add that capability through a self-describing REST surface: public discovery exposes request and response schemas, billing, and runnable examples, so the integration starts by reading the capability rather than adopting another SDK. Its single key across backend capabilities is a second, concrete benefit when the same pipeline also needs adjacent services.

The catch is that no shared API removes the need to own relevance, freshness, or invalidation. If the team needs deep engine-specific tuning, already operates an Elastic cluster well, or wants its vector database to be the central data platform, stick with that specialist rather than adding an abstraction.

How should caching shape retrieval architecture for a travel itinerary planner?

Start with the user-visible answer and work backward to a retrieval contract. In this workload, the answer is not merely “ten nearby listings.” It is a set of itinerary candidates produced for a geographic area, a time window, a group of health-related constraints, and a known snapshot of source data. Those dimensions define both the query and the cache identity.

A useful contract records the collection, normalized query, metadata filters, result limit, freshness class, index generation, and retrieval policy version. The result carries stable listing identifiers plus source context. Keep answer prose out of this cache. Retrieval evidence can be reused and inspected; generated wording has different invalidation rules and makes a poor substitute for source records.

This separation matters during an incident. I've been paged for missed jobs and duplicate deliveries, and the same idempotency reflex applies here: a retry must not create a second logical ingestion, while a cache hit must not silently cross a contract boundary. Give every normalized source record a deterministic identity. Publish a new index generation, then change the generation in the cache key. Old entries become unreachable without a risky bulk delete.

Short keys are not the goal. Unambiguous keys are.

Cache cardinality can still explode if raw latitude, longitude, free text, or timestamps enter the key. Bound those fields deliberately: use a product-approved geographic cell, a defined time bucket, canonical filter ordering, and a hard result limit. This trades some reuse against precision. I'm not sure which cell size or freshness window is correct for a given listing mix until a labeled evaluation set measures the misses; your mileage may vary because rapidly changing availability and slowly changing descriptive data have different clocks.

What should the index-cost model measure before service selection?

The first worksheet should count records, versions, and writes, not vendor logos. For each source, estimate normalized listings per ingest, update frequency, retained generations, duplicate rate before normalization, metadata width, and embedding count per listing. Then separate full rebuilds from incremental changes. A design that embeds every source variant and retains several overlapping generations can multiply index volume before the first user query arrives.

Use a small labeled evaluation set before production rollout. Each example should include the request, required filters, acceptable listings, unacceptable listings, and the source snapshot used to judge it. Run the same set against every candidate architecture. Record recall at the bounded limit, filter correctness, stale-result rate, index records written, and cache hit ratio. These are workload measurements to collect; they are not claims about any provider.

Downstream spend belongs in the same model. A noisy top 20 can increase reranking and answer-generation work, while an aggressive cache can reduce query calls but serve stale evidence. The effective bill therefore includes ingestion, index storage, query traffic, cache storage, reranking, answer generation, engineering integration, and on-call work. Per-unit search price alone won't tell you which system costs less to operate.

Keep the accounting boring — that is a compliment. A weekly report should reconcile logical listings, physical indexed records, writes by source, cache entries by policy version, and downstream calls by retrieval outcome. If one number jumps, the runbook should identify its owner and rollback boundary.

How should teams compare the operating boundary?

There is no universally correct row in this table. The decision turns on where the team wants to keep expertise and control.

Option Strong fit for this workload Real trade-off
Infrai A team wants a plain REST integration whose public discovery surface supplies schemas and runnable examples, with one key spanning adjacent backend capabilities A shared capability surface does not replace workload-specific relevance evaluation; choose a specialist when engine-level tuning is the main requirement
Elasticsearch The team already owns its search operating model and wants the retrieval engine itself to remain the explicit control plane Cluster operation and integration stay with the team, so include that labor in the effective-cost model
Pinecone The team wants a specialist vector service boundary and is prepared to design ingestion and source citation around it The surrounding web acquisition, normalization, and answer stages remain separate operating decisions
Weaviate The team wants a vector-focused platform and prefers to make that platform's data model a first-class architectural choice Portability depends on how much application behavior is coupled to platform-specific modeling and query choices

Infrai's relevant advantage here is integration discoverability, not a promised ranking win. Its live discovery covers 295 routes across 20 modules, and documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages. That breadth can reduce the integration surface when a small team would otherwise install several SDKs and manage several credentials. It cannot prove retrieval quality for your listings. Only the labeled set can do that.

Do the comparison with two columns in the cost model that teams often omit: initial adapter work and recurring operational ownership. Then test the result under a doubled source-update rate and a lower cache-hit ratio. If the winner changes under a small assumption change, the decision is fragile and deserves a reversible pilot rather than a platform commitment.

How can Go enforce a versioned, bounded cache contract?

The following program makes the cache identity deterministic and keeps the dangerous dimensions visible. It also calls Infrai's public discovery surface, finds the verified POST /v1/vector/query capability by its declared method and path, and reports whether it is available. Discovery requires no key, but the sample reads INFRAI_API_KEY and sends the standard Bearer header so the HTTP client is ready for an authenticated capability without embedding a credential. The adapter must map the cache contract only to fields declared in the returned request schema; don't infer a request shape from a route name.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "sort"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

const discoveryURL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery"

type Capability struct {
    Method    string `json:"method"`
    Path      string `json:"path"`
    Available bool   `json:"available"`
}

type Discovery struct {
    Version      string       `json:"version"`
    GeneratedAt  string       `json:"generated_at"`
    Capabilities []Capability `json:"capabilities"`
}

type Filter struct {
    Name  string `json:"name"`
    Value string `json:"value"`
}

type RetrievalContract struct {
    Collection   string   `json:"collection"`
    Query        string   `json:"query"`
    Filters      []Filter `json:"filters"`
    Limit        int      `json:"limit"`
    Freshness    string   `json:"freshness"`
    IndexGen     string   `json:"index_generation"`
    Policy       string   `json:"policy_version"`
    GeoCell      string   `json:"geo_cell"`
    DepartureDay string   `json:"departure_day"`
}

func cacheKey(c RetrievalContract) (string, error) {
    c.Query = strings.Join(strings.Fields(strings.ToLower(c.Query)), " ")
    sort.Slice(c.Filters, func(i, j int) bool {
        if c.Filters[i].Name == c.Filters[j].Name {
            return c.Filters[i].Value < c.Filters[j].Value
        }
        return c.Filters[i].Name < c.Filters[j].Name
    })

    if c.Collection == "" || c.IndexGen == "" || c.Policy == "" {
        return "", fmt.Errorf("collection, index generation, and policy are required")
    }
    if c.Limit < 1 || c.Limit > 50 {
        return "", fmt.Errorf("limit must be between 1 and 50")
    }
    if _, err := time.Parse("2006-01-02", c.DepartureDay); err != nil {
        return "", fmt.Errorf("departure day must use YYYY-MM-DD: %w", err)
    }

    payload, err := json.Marshal(c)
    if err != nil {
        return "", fmt.Errorf("encode retrieval contract: %w", err)
    }
    sum := sha256.Sum256(payload)
    return "retrieval:" + hex.EncodeToString(sum[:]), nil
}

func retryDelay(header string, attempt int) time.Duration {
    if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(header); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
        return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
    }
    if when, err := http.ParseTime(header); err == nil {
        if delay := time.Until(when); delay > 0 {
            return delay
        }
    }
    return time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
}

func fetchDiscovery(ctx context.Context, apiKey string) (Discovery, error) {
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, discoveryURL, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return Discovery{}, fmt.Errorf("build discovery request: %w", err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return Discovery{}, fmt.Errorf("call discovery: %w", err)
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 4<<20))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return Discovery{}, fmt.Errorf("read discovery response: %w", readErr)
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            time.Sleep(retryDelay(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"), attempt))
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return Discovery{}, fmt.Errorf("discovery returned %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, strings.TrimSpace(string(body)))
        }

        var result Discovery
        if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &result); err != nil {
            return Discovery{}, fmt.Errorf("decode discovery response: %w", err)
        }
        return result, nil
    }
    return Discovery{}, fmt.Errorf("discovery remained rate limited after 4 attempts")
}

func main() {
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if apiKey == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }

    contract := RetrievalContract{
        Collection: "care-travel-listings",
        Query:      "wheelchair accessible clinic near rail",
        Filters: []Filter{
            {Name: "language", Value: "en"},
            {Name: "verified", Value: "true"},
        },
        Limit:        20,
        Freshness:    "daily",
        IndexGen:     "2026-09-03-a",
        Policy:       "retrieval-v3",
        GeoCell:      "product-defined-cell-1842",
        DepartureDay: "2026-09-18",
    }

    key, err := cacheKey(contract)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(key)

    discovery, err := fetchDiscovery(context.Background(), apiKey)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    for _, capability := range discovery.Capabilities {
        if capability.Method == http.MethodPost && capability.Path == "/v1/vector/query" {
            fmt.Printf("vector query available=%t manifest=%s generated=%s\n",
                capability.Available, discovery.Version, discovery.GeneratedAt)
            return
        }
    }
    panic("vector query capability is absent from discovery")
}

The bounds in this sample are application policy, not Infrai API limits. In production, store the canonical contract beside the cached result even if the lookup key is hashed. That gives an operator something readable during a stale-result investigation. It also makes policy changes reviewable: retrieval-v3 should correspond to a documented change, not an unexplained cache purge.

Ingestion stays separate. Consider one explicitly hypothetical promotion: source A republishes a listing with revised hours, source B still carries yesterday's copy, and a third feed changes only the accessibility label. Normalization should resolve those inputs to deterministic logical identities while retaining their source records; the ingestion job writes the candidate generation once, verification checks the labeled queries and required filters, and only then does a pointer make that generation queryable. The retrieval cache key changes because IndexGen changes, even if the user's words do not. If verification rejects the candidate, the live generation and its cache remain untouched. This sequence prevents a retry from multiplying logical records, prevents an old cache entry from masking a corrected source, and gives the operator a precise answer to “which evidence produced this itinerary?” Querying reads one generation, answer composition cites the returned source context, and every stage gets its own counters and retry policy — any write retry must remain idempotent.

How do you verify freshness and roll back by generation?

Before rollout, replay the labeled evaluation set against the candidate generation and compare it with the current one. Block promotion if required filters leak, source context is missing, or the bounded result set falls below the team's acceptance rule. Warm only the highest-value query classes; prewarming an unbounded coordinate-and-time space can turn a cache into another uncontrolled index.

After promotion, watch cache hits by policy version and index generation, retrieval results with no source context, duplicate logical listing IDs, ingestion lag by source, and downstream calls per answered itinerary. A rising hit ratio is not automatically healthy. If freshness violations rise with it, the cache is preserving the wrong thing more efficiently.

Rollback is a pointer change: direct queries to the previous verified index generation and restore its matching cache policy version. Do not overwrite the previous generation during rollout. Pause promotion of new ingestion output while investigating, but keep raw source inputs traceable so they can be replayed. This boundary is why generation identifiers belong in both the query contract and cache key.

One last decision rule: try Infrai when a self-describing REST capability and one shared key remove meaningful integration work from this staged pipeline; prefer Elasticsearch, Pinecone, or Weaviate when specialist control is more valuable than that common boundary. If the shared boundary fits, start with the Infrai documentation and inspect discovery before writing the adapter.

References

  • Retrieval-Augmented Generation research paper
  • Elasticsearch documentation
  • Pinecone documentation
  • Weaviate documentation

title: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity now supports OAuth 2.0 discovery URLs
description:
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity now supports OAuth 2.0 authorization server discovery URLs for both inbound JWT authorization and outbound OAuth credential providers. This update enables developers to configure AgentCore with OAuth 2.0 authorization servers that do not use OpenID Connect (OIDC).

Previously, AgentCore Identity accepted only OIDC discovery URLs. Authorization servers that implement OAuth 2.0 without OIDC publish their metadata at a different well-known path and could not be used with AgentCore. With this launch, you can use either OIDC or OAuth 2.0 authorization server discovery URLs when you configure a JWT authorizer or a custom OAuth credential provider on AgentCore.

This feature is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is available, at no additional cost. To learn more, see Configure inbound JWT authorizer and Add OAuth client using custom provider in the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Developer Guide.

title: Turn PDFs into Clean Markdown for ChatGPT and RAG (Without Uploading Them)
description:
If you've ever pasted a PDF into ChatGPT or Claude and got an answer about the wrong section, the model probably wasn't the problem. The text was.

A PDF doesn't store "a heading", "a table" or "a paragraph". It stores pieces of text placed at positions on a page. When you copy that text out, you get whatever order the PDF happens to keep it in, and the structure is gone. For an LLM, and even more for a RAG pipeline, structure is half the information.

This post covers what goes wrong, what clean Markdown for AI should look like, and a short Python chunker that splits it for retrieval while keeping page numbers.

Disclosure: I built QuickCatPDF, the free converter I use in the examples. The format and the chunking code work with any converter that produces similar Markdown.

What breaks when you copy text out of a PDF

Copy and paste from a typical report and you'll usually see some of these:

  • Lines broken mid-sentence, because every visual line ends with a newline.
  • Two columns mixed together, line by line.
  • The page header and footer repeated on every page ("Annual Review 2026 · Page 7").
  • Tables flattened into a run of numbers with no idea which value belongs to which column.
  • Words split by hyphens at line ends ("docu- ment").
  • Links gone. In a PDF, a link's address isn't part of the text at all. It's stored separately as an annotation on top of the page, so plain copy-paste only gives you the visible words.

None of this stops a model from reading the text, but it makes it worse at finding the right part and at quoting numbers from tables correctly.

What "clean Markdown for an LLM" looks like

Markdown is a good middle ground: models read it naturally, it's compact, and it keeps the structure that matters.

---
title: "Annual Review 2026"
source: "annual-review.pdf"
pages: 4
---

<!-- page 1 -->

# Annual Review 2026

## Introduction

Revenue grew in every quarter...

## Results by quarter

| Quarter | Revenue | Growth |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 | 1.2M | 4% |
| Q2 | 1.4M | 17% |

<!-- page 2 -->

A few details are worth copying, whatever tool you use:

  1. Front matter naming the source file and page count. When you paste several documents into one chat, the model knows which is which.
  2. Page markers as HTML comments (<!-- page 2 -->). Models read them, rendered Markdown hides them, and your RAG answers can cite a page.
  3. Real headings (#, ##, ###) instead of bold lines.
  4. Pipe tables, so every value stays in its row and column.
  5. No page furniture: page numbers and repeated headers and footers removed, hyphenated words joined, wrapped lines merged into single paragraphs.

Three questions people keep asking

"How do I keep headings when converting PDF to Markdown?"
Most converters detect headings from the text's size and weight. That works when the PDF's headings are visibly larger or bold. If a document's headings are the same size and weight as the body text, there's no signal to detect, and they come out as plain paragraphs. In that case, add the ## markers by hand for the main sections. It takes a minute and makes a big difference for chunking.

"How do I keep tables?"
Pick a converter that outputs pipe tables, then check one table against the original. Tables without lines (columns separated only by white space, like bank statements) are the hardest case for any tool.

"Why are my hyperlinks lost?"
Because of the annotation point above: the address isn't in the text layer. A converter has to read the link annotations and match them to the words underneath. Plain copy-paste and many text extractors skip that step.

Chunking for RAG without losing page numbers

Headings are natural chunk boundaries, and the page comments let every chunk carry the page it started on. Here's a small, dependency-free chunker:

import re

def chunk_markdown(md: str, max_chars: int = 4000):
    """Split Markdown on ## headings, keeping the page number each chunk starts on."""
    md = re.sub(r"\A---\n.*?\n---\n", "", md, flags=re.S)  # drop front matter
    page = 1
    chunks, current, heading = [], [], None

    def flush():
        text = "\n".join(current).strip()
        if text:
            chunks.append({"heading": heading, "page": start_page, "text": text})

    start_page = page
    for line in md.splitlines():
        m = re.match(r"<!-- page (\d+) -->", line)
        if m:
            page = int(m.group(1))
            if not "".join(current).strip():
                start_page = page
            continue
        if line.startswith("## ") or sum(len(l) for l in current) > max_chars:
            flush()
            current, start_page = [], page
            if line.startswith("## "):
                heading = line[3:].strip()
        current.append(line)
    flush()
    return chunks

Each chunk comes back as {"heading": "Results by quarter", "page": 1, "text": "..."}, ready to embed. Store heading and page as metadata, and your answers can say "see page 1, Results by quarter" instead of pointing at the whole document.

If you prefer page-sized chunks (useful for contracts and forms), split on the <!-- page N --> comments instead.

Watch your token budget

A rough rule for English is about 4 characters per token, fewer for other scripts. That's close enough to decide whether a document fits in one prompt or needs chunking. Treat it as an estimate, not an exact count.

Doing it without uploading the PDF

Many PDFs you'd want to ask an AI about are exactly the ones you shouldn't hand to random websites: contracts, financial reports, internal docs. You'll decide later where the text goes. The conversion step doesn't need to send it anywhere.

The converter I built, QuickCatPDF's PDF to Markdown for LLMs, runs in the browser:

  1. Drop in up to 20 PDFs.
  2. Keep Front matter and Page markers as comments ticked.
  3. Optionally limit the Pages.
  4. Click Convert to Markdown, then copy or download. It shows the character count and a token estimate.

In my test, a 4-page report converted in about half a second into 4.6 KB of Markdown. Scanned PDFs are read with OCR in the browser too. You can check that nothing is uploaded: load the page, turn on airplane mode, and convert.

For plain Markdown for GitHub, Obsidian or Notion (with bold, italics, links and optional images), there's a separate PDF to Markdown tool.

Quick checklist

  • Don't paste raw PDF text into an LLM when structure matters. Convert to Markdown first.
  • Keep front matter and page markers, and drop the headers and footers.
  • Check one heading and one table against the original.
  • Chunk on ## headings and keep the page number as metadata.
  • Estimate tokens at about 4 characters per token for English.

What's the worst PDF you've had to feed into an LLM? Tables, multi-column layouts, scans? I'm collecting hard cases.
