title: Designing a 2-Tap UX for Gyms: Why Speed Beats Social Feeds
description:
Sweat dripping onto a smartphone screen under flickering gym fluorescent lights is the ultimate usability stress test. When you are between heavy sets, exhausted, and running on a strict rest timer, you do not want to scroll through a social feed, dismiss notification badges, or wait three seconds for a cloud round-trip to log your workout. Yet, modern fitness applications have increasingly bloated into social media clones packed with algorithmic feeds, leaderboards, and heavy animations.

At VanzaLabs, we asked a fundamental engineering question: what if a workout app behaved more like a calculator and less like Instagram? That core thesis led us to design a radical 2-tap interaction model for SPOT, our minimalist fitness tracking tool engineered specifically for high-intensity environments.

The Problem: Latency and Friction in the Iron Zone

Most mobile developers optimize for engagement loops—metrics like session length, daily active time, and ad impressions. In a gym, those metrics are actively toxic to the user experience. High-intensity training requires high cognitive focus. Every millisecond of UI latency or unnecessary tap introduces friction that breaks flow state.

Traditional fitness apps suffer from three architectural bottlenecks:

  1. Cloud Dependency: Requiring an active API round-trip to persist set weights and reps.
  2. UI Bloat: Navigation hierarchies buried three layers deep behind tabs for social sharing, messaging, and community challenges.
  3. Battery & Thermal Throttling: Complex UI frameworks rendering heavy lists and animations, causing devices to heat up in pockets.

When we prototyped our initial iterations, we measured time-to-log. Traditional apps averaged 7 to 12 taps and roughly 4.2 seconds of cognitive overhead per set. For a workout with 30 sets, that translates to over two minutes wasted purely on fighting user interfaces.

The Engineering Solution: Local-First and Zero Middleman

To achieve a frictionless 2-tap UX, we had to rethink the client architecture from the storage layer up. We adopted a strict local-first paradigm.

1. Zero Middleman Servers with Local SQLite

Instead of routing every set logged through an API gateway, session data is written directly to an embedded local database using optimized SQLite queries. We use lightweight abstractions to ensure write operations resolve in under 5 milliseconds. There are no middleman servers blocking the main thread waiting for network acknowledgments.

// Simplified local-first persistence layer
class WorkoutRepository @Inject constructor(
    private val localDatabase: SpotDatabase
) {
    suspend fun logSetQuickly(exerciseId: String, weight: Float, reps: Int) {
        val setEntity = SetEntity(
            timestamp = System.currentTimeMillis(),
            exerciseId = exerciseId,
            weight = weight,
            reps = reps
        )
        // Direct disk write with immediate UI state emission
        localDatabase.setDao().insert(setEntity)
    }
}

2. Optimistic UI and State Reductions

In SPOT, the UI state updates instantaneously. The user taps the weight, taps the reps, and the database write happens asynchronously in the background. If the app is closed abruptly, the local SQLite transaction log guarantees durability without needing complex conflict resolution algorithms.

3. Battery and Privacy Benefits

By minimizing network calls, we drastically reduced radio wake-ups, preserving battery life during long training sessions. Furthermore, because workout data stays local by default, user privacy is inherently protected. There is no telemetry profiling your squat PRs to serve targeted fitness supplements.

Practical Takeaways for Builders

If you are building tools for high-stakes, real-world environments—whether it is fitness trackers, inventory scanners, or point-of-sale systems—consider these architectural rules:

  • Measure the Thumb Zone: Design for single-handed use under physical fatigue. Vital actions must sit comfortably within the natural thumb arc.
  • Local-First is King: Never block user input on network availability. Gym basements famously have terrible cellular reception.
  • Kill the Feed: Strip away any feature that does not directly serve the core utility of the product. Speed is a feature.

Experience the Speed

Building tools that respect user time and cognitive load remains a core engineering philosophy for our team. If you want to experience an interface built entirely around raw utility and ultra-fast interactions, try out SPOT available now on the Google Play Store.

To explore more developer-focused tools and open experiments from our team, check out VanzaLabs.

title: Self-hosting a zero-trust network on one server with Lantern DSSE
description:
Lantern DSSE is an open-source (Apache-2.0), self-hosted zero-trust network: ZTNA and a secure web gateway that you run on your own servers. This post installs the 0.4.2 release on a single Linux server and connects a Windows PC to it.

Lantern DSSE is an experimental release. The single-server layout below is for trying it out: if that server stops, everything stops. Do not use it in production.

What Lantern DSSE does

It grew out of work on ransomware defense: if a device is compromised, which internal systems can it reach, and what can it send out?

  • Internal traffic. Observe which internal connections devices make, then limit each device to the applications it needs. Applications are reached through connectors that dial out to the Edge.
  • Out-of-band authentication with your IdP. For the internal destinations you mark, a connection such as SSH, RDP or SMB is held while the user signs in to your identity provider (OIDC) in a browser, and continues only after that.
  • Outbound traffic. Sites are allowed or denied by rule, and every decision is logged.
  • TLS inspection. For the traffic you choose, the Edge decrypts TLS with your organization's own certificate authority.

The same applies to AI agents. Prompts and guardrails shape what an agent tries to do, not what it can reach. We think the most dependable control is to decide access to each resource from an authenticated identity, outside the agent, and to log every decision.

What we are building

One server runs everything as containers.

What you need

  • One Linux x86-64 server with Docker Engine and Compose v2. I used a 4 vCPU, 16 GiB instance in AWS Tokyo with Ubuntu 24.04. You do not need Go or the source.
  • Port 443 open. Devices and administrators both come in through it.
  • The deployment's names resolving to the server, through DNS or hosts files. I used hosts files.
  • A Windows PC and the signed MSI from the release (DsseAgent-0.4.2-windows-x64.msi).

I did not limit port 443 by source address; the Console is protected by sign-in. Only SSH was limited to my own address.

1. Get the installer

Download the installer and the release manifest. The installer reads which container images to run from the manifest.

R=https://github.com/lantern-networks/dsse-core/releases/download/v0.4.2-experimental
curl -fLO $R/dsse-install-0.4.2-linux-amd64
curl -fLO $R/release-manifest.json
curl -fLO $R/SHA256SUMS
sha256sum -c --ignore-missing SHA256SUMS
sudo install -m 0755 dsse-install-0.4.2-linux-amd64 /usr/local/bin/dsse-install
sudo install -d -o "$USER" -g "$USER" -m 0755 /opt/dsse

2. Register the names

Choose a name for the deployment (one you control; example.test is a placeholder) and use the address the server actually has. The installer prints the line to add to the hosts file.

A='-up -deployment example.test -address 10.20.1.10 -admin-email admin@example.test
   -dir /opt/dsse/region-a -release-manifest release-manifest.json'
dsse-install $A -print-names | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts

It prints one line: the address followed by eight names. On the administrator's PC and on the Windows PC, point the same names at the server's public address.

3. Install with one command 

dsse-install $A

The installer runs six steps in order. For me it took about four minutes, including pulling the images.

Step What it does
1 Creates the deployment's certificate authorities, certificates and configuration
2 Starts the containers
3 Creates the first administrator
4 Restarts the control plane and the Edge
5 Turns on the authentication features
6 Checks the whole deployment

The last step passes when nothing fails. I got 50 checks passed out of 51, with one not applicable because no customer organization existed yet. If a step fails, fix the cause and run the same command again: it skips the finished steps and continues.

Three of the files it creates in /opt/dsse/region-a are worth knowing:

File Contents
admin-credentials.txt The first administrator's password, the key for an authenticator app, and recovery codes. Readable only by its owner, and never printed to the screen
deployment-anchor.pem The certificate of this deployment's root authority. It holds no private key, so you can hand it out. Used on the administrator's PC in step 4
authority/ The private keys of the authorities. Guard this above everything else

admin-credentials.txt has this shape, with some notes around it:

  password        <the password>
  second factor   <the TOTP secret>
  recovery codes  <recovery codes, separated by spaces>
Line Use
password The password for signing in to the Console
second factor The key you register in an authenticator app (in step 4). At sign-in you enter the six digits the app shows
recovery codes Entered instead of the six digits when the app is unavailable. Each code works once

A layout with several servers is installed with the same -up and a plan file; see the deployment guide.

4. Create an organization in the Console

Copy /opt/dsse/region-a/deployment-anchor.pem from the server to the administrator's PC and trust it. On Windows, in an elevated PowerShell:

Get-FileHash .\deployment-anchor.pem   # must equal sha256sum on the server
Import-Certificate -FilePath .\deployment-anchor.pem -CertStoreLocation Cert:\LocalMachine\Root

Before signing in, register the second factor value in an authenticator app on your phone (Google Authenticator, Microsoft Authenticator and so on):

  1. Open the screen that adds an account by typing a key (in Google Authenticator, "Enter a setup key").
  2. Give the account a name you will recognize, for example the address you passed as -admin-email.
  3. Enter the second factor value as the key (32 capital letters and digits), with the key type "time based".

When the app shows six digits that change every 30 seconds, it is registered. Sign-in fails if the phone's clock is far off.

Open https://console.region-a.<your deployment>/console.html in a browser and sign in with the -admin-email address, the password from admin-credentials.txt, and the six digits from the app.

The tenant_default organization that already exists belongs to the operator. Create a customer organization (a tenant) for your devices:

  1. Under Tenants, press + Add tenant and give it a display name. Leave Who runs it at its default, We run it for them.
  2. Press Manage on that organization in the list. Inside it, under Certificates & PKI → Certificates, press Let this deployment issue them for device identity and Let this deployment make one for traffic inspection. In the dialog that appears first, press Ask for 20 minutes.
  3. Under Device configuration, press Make the configuration, then Download everything for one device to get the set for Windows.

The set contains the configuration (install_profile.json), the key that verifies its signature (profile_signing_key.txt) and a one-time enrolment token (enrolment_token.txt). It does not contain the MSI: download DsseAgent-0.4.2-windows-x64.msi from the release and put it in the same folder as DsseAgent.msi.

5. Install on Windows

Check the signatures of the MSI and the configuration first. dsse-profileverify.exe checks the configuration; build it on Windows from a clone of the repository with go build -o dsse-profileverify.exe ./cmd/dsse-profileverify.

Get-AuthenticodeSignature .\DsseAgent.msi | Format-List Status,SignerCertificate
.\dsse-profileverify.exe -profile install_profile.json -pin profile_signing_key.txt

The MSI must be Valid with the signer LANTERN NETWORKS, INC., and the configuration must report "signed by the pinned key" (it then prints the configuration itself, which holds certificates and public keys but no secret). In real use, the key reaches the device by a different route from the configuration.

Install from an elevated PowerShell:

$msi = (Resolve-Path .\DsseAgent.msi).Path
$config = (Resolve-Path .\install_profile.json).Path
$token = (Resolve-Path .\enrolment_token.txt).Path
$pin = (Resolve-Path .\profile_signing_key.txt).Path
$log = Join-Path $PWD 'install.log'
$p = Start-Process msiexec.exe -Wait -PassThru -ArgumentList "/i `"$msi`" /qn /l*v `"$log`" CONFIG=`"$config`" TOKEN=`"$token`" PIN=`"$pin`""
$p.ExitCode

When it prints 0, start the agent. On its first start the device enrols in the organization.

Get-Service DsseSteer,DsseWfp
Start-Service DsseSteer
Get-CimInstance Win32_Service -Filter "Name='DsseSteer'" | Select-Object State,StartMode

It takes about half a minute before traffic goes through DSSE. It is ready when C:\Program Files\DSSE\dsse-steer.log shows steer_capture backend=wfp armed=true. The device also appears under Devices in the Console.

6. Check allow and deny

A new organization's Internet Access starts with one rule that allows and inspects everything. The idea is to make the traffic visible first and narrow it from there.

Add a rule that denies one site:

  1. Under Groups & Services, press + Add server and create the destination example.org.
  2. Under Internet Access, create a rule with example.org as the destination and Deny as the access. Give it a priority lower than the first rule's 100, for example 20 (the lower number wins).

In the PC's browser, an allowed site opens without a certificate warning, and the denied site shows a block page.

Logs & Audit records both the allowed and the denied requests, with the rule and the reason.

If you try it

If you try this in a lab, please tell us in an issue which version and operating system you used, what you tried, and where a step or the behaviour differed from what you expected. Do not include tokens, private keys or personal information. A star on GitHub is appreciated.

title: How we built an independent search engine with its own index
description:
Most "search APIs" are a thin layer over Google or Bing results. NestDaddy is not. It has its own crawler, its own inverted index, its own ranking and its own news collection, designed, built and operated end to end by our team.

This post walks through how the platform fits together and the engineering principles we follow. If you are thinking about building search yourself, or you want to know what sits behind the API you are calling, this is for you.

The shape of the platform

There are four parts, and each one is isolated so that no part can take another down:

  1. Crawler. Fetches pages, obeys robots.txt, extracts the readable text and stores it in PostgreSQL.
  2. Indexer. Turns new pages into posting lists in a RocksDB index that is built next to the live one.
  3. Swap. Every day, the new index replaces the live index in one atomic step, with an automatic rollback.
  4. Search. A BM25 ranker reads the live index, read-only, behind the web site, the REST API and an MCP server for AI agents.

The rule that ties them together: the search path never waits for the crawler or the indexer, and neither of them can compete with it for resources.

The crawler: polite, bounded, isolated

A good crawler is a polite one, so ours is built around clear limits.

  • robots.txt first. One fetch per site, cached for 24 hours. A 401 or 403 on robots.txt means "disallow everything".
  • Spread across hosts. Each batch claims URLs from the queue with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED and keeps at most 3 URLs per host, so a batch touches hundreds of different sites instead of hammering one. The same claim lets many crawler workers share one queue safely.
  • Bounded downloads. Every response is streamed and cut at 5 MB or 20 seconds, so no single site can slow the crawl down or flood it with data.
  • Isolation. The crawler runs in its own resource slice with dedicated CPU and memory limits and a low priority. Search traffic always comes first.

The index: RocksDB and posting lists

The index is an inverted index stored in RocksDB: for every term, a posting list of document IDs, plus per-document statistics for BM25.

We picked RocksDB over a search server for three reasons. It is a library, so there is no extra service to run. It is built for fast point lookups and multi-gets, which is exactly what a query does. And it can be opened read-only by many processes while another process builds the next version.

Text goes through a tokenizer (lowercasing, stop words, Porter stemming with a memoised stemmer) before it reaches the index, and the same tokenizer runs on every query.

Replacing the index safely, every day

The daily swap is deliberately boring:

  1. Take the writer lock so the indexer pauses.
  2. Hard-link the immutable SST files into a staging directory and copy the small metadata files (MANIFEST, CURRENT, OPTIONS, WAL). This takes about a second and uses no extra disk.
  3. Release the lock and verify the staging copy read-only: the document counter must not go down, sample terms must resolve, the newest indexed pages must be readable.
  4. Rename the live directory to a "previous" directory and the staging directory to live.
  5. Reload the search workers and run a live search check. If anything fails, roll back automatically.

Previous generations are kept, so going back is a rename, not a restore.

Ranking: BM25, measured

The ranker is BM25 with practical additions: a two-stage pre-score (rare terms first, then the top 3,000 candidates re-ranked by term frequency with one RocksDB multi-get), a domain match signal for navigational queries, and image documents kept out of web results.

We do not change ranking by feel. An evaluation suite of real queries, each with a judgment ("the right answer is this URL pattern" or "the homepage of this site"), runs against the live index after every change, and a change ships only when precision goes up. The November release moved every metric we track:

Metric Before After
Right answer at #1 (P@1) 45% 70%
Right answer in the top 3 60% 77.5%
Right answer in the top 10 70% 87.5%
Mean reciprocal rank 0.536 0.754

The changes behind it were classic search engineering: true document frequencies for IDF, an average document length measured from real documents, deterministic sampling, and keeping images out of web search.

Latency engineering

Fast search is mostly about removing surprises. Three practices matter most for us:

Linear-time text processing. Every regular expression on the query path is checked for backtracking. Patterns like \S+@\S+ are replaced by linear-time equivalents such as (?<!\S)(?=\S+@\S)\S+, which give the same output and stay fast on any input.

Keep the hot index in memory. A dedicated service checks which parts of the index file are resident (mincore) and reads back only what is missing, and it runs with a cgroup memory guarantee so the kernel keeps the index cached. One detail worth knowing: cgroup v2 memory protection is hierarchical, so the parent slice needs the same guarantee as the service.

Audit every scheduled job. Generic "free up memory" scripts such as echo 1 > /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches ignore cgroup protection and quietly undo all of the above. We review every scheduled job on the search path.

The result is sub-second search on fresh queries, measured on the same evaluation suite after every release.

What is next on the roadmap

Owning the whole stack means we can improve every layer ourselves. These are the upgrades in progress:

  • Deeper answers. The next index version adds full body text on a tiered storage design, so answers that live deep in a page rank where they should.
  • Numbers and more scripts. A new tokenizer that keeps short numbers ("windows 11", "iphone 17") and splits Chinese, Japanese and Thai text ships with the next index build.
  • Freshness at scale. A targeted recrawl of the most searched results and the most linked sites is running now, and the crawler is moving to a continuous multi-process pipeline.

Why build it at all

Because an index you own is an index nobody can switch off. Microsoft retired the Bing Search APIs in August 2025 and many apps lost their search overnight. Products that need raw results, news by country, or readable page text for AI agents need a source that answers in plain JSON and does not depend on someone else's roadmap.

That is what NestDaddy is for. You can try the search, news and page extraction APIs with a free 7-day key at nestdaddy.com/apis, or connect it to Claude, Cursor or any MCP client through nestdaddy.com/mcp.

If you are building something similar and want to compare notes, we would like to hear from you.

Originally published on the NestDaddy blog. NestDaddy is an independent search engine with its own index: nestdaddy.com.

title: Freelancer Retainers: Turn One-Off Projects Into Steady Monthly Income
description:
Every freelancer knows the feast-and-famine cycle. One month three clients pay at once and the bank account looks generous. The next month the inbox is quiet, the pipeline is empty, and the same bank account starts to feel thin. The work did not get worse. The income just stopped being steady.

A retainer fixes the steady part. It is a simple agreement: a client pays a fixed amount every month for a fixed amount of your time, whether they use all of it or not. In the sample, one freelancer replaced the scramble with three retainer clients at $1,300 a month each — $3,900 of income she could count on before the month began — and kept project work on top of it. The retainer did not replace freelancing. It gave freelancing a floor. Here are seven ways to build one, plus a 7-step setup so the first retainer starts this month.

1. Start with the clients who already come back

The easiest retainer client is the one who already hires you twice a year. They know your work, they trust your turnaround, and they have already decided you are worth paying. In the sample, the first retainer came from a client who had booked four separate projects in eight months — each one preceded by a new quote, a new negotiation, and a new wait for the invoice to clear.

Look at your last twelve months. Which clients came back more than once? Those are your retainer candidates. You are not selling them something new. You are offering to make the thing they already buy cheaper to buy: one agreement, one monthly invoice, no re-quoting every time.

2. Sell hours, not availability — and name the number

A retainer that promises "I'll be available" is a trap. Availability is infinite and unmeasurable, and the client will test it at 11 pm on a Sunday. A retainer that promises 10 hours a month is a product: the client knows what they bought, and you know what you owe.

In the sample, the smallest retainer is 10 hours a month at $65 an hour — $650, paid on the first of the month. The hours are named in the agreement, the rate is named, and the month is named. If the client needs an eleventh hour, it is billed at the same rate as extra work. Hours are countable. Availability is not. Sell what you can count.

3. Charge for the month, not for the work done

This is the part that feels strange at first: the client pays the full $650 even in a month when they only use 6 hours. That is not a trick. That is the point of a retainer. They are not buying 10 hours of typing. They are buying the guarantee that your 10 hours are theirs when they need them — the slot held, the turnaround kept, the queue jumped.

In the sample, unused hours roll over one month only, then expire. That keeps the deal honest: the client never feels cheated out of hours they paid for, and the freelancer never carries a mountain of banked hours into a busy month. A rollover cap of one month is the compromise that makes both sides comfortable.

4. Put the floor in writing — scope, rollover, and notice

A retainer without a written agreement is a handshake that will be remembered differently by each side. The agreement needs four lines: how many hours, what kind of work is included, what happens to unused hours, and how either side ends it.

In the sample, the notice period is 30 days, written into every agreement. Thirty days is long enough for the client to find a replacement and short enough that the freelancer is never trapped in a dead arrangement. The scope line matters most: "dashboard maintenance, monthly reports, and data cleaning" — not "Excel work," which means everything and nothing. Write the four lines before the first payment, not after the first argument.

5. Price the retainer below your project rate — slightly

A retainer client commits to paying every month, rain or shine. That commitment is worth something, so the rate reflects it. In the sample, the project rate is $65 an hour and the retainer rate is $60 — about 8% lower — in exchange for the client paying on the first of the month, every month, without being chased.

The discount is small on purpose. A retainer priced far below your normal rate becomes the cheapest work you do, and the client who pays least will demand most. Eight percent buys the commitment without selling the hours cheap. If a client asks for a bigger discount, the answer is fewer hours, not a lower rate.

6. Cap the number of retainer clients

Three retainer clients at 20 hours each is 60 hours a month of committed work — before any project work, before any admin, before any selling. In the sample, three is the cap. A fourth retainer would mean turning project clients away, and project work is where the higher rates and the new relationships live.

The cap protects the very thing the retainer was built for: steadiness without suffocation. When the retainer book is full, the answer to the next request is a waiting list, not a yes that squeezes the calendar until something breaks. Scarcity is also honest marketing: clients who know the slots are limited treat the agreement with more respect.

7. Invoice on the first, every month, without fail

The retainer only works if the money actually arrives on schedule. In the sample, the invoice goes out on the first of the month, every month, for the full amount, with the same line every time: "Monthly retainer — 10 hours, March." No chasing, no reminding, no "when you get a chance."

A client who pays late on a retainer is a client the retainer does not suit, and the 30-day notice exists for exactly that case. Two late payments in the sample means a conversation; three means the agreement ends. The retainer is a trade: steady work for steady pay. If the pay stops being steady, the trade is over.

Quick setup: a 7-step retainer checklist

  1. List every client who hired you more than once in the last twelve months — those are your first retainer candidates.
  2. Pick one and offer a named package: 10 hours a month at your retainer rate — in the sample, $650 at $65 an hour.
  3. Write the four lines: hours, scope, rollover (one month, then expiry), and 30-day notice to end it.
  4. Set the retainer rate slightly below your project rate — in the sample, about 8% lower — in exchange for payment on the first of every month.
  5. Cap your retainer book — in the sample, three clients — so committed hours never crowd out project work.
  6. Send the first invoice on the first of the month, same line every time, and track it like any other invoice.
  7. Review every quarter: which retainers pay on time, which ones use their hours, and which slot should be freed for a better client.

A retainer does not make freelancing safe. It makes it steady — and steady is what lets you say no to the bad project, wait for the good client, and stop starting every month at zero.

Tools mentioned: Freelancer Client Tracker ($10) — one page per client with retainer hours, rollover, and last invoice date, so no retainer ever drifts; Freelancer Time Tracker ($10) — the hours behind every retainer, so 10 hours a month stays 10 hours instead of quietly becoming 16; Freelancer Invoice Tracker ($10) — the first-of-the-month invoice log, so a late retainer payment is spotted the day it happens; Freelancer Budget Planner ($14) — the monthly plan where $3,900 of steady retainer income becomes a budget instead of a hope. title: Django's Tasks API Ships Without a Worker
description:
Halfway through a Django 6.0 upgrade on a client's compliance SaaS, I opened a branch called kill-celery. The plan was two hours of work: swap every @shared_task for the new built-in @task, drop the broker, delete the worker service, ship a smaller stack. I got as far as pasting a TASKS block into settings before I hit the sentence that closed the branch. Django's Tasks framework, in its own words, "does not provide a worker mechanism to run Tasks" — execution "must be handled by infrastructure outside Django, such as a separate process or service."

That is not a rough edge to be smoothed over in a point release. It is the declared scope of the feature, and it is the part most upgrade write-ups skip past on their way to the code sample.

What actually shipped

Django 6.0 arrived on December 3, 2025 with an API that standardises how background work is declared and enqueued, not how it is executed. You decorate a function, call .enqueue(), and get a TaskResult back:

# billing/tasks.py
from django.core.mail import send_mail
from django.tasks import task


@task(queue_name="emails", priority=10)
def email_users(emails, subject, message):
    return send_mail(subject, message, None, emails)

# settings.py
TASKS = {
    "default": {
        "BACKEND": "django.tasks.backends.immediate.ImmediateBackend",
        "QUEUES": ["default", "emails"],
    }
}

Two backends come in the box: ImmediateBackend, which runs the function inline the moment you enqueue it, and DummyBackend, which stores the result and never runs anything. The reference docs mark both as development and testing tools and say production systems should rely on backends that supply a worker process and a durable queue.

So the shape of the feature is: Django owns the interface, somebody else owns the execution. That is the same arrangement as DATABASES, CACHES and the storage API, and it is exactly what DEP 14, written by Jake Howard, set out to do — "provide an interface and base implementation for long-running background tasks in Django". The interface landed in core in September 2025 and shipped in 6.0.

The part that is not there

Read the API surface as a list of what a production queue needs, and the gaps are obvious. There is no worker. There is no retry policy — a task that raises has its exception and traceback recorded in TaskResult.errors and stops there. There is no periodic scheduling, no dead-letter queue, no concurrency controls, no durable storage at all unless the backend you pick provides it.

run_after exists on the task object and takes a timedelta or a timezone-aware datetime, and backends advertise whether they honour it through capability flags like supports_defer, supports_priority and supports_get_result. A one-shot delay is genuinely useful, but it is not a cron replacement, and a flag that tells you a backend cannot defer is not a scheduler. One review of the framework put it as "not a queue, not a worker system, and not a scheduler", which reads as harsh until you check it against the reference page and find it accurate.

If you were waiting for the next release to close the gap, it did not. Django 6.1 gave the task() decorator a **kwargs passthrough to the backend's task class and made Task and TaskResult picklable. No database backend, no worker command, no retries. The same release is where the interesting work went elsewhere: model field fetch modes, database-level on_delete options, and the dictionary-based MAILERS setting that deprecates the whole EMAIL_* family.

What I put behind the interface

Three options are worth considering, and the choice is mostly about what infrastructure you are already paying for.

A database backend, for small services. django_tasks_db.DatabaseBackend stores tasks in your existing database and ships a db_worker management command that processes them, plus a prune_db_task_results command for housekeeping — it lives in a separate package outside Django core. One team running it in production points at the operational win: because the queue is ORM rows, scheduled, completed and errored tasks are all visible in the Django admin without adding a monitoring stack. For a service that sends transactional email and runs the occasional long export, that is the whole requirement, and it removes Redis from the deployment diagram entirely.

The trade is durability and throughput. Every enqueue is a write and every poll is a query against the same database serving your web requests, so a task volume that would be trivial for a broker becomes contention for your connection pool.

Celery, when you already run a broker. If the project has Redis or RabbitMQ up for other reasons, the queue is already paid for, and Celery brings retries with backoff, beat scheduling, routing, rate limits and chords — none of which the Django interface will grow soon. Migrating to django.tasks here buys you a slightly nicer decorator and costs you all of that.

RQ, in the middle. Redis-backed, far less machinery than Celery, and a reasonable landing spot for a service that has outgrown database polling but does not need workflow primitives.

What I ended up doing on the compliance SaaS: kept Celery for the FMCSA sync jobs that need retries and a schedule, and moved two fire-and-forget email paths to django.tasks behind the database backend. The kill-celery branch became narrow-celery, which is a less satisfying name and a much smaller diff.

The transaction trap, which is now yours to handle

This is the failure mode I have debugged on three separate projects, and the new API does not save you from it. Enqueue a task inside transaction.atomic() and the worker — running in a different process, on a different connection — can pick the job up before your transaction commits and fail to find the row it was told to process. The Tasks docs are explicit about it and prescribe the standard fix:

from functools import partial

from django.db import transaction

from billing.tasks import generate_invoice_pdf


def close_period(request):
    with transaction.atomic():
        invoice = Invoice.objects.create(period=request.POST["period"])
        transaction.on_commit(partial(generate_invoice_pdf.enqueue, invoice_id=invoice.pk))

Note the partial. on_commit takes a callable with no arguments, so the common bug is calling .enqueue(...) immediately and handing on_commit the result. Celery users get a shortcut here instead: delay_on_commit() was added in Celery 5.4 and wraps the hook for you, at the cost of not returning a task ID, since nothing is sent to the broker until the transaction finishes. Django's interface has no equivalent, so the partial pattern is the one to standardise on in review.

The other constraint worth internalising early: task arguments and return values are serialized to JSON, so process_data.enqueue(datetime.now()) raises TypeError: Object of type datetime is not JSON serializable. Pass primary keys and ISO strings, re-fetch inside the task. That is good practice with any queue — it keeps tasks idempotent and avoids acting on a stale copy of an object — but here the framework enforces it rather than letting a pickle backend quietly hide the problem.

Why the interface is still worth adopting

I was ready to write this feature off as premature, and I have changed my mind on one point. The value is not that Django runs your tasks. It is that your application code stops naming the queue vendor.

Two concrete payoffs. First, tests: point TASKS at DummyBackend and assertions run against enqueued tasks without a broker, an eager-mode flag, or a mocked .delay. Second, migration cost: swapping the database backend for a Redis-backed one is a settings change plus a worker process, not a sweep through every module that imported shared_task.

That is a real architectural gain for a codebase that expects to outgrow its first queue — which, in my experience, is most SaaS backends around the point the first customer asks for scheduled reports.

The practical rule I would give anyone upgrading: adopt @task and .enqueue() for new background work, keep whatever runs your existing jobs, and do not delete the broker until you have picked and deployed a backend that has a worker in it. The API is stable and the ecosystem underneath it is not finished.

Sources

  • Django's Tasks framework — topic guide (6.1)
  • Tasks reference: backends, capability flags, TaskResult (6.1)
  • Django 6.0 released — 3 December 2025
  • Django 6.1 release notes
  • Django Enhancement Proposal 14: Background Workers
  • django-tasks-db — ORM-based backend and db_worker command
  • Using Django Tasks in production — Better Simple
  • Django 6.0 Tasks: a framework without a worker — Loopwerk
  • First steps with Django — Celery documentation

title: Flutter + Node.js: how I plan a mobile MVP
description:
A mobile MVP has two jobs: reach real users fast, and stay cheap to change. Flutter helps with the first, because one Dart codebase gives you both an iOS and an Android app. A small Node.js API helps with the second, because your business rules live in one place that a web dashboard or a second app can reuse later.

I am a freelance full stack developer with more than 20 years in corporate IT. This is the order I work in when a founder asks me to turn an idea into a working app.

1. Write one sentence first

Who is the user, and what is the one thing they must be able to do? "A customer places an order and sees its status" is enough. That sentence decides your screens and your tables. Then sketch the data: for an order flow, users, products, orders and order items. Getting this right early saves the most rework.

2. Design the API before the screens

Keep it plain REST with JSON: POST /auth/login, GET /orders, POST /orders, PATCH /orders/:id/status. In Node.js I use Express or Fastify with PostgreSQL or MongoDB, validation on every route and one consistent error format. Document the endpoints from day one so the app, the dashboard and later integrations share one contract.

3. Keep the Flutter architecture simple

Three layers are enough: a data layer that calls the API, a layer that holds state, and the widgets. Riverpod is lighter to start with, Bloc is stricter for larger teams; either works if you use it consistently. Generate Dart models from your API shapes so a backend change shows up as a compile error instead of a crash on a user's phone.

4. Build the UI from a few reusable parts

A button, an input, a list tile and a loading state, used everywhere, make the app look consistent without a long design phase. Handle empty lists, slow networks and expired sessions early. Users meet those on day one.

5. Plan auth, payments and push notifications

  • Auth: short-lived access tokens plus refresh tokens, kept in secure storage, never in plain preferences.
  • Payments: use a provider with a mobile SDK, such as Stripe, and let the API create and confirm the payment.
  • Push: Firebase Cloud Messaging covers both platforms; the API stores device tokens and sends a message when an order changes.
  • Third-party APIs: call them from the backend so keys stay secret and you can swap providers without a new app release.

6. Test what matters, on real phones

A few API tests for login, the core workflow and permissions, unit tests for the logic layer and widget tests for the main screens are enough for an MVP. Install weekly builds on real devices; simulators hide keyboard, notch and slow-network problems.

7. Automate the build and deploy

GitHub Actions can run tests and build the app on every push. The API runs in a Docker container behind HTTPS with secrets in environment variables and a daily database backup. Create the store accounts in your own name (Apple Developer $99 a year, Google Play a one-time $25) and leave time for review.

A realistic timeline

For a focused app with a small admin view: week one for scope, data model and API design; weeks two to four for core screens and endpoints, with an installable build each week; week five for payments, notifications and polish; week six for testing and store release. More user types or integrations add weeks.

Flutter or React Native?

Both can ship a good MVP. I lean to Flutter when you want a very consistent interface on both platforms and have no React mobile team. React Native makes sense if you already have React web developers to share.

Full guide with FAQ: How to Build a Flutter MVP Backed by a Node.js API

title: Docker's agent sandbox leaked through its copy command. Check every path that crosses the wall.
description:
Originally published on voirlabs.io by Ijlal Ishaq.

A sandbox for an AI agent is only as strong as the least guarded way in or out of it. Docker Sandboxes put a coding agent in its own virtual machine and let it see only the folders you approve, and that part held. The gap was the copy command next to it. By the end of this article you will know why that keeps happening, and what a file channel that respects the boundary looks like in code.

The allowlist held. The copy command did not ask it.

Docker Sandboxes runs agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Gemini CLI inside a microVM with its own kernel, filesystem and network. You grant it specific folders, usually the project workspace, and those folders are shared into the VM. Together they form an allowlist: the only parts of your machine the agent is supposed to reach.

On November 3, Peyton Kennedy of Endor Labs published CVE-2026-103916, a flaw he found in sbx cp, the command that moves files between the sandbox and your machine. The copy runs on your side, with your permissions, and never consults the allowlist. In Kennedy's words, the CLI "resolves symlinks in the paths it is given and acts on the resolution."

The agent controls those links, because the workspace is granted read and write. So it can replace a folder in the workspace with a link to somewhere else on your machine. Inside the VM the link points nowhere, so planting it gains the agent nothing on its own. It takes effect when you run an ordinary copy that passes through that folder. Kennedy shows both directions: a copy out of the sandbox overwrites a file outside the workspace, and a copy in pulls a host file into the sandbox.

The command did have a guard, the -L flag, but it checks only the last part of the path. A symlink can sit in any of four positions, and in the researcher's table "Three of the four positions are open." Endor Labs rates it high, 8.2 on CVSS 3.1.

The fix took two tries

Endor Labs reports that Docker first planned the fix for version 0.48.0 on October 13, and that "after the initial patch was live, the Docker team determined the fix was incomplete." Docker's own release notes for 0.51.0, dated November 3, confirm the final change: "sbx cp blocks symbolic links in mounted directories from escaping onto other host paths." If you run Docker Sandboxes, upgrade to 0.51.0.

This is also the second sbx cp escape this year. An earlier one, CVE-2026-17106, was fixed in 0.38.0, and Kennedy notes that its containment still works. It checked paths inside the archive being copied, not where the copy itself started or landed.

Why the second path gets missed

Kennedy's own summary is the part worth keeping: "the isolation primitive worked, and the failure was a second path to the host that the security model did not account for." He found the same shape earlier this year in another agent sandbox, brig.

The reason is ordinary. A sandbox is designed around its main channel, the shared folder, and that channel gets the allowlist and the tests. Side channels that move files on the operator's behalf, such as copy, export, download and artifact upload, look like the operator's own action, so they inherit the operator's trust. When the agent controls the path, that trust is spent wherever the agent points it.

Anything that lets an agent produce files on a real machine has these side channels: a build step that collects outputs, a tool that saves an attachment, a job that syncs a report to shared storage. Each one needs the boundary checked again, at the moment it touches the disk.

A copy that stays inside the workspace

Here is a sketch of how we would write the host side of a copy out of an agent's workspace in Node. It is ours, not Docker's code.

import { constants, promises as fs } from "node:fs";
import path from "node:path";

// Write bytes to a path inside the workspace, or refuse.
export async function writeInside(
  workspace: string,
  relPath: string,
  data: Uint8Array,
): Promise<string> {
  const root = await fs.realpath(workspace);
  const target = path.resolve(root, relPath);
  // Resolve every directory on the way, not only the file name.
  const dir = await fs.realpath(path.dirname(target));
  if (dir !== root && !dir.startsWith(root + path.sep)) {
    throw new Error(`refused: ${relPath} resolves to ${dir}`);
  }
  const file = path.join(dir, path.basename(target));
  // O_NOFOLLOW: if the file itself is a link, fail.
  const flags = constants.O_WRONLY | constants.O_CREAT |
    constants.O_TRUNC | constants.O_NOFOLLOW;
  const fh = await fs.open(file, flags, 0o644);
  try { await fh.writeFile(data); } finally { await fh.close(); }
  return file; // print it, so a person sees where it landed
}

Notice three things. The check runs on the resolved parent directory, which is exactly the position -L left open. The final open refuses to follow a link in the last position. And the function returns the real path, so the caller can print it; Kennedy points out that a successful sbx cp printed nothing, so a person watching had nothing to notice. A copy in is the same check on the source.

Where the sketch stops

A path check and the write that follows it are two steps. An agent that can rewrite its workspace while the copy runs could swap a folder for a link in between. On Linux, openat2 with RESOLVE_BENEATH makes the kernel enforce the boundary during the open itself, and Go code can use a library such as cyphar/filepath-securejoin, which Kennedy notes was already linked into the sbx binary. Use those where you can. The sketch shows the rule; the kernel enforces it.

If your agent never writes outside a VM and nothing it produces is copied back, none of this applies. The moment its output lands on a machine you use, it does.

What to take from it

  • Upgrade Docker Sandboxes to 0.51.0, and until you have, resolve a path yourself before you copy to or from a workspace.
  • List every channel that moves files between your agent and a real machine, not only the shared folder.
  • Check the boundary on each one after resolving every part of the path, at the moment of the write.
  • Show the resolved path whenever a copy succeeds.

If you are putting agents in front of real systems and want the file paths checked before they ship, book a conversation.

Sources

  • Endor Labs, Peyton Kennedy, "Docker Sandboxes vulnerability lets AI agents access sensitive files outside their sandbox (CVE-2026-103916)", November 3, 2026: https://www.endorlabs.com/learn/docker-sandboxes-vulnerability-lets-ai-agents-access-sensitive-files-outside-their-sandbox-cve-2026-103916
  • Docker, Docker Sandboxes release notes, version 0.51.0 (2026-11-03): https://docs.docker.com/ai/sandboxes/release-notes/

title: A One-Way Walkie-Talkie for the AI, and the Return Leg I Already Built
description:
He built himself a radio for the AI. He dictates a voice message into Telegram, WhatsApp or Signal; n8n transcribes it; and a session opens at once in Antigravity, Claude Code, Codex and Cursor, each carrying a short system prompt: you are working alongside three other LLMs, collaborate, agree who does what, and complete the task as well and as fast as possible, following the rules of the Bible and all our principles.

He says the fan-out genuinely helps - one model does not always cope, and three or four together find the concept well. The complaint is that the radio only transmits. To read the answers he opens four sessions in four tools by hand. What would be great, he says, is if the models talked to each other, took the task to some semicolon, and brought back one answer.

That thing is built. A skill on the shelf, version 1.0.0, whose contract is almost word for word the request: take the current question, connect the peers, read only messages addressed to that topic so their answers are separated from chat noise, and return one agreed decision or an honest refusal.

So the missing piece is not the mechanism, it is the trigger. The consensus skill is called from inside a session; the radio is fired by a voice message.

piece of the loop state
voice to text n8n, live, answers 200
fan-out to four CLIs built
shared session id across them requested 29 October
peers agree, one answer returns skill exists, 1.0.0
that answer arrives in Telegram the gap

And the thread got there independently. Eight substantive replies, and four of them proposed the same fix: why five inputs, invent an orchestrator and it will answer you in Telegram; better through an AI orchestrator that collects everything itself; one main one on the phone takes the commands and reports; and the sharpest - when several models discuss something without a moderator, nothing comes of it.

Four people arrived at the architecture his own rail policy already mandates: one orchestrator, everything else an executor. The post describes four peers negotiating with nobody in charge, which is the single configuration the canon rules out.

One commenter brought the part nobody else did: phones will not hand an app the headset and the microphone together, the one exception being a phone call. Their workaround is a custom board with a SIM, or a separate Android reflashed for it. That is the reason a two-way radio is hard on mobile specifically.

Another asked something measurable: do the Bible's rules fit in the context? They do not. The two always-loaded files on this machine come to 879,910 characters, about 405,000 tokens, and the Bible is a further 525 regulation files. Which is why the canon is pointers with bodies pulled on demand, and why the prompt says follow the rules rather than containing them. A peer told to follow rules it cannot fetch is being handed a slogan.

⚠️ Instrument notes. The n8n check is one unauthenticated request to the instance root: a 200 means the service answers, not that the workflow runs. Skills were read from the shelf, not exercised - no live consensus run was made for this post. Token figures are character counts divided by the measured Russian ratio of 2.17, so within about ten percent. The 525 count is by filename pattern on this machine. Thread metrics were read without logging in, so nested replies may be missing.

title: Responsive Design and Mobile Performance Fixes That Make a Real Difference
description:
Most "mobile problems" on websites come from a small set of repeat offenders: oversized images, layout jumps, unreadable text, tiny tap targets and too much JavaScript. The good news is that none of them need a full rewrite. You can fix most of them on an existing site, one change at a time.

This guide walks through twelve fixes, each with code you can adapt. It is ordered roughly from the easiest wins to fix issues to the more involved ones, and ends with how to measure the results so you know the work paid off.

Why mobile deserves its own attention

A phone is not just a small desktop. It usually has a slower CPU, a less stable network, a touch screen instead of a mouse, and a user who is often distracted or in a hurry. A page that feels fine on your development laptop over fast Wi-Fi can feel sluggish on a mid-range phone over a mobile connection.

Google's Core Web Vitals give us three useful measures of that experience:

LCP (Largest Contentful Paint): how quickly the main content appears.
CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift): how much the layout jumps around while loading.
INP (Interaction to Next Paint): how quickly the page responds when someone taps or types.

Every fix below maps to at least one of these, or to plain usability.

  1. Start with the viewport tag

Without it, mobile browsers render your page at a desktop-width canvas and then shrink it down, which makes everything tiny.

html
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">

Avoid adding maximum-scale=1 or user-scalable=no. They block pinch-zoom, which is an accessibility problem for people with low vision.

  1. Serve the right image size to each device

A 2400px-wide image on a 390px-wide phone wastes bandwidth and slows down LCP. Use srcset and sizes so the browser can pick the best file for the screen.

How it works: srcset lists the available files and their real widths. sizes tells the browser how wide the image will be displayed at different viewport sizes. The browser combines that with the device's pixel density and chooses a file.

Where your build pipeline allows it, also offer modern formats such as WebP or AVIF using the element:

Browsers that don't support a format simply fall back to the next option.

  1. Always set image dimensions to prevent layout shift

The width and height attributes in the examples above let the browser reserve the correct amount of space before the file downloads. Without them, text jumps down when the image finally appears, which is exactly what CLS measures.

Pair the attributes with this CSS so images remain fluid:

css
img {
  max-width: 100%;
  height: auto;
}

The browser uses the attributes to work out the aspect ratio, and the CSS lets the image shrink to fit its container. The same idea applies to embedded videos and iframes. The aspect-ratio property is a clean way to reserve space for them:

css
.video-embed {
  aspect-ratio: 16 / 9;
  width: 100%;
}
  1. Lazy-load below the fold, prioritize above it

A common mistake is lazy-loading everything, including the largest image at the top of the page. That delays LCP. Treat the hero or main product image as a priority and lazy-load the rest.

  1. Use fluid typography instead of a pile of breakpoints

clamp() lets text scale smoothly between a minimum and a maximum size, so you don't need a font-size rule at every breakpoint.

css
h1 {
  font-size: clamp(1.75rem, 1.2rem + 2.5vw, 3rem);
  line-height: 1.15;
}

body {
  font-size: clamp(1rem, 0.95rem + 0.25vw, 1.125rem);
  line-height: 1.6;
}

Keep body text at around 16px or larger on phones so nobody has to zoom to read it. Using rem units rather than px also respects the user's browser font-size settings.

  1. Build layouts that adapt without media queries

CSS Grid's auto-fit creates a card layout that reflows on its own as the container changes size:

css
.cards {
  display: grid;
  gap: 1rem;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(100%, 260px), 1fr));
}

The min(100%, 260px) part is important. Without it, a column with a 260px minimum can overflow a very narrow screen and cause accidental horizontal scrolling, one of the most common mobile bugs.

For simple one-dimensional layouts, Flexbox with wrapping does a similar job:

css
.row {
  display: flex;
  flex-wrap: wrap;
  gap: 1rem;
}

.row > * {
  flex: 1 1 240px;
}
  1. Use container queries for reusable components

Media queries respond to the viewport. But a card component might sit in a wide main column on one page and a narrow sidebar on another. Container queries let the component respond to the space it actually has.

css
.card-wrapper {
  container-type: inline-size;
}

.card {
  display: grid;
  gap: 0.75rem;
}

@container (min-width: 480px) {
  .card {
    grid-template-columns: 160px 1fr;
  }
}

This makes components more portable and reduces the number of one-off overrides in your stylesheet. Container queries are supported in all current major browsers.

  1. Make tap targets big enough

Small links and buttons are frustrating on touchscreens, and they cause mis-taps. A good rule is at least 44 by 44 CSS pixels. WCAG 2.2 sets 24px as a minimum for a pass, and Apple's and Google's guidelines suggest larger.

css
button,
.nav a {
  min-height: 44px;
  min-width: 44px;
  padding: 0.75rem 1rem;
}

Leave some space between neighbouring targets too. A row of tightly packed text links in a footer is a classic problem. Padding the links, instead of only increasing the gap, enlarges the tappable area.

  1. Tame fonts

Web fonts are a frequent cause of slow first paint and of text that flashes or jumps.

css
@font-face {
  font-family: "Inter";
  src: url("/fonts/inter-var.woff2") format("woff2");
  font-weight: 100 900;
  font-display: swap;
}
html
<link rel="preload" href="/fonts/inter-var.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>

Use font-display: swap so text appears right away in a fallback font.
Preload only the one or two font files used above the fold.
Serve WOFF2 and limit the weights and character sets to what you actually use.
Consider a variable font if you use several weights, since one file can replace many.

  1. Control third-party scripts and JavaScript weight

On mobile, JavaScript is often the biggest cost, because it has to be downloaded, parsed and executed on a slower CPU. It is also the main driver of poor INP.

html
<script src="/analytics.js" defer></script>
<script src="/chat-widget.js" async></script>

Practical steps:

Use defer for scripts that need the DOM and async for independent ones.
Audit your tags. Old tracking pixels, unused chat widgets and duplicate analytics are very common.
Split large bundles so each page loads only what it needs.
Break up long tasks. If a click handler does heavy work, yield back to the browser so the interface can update:

js
button.addEventListener("click", async () => {
  showSpinner();
  // Let the browser paint before heavy work
  await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 0));
  doHeavyWork();
});
  1. Respect user preferences

Responsive design is also about the person using the device, not only the screen size. Two media queries cost almost nothing and help a lot:

css
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  * {
    animation-duration: 0.01ms !important;
    animation-iteration-count: 1 !important;
    transition-duration: 0.01ms !important;
    scroll-behavior: auto !important;
  }
}

@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
  :root {
    --bg: #0f1115;
    --text: #e8eaed;
  }
}

Heavy animations can be uncomfortable for some users and drain battery. A dark theme also helps people who use their phone at night.

  1. Prevent horizontal scrolling and fix the usual suspects

Sideways scrolling on a phone makes a site feel broken. Common causes and quick fixes:

css
/* Long words or URLs breaking the layout */
p, li {
  overflow-wrap: anywhere;
}

/* Wide tables */
.table-wrap {
  overflow-x: auto;
}

/* Elements wider than the screen */
*, *::before, *::after {
  box-sizing: border-box;
}

To find the culprit, open DevTools in responsive mode at 320px width and look for the element that extends past the edge. Avoid hiding the problem with overflow-x: hidden on body as a first resort, since that can mask real layout bugs and break sticky positioning.

Measure before and after

Fixes only matter if you can see their effect. Use a mix of lab and real-world tools:

Lighthouse in Chrome DevTools, with mobile throttling turned on, for a quick lab test.
PageSpeed Insights to see real-user field data (Core Web Vitals) when your site has enough traffic.
Chrome DevTools Performance panel with CPU throttling to find long tasks.
A real mid-range phone on a mobile connection. Emulators hide a lot.

Change one thing at a time and re-test, so you know what helped. Lab scores fluctuate between runs, so compare trends rather than single numbers.

Common mistakes to avoid
Lazy-loading the main hero image.
Using fixed pixel widths on containers.
Hiding content on mobile instead of designing it properly for small screens.
Disabling zoom.
Loading every font weight "just in case".
Testing only at your own device's screen size.
Quick checklist
Viewport meta tag present
Responsive images with srcset, plus width and height
Hero image prioritized, others lazy-loaded
Fluid type with clamp()
Flexible grids with no horizontal scrolling at 320px
Tap targets at least 44px
Fonts preloaded, with font-display: swap
Scripts deferred and audited
Reduced-motion and dark-mode preferences respected
Tested on a real phone
Final thoughts

Good mobile performance rarely comes from one big trick. It comes from many small, sensible decisions: send fewer bytes, reserve space for what's coming, keep the main thread free, and make everything easy to read and tap. Start with the quick wins at the top of this list, measure, and work down.

Which of these has made the biggest difference on your projects? Let me know in the comments.

title: How Vercel Agent accesses production safely
description:
An agent working on production systems needs permission to act. A request like “fix this deployment” doesn’t tell you upfront which actions it will take or what access it will need. Grant agents broad access and a mistake can affect unrelated resources. Ask for approval at every step and the user has to approve individual actions before they know how the agent intends to solve the problem. Repeated prompts can turn that review into a habit of clicking approve.

Vercel Agent starts by investigating the problem, then proposes a plan showing what it would do and what access it would need. Approving that plan grants the additional permissions to carry it out, so the user can review the proposed fix before authorizing any changes.

The plan determines the permissions

For a broken production deployment, Vercel Agent might inspect recent deployments and build logs, then compare the failed deployment with the last known-good one. Read-only access lets that investigation run automatically. If it leads to a proposed redeploy, Vercel Agent requests the additional access in a plan the user can review and approve in one decision.

Access is defined by scopes, the named capabilities recognized by the Vercel authorization system. Any plan requesting access beyond the read-only baseline waits for approval as a whole, including any read-only tasks it contains. In this example, the investigation runs under a separate read-only plan before Vercel Agent proposes the redeploy:

Plan

Work

Requested scope

Investigate the failure

Inspect recent deployments and build logs, then compare the failed deployment with the last successful one

read:deployment

Redeploy the last known-good build

Create a deployment

read-write:deployment

A short read-only lookup can run without a plan. For longer investigations, Vercel Agent creates a read-only plan so the user can follow its tasks and progress while it runs automatically.

The plan connects what the user wants done to what Vercel Agent is allowed to do:

  • Intent: The outcome the user asks for.

  • Work: The tasks Vercel Agent proposes to achieve it.

  • Access: The scopes those tasks require.

  • Enforcement: The credentials and API checks that enforce access limits.

Each stored plan records its tasks and progress, with requested scopes attached to each task. The task descriptions explain why access is needed, and the scopes are combined across the plan.

The read-only baseline currently includes every registered scope beginning with read:. Plans need approval when they request access beyond that baseline or include supported external actions, such as opening a GitHub pull request. Read-only operations can still expose sensitive information, so automatic approval does not mean the work is harmless.

Vercel Agent can only use permissions the user already has

Vercel Agent runs as a Vercel App, which the user authorizes to act on their behalf within a team. That authorization is limited by the user’s existing permissions, so approving a plan cannot grant access the user does not have.

The Vercel OAuth service exchanges that authorization for shorter-lived tokens with specific scopes. These scopes define which capabilities the token permits, such as reading deployments or changing project settings. Vercel APIs check the token on each request to enforce those limits.

A user may authorize Vercel Agent for a team with dozens of projects. A redeploy plan requests deployment write access. Editing environment variables, changing domains, and managing team membership each require their own permissions.

Deployment write access is broader than a single redeploy. Naming deployment X in a plan does not, by itself, restrict the token to that deployment. The runtime, the software that coordinates Vercel Agent’s execution, checks that the plan is active before selecting its approved credential. Vercel APIs check each request against that credential’s permissions.

Approval determines which permissions Vercel Agent can use

When a user approves a plan that needs additional Vercel access, its requested scopes are checked again and a token is prepared containing the read-only baseline plus the approved permissions. The runtime, the software that coordinates Vercel Agent’s execution, checks that the plan is active before selecting its approved credential. That credential remains subject to its scopes, team, the user’s permissions, and expiry.

The credential used depends on the work:

Work

Credential

Read-only investigation

A baseline token with read-only scopes

Approved Vercel changes

A token with baseline scopes plus the approved additional scopes

External actions

Credentials and permissions specific to that provider

The model’s instructions tell it when to propose a plan and request approval. If it attempts an operation outside the token’s permissions, Vercel APIs reject the request, even if the model considers the action necessary to complete the task.

A single plan can include Vercel changes and a GitHub pull request. The user reviews both in one plan, while each provider uses separate permissions and credentials. GitHub pull-request access is tied to an owner and repository, so approval to open a pull request in acme/storefront applies to that repository even if the user also has access to acme/payments. Opening a pull request there requires its own approval.

Plans and tokens use the same permission definitions

A proposed plan can request a permission that has been renamed or removed. We initially maintained a separate permission list for Vercel Agent, which could fall out of sync with the OAuth service that issues its tokens. We moved to the same scope definitions so those mismatches could be caught during planning.

At session setup, Vercel Agent loads those definitions from the Vercel scope registry into an in-memory catalog. Fetching the registry requires authorization for the team, while the scope definitions themselves are shared across teams. The catalog supplies the definitions used at three stages:

  • Plan validation: Requested scopes are normalized, and unknown or malformed names are rejected before the plan is stored or presented for approval.

  • Approval: The requested scopes determine whether the plan fits within the read-only baseline or needs additional access.

  • Token preparation: Valid scopes define the credentials for approved work.

For example, a task to update firewall rules might request an outdated scope. The system rejects the proposed plan and returns valid scopes so Vercel Agent can correct it before requesting approval. This catches the mismatch during planning and requires an explicit correction instead of a fallback to broader access.

Fetching the registry adds latency and a service dependency, so Vercel Agent caches the catalog and uses that copy to check stored plans when they are loaded. Those checks reflect the cached definitions until the catalog is refreshed with changes from the registry.

Resuming work requires an active, approved plan

Vercel Agent may receive approval after the original chat request has ended, or lose its connection before carrying out an approved redeploy. The stored plan includes its state, who approved it, and when, alongside its tasks and requested permissions. That record connects the proposed work to the access the user authorized and allows the approval to be checked when work resumes.

Before resuming, the runtime reloads the plan and checks that it is active before selecting a credential with its approved permissions. A stopped plan fails that check, even if its token has time remaining before expiry.

If approval and a request to stop arrive together, the plan can move from waiting for approval to active only if the stop has not already changed its status. The runtime then checks again that the plan is active before using the approved credential.

If the investigation reveals that the current plan needs replacing, Vercel Agent can propose another. A replacement requesting elevated access needs its own approval, giving the user a chance to review the revised work and permissions together.

Where permissions need more precision

As Vercel Agent reached more of the platform, we had to correct access rules for actions that involve multiple resources or have different consequences. Attaching a domain can require both domain and project permissions, while staging a firewall rule and publishing it need different levels of access. Scopes need to capture these distinctions while keeping each plan’s access request manageable.

Matching those scopes to a proposed fix requires care throughout planning:

  • Choosing scopes: Vercel Agent chooses scopes with incomplete information, so it can request too little access and leave a task blocked, or too much and grant more authority than the work needs. Task-level guidance helps it choose, while validation catches invalid scope names. Even a valid scope can grant broader access than necessary.

  • Describing the work: “Redeploy the last successful build” gives the user a concrete action to assess, while scope names alone leave them to work out the consequences. The plan needs to explain the intended change and make clear which limits the token actually enforces.

  • Understanding denials: A denied operation could indicate a missing scope, an incorrect resource, or an operation that should remain blocked. Vercel Agent needs to distinguish those cases before requesting additional permissions.

Even with the right permissions, a redeploy requires judgment about whether the selected commit is safe to ship. That depends on the application, the failure, and the proposed fix. The user needs enough information to assess the choice, and Vercel Agent still has to execute it correctly.

Read-only investigation also needs controls for the information it retrieves, including sensitive project configuration and operational details. We chose a read-only baseline so Vercel Agent can investigate before asking for approval, and that choice needs continued review as scopes and the information they expose change. Other systems may need a narrower baseline. Separate controls must govern how retrieved information is handled and where it can go.

Vercel Agent can make a wrong decision or encounter malicious instructions in content it reads, such as build logs. Scoped credentials limit which operations it can perform in either case, but permitted operations can still cause harm. Plans therefore work alongside sandbox isolation, network policy, secret handling, rate limits, audit logs, and service authorization. Our work on security boundaries in agentic architectures explains the separation between an agent, its credentials, and the code it executes.

From investigation to approved action

Authority stays attached to the work that required it. The runtime selects the approved credential for an active plan, and its scopes define the operations Vercel Agent can perform. With the investigation already done, the user can assess a proposed fix and its requested access together.

Try Vercel Agent to investigate an issue in your project. Review what it finds and, if it proposes a change, assess the plan and requested access before approving it.

title: A three-state label queue where 100% reviewed and 0 labels can both be true
description:
Why one boolean is not enough

A common first draft for a local annotation or review queue adds a done boolean to every record. It becomes true when someone looks at the record and false before that. The problem appears at export time: the same field cannot say whether the record has a label. A record can be processed yet unlabelled, or unprocessed yet read downstream as finished. Separate two predicates first. reviewed means the record has been handled, including giving a label or explicitly abstaining. label_present means the record actually carries a label from the taxonomy.

local-label-queue is a small public tool I made; the source and samples are downloadable. It uses three states instead of two booleans: unlabelled, labelled, and abstained. The label field holds a taxonomy string only when status is labelled, and is null in the other two states. The tool has no done or has_label boolean field. An external system that defines done as reviewed makes labelled and abstained both true. One that defines done as label_present makes abstained and unlabelled both false. The three states keep the gap between the two predicates.

What the 12 synthetic records show

The bundled demo-annotations.jsonl contains 12 records: 2 labelled, 1 abstained, and 9 unlabelled. Every non-labelled row has label: null. Reviewed therefore counts 3, label_present counts 2, and the difference is the abstained row. Abstaining on every record gives a reviewed fraction of 1 while labelled stays 0. That shows abstention counts toward workflow progress but creates no label and implies nothing about label correctness. If a single boolean is defined as reviewed, it merges labelled with abstained. If it is defined as has_label, it merges abstained with unlabelled. Splitting the two questions keeps the legitimate state of 100% processed with zero labels from disappearing.

The two lines below fetch the public sample and count it. The result should match the description above.

curl -sL https://huggingface.co/spaces/WideChaos/local-label-queue/raw/d8068775077cd4149a39ec9a2c6cb0ab52045d54/demo-annotations.jsonl -o demo-annotations.jsonl
node --input-type=module -e 'const rows=(await import("node:fs")).readFileSync("demo-annotations.jsonl","utf8").trim().split("\n").map(JSON.parse);const c=rows.reduce((a,r)=>(a[r.status]=(a[r.status]||0)+1,a),{});console.log(c, rows.filter(r=>r.status!=="labelled"&&r.label!==null).length)'

The output should include { labelled: 2, abstained: 1, unlabelled: 9 }, with zero non-labelled rows whose label is not null. This checks state modeling and export fidelity. It does not check label correctness because the sample is original synthetic material, not human annotation or a gold standard.

This screenshot shows the public Space I deployed, displaying the same 12 synthetic records: 2 labelled, 1 abstained, and 9 unlabelled, with reviewed near 25% including the abstention. That share measures queue progress only; it says nothing about label correctness. The page also has no autosave.

revision and checkpoint serve different purposes

demo-checkpoint.json uses the same inventory and still shows 2/1/9, but its revision field is 7. revision counts changes, including undo operations. It is neither a processed count nor a labelled count. Reading it as completion progress creates false numbers.

The checkpoint is for resuming. The tool keeps decisions only in page memory; it has no autosave, browser storage, or cloud sync. Download the checkpoint explicitly before a refresh. On restore, it verifies the inventory hash and content hash, shows a preview, and replaces the current state explicitly rather than merging. JSONL export keeps every original group and text, not only labelled rows, so review all records before sharing the file with someone else.

SHA-256 is a recomputable consistency check. It detects a changed or truncated file but proves nothing about origin, label truth, or encryption, and it cannot stop someone from repacking a file after verification.
