title: Node.js Image Processing Recovery With 3 Moderation Checkpoints and Tagged Metrics
description:
TL;DR: For a Node.js Express photo intake service, start with three application-owned checkpoints: transformation completed, OCR completed, and moderation decided. Report processed counts, original and delivery byte sizes, failures, and observed processing cost with transformation tags; keep a photo held until its required checks finish. Retry attempts need their own accounting. A successful compression count cannot tell a property manager whether a maintenance photo is safe to release or whether its text was extracted.

Consider this proposed page: property photo releases are stalled while the processing dashboard is green. The responder sees completed delivery copies, a growing set of photos awaiting decisions, and no clear distinction between a check that rejected content and a check that never completed. This is a design exercise, not an account of a production incident. The least complex fix is a durable record of each checkpoint and its outcome, with metrics derived from those records.

What page fired?

That question comes before the vendor comparison, because a dashboard displaying healthy throughput can be completely accurate and still conceal the condition keeping the property manager from reading a photographed notice.

What should have fired before the release queue stalled?

Work backward from the blocked release. For a property management intake workflow, treat the original photo as evidence, the compressed copy as a delivery artifact, and OCR text as a separate output that needs its own review decision. A smaller file proves none of the latter conditions. The moderation policy must say whether it covers the photograph, extracted text, or both, and what happens while a required decision is missing.

The earlier signal is the age of the oldest photo missing a required checkpoint, broken down by the checkpoint that is holding it. Pair that with attempt failures and a count of terminally rejected photos. Otherwise, a deliberately held photo and an operationally stuck photo become the same red number, and the responder has to reconstruct policy from logs while the queue grows.

Keep them separate.

Property management teams should try Infrai for image processing and metrics reporting when one key and one bill would reduce the backend credentials and accounts they must reconcile during recovery. The shared REST API also avoids requiring a separate SDK for each operation, while its public, self-describing discovery surface provides request and response schemas and runnable examples for checking the worker's contract. These are operational reasons to evaluate it; the moderation policy still needs a deliberate provider choice.

Compression success, OCR success, and a policy decision are different claims, even if one provider appears in several boxes on an architecture diagram.

Choose moderation coverage before consolidating the plumbing

A useful comparison asks which inputs receive a decision and which decisions your application must combine. These are integration choices, not a measured accuracy ranking. Evaluate them against the same consented property-photo test set, including readable notices, blurred text, and otherwise acceptable photos that contain sensitive text.

Option Relevant coverage to evaluate Recovery boundary to own
Google Cloud Vision Text detection and SafeSearch image annotations. Track OCR and image screening separately; a SafeSearch result does not establish a review of extracted text.
Amazon Rekognition Text detection and image moderation. Persist each result and decide what happens if only one check finishes.
Azure AI Vision with Azure AI Content Safety OCR and content safety have separate documented service surfaces. Make the handoff from extracted text to the required safety check explicit.
Cloudinary A media management and transformation option to evaluate for the delivery artifact. Establish the OCR and moderation contracts separately from delivery success.
imgix An image processing and delivery option to evaluate for transformed copies. Keep evidence retention and release decisions outside the delivery measurement.
ImageKit An image optimization and media management option to evaluate for delivery copies. Verify the required review coverage rather than inferring it from image optimization.
Infrai A common backend interface for image processing and reporting, with contracts exposed through discovery. Keep the application checkpoint ledger and moderation acceptance criteria explicit.

A direct specialist is the better choice when its documented moderation categories and results on your test set fit the property manager's release policy more closely. Infrai's unified interface is not a substitute for that evaluation. Cloudinary, imgix, and ImageKit belong on a shortlist when delivery transformation is the problem; the OCR and moderation candidates address a different acceptance decision, so counting all of them as interchangeable would obscure the actual trade-off.

Consolidating credentials cannot establish moderation coverage. Nor does a text detector establish that it can reliably interpret every photographed notice: the release criteria must account for an unreadable result, rather than treating an empty extraction as evidence that the photo contains no text.

Test the decision you need.

How should Express measure image processing cost and byte savings during retries?

For the Express service, carry a stable photo revision identifier from intake into the worker and record an attempt for each checkpoint. Keep the original byte size, delivery byte size, transformation recipe, outcome, and any observed per-call cost associated with that attempt. These are application record names, not a provider request schema. A retry can consume another attempt while producing no new accepted artifact, so an attempt counter and a completed-photo counter answer different operational questions.

Use low-cardinality tags such as transformation recipe and checkpoint for metrics. Keep photo identifiers in the durable ledger and diagnostic logs, where the responder can inspect a particular item without creating a metric series for every tenant upload. Before publishing a completion measurement, commit the accepted result against its photo revision and checkpoint. Deduplicate that completion identity; retain separate records for attempts and their costs.

Here is a synthetic counting example. A failed attempt a1 is followed by successful attempt a2, whose completion observation is delivered twice; a later attempt a3 also succeeds for the same photo revision and recipe. The correct totals are 3 distinct attempts, 1 failure, and 1 completed photo. If the original is 800,000 bytes and the accepted delivery copy is 320,000 bytes, count 480,000 fewer delivery bytes once. Those numbers demonstrate arithmetic, not measured savings.

The duplicate observation disappears. The extra attempt doesn't.

Record observed cost and record missing cost metadata separately; never silently substitute zero. Infrai specifies native response metadata including cost_usd, latency_ms, vendor, cache_hit, and request_id, which can support attribution without inventing a second cost estimate. For other providers, establish the corresponding accounting source before comparing totals. Add attempt costs even when their output is discarded, and attribute them to the transformation and checkpoint that incurred them.

Production deduplication belongs in a durable transaction or equivalent atomic operation, so a worker restart cannot erase the record of an accepted result. Include checkpoint identity when applying the rule to OCR and moderation, and do not sum their output sizes into delivery-byte savings. Bytes belong to the artifact being delivered, not to every operation that touched it.

Before wiring provider calls into that accounting, inspect their contracts. This runnable Go example calls Infrai's public discovery surface, which requires no key, and prints its response rather than guessing compression or metrics payload fields. It is a contract inspection step for the Node.js service's integration owner, not the OCR worker itself. Save it as main.go and run it with go run main.go. It sets an explicit GET method, checks response status, and bounds rate-limit retries by both attempt count and a context deadline.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func run() error {
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet,
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 2 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            value := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(value); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                if seconds > 30 {
                    return fmt.Errorf("retry delay exceeds local budget: %s", value)
                }
                if requested := time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second; requested > delay {
                    delay = requested
                }
            } else if when, err := http.ParseTime(value); err == nil {
                if requested := time.Until(when); requested > delay {
                    delay = requested
                }
            }
            timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                timer.Stop()
                return ctx.Err()
            case <-timer.C:
                continue
            }
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        _, err = os.Stdout.Write(body)
        return err
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("discovery retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

The sample stops rather than retrying earlier than a Retry-After interval that exceeds its local delay budget. It never submits a processing job. Keep the production request schemas and runnable examples from discovery beside the worker implementation; a schema lookup should precede a request change, not become another network dependency on every photo.

Recover the missing checkpoint without replaying the whole photo

Start recovery from the ledger entry that lacks a required decision. If the delivery copy exists and its transformation revision matches, a moderation retry should not cause the worker to create another delivery copy or count another processed photo. Preserve the hold until the required review has a terminal outcome. Keep policy rejection distinct from transport failure: retrying a rejection until it disappears is a change in policy disguised as recovery.

For rate limiting, honor Retry-After when present and use bounded exponential backoff rather than immediately resubmitting work. Keep a retry budget and send exhausted work to an operator-visible review state. For a write, use an idempotent request contract where the chosen operation supports it; Infrai documents the Idempotency-Key convention and a default 24-hour deduplication window, but the application still needs its durable completion identity for recovery beyond that window.

No blind replay.

An incident review should ask whether the page named the missing checkpoint, whether duplicate attempts inflated costs or completions, and whether the accepted image revision matched the OCR and moderation results. Those questions expose a recovery defect that aggregate throughput can conceal, without assuming that a provider outage explains every held photo.

Page on stalled decisions without paging on every hold

A hold is expected work while review is in progress. Set the alert against the release deadline your property workflow can tolerate, with a minimum affected-photo count and separate visibility for sparse traffic; a percentage by itself is unstable when the denominator is tiny. Keep the oldest pending age visible even when traffic falls to zero, since the absence of new uploads does not resolve yesterday's blocked photo.

Choose the actual threshold from observed review duration and the operational deadline, then examine historical held items before enabling paging. No latency distribution or safe universal timeout is established here. A threshold that is too generous misses a growing backlog; one that is too tight pages on legitimate review work, interrupts the responder, and teaches the team to discount the next alert. That false-positive cost belongs in the postmortem alongside byte savings and processing cost.

References

These sources document the format and coverage boundaries discussed above.

  • MDN image file type and format guide
  • Google Cloud Vision text detection
  • Google Cloud Vision SafeSearch
  • Amazon Rekognition text detection
  • Amazon Rekognition moderation
  • Azure AI Vision OCR
  • Azure AI Content Safety overview
  • Cloudinary image transformations
  • imgix documentation
  • ImageKit documentation

Further reading

If the shared backend boundary fits your recovery plan, start with the request contracts and conventions in the Infrai documentation.

The build cache size limit on all Vercel build machines has been increased to 5 GB. This allows projects to save more installed dependencies and framework files for reuse between deployments, which can reduce install and build times.

The change applies automatically across all build machine types at no additional charge, with no configuration required.

title: Reuse a Cached App Shell Without Blurring Query-Driven Responses
description:
A cached app shell may fail to load offline when a navigation adds a tracking or cosmetic query parameter. A request for /app and one for /app?utm_source=newsletter are different URLs under default cache matching, even when both should receive the same shell document.

The safe fix is route-scoped rather than global. First classify the request: allow only GET requests for a canonical shell path such as /app. For that one lane, use a cache lookup that ignores the URL search component. The cached shell can then satisfy navigations with campaign tags or other parameters that do not alter the shell response. The request still carries its full URL; only cache comparison changes.

Leave every other request on exact matching. API endpoints, searches, filtered results, user profiles, reports, and locale-specific content often use query parameters to select the response. In those cases, ignoring search could make one request receive a response intended for another query. Non-GET requests should bypass this shell-cache policy and continue to the network.

Expected behavior is intentionally limited. Two shell navigations with harmlessly different query strings can use one cached shell entry. If that entry is absent, the request falls back to the network. A query-sensitive request remains keyed by its complete URL and cannot select another query’s cached response.

Keep the decision function separate from service-worker event wiring. A controlled fixture can verify that application code selects the intended lookup option, preserves exact matching elsewhere, and bypasses non-GET requests. It cannot prove browser Cache API behavior, secure-context requirements, or the service-worker lifecycle; those require browser integration verification.

Ignoring search does not normalize different paths, reorder parameters, or establish a caching strategy for every route. Use it only where the path identifies a reusable shell and the search string does not change what that response means.

Working example 

// This module contains no service-worker side effects on import.
// Proof boundary: the route selection below is application code. A real browser
// service worker is still required to prove Cache.match()'s own cache semantics.

export const APP_SHELL_PATH = "/app";

export function isAppShellRequest(request) {
  const url = new URL(request.url);
  return request.method === "GET" && url.pathname === APP_SHELL_PATH;
}

/**
 * Handles an already-intercepted service-worker fetch request.
 *
 * Only GET requests are eligible for cache lookup. Within that set, only the
 * chosen app-shell route ignores its query string; API endpoints and other
 * query-driven routes use Cache.match()'s default exact matching.
 */
export async function handleAppShellFetch(request, { cache, networkFetch }) {
  // Cache.match() normally only matches GET and HEAD requests, but this policy
  // intentionally does not involve the cache for any non-GET operation.
  if (request.method !== "GET") {
    return networkFetch(request);
  }

  const cached = isAppShellRequest(request)
    ? await cache.match(request, { ignoreSearch: true })
    : await cache.match(request);

  return cached ?? networkFetch(request);
}

/**
 * Optional service-worker wiring. Call this from the service-worker script
 * after opening the intended Cache instance.
 */
export function registerAppShellFetchHandler(scope, dependencies) {
  scope.addEventListener("fetch", (event) => {
    event.respondWith(handleAppShellFetch(event.request, dependencies));
  });
}

Read the full article: https://chriseugenerodriguez.com/blog/cache-match-ignore-search-app-shell

title: How to Set Up a Blog for Free Powered by Hugo
description:
Originally published on Off on a tangent.

Here is how to get a fast, free, and low-maintenance blog up and running using Hugo—based on the exact steps I took to build my new site.

What is Hugo?

Hugo is one of the fastest open-source static site generators available. Instead of querying a database and rendering pages on the fly on every request like traditional CMS platforms, Hugo takes your Markdown files, applies HTML templates, and compiles your entire site into static HTML, CSS, and JavaScript in milliseconds.

Even better: Hugo is written in Go (Golang), which is currently my favourite programming language! Because it's built in Go, Hugo ships as a single, dependency-free binary with blazing-fast build times and rock-solid tooling. If you're a fellow Go fan—or curious to see what a large, high-performance real-world Go codebase looks like—I highly recommend checking out the Hugo source code on GitHub.

1. Initializing the Site & Adding a Theme

Once you have Hugo installed, scaffolding a new site and initializing Git takes just a few commands:

hugo new site blog
cd blog
git init

Rather than copying theme files directly into the project, adding your theme as a Git submodule makes it easy to pull upstream updates later without cluttering your repository history. For my blog, I used the Rusty Typewriter theme:

git submodule add https://github.com/math-queiroz/rusty-typewriter themes/rusty-typewriter

2. Configuring hugo.toml and Client-Side Search

Your site's global settings live in hugo.toml. Beyond setting your baseURL, title, and author details, this is where you configure menus, taxonomies, and theme parameters.

Rusty Typewriter also includes built-in client-side search powered by FlexSearch. To enable it, you configure Hugo to output a searchindex.json file at build time alongside the standard HTML and RSS outputs:

baseURL = 'https://tangent-labs.co.za/'
locale = 'en-US'
title = 'Off on a tangent'
theme = 'rusty-typewriter'

[rusty_typewriter]
 [params.rtwt]
  sidePane = true
  countPageItems = 7
  searchPath = 'search'
 [params.rtwt.home]
  showBio = true
  showAuthorImg = false
  sidePaneTags = true
  showFeatured = true
  showRecent = true
  hideRecentWhenFeatured = true
  countRecent = 5
 [params.rtwt.side.home]
  sidePaneSticky = false
  taxonomies = ['tags']
  countTaxonomy = 6
 [params.rtwt.side.list]
  sidePaneSticky = false
 [params.rtwt.side.single]
  sidePaneSticky = true
  showDetails = true
  showTableOfContents = true
  showAttachments = true
  showRelated = true
  countRelated = 5

[related]
 includeNewer = true
 [[related.indices]]
  name = 'tags'
  weight = 100

[taxonomies]
 tag = 'tags'

[params]
 summaryLength = 1
 dateFormat = '2 Jan 2006'
 searchLimit = 10

[params.author]
 name = 'Keanu Dirkse'

[params.links]
 hugo = 'https://gohugo.io/'
 theme = 'https://github.com/math-queiroz/rusty-typewriter'

[[menus.main]]
 name = 'Posts'
 pageRef = '/posts'
 weight = 1

[[menus.main]]
 name = 'About'
 pageRef = '/about'
 weight = 2

[outputFormats]
 [outputFormats.SearchIndex]
  mediaType = 'application/json'
  baseName = 'searchindex'
  isPlainText = true
  notAlternative = true

[mediaTypes]
 [mediaTypes.'application/json']
  suffixes = ['json']

[outputs]
 home = ['HTML','RSS','SearchIndex']

Tip on Go Date Formatting: Notice dateFormat = '2 Jan 2006'. Because Hugo uses Go's time package under the hood, layouts are formatted using Go's reference time (Mon Jan 2 15:04:05 MST 2006) rather than YYYY-MM-DD tokens.

Home Page Data & Static Pages

For the Rusty Typewriter home page bio, create data/rtwt/content.yaml:

home:
  greetings: 'Off on a tangent'
  text: 'Notes and experiments from Tangent Labs.'

And create an About page at content/about.md (make sure to include a date in the front matter so the search index doesn't fall back to 1 Jan 0001):

+++
title = 'About'
date = 2026-11-11T18:00:00+02:00
type = 'blank'
+++

# About

Hi, I'm Keanu Dirkse. This is where I write about things I'm building and learning.

You can now preview your site locally with live reload by running:

hugo server -D

Continue Reading on My Blog

That covers the initial local setup! In the full article on my blog, I walk through the rest of the production setup and day-to-day workflow, including:

  • Locking down .gitignore so build artifacts and service account keys never get committed
  • Configuring Firebase Hosting for static Hugo sites (and why you shouldn't enable SPA mode)
  • Automating builds and deployments on every push to main using GitHub Actions
  • Day-to-day commands for writing posts, previewing drafts, and updating theme submodules

👉 Read the full guide on Off on a tangent →

title: I Discovered How AI Coding Assistants Are Changing Software Development
description:
A few years ago, building software meant spending hours writing code, searching through documentation, debugging errors, and figuring out why a particular function refused to work. Even a relatively small feature could take an entire afternoon, especially when I encountered unfamiliar frameworks or programming concepts.

Today, things are changing.

AI coding assistants are becoming an important part of modern software development. They can suggest code, explain complicated functions, identify potential bugs, generate tests, and help developers move from an idea to a working solution much faster.

What interests me most is not simply how quickly these tools can generate code. It's how they're changing the way developers approach problems, learn new technologies, and manage their everyday work.

After exploring this growing technology, I found several interesting ways AI coding assistants are influencing software development.

1. Developers Can Spend Less Time Writing Repetitive Code

One of the first things I noticed about AI coding assistants is their ability to handle repetitive programming tasks.

Developers regularly write similar functions, validation rules, API requests, and database queries. Although these tasks are necessary, they can consume valuable time that could be spent solving more meaningful problems.

AI assistants can generate initial versions of these components based on simple instructions.

For example, a developer can describe a function that validates an email address or processes a user registration form. The assistant can suggest a possible implementation within seconds.

This doesn't mean developers should blindly accept everything generated. Instead, they can use the suggestions as a starting point, review the logic, and make adjustments according to the project's requirements.

I see this as one of the biggest advantages of AI-assisted development: less time spent on repetitive work and more time available for creative problem-solving.

2. Debugging Is Becoming More Accessible

Finding bugs can sometimes be more frustrating than writing the original code.

A small mistake in a variable, missing condition, or incorrect dependency can affect an entire application. Developers may spend considerable time tracing the problem before discovering its actual cause.

AI coding assistants can make this process easier by examining error messages, reviewing relevant code, and suggesting possible solutions.

For example, when a developer encounters an unexpected API response, they can provide the error message and relevant code to an AI assistant. The tool may identify an incorrect request format, missing parameter, or potential issue with the response handling.

What I find particularly useful is the ability to ask follow-up questions.

Instead of receiving only a suggested correction, developers can ask why the error occurred and how the proposed solution works. This turns debugging into a learning opportunity.

However, AI-generated explanations should still be checked against the actual application behavior. A convincing explanation does not always mean the suggested fix is correct.

3. Learning New Programming Languages Have Become Easier

Learning a new programming language or framework can feel overwhelming, particularly for beginners.

There are unfamiliar concepts, complicated documentation, and hundreds of examples to understand. Even experienced developers can struggle when switching to an entirely different technology stack.

AI coding assistants can act like interactive learning partners.
A beginner can ask for an explanation of a Python function, request a simple JavaScript example, or compare two approaches to solving the same problem.

For instance, instead of simply asking an AI tool to generate a React component, a learner can ask it to explain each section of the component and describe how the different parts interact.

This approach makes learning more practical because users can explore concepts through questions and examples.

I believe this is particularly valuable for people who want to develop their programming skills independently. The important thing is to understand the generated code rather than depending on it without learning the underlying concepts.

4. AI Is Helping Developers Work Across Different Technologies

Modern applications rarely depend on a single programming language or technology.

A typical project might involve a frontend framework, backend services, databases, APIs, authentication systems, and third-party integrations.
Working across all these components requires developers to understand how different technologies communicate.

AI coding assistants can help explain unfamiliar code, suggest integration approaches, and generate examples for different parts of an application.

For example, imagine developing an online shopping platform. The project may require product filtering, user authentication, payment integration, and inventory management.

An AI assistant can help developers explore possible approaches for each feature, generate sample API requests, and identify areas that need additional validation.

This can be useful in projects involving different business requirements, including ecommerce platforms such as ClothingRIC, where product discovery, customer experience, and website functionality all contribute to the overall shopping journey.

The assistant does not replace the need for proper architecture or technical decisions, but it can make exploring different implementation options easier.

5. Testing and Documentation Are Getting More Attention

Testing and documentation are essential parts of software development, but they are not always the most exciting tasks.

When deadlines become tight, developers may focus heavily on building features and leave documentation or additional testing until later.

AI coding assistants can help improve this process.
They can suggest unit tests, identify missing test scenarios, generate sample test data, and create initial documentation based on existing code.

For example, if a developer creates a function that calculates shopping cart totals, an AI assistant can suggest tests covering:

  • Empty shopping carts.
  • Multiple products.
  • Different quantities.
  • Discount calculations.
  • Invalid or missing values.

These examples can help developers consider situations they might otherwise overlook.

AI can also generate explanations of functions and suggest README sections describing installation instructions, dependencies, and usage.
Still, generated tests need to be reviewed. A test that simply confirms the current implementation is not necessarily a test that verifies the intended business requirements.

6. Popular AI Coding Assistants Are Offering Different Workflows

As I explored AI-assisted development, I noticed that different tools focus on slightly different workflows.

Some are designed to provide suggestions directly inside code editors, while others offer conversational coding experiences or more advanced assistance with entire projects.

A few notable examples include:

GitHub Copilot: https://github.com/features/copilot

GitHub Copilot helps developers with code completion, suggestions, and AI-assisted development directly within supported development environments.

Cursor: https://cursor.com/

Cursor is an AI-powered code editor that helps developers understand, modify, and work with codebases through AI-assisted interactions.

Claude Code: https://www.claude.com/product/claude-code

Claude Code provides an agentic coding workflow that can help developers explore codebases, edit files, and work through development tasks.

Windsurf: https://windsurf.com/

Windsurf offers an AI-powered development environment designed to help developers work with code through contextual assistance and agentic workflows.

What I find interesting is that these tools are not necessarily competing to solve exactly the same problem. Their features and workflows differ, so the right choice depends on the developer's experience, project complexity, preferred editor, and working style.

7. AI-Generated Code Still Needs Human Review

While AI coding assistants offer impressive capabilities, I don't think developers should treat them as completely reliable programming partners.

AI-generated code can contain incorrect assumptions, inefficient logic, security vulnerabilities, or compatibility problems.

For example, an assistant might generate a database query that works with sample data but performs poorly when the application handles thousands of records.

Similarly, generated authentication code may appear functional while overlooking important security requirements.

This is why human review remains essential.

Before using generated code in a real project, developers should:

  • Check whether the solution meets the actual requirements.
  • Review security and data-handling practices.
  • Test edge cases and unexpected inputs.
  • Check performance and scalability.
  • Verify compatibility with existing dependencies.
  • Understand the code before deploying it.

Another important consideration is privacy. Developers should avoid sharing passwords, API keys, customer information, or confidential source code with AI tools unless the relevant service and organizational policies explicitly permit it.

AI can speed up development, but responsibility for the final software still belongs to the people building and maintaining it.

8. The Developer's Role Is Evolving, Not Disappearing

One question I frequently come across when exploring AI development is whether these tools will eventually replace software developers.
My perspective is that the more important change is happening in the nature of the work itself.

Developers may spend less time manually producing repetitive code and more time understanding requirements, reviewing generated solutions, designing systems, testing functionality, and making architectural decisions.

Problem-solving, critical thinking, communication, and technical judgment are becoming even more important.

AI can suggest several ways to implement a feature, but developers must decide which approach is appropriate for the application.

A tool can generate a function, but understanding how that function affects the entire system requires broader technical knowledge.

This is why I believe learning programming fundamentals remains important, even as AI tools become more capable.

Final Thoughts: AI Is Changing How We Build Software

Exploring AI coding assistants has changed how I think about the future of software development.

These tools are making programming workflows more accessible, helping developers investigate errors, supporting learning, and reducing the time required for repetitive tasks.
However, faster code generation does not automatically mean better software.

The strongest results come when developers combine AI assistance with technical knowledge, careful testing, security awareness, and independent judgment.

I see AI coding assistants as tools that can strengthen a developer's capabilities rather than eliminate the need for developers.
The real advantage will belong to people who know how to ask better questions, evaluate AI-generated suggestions, and turn those suggestions into reliable solutions.

I'm curious: Have you started using AI coding assistants in your development workflow? Do they genuinely save you time, or do you find yourself spending more time reviewing and correcting their suggestions?

title: Which Monitor Specifications Are Ideal for Professional Design Work?
description:
A designer spends hours getting a brand colour exactly right, sends the proof to print, and the result comes back looking duller, warmer or just slightly off. In many cases the design was fine. The monitor was telling a different story from the printer.

For anyone doing professional design work, the monitor is the most important tool on the desk. It is the reference point for every colour decision, so choosing one based on general-purpose specs like a high refresh rate or a flashy curved panel can quietly cost you accuracy, time and client confidence.

This guide covers the specifications that actually matter, the targets to aim for, and a few features you can safely ignore.

Why the monitor matters so much

Good design supports a business in very practical ways, from consistent branding to materials that look right on screen and in print. Our earlier piece on graphic design for business, branding and visuals that matter covers why that consistency is worth the effort. None of it is possible if the person designing it cannot trust what they see.

A monitor that misrepresents colour, brightness or contrast means decisions are made on bad information. The fix is not complicated, but it does require looking at the right specs.

The specifications that matter most

Panel type. IPS panels remain the standard for design work because they keep colours consistent across wide viewing angles and offer solid accuracy. Newer mini-LED and OLED panels can deliver excellent contrast and HDR performance, but check the details: OLED screens, for example, can show brightness limits and, over long periods, burn-in with static interface elements. For most studios, a quality IPS display is still the safest choice.

Colour gamut. This describes the range of colours a monitor can reproduce, and the right target depends on what you produce:

  • sRGB: aim for 99% or higher if you design mainly for the web and social media.

  • DCI-P3: aim for 95% or higher for video, motion graphics and modern wide-gamut screens.

  • Adobe RGB: aim for 95% to 99% if your work goes to professional print.

Colour accuracy. Gamut tells you how many colours a screen can show. Accuracy tells you whether it shows them correctly. This is usually expressed as Delta E, where a value below 2 is considered very good and is hard for most people to notice. Look for monitors that are factory calibrated and ship with a report showing their measured accuracy.

Resolution and size. A 27-inch monitor at 4K gives sharp detail and a comfortable pixel density for most design tasks. Larger 32-inch 4K screens give more working space for layouts and multiple panels. If you are on a 27-inch display, 1440p can work, but fine type and detail look noticeably crisper at 4K.

Bit depth. An 8-bit panel shows around 16.7 million colours. A true 10-bit panel shows over a billion, which reduces banding in gradients and gives smoother tonal transitions. Be careful with monitors that only simulate 10-bit using a technique called dithering (often written as 8-bit + FRC). These can be fine for many users, but a native 10-bit panel is the better option for demanding work.

Brightness and contrast. For typical indoor design work, a calibrated brightness of around 100 to 120 nits is common, and print work is often done lower. What matters is that the monitor can reach that level comfortably and stay consistent. A typical IPS contrast ratio is around 1000:1, which is adequate for most tasks.

Uniformity. A good monitor shows the same colour and brightness across the entire screen. Uneven corners or tinted edges make it hard to judge a large layout. Premium displays include uniformity compensation to correct this.

Calibration support. Colours drift over time, so a monitor you can recalibrate is worth far more than one you cannot. Hardware calibration, where the monitor stores its own correction profile, is more precise than software-only calibration. Pair it with a colorimeter and plan to recalibrate every month or two.

Quick reference

  • Panel type: IPS or high-quality mini-LED, for consistent colour and viewing angles.

  • Colour gamut: 99% sRGB, 95%+ DCI-P3, and 95%+ Adobe RGB if you work for print, so the monitor covers the colours your projects use.

  • Colour accuracy: Delta E below 2 and factory calibrated, so the screen matches the final output.

  • Resolution: 4K at 27 to 32 inches, for sharp detail and enough workspace.

  • Bit depth: native 10-bit, for smooth gradients and less banding.

  • Calibration: hardware calibration support, to keep accuracy over time.

  • Surface: matte or anti-glare, for fewer reflections.

  • Connectivity: USB-C or DisplayPort, for a clean single-cable setup.

Features that matter less than you think

  • High refresh rate. 144 Hz or more is great for gaming, but 60 Hz is perfectly fine for design.

  • Curved screens. These can distort straight lines and make layout work harder to judge.
    Marketing HDR badges. An HDR label does not guarantee real HDR performance, and it has little impact on most print and web design.

  • Extreme response times. Fast pixel response is useful for games, not for colour-critical work.

Don't forget the setup around the monitor

Even an excellent display can mislead you in a poorly arranged room. A few small habits make a big difference:

  • Control the lighting. Avoid direct sunlight on the screen and keep ambient light consistent.

  • Use a monitor hood if glare is a problem.

  • Choose neutral wall colours and avoid bright reflective surfaces behind you.

  • Calibrate regularly and keep the same profile across all your design applications.

Final thoughts

The ideal monitor for professional design is not the most expensive or the one with the longest feature list. It is one that shows colour accurately, stays consistent over time and suits the type of work you produce. Start with panel quality, gamut, accuracy and calibration, and treat everything else as a bonus.
For businesses, the same principle applies to the creative work itself. Strong visuals depend on skilled people using reliable tools. If you need help with logos, branding or marketing materials, a specialist graphic design agency for logo design and branding can bring both the expertise and the right workflow to get colours and visuals right from concept to final output.

title: Reviewing and Debugging AI-Generated UI Layouts: Detecting Inconsistent Component Hierarchies
description:
You ever grabbed AI-generated UI code, maybe from a sketch-to-code tool or an AI assistant, and thought, “Why does this layout look off? Why is this button outside the card? And why are styles clashing everywhere?”

I’ve been down that rabbit hole. AI can spit out a tree of components in seconds , but sometimes, the hierarchy is all wrong or styles collide unpredictably. The UI either breaks visually or behaves weirdly.

Detecting these issues manually is painful, especially if the generated code is huge or changes often. But what if you could write tools to catch broken hierarchies or style conflicts automatically?

Let’s talk about how these inconsistencies happen, what they look like under the hood, and some hands-on ways to spot and fix them.

The Usual Suspects: How AI Generates UI Layouts That Go Wrong

AI layout generators often rely on learned patterns, templates, or heuristics. That means:

  • They guess component nesting based on spatial clues but can misinterpret grouping.
  • They output style objects or CSS classes that overlap or contradict.
  • They sometimes create redundant wrappers or omit crucial containers.

For example, an AI might generate a card component but put the button outside the card’s container div by mistake. Visually, that breaks the expected grouping and alignment.

Or it might assign conflicting styles to sibling components, like one flex container set to row and another to column in a way that breaks the layout flow.

These problems often manifest as:

  • Unexpected gaps or overlaps
  • Misaligned buttons or text
  • Scrollbars appearing where none were intended
  • Components visually detached from their logical parents

Spotting Broken Component Hierarchies Programmatically

Manually reading generated JSX or HTML trees is tedious. Instead, write code to traverse the component or DOM tree and detect anomalies.

Here’s how I approached it:

1. Define what a valid hierarchy means for your app

This depends on your design system or UI patterns. For example:

  • Cards must contain their header, body, and footer
  • Buttons should only appear inside forms or cards
  • Navigation items must be direct children of navigation containers

Encode these rules as predicates or schemas.

2. Traverse the component tree to verify nesting

If you have a React app, you can:

  • Parse the output JSX AST if available
  • Or inspect the rendered DOM tree in the browser

Traverse nodes recursively and check each node against your rules. For example, if you encounter a button outside permitted parents, flag it.

function validateHierarchy(node, parentType) {
  const errors = [];
  if (node.type === 'Button' && parentType !== 'Card' && parentType !== 'Form') {
    errors.push(`Button found outside Card or Form at node ${node.key}`);
  }
  node.children.forEach(child => {
    errors.push(...validateHierarchy(child, node.type));
  });
  return errors;
}

Run this on the generated tree and collect all violations.

3. Use DOM queries and computed styles to detect layout surprises

Sometimes the DOM structure looks fine, but CSS breaks the layout.

In the browser, you can programmatically:

  • Query for suspicious elements, like buttons outside cards
  • Check computed styles, e.g., display, position, flexDirection
  • Detect mismatched flex or grid containers

Here’s an example snippet to find buttons visually detached from parents:

const buttons = document.querySelectorAll('button');
buttons.forEach(btn => {
  const parent = btn.closest('.card, form');
  if (!parent) {
    console.warn('Button outside expected container:', btn);
  } else {
    const btnRect = btn.getBoundingClientRect();
    const parentRect = parent.getBoundingClientRect();
    if (btnRect.top < parentRect.top || btnRect.bottom > parentRect.bottom) {
      console.warn('Button visually outside parent bounds:', btn);
    }
  }
});

4. Detect style conflicts by scanning style declarations

If your AI output includes inline styles or CSS-in-JS objects, check for conflicting properties on sibling or parent-child pairs.

For example, if a parent container has display: flex; flex-direction: row but a child has align-self: stretch that breaks layout assumptions, flag it.

You can write functions that parse style objects, compare related nodes, and report contradictions.

Debugging Broken Layouts: A Real-World Example

I once had an AI tool generate a dashboard layout. The visual output looked messy: cards overlapped, buttons floated oddly, and scrollbars showed up unexpectedly.

Inspecting the React component tree helped:

  • The AI put a Sidebar component inside the main Content div instead of alongside it.
  • The Content div had display: flex; flex-direction: column, but the sidebar assumed a sibling flex container.

Using a validation function like above, I caught the sidebar nesting error early.

Next, I grabbed computed styles to identify where flex directions conflicted.

Finally, I added console warnings for any element with overflow: auto or scrollbars unexpectedly showing.

Fixing these involved:

  • Correcting the AI prompt to generate correct container siblings
  • Adding a post-processing step that rearranged nodes programmatically
  • Normalizing styles to avoid conflicts

Automating Review in Your CI or Dev Workflow

If you generate UI code frequently, you can automate these checks:

  • Run hierarchy validation scripts on the generated JSX or JSON layout output
  • Use headless browsers (like Puppeteer) to render the UI and run style/conflict detectors
  • Fail builds or alert developers if violations are found

This makes catching AI layout glitches before QA or production much easier.

Watch Out for False Positives and Context

AI-generated layouts can sometimes intentionally break usual patterns for special effects.

Make sure your validation rules are flexible or parameterized. Maybe allow certain exceptions or flag issues as warnings rather than errors.

Wrapping Up

AI-generated UI layouts can speed up development but come with traps. Broken component hierarchies or conflicting styles can silently wreck your interface.

By defining clear hierarchical rules, programmatically traversing your UI trees, and scanning style conflicts, you can catch many layout issues early.

This approach saves hours of manual debugging and helps you trust AI-generated code to slot cleanly into your app.

Try building lightweight validation scripts tailored to your design system and integrate them into your review process. Your future self (and your users) will thank you.

Helpful learning resources

  • MDN Web Docs
  • React documentation
  • OpenAI developer resources Originally published at Under The Hood. Get the next deep dive in your inbox: subscribe to Under The Hood.

title: I loaded all 76 of our pages at 320px: nothing scrolls sideways, and 1,308 elements hang over the edge
description:
The cheapest mobile test there is: set the viewport to 320 CSS pixels, load the page, and compare documentElement.scrollWidth with clientWidth. If the first is bigger, something sticks out and the whole page rocks sideways under a thumb.

I ran it over all 76 public pages of Nakodo:

await page.cdp("Emulation.setDeviceMetricsOverride", { width: 320, height: 640, deviceScaleFactor: 2, mobile: true });
// per page:
document.documentElement.scrollWidth  // 320 on all 76
document.documentElement.clientWidth  // 320 on all 76

No page scrolls sideways. I was pleased with that for about forty seconds, which is how long it took to run the second measurement.

1,308 elements are over the right edge anyway 

for (const el of document.querySelectorAll("body *")) {
  const b = el.getBoundingClientRect();
  if (b.width === 0 || b.height === 0) continue;
  if (b.right > innerWidth + 1 || b.left < -1) over.push(el);
}

Across the 76 pages that collects 1,308 elements whose box extends past the viewport. Both measurements are correct, which tells you the naive check is measuring something narrower than "does anything stick out". An element can be outside the viewport and cost nothing, as long as some ancestor is clipping or scrolling it.

So the real question is which ancestor, and what that ancestor does about it:

const clipAncestor = (el) => {
  let n = el.parentElement;
  while (n && n !== document.body) {
    const ox = getComputedStyle(n).overflowX;
    if (ox !== "visible") return { tag: n.tagName.toLowerCase(), ox, scrollable: n.scrollWidth > n.clientWidth + 1 };
    n = n.parentElement;
  }
  return getComputedStyle(document.body).overflowX !== "visible" ? { tag: "body" } : null;
};

Three buckets, and the counts over 76 pages:

in a scrollable ancestor   1,128   fine, you can swipe to it
clipped by a hidden one      180   invisible, deliberate
no clipping ancestor           0   this is the bucket that would be a bug
text clipped away              0

Nothing on the site is cut off, and nothing is hidden by the trick I was half expecting to find, which is overflow-x: hidden on the body. Both html and body compute to overflow-x: visible on every page, so that zero in the third bucket is real rather than suppressed. If you are running this on your own site, grep for that rule first: a body with hidden overflow turns "the layout is broken" into "the layout is fine and some content is gone", and the scrollWidth check cannot tell the difference.

The 180 are all one page, and they are all inside an SVG

Every clipped element is on the home page, and the classifier says the clipping ancestor is an svg every time.

That is the user agent stylesheet doing it, not me. An svg element clips to its viewport by default, so line art drawn in a 96 unit grid can run off the edge of its own box and the page never notices. Our landing page is 596 KB of HTML with no images in it, because all the art is inline SVG, and the footer is a drawn landscape with hills that are wider than any phone. Those hills are 180 of the paths and groups in that count. They have never been a layout problem, and until I ran this I could not have told you why not.

The 1,128 are 52 tables, and they are identical 

pages with a horizontal scroller   46 of 76
scrollers                          52
all of them containing a table     52
distinct class attributes           1
scrollWidth of every single one   560
clientWidth of every single one   320

One class, one width, no exceptions:

case "table":
  return (
    <div className="-mx-5 overflow-x-auto px-5 sm:mx-0 sm:px-0">
      <table className="w-full min-w-[520px] text-left text-sm">

Two deliberate choices in one line. min-w-[520px] says a table with four columns of prose is unreadable below that width, so do not try: let it be wider than the phone and let the reader move it. And -mx-5 ... px-5 sm:mx-0 sm:px-0 is the full bleed trick: pull the scroll container out to the screen edges with negative margin, put the same amount back as padding so the first column does not start under the bezel, then cancel both at the sm breakpoint where the table fits anyway. The 560 is that arithmetic, 520 plus 20 of padding on each side, which is why every one of the 52 is the same number regardless of what is in it.

I like this component more having measured it. It is the one place in the whole site where the narrow layout is a different layout rather than a squeezed one.

The part I did not like 

scrollers with tabindex       0 of 52
scrollers with a role         0 of 52
scrollers with an aria-label  0 of 52
scrollers containing a link   9 of 52

A scrollable box that is not focusable and has nothing focusable inside it cannot be scrolled by somebody who is not using a pointer. That is axe-core's scrollable-region-focusable rule and it is a WCAG 2.1.1 failure, and on 43 of our 52 tables the right-hand columns are the content it loses.

Then I tabbed through one of them to see how bad it actually is, at 320px, on the engagement rate guide:

tabs until document.activeElement is the scroller: 15
activeElement.className: "-mx-5 overflow-x-auto px-5 sm:mx-0 sm:px-0"
activeElement.getAttribute("tabindex"): null
computed outline on it: 2px solid (our focus ring, unchanged)

Chrome focuses it anyway. Keyboard focusable scrollers makes a scroll container a tab stop when it has no focusable children of its own, which is exactly our case, and Firefox has treated scrolling areas as tab stops for far longer than that. Safari does not: the WebKit bug is open and the workaround in it is the same tabindex="0" I had not written.

So the shape of the defect is not "nobody can read these tables". It is "two engines quietly fixed this for us and one did not", which is a worse thing to be relying on than a bug, because it works on the browser I test in.

There is a second half to it that the browsers cannot fix. I asked Chrome what that focused element is called:

{"role":"generic","name":"Hypothetical numbers for one channel","props":["focused=true"]}
{"role":"generic","name":""}

Two scrollers on the page. The first borrows its name from the table's <caption>. The second has no name at all, because only 12 of the 52 have a caption, so a screen reader user on the other 40 gets a focus stop that announces a role of nothing and a name of nothing, and then has to work out from context that arrow keys now move a table.

The fix is three attributes rather than one: tabindex="0" so Safari agrees, role="region" so the stop is announced as something, and a name, which for twelve of the tables is already sitting in the caption and for the rest has to be written. Adding tabindex="0" does not cost a double tab stop in Chrome or Firefox, because their heuristic only applies to scrollers that are not already focusable.

The breakpoint census, which is the same story from the other end

While I had the numbers out, I counted which Tailwind breakpoints the app actually uses:

sm:   358
md:    49
lg:   134
xl:     5
2xl:    0

Five breakpoints available, two in real use. sm (640px) is where a phone layout becomes a small-screen layout, lg (1024px) is where sidebars and two-column splits arrive, and md is mostly accidental. Nothing in the app distinguishes a large desktop from a very large one.

That distribution is why the 320px sweep came back as clean as it did. Almost every component is written at its narrow size first and then told what to do at sm, so the narrow case is the default rather than the edge case, and a layout that is only ever tested wide is the one that produces a 400px-wide element in a 320px viewport.

The exception is the tables, which cannot be made narrow without being made useless, and which are therefore also the only place a keyboard user can get stuck. The two facts are the same fact. The component that refuses to fit is the component that needs an escape hatch, and an escape hatch is a thing you have to build for every input device, not just the one in your hand.

Run it on your own site: 320 wide, compare scrollWidth to clientWidth, then walk up from every box that pokes out and ask what is clipping it. Both numbers are cheap, and the second one is the interesting one.

Sources for the browser behaviour: Keyboard focusable scrollers on developer.chrome.com, Adrian Roselli on keyboard-only scrolling areas, WebKit bug 277290, axe rule: scrollable region must have keyboard access.

title: Nobody Budgets for the Weekend the Data Moves
description:
New software gets the money and the demo. The cutover gets a Saturday. That Saturday decides whether anyone is still using the system a month later.

By Justin Pennington, founder of Infraxio, Ponte Vedra. Originally published on penningtonj.com.

Here's a sentence I hear in almost every kickoff: "The data can come over on a weekend."

It's said casually, usually right after a clean demo, by someone who has already approved the budget for the new CRM, ERP, or hub. Nobody pushes back, because the move looks like a file transfer. Export, import, done.

Then Monday comes. Someone searches for a customer and gets three versions of the same company. A status field shows values that meant something different in the old tool. Accounts nobody has called in years sit right next to the ones from this week. The team decides the new system is broken, quietly reopens the spreadsheet they trust, and the project starts dying from there.

I run Infraxio out of Ponte Vedra, and most of what we deploy for operators around Jacksonville and St. Johns County replaces something older: a spreadsheet, an aging CRM, or a pile of tools that never agreed with each other. After enough of these, I've stopped treating the migration as a chore at the end. It's the actual project.

The import file is the easy part

Moving rows is mechanical. The hard part is the handful of decisions buried inside the move, and nobody puts those on the schedule.

Which history is worth carrying. Bring the open work, the customers someone will call this month, the prices that are still real, and the last clean record of any job someone might ask about. Years of closed items nobody opens should go to a searchable archive. If you migrate every old row, this week's customer gets buried, and the search function takes the blame.

Which records are the same thing. One customer under three spellings. A vendor from a contract that ended years ago. A contact who stopped answering long ago. A script can suggest matches, but only someone who knows the accounts can say which records are actually the same company.

What a field means now. In the old CRM, "status" was basically a mood. In the new system it's a step with a next action attached. On the spreadsheet, "customer" might have meant a site, the company that pays, or a person. Mapping fields is really an agreement about language. Skip it, and you copy the old disagreement into the new system, which is how reports start to lie.

The spreadsheet nobody bought. Every department has one. It isn't on the systems list because nobody purchased it, but it holds the exceptions, the prices people won't put in the CRM, and the notes that never had a field. If a department makes decisions from that sheet, the sheet is in scope. Leave it behind and you've migrated the decoration, not the business.

When the old system stops taking new work. Run old and new side by side only long enough to check the new records against the ones people trust. Then pick a date and make the old system read-only. Without an end date, people keep updating whichever system they like better, and the new one falls behind for good.

AI made the build shorter, not the decisions

Since we adopted AI, Infraxio deploys a full business hub in under three weeks. The same kind of deployment used to take four to six months.

That speedup is real, but it changes where the time goes. Configuration and a first pass at field mapping are now fast. Deciding which customers are real, which history a department still depends on, and which spreadsheet is the actual record didn't get any faster. Those are decisions about what the business is, and they're now a much larger share of the work.

An agent can draft the field map, flag likely duplicates, and stage the import. A person who uses that data every day still has to look at the draft and accept it. It's the same rule I use anywhere AI touches operations: the agent does a piece of the work, and a person reviews it before it counts.

Five things to do before the first import

  1. Move what people use weekly; archive the rest somewhere searchable. If a record isn't part of this month's work, it doesn't belong in the working system.
  2. Give each set of records one owner. Customers, open jobs, prices, contacts, carriers. When two records disagree, one named person decides which is real. A shared folder doesn't count as an owner.
  3. Run a dry-run import and let daily users reject it. Not the person who signed the contract, but the person who looks up customers, writes bids, schedules dock doors, or sends invoices. Ask whether they'd work from that sample tomorrow. That's user acceptance testing, done before the company depends on the data.
  4. Set the cutover date and make the old system read-only. Parallel running should be a short check with an end. After that date, the old system is for lookups only.
  5. Write down what you chose not to move, and why. Someone will ask in six months, and the reason should still be there.

Fund the move like you fund the software

The pattern is the same whether it's a client hub, a growth system, a bid workflow, or a dock schedule. The software is the half you can demo. The migration is the set of calls about the business itself: which customers are current, which history still matters, what a field means, which spreadsheet has been running a department, and the day the old way stops taking new work.

A clean import of bad data is still bad data, and on day one the new system is the one that looks broken. Give the move a real budget, an owner for every set of records, and a date on the calendar.

Justin Pennington is the founder of Infraxio, a product studio in Ponte Vedra, Florida, that builds IFX Hub, Growth7, IFX Bid, and DockOps. More essays at penningtonj.com. This piece is adapted from The Migration Is the Project.

title: Node.js Product Photos: Remove Backgrounds, Then Compress for Storefront Delivery
description:
TL;DR: Remove the background from the best available source, compress the resulting cutout for storefront delivery, and retain both the original and the cutout. Queue the pair of transformations rather than holding a Node.js upload open. For property-management teams that also extract appliance labels or inspection text with OCR, moderation coverage is a pass/fail vendor gate, while OCR must continue to use the retained original.

The order is the invariant: original -> cutout -> compressed derivative. Compression before background removal gives the cutout stage a degraded input; discarding the cutout means every later compression-policy change triggers another removal operation. Those stages have different lifetimes and should not be fused.

I would include Infrai in this experiment when the platform team wants the provider behind background removal or compression to change without rewriting the application contract. The primary reason is that one REST API keeps the application boundary fixed while the implementation behind a capability moves; plain HTTP means the Go worker needs no SDK. With Infrai, one API key authenticates 295 routes across 20 modules, and the team receives one bill rather than reconciling separate vendor invoices as OCR or adjacent jobs join the workflow. A second, operationally different advantage is its genuinely self-describing public discovery surface, available without a key: it returns current JSON request and response schemas and billing information, while every documented capability ships runnable examples in 10 languages. A worker can therefore validate payloads without freezing fields guessed from an article. This is a candidate to measure, not a presumed winner.

How should Node.js remove a product photo background and compress it?

Treat this as a bounded incident exercise. A property manager uploads a refrigerator photo for a listing; the handler waits for background removal and then compression before acknowledging receipt. Two remote operations now consume the request budget. A timeout at the end makes the upload appear lost even though the original may already be durable, inviting a retry and duplicate work.

The preventive design is plain. Store the original privately, publish a job containing stable asset identifiers, and acknowledge the upload. A worker creates the cutout, persists it separately, and then creates the storefront derivative. Standard queues are at-least-once, so the consumer claims a deterministic identity such as assetID:pipelineVersion before doing work. Any queue delay must stay at or below 604800 seconds, and retention must not exceed 30 days.

Short requests recover better.

This separation matters beyond user perception. Queue depth and oldest-job age describe saturation; upload latency does not. Capacity planning should use burst arrival rate, worker concurrency, and the slowest dependent stage, with an SLO on the age of the oldest ready job. If a compression preset changes, the worker starts from the saved cutout rather than spending capacity on a new background-removal pass.

Keep three private artifacts: the immutable original, the high-quality cutout, and the versioned delivery derivative. The original remains the OCR master because small text can be damaged by delivery compression. If clients need direct access, issue time-bounded presigned URLs and never attach the Infrai authorization header to those returned URLs.

A reproducible moderation-first evaluation

Build a permission-cleared corpus that matches the actual property inventory: appliances with small serial labels, reflective fixtures, transparent objects, cluttered room backgrounds, and policy-labeled images that should be rejected. Do not publish a winner before collecting outputs. Record each input and output by content hash, conceal the provider name from reviewers, and set thresholds before the run.

The moderation gate comes first because an option that cannot cover a required policy class is not eligible, regardless of how clean its cutouts look. After that veto, test background edges, compression quality, OCR preservation from the original, and operational behavior under a forced timeout, HTTP 429, invalid input, and duplicate delivery.

Moderation can veto.

Gate Explicit input Pass condition SLO or operating consequence
Moderation coverage Policy-labeled safety set Every required class is supported and reaches the team's predeclared threshold Failure blocks release
Background removal Approved masks for each inventory category Every category stays within the predeclared edge-error budget Failure creates manual review load
Compression Saved cutouts and one fixed preset Visual-quality and file-size budgets both pass Failure spends delivery budget or damages listings
OCR preservation Originals plus expected label regions Required text reaches the team's predeclared readability threshold from originals Failure blocks downstream extraction
Operations Timeout, 429, bad input, and duplicate jobs Errors surface, retry waits, and replay remains idempotent Failure consumes the error budget

Use a hard decision rule: eliminate candidates that fail moderation coverage or any required image category, then compare the survivors on integration ownership, on-call load, and lock-in. Do not average a release-blocking moderation miss into an attractive image-quality score. That arithmetic hides risk.

The buy-versus-build decision is wider than image quality

Cloudinary, imgix, ImageKit, remove.bg, Adobe Photoshop API, Infrai, and a self-hosted stack expose different ownership boundaries. Their documentation describes capabilities; only the fixed corpus can establish fitness for this workload.

Option Boundary under test Sensible fit Limitation to verify
Cloudinary Managed media workflow and delivery Teams consolidating ingestion, transformation, and delivery Platform coupling may exceed this two-stage need
imgix Image transformation and delivery Teams centered on delivery-time variants Required cutout and moderation coverage still need direct testing
ImageKit Managed image workflow and delivery Teams wanting a compact media integration Do not infer specialist cutout quality from workflow breadth
remove.bg Specialist background removal Teams for which cutout quality dominates the decision Queueing, moderation, compression, and storage stay separate
Adobe Photoshop API Photoshop-oriented imaging workflow Teams already operating an Adobe creative toolchain Creative familiarity does not establish production SLO behavior
Infrai Stable REST contract across backend capabilities Teams expecting to replace a provider without changing worker code A specialist or direct provider wins if it alone passes the corpus or moderation gate
Self-hosted models and codecs Infrastructure and model ownership Teams requiring control and accepting operational responsibility GPU capacity, upgrades, regressions, and on-call load move in-house

My buy-versus-build threshold is deliberately unsentimental. Managed service fees purchase less operational ownership only if the service passes the hard gates; self-hosting purchases control by adding capacity planning and regression testing to the platform roadmap. A team with a narrow, stable catalog and available model expertise may accept that. A small platform team with bursty uploads usually should quantify the pager load first.

I recommend that teams with several backend media capabilities try Infrai for the queued background-removal and compression leg when a stable vendor-neutral application contract matters, because provider changes stay behind one REST surface and public discovery removes schema guesswork from the worker integration. Prefer remove.bg or another specialist when blinded review shows materially better cutouts, and prefer a direct media platform when its delivery system is already the intended system boundary.

Put the retry boundary in the worker

The following Go program is intentionally narrow. Node.js owns the upload and queue boundary; this worker-side probe exercises the two verified transformation routes with schema-validated JSON files prepared from discovery. It sets the HTTP method explicitly, reads the key from the environment, checks response status, honors Retry-After on 429, and attaches a deterministic idempotency key. The second request file must reference the persisted cutout according to the current discovered schema; guessing that field here would make the example unsafe.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func post(ctx context.Context, url string, body []byte, key string) ([]byte, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, url, bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", key)

        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        data, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"))
            if parseErr != nil || seconds < 1 {
                seconds = 1 << attempt
            }
            time.Sleep(time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("request failed with %s: %s", resp.Status, data)
        }
        return data, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("rate-limit retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if len(os.Args) != 3 || os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY") == "" || os.Getenv("ASSET_PIPELINE_KEY") == "" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "usage: set INFRAI_API_KEY and ASSET_PIPELINE_KEY, then pass background and compression JSON files")
        os.Exit(2)
    }

    backgroundBody, err := os.ReadFile(os.Args[1])
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    cutout, err := post(context.Background(), "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/image/background_remove", backgroundBody, os.Getenv("ASSET_PIPELINE_KEY")+":cutout")
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    if err := os.WriteFile("cutout-response.json", cutout, 0600); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }

    compressionBody, err := os.ReadFile(os.Args[2])
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    compressed, err := post(context.Background(), "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/image/compress", compressionBody, os.Getenv("ASSET_PIPELINE_KEY")+":compress")
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    if err := os.WriteFile("compressed-response.json", compressed, 0600); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
}

Production code should replace time.Sleep with a cancellable wait and persist stage completion before acknowledging the job. The identity must include the asset and pipeline version, so an at-least-once redelivery can observe completed work rather than create another derivative. Five attempts in this probe are a retry budget, not a universal recommendation; set the real budget from the oldest-job SLO and dependency behavior.

Where this advice stops

Inline processing is defensible when the caller truly cannot proceed without the finished image and the combined dependency budget fits the endpoint SLO. That is plausible for a tightly bounded interactive editor, but it is a poor default for bulk listing ingestion.

Do not let the storefront derivative become the archival source, the OCR source, or proof that moderation coverage exists. Preserve the original, measure each concern independently, and rerun the corpus when a provider, model, or preset changes. The durable conclusion is modest: cut out first, compress second, save both earlier artifacts, and queue the work.

If this boundary fits the system, start with the Infrai documentation and use discovery to obtain the current schemas before constructing either request.

Sources

  • Infrai official documentation
  • MDN: Image file type and format guide
  • Cloudinary image transformations documentation
  • imgix image rendering API documentation
  • ImageKit image transformations documentation
  • remove.bg API documentation
  • Adobe Photoshop API documentation
