title: Strangle, don't rewrite: patterns around a COBOL core to modern Java
description:
Say your bank runs its ledger on a COBOL core, and the mobile team wants a modern account inquiry API. Nobody wants a big-bang rewrite of the core, so someone draws a facade in front of the mainframe and says the magic words: Strangler Fig. Route one operation at a time to new code, and let the old system shrink.

That's the right starting point, and Martin Fowler's Strangler Fig Application page explains it well. The trouble starts the day after the facade goes in. The new service has to read packed decimals out of copybook records. It has to know whether a balance is posted or only memo-posted. It has to prove it computes the same interest as the old code before anyone flips a route. And once it publishes events, it has to survive the broker delivering the same event twice.

That work falls to the patterns you add around the facade. This article covers the hands-on part: the Java code for three of those patterns (an anti-corruption layer, a parallel run with mismatch classification and a transactional outbox with an idempotent consumer), plus the read side you put next to them. Everything comes from a small Java 25 module in legacy-modernization-patterns on GitHub, with no Spring and no database, so you can run it on a laptop in seconds.

If you want the "why" behind not rewriting legacy systems blind, I wrote about that earlier in Stop rewriting legacy systems, use AI to understand them first. This one stays close to the code.

The pattern map

Here's where each pattern sits around the facade, and which package in the repo implements it:

The facade is the interception point. It starts as a pure pass-through (100% of traffic to legacy, no behavior change), and you only flip a route after the patterns below have done their job. Rolling back means changing a route, with no deployment involved.

The module is organized by pattern:

Package Pattern Main class
acl Anti-Corruption Layer AccountTranslator
interest Branch by Abstraction, Parallel Run InterestCalculatorToggle, ParallelRun
outbox Transactional Outbox, Idempotent Consumer OutboxRelay, IdempotentConsumer
posting Safe financial writes (unknown outcome) SafePostingClient

I'll skip posting here. It deserves its own article, and the repo has it if you're curious.

Step 1: the anti-corruption layer

The ACL is the boundary between the legacy world and your domain model. On a mainframe that means a few concrete jobs: EBCDIC to UTF-8, packed decimal (COMP-3) to BigDecimal, fixed-width copybook records to typed objects and legacy return codes to domain outcomes. The example record in the repo is 20 bytes: a 10-byte account ID, a 1-byte type flag, a 7-byte COMP-3 balance and a 2-byte return code. The ID, flag and return code are EBCDIC text (code page IBM037); the balance is COMP-3.

Decoding COMP-3

Packed decimal stores two digits per byte, one per nibble, and puts the sign in the last nibble: C or F for positive, D for negative. So the bytes 01 23 45 6C with scale 2 are 1234.56. Here's the decoder from examples/account-modernization/src/main/java/com/wallaceespindola/modernization/acl/PackedDecimal.java, trimmed to the main method and the sign check:

public static BigDecimal decode(byte[] bytes, int scale) {
    if (bytes == null || bytes.length == 0) {
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("Empty packed decimal");
    }
    BigInteger digits = BigInteger.ZERO;
    int last = bytes.length - 1;
    for (int i = 0; i <= last; i++) {
        digits = append(digits, bytes[i] >> 4 & 0xF);
        if (i < last) {
            digits = append(digits, bytes[i] & 0xF);
        }
    }
    boolean negative = isNegative(bytes[last] & 0xF);
    return new BigDecimal(negative ? digits.negate() : digits, scale);
}

private static boolean isNegative(int signNibble) {
    return switch (signNibble) {
        case SIGN_POSITIVE_C, SIGN_POSITIVE_F -> false;
        case SIGN_NEGATIVE -> true;
        default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid packed sign nibble: " + signNibble);
    };
}

Two details matter. The high nibble of the last byte is a digit, the low nibble is the sign, which is why the loop skips the low nibble only on the last byte. And anything unexpected (a digit nibble above 9, an unknown sign) throws (the digit check lives in append, omitted above). You don't want a corrupt record to quietly become a balance of zero. LegacyAccountRecord.parse catches that exception and rethrows it as a LegacyTechnicalException, so callers see one kind of legacy failure.

Semantic translation

Once the bytes are decoded, you still have to decode the meaning. On many cores, the same balance field can hold a ledger (posted) balance or a memo-posted (pending) one, depending on a record type flag. If that flag leaks into your API, every consumer has to learn what 'M' means, and you've just copied the legacy model into the new system.

Here's the translator from examples/account-modernization/src/main/java/com/wallaceespindola/modernization/acl/AccountTranslator.java, trimmed to the two methods:

public AccountLookup translate(byte[] raw) {
    LegacyAccountRecord record = LegacyAccountRecord.parse(raw);
    return switch (record.returnCode()) {
        case OK -> new Found(new AccountBalance(record.accountId(), record.balance(), typeOf(record.typeFlag())));
        case NOT_FOUND -> new NotFound(record.accountId());
        case BLOCKED -> new Blocked(record.accountId());
        default -> throw new LegacyTechnicalException("Legacy return code " + record.returnCode());
    };
}

private static BalanceType typeOf(char flag) {
    return switch (flag) {
        case LEDGER_FLAG -> BalanceType.POSTED;
        case MEMO_POSTED_FLAG -> BalanceType.PENDING;
        default -> throw new LegacyTechnicalException("Unknown record type flag " + flag);
    };
}

Return codes "00", "04" and "08" become Found, NotFound and Blocked, three records of a sealed AccountLookup interface, so the compiler makes callers handle each case. Flags 'L' and 'M' become BalanceType.POSTED and BalanceType.PENDING. Nothing named typeFlag or returnCode leaves the acl package.

A few rules I'd hold the ACL to:

  • One ACL per bounded context: an account ACL, not a "mainframe ACL" that every team adds to.
  • Translation only: no business rules. Once it starts deciding things, it's a new monolith with extra latency.
  • Retire it with the legacy capability: an ACL with no legacy system behind it is dead weight.

Step 2: the read side, pending and posted

The first capability most teams move is account inquiry, because reads are low risk and high volume. The usual shape is change data capture (CDC) from the legacy store into a read model, with the ledger staying the system of record. That's CQRS without event sourcing: the mainframe ledger is already the write model.

The repo doesn't ship a CDC pipeline (it would need a database and a broker), but the ACL above is exactly what the translation step needs. Raw CDC records are legacy-shaped. If you write them straight into the read model, the new model inherits the old schema, flags included. So run them through the same kind of translation, and store POSTED and PENDING as separate, explicit values.

Many cores memo-post during the day and hard-post in the end-of-day batch, and CDC sees both. If the read model has one "balance" column, customers will watch their balance jump around at night. With pending and posted modeled explicitly, the UI can show both and nothing surprises anyone.

Two more things to put in place before you route reads to the new service:

  • A lag SLO with a fallback route: if CDC falls behind, the facade sends balance reads back to legacy through the ACL. That keeps the step reversible.
  • Per-key ordering and dedup: partition by account ID, and drop duplicates by source log position.

Step 3: the parallel run

Before the facade sends real customers to new logic, you want evidence that the new logic agrees with the old one. A parallel run computes both, compares them, records the result and serves the legacy answer. The repo does this for monthly interest, behind a Branch by Abstraction toggle with three modes: LEGACY, SHADOW and MODERN.

The two calculators disagree on purpose. The legacy one uses 30/360, truncates the intermediate result to four decimals, then rounds half-up (COBOL ROUNDED). The modern one uses actual days over 365 and rounds half-even. Those are exactly the differences that show up in real parallel runs: rounding mode, day-count convention and intermediate truncation.

Here's the core of examples/account-modernization/src/main/java/com/wallaceespindola/modernization/interest/ParallelRun.java, trimmed to the two methods that matter:

@Override
public BigDecimal monthlyInterest(BigDecimal balance, BigDecimal annualRate, YearMonth month) {
    BigDecimal legacyResult = legacy.monthlyInterest(balance, annualRate, month);
    BigDecimal modernResult = modern.monthlyInterest(balance, annualRate, month);
    BigDecimal difference = modernResult.subtract(legacyResult).abs();
    comparisons.add(new Comparison(balance, annualRate, month, legacyResult, modernResult, difference,
            classify(difference, month)));
    return legacyResult;
}

private MismatchCategory classify(BigDecimal difference, YearMonth month) {
    if (difference.signum() == 0) {
        return MismatchCategory.MATCH;
    }
    if (difference.compareTo(ONE_CENT) <= 0) {
        return MismatchCategory.ROUNDING;
    }
    if (difference.compareTo(tolerance) <= 0) {
        return MismatchCategory.WITHIN_TOLERANCE;
    }
    boolean oddMonthLength = month.lengthOfMonth() != DAYS_IN_LEGACY_MONTH;
    return oddMonthLength ? MismatchCategory.DAY_COUNT : MismatchCategory.UNEXPLAINED;
}

The last line of monthlyInterest is the important one: it always returns legacyResult. So shadow mode has no customer-visible effect. (In a real system you'd also stub notification and payment adapters on the shadow path, and enforce that in configuration.)

The classification is what makes the output usable. A raw list of mismatches turns into a spreadsheet nobody reads. Buckets turn it into a triage conversation: rounding noise, within tolerance, a known day-count difference or something a human has to look at. With a balance of 1000 at 5% in January, the tests show legacy at 4.17 and modern at 4.25. The difference of 0.08 is above the one-cent tolerance, and January has 31 days, so it lands in DAY_COUNT, not UNEXPLAINED. ParallelRunReport then counts comparisons per category.

The classifier is a heuristic, and the Javadoc in the repo says so. In a real run you'd grow the categories as you explain differences (business date vs system date, time zones), and only UNEXPLAINED should block a cutover. Once the counts look right, the rollout goes shadow, then canary (a small segment gets the modern result while legacy is still computed and compared), then full cutover with legacy kept warm for a rollback window.

Step 4: the outbox and the idempotent consumer

When the new service starts owning business events (a notification, a fraud signal), it needs to change its own state and publish an event without the two drifting apart. Writing to the database and then calling the broker is a dual write, and a crash between the two loses the event or publishes one for a change that never committed.

The transactional outbox fixes that: the state change and an outbox row commit in one local transaction, and a relay publishes outbox rows later. The repo models the transaction with InMemoryUnitOfWork, which commits ledger rows and outbox rows together or not at all. The relay, from examples/account-modernization/src/main/java/com/wallaceespindola/modernization/outbox/OutboxRelay.java, trimmed to its one method:

public int relayOnce() {
    int sent = 0;
    for (OutboxEvent event : store.unpublished()) {
        try {
            publisher.publish(event);
        } catch (RuntimeException e) {
            LOG.log(Level.WARNING, "Publish failed for {0}, will retry: {1}", event.eventId(), e.getMessage());
            break;
        }
        store.markPublished(event.eventId());
        sent++;
    }
    return sent;
}

It stops at the first failure to keep the order, and it marks an event as published only after the broker accepted it. That second rule means a crash after publish and before markPublished sends the event again on the next run. Delivery is at-least-once, and there's no way around that on the producer side.

So the consumer has to make duplicates harmless. Here's examples/account-modernization/src/main/java/com/wallaceespindola/modernization/outbox/IdempotentConsumer.java, trimmed to the method:

public synchronized boolean accept(OutboxEvent event) {
    if (inbox.contains(event.eventId())) {
        return false;
    }
    handler.accept(event);
    inbox.add(event.eventId());
    return true;
}

The inbox is a set of processed event IDs. A redelivered event returns false and the handler never runs twice. In production, the inbox is a table keyed by event ID, and you insert into it in the same transaction as the consumer's own state change. Otherwise you've moved the dual-write problem from the producer to the consumer.

On the mainframe side, the same idea exists: write the event to a Db2 outbox table, or put it on MQ, inside the same CICS unit of work as the business update. For the relay you can poll, as the example does, or tail the outbox table with CDC, which avoids polling load and keeps commit order.

Things that will trip you up

A leaky ACL. If a legacy field name, a return code or a record shape shows up in a new API or event, the ACL has a hole. Review contracts for it the same way you review for secrets.

Rounding that isn't a bug. COBOL ROUNDED is half-up by default, while Java's BigDecimal needs an explicit RoundingMode. Plenty of "mismatches" in a parallel run come from this one line, so classify them as a group instead of chasing them one by one.

Shadow traffic with side effects. A shadow path that sends a real notification or books a real entry is worse than no parallel run. Stub every adapter with a side effect, and enforce it in configuration so it doesn't depend on someone catching it in review.

A consumer that is "mostly" idempotent. An inbox that is updated after the handler commits, in a separate transaction, will process a duplicate eventually. Write the inbox row in the same transaction as the handler's changes.

The perpetual strangler. Facades, ACLs, CDC pipelines and parallel-run harnesses are transitional architecture. Each one needs a removal date, or you end up running and paying for both stacks indefinitely. Patterns of Legacy Displacement by Ian Cartwright, Rob Horn and James Lewis calls this out well.

Where it doesn't pay off

This toolkit has a cost: you build, run and later delete everything in it. If the legacy capability is small enough to replace in one well-tested release, coexistence may cost more than the cutover. If it's stable, cheap to run and not blocking anyone, retaining it behind an API is a good outcome. And if there's no interception point at all (no API, queue or data boundary), the facade has nowhere to go, so you start with event interception or encapsulation first. There's no adoption data here. Choose the patterns per capability, and add each one only where it solves a problem you actually have.

Recap

  • The strangler facade decides where traffic goes. It starts as a pass-through and every flip is a routing change you can undo.
  • The ACL decodes COMP-3 and EBCDIC, but its real job is semantics: return codes become domain outcomes, flags become POSTED and PENDING.
  • The read side keeps pending and posted apart, has a lag SLO and falls back to legacy when it's behind.
  • The parallel run serves the legacy answer, compares and classifies, so you triage categories instead of rows.
  • The outbox gives you at-least-once publishing without dual writes, and the idempotent consumer makes the "at least" part safe.

Try it yourself

You need Java 25 and Maven. Clone the repo and run the build:

cd examples/account-modernization && mvn verify

All 36 tests should pass in a few seconds. Good places to start reading are PackedDecimalTest (the byte-level examples), ParallelRunTest (the classification cases, including the 4.17 vs 4.25 one) and OutboxTest (a broker that fails, then recovers and gets the same event again). Then pass a tolerance of 0.10 to ParallelRun and rerun the January case: the 0.08 DAY_COUNT gap becomes WITHIN_TOLERANCE. The pattern catalog behind the code, including the phases and exit criteria, is in docs/legacy-modernization-patterns-context.md.

Which of these patterns did your team find hardest to get right around a legacy core: the ACL, the parallel run or the outbox? I'd like to hear in the comments.

title: Crypto Withdrawal Risk Monitoring: How CDC Helps
description:
When a withdrawal sits in review, the customer wants to know when it will go through. Your team needs an answer too. Sometimes, the risk service is still waiting for the account data it needs to decide.

Imagine a customer changes their security settings, adds a withdrawal address, and then requests a large withdrawal. There may be a reasonable explanation for all three actions. But your risk system needs to see them together to assess the request.

That becomes harder when the records live in separate systems and arrive at different times. Crypto withdrawal risk monitoring may then rely on an account view that is already out of date. A legitimate request can wait longer, while a suspicious pattern may take longer to surface.

Change data capture (CDC) helps close this gap by continuously delivering committed database changes to downstream systems. BladePipe handles this data delivery layer, with full data loads and ongoing CDC synchronization.

Let's follow a withdrawal workflow built around that delivery layer. We'll look at how account changes reach the risk system and how a decision can affect a withdrawal before funds leave.

Where Crypto Exchanges Can Stop a Withdrawal

Before looking at the data pipeline, it helps to locate the point where a decision can still change the outcome. A withdrawal usually passes through security checks, balance validation, funds reservation, review, wallet execution, and blockchain confirmation.

The order varies by exchange. What matters is whether the risk decision arrives while the exchange can still hold or reject the request.

Stage What needs to be checked Limits of control
Request submission Identity, withdrawal permissions, destination, and available balance Checks must use the source-of-truth transactional system
Awaiting review Recent activity, withdrawal history, and account relationships The workflow can support holds, rejection, or manual review
Wallet execution Whether approval remains valid and relevant state has changed The ability to pause depends on the wallet interface and execution progress
Broadcast or completion Whether further suspicious activity is underway Changing an internal status generally cannot reverse a transaction already sent

This is why the status shown in an internal dashboard needs a closer look. “Under review” does not prove that funds have not been sent. Check when your workflow calls the wallet and when the transaction is broadcast.

If review must finish before execution, every path to the wallet has to respect that requirement. That includes automated jobs, manual actions, and retries. Once that control point is clear, you can work backward to the data the review needs.

How BladePipe Delivers Data for Withdrawal Reviews

For the account in our example, the review might need recent security changes, withdrawal history, and links between the destination address and other accounts. Those inputs may come from different databases.

If each database feeds the risk system through a scheduled batch job, the review may wait for the next refresh. With BladePipe, you can load the existing records first, then keep delivering changes through CDC. This gives downstream consumers a starting dataset and ongoing updates.

For example, a MySQL-to-Kafka DataJob can deliver account and withdrawal table changes to Kafka for your risk consumers to process. Those consumers link the records and evaluate activity. The full path looks like this:

Commit the change → BladePipe CDC → downstream risk processing → decision → current-state checks → allow or block processing.

The important handoff comes after delivery. A new record needs to trigger an evaluation or update an existing one. Otherwise, the data can be current while the withdrawal keeps waiting.

Example: A Security Change Followed by a Withdrawal

Let's follow the same account through a simplified example of that workflow.

  1. Account activity commits. A user changes security settings and adds a withdrawal address. The source systems save those changes.
  2. A withdrawal is requested. The withdrawal service checks the balance and permissions, then creates a pending request.
  3. BladePipe delivers the changes. It captures the committed updates from the configured source tables and sends them to Kafka. The downstream risk consumer links account updates and withdrawal records using account and request identifiers.
  4. The risk system evaluates the request. It checks that the required inputs have arrived, then applies rules to recent activity. A rule may send the request for additional review.
  5. The withdrawal service applies the decision. It verifies the request version, account restrictions, and current status before making a controlled state transition. A canceled or changed request must not use an old approval.
  6. The outcome is recorded. The system saves the decision, supporting evidence, and whether the hold or approval actually took effect.

At the evaluation step, one detail is easy to miss. The withdrawal record may arrive before a related security update. Set a freshness limit for approval inputs, and define how the workflow handles late data or a missing decision.

That gives you a specific delay to reduce: the time spent waiting for data. Manual review, wallet processing, and blockchain confirmation still take their own time. Keeping those delays separate makes it easier to see whether the pipeline is helping.

Real-Time Withdrawal Risk Monitoring with CDC

So far, we have followed one request. The same incoming data can also help your team spot activity across several requests or accounts. A withdrawal that looks ordinary on its own may deserve attention when others quickly follow it.

For example, several accounts might send funds to the same address within a short period. To assess that pattern as it develops, a Kafka-based setup can extend the BladePipe pipeline with continuous calculations:

Database → BladePipe CDC → Kafka → stream processing engine → risk decision → operational action.

As events arrive, the stream processor updates withdrawal counts, cumulative amounts, and linked-account counts over a recent time window. A calculation covering the last five minutes can update with every event. It need not wait five minutes before producing a result.

If that pattern triggers a rule, the resulting decision might hold pending withdrawals or require additional authentication. It could also send the case for manual review. Recording the action's outcome lets your team check that the response actually happened.

The useful response depends on how far the withdrawals have progressed. Once funds have been sent, intervention generally focuses on limiting further losses. Shared addresses and similar behavior remain indicators to investigate, rather than proof of fraud.

If you are building this with Kafka, our Kafka CDC architecture guide explains the delivery layer in more detail. Our guide to when to use Kafka can help you compare it with simpler options.

Avoid Double Counting Withdrawal Events

Those rolling counts are only useful if they count the right thing. One withdrawal may generate several updates as it moves from pending review to processing, sent, and completed. Treating every update as a new withdrawal would make ordinary activity look much busier than it is.

Before using the feed in a risk rule, agree on a few definitions:

  • What is being measured? Requested, pending, or completed withdrawal amounts?
  • What needs to be adjusted? How do cancellations, failures, and reversals affect the totals?
  • What counts as a duplicate? How are retries and replayed records tied back to the same withdrawal? Which event ID and request version identify an update?
  • Which time matters? Are windows based on when an event occurred or when it was processed, and how are late events handled?

These definitions also help you decide what to retain. Current state answers “Can this account withdraw now?” Event history explains what happened before the request and whether the pattern is unusual.

For the security-change example, the latest account row may not preserve the sequence you need to review. Retain the relevant history and connect it with login devices, the origin of the action, and audit logs. That context helps the risk system interpret the change.

Reliable Event Delivery with CDC and the Outbox Pattern

Once you know what each event should mean, you need a reliable way to deliver it. A common approach is to update the database and then publish a message. If the application fails between those writes, the withdrawal can exist in the database without a matching event reaching the risk system.

CDC can capture the committed database change and deliver it downstream. You can capture business tables directly or use an outbox table for explicit business events:

Approach Typical use What it requires
Capture changes directly from business tables Maintain account views, withdrawal status, and analytics data Consumers must understand the schema and the meaning of each change
Transactional outbox Publish explicit business events such as “withdrawal requested” The application writes the business record and event record in one database transaction; CDC then delivers the event

With an outbox, the application saves the withdrawal update and event record in one database transaction. CDC then delivers the event record. This closes the gap between saving the business change and recording the event that needs to be published.

Delivery can still involve retries, so consumers need to recognize an event they have already handled. Give each business event a unique ID for deduplication. For a Kafka-based design, choose a message key that keeps related events in the same partition, and define how consumers handle their order.

That retry handling matters all the way to execution. An external wallet operation sits outside the outbox database transaction. Your application still needs to prevent a replayed event or repeated request from causing a second withdrawal.

You may already have a transactional job queue or another reliable event mechanism. In that case, compare its delivery and recovery behavior with what CDC would add. The goal is a dependable path from committed data to the consumer that needs it.

Where a Real-Time Data Warehouse Fits

The consumers will need different views of the same activity. A stream processor can maintain the recent counts used by a rule. An investigator may need months of history to understand how several accounts are related.

A real-time data warehouse can support those longer histories and flexible queries. It still depends on timely delivery: a one-second query against data refreshed hourly can return a view that is almost an hour out of date.

BladePipe can deliver database changes to Kafka or a supported analytics destination. That lets you build the delivery path around what each consumer needs:

  • Stream processing supports continuous monitoring, windowed calculations, and rule evaluation.
  • A real-time warehouse supports historical analysis, account relationships, and investigations.
  • Both can be used when the workload calls for them.

Whichever layer produces a risk result, feed it back into the review workflow described earlier. The withdrawal service should still check the current balance, permissions, and request state in the authoritative transactional system before execution.

Measure Review Time and Time to Effective Control

With the delivery and processing layers connected, you can check whether the workflow is improving. Start with the two outcomes that brought us here: less waiting for legitimate requests and earlier action on suspicious activity.

They need separate timelines:

Goal Timeline to measure
Shorten legitimate withdrawal reviews Request submitted → data available → decision complete → withdrawal cleared for processing
Limit further losses Suspicious pattern becomes detectable → decision complete → control takes effect

Within each timeline, measure data delivery, decision time, and action time separately. If data arrives quickly but reviews remain slow, you know where to look next. If a decision is prompt but a hold takes too long, the delay is closer to execution.

For the delivery part, check BladePipe task progress alongside downstream processing lag. BladePipe records offsets so its full-load and incremental tasks can resume from the last recorded position after a restart. Include consumer recovery in the same test, since resumed delivery may involve records that need deduplication.

Review false-positive rates and manual review volume alongside those timings. A faster rule that sends too many legitimate requests to reviewers may create a new queue. Also test peak load, backlogs, replay, and downstream outages to see how the workflow behaves under pressure.

This focus on timing also helps you decide where continuous processing is worth the effort. Historical backfills, independent reconciliation, feature recomputation, and model training can still use batch processing. Prioritize the paths where waiting changes the outcome.

Build the Data Pipeline Around One Withdrawal Workflow

You do not need to rebuild every pipeline at once. Choose one crypto withdrawal risk monitoring workflow where waiting for data causes a recurring problem. Identify the records it needs, agree on an acceptable delay, and trace the decision through to the withdrawal service.

With BladePipe handling the initial load and ongoing database changes, your team can focus on connecting that data to risk rules and withdrawal controls. Start with the tables needed for the chosen workflow, then check how the full path behaves when data arrives late or processing restarts.

For a MySQL-based setup, our guide to syncing MySQL data to Kafka with BladePipe walks through the delivery side. Use your own sources, consumers, and recovery scenarios to test the full workflow. Once the results show where it helps, you can decide which workflow to connect next.

title: How to Build Private Retrieval for Financial Research Dashboards: A Cost-Aware Playbook
description:
Index cost is the constraint that changes this design. For a financial research dashboard that also aggregates game listings from several feeds, I would keep sensitive fields out of the shared semantic index, attach an explicit access scope to every chunk, and retrieve in two stages: cheap metadata filtering first, embeddings second.

Short answer: build a policy-aware retrieval layer around a small, partitioned index, then prove its behavior with adversarial privacy tests before tuning recall. A giant all-purpose vector store is easy to demo and expensive to govern.

The result is less glamorous than a single search call. It is easier to explain to a reviewer, though, and the explanation is part of the product.

Start with a data contract, not an embedding model

The first implementation mistake is treating a document as the security boundary. A quarterly filing, a broker note, and a game listing can share a text format while having completely different readers. The unit that needs a policy is the chunk, and the policy must survive ingestion, indexing, retrieval, and citation rendering.

I use a narrow record contract. It keeps the raw text in a controlled store and puts only the searchable representation plus labels in the index.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import FrozenSet


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Chunk:
    chunk_id: str
    source_id: str
    text: str
    tenant: str
    scopes: FrozenSet[str]
    contains_personal_data: bool
    published_at: str


def can_read(chunk: Chunk, user_scopes: set[str], tenant: str) -> bool:
    return (
        chunk.tenant == tenant
        and chunk.scopes.issubset(user_scopes)
        and not chunk.contains_personal_data
    )

That last boolean is not a complete privacy system. It is a forcing function: the ingestion job must make a decision instead of silently indexing everything. In production, a separate redaction service can replace or enrich it, with an audit record linking the redacted version to the source object.

For the game-listing feed, tenant can identify a publisher account and scopes can distinguish public catalog data from unreleased launch dates. For the dashboard, the same fields can represent a fund, desk, or subscription tier. The shape stays stable while policy values change.

How should retrieval handle privacy controls, citations, and index cost?

A useful query path has four observable checkpoints: authenticate the caller, apply structured filters, run semantic search over the remaining candidates, and authorize every citation before it leaves the service. Logging those checkpoints gives an operator a reason when a result is absent.

Here is a deliberately boring interface for the middle two steps. It is plain Python so the policy can be tested without a hosted search dependency.

from collections.abc import Iterable


def metadata_candidates(
    chunks: Iterable[Chunk],
    *,
    tenant: str,
    user_scopes: set[str],
    as_of: str,
) -> list[Chunk]:
    return [
        chunk
        for chunk in chunks
        if chunk.tenant == tenant
        and chunk.published_at <= as_of
        and chunk.scopes.issubset(user_scopes)
        and not chunk.contains_personal_data
    ]


def citation_payload(chunk: Chunk, user_scopes: set[str], tenant: str) -> dict[str, str]:
    if not can_read(chunk, user_scopes, tenant):
        raise PermissionError("citation is outside the caller scope")
    return {"source_id": chunk.source_id, "chunk_id": chunk.chunk_id, "text": chunk.text}

The semantic ranker runs only on metadata_candidates. That ordering matters for privacy, but it also controls index cost at scale: a cheap filter can prevent an embedding search from touching unrelated tenants and old versions. Keep the filter dimensions low-cardinality and measurable. If every document gets a unique, high-cardinality label, the filter itself becomes a slow secondary index.

The retrieval-augmented generation paper describes combining a parametric generator with a non-parametric memory, which is a useful mental model here: retrieval is a separate memory system with its own freshness and access rules, not a prompt field that can be patched after generation. The model should receive only authorized passages. Do not ask it to hide passages it was already given.

A small evaluation harness catches the expensive mistakes

Before choosing chunk sizes or a database, make a fixture with three classes of queries: an analyst asking for public revenue data, a desk user asking for restricted research, and a cross-tenant query that should return nothing. Add game-listing queries with unreleased metadata to make the same boundary concrete outside finance.

I keep expected outcomes as data, then run them on every ingestion change.

def evaluate(cases: list[dict], chunks: list[Chunk]) -> dict[str, float]:
    allowed = denied = 0
    for case in cases:
        found = metadata_candidates(
            chunks,
            tenant=case["tenant"],
            user_scopes=set(case["scopes"]),
            as_of=case["as_of"],
        )
        got = {item.chunk_id for item in found}
        expected = set(case["expected_ids"])
        if got == expected:
            allowed += 1
        if not (got & set(case.get("forbidden_ids", []))):
            denied += 1
    total = len(cases) or 1
    return {"exact_scope_rate": allowed / total, "denial_rate": denied / total}

Exact matching is intentionally strict for this fixture. A production harness can add recall, citation precision, latency percentiles, and token counts, but privacy leakage is a binary failure. I also test stale records: a query with an as_of date must not surface a later filing or a future game launch. In one fixture, the public analyst sees two annual-report chunks and the desk user sees those plus a restricted channel-check note; the cross-tenant request sees zero. That tiny matrix catches a surprising number of regressions because a developer can change a default filter, refresh a snapshot, or re-embed a document without touching the answer prompt. I keep the expected IDs in version control and require the same policy version in the test report as in the index metadata, so a passing score cannot be detached from the rules that produced it.

One practical trap is measuring only answer quality. A fluent answer assembled from a forbidden chunk is still a failed request. Track policy-denial counts, empty-result rates by scope, and the number of citations rejected at the final gate. Those metrics tell you whether a recall change actually altered exposure risk.

Where this architecture does not fit

The catch is operational complexity. Partitioned indexes and a second authorization check cost engineering time, and they can reduce recall when metadata is incomplete. This approach is not suitable when the corpus is entirely public, tiny, and disposable; a conventional full-text index may be clearer. Stick with a simpler pipeline until you have a real tenant boundary or a retention requirement.

It is also a poor fit for workloads that need millisecond, globally replicated search with no tolerance for a policy lookup. In that case, choose a search system with native document-level security and validate its enforcement independently. Your mileage may vary because provider-specific filter semantics and replication guarantees differ; the contract and tests should remain yours.

The notebook version should expose the same four checkpoints as the deployed service, with fixtures standing in for the source feeds. Package the policy function, candidate filter, ranker adapter, and citation gate as separate modules. That makes a code review about decisions rather than a wall of prompt strings.

For observability, emit a request ID, tenant, policy version, candidate count, ranked count, denied-citation count, and token estimate. Never log raw restricted text by default. Retain enough identifiers to replay a decision against a quarantined copy of the source.

Finally, set a budget in the evaluation harness. If a new chunking strategy doubles indexed tokens without improving scope-safe recall, reject it before it reaches the dashboard. The right retrieval design is the one whose privacy behavior is testable, whose citations are explainable, and whose index bill grows for a reason.

References

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://www.nist.gov/privacy-framework
  • https://owasp.org/www-project-top-ten/

title: Building Reliable Inventory and Booking Workflows for a Multi-Provider Rental Marketplace
description:
Introduction

At first glance, building a vehicle rental marketplace looks like a standard catalog application: let providers upload vehicles, index the attributes, and render search results. In practice, static catalog engineering breaks down the moment two customers try to book the same vehicle for overlapping dates, or when an independent fleet operator updates offline availability mid-session.

In a multi-provider ecosystem like MotoShare Gulf—which connects customers with independent vehicle owners and local rental businesses across the UAE, particularly in Dubai and Abu Dhabi—the core engineering challenge is state synchronization over time. A vehicle appearing in search results simply confirms that a listing exists and matches static filters. It does not guarantee that the physical asset is operationally ready, unencumbered by maintenance, or free of overlapping reservation holds for a specific Friday-to-Monday window.

To operate reliably, a rental marketplace requires more than a vehicle listing database. It demands consistent inventory records, date-aware availability checks, strict reservation conflict prevention, clear provider ownership boundaries, and resilient booking workflows.

Modeling a Multi-Provider Vehicle Inventory

A common early mistake in marketplace design is conflating the physical asset with the public listing. When a single table stores vehicle VINs, daily pricing, marketing descriptions, and active booking flags together, schema rigidity quickly follows. If a provider pauses a listing for seasonal maintenance or lists the same vehicle under different regional delivery terms, mutating a monolithic record risks corrupting historical reservation references.

Separating physical assets, provider ownership, commercial listings, and time-bound reservations creates a clean relational foundation:

CREATE TABLE providers (
    provider_id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    business_type VARCHAR(32) NOT NULL, -- 'fleet_operator' | 'individual_owner'
    verification_status VARCHAR(32) NOT NULL,
    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()
);

CREATE TABLE locations (
    location_id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    emirate VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL, -- e.g., 'Dubai', 'Abu Dhabi'
    zone_name VARCHAR(128) NOT NULL,
    coordinates POINT
);

CREATE TABLE vehicles (
    vehicle_id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    provider_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES providers(provider_id),
    category VARCHAR(32) NOT NULL, -- 'motorcycle' | 'sports_bike' | 'standard_car' | 'luxury_car'
    make VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL,
    model VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL,
    model_year INT NOT NULL,
    vin_hash VARCHAR(128) UNIQUE NOT NULL,
    operational_status VARCHAR(32) NOT NULL -- 'active' | 'maintenance' | 'retired'
);

CREATE TABLE vehicle_listings (
    listing_id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    vehicle_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES vehicles(vehicle_id),
    location_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES locations(location_id),
    listing_status VARCHAR(32) NOT NULL, -- 'published' | 'unlisted' | 'suspended'
    daily_rate_minor_units BIGINT NOT NULL,
    currency CHAR(3) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'AED',
    min_rental_hours INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 24
);

CREATE TABLE reservations (
    reservation_id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    vehicle_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES vehicles(vehicle_id),
    listing_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES vehicle_listings(listing_id),
    customer_id UUID NOT NULL,
    start_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    end_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    status VARCHAR(32) NOT NULL, -- 'held' | 'confirmed' | 'cancelled' | 'completed'
    hold_expires_at TIMESTAMPTZ,
    idempotency_key VARCHAR(128) UNIQUE NOT NULL,
    CONSTRAINT valid_period CHECK (end_at > start_at)
);

Notice that reservations references both listing_id (capturing the commercial terms at booking time) and vehicle_id (anchoring availability to the physical unit). Even if a provider edits pricing or unpublishes a listing later, the underlying physical vehicle identity and provider ownership remain immutable for active and historical bookings.

Designing Date-Based Availability Checks

Availability in a rental system is never a boolean column (is_available = true). Instead, availability is a derived query across multiple state layers:

  1. Listing Visibility: Controls whether customers can discover the listing (published vs. unlisted).
  2. Operational Availability: Reflects whether the physical vehicle is roadworthy or blocked by the provider for servicing, inspection, or offline use.
  3. Temporary Reservation Holds: Short-lived locks created when a customer initiates checkout or awaits provider approval.
  4. Confirmed Reservations: Committed bookings that block the vehicle for the requested interval, plus any mandatory turnaround buffer for cleaning and inspection.
  5. Cancelled or Expired Reservations: Historical records that no longer block calendar intervals once transitioned out of active states.

Two half-open time intervals $[A_{\text{start}}, A_{\text{end}})$ and $[B_{\text{start}}, B_{\text{end}})$ overlap if and only if:

$$A_{\text{start}} < B_{\text{end}} \quad \text{AND} \quad A_{\text{end}} > B_{\text{start}}$$

Using half-open intervals allows back-to-back bookings (e.g., Reservation A ends at 10:00, Reservation B starts at 10:00) without false conflicts, though production systems typically inject an explicit turnaround buffer (such as 2 hours) to end_at before running the check.

interface TimeWindow {
  startAt: Date;
  endAt: Date;
}

interface ExistingBooking {
  id: string;
  startAt: Date;
  endAt: Date;
  status: 'held' | 'confirmed' | 'cancelled' | 'completed';
  holdExpiresAt?: Date;
}

/**
 * Illustrative overlap check.
 * Assumptions: Timestamps are normalized to UTC; turnaround buffers are pre-applied.
 * Limitations: In-memory evaluation only; must be paired with database-level locking
 * to prevent race conditions between read and write operations.
 */
function isVehicleAvailable(
  requested: TimeWindow,
  bookings: ExistingBooking[],
  now: Date = new Date(),
  turnaroundBufferMs: number = 2 * 60 * 60 * 1000
): boolean {
  if (requested.endAt <= requested.startAt) {
    throw new Error('Invalid rental period: endAt must be after startAt');
  }

  for (const booking of bookings) {
    if (booking.status === 'cancelled' || booking.status === 'completed') {
      continue;
    }

    // Ignore expired temporary holds even if a background cleanup worker has not run yet
    if (
      booking.status === 'held' &&
      booking.holdExpiresAt &&
      booking.holdExpiresAt <= now
    ) {
      continue;
    }

    const effectiveEnd = new Date(booking.endAt.getTime() + turnaroundBufferMs);

    const overlaps =
      requested.startAt < effectiveEnd && requested.endAt > booking.startAt;

    if (overlaps) {
      return false;
    }
  }

  return true;
}

Evaluating holdExpiresAt <= now directly inside the availability predicate ensures stale holds release capacity immediately at the exact millisecond of expiration, rather than relying solely on asynchronous cron jobs.

Preventing Double Bookings

When two customers attempt to book the same vehicle for overlapping dates within milliseconds of each other, standard SELECT followed by INSERT application logic fails due to Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use (TOCTOU) race conditions. Both transactions read zero conflicts simultaneously and both insert confirmed rows.

Backend engineers have several mechanisms to prevent double bookings, each carrying distinct trade-offs:

Mechanism How It Works Trade-Offs
Database Exclusion Constraints Uses PostgreSQL EXCLUDE USING GIST on tstzrange(start_at, end_at) scoped by vehicle_id. Guarantees zero overlapping active rows at the storage engine level; requires careful indexing when filtering out cancelled states.
Pessimistic Row Locking Executes SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the parent vehicles row before checking reservations. Serializes concurrent booking attempts per vehicle cleanly; increases lock contention on high-demand vehicles during traffic spikes.
Optimistic Concurrency Control Uses a version integer on the vehicle calendar and retries on UPDATE ... WHERE version = expected. High throughput under low contention; requires retry loops and degrades under heavy flash-crowd contention.
Temporary Holds + TTL Places a 10–15 minute held state during payment or provider review, paired with an idempotency key. Prevents users from losing a vehicle mid-checkout; introduces inventory lockup if malicious clients hoard holds without paying.

In practice, combining pessimistic locking on the parent vehicles record inside an ACID transaction with idempotency keys provides deterministic safety without complex retry storms:

from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone
import psycopg2

def create_reservation_hold(
    conn,
    vehicle_id: str,
    listing_id: str,
    customer_id: str,
    start_at: datetime,
    end_at: datetime,
    idempotency_key: str,
    hold_minutes: int = 15,
) -> dict:
    """
    Illustrative transactional reservation hold using PostgreSQL row-level locking.
    Assumptions: PostgreSQL database with READ COMMITTED isolation; UTC timestamps.
    Limitations: Serializes concurrent requests for the same vehicle_id; requires
    external payment/provider confirmation flow to promote 'held' to 'confirmed'.
    """
    now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
    hold_expires_at = now + timedelta(minutes=hold_minutes)

    with conn:  # Begins transaction; commits on exit, rolls back on exception
        with conn.cursor() as cur:
            # 1. Idempotency check for safe client retries
            cur.execute(
                """
                SELECT reservation_id, status
                FROM reservations
                WHERE idempotency_key = %s
                """,
                (idempotency_key,),
            )
            existing = cur.fetchone()
            if existing:
                return {"reservation_id": existing[0], "status": existing[1], "replayed": True}

            # 2. Lock parent vehicle row to serialize concurrent booking requests
            cur.execute(
                """
                SELECT operational_status
                FROM vehicles
                WHERE vehicle_id = %s
                FOR UPDATE
                """,
                (vehicle_id,),
            )
            vehicle = cur.fetchone()
            if not vehicle or vehicle[0] != "active":
                raise ValueError("Vehicle is not operationally available")

            # 3. Check for overlapping active holds or confirmed reservations
            cur.execute(
                """
                SELECT 1
                FROM reservations
                WHERE vehicle_id = %s
                  AND status IN ('confirmed', 'held')
                  AND (status = 'confirmed' OR hold_expires_at > %s)
                  AND start_at < %s
                  AND end_at > %s
                LIMIT 1
                """,
                (vehicle_id, now, end_at, start_at),
            )
            if cur.fetchone():
                raise RuntimeError("Booking conflict: overlapping reservation exists")

            # 4. Insert temporary hold atomically
            cur.execute(
                """
                INSERT INTO reservations (
                    vehicle_id, listing_id, customer_id,
                    start_at, end_at, status, hold_expires_at, idempotency_key
                )
                VALUES (%s, %s, %s, %s, %s, 'held', %s, %s)
                RETURNING reservation_id
                """,
                (
                    vehicle_id,
                    listing_id,
                    customer_id,
                    start_at,
                    end_at,
                    hold_expires_at,
                    idempotency_key,
                ),
            )
            reservation_id = cur.fetchone()[0]
            return {"reservation_id": reservation_id, "status": "held", "replayed": False}

Managing Multiple Provider Workflows

A multi-provider marketplace rarely serves a uniform supplier base. Commercial rental agencies manage multi-car fleets with dedicated dispatch teams, whereas individual owners listing a personal motorcycle or weekend sedan operate asynchronously and may require manual review before accepting a handoff.

If both the marketplace platform and the provider can mutate availability arbitrarily without clear boundaries, split-brain inventory states occur. Effective systems enforce strict ownership and event boundaries:

  • Provider-Scoped Mutations: Authorization middleware must enforce that provider_id claims match the owner of the target vehicle_id before allowing updates to pricing, pickup locations, or maintenance blocks.
  • Request-to-Book vs. Instant-Book Modes: Depending on provider settings, a customer request either confirms immediately upon payment authorization or transitions into a pending_provider_approval hold with a strict SLA timer.
  • Out-of-Band Availability Sync: When a local fleet operator rents a car to a walk-in customer, they must be able to create an offline_block interval on the vehicle calendar. If an offline block overlaps an unconfirmed hold, the system should automatically void the hold and notify the customer before payment capture.

* Symmetric Cancellation Handling: Cancellations initiated by either party must trigger deterministic state transitions, release date intervals atomically, and emit domain events for refund calculation and search index updates.

Designing a Search and Discovery Layer

Search queries in a regional rental marketplace combine geospatial filters, vehicle taxonomy, and temporal availability. A user browsing for motorcycle rental Dubai has fundamentally different discovery constraints than someone comparing options for car rental Abu Dhabi, motorcycle rental Abu Dhabi, or car rental Dubai.

To keep search latency low without serving stale availability, engineering teams typically separate discovery into two stages:

  1. Candidate Filtering (Search Index): An inverted index (such as OpenSearch or Elasticsearch) filters listings by emirate, delivery radius, category, pricing tier, and listing_status = 'published'.
  2. Real-Time Availability Verification (Relational Store): Before rendering final bookable badges or accepting a checkout intent, the API cross-references candidate vehicle_ids against the authoritative reservations table for the user's exact [start_at, end_at) window.

Displaying clear UI distinctions—such as "Available for your dates" versus "Listed in Dubai — select dates to verify availability"—prevents user frustration when popular vehicles are already booked during peak holiday weekends.

Handling Different Vehicle Categories

Treating every vehicle as a generic row with make, model, and daily_rate breaks down across diverse automotive segments. Two-wheelers, daily commuters, and high-value performance vehicles require category-specific schemas and validation rules:

  • Motorcycles and Sports Bikes: Search intents like Ducati motorcycle rental Dubai or sports bike rental Abu Dhabi involve rider-specific constraints that do not apply to sedans. Data models must capture engine displacement (cc), seat height, ABS/traction control equipment, included riding gear, and motorcycle-specific license class endorsements.
  • Standard Passenger Cars: Queries for car rental Dubai or car rental Abu Dhabi emphasize seating capacity, luggage volume, transmission type, fuel policy, and daily mileage allowances.
  • Luxury and Exotic Vehicles: Customers searching for luxury car rental Dubai or luxury car rental Abu Dhabi encounter stricter risk controls. The booking engine must enforce higher security deposit holds, minimum driver age thresholds (often 25+), multi-year license tenure checks, and higher excess mileage rates.

Using a JSONB category_attributes column paired with versioned JSON Schema validation per vehicle category allows the platform to enforce strict domain rules without proliferating dozens of sparse, nullable columns. Note that category taxonomy defines how vehicles are validated and discovered—it never implies live availability for any specific model until date-range checks pass.

Marketplace Architecture and Technology Choices

To isolate read-heavy discovery traffic from write-critical reservation transactions, a modular service boundary is effective. Note that the following diagram represents a conceptual architecture recommendation for marketplace engineers—not a claim regarding MotoShare Gulf's internal infrastructure or software stack.

Synchronous vs. Asynchronous Boundaries

  • Synchronous Paths: Availability checks, reservation hold creation, idempotency verification, and payment authorization must execute synchronously so the user receives immediate, deterministic feedback.
  • Asynchronous Paths: Search index updates, provider SMS/email notifications, invoice PDF generation, and analytics aggregation should run asynchronously via a transactional outbox pattern. If a notification provider experiences latency, it should never block or roll back a committed database reservation.

Supporting Rental Business Operations

For local rental agencies and independent fleet owners, marketplace visibility is only half of the operational picture. Providers still need day-to-day operational tooling to track fleet maintenance schedules, manage active reservation calendars, verify customer documents, reconcile security deposits, and monitor fleet utilization.

In its public positioning, MotoShare Gulf advertises free vehicle rental management software UAE alongside its consumer marketplace to help local rental businesses digitize fleet records, bookings, and daily operations. From a systems engineering perspective, unifying provider fleet management with marketplace availability eliminates the primary source of double bookings: manual spreadsheet syncs between an agency's back-office desk and its online listings. When a provider logs a walk-in booking or scheduled service directly inside their fleet dashboard, the underlying vehicle calendar updates immediately across all channels.

Engineering Lessons for Marketplace Developers

  1. Treat availability as date-dependent data. Never store availability as a static boolean flag on a vehicle record; always compute it against half-open time intervals and active reservation states.
  2. Keep reservation state transitions explicit. Enforce a strict finite state machine (held → confirmed → completed / cancelled) so invalid transitions—such as confirming an expired hold—fail fast.
  3. Protect booking operations against concurrency. Pair database-level locking or exclusion constraints with client idempotency keys to eliminate race conditions during simultaneous booking requests.
  4. Separate provider ownership from customer-facing listings. Anchor reservations to immutable physical vehicle IDs and provider ownership records rather than mutable marketing listings.
  5. Make failure and cancellation workflows part of the original design. Build hold expiration, offline provider blocks, and symmetric cancellation rollbacks into day-one schemas rather than patching them in after launch.

Conclusion

Reliable rental marketplaces—whether serving commercial fleets or peer-to-peer car rental UAE networks—succeed on data integrity rather than catalog volume alone. When inventory models separate physical vehicles from commercial listings, availability queries evaluate overlapping intervals accurately, and reservation writes execute inside atomic transactions, both providers and renters gain predictable outcomes. For backend engineers building two-sided booking platforms, investing early in explicit state machines and concurrency control prevents the edge-case failures that erode marketplace trust at scale.

title: Cloud Object Storage for User Avatar Uploads: Node.js Tenant Isolation Explained in 4 APIs
description:
A gaming service that stores signed tournament waivers has a stricter problem than avatar uploads: each file needs a tenant boundary and an explicit deletion deadline. The practical answer is private object storage behind a server API, with short-lived presigned access and a lifecycle rule of at least one day.

Keep it private.

Short answer: choose the service whose request path lets your server enforce tenant_id, whose objects stay private, and whose deletion policy you can observe. Amazon S3 is the broadest specialist baseline. Cloudflare R2 is a sensible S3-compatible alternative. Supabase Storage fits teams already centered on Supabase. Infrai fits a platform team that wants storage beside other backend capabilities behind one REST contract, provided the missing storage controls are acceptable.

The cost is more than bytes. It includes the second SDK, another credential, lifecycle configuration, retry semantics, and the operational work of proving that tenant A never receives tenant B's signed document.

What changes when the object is a signed document?

Before: the upload path treats a filename as an address. After: the server creates an opaque key from a tenant and document identifier, writes privately, and issues access only for a bounded request.

Think of the flow as a short diagram in words: client sends metadata to the API; API authenticates the tenant; API writes tenants/{tenantId}/documents/{documentId}.pdf; API returns a presigned URL for the next operation; a scheduled deletion process removes the object after the contractual deadline. The bucket is shared only if the key namespace and authorization checks are shared deliberately.

That last sentence is the important one. A bucket is not a tenant boundary by itself. The application must validate ownership before it creates a key, presigns a URL, or deletes an object. Keep the object ACL private or signed-only. A public URL is the wrong shape for a document that has an explicit retention end.

For gaming, the data model might contain a player or team identifier, a tenant identifier, a document identifier, and delete_at. Store the deadline in your database as the source of truth. Use object storage lifecycle as a second line of enforcement, not as the only audit trail. A one-day minimum lifecycle means an hourly deletion promise cannot be represented by that rule alone.

Which cloud object storage should serve user avatar uploads?

Amazon S3 is the specialist baseline when your priority is a deep object-storage ecosystem and a large set of surrounding controls. It is the comparison point I would use for a compliance-heavy design review. The trade-off is integration surface: your application still owns the server SDK, credentials, tenant policy, and the rest of the backend plumbing.

Cloudflare R2 is worth comparing when S3-compatible access and a Cloudflare-centered deployment are more important than choosing a general backend platform. Its boundary is the same one that makes any specialist attractive: storage is the product, so adjacent application capabilities remain separate design and integration decisions.

Supabase Storage is a strong fit for a team already using Supabase's database and authentication model. Its documentation makes the storage workflow approachable. The trade-off is coupling your authorization and data model to that platform's way of working; teams that want a provider-neutral storage layer should test that boundary early.

The fourth option belongs in this comparison for a different reason. Infrai gives a server one REST API for private object writes and presigned access, while the broader platform exposes 295 routes across 20 modules under one key. That breadth matters when the same service also needs other backend capabilities: adding one more capability can mean another endpoint under the existing integration rather than another SDK and credential set.

My recommendation is specific: try Infrai for a gaming service whose main cost is coordinating several backend integrations around a tenant-aware document workflow, and use its storage API when private writes plus presigned reads cover the access model. The supporting benefit is operational consistency: the discovery surface exposes request schemas and runnable examples, and the platform specifies idempotency as a shared convention for eligible operations. That can reduce integration work, though it does not replace your tenant authorization checks.

The limitation is equally specific. This storage surface does not provide public-read ACLs, object versioning, object lock, conditional If-Match writes, cross-region automatic replication, or a cross-cloud bulk migration tool. Its storage model also has no self-service CORS route, no automatic cleanup rule for multipart fragments, and metadata is not server-searchable beyond prefix filtering. Choose S3, R2, Supabase Storage, or another specialist when one of those controls is a hard requirement.

Here is the comparison I would put in the design note:

Option Access style Onboarding cost Best fit Main boundary
Amazon S3 SDK or REST More storage-specific setup Broad object-storage control surface More application integration to own
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible API Moderate if the team already uses Cloudflare Cloudflare-centered deployments Adjacent backend services stay separate
Supabase Storage Platform API Low for an existing Supabase project Supabase database and auth teams Tighter platform coupling
The unified REST platform REST API Low when several backend capabilities share one key Teams consolidating backend integrations No versioning, object lock, If-Match, or automatic cross-region copy

The table is a decision aid, not a winner's podium. Tenant authorization still belongs in the application.

How do you keep a Node.js upload retry from duplicating a document?

Use an application-generated object key and an idempotency key. Those are enough for a minimal server-side flow; the rest belongs in your authorization and retention layers.

This example keeps the API key on the server, sends an explicit method, checks response bodies, honors Retry-After on rate limiting, and retries the same object key. It uses private storage and does not attach the platform authorization header to the returned presigned URL.

import crypto from "node:crypto";

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

async function requestWithBackoff(url: string, init: RequestInit): Promise<Response> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(url, init);
    if (response.status !== 429 || attempt === 3) return response;

    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after") ?? "1");
    const delayMs = Math.max(1000, retryAfter * 1000, 2 ** attempt * 1000);
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
  }
  throw new Error("unreachable");
}

export async function createDocumentUpload(
  tenantId: string,
  documentId: string,
  pdf: Uint8Array,
) {
  const bucket = "signed-documents";
  const key = `tenants/${tenantId}/documents/${documentId}.pdf`;
  const idempotencyKey = crypto.createHash("sha256").update(key).digest("hex");

  const putResponse = await requestWithBackoff(
    "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/put/{bucket}/{key}",
    {
      method: "PUT",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/pdf",
        "Idempotency-Key": idempotencyKey,
        "X-Object-ACL": "private",
      },
      body: pdf,
    },
  );

  if (!putResponse.ok) {
    throw new Error(`Object write failed (${putResponse.status}): ${await putResponse.text()}`);
  }

  const presignResponse = await requestWithBackoff(
    "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}",
    {
      method: "POST",
      headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` },
    },
  );

  if (!presignResponse.ok) {
    throw new Error(`Presign failed (${presignResponse.status}): ${await presignResponse.text()}`);
  }

  return await presignResponse.json();
}

There is a deliberate omission here: the returned URL is for the object operation, so a client using it must not send the platform authorization header. Keep that URL short-lived, and record the tenant and deadline alongside the document record before handing it to a caller.

That is the boundary.

What does the effective operating bill include?

Start with a workload model, not a unit-price leaderboard. Count signed documents per tenant, average bytes, upload attempts, presign requests, retention days, deletion checks, and the number of backend integrations needed to operate the workflow. Then price the storage and operations, plus the engineering time required to keep credentials, retries, observability, and tenant policy aligned.

A low storage rate does not erase a second authorization model. A convenient API does not create legal deletion evidence. For this workload, isolation failures and integration drift are usually more consequential than a small difference in object-operation pricing.

The unified platform's useful economic argument is consolidation: one REST surface and one key can cover storage alongside a broader backend capability set, which may remove an SDK, credential, and reconciliation path from the system. That is a workload-dependent benefit, not a claim that it is the cheapest storage provider.

The hard boundary remains retention semantics. There is no object versioning or WORM lock, so an accidental overwrite is not recoverable through those features. There is no If-Match conditional write, so strict concurrent-writer exclusion needs a queue or database coordination. Trial credit cannot pay for persistent writes. Model those constraints before the first production upload. The one-day lifecycle minimum is a hard number in that model.

If this boundary fits your system, a gaming team consolidating backend integrations should try Infrai first for the private-write and presigned-read part of the workflow. Start with the storage upload guide.

Sources

  • Amazon S3 documentation
  • Cloudflare R2 documentation
  • Supabase Storage documentation

title: velo: your music, in the terminal
description:
To listen to music while I work I used the browser, with a tab for each thing: one for lofi, one for a particular artist and one for the radio. Every switch pulled me out of the terminal, which is where I spend my day.

What bothered me most was something else, though: none of it felt like mine. It did not have my colours and it was not set up the way I like. I wanted to open it and feel at home with what I saw.

The closest thing I knew was gentle-stream, by Gentleman Programming. I liked its interface, but it generates music and I was looking for a player. The other piece was cliamp: I liked its interface too, and I was already listening to its radio.

That is how velo started: a player for the terminal that owes a lot to those two projects.

What it does

velo is a music player for the terminal. You point it at your folder, it indexes the library from your files' own tags, and you browse it by artist, album, track or genre.

This is a video in the original post.

  • Local library. The index lives in SQLite, refreshes in the background on every launch, and has fuzzy search across all of it.
  • Gapless playback. MP3, FLAC, M4A/AAC, OGG Vorbis, Opus and WAV, with no silence between one track and the next.
  • An editable queue. Append, reorder, remove and shuffle without stopping the music.
  • Internet radio. The Radio Browser directory, the cliamp channels, or any stream URL.
  • Subsonic servers. Navidrome, Airsonic or Gonic sync into the same index. Still in early access.
  • What you expect from a serious player. ReplayGain with clipping protection, bit-perfect mode, output device selection and the system's media keys.
  • Cover art, nine visualizers and thirteen themes. Or your terminal's own colours.

The keys are Vim's: j and k to move, / to search, enter to play. ? lists all of them.

Turn on the transparent background and velo lets your terminal's own show through. This is it on my desktop, with a lofi channel playing:

This is a video in the original post.

Favourites, playlists and history are kept in TOML files you can open and edit. And there is no telemetry: velo only contacts what you point it at, plus one request a day to GitHub to learn whether a newer version exists, which one line of configuration turns off.

What already existed

There are many terminal players and several are very good. The truth is I did not try most of them in depth. I looked at them as references while I designed velo, to see what each one solved and how.

One decision came out of that. Some of the best known, like ncmpcpp and rmpc, are MPD clients: before you hear a song you have to install, configure and keep a separate server running.

I wanted the opposite: one binary. You install it, tell it where your music is, and it plays. No daemon, no server and no account.

How it works inside

The audio callback only copies memory. The operating system asks velo for samples every few milliseconds, and if they arrive late you hear a click. So the expensive work (decoding, resampling, applying ReplayGain) happens on another thread, one buffer ahead. The two threads talk through a lock-free ring buffer. The callback measures how many samples are ready, copies them and fills the rest with silence. It does not allocate, take a lock or write a log.

Gapless means gapless. The next track is decoded before the current one ends and joined to it with no silence inserted. Lossy encoders add padding at the start and end of every file, and velo trims it at the seam. On a live album or a concept album, you can hear the difference.

One binary, for real. Every dependency had to pass that rule. SQLite is compiled in. Symphonia, the library that decodes the other formats, has no Opus decoder, so libopus is built statically. For media keys on Linux I chose a pure Rust D-Bus implementation, because the default one required a system library to be installed.

Remote servers go through a cache. A Subsonic track is downloaded once, untranscoded, and played from disk. That way seeking, gapless playback and ReplayGain work exactly as they do for a local file.

How I built it

The repository does not hide it, so I will say it myself: velo went from its first commit to version 1.0.0 in six days, with 479 commits and 75 published versions. I did not write those 70 thousand lines of Rust by hand. AI agents wrote them, with the same system I described in my AI dev stack.

What I did was direct. Every feature started as a document with numbered requirements that quote my own words, and every task was closed against those requirements. There are 21 of those documents in the repository's odd/tasks folder, in plain sight.

The code is not accepted on faith either. There are more than 1,200 tests, and a single script runs the formatter, the linter with warnings treated as errors, and every test. It is the same one continuous integration runs.

Not everything went to plan. velo was my first time with many of these technologies and with nearly every audio concept. Gapless, ReplayGain and bit-perfect were the most technical terms for me, and I did not fully understand what they implied. So when the agent proposed a scope I accepted it, and on top of that I asked for Subsonic servers, which I hardly use. It is in the project's first document, in my own words. Later there were moments when I did not know enough to question it, and I simply let it continue.

velo ended up bigger than I needed. That was not a bad thing: those features left the application more complete. But it made one thing clear to me: when you do not understand the subject, you stop directing and start approving.

Try it

velo runs on macOS and Linux. With Homebrew:

brew install alvaldes/tap/velo

Or with the install script, which verifies the checksum and does not ask for sudo:

curl -fsSL https://alvaldes.github.io/velo/install.sh | sh

Then run velo, press o and type the path to your music folder. On the site there is a player you can press play on before installing anything.

To see cover art you need a terminal that speaks the kitty, sixel or iTerm2 protocol. Windows is untested.

It is open source, under the MIT license. If something does not work or you have an idea for an improvement, open an issue in the repository.
