title: Content Negotiation Comes to GitLab Pages: Serving Semantic Web Formats with Standard HTTP Headers
description:
Static websites are often treated as HTML-only applications. But the web has always supported multiple representations of the same resource: HTML for browsers, JSON for applications, RDF for linked-data clients, and Turtle or N-Triples for semantic web tools.

Until now, GitLab Pages primarily resolved extensionless URLs to HTML files. That meant a request such as:

GET /alice
Accept: text/turtle

could still return an HTML document, even when a Turtle representation was available on disk.

This limitation made it difficult to publish semantic web content using clean, extensionless URLs.

The Problem

A project might contain several representations of the same resource:

public/resource.html
public/resource.rdf
public/resource.ttl
public/resource.jsonld

Different clients may prefer different representations.

A browser may request HTML:

Accept: text/html

A linked-data client may request RDF/XML:

Accept: application/rdf+xml

Another client may prefer Turtle:

Accept: text/turtle

Without content negotiation, all these requests resolve to the same default representation or fail to find the requested format.

The goal was to let GitLab Pages select the appropriate representation based on the client's HTTP Accept header, without requiring extensions in the URL.

Implementing Accept Header Negotiation

GitLab Pages now parses the HTTP Accept header and uses the client's preferences when resolving extensionless paths.

Supported formats include:

Media type Extension
application/rdf+xml .rdf
text/turtle .ttl
text/n3 .n3
application/n-triples .nt
application/ld+json .jsonld
application/rdf+xml .owl
text/html .html

Supporting quality values

HTTP content negotiation allows clients to express preferences using quality values (q).

For example:

Accept: text/turtle;q=0.9, application/rdf+xml;q=0.8

In this example, the Turtle representation is preferred over RDF/XML when both files exist.

The parser also considers media-type specificity:

Accept: text/turtle, text/*, */*

An exact media type takes precedence over a type wildcard, which takes precedence over the global wildcard.

This makes representation selection follow standard HTTP semantics instead of relying on a fixed extension preference.

Safe Fallback Behavior

Content negotiation is designed to preserve existing GitLab Pages behavior.

If the requested representation does not exist, GitLab Pages falls back to the HTML representation:

/resource.ttl  -> resource.ttl
/resource      -> resource.html

Direct requests containing an explicit extension continue to bypass negotiation.

The feature is also protected by a feature flag:

FF_ENABLE_CONTENT_NEGOTIATION

This allows the behavior to be enabled progressively without changing the default behavior for existing deployments.

Correct Caching with Vary

Different clients can receive different representations for the same URL. Shared caches must know that the response depends on the Accept header.

Negotiated responses therefore include:

Vary: Accept

This prevents a cached Turtle response from accidentally being served to a client requesting HTML.

The implementation also keeps variant-specific ETags distinct so that conditional requests do not incorrectly return 304 Not Modified for a different representation.

This is an important detail: content negotiation is not complete if the server selects the correct representation but caching does not distinguish between variants.

Better Acceptance Testing

The acceptance tests now use the repository's shared fixture convention instead of creating ZIP files at runtime.

The fixture contains:

shared/pages/group/content-negotiation/public/
├── resource.html
├── resource.rdf
├── resource.ttl
├── resource.jsonld
└── dir/
    ├── index.html
    └── index.ttl

The GitLab API stub registers the domain through the normal apiResponses map, matching the conventions used by the rest of the repository.

This makes the tests:

  • Easier to understand
  • More deterministic
  • Closer to real GitLab Pages behavior
  • Free from temporary archive servers
  • Safer because test assertions do not run inside background HTTP handlers

Using shared fixtures also makes it easier to extend the acceptance tests when additional representations or directory-index scenarios are introduced.

Validation

The implementation was validated with:

go test ./internal/serving/disk ./test/acceptance -short -count=1
go test ./... -short -count=1
go vet ./internal/serving/disk ./test/acceptance ./test/gitlabstub

All targeted tests and the short repository test suite passed.

Why This Matters

Content negotiation makes GitLab Pages more useful for projects that publish structured and linked data while preserving the familiar extensionless URL experience.

Authors can publish multiple representations:

/alice

And let clients request the format they understand:

Accept: text/html
Accept: text/turtle
Accept: application/ld+json

This brings standards-based representation selection to GitLab Pages without requiring application code, routing frameworks, or custom servers.

GitLab Pages remains static, simple, and fast — while becoming more capable for semantic web publishing.

References

  • Merge Request: gitlab-org/gitlab-pages!1384

title: Recover Pending Payments Without Making Customers Wait
description:
Moving provider status checks into background reconciliation while keeping transaction reads fast and current.

A transaction marked processing creates two competing needs. Customers want a fast transaction list, while the platform needs to check whether the external provider has reached a final state.

Calling the provider synchronously every time the customer opens the transaction screen couples product latency to an external network. A slow or unavailable provider can make the entire history page feel broken.

A better pattern is stale-while-revalidate for payment status.

The transaction endpoint returns the current local state immediately. If a processing transaction has not been checked recently, it schedules a background status task using a deterministic key such as:

status-check:{provider}:{provider_reference}:{check_window}

The worker queries the provider, records the observation, and applies a guarded state transition. The next app refresh or websocket update reflects the new state.

Define eligibility for polling

Do not check every transaction on every read. A status scheduler should consider the local state, provider, last check time, age, retry count, and next eligible check time.

Use shorter intervals for newly processing transactions and progressively back off. Stop polling terminal records. Move unusually old transactions into an exception queue rather than querying forever.

Separate query success from payment success

A provider can return HTTP 200 because the status query succeeded while the payment remains pending. Normalize the financial status from the correct payload field. Unknown values remain unknown; they must not become successful because the transport worked.

Store both the raw sanitized observation and normalized status. This gives operations evidence when mappings need correction.

Guard transitions and effects

Workers, webhooks, and staff actions may all update the same transaction. Lock the local record and use an explicit transition table. A late pending observation cannot move a completed transaction backward.

When the new state requires a credit, debit, release, or refund, protect that effect with a unique ledger reference. Status idempotency and financial idempotency are related but separate guarantees.

Provide operational controls

Staff needs actions to check one transaction, bulk-check eligible pending transactions, and request provider webhook replay when supported. These commands should queue work rather than keep the browser waiting.

Display last checked time, next check time, attempt count, latest provider state, and any operational error. Bulk actions should report queued, skipped, and ineligible counts.

Notify only on meaningful transitions

A repeated processing result should not notify the customer. Trigger messages after a committed transition into a meaningful state and deduplicate them by transition event identity.

Background status recovery makes the application responsive without abandoning eventual accuracy. The local transaction remains the fast read model; external status becomes asynchronously refreshed evidence.

Implementation checklist

Persist last_checked_at, next_check_at, attempt count, latest provider status, and the provider reference used for lookup. Make the queue task unique for a transaction and time window. Apply exponential backoff with a maximum age and move exhausted cases into a visible exception state.

Instrument provider latency, status changes per check, checks that return no result, terminal recovery rate, and the age of the oldest processing transaction. These metrics distinguish a slow provider from a broken worker or an incorrect status mapping.

title: osFoundry는 왜 Codex CLI에 변경을 푸시하지 않고 리소스마다 커서로 폴링하게 할까
description:
osFoundry MCP 서버에서 "뭔가 바뀌면 알고 싶은" 클라이언트가 쓸 수 있는 걸 이 Mac에서 토큰 없이 전부 두드려 봤다.

$ uv run --with tiktoken --with jsonschema python3 watch_sim.py
== Part 1: live wire, 8 calls each, ms ==
initialize                   HTTP 200  median  414.7  p90  757.8
tools/list                   HTTP 200  median  606.8  p90  716.7
resources/subscribe          HTTP 200  median  450.6  p90  550.2
GET (stream)                 HTTP 405  median  423.9  p90  475.4
tools/call poll (no token)   HTTP 401  median  322.0  p90  463.9
initialize capabilities: {"tools": {"listChanged": false}}
resources/subscribe -> {"code": -32601, "message": "Method not found"}
GET body -> ''
poll without token -> isError True | Authentication required
rate limit headers: limit 2000, reset in 61 s

푸시 경로는 세 개 다 닫혀 있다. initialize가 선언하는 건 tools뿐이고 그마저 listChanged: false라서, 툴 목록이 바뀌어도 알려 주지 않는다. resources/subscribe는 "Method not found"다. Streamable HTTP 서버라면 서버→클라이언트 스트림을 열어 줄 MCP URL로의 GET은 405를 돌려준다. 남는 건 읽기 전용 툴 하나뿐이다.

{"name": "poll_resource_events",
 "description": "Resume from an event sequence for one granted channel, Note, knowledge base, record, or session.",
 "inputSchema": {"properties": {
     "resource_type": {"enum": ["message_channel", "note", "knowledge_base", "record_channel", "room",
                                "gitnest_repository", "agent_session", "team_session", "loop_session",
                                "graph_session"]},
     "resource_id": {"type": "string"},
     "after_sequence": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 0},
     "limit": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 1, "maximum": 100}},
   "required": ["resource_type", "resource_id"], "additionalProperties": false},
 "annotations": {"readOnlyHint": true, "openWorldHint": false, "destructiveHint": false},
 "securitySchemes": [{"type": "oauth2", "scopes": ["osfoundry:read"]}]}

핵심은 "one granted"와 "resume from an event sequence" 두 표현이다. 이 글에서는 이 두 표현을 클라이언트 쪽을 Python으로 다시 만들어서 확인한다. 이 Mac에는 codex 바이너리가 없어서 클라이언트 역할은 스크립트가 했다. osFoundry 서버 코드는 공개돼 있지 않다. Part 1과 2는 라이브 서버고, Part 3은 재현이라 응답 모양과 활동 빈도는 재현 쪽에서 정한 값이다.

왜 푸시가 아니라 폴링일까, 특히 Codex라면

Codex CLI는 상주 프로세스가 아니다. 실행하면 돌고, 턴 하나를 처리하고, 끝나거나 사용자 입력을 기다린다. 푸시를 받으려면 세션과 세션 사이에도 누군가 귀를 열고 있어야 하는데, 노트북에선 대개 아무도 없다. 시퀀스 커서는 이런 생활 방식에 딱 맞는다. 클라이언트는 리소스마다 정수 하나만 들고 있다가, 내키는 때 돌아와서 그 뒤로 무슨 일이 있었는지 물으면 된다.

위의 ms 숫자는 일본에서 Apple M1으로 잰 거라 서버보다 경로 얘기에 가깝다. 더 중요한 건 레이트 리밋 헤더다. 인증 안 된 응답에 X-RateLimit-Limit: 2000이 붙고, 리셋은 61초쯤 뒤다. 로그인한 클라이언트도 같은 한도인지는 확인 안 했다. 그래도 리소스 30개를 30초마다 폴링해 봐야 분당 60요청이다. Codex로 변경을 지켜볼 때 발목을 잡는 건 서버 부하가 아니라 Codex 자신의 턴 수다. 폴링 한 번이 곧 모델이 툴을 부르고 결과를 읽는 한 턴이다.

폴링해도 되는 대상은 어떻게 찾을까

호출 두 개면 되고, 스키마만 봐도 설계 의도가 꽤 드러난다.

list_granted_resources   osfoundry:read  ro=True required=[] props=[]
list_project_resources   osfoundry:read  ro=True required=['project_id', 'resource_type'] props=['project_id', 'resource_type', 'search', 'offset', 'limit']
poll_resource_events     osfoundry:read  ro=True required=['resource_type', 'resource_id'] props=['resource_type', 'resource_id', 'after_sequence', 'limit']
59 tools on server; these three = 591 of 12662 tokens (4.7%, cl100k_base)
poll_resource_events types: 10 | list_project_resources types: 9 | only pollable: ['graph_session']

list_granted_resources는 인자를 하나도 안 받고, 억지로 넣으면 스키마가 튕긴다.

list_granted_resources   no arguments           ok
list_granted_resources   project_id passed      REJECT additionalProperties

클라이언트가 뭔가를 요청하는 툴이 아니라, 서버가 "네가 가진 건 이거다"라고 알려 주는 툴이다. initialize의 instructions도 "Use list_granted_resources first."로 시작한다. 돌아오는 건 연결에 추가된 프로젝트와 개별로 허용된 리소스다. 웹 클라이언트(ExternalAssistantsPanel.tsx)로 치면 Projects 영역과 "Older individual access" 영역이다.

list_project_resources는 resource_type이 필수다. "이 프로젝트 안에 있는 거 전부" 같은 목록은 없어서, 전체를 파악하려면 타입마다 한 번씩 아홉 번 불러야 한다. 한 타입에 50개가 넘으면(limit 최대 50, offset으로 페이지 넘김) 더 늘어난다. 설명문에는 프로젝트 단위 접근의 유일한 예외도 적혀 있다. "Ordinary Message channels require a separate invitation."

graph_session은 폴링은 되는데 목록에는 안 나온다. Graph는 오너의 데스크톱에 있고, 오너가 데스크톱 앱에서 공유한 다음에야 list_graph_sessions로 들어온다.

커서는 왜 서버가 아니라 클라이언트가 들고 있을까

osFoundry에는 두 방식이 다 있다. 에이전트 네트워크의 wait_for_messages는 커서를 서버가 들고 있어 준다. "Without after_sequence it resumes where your last call stopped"라고 돼 있고, timeout_s로 최대 50초까지 롱 폴링도 된다. poll_resource_events에는 둘 다 없다. timeout_s는 튕기고 설명엔 "resume from"뿐이니, 번호는 클라이언트가 챙겨 와야 한다.

wait_for_messages props: ['after_sequence', 'timeout_s', 'limit'] timeout_s max 50 | poll_resource_events has timeout: False
poll_resource_events     timeout_s 30           REJECT additionalProperties

서버가 커서를 들고 있으면 듣는 쪽이 하나일 땐 편하다. 그런데 연결 하나를 클라이언트 둘이 같이 쓰면 깨진다. 같은 로그인으로 터미널 두 개에서 Codex를 열면 딱 그 상황이다. 재현에서 채널 이벤트 600개를, 랜덤하게 번갈아 폴링하는 터미널 두 개에 흘려 봤다.

two terminals, client cursor: A saw 600/600, B saw 600/600
two terminals, server cursor: A saw 305/600, B saw 295/600

연결마다 서버가 커서를 하나 들고 있으면, 한쪽이 커서를 밀 때마다 다른 쪽은 그만큼 놓쳐서 각자 절반 정도만 본다. 요청에 after_sequence를 넣는 방식이면 둘 다 전부 보고, 서버는 읽는 쪽 상태를 하나도 안 들고 있어도 된다. 여러 툴이 제각각 읽어 가는 리소스 로그라면 커서 주인은 클라이언트가 맞다.

스키마상 after_sequence는 필수가 아니지만, 빼면 어떻게 되는지는 어디에도 안 적혀 있다. 거기 기대지 말자. 번호를 저장해 두고 매번 보내는 게 안전하다.

페이지가 꽉 차면 몇 번 불러야 할까

limit은 100이 끝이다. 대량 임포트 뒤라면 노트 하나에 이벤트가 수백 개 쌓여 있을 수 있다. 마지막 시퀀스부터 다시 부르고, 페이지가 꽉 차지 않은 채로 올 때까지 반복해서 비운다.

burst of 350 events, limit 100:  4 calls to drain, cursor ends at 350
burst of 350 events, limit  50:  7 calls to drain, cursor ends at 350
burst of 350 events, limit  20: 18 calls to drain, cursor ends at 350

100으로 부르면 된다. 재현에서 응답 크기는 빈 페이지가 17토큰, 이벤트 하나짜리가 41토큰이었다(cl100k_base). 모양은 재현 쪽 거지 osFoundry 게 아니지만, 자릿수 감은 충분하다. 빈 폴링은 읽는 비용이 싸고, 폴링 비용은 거의 턴 수로 정해진다.

리소스 30개를 얼마 간격으로 폴링해야 할까

재현에서는 프로젝트 하나에 목록으로 뽑을 수 있는 아홉 타입의 리소스 30개를 두고 활동량을 한쪽으로 몰았다. 바쁜 게 3개(분당 이벤트 1개), 적당한 게 7개(10분에 1개), 조용한 게 20개(2시간에 1개). 빈도는 가정이다. 8시간짜리 하루를 시드 5개로, 가상 시계 위에서 돌렸다.

every 30 s, all 30                 calls/hour   3600  empty  94.7%  seen late median   14.9 s  p90   27.0 s  max     30 s  (1843 events/day)
every 5 min, all 30                calls/hour    360  empty  78.0%  seen late median  150.9 s  p90  271.1 s  max    300 s  (1843 events/day)
30 s, x2 when empty, cap 10 min    calls/hour    502  empty  70.2%  seen late median   34.9 s  p90  206.4 s  max    599 s  (1843 events/day)
30 s, x2 when empty, cap 30 min    calls/hour    420  empty  65.3%  seen late median   35.6 s  p90  238.4 s  max   1799 s  (1843 events/day)
server window for comparison: 2000 requests per ~61 s

고정 30초는 빠르지만 95%가 헛방이다. 시간당 3,600번 부르고 거의 다 비어 있다. 고정 5분은 싸지만, 바쁜 채널까지 포함해서 전부 느리다. 리소스별 백오프(빈 폴링마다 그 리소스의 간격을 두 배로 늘리고, 이벤트가 오면 처음으로 되돌림)는 호출 수를 싼 쪽에 가깝게 맞추면서 지연 중앙값은 빠른 쪽에 가깝게 유지한다. 바쁜 리소스는 30초에 머물고 조용한 것만 멀어지기 때문이다. 대가는 상한값이다. 30분으로 두면 조용한 리소스의 첫 변경은 최대 30분까지 기다릴 수 있다.

Codex 입장에선 이 표가 오히려 타이머를 아예 안 돌릴 이유가 된다. 사람이 "뭐 바뀌었어?"라고 물을 때 저장해 둔 커서로 한 바퀴 돌면, 지켜보는 리소스 하나당 호출 한 번으로 그 시점까지의 변경을 지연 0으로 잡는다. 백오프 표는 Codex든 뭐든 계속 지켜보게 돌려 두는 스크립트를 위한 거다.

오너가 접근을 회수하면 어떻게 될까

오너가 4시간 07분 시점에 프로젝트를 뺐다고 하자. 커서 30개가 전부 이제 못 읽는 리소스를 가리킨다. 문제는 클라이언트가 그걸 언제까지 폴링하느냐다.

owner removes the project at 4 h 07 min (30 resources lose access):
  re-list grants every 10 min    failed polls after removal  180, list_granted_resources calls 25
  re-list grants every 60 min    failed polls after removal 3180, list_granted_resources calls 5
  re-list grants on first error  failed polls after removal    1, list_granted_resources calls 5

타이머로 그랜트를 다시 확인하면 호출이 늘거나, 실패하는 폴링을 수천 번 쌓거나 둘 중 하나다. 처음 거절당한 순간을 "그랜트 다시 읽기" 신호로 쓰면 실패 한 번과 list_granted_resources 호출 한 번이면 끝난다. 그다음 목록에서 사라진 리소스의 커서를 버리면 된다. 나중에 오너가 프로젝트를 다시 넣어 주면 그 리소스들은 처음부터 새로 시작한다.

스키마는 어디서 막을까

나머지 케이스도 라이브 inputSchema에 jsonschema(Draft 2020-12)로 돌려 봤다.

list_project_resources   no resource_type       REJECT required
list_project_resources   limit 50               ok
list_project_resources   limit 51               REJECT maximum: limit
list_project_resources   graph_session          REJECT enum: resource_type
list_project_resources   search 101 chars       REJECT maxLength: search
poll_resource_events     no after_sequence      ok
poll_resource_events     graph_session          ok
poll_resource_events     after_sequence -1      REJECT minimum: after_sequence
poll_resource_events     limit 100              ok
poll_resource_events     limit 101              REJECT maximum: limit
poll_resource_events     resource_type project  REJECT enum: resource_type

다들 제일 먼저 해 보는 게 resource_type: "project"다. 프로젝트는 로그를 가진 리소스가 아니라, 리소스를 보이게 해 주는 그랜트 단위다.

스크립트 전체는 M1에서 20.2초 걸렸고, 그중 대부분이 네트워크 호출 40번이었다. 유저 CPU 시간은 0.91초였다.

직접 만든다면

  • 로그는 리소스마다 하나로 두고, 커서는 클라이언트가 들게 한다. 연결 하나를 둘이 읽어도 이벤트를 뺏어 가지 않고, 서버는 읽는 쪽 상태를 저장할 필요가 없다.
  • 그랜트 목록은 인자 없는 전용 툴로 만들고, 클라이언트가 거기서 시작하게 한다. 찾을 수 있는 건 오너가 허용한 것뿐이어야 한다.
  • 페이지 크기에 상한을 두고, 다 비우는 법(마지막 시퀀스부터, 덜 찬 페이지가 올 때까지 다시 부르기)을 정해 둔다.
  • 백오프는 전역이 아니라 리소스별로. 바쁜 건 빠르게, 조용한 건 싸게.
  • 폴링이 처음 거절되면 그랜트를 다시 읽고, 사라진 커서는 재시도하지 말고 버린다.
  • 커서는 이벤트를 처리한 다음에 기록한다. 중간에 죽어도 건너뛰는 게 아니라 다시 읽게 된다.

연결마다 툴이 어떻게 정해지는지는 툴 스코프 페이지, 프로토콜의 짧은 정의는 MCP 용어 설명에 있다.

title: 🔥 How I’m Building an AI-Powered Bank Statement Analyzer with Python
description:
Hi everyone! 👋

I'm a Python developer with 12+ years of experience in backend engineering. Recently, I started building my own SaaS product called StatementIQ to simplify bank statement analysis using AI.

When I started working on this, I quickly realized that analyzing bank statements in production is much harder than just extracting raw text from a PDF.

The Real-World Engineering Challenges

Building a reliable parser means handling messy edge cases:

  • Inconsistent Formats: Every bank has a completely different layout, multi-line descriptions, and column structure.
  • Locked & Scanned Files: Handling password-protected PDFs alongside OCR fallbacks for scanned copies.
  • Transaction Categorization & Insights: Accurately identifying salaries, EMIs, recurring expenses, and cashflow patterns without hallucinating numbers.
  • Scale & Determinism: Processing large multi-page financial statements quickly while keeping the output strictly structured (JSON) and reliable.

Under the Hood (Tech Stack & Learnings)

My goal is to build a production-grade tool, not just another wrapper or demo project. Through this journey, I'm diving deep into:

  • Backend & Data Processing: Python (FastAPI/Django), PostgreSQL, and asynchronous task queues for handling heavy files.
  • AI & LLMs: Combining deterministic rule-based parsing with LLMs (including self-hosted models via Ollama) for fallback column mapping and categorization.

I'm actively improving the product and shipping new features step by step. You can check out the live project here: 👉 StatementIQ

I’d love to connect with fellow Python developers, AI engineers, and anyone building in the FinTech space!

Question for the community:

When building real-world AI applications on messy documents, what has been your biggest bottleneck—data quality, accuracy, or latency/performance?

Thanks for reading!

— Nitesh Kumar Singh (Portfolio)

title: Copiar una base NoSQL no es exportar JSON: lo que aprendimos haciendo backups de Firestore
description:
Autor: Carlos Jimenez Laura
Curso: Base de Datos II · Universidad Privada de Tacna
Actividad: Estrategias de copia de seguridad NoSQL, desarrollada junto con Arturo Cutipa Flores
En PostgreSQL ejecutas pg_dump y obtienes un archivo que recrea la base. En Firestore, con el plan gratuito, no existe un equivalente: la exportación administrada exige un plan de pago y un bucket de Cloud Storage. La idea obvia es leer todos los documentos y guardarlos como JSON, y esa copia parece correcta hasta que intentas restaurarla.
En este artículo cuento qué se pierde con esa idea y cómo lo resolvimos en StockSeguro, un inventario con copias automáticas, cifradas y comprobadas.

Enlaces del proyecto
• Aplicación: https://stockseguro-firestore.onrender.com
• Repositorio público: https://github.com/CRJL19/firestore-backups
• Video: https://youtu.be/56mY6DRLr8U

Figura 1. StockSeguro con el panel de copias de seguridad.

Las opciones que teníamos

Elegimos la copia lógica porque era lo posible con nuestro presupuesto, no porque sea la mejor en general. Para una base grande en producción, recomendaría la nativa.

Cuatro formas de perder datos sin enterarte

1. JSON no conoce los tipos de Firestore
Un documento nuestro tiene un Timestamp, un GeoPoint y una referencia a su proveedor. JSON.stringify los convierte en objetos corrientes, y al restaurar ya no son esos tipos. La referencia deja de ser una referencia y ninguna consulta por fecha vuelve a funcionar.

Por eso cada tipo especial se guarda con una etiqueta:

Y hay una decisión deliberada al final de esa función: un tipo desconocido lanza un error. Prefiero que falle la copia a que parezca correcta y le falten datos.

2. Las subcolecciones no vienen con su padre
Leer products no trae products/{id}/movements. Hay que recorrerlas. Y hay un caso peor: una subcolección puede colgar de un documento que ya no existe. Firestore lo llama documento fantasma, y un collection.get() no lo devuelve, así que sus hijos quedarían fuera.
listDocuments() sí los incluye:

Una de nuestras pruebas crea justo ese caso, borra todo, restaura y comprueba que el hijo volvió.

3. Una copia que tarda no es una foto
Si la app sigue escribiendo mientras copias, puedes guardar un producto de hace un minuto con los movimientos de ahora. Resolvimos esto leyendo los documentos dentro de una transacción de solo lectura, de modo que todo corresponde a un mismo instante:

4. Un borrado no deja rastro
La copia incremental lee lo que cambió según updatedAt, pero un documento borrado ya no tiene ese campo: simplemente deja de existir, y la consulta no puede verlo. Sin más, al restaurar reaparecerían productos eliminados.
Por eso la app deja una marca en la misma operación que borra:

La estrategia completa
• Copia completa cada 7 días, que corrige cualquier desviación acumulada.
• Copia incremental diaria, que gasta menos cuota porque lee menos documentos.
• Restauración selectiva: --only products/abc123 recupera un producto y sus movimientos sin tocar el resto.
• Cifrado AES-256-GCM, necesario porque los artifacts de un repositorio público se pueden descargar con cualquier cuenta de GitHub.
• Objetivo de pérdida (RPO): 24 horas. El panel de la app avisa si la última copia supera las 26.
Restaurar una incremental significa aplicar la cadena en orden: la completa y luego cada incremental. Dentro de cada copia, los borrados se aplican antes que los documentos, porque un documento presente en una copia existía al hacerla, aunque se hubiera borrado y creado de nuevo.

El problema que no se resuelve del todo
La copia incremental depende de un contrato: todo se escribe a través de la app, con updatedAt y sus marcas de borrado. Alguien que borre un documento desde la consola de Firebase lo rompe, y la incremental no se entera.
No pudimos evitarlo, pero sí detectarlo. Cada copia guarda los conteos reales del origen con consultas de agregación, que son baratas. Si al restaurar los números no coinciden, la verificación falla:
products: la copia dice 1 y la restauración tiene 2
Una prueba automática reproduce ese caso. La solución entonces es una copia completa. Queda un hueco que prefiero admitir: una modificación externa que no cambie los conteos solo se recoge en la siguiente completa.

Cómo se publica y se automatiza
El código está en un repositorio público de GitHub, y todo se ejecuta con GitHub Actions:
• Cada git push ejecuta las 39 pruebas contra el emulador de Firestore, construye la imagen Docker y despliega en Render, un proveedor público en la nube.
• Cada día, a las 03:00 hora de Perú, un workflow hace la copia, la restaura en un emulador y solo si coincide la guarda.
Las copias se hacen con una cuenta de servicio de solo lectura, y la base está en Firestore, sobre Google Cloud.

Resultados
En producción, con Firestore real, la primera copia completa dio esto:

Figura 2. Resumen de la copia verificada en GitHub Actions.

Después dejamos el workflow funcionando solo. Del 2 al 12 de noviembre se ejecutó todos los días y guardó 12 copias, todas verificadas antes de guardarse: 2 completas, la segunda creada automáticamente al cumplirse los 7 días, y 10 incrementales. Cada incremental cifrada pesa unos 650 bytes, frente a 1,8 KB de una completa.
El simulacro de desastre lo hicimos en el emulador local, con los mismos comandos que usa GitHub Actions: una copia completa, un cambio de stock y un borrado, una incremental, la base vaciada y la restauración de la cadena. Volvieron los 25 documentos esperados en 237 ms, con el stock actualizado y sin el producto eliminado. En producción, la restauración existe como un workflow manual, pero no la ejecutamos para esta demostración.
Un dato que me sorprendió: esa incremental, hecha segundos después de la completa, copió 26 registros frente a 27. No es un error. Cada incremental relee los últimos 5 minutos por seguridad, porque copiar de más es inofensivo y copiar de menos no lo es. El ahorro aparece cuando las copias están separadas por horas.

Limitaciones
• Dos ubicaciones, no tres. Hay datos en Firestore y copias en GitHub. La regla 3-2-1 pediría una tercera.
• Enteros y decimales. El SDK de JavaScript no distingue 1 de 1.0. Tampoco se conservan createTime ni updateTime, que asigna el servidor.
• Memoria. Cada copia se procesa completa en memoria, adecuado para miles de documentos, no para millones.
• La clave de cifrado. Si se pierde, las copias no sirven de nada, así que hay que guardarla también fuera de GitHub.

Qué me llevo
En una base relacional el esquema y la herramienta de volcado resuelven casi todo por ti. En NoSQL, el esquema vive en la aplicación, y por eso la estrategia de copia también: tuvimos que cambiar cómo borra la app para poder copiar bien.
Lo otro que me llevo es desconfiar de una copia hasta verla restaurada. Mi compañero Arturo cuenta en su artículo cómo automatizamos esa comprobación.

title: Cuando la comunidad se encuentra, la tecnología deja huella: así se vivió el AWS Student Community Day 2026 en el IPN, CDMX.
description:
El 4 de noviembre se celebró el segundo AWS Student Community Day en México, esta vez con sede en el IPN, en Ciudad de México. Organizado por comunidades de estudiantes de AWS, el encuentro reunió a personas de escuelas de distintos puntos del país. Ver llegar camiones desde Oaxaca, Hidalgo y el Estado de México fue una buena manera de entender el tamaño de lo que habían conseguido.

Para una comunidad que apenas comienza a abrirse camino en el mundo de la tecnología, organizar un evento de esta magnitud no es poca cosa. Y, sin embargo, ahí estaban: convirtiendo las ganas de aprender y compartir en un encuentro para recordar. Si quieres conocer más sobre el evento, puedes visitar su sitio oficial.

Una comunidad joven, muchas ganas de participar

La comunidad de AWS User Group Ciudad de México fue invitada como comunidad aliada. Además, los tres organizadores tuvimos la oportunidad de participar, ya fuera dando una charla o apoyando en distintas actividades.

Para nosotros fue especialmente emocionante: la comunidad apenas iba por su quinto mes de actividad y ya estábamos compartiendo espacio con estudiantes y comunidades de todo México. Nada mal para un grupo que todavía está dando sus primeros pasos.

De las historias familiares a Amazon KDP

Vania Lockheart fue una de las primeras personas en participar por parte de nuestra comunidad. En su charla compartió la travesía creativa de escribir un libro familiar: desde tomar una cámara y comenzar a grabar historias hasta utilizar AWS para crear los escritos.

También contó cómo trabajó las correcciones con el equipo editor, los ajustes a los manuscritos, el diseño de la portada y, finalmente, la publicación en Amazon KDP. Un recorrido paso a paso que mostró todo el trabajo que hay detrás de convertir una historia familiar en un libro.

El poder de un sticker

Después llegó el momento de dar a conocer la comunidad. Sacamos el primer sticker y, como si alguien hubiera dado una señal secreta, los asistentes comenzaron a hacer fila para llevarse llaveros y calcomanías.

El swag no duró ni treinta minutos. Nos tomó por sorpresa: sabíamos que los regalos suelen ser populares, pero no esperábamos que desaparecieran con tanta rapidez.


Más tarde estuvimos en el booth oficial de AWS entregando material a los asistentes y contando qué hacemos en el user group. El material que se había apartado también empezó a irse rápidamente, mientras más personas conocían nuestra comunidad.

Edwin y Vania se encargaron de compartir información en el booth, mientras John daba asesorías en un taller de Claude Code. John, una disculpa: no tengo fotos tuyas dando asesorías, pero tu participación también merece quedar en esta historia.

Aprender AWS, paso a paso

Ya casi al final del día, Edwin impartió un taller sobre construcción de métricas con servicios serverless, un tema que le apasiona. Explicó con detalle qué se hacía en cada paso, cómo se activaba cada servicio y por qué estaba ahí.

Se sintió como una clase para comenzar con AWS desde cero y llegar a construir un primer proyecto de métricas. Y, por la reacción de los asistentes, fue una experiencia que disfrutaron mucho.

Nos vemos en el siguiente

Así vivimos el AWS Student Community Day desde la comunidad de AWS User Group Ciudad de México: compartiendo conocimientos, conociendo a quienes están comenzando y descubriendo que incluso una comunidad joven puede encontrar muchas formas de aportar.

Esperamos seguir participando en encuentros como este, ya sea apoyando las actividades o compartiendo lo que sabemos. Al final, las comunidades crecen precisamente así: cuando alguien se anima a construir algo y los demás deciden sumarse.

title: How to Scrape Goodreads with Node.js: Book Search, Rating Distributions, Reviews, Author Lists, and a Ratings Tracker (2026)
description:
Goodreads is still where most readers log what they read, so it's where the numbers are: how many people rated a book, how those ratings split across one to five stars, what the most-liked reviews say, and which of an author's books carry their reputation. If you build a reading app, do comp titles for a publisher, or just want to know whether a book you're about to pitch is growing, you'll want that data in a script.

Then you search for "Goodreads API" and find out it's gone. This post covers what's left officially, what goodreads.com hands a plain script today, and then builds goodreads.mjs, one Node.js file with no npm dependencies (built-in fetch and node:sqlite, so Node 22.13+). It has six commands:

  1. probe checks what goodreads.com returns to a script and reads the data embedded in a book page
  2. search finds books by title or ISBN
  3. book prints details and the full one-to-five-star rating distribution
  4. reviews pages through community reviews with a cursor and summarizes them
  5. author lists an author's books and shows how concentrated their ratings are
  6. track stores rating snapshots in SQLite and reports new ratings per day between runs

Every command was run on November 13, 2026 on a rented Linux VM (Node 24.22.1), and each output block below is pasted unedited from that session.

Read this first. Goodreads' Terms of Use forbid this kind of collection. Section 1 ("Use of Our Service") of the terms at goodreads.com/about/terms (last revised April 28, 2021) says your license to use the site does not include "any collection and use of any book listings, descriptions, reviews or other material included in the Service" or "any use of data mining, robots, or similar data gathering and extraction tools." So scraping Goodreads is against its terms, whoever does the fetching. Read the terms yourself and think about the legal risk for your use case before you run anything here, and use the official options below wherever they cover what you need. Reviews are also personal writing by real people: don't republish them, and keep only what you need.

Is there still a Goodreads API?

Not for new projects. In December 2020 Goodreads stopped issuing new developer keys and said it planned to retire the public API. Today goodreads.com/api just redirects to the homepage (you'll see the 302 in Step 1). Old keys you may find in blog posts and GitHub repos don't help a new project.

What you can still use without scraping:

  • Your own library export. Under My Books, "Import and export" gives you a CSV of your own shelves, ratings, and review dates. If you only need your own reading data, stop here.
  • Open Library. The Internet Archive's Open Library API is open and has ISBN, work, and author lookups. It has ratings too, but far fewer: on November 13 it had about 200 ratings for Project Hail Mary, versus about 1.94 million on Goodreads.

If you need Goodreads' own ratings, distributions, or reviews, there's no official route left. That's what the rest of this post is about.

Step 1: See what goodreads.com sends a script

Book pages are a Next.js app. The HTML contains a <script id="__NEXT_DATA__"> tag with the page's Apollo GraphQL cache, so you don't need to parse markup. The cache holds Book:..., Work:..., Review:..., and User:... entries. The rating statistics live on the work (all editions together), not on the edition you asked for.

#!/usr/bin/env node
// goodreads.mjs - Goodreads book, review, and author data in Node.js (22.13+), no npm dependencies.
// Usage: node goodreads.mjs <probe|search|book|reviews|author|track> ...
import { DatabaseSync } from "node:sqlite";
import { writeFileSync } from "node:fs";

const KEY = process.env.SCRAPEATLAS_API_KEY ?? "";
const API = "https://api.scrapeatlas.com/v1/goodreads";
const UA = "Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/130.0 Safari/537.36";
const sleep = (ms) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms));

async function get(url, headers = {}) {
  const r = await fetch(url, { headers, redirect: "manual", signal: AbortSignal.timeout(30_000) });
  return { status: r.status, location: r.headers.get("location"), text: await r.text() };
}

function nextData(html) {
  const m = html.match(/<script id="__NEXT_DATA__" type="application\/json">(.*?)<\/script>/s);
  if (!m) throw new Error("no __NEXT_DATA__ on the page (layout changed or you got a block page)");
  return JSON.parse(m[1]).props.pageProps.apolloState;
}

function bookFromApollo(state) {
  const values = Object.entries(state);
  const book = values.find(([k, v]) => k.startsWith("Book:") && v.title)?.[1];
  const work = values.find(([k]) => k.startsWith("Work:"))?.[1];
  const reviews = values.filter(([k]) => k.startsWith("Review:")).map(([, v]) => v);
  return {
    title: book.title,
    isbn13: book.details?.isbn13,
    pages: book.details?.numPages,
    genres: (book.bookGenres ?? []).map((g) => g.genre.name),
    averageRating: work.stats.averageRating,
    ratingsCount: work.stats.ratingsCount,
    ratingsCountDist: work.stats.ratingsCountDist, // [1-star, 2-star, 3-star, 4-star, 5-star]
    textReviewsCount: work.stats.textReviewsCount,
    embeddedReviews: reviews.length,
  };
}

async function probe(bookId) {
  const page = `https://www.goodreads.com/book/show/${bookId}`;
  let real;
  for (const ua of ["curl/8.5.0", "", null, UA]) {
    const res = await get(page, ua === null ? {} : { "user-agent": ua, "accept-language": "en-US,en;q=0.9" });
    const label = ua === null ? "Node default UA" : ua === "" ? "empty UA" : ua.slice(0, 15);
    console.log(`GET /book/show/${bookId} [${label.padEnd(15)}] -> ${res.status}, ${res.text.length} bytes`);
    if (ua === UA) real = res;
  }
  const b = bookFromApollo(nextData(real.text));
  console.log(`  __NEXT_DATA__: "${b.title}" avg ${b.averageRating}, ${b.ratingsCount} ratings, dist ${JSON.stringify(b.ratingsCountDist)}`);
  console.log(`  genres: ${b.genres.slice(0, 5).join(", ")} | ${b.textReviewsCount} text reviews, ${b.embeddedReviews} embedded in the HTML`);
  const more = real.text.match(/\/book\/show\/\d+\/reviews\?reviewFilters=[^"]+/);
  console.log(`  "more reviews" link: ${more ? more[0].slice(0, 60) + "..." : "none"}`);
  const ac = await get(`https://www.goodreads.com/book/auto_complete?format=json&q=${encodeURIComponent(b.title)}`, { "user-agent": UA });
  const hits = JSON.parse(ac.text);

  console.log(`GET /api                                     -> ${api.status} ${api.location ?? ""}`);
}

Step 2: A small API client

Reading the book page yourself works for a single book's stats. Paging through reviews means reverse-engineering the reviewFilters cursor that robots.txt asks crawlers to stay away from, and search results and author lists are more page types to parse, each of which can break on its own. So from here on, the script reads Goodreads through ScrapeAtlas*. Its OpenAPI spec lists five Goodreads routes: /v1/goodreads/search, /book, /book-reviews, /author, and /author-books. You call them with GET and pass your key in the x-api-key header. Each successful call, partial results included, costs 1 credit. Failed calls are free. Using an API doesn't change the terms: Goodreads' rules still apply to the data, whoever fetches it.

async function sa(path, params) {
  if (!KEY) throw new Error("Set SCRAPEATLAS_API_KEY first.");
  const qs = new URLSearchParams(Object.entries(params).filter(([, v]) => v != null && v !== ""));
  for (let attempt = 1; ; attempt++) {
    const r = await fetch(`${API}/${path}?${qs}`, { headers: { "x-api-key": KEY }, signal: AbortSignal.timeout(120_000) });
    const body = await r.json().catch(() => ({}));
    if (r.ok && body.success !== false) return body;
    const code = body.failure?.code ?? `http_${r.status}`;
    const retry = r.status === 429 || r.status >= 500;
    if (!retry || attempt === 3) {
      const err = new Error(`${path}: ${code} - ${body.failure?.message ?? r.statusText}`);
      err.code = code;
      throw err;
    }
    await sleep(2000 * attempt);
  }
}

// Accepts 54493401, "54493401-project-hail-mary", or a full goodreads.com URL.
function idOf(x) {
  const m = String(x).match(/(?:show\/)?(\d+)/);
  if (!m) throw new Error(`not a Goodreads id or URL: ${x}`);
  return m[1];
}

sa() retries 429 and 5xx up to three times and throws errors that carry the API's failure.code (for example not_found), so the commands can tell a missing book from a network problem. idOf() takes 54493401, 54493401-project-hail-mary, or a full book or author URL.

Step 4: Book details and the rating distribution

The average rating hides most of the story. Two books with a 4.2 can look completely different: one where nearly everyone gave 4 stars, and one that splits between 5 and 1. The distribution shows which one you have.

function ratingStats(dist) {
  const counts = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5].map((s) => dist[s] ?? 0);
  const total = counts.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
  const mean = counts.reduce((a, c, i) => a + c * (i + 1), 0) / total;
  const share = (stars) => stars.reduce((a, s) => a + counts[s - 1], 0) / total;
  return { counts, total, mean, five: share([5]), low: share([1, 2]) };
}

function bar(n, max, width = 30) {
  return "#".repeat(Math.round((n / max) * width));
}

async function book(ref) {
  const { book: b } = await sa("book", { id: idOf(ref) });
  const st = ratingStats(b.ratingsDistribution);
  const max = Math.max(...st.counts);
  console.log(`${b.title} - ${b.authors.map((a) => a.name).join(", ")} (${b.work?.firstPublishedAt?.slice(0, 4) ?? "?"})`);
  console.log(`  ${b.format ?? "?"}, ${b.pages ?? "?"} pages, ISBN13 ${b.isbn13 ?? "-"}, ${b.publisher ?? "-"}`);
  console.log(`  avg ${b.averageRating} from ${b.ratingsCount} ratings (mean of distribution: ${st.mean.toFixed(3)}), ${b.reviewsCount} text reviews`);
  for (let s = 5; s >= 1; s--) {
    const n = st.counts[s - 1];
    console.log(`  ${s}* ${String(n).padStart(9)} ${(100 * n / st.total).toFixed(1).padStart(5)}%  ${bar(n, max)}`);
  }
  console.log(`  5-star share ${(100 * st.five).toFixed(1)}%, 1-2 star share ${(100 * st.low).toFixed(1)}%`);
  console.log(`  genres: ${b.genres.slice(0, 6).map((g) => g.name).join(", ")}`);
  const wins = (b.awards ?? []).filter((a) => a.designation === "WINNER");
  if (b.awards?.length) console.log(`  awards: ${b.awards.length} listed, ${wins.length} wins (${wins.slice(0, 3).map((a) => a.name).join(", ")})`);
  if (b.series?.length) console.log(`  series: ${b.series.map((s) => s.position ? `${s.title} #${s.position}` : `${s.title} (no position given)`).join(", ")}`);
  return b;
}

Step 5: Reviews with cursor pagination

/v1/goodreads/book-reviews returns 30 reviews per page and a nextCursor. Pass it back as cursor to get the next page. The function below stops when there's no cursor or a page brings nothing new, deduplicates by review ID, and can write everything to JSONL.

async function reviews(ref, pages = 3, out = null) {
  const id = idOf(ref);
  const seen = new Map();
  let cursor = null;
  let total = null;
  for (let p = 1; p <= pages; p++) {
    const res = await sa("book-reviews", { id, cursor });
    total = res.totalCount;
    let fresh = 0;
    for (const r of res.reviews) if (!seen.has(r.id)) { seen.set(r.id, r); fresh++; }
    console.log(`page ${p}: ${res.reviews.length} reviews (${fresh} new), totalCount ${res.totalCount}`);
    cursor = res.nextCursor;
    if (!cursor || fresh === 0) break;
    await sleep(500);
  }
  const all = [...seen.values()];
  if (out) writeFileSync(out, all.map((r) => JSON.stringify(r)).join("\n") + "\n");
  summarizeReviews(all, total);
  if (out) console.log(`saved ${all.length} reviews to ${out}`);
  return all;
}

function summarizeReviews(all, total) {
  const byStar = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5].map((s) => all.filter((r) => r.rating === s).length);
  const words = all.map((r) => (r.text ?? "").split(/\s+/).filter(Boolean).length).sort((a, b) => a - b);
  const median = words[Math.floor(words.length / 2)] ?? 0;
  console.log(`\n${all.length} unique reviews of ~${total}; stars 5..1: ${byStar.slice(1).reverse().join(" / ")}; unrated: ${byStar[0]}`);
  console.log(`median length ${median} words; spoiler-flagged ${all.filter((r) => r.spoiler).length}; written by Goodreads authors ${all.filter((r) => r.reviewer?.isAuthor).length}`);
  const years = {};
  for (const r of all) years[r.createdAt.slice(0, 4)] = (years[r.createdAt.slice(0, 4)] ?? 0) + 1;
  console.log(`created per year: ${Object.entries(years).sort().map(([y, n]) => `${y}:${n}`).join(" ")}`);
  console.log("most-liked:");
  for (const r of [...all].sort((a, b) => b.likeCount - a.likeCount).slice(0, 3)) {
    console.log(`  ${r.rating}* ${String(r.likeCount).padStart(6)} likes  ${r.reviewer.name.slice(0, 28)}: "${(r.text ?? "").replace(/\s+/g, " ").slice(0, 70)}..."`);
  }
}

Two things here will mislead you if you don't know them:

  • The order isn't random. Reviews come in Goodreads' default order, which puts popular, much-liked reviews first. In these 120, 14 of the 116 star-rated reviews are 1 or 2 stars (12%).   • totalCount moves around. It came back as 265185 and 265252 on different pages of the same run, and the book's reviewsCount was 265795. Treat it as an estimate.

Also: rating is 0 when someone wrote a review without picking stars (4 here). Each review has both text and textHtml, and the HTML can contain images and quotes. reviewer.isAuthor marks Goodreads author accounts, which is useful if you want to separate fellow writers from regular readers. Two reviews are from 2020, before the book came out in May 2021. Those are most likely advance-copy readers.

Step 7: A ratings tracker in SQLite

A single snapshot can't tell you whether a book is gaining readers. Two snapshots can. track stores the totals and all five buckets for each book, then compares the newest snapshot with the previous one.

function openDb(file) {
  const db = new DatabaseSync(file);
  db.exec(`CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS snapshot (
    book_id INTEGER, taken_at TEXT, title TEXT, avg REAL, ratings INTEGER, reviews INTEGER,
    s1 INTEGER, s2 INTEGER, s3 INTEGER, s4 INTEGER, s5 INTEGER,
    PRIMARY KEY (book_id, taken_at))`);
  return db;
}

async function track(refs, dbFile = "goodreads.db") {
  const db = openDb(dbFile);
  const prevStmt = db.prepare("SELECT * FROM snapshot WHERE book_id = ? ORDER BY taken_at DESC LIMIT 1");
  const insert = db.prepare("INSERT INTO snapshot VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)");
  const now = new Date().toISOString();
  for (const ref of refs) {
    let b;
    try {
      ({ book: b } = await sa("book", { id: idOf(ref) }));
    } catch (e) {
      console.log(`${ref}: skipped (${e.code ?? e.message})`);
      continue;
    }
    const d = b.ratingsDistribution;
    const prev = prevStmt.get(b.id);
    insert.run(b.id, now, b.title, b.averageRating, b.ratingsCount, b.reviewsCount, d[1], d[2], d[3], d[4], d[5]);
    if (!prev) {
      console.log(`${b.title.slice(0, 34).padEnd(34)} first snapshot: ${b.ratingsCount} ratings, avg ${b.averageRating}`);
      continue;
    }
    const hours = (Date.parse(now) - Date.parse(prev.taken_at)) / 3.6e6;
    const added = b.ratingsCount - prev.ratings;
    const deltas = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5].map((s) => d[s] - prev[`s${s}`]);
    console.log(`${b.title.slice(0, 34).padEnd(34)} +${added} ratings in ${hours.toFixed(1)}h (${(added / hours * 24).toFixed(0)}/day), +${b.reviewsCount - prev.reviews} reviews, avg ${prev.avg} -> ${b.averageRating}`);
    console.log(`${"".padEnd(34)} new ratings by star 5..1: ${deltas.slice().reverse().map((x) => (x >= 0 ? "+" : "") + x).join(" / ")}`);
  }
}

That's a useful result, because it shows a trap. Project Hail Mary and Sunrise on the Reaping didn't move at all in half an hour. That's almost certainly not because nobody rated them. Goodreads refreshes these counters in batches: between 04:01 and 04:04 UTC that morning, Project Hail Mary jumped from 1,938,620 to 1,938,684 ratings, then stayed exactly there for over half an hour, and the book page itself (fetched directly at 04:36 UTC) showed the same frozen number. The Martian happened to get a refresh in between, so its "768/day" is just 15 ratings extrapolated from a 28-minute window.

So don't run the tracker every few minutes. Run it once a day at the same time, and look at trends over a week or more. The per-star deltas are where it gets interesting over time: if a book's new ratings start landing in the 1- and 2-star buckets while the average still reads 4.4, the average is being held up by old ratings.

To run it every day, a cron line is enough:

15 6 * * * cd /opt/goodreads && SCRAPEATLAS_API_KEY=... node goodreads.mjs track 54493401 214331246 18007564 >> track.log 2>&1

Each track run costs one credit per book. The database is a single snapshot table, so SELECT taken_at, ratings, s5, s1 FROM snapshot WHERE book_id = 54493401 gives you a chart-ready series.

The CLI 

const [cmd, ...args] = process.argv.slice(2);
const flag = (name, def) => {
  const i = args.indexOf(`--${name}`);
  if (i === -1) return def;
  const v = args[i + 1];
  args.splice(i, 2);
  return v;
};

try {
  if (cmd === "probe") await probe(idOf(args[0] ?? "54493401"));
  else if (cmd === "search") { const page = Number(flag("page", 1)); await search(args.join(" "), page); }
  else if (cmd === "book") for (const a of args) { await book(a); console.log(); }
  else if (cmd === "reviews") { const pages = Number(flag("pages", 3)); const out = flag("out", null); await reviews(args[0], pages, out); }
  else if (cmd === "author") { const pages = Number(flag("pages", 2)); await author(args[0], pages); }
  else if (cmd === "track") { const db = flag("db", "goodreads.db"); await track(args, db); }
  else console.log("usage: node goodreads.mjs <probe|search|book|reviews|author|track> ...");
} catch (e) {
  console.error(`error: ${e.message}`);
  process.exitCode = 1;
}

Gotchas I hit, collected

  • The official API is gone. /api redirects to the homepage. Old tutorials with key= URLs won't help.
  • Check the body, not the status. Empty UA → 403. Everything else gave a mix of 200, 202, and 503 within minutes, from the same IP.
  • Only 30 reviews per book page. More need the reviewFilters cursor, which robots.txt disallows.
  • Stats belong to the work. All editions share them. Key on work.id.
  • Title search returns summary spam. Search by ISBN, or check the author and ratingsCount.
  • Counts differ between surfaces. Search, book page, and author list can be a dozen or so ratings apart at the same moment.
  • Review order is popularity, not a sample. Low-star reviews are over-represented among the most-liked.
  • rating: 0 means no stars, not a zero-star review.
  • series[].position can be null, and publishedYear is often null for editions and box sets.
  • Bibliographies include anthologies and forewords. Filter on the first author's ID.

Wrapping up

  • There's no Goodreads API for new projects. Your own CSV export and Open Library cover some needs.
  • Book pages embed a full Apollo cache with rating distributions, genres, awards, and 30 reviews, but the site answers a script inconsistently.
  • The five-bucket distribution says more than the average does, and it lets you check your parsing.
  • Reviews show what's popular, not what's typical. Don't estimate sentiment from the first pages.
  • Two SQLite snapshots are enough to measure new ratings per day and which star buckets they land in.

What do you use Goodreads data for: reading apps, comp titles, or something else? I'd like to hear how you deal with the summary-book spam in search.

*I build it.

title: image.to.design + Design Shapes: The Deadly Combination Every Figma Designer Needs
description:
Most designers treat their Figma plugin stack as either/or. You pick a screenshot importer, or you pick a UI reconstructor. What almost no one realizes is that the two most talked-about tools in this space — image.to.design and Design Shapes — do completely different things. Used together, they cover the entire design pipeline with zero overlap.

This is the combination that changes how fast you work.

What image.to.design actually does

image.to.design by divRIOTS is a raw asset importer. You give it a URL, a screenshot, or a PDF, and it brings the visual content into Figma as-is — bitmap images, extracted colors, fonts where it can identify them. It is excellent at what it does: getting visual material off the web and into your canvas fast.

What it does not do is reconstruct the UI. The imported result is a flat image or a loose collection of elements. There are no auto-layout groups, no component structure, no SVG icons — just the pixels, organized roughly.

That is not a criticism. That is by design. image.to.design is an asset pipeline tool, not a UI analysis tool.

What Design Shapes actually does

Design Shapes (by Crafttor) works from the other end. You give it a screenshot of a UI — a mobile app, a web page, a dashboard — and it uses AI to reconstruct the interface as editable Figma layers. It identifies interface elements, matches icons to Lucide SVG vectors, groups rows and columns with real auto-layout, and extracts the color palette as Figma Variables bound to every fill.

The output is not a flat image. It is a working layer tree: named frames, text nodes, matched SVG icons, and design tokens — ready to edit.

What Design Shapes does not do is import arbitrary web content, PDFs, or raw brand assets. It is purpose-built for UI reconstruction, not asset harvesting.

The gap between them is exactly zero

This is what makes the combination unusual: the tools do not compete. They do not even touch the same part of the workflow.

image.to.design fills your canvas with raw material. Design Shapes turns UI screenshots into editable structure. One ends where the other begins.

The four-step workflow

Step 1 — Grab assets with image.to.design. Paste the competitor's URL or drop in a PDF brand deck. Import logos, illustrations, and reference images straight into Figma as raw material.

Step 2 — Screenshot the UI you want to reconstruct. Capture the mobile app, landing page, or dashboard you need to work from — your own or a reference.

Step 3 — Run Design Shapes on the screenshot. In one click, the flat screenshot becomes a structured layer tree with auto-layout groups, Lucide SVG icons, and color tokens extracted as Figma Variables.

Step 4 — Combine on canvas. Drag your imported assets alongside the reconstructed UI. You have both: the raw brand material and the editable structure, in the same file.

Who this workflow is built for

Competitive analysis — Import a competitor's site with image.to.design, then reconstruct their app UI with Design Shapes. You get their brand assets and their interface architecture in a single Figma file, fully editable.

Client presentations — Grab a client's existing PDF or web presence with image.to.design, reconstruct their current app UI with Design Shapes, and have a redesign-ready file inside an hour.

Design handoff — Use image.to.design for marketing assets and illustrations, Design Shapes for the UI components that engineers will implement. Everything in one file, everything structured.

The credit math

image.to.design has its own pricing. Design Shapes starts free — 5 credits when you sign up, plus a daily free credit that expires at midnight. Paid plans start at $9 for 60 credits.

For most projects, the full four-step workflow above costs one Design Shapes credit. Neither tool charges you for the other's work.

Start with the free tier

Design Shapes gives you enough free credits to run the full workflow on your first real project before you spend anything. Install it from the Figma plugin page, run it on a screenshot you already have, and see the layer tree it produces.

Then stack it with image.to.design and you have the full pipeline.

title: I ranked 7 Android cloud services by one question: will the device still be the same device in three months?
description:
Disclosure first: I work with DuoPlus, on the growth side. So yes, it's on this list, and yes, it's near the top. I'll tell you where it falls short too, and I checked every other product's claims against its own website this week instead of going from memory.

Why this list exists: most cloud phone and device cloud roundups rank by "how many devices" or "how cheap." That's not what breaks for the teams I talk to. They're small QA shops, two-person dev teams, agencies looking after a dozen client apps. The question that actually costs them time is boring: when I open this Android environment next month, is it still logged in, still configured, still mine? Or am I starting from zero again?

So that's the ranking criterion. Fit for small dev/QA teams and agencies that need stable, isolated Android environments that last. Not gaming, and not one-off test runs (though some tools below are great at those).

1. DuoPlus

https://www.duoplus.net/share/market

DuoPlus gives you real ARM Android cloud phones, on Android 10, 11, 12 and 15. Each one is an isolated, independent device environment with its own data and login state, and it stays a fixed, long-term environment, so the phone you set up for a client in March is the same phone in June.

The part agencies care about is handover. You can share a device with a teammate in one click and they pick it up already logged in. When someone goes on leave, nobody spends an afternoon re-entering passwords and waiting on 2FA codes from the client.

Other things I actually use: per-device proxy and region settings, local environments in 150+ countries/regions, bulk install/uninstall/launch of apps across a batch of devices, root, and an API. Billing is per-minute. There are browser, desktop and mobile clients. There are also cloud numbers, which I use for testing our own app's signup and OTP flows without passing someone's personal SIM around the office.

Fits: agencies holding client app accounts long-term, small QA teams that want persistent devices they can hand to each other, anyone doing regional checks.

Drawbacks, honestly: it's Android only, so if your release checklist includes iOS you need a second tool. And it's not a test-automation grid with built-in reporting. If what you want is "upload APK, run Espresso suite on 40 device models, get a video per failure," the next three entries do that better.

2. Genymotion SaaS

https://www.genymotion.com/

Genymotion is the one I'd point a pure dev team at. Their site lists Genymotion SaaS ("optimized for team work, CI/CD and agentic AI"), a PaaS version on AWS, Alibaba, GCP and Azure, and Genymotion Desktop for PC and Mac. Integrations they name: Detox, GitHub Actions, CircleCI, Bitrise, Jenkins.

These are Android virtual devices built to be spun up from a pipeline, and they also pitch browser-based support and demo use.

Fits: dev teams that want Android devices wired into CI, plus support teams that need to reproduce a customer's bug from a browser tab.

Less ideal when: you need one specific device to hold a client's logged-in state for months and get passed between people. That's not what a CI emulator is shaped for.

3. AWS Device Farm

https://aws.amazon.com/device-farm/

Real physical phones and tablets hosted by AWS. You can run automated tests (Appium, Espresso, Calabash, or their built-in suite with no scripting), do manual remote sessions, and get videos, logs and performance data back. You can set location, language and network conditions.

The interesting bit for this list: their private device lab option gives you iOS and Android devices for your exclusive use and, per their page, lets you persist settings between sessions. That gets much closer to "my device stays my device."

Fits: teams already on AWS who need real hardware coverage, including iOS, hooked into Jenkins or Android Studio.

Less ideal when: you're a five-person agency without anyone who wants to own AWS config. And the shared pool is built for test runs, not long-lived logged-in accounts.

4. BrowserStack App Live

https://www.browserstack.com/app-live

BrowserStack says 30,000+ real iOS and Android devices. You can upload dev APK/AAB/IPA builds or install production apps from the stores, debug with logs and crash reports, and test on up to four devices at once. Their Custom Device Lab adds exclusive device access with options like app persistence and SIM binding.

Fits: QA teams who need wide model coverage across iOS and Android, fast.

Less ideal when: the job is keeping a handful of long-term environments for ongoing client work. You'd be paying for breadth you don't use, and persistence lives in the custom lab tier, not the default.

5. GeeLark

https://www.geelark.com/

GeeLark offers ARM-based cloud phones for Android apps plus multi-account browser profiles for web, both in one workspace. Team features are solid on paper: team members can be added free, roles and permissions, operation logs, groups/tags/notes for organising profiles. They also mention MCP so you can connect an AI agent to manage the phones and profiles, and they list GPS/SIM simulation across 150+ countries.

Fits: social and marketing teams who want phones and browser profiles managed side by side, with scheduling and AI content tools on top.

Less ideal when: you're a dev/QA team. A big chunk of the product is about posting, content generation and engagement automation, which you'll pay attention to (and maybe pay for) without needing.

6. VMOSCloud

https://www.vmoscloud.com/

VMOSCloud runs Android cloud phones with a strong lean toward social media automation: an AI workflow feature that turns text prompts into actions, a Synchronizer that mirrors one device's actions across many, and a Team Hub with roles and permissions. Their homepage lists Google Play Integrity, SafetyNet and Widevine L1. "App Test" appears in their industry list, though most of the page is about growing social accounts.

Fits: operators running many social accounts who want synchronized control.

Less ideal when: you want a dev-first tool. I'd also read their data policy closely if you plan long-term use: their FAQ says data is automatically deleted once the subscription ends, which is fine, just plan exports around it.

7. Redfinger

https://www.cloudemulator.net/

One of the older names. Redfinger has Android, Windows, web and iOS access, a Redfinger for Business line, and servers in the US, Taiwan and Singapore. Their site mentions device simulation for testing alongside gaming and cross-border marketing.

Fits: individuals and small teams who want a simple cloud Android device on several platforms.

Less ideal when: you need team handover and region coverage beyond those three server locations.

Honourable mentions: LDCloud and UgPhone

Both are positioned mainly for gaming. LDCloud (https://www.ldcloud.net/) leads with 24/7 AFK play, multi-instance and sync operation. UgPhone (https://www.ugphone.com/) lists tiers on Android 10, 12 and 13 with servers in places like Hong Kong, Germany, Japan, the USA and Singapore. For client QA work, I wouldn't start here.

How I'd actually choose

If I'm honest, the decision usually comes down to one question. Is the device disposable (run tests, throw away) or durable (holds state, gets handed between people for months)?

Disposable: Genymotion, AWS Device Farm, BrowserStack. Pick by whether you need iOS and how much CI you already have.

Durable: that's where DuoPlus, GeeLark, VMOSCloud and Redfinger sit, and I'd rank them by how painless handover and regional setup are for a non-engineer on your team. That's why DuoPlus is first on my list.

Plenty of teams end up with one of each. What hurts is using a disposable tool for durable work and wondering why everyone keeps logging in again.

If you've ranked these differently for your own team, I'd like to hear why in the comments, especially if you run client work on BrowserStack's custom lab.

title: Measuring the Per-Image Cost of GPT-Image 2.6: Does Higher Quality Improve the Image?
description:
GPT-Image 2.6 was released a week ago. How much does it actually cost to make one image, and do the images change as much as the quality level suggests?

The official documentation lists token prices, but not per-image prices for medium and higher quality levels in GPT-Image 2.5 and 2.6. So I generated 69 images while changing the model and quality level, then calculated the cost from the token counts in the responses. I also cover the process and results in the video.

How I compared the models

I compared gpt-image-2, GPT-Image 2.5 Flare and Sunburst, and GPT-Image 2.6 Flare and Sunburst. The prompts were for a jazz poster with text, a product photo of an earbud case with a “UNION” label, and a winter-night tteokbokki street stall with a sign in Korean.

I used five quality levels: low, medium, high, xhigh, and max. I requested 1024×1024 images and generated one image for each combination, for a total of 69 images. The total cost was $5.63. gpt-image-2 does not support xhigh or max, so those requests returned a 400 error.

The price of one 1024×1024 image

I calculated the price using $30 per 1 million output tokens and $5 per 1 million input text tokens. The prices below are for one image. For GPT-Image 2.5 and 2.6, Flare and Sunburst had the same price at every quality level.

Quality gpt-image-2 2.5 2.6
low $0.006 $0.006 $0.025
medium $0.053 $0.013 $0.044
high $0.211 $0.053 $0.053
xhigh unsupported $0.094 $0.094
max unsupported $0.211 $0.211

All 69 images, by-quality view and 1:1 zoom: https://bgprogramming.com/dev/image-model-comparison

For 2.6, the price goes from $0.025 at low to $0.211 at max, a difference of about 8.5 times. For 2.5, the price goes from $0.006 at low to $0.211 at max, or 35 times. Compared with 2.5 low, 2.6 low costs 4 times as much.

Do images change when you raise the quality level?

I compared the same street stall image from low to max with 2.6 Sunburst. The composition stayed almost the same as I raised the quality level. I saw small differences in textures such as knit fabric, steam, and wood grain. They were easier to see when I zoomed in on the original at 1:1. At thumbnail size, it was hard to tell them apart.

Even at low, the English and Korean text was accurate, including the small Korean menu board. The price goes up, but with the three prompts I tested and at thumbnail size, the differences between quality levels were not large.

Model differences mattered more than quality levels

For the jazz poster, 2.5 added small text I had not requested. One example was “GOOD MUSIC BRINGS US TOGETHER.” Raising the quality level did not fix this, and the text was not present in 2.6. Even at the same low level, the scene from 2.6 was more crowded.

The price difference also depended on the model. At high, gpt-image-2 cost $0.211 and 2.6 cost $0.053. Generation time also differed: gpt-image-2 high took an average of 105 seconds, while 2.6 Flare high took 10 seconds.

Flare and Sunburst: same price, different speed

2.6 Flare and Sunburst had the same price at every quality level. In this comparison, the speed difference was clear. The times below are averages across the three prompts.

Quality Flare Sunburst
low 7 seconds 25 seconds
medium 9 seconds 30 seconds
high 10 seconds 54 seconds
xhigh 17 seconds 81 seconds
max 31 seconds 142 seconds

Sunburst was 2–5 times slower than Flare. Flare low took 7–8 seconds in all three runs. That does not mean Flare is a lower-quality model. Text accuracy was the same at low.

OpenAI describes Sunburst’s strengths as medium and higher quality, and consistency during iterative editing. In my comparison, the difference between medium and high was not clear, and I did not measure iterative editing. I might consider Flare when users are waiting or when I need to generate several drafts, and Sunburst when I need to revise the same image multiple times or keep a character consistent. That is my judgment based on these measurements.

Token counts looked fixed — limitations of this comparison

For the same model and quality level, the output token count was the same across different prompts. For example, 2.6 low used 824 tokens, and medium used 1,449 tokens. The counts were the same for a simple poster and a night scene with people and signs.

This is based on only three prompts, so I cannot say it is a general rule. But in this test, output token counts seemed to be fixed by resolution and quality level rather than by image complexity.

I also generated only one image for each combination, so the composition could change if I generated it again. I used only three types of prompts, and I did not test iterative editing. Please treat the prices here as results from this test of one 1024×1024 image.

What I changed afterward

My channel thumbnail tool was set to gpt-image-2 high. After this comparison, I decided to use GPT-Image 2.5 Sunburst at low.

When I made this video’s thumbnail with gpt-image-2, “8.5 times,” which I had written in the first line of the prompt as an explanation, appeared as text in the image. The phrase “The highest quality costs 8.5 times more!” (originally in Korean) appeared in two places, even though I had not requested it. I removed that sentence, added “No other text,” and generated the image again.

Three things to check

First, compare images at the size you will actually use, starting with the lowest quality level. Raise it only if the results are not good enough.

Second, check the cost per image instead of looking only at the token price. You can calculate the cost by recording the token counts in the response.

Third, when a new model comes out, compare it using the prompts you already use.

When generating images, which matters most to you: speed, price, or quality?
