title: The health check that took down Outlook: inside the Microsoft 365 outage of November 12
description:
On Thursday lunchtime, Outlook stopped opening. Not for one company, and not in one country. People clicked their inbox and got nothing. They refreshed. They restarted the app. They tried their phone. Nothing worked, and the usual fixes did nothing at all, because the problem was not on their side of the screen.

By 1:09 p.m. Eastern time, Downdetector had logged 128,874 problem reports for Outlook. Independent traffic measurements put Exchange Online, the service behind Outlook mailboxes, at about 89 percent below its normal level for more than nine hours. Teams, SharePoint, Copilot and the Microsoft 365 admin centre broke along with it, because they all lean on the same mail service.

This is the story of what happened next, told from Microsoft's own incident log. It is worth reading closely, because the villain of this outage was not a hacker, a traffic spike, or a bad deploy. It was the safety system that was supposed to protect the service.

The day, hour by hour

All times are Eastern, Thursday November 12, 2026, unless stated otherwise.

11:17 a.m. Microsoft opens the incident internally. Almost nobody outside the company notices anything yet.

12:25 p.m. Outlook problem reports start climbing on Downdetector.

12:35 p.m. Kentik, a company that watches internet traffic, sees Exchange Online traffic fall off a cliff.

12:54 p.m. Microsoft's first public post. It talks about users "in the Americas", as if this is a regional problem.

1:07 p.m. The wording changes to "users in any region". It is not regional.

1:09 p.m. Downdetector peaks at 128,874 Outlook reports.

2:18 p.m. Microsoft corrects its own first theory. The elevated load, it writes, "isn't driven by an overall increase in traffic, but by a large number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable, which is shifting load onto the remaining infrastructure." Read that sentence twice. The traffic did not grow. The fleet shrank.

2:43 p.m. The missing servers have a cause: they are failing automated health checks, and the load balancer is pulling them out of service because of it.

2:57 p.m. The suspect narrows. The failed health checks "may originate from a specific component on the affected servers that's responsible for processing them." Microsoft starts deploying a change to bypass that component, and takes steps to stop more servers being removed from service.

3:56 p.m. An alternative health check method works on a subset of servers, and those servers come back. Progress, at last.

5:00 p.m. The setback. The fixes so far "have not provided the anticipated relief." Servers that were returned to service "can become unresponsive again once they begin receiving traffic."

8:06 p.m. A sharper finding: "a process on the affected servers responsible for establishing secure connections becomes overwhelmed, causing the servers to stop processing requests." In the same update, Microsoft starts reverting "a recent network configuration change that correlates with the start of impact."

Overnight. A patch to an upstream authentication and routing component starts showing positive results. Microsoft extends the window for delayed email from 24 hours to 48 hours, so messages sitting in queues are not bounced while recovery continues.

Friday morning. Recovery moves region by region, Asia first, then Europe, then North America. At 8:00 a.m. Eastern on Friday, the incident is still open. Some users are still seeing intermittent problems and delayed mail. Microsoft says there is no evidence of malicious activity, and promises a full post-incident report with root cause once the service is fully restored.

That report has not been published yet. Everything above comes from Microsoft's incident log as it stood on Friday morning, and the details may change when the report lands. The lesson does not depend on the details.

What a health check is, and how it can turn on you

A load balancer is a traffic cop. It stands in front of a fleet of servers and hands each incoming request to a server that is ready for it. To know which servers are ready, it asks them, every few seconds, a simple question: are you okay? That question is a health check, and a server answers it by running a small check and replying yes or no.

If a server answers no, or does not answer at all, the load balancer stops sending it traffic. That is the whole point. A sick server should not get more work.

Now imagine the part of the server that answers that question is itself broken. The server is fine. It could handle mail. But it cannot say so, because the component that processes the health check is the thing that failed. The load balancer hears silence, concludes the server is dead, and pulls it out of rotation.

That is what Microsoft's log describes. And here is where it turns into a cascade, which is the word engineers use when one failure causes the next failure, which causes the next.

Every server that gets pulled hands its share of the work to the servers still standing. Those servers now carry more load than they were built for. Their processors run hotter. They slow down. Some of them start failing their own health checks, and get pulled too. Each removal makes the next one more likely. The fleet does not fail all at once. It fails one server at a time, faster and faster, like a row of dominoes that leans a little harder with each fall.

Microsoft saw this happening in real time. At 2:18 p.m. it wrote that load was shifting onto the remaining infrastructure. That is the cascade, described in Microsoft's own words.

The second trap: bringing servers back

Fixing a cascade is not as simple as fixing the broken part and turning the servers back on. Microsoft learned that at 5:00 p.m., when servers it had returned to service went unresponsive again as soon as traffic reached them.

Think about what happens the moment a server comes back. Every client that has been retrying for hours, every phone that has been polling for new mail, every app that has been hammering refresh, all rush in at once. The server is healthy, but it is healthy in the same way a shop is healthy at the moment the doors open after a crowd has waited outside all day. The first minute is the hardest minute it will ever have.

There is a second reason that first minute is so hard, and it is the detail Microsoft found at 8:06 p.m., that a process for establishing secure connections was getting overwhelmed. When your app connects to a mail server, the first thing that happens is a handshake, a short exchange that sets up an encrypted connection. That handshake is the most processor hungry part of accepting a connection, far more expensive than sending the mail itself. During normal operation, handshakes are spread out across the day. After an outage, millions of them arrive in the same minute, because every client is reconnecting at the same time. The server spends all of its processor time saying hello, and has none left to do any work.

So the recovery has to be slow on purpose. Microsoft did exactly that: traffic limits in specific locations, a narrower set of connections allowed through, then gradually widening. Let a few servers prove they are stable under a little traffic before you give them a lot. It feels slow. It is the only thing that works.

The guard you can build this week: separate alive from ready

Most small services have one health endpoint, and it answers one question: is the process running? That is a liveness check, and it is the wrong question to ask a load balancer. A process can be alive and still unable to take traffic. What the load balancer needs is a readiness check: is it safe to send this server real work right now?

Here is the difference in Go. Two endpoints, two different questions.

// /healthz answers one question: is this process alive?
func healthz(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    w.WriteHeader(http.StatusOK)
    w.Write([]byte("ok"))
}

type gate struct {
    sem chan struct{} // one slot per request we are willing to run
}

func newGate(limit int) *gate {
    return &gate{sem: make(chan struct{}, limit)}
}

// /readyz answers a different question: is it safe to send
// this server more work right now?
func (g *gate) readyz(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    // If the server is 90 percent full, say not ready.
    // The load balancer will wait. It will not pull the
    // server out of rotation, and the server gets a chance
    // to drain instead of being declared dead.
    if len(g.sem) >= cap(g.sem)*9/10 {
        w.WriteHeader(http.StatusServiceUnavailable)
        return
    }
    w.WriteHeader(http.StatusOK)
    w.Write([]byte("ok"))
}

Pair that with a shedder, a piece of middleware that refuses new work fast when the server is full, instead of accepting it and dying slowly:

func (g *gate) shed(next http.Handler) http.Handler {
    return http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        select {
        case g.sem <- struct{}{}:
            defer func() { <-g.sem }()
            next.ServeHTTP(w, r)
        default:
            // Full. Refuse in microseconds, with a 503 the
            // client can retry, instead of queueing work
            // that will time out anyway.
            http.Error(w, "busy, try again", http.StatusServiceUnavailable)
        }
    })
}

The threshold matters, and it is worth testing at the boundary. Run a load test that fills the server to 89 percent of its limit, then 90, then 100. At 89 it should still report ready. At 90 it should report not ready. At 100 it should refuse fast. If those three numbers do not behave, the guard is decoration.

The guard on the other side: retry like a polite guest, not a crowd

The cascade also had a client side. Every Outlook app, every phone, every integration kept retrying, and when the servers came back, all of those retries landed at once. You cannot fix Microsoft's clients. You can fix yours.

A retry that waits the same amount of time every time is a crowd that knocks on the door in unison. A retry with backoff waits longer after each failure, and jitter, a small random amount added to the wait, spreads the retries out so they do not all land in the same second.

import random
import time
import requests

def get_with_backoff(url, tries=5):
    delay = 0.5  # start by waiting half a second
    for attempt in range(tries):
        try:
            resp = requests.get(url, timeout=5)
            if resp.status_code < 500:
                return resp  # a 4xx is our mistake, not the server's
        except requests.RequestException:
            pass  # network error: treat it like a 5xx and retry
        # Wait longer each time, and add jitter so every client
        # does not retry at the same instant.
        time.sleep(delay + random.uniform(0, delay))
        delay *= 2
    raise RuntimeError("service still down after retries")

And one step further, a circuit breaker: a small counter that stops calling a service entirely after a few failures in a row, and only tries again after a cooling off period. It is the client side version of the same idea: when something is struggling, the kindest thing you can do is stop hitting it.

Three questions to take back to your own systems

First, what does your health check actually measure? If the check runs through the same component that does the real work, a failure in that component looks like a dead server, and your load balancer will do exactly what it did to Microsoft: remove healthy capacity in the middle of a crisis. Check the check.

Second, do you separate alive from ready? A server that is alive but full should shed load, not be declared dead. A server that is dead should be declared dead. One endpoint cannot answer both questions.

Third, have you tested the return to service, not just the failure? Kill a server in staging, bring it back, and watch what happens in the first minute under real traffic. If it falls over again the moment traffic reaches it, you have the same second trap Microsoft hit at 5:00 p.m., and you can fix it before your users find it for you.

The uncomfortable part of this outage is how ordinary each piece was. A component that answers health checks. A load balancer doing its job. Clients retrying, as clients do. None of it was exotic. That is the point. The systems that take down a whole service are rarely exotic. They are ordinary parts, arranged so that the safety system itself can become the failure.

So here is the question to take back to your own systems: which of your health checks is measuring the thing that checks, instead of the thing itself, and how would you know?

Sources: Microsoft incident log for EX1550543 and MO1550821, as published in the Microsoft 365 admin centre and mirrored publicly by the University of Pennsylvania; Downdetector and Kentik figures as reported in the Enrow write-up of the outage. Microsoft has not yet published a root cause; it has promised a full post-incident report once the service is fully restored.

title: RabbitMQ for Beginners: Let Your Services Talk Without Waiting on Each Other
description:
RabbitMQ is a message broker — a post office for your software. Instead of services calling each other directly and waiting for a reply, they send messages to RabbitMQ, which delivers them when the other service is ready. That simple idea makes systems faster, more reliable, and much easier to scale.

What makes RabbitMQ different? First, it decouples services: the sender does not need to know who will read the message, or when. Second, it is durable: messages can be stored on disk, so nothing is lost if a service restarts. Third, it supports patterns like work queues, publish-subscribe, and routing, so one tool covers many communication needs.

Here is the simplest example. A producer sends a task to a queue, and a worker picks it up when ready. In Node.js with the amqplib library, the producer looks like this:

const amqp = require("amqplib");

async function send() {
  const connection = await amqp.connect("amqp://localhost");
  const channel = await connection.createChannel();
  await channel.assertQueue("tasks", { durable: true });
  channel.sendToQueue("tasks", Buffer.from("Send welcome email to Priya"), {
    persistent: true,
  });
  console.log("Task sent");
  await connection.close();
}

send();

And the worker:

const amqp = require("amqplib");

async function work() {
  const connection = await amqp.connect("amqp://localhost");
  const channel = await connection.createChannel();
  await channel.assertQueue("tasks", { durable: true });
  channel.consume("tasks", (msg) => {
    console.log("Working on:", msg.content.toString());
    channel.ack(msg);
  });
}

work();

The producer never waits for the worker. If ten tasks arrive at once, you can start ten workers and they share the load automatically.

Where is RabbitMQ used? It is used for background jobs (sending emails, resizing images), for connecting microservices, and for handling traffic spikes. When a website gets a sudden rush of orders, RabbitMQ holds them in a queue instead of letting the system fall over.

Who should learn RabbitMQ? Backend developers, anyone building microservices, and developers who need background jobs. If your app does slow work — emails, payments, image processing — a message queue is the tool that keeps your website fast while the slow work happens in the background.

RabbitMQ's limits are worth knowing. It adds a new piece of infrastructure to run and monitor, messages can pile up if workers fail, and debugging a distributed queue takes practice. Start with one queue and one worker, and add complexity only when you need it.

Your first step today: run RabbitMQ locally with Docker, send one message from the producer above, and watch the worker receive it. In a week you will be designing systems around queues instead of direct calls.

Quick Summary

A useful app makes everyday tasks easier, whether customers are booking a service, sellers are managing orders, or a startup is testing a business idea. It should be simple to use, reliable, and ready to improve as needs change.

What Is Bubble App Development?

Bubble app development means building an application with Bubble’s visual editor. An app can include pages, user accounts, forms, saved information, payments, and actions that run when a user completes a task.

  • Internal business tools: Dashboards and forms for managing leads, tasks, stock, or daily work.
  • Startup MVPs: First versions that let a team test an idea with real users before investing in a larger product.

Not every feature fits every project. Review users, data, steps, and outside services before choosing Bubble.

What Do Bubble App Development Services Include?

A good development partner starts with the problem the app must solve and supports the work through launch and future updates.

Custom app development turns business needs into a solution built around users, tasks, and rules instead of adding features just because they look impressive.

Web app development creates browser-based products such as SaaS tools, marketplaces, portals, and customer systems. The design should be easy to use on large and small screens.

Mobile app development starts by confirming whether you need a mobile-friendly web app or a native iOS and Android app. The choice depends on how people will use the product and which phone features it needs.

AI features and integrations connect an app with outside tools, payment services, or AI features when they solve a real task. Each connection should be checked for access, cost, and reliability.

App improvement and support may include fixing errors, reviewing slow workflows, improving how information is stored, adding features, and keeping the app useful after launch.

UncannyCS lists custom Bubble apps, web applications, mobile-friendly apps, AI features, plugin and API connections, migration, optimization, and maintenance among its services. Review its Bubble app development services to learn more about its approach.

How Does a Bubble App Project Move From Idea to Launch?

A clear process helps prevent missed requirements and avoidable changes. A typical project should cover six stages:

  1. Understand the need. Discuss the users, business goals, problem, and tasks the app must support.
  2. Set the first version’s scope. Separate launch essentials from features that can wait.
  3. Plan the screens and user journey. Map how people sign up, move through the app, enter details, and complete key actions.
  4. Build the app. Set up pages, data, user access, workflows, and agreed integrations in Bubble.
  5. Test real situations. Check user roles, forms, payments, notifications, mobile layouts, and errors. Fix issues before release.

How Do You Choose a Bubble Development Company in the USA?

Is Bubble the Right Choice for Every App?

title: The anti-flicker tax: what hiding your page does to LCP
description:
If you've run a test from a visual editor, you've probably seen it: the page loads with the old headline, and a beat later the new one snaps into place. That's flicker. Client-side testing tools all have to deal with it, because their script applies the variant after the browser has started painting.

From inside the browser you can either show the original and swap it, so the visitor sees the flash, or hide the page until the script is done. The second option is the "anti-flicker snippet", and most tools turn it on by default.

How long the page stays hidden

An anti-flicker snippet makes the page invisible, usually with opacity: 0 on the body or a class like Google Optimize's async-hide. It reveals the page when the testing script finishes or a timeout fires, whichever comes first, so the timeout is your worst case. The defaults are generous:

  • Google Optimize shipped its snippet with a 4,000 ms default (Google's developer docs). Optimize shut down on September 30, 2023, but copies of that snippet are still sitting in plenty of <head> tags.
  • Webflow Optimize also defaults to 4,000 ms. Enterprise plans can set anything from 0 to 30,000 ms, and Webflow's help page warns that lower values bring back flicker (Webflow help).

Optimizely recommends loading its snippet synchronously in the head instead (Optimizely support), which blocks rendering until the script has downloaded and run.

On fast wifi with a warm cache, the script usually wins and the page appears within a few hundred milliseconds. On a slow phone, your visitor waits for the timeout.

What it does to Core Web Vitals

Largest Contentful Paint can't happen while the page is invisible, so LCP absorbs the whole wait. Vercel's guide on A/B testing and Core Web Vitals says the failsafe commonly sits at 4 seconds and LCP takes all of it (Vercel KB). Google rates LCP as good at 2.5 seconds or less, measured at the 75th percentile (web.dev).

Published measurements are rare. DebugBear tested one site and recorded an LCP of about 6.0 seconds with body hiding and about 2.7 seconds with the hiding overridden (DebugBear). That's one site, and your numbers will differ, but they'll move in the same direction.

The same Vercel guide also covers layout shift. Without anti-flicker, swapping content in can push CLS past 0.1. With it, CLS can look healthy for the wrong reason, since the browser doesn't record shifts that happen while the page is hidden. A clean CLS score on a tested page might only mean nobody could see the problem.

The browser team's own advice

Chrome's guidance on flicker-free client-side testing suggests blocking="render" with a strict execution budget of under 100 ms, says not to combine it with anti-flicker snippets, and recommends testing on the server wherever you can (Chrome for Developers). The people who build the browser think the cleanest fix is to stop deciding in the browser.

Deciding before the first byte

A Next.js server already renders the page, so it can render the right variant from the start. You can build that yourself in about 100 lines; our guide to A/B testing in the App Router shows how. evolveAB does the assignment in the Next.js proxy, which reads a signed config bundle from memory (no network call), sets a sticky cookie and rewrites the request to that variant's cached render. The HTML arrives with the variant already in it, so there's nothing to hide or swap and no testing script blocking the head.

That has a cost too. Our code in the proxy takes 0.1 to 0.35 ms, but on Vercel any proxy adds roughly 20 ms to a first page view; one that does nothing measured 18 to 23 ms in our tests. Twenty milliseconds before the first byte is an easy trade against up to four seconds of blank page, as long as nobody pretends it's zero.

We also measure each variant's page speed in visitors' browsers and compare it with control. Once there are enough page views to be sure, auto-rollback pauses a variant that's clearly slower: LCP 20% worse, CLS up by 0.05 or INP 50 ms slower. A variant shouldn't win on sign-ups by quietly making the page slower.

Measuring it on your own site

You don't need to switch tools to see what anti-flicker costs you. Run a throttled Lighthouse or WebPageTest trace on a tested page and look at the gap between first byte and first paint, then find the timeout in your snippet (it's usually a plain number in the code). If it says 4000 and your mobile LCP hovers around 2.5 seconds, you know where part of it goes.

Originally published on the Evolve blog.

title: Running Agent Skills Code With OpenSandbox
description:
Agent skills give coding agents reusable instructions for tasks such as preparing a release. They can also include executable code: a script that checks a file or produces a report another step will use.

When that work reaches a delivery pipeline, we need a way to decide whether the result is good enough to publish. Where should the skill's code run, and how should its output affect that decision?

OpenSandbox provides APIs for creating temporary environments and running commands. I wanted to test how it could run a skill's helper between building a Python package and publishing it, with GitHub Actions enforcing the result.

I built a small workflow around a skill that checks a release manifest—the file listing a package and its version. The experiment tests whether valid input can reach publication, while a missing version or an incorrect report stops the release.

Where does the check fit?

The pipeline has three jobs: build, check, and publish. The build creates a wheel, Python's installable package format, and its release manifest. The check runs the skill's helper. Publication depends on both jobs succeeding.

The OpenSandbox check sits between building the candidate and publishing it. Code review and application tests belong to the broader delivery process.

The publish job declares these dependencies:

publish:
  needs: [build, check]
  runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
  timeout-minutes: 5
  permissions:
    contents: write

GitHub Actions skips dependent jobs when a prerequisite fails. A failed check prevents the publish job from starting.

What code comes from the skill?

This example's release-checking skill supplies a Python CSV validator and SKILL.md instructions describing its input and output requirements.

The valid manifest has one package:

package,version
opensandbox-release-demo,0.1.0

The helper requires both fields and unique package names. It returns JSON containing the row count and package identities. A missing version produces a diagnostic naming the row and exits with status 7.

The delivery job invokes a reviewed helper explicitly. An agent can follow the skill while preparing release files, while CI runs the same executable check before publication. The pipeline's acceptance rules determine whether that release step can continue.

How does OpenSandbox run the check?

The check job starts an OpenSandbox server on its GitHub runner. Its Python client creates a temporary environment, uploads the skill and manifest, verifies file readback, and runs the helper through the OpenSandbox SDK.

The complete client includes this command invocation:

execution = await sandbox.commands.run(
    command, opts=RunCommandOpts(timeout=timedelta(seconds=30))
)

The server and SDK are pinned to version 1.2.0. The sandbox uses a Python image pinned by digest, a three-minute lifetime, and explicit resource limits. It receives the skill files and synthetic manifest; the GitHub publication token belongs to the publish job.

The caller reads the expected package name and version from the built wheel's metadata. It accepts the report only when execution succeeds and the returned fields match that candidate. Before publication, it also rechecks the wheel and manifest checksums against the accepted evidence.

A finally block requests sandbox destruction even after rejection. The caller then checks for a 404 from a new lifecycle client. A cleanup failure leaves the release check blocked.

What passed, and what blocked publication?

I ran three separate GitHub Actions executions at the same source revision. Each execution built its own candidate before reaching the OpenSandbox check.

Scenario Helper exit Check job Publish job
Valid manifest 0 Passed Created prerelease
Missing version 7 Failed Skipped
Incorrect report 0 Failed Skipped

The missing-version case changes the CSV input. The wrong-report case uses a separate control script that returns 99 rows while exiting successfully. The caller expects one package, so it rejects that report.

The valid run created a demo prerelease. I downloaded its wheel without signing in, matched its checksum to the accepted candidate, and installed it in a fresh environment. Both rejected runs had skipped publish jobs and returned 404 for their expected release tags. All three sandbox cleanup lookups also returned 404.

The retained evidence connects each decision to its source revision, helper, candidate checksums, process output, and cleanup lookup. A failed run's JSON record remains available even though its publish job was skipped.

When should a team use this pattern?

I'd consider OpenSandbox when an agent application needs to create temporary environments for individual script jobs, with a defined runtime, selected input files, and collected results. This release check shows how that execution service can participate in an automated delivery decision.

For a simple validator, your existing CI container may already provide a suitable environment. Compare that support with the lifecycle work an OpenSandbox service adds. The recommendation depends on your agent application's execution needs.

The companion repository includes the workflow, skill, tests, and reproduction commands. This check covers manifest fields and agreement with the built package; teams still define their other testing, approval, and deployment requirements.

The useful result is a release check your team can inspect, rerun, and enforce before publication. The skill supplies the procedure, OpenSandbox runs its helper, and the pipeline acts on the observed result.

If your agent workflow needs that execution step, check out OpenSandbox.

title: Opening a 50 GB text file without reading it
description:
Most text editors open a file by reading all of it. That is fine for a source file and hopeless
for a 50 GB log: the work done before the first screen grows with the file, and no processor
saves you from that. BigText, a free and open-source editor for Windows, Linux and macOS, is
built on the opposite rule:

The time and memory of every operation depend on the text on screen, not on the size of the
file.

This article is about the five decisions that make that rule hold, what they measure at on a
50 GB file, and what I learned building the editor with an AI model.


BigText opens a 50 GB log at once, jumps to its end and its middle, searches it with a regular expression and follows a growing log.

A fast machine does not help

All the numbers below come from one machine:

Part
Model HP Z2 Tower G1i Workstation
CPU Intel Core Ultra 9 285, 24 cores
Memory 192 GB DDR5-5600
GPU NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090
Disks 2 × 1 TB Samsung NVMe SSD
OS Windows 11 Pro

On a machine like this everything should be instant, and for years opening a big log, CSV export
or SQL dump was not. The editor would think for a long time, the window would freeze, sometimes
it would refuse the file.

The reason is simple. Notepad++ allocates a buffer for the whole file and warns above 2 GB that
opening it may take minutes
(source).
VS Code keeps roughly the size of the file in memory
(VS Code blog).
Reading a file from start to end and splitting it into lines is one sequential pass, usually on
one thread: one of the 24 cores works and the rest wait. The GPU has nothing to do with it.

That pass is easy to measure, because BigText makes it too, in the background, to build its line
index. For the 50 GB file it takes 17–18 seconds on this machine, with the file already in the
operating system's cache, that is, in RAM. An editor that makes this pass before it shows the
first line keeps you waiting at least that long in the best case. If the file does not fit in
memory, it does not open at all.

The problem is not the hardware but the algorithm. If the work before the first screen is
proportional to the file, no processor helps.

The idea: read what the screen needs

A screen holds fifty or sixty lines, a few kilobytes of text. Showing the first screen of a 50 GB
file does not require reading 50 GB. Five decisions follow from that.

1. The file is mapped, not loaded, and in windows

Memory mapping (mmap, MapViewOfFile on Windows) ties a file to the program's address space
without reading anything. The actual read happens when the program touches a byte, and only for
that page. Opening a file this way costs the same whatever its size.

There was a surprise here. On Windows, mapping a 50 GB file as one view costs almost 100 MB of
memory by itself: the system keeps 8 bytes of bookkeeping for every 4 KB page. Memory use
depended on the file size again; with a 50 GB file open the process took 205 MB.

So the single view became a cache of windows: 288 MB each, starting every 256 MB so that a line
near a boundary always fits in one of them, with at most six mapped at a time. Memory dropped from
205 MB to 107 MB and stopped depending on the file size.

2. Opening reads the first megabyte

When a file opens, a worker thread reads its first megabyte. From that sample it decides the
encoding (UTF-8, UTF-16, Windows-1251 and others), the line endings and whether the file is
binary. That takes 1.1–1.4 ms. Then the lines that fit on the screen are drawn, and the file is
open.

3. The screen is anchored to a byte offset, not a line number

An ordinary editor knows its position as "I am at line one million", and to know that it has to
count every line before it. BigText knows "I am at byte 26,843,581,344". The scrollbar is
proportional to bytes too. Jumping to the middle of the file counts nothing: it reads a few
kilobytes there, finds the nearest line start and draws.

The line number is shown at once anyway. At first it is an estimate with a ~ in front of it;
when the index reaches that part of the file, the exact number replaces it.

4. A sparse line index: one number per 64 KB

Storing where every line starts is expensive. My test file has 453,565,956 lines; a full table of
offsets would take 3.4 GB. BigText splits the file into 64 KB blocks and stores one number per
block: how many lines came before it.

file:   [ 64 KB ][ 64 KB ][ 64 KB ][ 64 KB ] ...   819 thousand blocks
index:     0        554     1,107    1,661   ...   lines before each block (example)

For the 50 GB file the index is 8.12 MB, 0.016 % of the file. "Go to line N" finds the block by
binary search and then scans at most 64 KB of text, counting newlines with SIMD.

The index is built in the background from the start of the file, at about 2.9 GB/s: 17–18 seconds
for 50 GB. The editor works normally meanwhile: scrolling, jumping and searching all work.

5. The UI thread never waits

The UI thread reads only the bytes on screen. Indexing, search, replace and save run on worker
threads, each with a progress bar and a cancel button. The goal is that no frame takes more than
16 ms. While the 50 GB file was being indexed, a page-down frame took 1.2 ms on average.

There is one more edge case. A file can be a single enormous line, such as a 2 GB minified JSON
document. Such lines are split softly every 64 KB, so working out any line never reads more than
128 KB.

Measurements

The numbers come from a release build of BigText 0.4.1 and its own benchmark
(bigtext --bench-ui). Each file was measured three times, with the files in the OS cache.

1 GB 10 GB 50 GB
Lines 9,069,553 90,713,192 453,565,956
Open request → first screen of text painted 31–32 ms 31–32 ms 31–35 ms
of which opening the file and detecting the encoding 1.3–1.4 ms 1.3 ms 1.3 ms
Background indexing 0.4 s 3.7 s 17.4–17.7 s
Index size 130 KB 2.03 MB 8.12 MB
Memory of the idle editor 98–99 MB 100–101 MB 107–109 MB

The important row is the second one: the file grew fifty times and the time to open did not
change. Six more runs on the 50 GB file gave 35 ms at worst.

Memory hardly changed either. Most of the 100 MB is the graphical interface itself: the core
without a window holds the 50 GB file and its index in 12.1 MB.

What the 30 ms means needs saying precisely. Opening the file and detecting the encoding take
1.2 ms and laying out the first screen of text 0.03 ms; the rest is waiting for the window's next
frames. The benchmark stops the clock when the editor has painted the text, which does not
include the frame reaching the monitor, and it opens the file in the program's first frame.

In a window that is already running there are two cases. With another file open, the 50 GB file
opened in a new tab in 10 ms. The first file opened into an empty window took 0.1–0.2 s to show:
the editor's own work is again a few milliseconds, and the rest is the GPU driver or the
compositor presenting the first frame with a document in it. The cause of that one slow frame is
not known yet; a second file in the same window paints in about 10 ms.

Other numbers on the 50 GB file:

  • Go to line before the index was ready: no frame above 2.1 ms.
  • Plain-text search: 4.0–4.3 GB/s, the whole file in 12 seconds.
  • Regular-expression search: 3.6–4.3 GB/s.


A regular expression found 830 matches in the 50 GB file in 15.5 seconds. The results list is under the text; a click jumps to a match.

Editing and saving

Viewing is half of it; big files also need editing. BigText uses a piece table, an old and proven
structure. The original file is never touched. Typed text goes into a separate buffer, and the
document is a list of pieces: "this part of the original, then this part of the buffer". A
thousand edits in a 50 GB file take a few kilobytes.

Saving streams the result into a temporary file in the same folder, flushes it to disk and only
then replaces the original atomically (ReplaceFileW on Windows, which keeps attributes and
permissions). If something fails on the way or the power goes off, the original stays intact.

The 25th gigabyte of the same file in hex view. Jumping there is instant too.

I built it with Claude

I built BigText with Anthropic's Claude model, through Claude Code. Claude wrote the code. My
part was to say precisely what was needed, check the result and choose the next step. Every one
of the 174 commits in the repository names Claude as co-author.

It started with one document: the goal of the program, eight architecture rules that must not be
broken, measurable speed targets and a list of edge cases that must not break it. It is in the
repository as prompt.md. Four of its requirements:

  • Never read the whole file into memory.
  • Never block the UI thread; no task on it may take more than 16 ms.
  • Do not use ready-made editor components: they all keep the whole document in memory.
  • Measure the speed targets and report real numbers.

Claude first wrote a plan (PLAN.md), then worked through it in stages: opening and viewing,
search, replace, editing and saving, encodings. After each stage it measured on the test files
and compared the result with the target.

  • 24 October, 09:46: the first commit.
  • 24 October, 14:38: version 0.1.0, five hours later.
  • 29 October: version 0.4.1, the one measured above.
  • 10–12 November: versions 0.5.0 to 0.7.3.

Today the project has 151 Rust files, about 70,000 lines of code including tests, 335 tests and an
in-app GUI self-test that drives the real window with synthetic mouse and keyboard input through
229 checks.

Four lessons:

  1. Make the goal measurable. Not "it should be fast" but "the first screen in under 200 ms" and "under 200 MB of memory with a 50 GB file open". A goal like that can be checked.
  2. Write the architecture rules down first. The decisions that mattered most were made before any code was written.
  3. Measurement beats guessing. Memory dropping from 205 MB to 107 MB was not in the plan; it came out of a measurement.
  4. Give the AI tests it can run itself. When the GUI self-test was added, it found four bugs, which were then fixed.

What else it does

Besides opening big files, BigText:

  • searches with regular expressions, filters lines like grep and replaces across the whole file;
  • follows growing logs like tail -F, jumps to a time, filters by level and opens logs on servers over SSH;
  • opens CSV and TSV as tables with sorting, statistics and pivots, and JSON with a structure view;
  • compares two huge files;
  • reads files inside .gz, .zst, .zip and .tar without unpacking them by hand;
  • highlights code in about two dozen languages and formats, with a folder side bar and go-to-file, for the files that are not huge.

Two logs compared: four differences in 425 thousand lines, found in 0.04 seconds.

Try it, or measure it yourself

BigText runs on Windows, Linux and macOS. It is free and open source under the MIT license, and
its interface is in eight languages. The test-file generator and the benchmark come with the
portable downloads:

gen-testfiles --only random-lines-10g.txt
bigtext --bench-ui testdata/random-lines-10g.txt --report report.txt

The 50 GB file is the 10 GB one joined five times.

  • Website: https://erkinbek.github.io/bigtext/
  • Downloads: https://github.com/Erkinbek/bigtext/releases/latest
  • Source: https://github.com/Erkinbek/bigtext

If you have a file your editor cannot open, try it in BigText and tell me how it went.

A note on this article: like the code, it was written with Claude, from the project's notes and measurements. I checked it before publishing, and the replies in the comments are mine.

title: How Many Closed Findings Before You Trust a Routing Change
description:
How Many Closed Findings Before You Trust a Routing Change

This week X spent its energy arguing about whether a headline number is real. A vLLM post claims DeepSeek V4.1 Flash runs 58× the throughput of GB300 NVL72 on Vera Rubin hardware. The replies immediately asked how it was measured, and at what concurrency. Another post pointed out that DeepSeek's cheapest price is a caching artifact: input the model has already seen costs $0.003 per million tokens off-peak instead of $0.15 — fifty times less — so a "cheap" agent run may just be a well-cached one. A third thread argues over forensic evidence about what hardware trained the newest models at all.

Nobody on that timeline is arguing about the models. They are arguing about the evidence. That is the same question, one level down, that decides whether your routing change is real: your dashboard says a task type got better, or that the small model can take more work. How many closed findings do you need before you believe it — and act on it?

A reader asked the version of this question that stuck with me all week. Under my November 6 post, Agentic Affairs asked: before each category of conclusions accumulates 20 entries, does the median mean anything at all? We spent the week stress-testing that question in the comments. This post is the answer we arrived at — and the rule we now run.

The median of three is a rumor

Take a task type with three closed findings, measured as cost per completed task: $0.01, $0.02, $0.90. The median is $0.02. It looks cheap. One more finding arrives at $0.85 — a second expensive case, the kind that shows up once the small model meets the edge of its competence. The four values are $0.01, $0.02, $0.85, $0.90, and the median is now $0.44. One observation moved it more than twentyfold.

That is what "before 20 entries" means in practice. With a handful of findings, the median is not a summary of the category. It is one observation wearing a summary's clothes. It will move again with the next finding, and the direction of the move tells you nothing about the category — it tells you about the finding that just arrived.

The median is not special here. Any statistic computed on a handful of observations has the same disease: the next observation can rewrite it. The median is just the statistic people reach for when they want to sound robust, which makes its early instability more dangerous, not less. A mean that jumps is obviously unstable. A median that jumps looks like a contradiction — and teams resolve contradictions by picking the version they already believed.

One flip moves the number more than you think

The same arithmetic governs success rates, which is where routing decisions actually get made. One closed finding flipping from success to failure moves the rate by 1/n, where n is the number of closed findings:

  • 5 closed findings: one flip moves the rate 20 points
  • 10 closed findings: one flip moves it 10 points
  • 20 closed findings: one flip moves it 5 points
  • 30 closed findings: one flip moves it 3.3 points
  • 100 closed findings: one flip moves it 1 point

Read that table as a decision rule. If your bar for promoting a task type to the cheaper tier is a success rate above 95%, and you have 5 closed findings, a single late failure takes you from 100% to 80% — twenty points below the bar, on one observation. You did not learn the task type is bad. You learned you never had a measurement.

Our rule, after a week of arguing about it in the comments, is a 30-closed-finding floor before any routing change: no task type moves up or down a tier until 30 of its findings are closed. I will be explicit that 30 is our operating rule, not a universal constant — it is the point where one flip stops being able to move the rate by more than a rounding error, and where the median stops jumping by multiples. Your floor will differ with your volume and your cost of being wrong. What should not differ is having a floor, written down, before the decision arrives. A floor chosen in the middle of a debate is not a floor. It is a preference.

Count flips, not percentages

There is a second trap that a floor alone does not fix. When a task type has a near-zero failure baseline, one late failure doubles the failure rate. One failure in a hundred closed findings is a 1% failure rate; a second is 2%. The percentage doubled. The evidence grew by one finding.

This is the flip-count rule we argued out in the thread: at low baselines, ask how many flips moved, not what percentage moved. The percentage is the headline; the flip count is the evidence. A routing change justified by "the failure rate doubled" that rests on a single additional failure is a decision made on one observation — the same mistake as the median of three, wearing a more alarming costume.

The same logic applies in reverse. A task type that goes from 2 failures in 100 to 1 in 100 has "halved its failure rate" on the strength of one finding not failing. Do not promote on that either.

What counts as "closed" — and what never does

A floor of 30 means nothing if the 30 are not actually closed. A finding is closed when its real outcome is known — not when the model answered, not when a cheap check passed. That is the attribution-window argument from my last post, and it has a practical consequence here: the count that matters is closed findings, not total findings.

We split every interval into three buckets, a distinction a reader (Tom Jones) pushed us to make explicit:

  • Verified clean — the outcome is confirmed good.
  • Verified failed — the outcome is confirmed bad, with a reason.
  • Timed out, still unclosed — the window passed with no outcome signal.

The third bucket is the one that corrupts the count. An unclosed finding is not a success. It is an unknown, and it must be displayed as unknown — never folded into the clean column to make the numbers look better. A category with 25 verified-clean findings and 5 unclosed ones has 25 closed findings, not 30. It has not met the floor.

Backfill — findings whose outcome arrives late — gets the same discipline. A reader (Emily Woods) put it precisely in a comment this morning: backfill corrects the record; it does not rewrite the published numbers. Keep both columns — the state at the original deadline, and the final result — and judge a late backfilled success against the original deadline's timestamp, not against today's. And if the same task type keeps producing late backfills, that is itself a signal: the deadline is wrong, and it should be recalibrated openly and recorded as a decision — not quietly absorbed by letting each backfill rewrite history.

The quiet types never graduate — and that is fine

Every pipeline has task types that almost never run. A rare document shape, a seasonal request, a customer-specific format. They will never accumulate 30 closed findings, and most will never reach 10. The question is what happens to them, because the wrong answer is to either promote them on thin evidence or let them clog the review queue forever.

Our answer, worked out in the thread: a 10-finding threshold gates graduation out of the watchlist, and the watchlist itself has a 25-item hard cap with a quarterly manual review. A quiet type sits on the watchlist until it either accumulates 10 closed findings or the quarterly review retires it. It never gets promoted on 3 findings because someone is impatient, and it never blocks a decision about the types that do have evidence. The cap matters: without it, the watchlist grows until nobody reviews it, and the review stops being a review.

The honest caveat, which I gave in the thread and repeat here: the 10-finding threshold is a starting guess, and the quarterly review is a process, not a measurement. We have not run the 8-week replay that would calibrate these numbers — re-scoring the same tasks at 3, 7, and 14 days to see where the numbers stop moving. Until that replay runs, treat every number in this post that describes our own thresholds as a documented guess with a calibration plan, not a measured constant. That is the difference between a rule and a superstition: the rule says how it will be checked.

Slow drift beats the two-window rule

The two-window rule from my first post in this series — require the success rate to stay below the bar for two consecutive windows before moving a task type — catches steps. It does not catch slopes. A task type whose failure rate creeps from 1% to 2% to 3% across six weeks never trips a two-window alarm, because no single window looks bad enough. By the time it does, the redos have been quietly compounding for a month and a half.

That was another reader question from the week — the slow-drift alert — and the answer is that drift needs its own detector, separate from the window rule: a trend line on the closed-finding rate per task type, with an alert when the slope, not the level, crosses a bar. We do not have a good slope bar yet, and I will not invent one here. The point is structural: a rule that only looks at levels will miss every failure that arrives gradually, and most real failures arrive gradually.

What a thin-evidence decision costs

Keep the same pipeline from the last two posts, so the numbers stay comparable: a day's work needs 10 GPU-hours — 8 hours of chores on an RTX 4090 at $0.89 per GPU-hour ($7.12) and 2 hours of final answers on an H100 at $2.69 ($5.38). Total: $12.50 per day.

Now promote a task type to the cheap tier on 5 closed findings, all successful — a 100% provisional rate. The window closes and the 30-finding truth is 27 successes in 30: a 90% final rate. Out of 1,000 tasks a day, 100 now need a large-model redo. Assume a redo takes about 2 minutes of H100 time — your number will differ, measure yours: 100 × 2/60 hours × $2.69 = $8.97 a day in redo cost, on top of the $12.50 day. A decision made on 5 findings added 72% to the daily bill.

And the redo price is moving against you this week. RunPod's own pricing page now lists the H100 SXM at $4.39 per GPU-hour on Secure Cloud, up from $3.99 — the Community Cloud rate is unchanged at $2.69. Lambda's published rate rises to $4.59 on Monday, November 16, from $3.99. At the new Secure Cloud rate, those same 100 redos cost 100 × 2/60 × $4.39 = $14.63 a day — more than the entire original day's work. The cost of deciding on thin evidence is not fixed. It rises with the price of the model you redo on, and that price rose this week.

That is the whole argument in one number: the evidence threshold is not bureaucracy. It is the cheapest insurance you can buy against a redo bill that now costs more than the work itself.

We measure our own funnel the same way

This is not theory we exempt ourselves from — and this post is itself the example. Our site recorded 5 clicks and 190 impressions in Google Search Console over the latest 28-day window (October 16 to November 12, 2026), and our GPU cost calculator page recorded zero impressions again — it does not appear in the Search Console page table at all. That zero is a fact about the window, not a verdict on the page.

The discussion that produced this post is the same discipline applied to our own writing. The median question arrived when the thread under my November 6 post had 9 comments. We did not write this post then. We waited while readers stress-tested it — the flip-count rule, the quiet-types threshold, the watchlist cap, the backfill discipline, the slow-drift alert — and by today that article has 66 comments, up from 27 on the morning of November 9 and 42 on November 10. Across our 9 published articles we now have 90 comments and 5 reactions. This post is written on closed findings: questions that were asked, answered, and left standing after a week of replies. A post written on 9 comments would have been a median of three.

The bottom line

Do not ask "what is our success rate?" Ask "how many closed findings is that rate standing on, and how far would one more finding move it?" If the answer is fewer than your floor, you do not have a measurement. You have a rumor with a confidence interval wider than the decision — and this week, on X and everywhere else, rumors about numbers are exactly what everyone is arguing about.

If you want to skip the spreadsheet, our free GPU cost calculator prices the same trade-off — workload, GPU tier, and hourly rates — so you can see what a routing change costs before you make it: https://qisuanai.com/gpu-cost-calculator/

Prices: RunPod and Lambda public pricing pages, re-checked November 13, 2026 — RunPod Secure Cloud RTX 4090 $0.89, H100 SXM $4.39 (was $3.99), Community Cloud H100 SXM $2.69; Lambda H100 $4.59 and A100 (80 GB) $3.19 effective November 16, 2026, current rate behind login. DeepSeek API prices per DeepSeek's Models & Pricing page as reported November 9, 2026: deepseek-flash $0.30 input / $1.20 output per million tokens at peak, half off-peak; cache hits $0.006 / $0.003. X posts cited as discussion, not facts: vLLM's 58× throughput claim and the replies questioning its measurement conditions; the cache-hit price question; the hardware-forensics thread. The worked example is arithmetic on GPU-hours, not a production benchmark — your redo times and true rates will differ, and they are the numbers that decide your actual bill. The 30-finding floor, 10-finding threshold, and 25-item watchlist cap are our operating rules, stated as such; the 8-week replay that would calibrate them has not run yet, and the 7-day attribution window is a starting guess. Thread data: discussion under "Don't Scale Your LLM Routing on Request Volume" (November 6, 2026) and "Your Routing Dashboard Lies Until the Attribution Window Closes" (November 10, 2026), including Agentic Affairs' median question, the flip-count rule, the quiet-types and watchlist-cap discussion, Tom Jones' three-bucket split, and Emily Woods' backfill discipline.

title: Designing PixoPet: Turning Apple Health Data Into Virtual Pet Growth
description:
What if your virtual pet could grow while you're going about your day? That's the idea behind PixoPet, an iPhone virtual pet app I've been working on with a small team. Instead of relying entirely on in-game tasks, PixoPet connects sleep, focus, and movement with pet growth.

The concept sounds simple, but designing the experience raised a few interesting UX questions.

1. Making activity tracking less of a chore

Most habit trackers ask users to manually record their progress. That works for some people, but it also creates more tasks to manage. For PixoPet, we wanted to use activity data that already exists on the user's iPhone. With permission, PixoPet reads supported sleep and step data from Apple Health. Focus activity is tracked through an iOS Focus configuration. These activities contribute to growth energy, which users can allocate toward their virtual pet.

The goal is to make progress feel connected to everyday life without requiring constant manual check-ins.

2. Helping users understand where their energy comes from

Automatic tracking is convenient, but it can also make progress feel unclear. If someone opens an app and sees 500 EXP, how do they know where it came from? In PixoPet, we separate growth energy into Sleep, Focus, and Move so users can see how different activities contribute. We also show the energy available for allocation and the pet's current level progress.

This makes the relationship between real-world activity and virtual rewards easier to understand.

3. Making progression more meaningful than a number

Leveling up is satisfying, but we wanted the reward to feel connected to the pet itself. As a PixoPet grows, it can unlock new actions, backgrounds, stories, and achievements. Rather than only showing a progress bar, these rewards give users something new to discover in their pet's world.

4. Designing for imperfect days

One challenge we're still exploring is how to make activity-based progression encouraging without adding pressure. People don't sleep well or stay active every day. A self-care app should recognize that routines change. We're continuing to think about how to reward progress while keeping the experience flexible and approachable.

What we're learning

Working on PixoPet has made me think more carefully about the balance between automatic data collection, clear feedback, and meaningful rewards. Reducing manual interactions is useful, but users still need to understand how their data is used and what they get from it. PixoPet is available on iPhone, and we're continuing to improve the experience. I'm part of the PixoPet team and would love to hear how other developers and designers approach similar challenges.

How do you balance automatic tracking with clear user feedback in your own apps?

PixoPet on the App Store:
https://apps.apple.com/gb/app/pixopet-self-care-pet/id6806964547
