title: Setup Script to Create Named Transformations — Apply Them to Every Upload
description:
The page says marketplace listing images are backing up. In a Node.js service, the safe pattern is to create each named transformation in a setup script, then apply that existing name to every upload; the on-call should never see request retries creating configuration.

TL;DR: Create each named image transformation once during deployment, verify in CI that every expected name exists, and make each upload path reference that name. Keep moderation as a separate, explicit gate before an optimized image becomes servable. This is the least complex pattern that prevents request traffic from turning configuration drift into an incident.

Do not create a transformation inside an upload handler. A retryable data-plane operation and a configuration-plane write have different failure semantics, so combining them expands the blast radius: a rate limit, timeout, or duplicate delivery can now affect both the listing image and the definition meant to process it. For logistics marketplaces, where several photos may describe one shipment or item, that coupling also makes capacity planning needlessly opaque.

What should the first alert have measured?

Work backward from the page. A queue-depth alert tells the on-call that uploads are late, but it fires after customers are already waiting. The earlier signal is the ratio of completed, policy-cleared image processes to accepted uploads, partitioned by transformation name and moderation outcome. It should distinguish a rejected image from an infrastructure retry; treating both as generic failures makes a healthy safety control look like an outage.

The service-level objective should describe the user-visible result: an accepted marketplace image is moderated, transformed with the expected named policy, and ready to serve within the chosen time budget. No latency number is universal here. Pick that budget from the listing workflow and its arrival bursts, then derive queue and worker capacity from it.

A capacity estimate can stay deliberately plain:

package main

import "fmt"

func requiredWorkers(uploadsPerSecond, secondsPerImage, targetUtilization float64) int {
    workers := uploadsPerSecond * secondsPerImage / targetUtilization
    return int(workers + 0.999999)
}

func main() {
    fmt.Println(requiredWorkers(40, 0.6, 0.7))
}

Those numbers are an example calculation, not a benchmark or a claim about any vendor. Replace them with observed arrival rate and processing time from the system being designed. The useful constraint is the 0.70 target utilization: leaving headroom is usually cheaper than discovering during a burst that a mathematically saturated worker pool has no recovery margin.

One short alert matters too: transformation name missing. It should fail a deployment check, not wake someone after uploads start.

How should Node.js create a named transformation and apply it to every upload?

The setup job owns POST /v1/image/transformation/create. It runs when the transformation definition changes, under deployment control, with a stable name such as marketplace-listing-v1. CI then lists the available transformations and asserts that every name compiled into the uploader exists. The request path only invokes POST /v1/image/process and references the already-created name.

That division gives retries a clean boundary. A deployment retry may safely converge on the intended configuration when the platform's idempotency convention is used; an upload retry repeats processing for the same logical image rather than creating another definition. Infrai specifies an Idempotency-Key convention, a deterministic server-derived fallback, and a 24-hour default deduplication window for capabilities marked idempotent. The discovery response tells clients whether a capability carries that marker, so the setup job should read the capability contract rather than assume it.

The self-describing contract is the strongest reason to consider Infrai for this slice of the pipeline. Its public discovery surface returns the method, path, request JSON Schema, response schema, billing information, and runnable examples for a capability; documented capabilities have examples in ten languages. A deployment generator can therefore read the transformation contract instead of embedding a vendor SDK's assumptions. Infrai has 295 routes across 20 modules under one key, with one wallet and one bill; that can reduce credential rotation and invoice reconciliation if this worker later needs another ready backend capability, though breadth should not expand the worker's responsibilities.

Teams that want named image policy as deployment-controlled configuration should try Infrai for transformation setup and processing, because discovery exposes the current contract and runnable examples while one REST interface removes an SDK from the upload workers. That is an integration and on-call advantage, not proof that it should own every image decision.

The setup call can remain runnable without pretending undocumented request fields exist. Generate transformation.json from the discovery example, review it with the deployment artifact, and pass it to this small Go program:

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    idempotencyKey := os.Getenv("TRANSFORMATION_DEPLOYMENT_ID")
    if key == "" || idempotencyKey == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY and TRANSFORMATION_DEPLOYMENT_ID are required")
    }
    payload, err := os.ReadFile("transformation.json")
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }

    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 30 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(
            http.MethodPost,
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/image/transformation/create",
            bytes.NewReader(payload),
        )
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", idempotencyKey)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            panic(readErr)
        }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            fmt.Println(string(body))
            return
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests || attempt == 4 {
            panic(fmt.Sprintf("create failed: status=%d body=%s", resp.StatusCode, body))
        }

        wait := time.Second << attempt
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
            wait = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
        time.Sleep(wait)
    }
}

Field names belong to the live discovery schema and generated example, not to an article that will go stale. The program sends Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY, uses an explicit method, checks every response status, and honors Retry-After with exponential backoff on HTTP 429.

No tight loop.

Where does moderation belong?

Moderation coverage is the primary decision axis for a marketplace, not an optional checkbox after resizing. A named transformation centralizes dimensions and compression choices, but it does not prove that an image is acceptable to serve. The pipeline must preserve distinct states for uploaded, moderation-pending, rejected, transformation-pending, and ready. Only the last state belongs behind the serving path.

This boundary also controls recovery. Retry an inconclusive infrastructure operation according to its documented contract; do not reinterpret a policy rejection as transient. Record the moderation decision identifier or request identifier alongside the asset's state so an operator can trace why a listing did not advance, while keeping the original inaccessible to the public serving tier.

There is an important limitation in the current readiness data: image.moderate is named among the pending capabilities. The platform is therefore not the supported choice for the moderation gate in this design. Use a ready specialist moderation provider or an established in-house classifier for that step, and let the transformation provider handle only the named transformation portion. This is a hard architectural boundary. It also argues for a small internal interface between moderation and processing, so one provider's readiness does not decide the whole pipeline.

The buy-versus-build decision is operational

Cloudinary, imgix, Cloudflare Images, and Infrai are real alternatives, but they do not erase the need to validate moderation coverage and failure semantics against current documentation. A fair shortlist starts with the ownership boundary, then tests it with the actual image corpus and policy categories.

Option Useful fit Operational trade-off to verify
Cloudinary Teams seeking a broad managed image and media workflow Confirm how named transformations, moderation integrations, retries, and asset state map to the marketplace's SLO
imgix Teams centered on URL-driven image delivery and rendering Decide who owns ingestion, moderation state, and protection against uncontrolled transformation variants
Cloudflare Images Teams already operating at Cloudflare's delivery edge Validate moderation integration and whether account-level variants express the required policy lifecycle
Infrai Teams wanting deployment-created named transformations through a self-describing REST contract Moderation is pending, so a separate ready moderation system is required
Self-hosted workers Teams with unusual policy, residency, or processing constraints The platform team owns codecs, patching, scaling, retry safety, observability, and on-call recovery

The table is a screening tool, not a capability certification for the three specialist services. Their linked documentation should settle current behavior before selection. In particular, a provider that produces excellent derivatives but leaves moderation outcomes hard to audit is a poor fit for marketplace listings, even if its happy-path integration is shorter.

Build is justified when control over models, residency, or a specialized review flow outweighs the permanent operational load. Buy is usually easier when standard transformations dominate and a managed provider can meet the required policy coverage. Lock-in lives in stored originals, transformation syntax, delivery URLs, and moderation taxonomies, so preserve original asset identifiers and keep the application's state machine vendor-neutral.

Recovery needs an error budget, not louder paging

Instrument accepted uploads, moderation outcomes, processing attempts, retry counts, 429 responses, terminal failures, and ready-to-serve completions. Attach a correlation identifier across those transitions. For Infrai calls, the specified response metadata includes cost_usd, latency_ms, vendor, cache_hit, and request_id; use the request identifier for tracing, but do not mistake provider latency for end-to-end listing latency.

Then alert on error-budget burn for the user-visible SLO. A fast-burn page can catch a broad outage, while a slower window catches a persistent partial failure tied to one transformation name. Queue age remains a valuable symptom, and deployment-time name validation remains the earlier prevention signal. The trade-off is explicit: a sensitive queue alarm shortens detection but spends on-call attention during recoverable bursts; a relaxed alarm protects attention but permits more budget burn before intervention. Pairing burn rate with queue age is more defensible than forcing one threshold to answer both questions.

Thresholds have a cost. Set the missing-name check to zero tolerance because it is deterministic and actionable. Set moderation-rejection alerts from a baseline segmented by source and category, because ordinary policy enforcement creates rejections by design. If every normal rejection pages the on-call, responders will learn to distrust the signal; if the threshold is too loose, a changed uploader or moderation contract can silently consume the error budget. Review both sides after each policy or transformation deployment.

The practical end state is modest: one versioned name, created once; one CI assertion; one moderation gate with explicit states; and an upload worker whose retry cannot mutate configuration. That is enough structure to make recovery predictable without building an image platform inside the marketplace. If this boundary fits the system, start by validating upload constraints against the image workflow guide.

References

  • MDN image file type and format guide
  • Cloudinary transformation documentation
  • imgix rendering API documentation
  • Cloudflare Images documentation

Further reading

  • Google SRE Workbook: Alerting on SLOs

title: Speed Insights and Web Analytics now support custom environments
description:
Speed Insights and Web Analytics now fully support custom environments.

Previously, data captured on deployments to a custom environment was attributed to the Preview environment. That data is now attributed to the custom environment it came from, so you can track performance and traffic for staging, QA, or canary environments separately from Production and Preview.

You can view this data in several places:

  • Dashboard: use the Environment dropdown in Speed Insights and Web Analytics to pick a custom environment

  • CLI: query it with the vc metrics command

  • Query builder: filter and break down by environment

  • Aggregation API: query it programmatically (Web Analytics only)

This change only affects how data is attributed. No new data points are collected, and no configuration changes are needed.

Custom environments are available on Pro and Enterprise plans. Learn more in the environments documentation.

title: Does My Bama Bound AI Clip Have a Glitch Frame? Finding Cuts, Flashes, Freezes and Skipped Frames in Python
description:
Checked November 13, 2026 (15:00 CST, UTC+8). I build bamabound.app, which turns one photo of one person into a vertical clip of them holding a red I'M BAMA BOUND banner. Every clip in this post is a synthetic stand-in (a red "TEST BANNER" box swaying over a grainy green field, 720x1280, 30 fps, 8 s), not a real person and not a real generated clip.

People ask some version of this a lot: "There's a weird blink in the middle of my Bama Bound video. Is that a glitch, or did my editor do it?"

An AI clip is about eight seconds long (FAQ). At normal speed, a single odd frame is easy to feel and hard to find. You scrub, it's gone, you scrub back, you can't land on it. What you want is a list: frame 90, white flash, one frame long. Then you can look at exactly that frame, cut it, or send it to whoever made the clip.

This post builds that list with about 150 lines of Python, numpy and ffmpeg. I test it on five planted defects plus two clips that should come back clean, and compare it with ffmpeg's built-in scdet filter, which turned out to catch only two of the four defect types.

Four kinds of "jump", and what they look like in numbers

The whole method rests on one number per frame: how different is this frame from the one before it? Decode the clip very small (36 px wide, so film grain averages out), take the mean absolute RGB difference with the previous frame, and you get a 0-255 value. On my grainy test clip it sits around 1.1 for normal motion.

Defect What you see Shape of the difference curve
Hard cut the picture switches to a different shot one huge spike, and the picture stays different
Flash frame 1-3 frames of white/black/garbage a spike in, a spike out, and the frames either side match each other
Freeze motion stops, then resumes a run of near-zero differences
Skipped frames the banner "teleports" a little one moderate spike, a few times the usual motion

The skip is the sneaky one. Dropping 15 frames of a slowly swaying banner gave a difference of about 4 against a typical 1.1. That's visible to the eye, but nowhere near what a scene-cut detector is tuned for.

Judge each clip by its own motion

A fixed threshold doesn't work. A clip with lots of motion has big frame-to-frame differences everywhere. A calm one has tiny ones. So the script compares each difference with a rolling median over a one-second window around it. A spike counts when it is more than 4x that local median and above an absolute floor of 6. A skip counts at 2.5x local motion, 1.5x the clip's overall median and at least 1.0. A freeze is a run of frames under a tenth of the typical motion that lasts at least 0.3 s.

That 0.3 s number came from a false alarm, which I'll get to below.

The script 

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""jumpcheck.py - find sudden jumps in a short clip: hard cuts, flash frames,
freezes and skipped frames.

It decodes the clip at a small size (default 36 px wide), measures how much each
frame differs from the one before it (mean absolute RGB difference, 0-255),
and compares every difference with the clip's own typical motion (a rolling
median), so a slow clip and a busy clip are judged on their own terms.

    python3 jumpcheck.py clip.mp4            # human-readable report
    python3 jumpcheck.py clip.mp4 --json     # machine-readable
    python3 jumpcheck.py clip.mp4 --csv d.csv  # per-frame differences

Exit code 0 = nothing found (keyframe pulses are listed but not counted),
1 = at least one cut/flash/freeze/skip, 2 = could not read clip.
Needs ffmpeg/ffprobe on PATH and numpy.
"""
import argparse, json, subprocess, sys
import numpy as np


def probe(path):
    out = subprocess.run(
        ["ffprobe", "-v", "error", "-select_streams", "v:0", "-show_entries",
         "stream=width,height,avg_frame_rate", "-of", "json", path],
        capture_output=True, text=True, check=True).stdout
    s = json.loads(out)["streams"][0]
    num, den = s["avg_frame_rate"].split("/")
    return int(s["width"]), int(s["height"]), float(num) / float(den)


def frames(path, w, h):
    cmd = ["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-i", path, "-an", "-vf",
           f"scale={w}:{h}:flags=area", "-pix_fmt", "rgb24", "-f", "rawvideo", "-"]
    raw = subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, check=True).stdout
    n = len(raw) // (w * h * 3)
    return np.frombuffer(raw[: n * w * h * 3], np.uint8).reshape(n, h, w, 3).astype(np.int16)


def keyframes(path):
    """Indices of I-frames. Low-bitrate encodes 'pulse' on every keyframe,
    which looks like a small skip but is just the encoder refreshing detail."""
    out = subprocess.run(
        ["ffprobe", "-v", "error", "-select_streams", "v:0", "-show_entries",
         "frame=pict_type", "-of", "csv=p=0", path],
        capture_output=True, text=True, check=True).stdout.split()
    return {i for i, t in enumerate(out) if t.strip(",") == "I"}


def diff(a, b):
    return float(np.abs(a - b).mean())


def analyse(path, small_w=36, spike=4.0, floor=6.0, freeze_ratio=0.1, min_freeze_s=0.3):
    W, H, fps = probe(path)
    small_h = max(2, round(small_w * H / W / 2) * 2)
    f = frames(path, small_w, small_h)
    n = len(f)
    kf = keyframes(path)
    min_freeze = max(2, int(round(min_freeze_s * fps)))
    d = np.zeros(n)
    for i in range(1, n):
        d[i] = diff(f[i], f[i - 1])
    # typical motion around each frame: median of a 1-second window, excluding frame 0
    win = max(5, int(round(fps)))
    base = np.zeros(n)
    for i in range(1, n):
        lo, hi = max(1, i - win), min(n, i + win + 1)
        base[i] = np.median(d[lo:hi])
    typical = float(np.median(d[1:])) if n > 1 else 0.0
    events, i = [], 1
    is_spike = lambda k: d[k] > max(spike * base[k], floor)
    while i < n:
        if is_spike(i):
            # flash: spike in, spike out within 3 frames, and the frames either side match
            back = None
            for k in range(1, 4):
                j = i + k
                if j < n and is_spike(j) and diff(f[i - 1], f[j]) < max(spike * base[i], floor) / 2:
                    back = j
                    break
            if back:
                events.append({"type": "flash", "frame": i, "frames": back - i,
                               "time": round(i / fps, 3), "diff": round(float(d[i]), 2)})
                i = back + 1
                continue
            # does the picture stay changed? compare a frame before with a frame after
            after = min(n - 1, i + 2)
            kind = "cut" if diff(f[i - 1], f[after]) > max(spike * base[i], floor) else "jump"
            events.append({"type": kind, "frame": i, "time": round(i / fps, 3),
                           "diff": round(float(d[i]), 2), "typical": round(float(base[i]), 2)})
        elif d[i] < freeze_ratio * max(typical, 1e-6):
            j = i
            while j < n and d[j] < freeze_ratio * max(typical, 1e-6):
                j += 1
            if j - i + 1 >= min_freeze:
                events.append({"type": "freeze", "frame": i - 1, "frames": j - i + 1,
                               "time": round((i - 1) / fps, 3),
                               "seconds": round((j - i + 1) / fps, 3)})
            i = j
            continue
        elif d[i] > max(2.5 * base[i], 1.5 * typical) and d[i] > 1.0:
            events.append({"type": "keyframe" if i in kf else "skip", "frame": i, "time": round(i / fps, 3),
                           "diff": round(float(d[i]), 2), "typical": round(float(base[i]), 2)})
        i += 1
    return {"file": path, "frames": n, "fps": round(fps, 3), "size": f"{W}x{H}",
            "typical_diff": round(typical, 3), "max_diff": round(float(d.max()), 2),
            "events": events}, d


def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__.split("\n")[0])
    ap.add_argument("clip")
    ap.add_argument("--json", action="store_true")
    ap.add_argument("--csv")
    ap.add_argument("--width", type=int, default=36, help="analysis width in px (smaller = less grain)")
    ap.add_argument("--min-freeze", type=float, default=0.3, help="seconds of no change that count as a freeze")
    ap.add_argument("--spike", type=float, default=4.0, help="x typical motion that counts as a spike")
    a = ap.parse_args()
    try:
        rep, d = analyse(a.clip, small_w=a.width, spike=a.spike, min_freeze_s=a.min_freeze)
    except (subprocess.CalledProcessError, KeyError, IndexError, ValueError) as e:
        print(f"could not read {a.clip}: {e}", file=sys.stderr)
        return 2
    if a.csv:
        with open(a.csv, "w") as fh:
            fh.write("frame,time,diff\n")
            for i, v in enumerate(d):
                fh.write(f"{i},{i / rep['fps']:.3f},{v:.3f}\n")
    if a.json:
        print(json.dumps(rep, indent=2))
    else:
        print(f"{rep['file']}: {rep['frames']} frames @ {rep['fps']} fps, {rep['size']}, "
              f"typical frame-to-frame diff {rep['typical_diff']}, max {rep['max_diff']}")
        if not rep["events"]:
            print("  no cuts, flashes, freezes or skips found")
        for e in rep["events"]:
            extra = {k: v for k, v in e.items() if k not in ("type", "frame", "time")}
            print(f"  {e['type']:6} at {e['time']:6.3f}s (frame {e['frame']})  {extra}")
    real = [e for e in rep["events"] if e["type"] != "keyframe"]
    if any(e["type"] == "keyframe" for e in rep["events"]):
        print("  (keyframe = small pulse on an I-frame, usually encoder refresh; not counted)")
    return 1 if real else 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

Run it:

python3 jumpcheck.py clip.mp4          # report, exit 1 if anything found
python3 jumpcheck.py clip.mp4 --json   # for CI or a batch script
python3 jumpcheck.py clip.mp4 --csv diffs.csv   # plot the curve yourself

Planting defects to test it

You can't trust a detector you've only run on clean clips. make_glitch.sh takes any clip and plants one known defect at a known frame:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Make a test copy of a clip with one known defect, to check a jump detector.
#   ./make_glitch.sh in.mp4 cut|flash|freeze|drop|lowbitrate N out.mp4
#   cut        N ignored: from 4 s on, the picture is flipped and hue-rotated (a "different shot")
#   flash      N white frames starting at frame 90
#   freeze     frame 150 held for N frames (same total length)
#   drop       N frames removed starting at frame 120 (clip gets shorter, motion jumps)
#   lowbitrate N ignored: CRF 38 with a keyframe every 30 frames (encoder pulse, not a defect)
set -euo pipefail
in=$1; kind=$2; n=$3; out=$4
enc=(-c:v libx264 -preset veryfast -crf 20 -pix_fmt yuv420p)
case $kind in
  cut) ffmpeg -v error -y -i "$in" -filter_complex \
        "[0:v]split[a][b];[a]trim=0:4,setpts=PTS-STARTPTS[a2];[b]trim=4,setpts=PTS-STARTPTS,vflip,hue=h=120[b2];[a2][b2]concat=n=2:v=1:a=0,fps=30[v]" \
        -map "[v]" -map 0:a? "${enc[@]}" -c:a copy "$out" ;;
  flash) ffmpeg -v error -y -i "$in" -vf "drawbox=0:0:iw:ih:color=white:t=fill:enable='between(n,90,$((90+n-1)))'" \
        "${enc[@]}" -c:a copy "$out" ;;
  freeze) ffmpeg -v error -y -i "$in" -filter_complex "[0:v]split[a][b];[a][b]freezeframes=first=150:last=$((150+n-1)):replace=150[v]" \
        -map "[v]" -map 0:a? "${enc[@]}" -c:a copy "$out" ;;
  drop) ffmpeg -v error -y -i "$in" -vf "select='not(between(n,120,$((120+n-1))))',setpts=N/30/TB" -an -r 30 "${enc[@]}" "$out" ;;
  lowbitrate) ffmpeg -v error -y -i "$in" -c:v libx264 -preset veryfast -crf 38 -g 30 -pix_fmt yuv420p -c:a copy "$out" ;;
  *) echo "unknown kind $kind" >&2; exit 2 ;;
esac
echo "wrote $out ($kind $n)"

The base clip comes from a small synthetic generator (make_field_test_clip.sh: gradient sky, noisy field, red box with white text swaying on a sine, beeps over a hum). It's in the same folder as the scripts.

Results

Same base clip, one defect at a time:

Test clip jumpcheck.py found Exit
clean clip, grain 18 nothing (typical diff 1.07, max 1.54) 0
hard cut at 4.0 s cut at frame 120, diff 102.3 vs local 1.12 1
1 white frame at 3.0 s flash at frame 90, 1 frame 1
2 white frames at 3.0 s flash at frame 90, 2 frames 1
frame 150 held 15 frames freeze at 5.0 s, 0.5 s 1
15 frames dropped at 4.0 s skip at frame 120, diff 4.06 vs 1.11 1
clean clip, no grain nothing (typical 0.245) 0
clean clip scaled to 480x854 nothing 0
clean clip re-encoded CRF 38, keyframe every 30 7 keyframe pulses listed, not counted 0
file that doesn't exist error message 2

For comparison: ffmpeg's scdet

ffmpeg ships a scene-change filter, so the obvious question is why not just use it:

ffmpeg -i clip.mp4 -vf "scdet=threshold=10,metadata=print:file=scd.txt" -f null -

On the same planted clips at threshold=10:

Defect Highest lavfi.scd.score Flagged?
clean 0.17 no
hard cut 24.5 (frame 120) yes
1 white frame 36.8 (frame 90) yes, but only the entry. The exit frame scored low, so it looks just like a cut
15-frame freeze 2.4 no
15 dropped frames 0.9 no

That isn't a bug. scdet is built to find scene changes, and its score is roughly "how much did the frame difference jump compared with the previous difference". The return from a flash is a big difference right after another big difference, so it scores low. Freezes and small skips aren't scene changes at all. If all you need is real cuts, scdet is fine. To tell a flash from a cut, or catch the quieter defects, you need the raw curve.

Two false alarms that shaped the defaults

1. Low-bitrate keyframe "pulses." I re-encoded the clean clip at CRF 38 with a keyframe every 30 frames. The first version of the script reported seven "skips" at frames 29, 58, 87 and so on, exactly 29 frames apart. ffprobe -show_entries frame=pict_type showed an I-frame at every one of them. At low bitrate, every keyframe refreshes detail the P-frames had smeared away, and that registers as a small jump. The script now asks ffprobe for I-frame positions, labels those events keyframe and leaves them out of the exit code.

The cost of that choice is that a real skip landing on a keyframe gets hidden. This happened once in the dataset grid I mention below. Before I made the test clip deterministic, a 10-frame drop got labelled keyframe because x264 had put an I-frame right at the jump. If you have a clip that already feels wrong, also read the keyframe lines.

2. Slow motion looks like a freeze. With grain turned off, the test banner moves less than a pixel per frame at the slow ends of its sway. After encoding, some frames come out identical. The first version flagged eight "freezes" of 3-7 frames (0.1-0.23 s) in a perfectly fine clip. Raising the minimum to 0.3 s removed all of them and still caught the planted 15-frame freeze. A 0.1 s pause in an AI clip is rarely what people mean by "it froze".

Where it stops working

  • Tiny skips are invisible. On the grainy clip, dropping 1, 2 or 5 frames wasn't detected. The motion jump is smaller than the grain. On the grain-free clip, 5 dropped frames were caught (diff 1.59 vs typical 0.244) but 1-2 weren't. Freezes of 3 and 6 frames were not reported (by design, under 0.3 s); 9 and 15 were. A full grid of these cases is in the dataset linked at the end.
  • A cut to a similar-looking shot can slip through. My cut fixture flips the picture and rotates the hue, so it's an obvious change. A cut between two nearly identical framings won't produce a big spike.
  • The freeze after-effect. When a freeze ends, the motion catches up in one frame. On the grain-free clip that catch-up was also reported as a skip. It isn't a second defect, just the other end of the same freeze.
  • Thresholds were tuned on synthetic clips. Real footage with camera shake will need --spike raised.

What to do with the list

  • It's your own edit. Look at the reported frame first. Flashes and freezes usually come from a transition, a bad cut point or a dropped frame in the export. Trim with frame accuracy (re-encode, don't stream-copy) and run the check again.
  • The clip came out of the generator like that. The studio's help page separates a failed generation from one that looks wrong. Looking different from your photo isn't a failed order on its own. If you write to support, a frame number and a timestamp make the report concrete. The address is on the help page.

For reference, the pricing page listed these per-clip prices when I checked on November 13, 2026: 480p $7.98, 720p $9.98, 1080p $16.98, 4k $24.98, tax added at checkout. Check the page itself before you rely on them.

Measured grid

I ran the planted defects at several sizes (flash 1-3 frames, freeze 3-15, drop 1-15) on a grainy and a grain-free source, with fixed random seeds so it reproduces exactly. The 30 rows are in the bamabound-guides dataset on Hugging Face (config jump_detection), along with the script that rebuilds them.

title: How to Run Two Claude Desktop Accounts on One Mac (With Separate Dock Icons and Shared Context)
description:
I run my daily operations and recurring routines inside Claude Desktop's Code tab: morning check-ins at 08:45, weekly planning, Telegram community digests, and weekly SEO and AEO checks for this blog.

Running everything on a single account has a structural flaw. Paid Claude plans have a session limit that resets every five hours, plus weekly limits. When a heavy coding or video-rendering session burns through that session limit in 45 minutes, every scheduled task on that account hits the same wall and stalls.

I wanted two Claude accounts running in parallel on the same Mac mini:

  1. Account 1 (Routines): my existing account, left completely untouched, so all scheduled tasks, mail connectors and morning check-ins keep running on autopilot.
  2. Account 2 (Engineer): a second account dedicated to hands-on coding, debugging and content work.

And I needed two things most multi-account guides skip: the two accounts had to share the same project memory and skills without duplicating scheduled tasks, and they needed different icons in the macOS Dock so I wouldn't click the wrong window twenty times a day.

Short answer

You don't need to log out and back in, and you don't need to migrate your existing scheduled tasks. Leave your original Claude.app untouched for routines, and launch a second instance for daily work by passing both --user-data-dir (which isolates the Electron desktop app) and CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR (which isolates the Claude Code engine). To give the second window its own teal Dock icon and an "Engineer" label without breaking Apple's code signature, launch an unmodified APFS clone (cp -cR) at ~/Applications/Engineer.app through a small launcher, and symlink only skills, agents and projects between the two config folders.

Why --user-data-dir alone isn't enough

Most guides for running multiple Claude accounts focus either on the terminal CLI or on the chat window. If you use the Code tab inside Claude Desktop, two separate layers store your login and state:

Layer Setting What it isolates
Claude Desktop (Electron) --user-data-dir Desktop login, claude_desktop_config.json (MCP servers), the sidebar session list
Claude Code engine CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR Code tab credentials (a macOS Keychain entry), scheduled-tasks/, projects/, settings.json

Where each account keeps them:

Layer Account 1 (Routines) Account 2 (Engineer)
Claude Desktop ~/Library/Application Support/Claude ~/Library/Application Support/Claude-Work
Claude Code ~/.claude (variable left unset) ~/.claude-work

If you only pass --user-data-dir, the Desktop window opens a new account, but the Code tab inside it still uses ~/.claude and bills your original account. To isolate both, you have to pass both.

One macOS Keychain trap: leave CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR unset for your original account. Pointing it at ~/.claude explicitly can make Claude Code look up a different Keychain entry than the default, so your existing login seems to disappear. Only set the variable for the second account.

What didn't work: editing Info.plist, and a plain AppleScript launcher

Before landing on the working setup, I hit two dead ends that come up in almost every forum thread on this:

  • Dead end 1: editing Info.plist and re-signing the app. Some guides suggest duplicating Claude.app, changing CFBundleName and CFBundleIdentifier in Info.plist, replacing the binary with a wrapper script, and running codesign. On recent macOS and Electron builds, modifying any file inside the signed bundle strips Anthropic's entitlements. The app crashes on launch with EXC_BREAKPOINT (SIGTRAP) inside Electron Framework.
  • Dead end 2: a plain AppleScript launcher pointing at /Applications/Claude.app. An osacompile applet that runs open -n -a "/Applications/Claude.app" works without crashing. But even if you paste a custom icon onto the launcher in Finder, the launcher exits in a tenth of a second and /Applications/Claude.app is what stays in the Dock. You end up with two identical orange Claude icons in the Dock and in window switchers.

The fix: an unmodified APFS clone, a launcher and a recolored icon

The trick is to separate the launcher from an unmodified APFS clone:

  1. Copy /Applications/Claude.app to ~/Applications/Engineer.app with cp -cR. On APFS this creates a clone: it finishes instantly, uses no extra disk space, and leaves every file inside Contents/ untouched, so Gatekeeper and Electron never complain.
  2. Attach a custom icon to the outside of the bundle with macOS's NSWorkspace API. Finder stores custom icons in an extended attribute (com.apple.FinderInfo and an Icon\r file), outside the code-signing seal.
  3. Create a tiny launcher at /Applications/Engineer.app that starts ~/Applications/Engineer.app with --env "CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR=..." and --args "--user-data-dir=...".

Because the running process is ~/Applications/Engineer.app, the Dock shows its custom icon and Engineer as the tooltip.


The two icons I keep in the Dock: the original Claude app for routines, and the recolored Engineer clone for hands-on work. Both icons are taken from the apps on my Mac.

In the real Dock, hovering over each icon shows its own name:


Hovering over the teal icon: Engineer.


Hovering over the orange icon: Claude.

Step 1: Create the isolated Engineer app and launcher

Open Terminal and run:

mkdir -p "$HOME/Applications" "$HOME/.claude-work" "$HOME/Library/Application Support/Claude-Work" &&
rm -rf "$HOME/Applications/Engineer.app" "/Applications/Engineer.app" &&
cp -cR "/Applications/Claude.app" "$HOME/Applications/Engineer.app" &&
osacompile -o "/Applications/Engineer.app" \
  -e 'do shell script "open -n -a \"$HOME/Applications/Engineer.app\" --env \"CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR=$HOME/.claude-work\" --args \"--user-data-dir=$HOME/Library/Application Support/Claude-Work\""'

Step 2: Recolor the original Claude icon to teal

Instead of hunting for a third-party PNG, you can use macOS's built-in CoreImage (CIHueAdjust) from Terminal. It takes Claude's official icon, keeps the transparent rounded corners and the white starburst, rotates the orange background 180 degrees to teal, and applies it to both Engineer.app bundles:

osascript -l JavaScript -e 'ObjC.import("Cocoa"); ObjC.import("CoreImage"); var ws = $.NSWorkspace.sharedWorkspace; var orig = ws.iconForFile("/Applications/Claude.app"); orig.setSize($.NSMakeSize(512, 512)); var ci = $.CIImage.imageWithData(orig.TIFFRepresentation); var f = $.CIFilter.filterWithName("CIHueAdjust"); f.setValueForKey(ci, "inputImage"); f.setValueForKey(3.14159, "inputAngle"); var rep = $.NSCIImageRep.imageRepWithCIImage(f.valueForKey("outputImage")); var img = $.NSImage.alloc.initWithSize($.NSMakeSize(512, 512)); img.addRepresentation(rep); ws.setIconForFileOptions(img, "/Applications/Engineer.app", 0); ws.setIconForFileOptions(img, ObjC.unwrap($.NSHomeDirectory()) + "/Applications/Engineer.app", 0);' && killall Dock Finder

If you prefer emerald green instead of blue, change 3.14159 to 2.1.

Step 3: Sign in to the second account without the deep-link mix-up

Claude Desktop signs in through your browser and passes the login back through a claude:// deep link. If two Claude instances are open at the same time, macOS often hands that callback to the wrong window.

For the first login only:

  1. Quit your original Claude app (Cmd + Q).
  2. Open Engineer from /Applications and sign in with your second Claude account (or use the email verification code instead of clicking the magic link).
  3. Switch to the Code tab inside Engineer and confirm that /status shows your second account.

Keeping both accounts in sync (without duplicating scheduled tasks)

Two isolated folders mean the new account starts empty: none of your installed skills, subagents, MCP servers or conversation transcripts are there.

The key is selective symlinking:

ln -sfn "$HOME/.claude/skills" "$HOME/.claude-work/skills" &&
ln -sfn "$HOME/.claude/agents" "$HOME/.claude-work/agents" &&
ln -sfn "$HOME/.claude/projects" "$HOME/.claude-work/projects" &&
cp "$HOME/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json" \
   "$HOME/Library/Application Support/Claude-Work/claude_desktop_config.json"

Here is why this split works:

  • What stays separate (scheduled-tasks/ and credentials): local scheduled tasks live under ~/.claude/scheduled-tasks/<task-name>/SKILL.md. By not symlinking scheduled-tasks/, all routines stay on Account 1. If you symlinked that folder, both open apps would fire every scheduled task twice.
  • What is shared on disk (skills/, agents/, projects/): Claude Code stores session transcripts and per-project auto memory (MEMORY.md) under ~/.claude/projects/, grouped by working directory, regardless of which account paid for the tokens. Symlinking projects/ lets either account resume or search conversations started by the other.
  • Project-level context (CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md): because both accounts open the same project folders on disk, shared files like CLAUDE.md, Now.md and project logs are read and updated by both accounts in real time.

Pairing each Claude account with its own Chrome profile

Several of my scheduled tasks read signed-in pages in Chrome through the Claude in Chrome extension. If two Claude instances try to share a single Chrome profile, they fight over the connection.

A Claude Desktop instance connects to Chrome through Anthropic's bridge and only sees Chrome extensions signed in to the same Claude account. That makes isolating browsers straightforward:

  1. Leave your original Chrome profile as it is. Its Claude in Chrome extension is already signed in to Account 1 (Routines). Keep the web sessions your scheduled tasks read (Search Console, Bing Webmaster Tools, Telegram Web, analytics dashboards) logged in there.
  2. Create a second Chrome profile for Engineer. Install the Claude in Chrome extension in the new profile and sign the extension in to Account 2.
  3. Lock the pairing once. With both Chrome profiles open, type /chrome inside an Engineer Code session (or ask it to switch browser) and approve the connection in the new Chrome window. Claude remembers the paired browser for future sessions.

Two gotchas to keep in mind

  1. Launch order matters (Claude.app first, Engineer.app second). Both apps share the same internal CFBundleIdentifier, so clicking the stock orange Claude.app icon while Engineer is already running tells macOS LaunchServices to focus the running Engineer window instead of starting a new process. Always start your main Claude.app first (it runs your background routines anyway, so it stays open all day), then launch Engineer.app. Because the Engineer launcher passes open -n, it always opens its own window.
  2. After a Claude Desktop update, refresh the clone. When /Applications/Claude.app auto-updates, your APFS clone at ~/Applications/Engineer.app stays on the previous build until you re-run the cp -cR and icon commands above.

Checklist

  1. Keep Account 1 (scheduled tasks and routines) on the default /Applications/Claude.app and ~/.claude.
  2. Create an unmodified APFS clone at ~/Applications/Engineer.app and a launcher at /Applications/Engineer.app that passes both --env "CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR=$HOME/.claude-work" and --args "--user-data-dir=$HOME/Library/Application Support/Claude-Work".
  3. Run the CoreImage one-liner to give Engineer a teal Claude icon in the Dock and window switcher.
  4. Quit the main app once, sign in to Account 2 inside Engineer, then reopen the main app.
  5. Symlink skills, agents and projects from ~/.claude to ~/.claude-work, copy claude_desktop_config.json, and leave scheduled-tasks unlinked.
  6. Sign a second Chrome profile's Claude extension in to Account 2 and pair it with /chrome.

If you're building AI-native workflows around your business, or want a hand setting up a system like this without breaking your existing tools, get in touch.

Originally published on my blog.

title: One of the amazing react feature!!
description:
Context API is a react feature used to share data between multiple components without using props methods.

By using props method here comes the issue named props drilling ,shows that the same data have pass through each component, if some components doesn't need that data but also have access of it.

So to avoid this we using context

How Context API works
Context API mainly involves three things:

  1. createContext() – Creates a context.
  2. Provider – Makes data available to child components.
  3. useContext() – Allows components to access that data.

title: How we cut our homepage from 4 MB to 179 KB and reached Lighthouse 100
description:
Two PNG images made up almost all of quantumines.com's 4 MB homepage. Serving them as AVIF and WebP at the size each screen needs cut the page to 179 KB and the mobile Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) from about 17 seconds to 1.8 seconds. Self-hosted fonts with size-matched fallbacks, two colour fixes and an accessible-name fix took the remaining Lighthouse scores to 100. We made all of these changes on 10 November 2026 in one commit. This write-up lists each one, with the code, so another small team can repeat it in an afternoon.

Where did the 4 MB come from?

The network list in Lighthouse and Chrome DevTools answered that quickly. The homepage loaded a 2.0 MB PNG for the hero sculpture and a 2.1 MB PNG for the product artwork, both exported straight from a design tool at full quality. Everything else on the page, HTML, CSS, JavaScript and icons, was small. A 1.6 MB logo PNG was also referenced from our structured data, though not displayed.

On a phone over a throttled mobile connection, which is what Lighthouse simulates, two megabytes take many seconds to arrive. And because the hero is the largest thing on screen, it is the element LCP measures: until it finishes, the page counts as not loaded.

quantumines.com homepage before and after (Lighthouse mobile, 10 November 2026)

Measure Before After
Total page weight about 4 MB 179 KB
Largest Contentful Paint (mobile) about 17 s 1.8 s
Accessibility score 96 100
All four Lighthouse categories not all 100 100 / 100 / 100 / 100
Cumulative Layout Shift not recorded 0

Step 1: serve images as AVIF and WebP, at the right size

We exported each large image three times (480, 768 and 1,024 pixels wide for the hero) in AVIF and in WebP, and let the browser pick with <picture>, srcset and sizes. The 1,024-pixel hero dropped from 2.0 MB as PNG to 44 KB as AVIF; a phone downloads the 480-pixel AVIF, which is 12.5 KB.

<picture>
  <source type="image/avif"
    srcset="assets/hero-480.avif 480w, assets/hero-768.avif 768w, assets/hero-1024.avif 1024w"
    sizes="(max-width: 760px) 100vw, 55vw">
  <source type="image/webp"
    srcset="assets/hero-480.webp 480w, assets/hero-768.webp 768w, assets/hero-1024.webp 1024w"
    sizes="(max-width: 760px) 100vw, 55vw">
  <img id="hero-image" src="assets/hero-1024.webp"
    alt="Sculpture of mint metal, glass and textured stone"
    width="1024" height="1280" fetchpriority="high">
</picture>

Three details matter. The width and height attributes let the browser reserve the space before the image arrives, so nothing jumps. fetchpriority="high" tells it to fetch the LCP image before other images. And the hero is never lazy-loaded: lazy loading the largest image on screen delays exactly the thing LCP measures. The product artwork, further down the page, got the same AVIF and WebP treatment at 768 and 1,536 pixels.

The 1.6 MB logo in our Organization schema was replaced with a 512-pixel PNG of 137 KB. Search engines don't need more than that, and it no longer turns up in audits.

Step 2: self-host the fonts and stop the text from jumping

The site used Manrope and DM Sans from Google Fonts. That meant a render-blocking stylesheet request to another domain, then the font files from a third. We downloaded the variable versions of both (they are under the SIL Open Font License), serve them as WOFF2 from our own domain and preload them:

<link rel="preload" href="/fonts/manrope-var.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>
<link rel="preload" href="/fonts/dm-sans-var.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>

With font-display: swap, text appears at once in a fallback font and switches when the web font arrives. The switch can move text, because Arial is wider or taller than the real font. So we defined fallback faces measured against Arial, with size-adjust and the ascent and descent overrides, and listed them right after the real font:

@font-face {
  font-family: 'Manrope Fallback';
  src: local('Arial'), local('Liberation Sans'), local('Helvetica');
  size-adjust: 94.9%;
  ascent-override: 112.4%;
  descent-override: 31.6%;
  line-gap-override: 0%;
}
--display: 'Manrope', 'Manrope Fallback', sans-serif;

Together with the image dimensions, this is why Cumulative Layout Shift is 0.

Step 3: fix the last accessibility points

Accessibility was at 96. Lighthouse flagged two things. Some muted text in the light theme was below the 4.5:1 contrast ratio that WCAG requires for normal text, so we darkened those colours until each passed. And the mobile menu button's accessible name didn't match its visible label "Menu", which confuses people who use voice control: they say what they see. Making the name match the label fixed it. Both changes took minutes; finding them is what the audit is for.

Step 4: cache by file type

Our Node server sets Cache-Control from the file extension. Fonts never change under the same name, so browsers may keep them for a year. Images can be kept for a week and refreshed in the background. HTML, CSS and JavaScript are checked again after an hour, so a deploy shows up quickly:

ext === '.woff2' ? 'public, max-age=31536000, immutable'
: /^(\.avif|\.webp|\.png|\.jpe?g|\.svg|\.ico)$/.test(ext)
  ? 'public, max-age=604800, stale-while-revalidate=86400'
  : 'public, max-age=3600'

Step 5: make the next page feel instant

Two newer browser features cost a few lines each. Speculation Rules tell Chrome to prefetch a same-site page when the visitor hovers over its link, so the click usually lands on a page that is already downloaded. We exclude anything with side effects or private data, such as log-in, the app, admin pages and the API:

<script type="speculationrules">
{"prefetch":[{"source":"document","where":{"and":[
  {"href_matches":"/*"},
  {"not":{"href_matches":["/login","/app/*","/admin/*","/api/*","/logout"]}}
]},"eagerness":"moderate"}]}
</script>

Cross-document view transitions add a short cross-fade between pages with one CSS rule, turned off for people who ask their system for reduced motion:

@view-transition { navigation: auto; }
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  @view-transition { navigation: none; }
}

Browsers that don't support either feature ignore them, so there is no downside for anyone.

How do we keep it at 100?

Scores drift as pages are added. Every time the site is rebuilt, we run Lighthouse on the homepage, the newest post and one product page, and fix anything below 95 before it goes live. New images must be AVIF or WebP with width, height and srcset. Each page's preview image for social media is generated at build time, so nobody uploads a multi-megabyte PNG by hand. The same discipline carried over to adding WebMCP for AI agents: the site still scores 100 in all four categories with it.

What would we tell another small team?

  • Open the network list before touching code. On most small sites one or two images are most of the weight.
  • Fix the LCP image first: modern format, right size, fetchpriority="high", never lazy.
  • Give every image width and height, and give web fonts a size-matched fallback. That is most of CLS.
  • Treat accessibility warnings as bugs. They are usually quick to fix and they affect real people.
  • Re-run the audit on every build, not once a quarter.

Frequently asked questions

Is AVIF supported in all browsers?

AVIF works in current versions of Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari. The <picture> element falls back to WebP and then to the <img> source, so older browsers still get an image.

What is a good Largest Contentful Paint?

Google's Core Web Vitals treat an LCP of 2.5 seconds or less as good, measured at the 75th percentile of real page loads. quantumines.com's homepage measures 1.8 seconds in Lighthouse's mobile test.

Does a Lighthouse score of 100 guarantee good Core Web Vitals?

No. Lighthouse is a lab test on one simulated device. Core Web Vitals in Search Console come from real visitors' browsers. A high lab score makes good field data likely, but the field data is what Google uses.

Quantumines is a technology and product studio in Lahore, Pakistan, founded by Muhammad Ali Raza (Ali Arbi). We build websites and web apps for clients with the same standards; see our services.

title: Tracking the stablecoin supply drop with 30 lines of Node
description:
Why this number now

On 11 November 2026, Glassnode reported that the supply of major stablecoins fell $14.2 billion over 30 days, the largest 30-day contraction since June 2022 (The Block, Cointelegraph, Crypto Briefing). Stablecoin supply only shrinks when holders redeem tokens with the issuer, so analysts read it as cash leaving the crypto market.

Outlets quoted different totals for the remaining supply: "just below $280 billion" in one, "$290 to $293 billion" in another. I wanted to see the raw series myself, and DefiLlama publishes it for free with no API key.

The script

It uses built-in fetch (Node 18+) and two public endpoints:

  • https://stablecoins.llama.fi/stablecoincharts/all returns one point per day with totalCirculatingUSD.peggedUSD.
  • https://stablecoins.llama.fi/stablecoins returns every stablecoin with circulating and circulatingPrevMonth. 
// supply-change.mjs
// Usage: node supply-change.mjs [days]
const DAYS = Number(process.argv[2] || 30);
const usd = (n) => `${n < 0 ? '-' : ''}$${(Math.abs(n) / 1e9).toFixed(2)}B`;

// 1. Total supply of USD-pegged stablecoins, one point per day
const chart = await (await fetch('https://stablecoins.llama.fi/stablecoincharts/all')).json();
const total = chart.map((d) => ({
  day: new Date(Number(d.date) * 1000).toISOString().slice(0, 10),
  v: d.totalCirculatingUSD?.peggedUSD ?? 0,
}));
const now = total.at(-1);
const then = total.at(-1 - DAYS);
const pct = ((now.v / then.v - 1) * 100).toFixed(2);
console.log(`Total: ${usd(then.v)} on ${then.day} -> ${usd(now.v)} on ${now.day} (${usd(now.v - then.v)}, ${pct}%)`);

// 2. The six largest USD stablecoins: today vs a month ago
const { peggedAssets } = await (await fetch('https://stablecoins.llama.fi/stablecoins?includePrices=false')).json();
const rows = peggedAssets
  .filter((a) => a.pegType === 'peggedUSD')
  .map((a) => ({ sym: a.symbol, now: a.circulating?.peggedUSD ?? 0, month: a.circulatingPrevMonth?.peggedUSD ?? 0 }))
  .sort((a, b) => b.now - a.now)
  .slice(0, 6);
for (const r of rows) {
  const d = r.now - r.month;
  console.log(`${r.sym.padEnd(6)} ${usd(r.now).padStart(9)}  ${d >= 0 ? '+' : ''}${usd(d)}`);
}

What it printed

I ran it at 01:50 UTC on 13 November 2026:

Total: $303.97B on 2026-10-14 -> $287.71B on 2026-11-13 (-$16.26B, -5.35%)
USDT    $175.48B  -$8.43B
USDC     $69.45B  -$3.69B
USDS      $5.38B  -$1.58B
USDe      $4.90B  +$0.14B
DAI       $4.66B  -$0.08B
USD1      $3.17B  -$1.04B

My window ends three days after Glassnode's and DefiLlama tracks more coins, so -$16.26B versus -$14.2B is expected. The direction matches, and USDT plus USDC make up about $12.1B of the drop, close to the "nearly $11 billion" The Block reported for those two.

Things that tripped me up

  • date in the chart endpoint is a Unix timestamp in seconds, as a string. Number(d.date) * 1000 before building a Date.
  • circulatingPrevMonth is a rolling value from DefiLlama's side, so it won't line up with the chart's day-30 point to the cent. Use the chart for the total and the per-coin fields for the breakdown.
  • Filter on pegType === 'peggedUSD'. Without it, euro and gold tokens end up in your top six.
  • Different trackers include different coins. That explains most of the disagreement between published totals.

Ideas to extend it

  • Run it daily from a cron job and alert when the 30-day change flips positive. Glassnode called that the first sign of new money coming in.
  • Break USDT down by chain with the chainCirculating field to see which networks lost the most.

Sources: Glassnode via The Block (11 Nov 2026), Cointelegraph (12 Nov 2026), Crypto Briefing (11 Nov 2026), DefiLlama stablecoin API.

title: Our Restaurant TV Menu Never Showed Page 5: A Polling Refresh, a Rotating Carousel and Array Identity in React
description:
We build a point-of-sale and QR menu product for cafes and restaurants. One small feature is a TV menu: a public URL that the restaurant types into the browser of the smart TV hanging in the dining room. It shows the whole menu in large type, product names on the left, prices on the right. No ordering, no clicks. Customers look at it and tell the waiter what they want.

Two requirements shaped the screen. First, the TV must never need a human. If the owner changes a price in the admin panel, the TV has to pick it up on its own, so the page polls the menu endpoint every 60 seconds. Second, the menu must never scroll. A cafe with 20 items gets one screen with big letters. A restaurant with 300 items gets split into pages, and the pages rotate every 15 seconds.

Both requirements worked in testing. Together they produced a bug that only shows up with a long menu: the TV never showed anything after page 4.

The setup

Stripped down, the component looked like this:

const [sections, setSections] = useState<Section[]>([]);
const [page, setPage] = useState(0);

// 1. Poll the menu every 60 s
useEffect(() => {
  const load = async () => {
    const menu = await api.fullMenu(slug);
    setSections(menu.sections);
  };
  load();
  const t = setInterval(load, 60_000);
  return () => clearInterval(t);
}, [slug]);

// 2. Measure rendered heights, split into pages
const pages = useMemo(() => paginate(sections, columns, measurement),
  [sections, columns, measurement]);

// 3. Data or layout changed: go back to the first page
useEffect(() => { setPage(0); }, [sections, columns, measurement]);

// 4. Rotate pages
useEffect(() => {
  if (pages.length < 2) return;
  const t = setInterval(() => setPage(p => (p + 1) % pages.length), 15_000);
  return () => clearInterval(t);
}, [pages.length]);

Effect 3 is reasonable on its own. If the owner deletes a category and the menu shrinks from 9 pages to 6, the current page index might point past the end. Resetting to page 0 when the data changes is the simple, safe answer.

What actually happened

Every 60 seconds, effect 1 called setSections with a freshly parsed array from the API. The content was identical to the previous response, but the array was new. React compares dependencies with Object.is, so to React the sections had changed.

That set off a chain:

  1. sections changed, so the measurement effect re-ran and produced a new measurement object.
  2. sections and measurement changed, so effect 3 ran and set the page back to 0.
  3. pages.length was still 9, so the rotation interval was not restarted. It just kept ticking from wherever it was.

With a 15-second page duration and a 60-second refresh, the timeline looked like this:

Time What the TV shows
0 s page 1
15 s page 2
30 s page 3
45 s page 4
60 s refresh: back to page 1
75 s page 2

A full tour of 9 pages takes 135 seconds. The refresh fired every 60. Pages 5 to 9 were never displayed. Ever. Small menus were fine because they fit on 4 pages or fewer, and so did our test data.

The bug was invisible in development for the same reason. Nobody sits and watches a carousel for two minutes. And when you reload the page to check something, you start at page 1 anyway, which looks correct.

Why the usual checks missed it

There was nothing to catch. No error, no warning, no failed request. The network tab showed a successful request every minute. React DevTools showed the component re-rendering once a minute, which is what polling is supposed to do. Each piece did what it was written to do. The bug lived in the interaction between two timers with different periods and a reset rule that treated "new object" as "new data".

For a restaurant, that means whatever sits at the end of the menu, often desserts and drinks, simply does not exist on the TV.

The fix: only touch state when the content changes

The fix was to stop handing React a new array when nothing had changed. We build a signature from the fields that actually affect what the TV draws and compare it with the last one:

const signatureRef = useRef<string>("");

const load = async () => {
  const menu = await api.fullMenu(slug);
  const next = menu.sections ?? [];
  const signature = JSON.stringify(
    next.map(s => [
      s.id, s.name, s.image,
      s.products.map(p => [
        p.id, p.name, p.price, p.isAvailable, p.soldOut, p.description,
        (p.priceOptions ?? []).map(o => [o.id, o.name, o.price]),
      ]),
    ])
  );
  if (signature !== signatureRef.current) {
    signatureRef.current = signature;
    setSections(next);
  }
};

Now an unchanged response does nothing. No new array, no new measurement, no reset. The carousel keeps rotating through all 9 pages. When the owner changes a price, the signature changes, the menu re-renders with the new price and the reset to page 1 is the correct behaviour, because the layout may have changed.

A few notes on the choice:

  • Why not compare the whole response? The API also returns things the TV ignores, such as timestamps and fields used by the ordering screen. Including them would make the signature change for reasons the customer cannot see. The signature lists exactly what is drawn.
  • Why JSON.stringify and not a deep-equal library? The menu is a few hundred products at most. Stringifying it once a minute costs less than a millisecond on a TV browser, and the code is obvious to the next person who reads it.
  • Why a ref and not state? The signature is bookkeeping. Storing it in state would itself cause a render.

The general lesson

The pattern is common: a polling hook or a WebSocket feed sets state on every message, and somewhere downstream an effect treats "the dependency changed" as "the data changed". In most components this costs an extra render and nobody notices. It becomes a bug when the downstream effect does something visible or stateful: resets a page, clears a form, scrolls to the top, restarts an animation, refetches something else.

What we check now when a component both polls and holds UI state:

  1. Does the fetch set state unconditionally? If so, ask whether an unchanged response should be a no-op. It usually should.
  2. Which effects depend on the polled data, and do any of them reset something? Reset effects are where identity changes turn into user-visible behaviour.
  3. Are there two timers with different periods? A refresh interval and a rotation interval, a refresh and a debounce, a refresh and a toast timeout. Write down the timeline for the longest realistic case, like we did in the table above. Ten seconds with a pencil would have found this bug.
  4. Test with production-sized data. A short test menu fits on a page or two. The bug needed more than four.

Libraries like TanStack Query help here because they keep referential identity for unchanged data through structural sharing. If you write the polling yourself, you get to do that part yourself.

A related design choice

The same screen does not hide sold-out products. They stay in place, dimmed, with a "SOLD OUT" label. Removing them would reflow the whole menu and move items between pages every time stock changed, which is the same kind of surprise from the customer's side: the thing you were reading a moment ago is somewhere else now.

We write about the products behind this, restaurant POS and QR menus among them, at alestaweb.com. The TV screen itself is one URL and a smart TV browser, which is about as low-tech as a feature gets. It still managed to hide more than half of a long menu.

title: Travel Itinerary Retrieval: Document Lineage and Freshness for Planner Systems Explained
description:
When an itinerary changes, retrieve the newest valid document for the trip, but keep the older version available for explanation. That is the decision rule: current answers need an explicit version boundary, not a larger top-k.

Short answer: store each itinerary revision as an immutable document, retrieve by a stable trip key plus an “active at” timestamp, and carry the revision ID into every chunk and citation. A planner can then answer “what is booked now?” without losing the ability to explain what changed.

This is a retrieval architecture problem, not a vector-database shopping problem. A travel itinerary planner may have a booking confirmation, an airline schedule update, a hotel message, and a manually edited day plan that all refer to the same trip. Similar wording does not make those records interchangeable.

How can a travel itinerary planner retrieve the right document version?

Start with two identities: trip_id identifies the journey, while revision_id identifies one immutable snapshot of its source document. A chunk gets both IDs, along with effective_from, effective_until, source_type, and a content hash. The active revision is a query decision; the source document itself never gets rewritten in place.

That distinction fixes a common failure mode. A team overwrites “Paris-plan.md” after a train time changes, re-embeds the file, and later discovers that an answer cites a chunk whose text no longer matches the booking record. The index may be fresh, but the evidence trail is gone. Version lineage gives the answer layer something stable to display and gives an evaluator a precise target.

The retrieval flow is deliberately plain. Normalize the user's trip reference, resolve the permitted revision set, search only chunks in that set, then group results by revision_id before composing an answer. A reranker may improve ordering, but it must not decide which revisions are valid. Freshness and authorization happen before ranking.

Keep history.

Here is a small, runnable Python sketch. It uses an in-memory list so the version rule is visible without hiding it behind a framework.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime, timezone


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Chunk:
    trip_id: str
    revision_id: str
    text: str
    effective_from: datetime
    effective_until: datetime | None
    source_type: str


def active_chunks(chunks: list[Chunk], trip_id: str, at: datetime) -> list[Chunk]:
    candidates = [
        chunk
        for chunk in chunks
        if chunk.trip_id == trip_id
        and chunk.effective_from <= at
        and (chunk.effective_until is None or at < chunk.effective_until)
    ]
    newest_by_revision = {}
    for chunk in candidates:
        newest_by_revision.setdefault(chunk.revision_id, []).append(chunk)
    if not newest_by_revision:
        return []
    newest_revision = max(
        newest_by_revision,
        key=lambda revision: max(
            item.effective_from for item in newest_by_revision[revision]
        ),
    )
    return newest_by_revision[newest_revision]


now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
records = [
    Chunk(
        trip_id="trip-204",
        revision_id="rev-08",
        text="Rail from Lyon to Paris departs at 09:40 on 2026-06-18.",
        effective_from=datetime(2026, 5, 2, tzinfo=timezone.utc),
        effective_until=None,
        source_type="rail_confirmation",
    ),
    Chunk(
        trip_id="trip-204",
        revision_id="rev-07",
        text="Rail from Lyon to Paris departs at 08:55 on 2026-06-18.",
        effective_from=datetime(2026, 4, 11, tzinfo=timezone.utc),
        effective_until=datetime(2026, 5, 2, tzinfo=timezone.utc),
        source_type="rail_confirmation",
    ),
]

for chunk in active_chunks(records, "trip-204", now):
    print(chunk.revision_id, chunk.text)

The example chooses one active revision after filtering. In production, keep the previous revision available for a “what changed?” request, but do not mix it into a current-plan answer unless the prompt asks for history. That one separation prevents an old departure time from winning because it happens to be semantically closer to the question.

The data model that keeps freshness explainable

Versioning works best when the ingestion record is richer than a file path. I use an event-like record for every source update: the source identifier, observed time, effective time, revision ID, parser version, and a pointer to the raw payload. Chunks inherit the revision ID; they do not invent their own notion of freshness.

There are two clocks here. observed_at says when the system received a message. effective_from says when the itinerary should be treated as true. An airline notice received late can have an earlier effective time than a message received on time. If the planner stores only ingestion time, a delayed notice can appear to be the newest truth.

Chunk boundaries still matter. Split around semantic units such as a reservation, a transfer, or a day-level activity, and repeat the trip and revision metadata on every chunk. A tiny chunk that says “09:40” is not useful by itself; a chunk that includes the date, station, and revision can be cited without asking the model to reconstruct context from a neighbor.

Do not silently merge revisions during indexing. If a new confirmation supersedes an old one, mark the old revision inactive for current retrieval and retain it for history. A delete operation should be an explicit policy decision, because legal retention, customer support, and debugging may require the original payload even after it leaves the active index.

What should chunking and freshness mean for itinerary answers?

Chunking is a precision decision. Smaller units make it easier to exclude an unrelated day or reservation, while larger units preserve context such as a multi-leg connection. Freshness is a truth decision. A chunk can be highly relevant and still be wrong for the requested travel date.

I keep these signals separate in the candidate record:

Signal Question it answers Failure when omitted
Similarity Does this passage discuss the request? A matching phrase from the wrong trip can surface.
Revision validity Is this version active for the requested time? A cancelled train can look current.
Provenance Which source and revision support the claim? The answer cannot explain its evidence.
Scope Is this chunk allowed for the caller? A support agent may see another traveller's data.

The ranker should consume candidates only after validity and scope filters have run. I also make the answer contract preserve source_type, revision_id, and the relevant effective time in the citation object. That is enough for a UI to show “rail confirmation, revision 08” beside a departure time rather than presenting an untraceable sentence.

Here is the evaluation case I would put in a notebook before wiring a production endpoint: ask for the current departure, ask what changed since yesterday, ask about an old revision explicitly, and ask a question about a different trip with similar city names. The expected result is not just a text string. It is a selected revision, an allowed evidence set, and a refusal when no valid evidence exists.

One subtle trap is a partial update. A hotel message may revise check-in time without replacing the whole itinerary. Treating that message as a complete new snapshot can erase unchanged reservations. Imagine rev-08 contains the rail confirmation, two hotel stays, and a museum booking. A later message says only “late check-in is available until 22:00.” If ingestion stores that message as a full replacement, the next query can retrieve a revision with a correct check-in note but no hotel address, because the address lived only in rev-08. If ingestion appends the note to the old chunks without a new revision, a historical question can accidentally inherit a future policy. The repair is architectural: either build a complete materialized revision from all authoritative components, or label the message as a patch and resolve it before retrieval. Record which source supplied each field, and make the resolver fail closed when two authoritative updates overlap without an ordering rule. Then test a sequence such as confirmation, amendment, delayed amendment, and cancellation. The expected output should name the selected revision and the fields it changed, not merely produce a fluent itinerary. Mixing snapshot and patch models produces answers that are current in one field and stale in another.

A practical rollout and the uncomfortable limits

Ship the ingestion ledger before the chatbot. Log every revision transition and make the active-revision query inspectable. Then run a shadow set containing changed train times, duplicate booking numbers, late-arriving notices, and two trips with the same destination. Compare the selected revision and citation metadata, not only the generated prose.

I budget tokens around the evidence that survives filtering. Sending five chunks from three revisions to the answer model is expensive and confusing; sending one well-scoped chunk with a clear source label is usually easier to evaluate. The notebook-to-prod handoff should record the candidate count, selected revision, and prompt tokens so a quality improvement does not hide a cost regression.

The catch is that immutable revisions add storage, metadata, and lifecycle work. They are not suitable when the source system itself has no meaningful revision or effective time and the product only needs a disposable summary. In that case, a simpler cache with a short expiry may be the honest choice. Stick with a revisioned design when users can dispute an answer, when schedule changes matter, or when support staff must reconstruct a past itinerary.

I’m not sure one global freshness window can serve every travel source. Airline schedules, restaurant reservations, and a traveller’s handwritten note have different update semantics. Let the source owner define the policy, then encode that policy in tests. Your mileage may vary, but the uncertainty should live in a named rule rather than in the model's confidence score.

Three words: version first, rank second.

References

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110
