title: How to Add Booking to a Next.js App With a REST API (2026)
description:
Originally published on opencals.com. The original stays updated; check it for the latest version.

Adding a booking page to a Next.js app looks like a weekend project until you start it. The UI is the easy part. The hard part is everything the calendar needs to know before it can show a single open slot: which staff are working, how long the service takes, what's already booked, how much buffer to leave between appointments, and whether two people can hold the same slot at once. That logic is where booking projects quietly turn into month-long ones.

This guide takes the other path. Instead of building the scheduling engine yourself, you call a booking API for the availability, cart, and payment logic, and you keep full control of the Next.js frontend. I built Opencals as exactly that kind of API, so the code here uses it — but the shape of the problem is the same whichever backend you pick, and I'll flag the parts that are universal.

Key takeaway

The frontend of a booking flow is a few forms and a calendar grid. The backend is real-time availability across staff, services, and existing bookings — plus payments. Calling a booking API lets you own the first part and hand off the second.

What "add booking" actually involves

Before any code, it helps to name the pieces. A working booking flow has four moving parts, and most half-finished projects stall because they underestimated one of them.

1. A service catalog

What can be booked — a 60-minute session, a color treatment, a group class — each with its own duration, price, and the staff who can deliver it. This is your booking homepage data.

2. Real-time availability

Given a service and a date range, which slots are actually open? This has to account for existing bookings, staff hours, buffer time, and multi-staff conflicts. It is the single hardest piece to build well.

3. A cart and checkout

Holding a slot while the customer enters details and pays, then confirming the booking only if payment succeeds. Slots are a scarce resource, so this needs to be race-safe.

4. Post-booking management

Confirmation, reminders, and letting customers reschedule or cancel without emailing you. Easy to skip on day one, painful to add later.

If you build all four yourself, you're writing a scheduling engine. If you call an API, you're wiring four typed methods into React components. This guide does the second.

Prerequisites

You need a Next.js 14+ app using the App Router, Node 18+, and a booking API key. With Opencals that's a private storefront key (prefixed spk_), created in the dashboard under Users → your user → API Keys; any booking API will have an equivalent. Install the SDK:

npm i @opencals/storefront-sdk

Then set the key in your environment. Keep it server-side — a private storefront key can create real bookings, so it does not belong in client bundles.

# .env.local
OPENCALS_API_KEY=spk_your_key_here

Why server-side

Anything that creates a booking or a payment should run in a Route Handler or Server Action, never in a client component. The browser calls your Next.js API routes; your routes call the booking API with the secret key. This is the same pattern you'd use for a Stripe secret key.

Step 1 — Initialise the SDK once

Create a small module that configures the client. setupOpencals sets up the SDK's shared client, so you call it once and every service call after that uses the key. Import this module at the top of any server file that calls the API.

// lib/opencals.ts — import from server code only
import { setupOpencals } from "@opencals/storefront-sdk";
import { nextBuyerIp } from "@opencals/storefront-sdk/next";

setupOpencals({
  apiKey: process.env.OPENCALS_API_KEY, // spk_…
  buyerIp: nextBuyerIp,
  throwOnError: true, // failed calls throw OpencalsApiError instead of returning { error }
});

nextBuyerIp forwards each visitor's IP on sign-in, cart and checkout calls, so the API rate-limits per visitor instead of treating your server as one very busy customer. It skips GET requests on purpose, so your cached pages stay static.

If you prefer raw fetch over an SDK, the same call is a GET with the key in an X-Api-Key header — the SDK just gives you typed responses. Both work; typing saves you from guessing the shape of a nested availability object at 11pm.

curl https://api.opencals.com/storefront/products \
 -H "X-Api-Key: spk_your_key"

Step 2 — List services on a Server Component

The App Router lets you fetch on the server and stream HTML, which is ideal for a service catalog — it's public data, good for SEO, and doesn't need to be interactive.

// app/book/page.tsx
import "@/lib/opencals";
import { ProductService } from "@opencals/storefront-sdk";
import { ServiceCard } from "./service-card";

export default async function BookPage() {
 const { data: page } = await ProductService.list({
    query: { status: ["active"], take: 50 },
    throwOnError: true,
 });

 return (
 <main className="grid gap-4">
 {page.data.map((service) => (
 <ServiceCard key={service.id} service={service} />
 ))}
 </main>
 );
}

The list comes back as { data, meta }, fully typed. Each service carries its price (in minor units), duration (seconds), beforeGap/afterGap buffers and a variants array, each variant with its own price and duration. formatPrice and formatDuration from the SDK turn those into display strings. You render, you don't compute.

Step 3 — Fetch real-time availability

This is the endpoint that would have taken you weeks to write. You pass a service and a date, optionally a staff member or location, and you get back the slots that are open right now.

// app/api/availability/route.ts  (Route Handler)
import { NextRequest, NextResponse } from "next/server";
import "@/lib/opencals";
import { ProductService } from "@opencals/storefront-sdk";

export async function GET(req: NextRequest) {
 const { searchParams } = new URL(req.url);

 const { data: slots } = await ProductService.getCurrentAvailabilities({
    path: { productId: searchParams.get("productId")! },
    query: {
      date: searchParams.get("date")!, // YYYY-MM-DD
      staffMemberId: searchParams.get("staffMemberId") ?? undefined,
      timezone: "Europe/Warsaw", // your store's timezone
 },
 });

 return NextResponse.json({ slots });
}

Each slot is { fromDate, fromTime, toDate, toTime, staffMemberIds, attendees, maxAttendees }, and the list already leaves out times that are booked, outside staff hours, or too close to another appointment given the service's buffers. Your calendar component fetches this route when the user picks a date and renders whatever comes back — no client-side conflict math. For a month view, getCurrentAvailabilitiesMerged returns the broad open windows so you can grey out full days.

The universal part

Every booking backend worth using exposes an availability endpoint like this. If a tool only gives you raw calendar events and expects you to compute open slots yourself, you haven't offloaded the hard part — you've just moved it. Availability calculation is the feature to evaluate first.

Step 4 — Hold the slot with a cart

A slot is a scarce resource. Between "customer clicked 2pm" and "customer paid," you don't want someone else grabbing it, and you don't want to create a real booking that might never be paid for. A cart holds the slot for a short window: you create (or reuse) a cart, then create the appointment inside it.

// app/api/cart/route.ts
import { NextRequest, NextResponse } from "next/server";
import { cookies } from "next/headers";
import "@/lib/opencals";
import { AppointmentService, CartService } from "@opencals/storefront-sdk";

export async function POST(req: NextRequest) {
 const { slot } = await req.json(); // one slot from step 3
 const jar = await cookies();

 const { data: cart } = await CartService.createOrGet({
    headers: { "X-Cart-Id": jar.get("cartId")?.value ?? "" },
 });

 await AppointmentService.create({
    body: {
      slot: {
        productId: slot.productId,
        fromDate: slot.fromDate,
        fromTime: slot.fromTime,
        toDate: slot.toDate,
        toTime: slot.toTime,
 },
      numberOfAttendees: 1,
      cartId: cart.id,
 },
 });

  jar.set("cartId", cart.id, { httpOnly: true, sameSite: "lax" });
 return NextResponse.json({ cartId: cart.id });
}

The cart ID lives in an httpOnly cookie, and every cart and checkout call names its cart with the X-Cart-Id header. Times are UTC. If two people try to hold the same slot at the same moment, one succeeds and the other gets a clear error, so your UI can say "someone just took that time" instead of double-booking.

Step 5 — Check out and pay

Checkout turns a held cart into a paid booking in two server calls with the card confirmation in between. start attaches the customer, re-checks the cart and creates the payment; the browser confirms the card with Stripe; submit places the order.

// app/api/checkout/start/route.ts
import { NextRequest, NextResponse } from "next/server";
import { cookies } from "next/headers";
import "@/lib/opencals";
import { CheckoutService } from "@opencals/storefront-sdk";

export async function POST(req: NextRequest) {
 const { email, firstName, lastName } = await req.json();
 const cartId = (await cookies()).get("cartId")!.value;

 const { data: checkout } = await CheckoutService.start({
    headers: { "X-Cart-Id": cartId },
    body: { provider: "stripe", customer: { kind: "new", email, firstName, lastName } },
 });

 // The browser needs these to mount a Stripe Payment Element.
 return NextResponse.json({
    clientSecret: checkout.clientSecret,
    publishableKey: checkout.publishableKey,
    stripeAccountId: checkout.stripeAccountId,
 });
}

// app/api/checkout/submit/route.ts — called after stripe.confirmPayment() succeeds in the browser
import { NextRequest, NextResponse } from "next/server";
import { cookies } from "next/headers";
import "@/lib/opencals";
import { CheckoutService } from "@opencals/storefront-sdk";

export async function POST(req: NextRequest) {
 const { paymentIntentId } = await req.json();
 const cartId = (await cookies()).get("cartId")!.value;

 const { data: result } = await CheckoutService.submit({
    headers: { "X-Cart-Id": cartId },
    body: { stripePaymentIntentId: paymentIntentId },
 });

 return NextResponse.json(result);
}

The Stripe publishable key comes back from start, from the store's own Stripe connection, so there is no Stripe key to configure in your app. If the card wasn't authorised (declined, 3-D Secure not finished), submit answers 402 with the code PAYMENT_NOT_AUTHORIZED, no order is placed and the cart is untouched, so the customer can try again. A second start or submit on the same cart while one is running gets CHECKOUT_IN_PROGRESS instead of a duplicate order. The slot only becomes a real booking once the payment is authorised.

Step 6 — Let customers manage their own bookings

The reschedule-and-cancel flow is the one teams skip first and regret most, because without it every change becomes a support message. These calls run as the signed-in customer: AuthService.signIn returns an accessToken, and you send it as a Bearer token next to your store key, so the customer only sees and touches their own bookings.

// server code, with the customer's accessToken from AuthService.signIn
import "@/lib/opencals";
import { AppointmentService } from "@opencals/storefront-sdk";

const asCustomer = { Authorization: `Bearer ${accessToken}` };

const { data: upcoming } = await AppointmentService.list({
  headers: asCustomer,
  query: { status: ["scheduled", "pending"], orderBy: "from", order: "ASC" },
});

await AppointmentService.reschedule({
  headers: asCustomer,
  path: { appointmentId },
  body: { slot: newSlot }, // a slot from getCurrentAvailabilities, fetched with excludeAppointmentId
});

Pass excludeAppointmentId when you fetch availability for a reschedule, so the appointment's own slot isn't shown as taken. The store's reschedule and cancel windows still apply. Wire these into an account page and the reschedule requests that used to hit your inbox now resolve themselves.

Putting it together

The full flow, from the frontend's point of view, is six typed calls in five steps:

1. List services

ProductService.list() → render the catalog on a Server Component.

2. Check availability

ProductService.getCurrentAvailabilities() → the open slots for a date, computed server-side.

3. Hold the slot

CartService.createOrGet() + AppointmentService.create() → the chosen slot is held in a cart while the customer checks out.

4. Start checkout

CheckoutService.start() → the customer is attached and a payment is created for the browser to confirm.

5. Place the order

CheckoutService.submit() → the held slot becomes a real, paid booking.

Everything hard about scheduling — the availability math, the race conditions, the payment-to-booking handoff — lives behind those calls. Your Next.js app stays a frontend: forms, a calendar grid, and route handlers that proxy to the API with your secret key.

When not to use an API for this

Honest caveat, because not every project needs this. If you're a solo consultant booking 1:1 calls and you don't take payment up front, a hosted tool like Calendly is simpler and you shouldn't build anything. An API earns its keep when you need a custom-branded flow, multiple staff or locations, payments at booking, or booking embedded inside a product you already own. That's when owning the frontend while renting the backend is the right trade — and the links below cover the endpoint surface, the architecture, and the typed SDK.

Where to go from here

  • Booking API guide: The endpoint-level reference: auth model, core routes, and the full booking flow in raw REST.
  • Booking SDK: The typed TypeScript SDK used in this guide — services, availability, cart, and checkout end to end.
  • Headless booking system: The architecture behind building a custom booking frontend on any stack.
  • Opencals for developers: API docs, the OpenAPI spec, and how to get a storefront key.
  • Build a booking website: Three approaches compared, from no-code to a fully custom build.

Frequently asked questions

Can I add booking to Next.js without a third-party API?

Yes, but you're then building a scheduling engine: real-time availability across staff and services, buffer logic, race-safe slot holding, and payment-to-booking handoff. For a single service with no payments that's doable in a weekend. For anything with multiple staff, locations, or paid bookings, the availability and concurrency logic is where most of the effort goes — which is what an API removes.

Where do I keep the booking API key in Next.js?

Server-side only — in an environment variable read by Route Handlers or Server Actions. A storefront key can create real bookings and charges, so it must never ship in a client bundle. The browser calls your own Next.js API routes; those routes call the booking API with the secret key.

Does this work with the App Router and Server Components?

Yes. Public reads like the service catalog fit Server Components and stream as HTML, which is good for SEO. Anything that mutates — cart, checkout, reschedule — goes in Route Handlers or Server Actions so the secret key stays on the server.

How is a booking API different from a calendar API like Google Calendar?

A calendar API stores and returns events. A booking API computes availability — it knows service durations, staff assignments, buffers, and existing bookings, and returns the slots a customer can actually book. With a calendar API you'd still have to write all of that logic yourself on top of raw events.

Can customers reschedule or cancel on their own?

Yes. The customer signs in through the API (AuthService.signIn returns an access token), and your server calls AppointmentService.list, reschedule and cancel with that token as a Bearer header next to the store key, so each customer only sees their own bookings. The store's reschedule and cancel windows still apply. Wire them into an account page and the change requests you'd otherwise answer by email resolve themselves.

title: Death to long-lived static credentials
description:
Fifteen years ago, TLS was something you'd use to protect the most sensitive areas of your app. Then Google, Let's Encrypt, the EFF, and others led the push for HTTPS everywhere, making encryption the default for every request. Without it, anyone between the browser and server can read and tamper with the traffic.

OAuth, OIDC, DBSC, and related standards already provide building blocks for secure authentication, but standards alone do not make secure methods the norm. HTTPS needed tooling that made encryption easy and a sustained push that made it expected. Machine-to-machine authentication still resembles HTTPS in 2010, with some vendors and enterprises leading the way while long-lived static credentials remain the default for many SaaS vendors and infrastructure providers.

At Vercel, we want to make fast and secure the default across the web, including in our own services and the integrations in our Marketplace. We’ve built OIDC UI, a shadcn/ui registry that gives providers trust-policy forms and token verification code. We’re expanding OIDC support across Vercel and setting new authentication requirements for Marketplace providers.

Long-lived static credentials are insecure

Long-lived static credentials are secrets such as API keys and database passwords that applications keep reusing, often with no expiration. As agents take on more useful work, we give them access to our systems, tools, and data through credentials that can grant permissions far beyond the task at hand.

Those credentials can leak into a code repository or chat, be stolen when a service or dependency is compromised, or be exposed when prompt injection leads an agent to reveal them. However it happens, an attacker can use the credential with the permissions it grants until it expires or is revoked. Recent credential-theft and supply-chain incidents across the industry show why encryption at rest isn’t enough when malicious code can read an application’s credentials in production.

Rotating exposed credentials takes time and coordination across the systems that use them, and mistakes can disrupt production. At Vercel, we’ve previously spent thousands of engineering hours on multiple, very painful key rotations out of an abundance of caution, and we never want to have to do this again.

Better solutions already exist

With OIDC, your application can authenticate without storing a long-lived provider key. A trusted issuer provides a signed, short-lived token identifying the application, and the receiving service verifies that token before deciding what access to grant.

A stolen token stops working when it expires, limiting how long that copy can be used even if the leak goes unnoticed. Your application can obtain fresh credentials programmatically, removing the need to distribute and manually rotate a persistent provider key across the systems that use it.

We’ve been prioritizing OIDC across Vercel so applications can access Blob, AI Gateway, and Sandbox without storing long-lived keys for those services. Our OIDC federation has been generally available since 2024, letting applications running on Vercel exchange Vercel-issued identity tokens for temporary AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure credentials under configured project and environment trust policies. But for developers to stop managing long-lived keys, that support has to extend to all the services their applications depend on.

The rest of the web hasn’t followed

We surveyed more than 1,000 SaaS vendors and found that only 8.4% supported secure authentication methods.

But getting vendors to support secure authentication is only part of the problem. Even when a service offers a secure method, developers often choose a static key because it can be simpler to use. We see three main barriers to broader adoption:

  • Tooling and setup that make secure authentication more complicated than using a static key.

  • Added latency from fetching or exchanging tokens on the request path.

  • Weak incentives for vendors to offer and prioritize secure authentication.

Our goal is to make secure authentication the default on Vercel, while also using our Marketplace to help push more vendors to support it.

Our commitment to a more secure web

We have a responsibility to make this change practical across the services we run, the tools developers use, and the integrations we build with partners.

Make secure authentication easier to use

Using a secure token has to be easier than pasting a key, or developers will keep pasting keys. On Vercel, code retrieves an OIDC token with a function call, and a custom audience specifies the service intended to receive it.

With Vercel Connect, applications and agents use their deployment identity to request provider tokens at runtime, without having to store long-lived provider secrets in environment variables. Once the connector is configured and linked to the project and the user’s account is connected, code can request a token for that user with scopes the provider supports.

We’re also extending OIDC support across the Vercel API and CLI to remove the need for long-lived Vercel tokens in deployment workflows.

OIDC UI for API providers

OIDC UI is a shadcn/ui component registry with a trust-policy configurator and a server-side token verifier. It includes provider forms for Vercel, GitHub, GitLab, Google, Bitbucket, AWS, Azure, and custom OIDC issuers. A provider can let customers configure trust for a particular Vercel project’s production environment, then verify incoming tokens against that policy without building the configuration interface and verification code from scratch.

Reduce the performance cost of secure authentication

A static key in an environment variable is already available when a function runs, so reading it requires no network request. Fetching a token or exchanging it for provider credentials can add network latency, so reducing those calls is part of making secure authentication practical.

Vercel Functions receive a platform-issued token in the request header, which the SDK reads without fetching another. The platform reuses unexpired tokens, while Vercel Connect caches provider tokens in process and refreshes them near expiry. Custom-audience and provider exchanges require network calls.

For example, an application can use the Azure SDK to access Cosmos DB with temporary credentials instead of a database key. With Azure configured to trust the Vercel project and its default token audience, the callback supplies a Vercel OIDC token to ClientAssertionCredential, which exchanges it for the Azure access token used by CosmosClient.

Give providers an incentive to support secure authentication

The Vercel Marketplace offers access to third-party databases, content management systems, observability tools, and more. Our goal is for all of these vendors to support short-lived, identity-based authentication, whether they accept OIDC tokens directly or exchange them for temporary credentials. We’re working to make integrations configure that authentication automatically when developers connect a service, so it does not require a separate setup step.

HTTPS everywhere did not win on ergonomics alone. Chrome put a “Not secure” label on plain HTTP, and then it set deadlines. Now we are setting ours. By November 30, 2026, vendors who do not support OIDC auth from Vercel to their services and use long-lived secrets for authentication will have a similar “Not secure” message on their listing. By January 2027, vendors who do not offer secure auth will be delisted. We are holding the Vercel API and our own native integrations to the same bar.

From static to dynamic

Fifteen years ago, encrypting every request felt like overkill. Today, the padlock is so normal that we only notice when it's missing. Secure authentication between services should become just as routine, so developers can connect the systems they need without storing another long-lived secret. Going from static to dynamic has always been the Vercel mission. It started with pages, and now it’s credentials.

Additional resources

  • OIDC federation covers how deployments get short-lived identity tokens, with guides for AWS, GCP, Azure, and your own API.

  • Custom OIDC token audiences scopes each token to the one service meant to receive it.

  • Vercel Connect requests short-lived, scoped provider tokens at runtime, so code and agents never store credentials.

  • Vercel Connect guides walk through building agents this way, from Slack bots to GitHub agents.

title: PostgreSQL Commands – Step-by-Step Guide
description:
PostgreSQL is an open-source relational database management system (RDBMS) used to store, manage, and retrieve data.

Step 1: Check whether PostgreSQL is installed

Run:

psql --version

Step 2: If PostgreSQL is not installed

On Linux Mint / Ubuntu, install it using:

sudo apt update
sudo apt install postgresql

Step 3: Switch to PostgreSQL user

sudo -i -u postgres

Then open PostgreSQL:

psql

Purpose: Switches the current terminal session to the postgres Linux user.

sudo --> Executes a command with elevated privileges
-i --> Starts an interactive login shell
-u --> Specifies the user
postgres --> PostgreSQL system user

Step 4: Check PostgreSQL version

Select version();

Step 5: Get Help

\h

Purpose: Displays help about SQL commands in PostgreSQL.

Step 6: List All Databases

\l

Purpose: Displays all databases available in the PostgreSQL server.

Step 7: Create a Database

CREATE DATABASE movie;

Purpose: Creates a new database named movie.
Note: SQL commands should end with a semicolon (;).

Step 8: Quit the PostgreSQL Terminal

\q

Step 9: Connect to a Database

\c movie

Purpose: Connects to the database named movie.

Step 10: Clear the Terminal Screen

Ctrl + l

Step 11: Display Tables

\d

Purpose: Displays the tables, views, sequences, and other relations in the current database.

Step 12: Display Table Structure

\d movie;

title: How can an AI startup get free GPU and cloud credits?
description:
Most free GPU time for an AI startup comes from AWS Activate, the Google for Startups Cloud Program and Microsoft for Startups, with smaller grants from GPU providers such as RunPod. Nodus can run your training and fine-tuning jobs inside your own credited AWS, Google Cloud or Azure account (Beta), spending those credits first and moving to Nodus capacity when they run out. The catch is that a credit is only worth the GPU hours it buys before it expires, and quota waits, high list prices and expiry dates all shrink that number.

We build Nodus. Every program fact below links to the program's own page, the GPU arithmetic is shown once, and we checked each page on November 13, 2026. If you are still choosing a platform rather than chasing credits, read the best GPU cloud for an AI startup first.

Which startup credit programs can actually pay for GPUs?

The three hyperscalers are the only programs that reach six figures, and all three cover their own GPU virtual machines. GPU providers give less, but their credits go straight to GPU time.

Program Credits Who qualifies How you apply Expiry
AWS Activate Founders $1,000, up to $5,000 for select startups Self-funded, founded in the last 10 years, pre-Series B Directly "Usually" 1 to 2 years, by package
AWS Activate Portfolio Up to $200,000 Backed by an Activate Provider, pre-Series B, round in the last 12 months With your provider's Org ID Same
Google for Startups, Start tier $2,000 Founded in the past 2 years, working MVP, plans to raise Directly Not stated
Google for Startups, AI tier Up to $250,000 in year 1, up to $100,000 more in year 2 Pre-seed or seed in the last 5 years or Series A in the last 12 months, building on Gemini Directly, investors can verify stealth teams Over 2 years
Microsoft for Startups Up to $5,000 after business verification, up to $150,000 over time Early-stage software startups Directly Not stated
RunPod Startup Program $1,000 (raised under $1M), $5,000 (verified VC), bonus on $25,000+ commits By funding raised Online form 1 year after issue
Modal for Startups Not published New to Modal, seed to Series A via partner VCs or over $1M raised Online form Not stated

Programs checked November 13, 2026. AWS's eligibility details come from its Activate credits guide. Google's year-2 line reads "20% up to an additional $100,000"; startups that are not AI-first get up to $100,000 in year 1.

A few details in that table decide more than the headline amount. Activate Providers include accelerators, angel investors and VC firms, and AWS names Y Combinator, Sequoia and Andreessen Horowitz among them. Google's AI tier is designed for startups that "use or plan to use Gemini" as a foundation of their product. It also excludes teams that already received more than $5,000 in Google Cloud credits. AWS also runs an invite-only tier of $200,000 or more for AI startups after Activate Portfolio, reached through an account manager.

Does NVIDIA Inception give you cloud credits?

Not directly. NVIDIA Inception is a free program with no fees or equity, open at any funding stage. Members must be incorporated, under 10 years old, have a working website and a clear use for NVIDIA technology.

Its credit benefit is access: members can request "free cloud credits from NVIDIA and partners" through the Inception portal, with amounts set per offer and not published. The other benefits are training courses, VC introductions and preferred hardware pricing, which NVIDIA describes as a rebate on the supplier's price. Join it because it costs nothing, but do not plan your compute budget around it.

In what order should a startup apply for credits?

Apply in the order your funding windows close, and only when you have work ready to run. Credits start expiring when they are issued, and several programs gate on how recent your last round was. This is our decision rule, built from the eligibility lines above.

  1. No investor yet. Apply to Microsoft for Startups first, since business verification gets you up to $5,000, the largest starting grant here for a team without investors. Add Google's $2,000 Start tier if you were founded in the last two years, and AWS Activate Founders for $1,000. Join NVIDIA Inception, and RunPod's $1,000 Starter tier if you want its pods or serverless endpoints.
  2. Accelerator or seed fund. Ask whether your backer is an AWS Activate Provider and get its Org ID, because Portfolio credits must be claimed within 12 months of your latest round. Apply to Google's AI tier in the same quarter if you build on Gemini. Pick the cloud where your first real training run will happen and apply there first.
  3. Series A or later. Google's AI tier needs the Series A to be under 12 months old, so apply right after the round closes. AWS Activate stops at pre-Series B, and its larger AI tier is invite-only through your account manager. A RunPod Growth commit is a discount on prepaid spend, not free compute.

One rule covers all three stages. Never take a grant you cannot spend before it expires on a GPU you can actually get.

How many H100 hours does a credit stack really buy?

Far fewer than the dollar figure suggests, because hyperscaler on-demand GPU prices are high. We priced one NVIDIA H100 hour on each cloud's own listed on-demand rate for its 8 x H100 machine.

Cloud 8 x H100 machine Listed price per hour Per H100-hour
AWS, p5.48xlarge (US East, N. Virginia) 8 x H100 $55.04 $6.88
Google Cloud, a3-highgpu-8g 8 x H100 $88.49 $11.06
Azure, ND96isr H100 v5 (East US) 8 x H100 $98.32 $12.29

Prices checked November 13, 2026 on AWS EC2 on-demand pricing, Google Cloud accelerator-optimized pricing and the Azure retail prices API behind Azure's Linux VM pricing page. Per H100-hour is the machine price divided by 8.

Take a seed-stage AI startup with an Activate Provider behind it that wins the year-1 maximum on AWS and Google, plus Microsoft's $5,000 verification tier. That is $455,000 of credit.

  • AWS: $200,000 / $6.88 = 29,069.8 H100-hours.
  • Google Cloud: $250,000 / $11.06125 = 22,601.4 H100-hours.
  • Azure: $5,000 / $12.29 = 406.8 H100-hours.


A $455,000 stack buys about 52,078 H100-hours, roughly one 8-GPU machine running for 271 days.

The total is 52,078.0 H100-hours, or 6,509.8 hours of one 8 x H100 machine, which is 271.2 days of continuous use. At Nodus's listed $2.60 per H100-hour, the same 52,078.0 hours would cost about $135,403. That is the honest way to value a credit stack: in GPU-hours at a price you could otherwise pay, not in the headline dollars.

A team with no investor gets a much smaller stack: $1,000 from AWS, $2,000 from Google and $5,000 from Microsoft.


Without an investor, Microsoft's verification tier buys more H100 time than the AWS and Google grants combined.

Those three grants buy 145.3, 180.8 and 406.8 H100-hours, 733.0 in total. That is one 8 x H100 fine-tune of about 92 hours, which is real work but not a training budget.

Which gotchas make startups lose their credits?

Most lost credit comes from four rules in the programs' own terms and docs, not from bad luck.

  • GPU quota starts at zero on AWS. The default quota for "Running On-Demand P instances", the family that includes H100 machines, is 0 vCPUs, so you must request an increase before credits can buy any H100 time. Google gives new projects a global GPU quota and asks you to request more per GPU model and region. Azure grants GPU machines through per-family vCPU quota requests.
  • Credits expire while you wait. AWS says Activate credits "usually expire within 1-2 years", and RunPod credits expire one year after issue. Apply when the quota request and the workload are ready, not on the day you hear about the program.
  • Marketplace and support are excluded. AWS promotional credit terms exclude AWS Marketplace, enterprise support tiers and upfront fees for Savings Plans and Reserved Instances. Google excludes all third-party products, including Marketplace and Model Garden listings. Microsoft excludes support plans, Marketplace purchases and third-party models.
  • You cannot steer AWS credits. They apply automatically to all eligible charges, so a forgotten database or idle machine eats the same balance as your training runs.

How does Nodus help you spend cloud credits first?

Nodus can run your jobs in your own connected AWS account, GCP project or Azure subscription, so it spends your cloud credits before Nodus capacity. This is a Beta feature described in the cloud accounts docs.

Connecting starts read-only. For AWS, the role Nodus assumes can only list instances, read daily cost, read your credit balance and expiry, and read GPU quotas. That last point matters here: you see the credit left, the date it expires and whether your quota can take an H100 job in one place.

Running work is a separate upgrade with a spending limit you set. Single-node Jobs and TrainingJobs then go to your connected accounts first. When the account is full or out of credit, the default behavior runs the work on Nodus capacity at Nodus rates.

You can instead make Jobs wait for your approval or wait for your account. The job page shows whether each attempt ran in your account or on Nodus capacity.

For a GPU job in your own account, Nodus charges a route fee of $0.02 per device-hour, and your cloud bills the machine and disk against your credits. Multi-node runs and Sandboxes use Nodus capacity.

What should you use when the credits run out?

Pay the lowest rate for work that finishes. Nodus lists an H100 at $2.60 per hour on the pricing page, against the $6.88 to $12.29 per H100-hour hyperscaler list prices above.


After credits, the same dollar buys 2.65 times more H100 time at Nodus's listed rate than at AWS on-demand.

The 2.65 comes from $6.88 / $2.60. List price is not the whole bill, and we break down idle time and failed runs in what an H100 or B200 hour really costs per finished job. Nodus has no public starter credit right now: its credits guide says the $30 starter offer has ended, so new accounts add prepaid credit or redeem an approved promo code. If an agent launches your jobs, cap its spending first, as we show in how to limit an AI agent's GPU spending.

FAQ

Can you stack AWS, Google and Microsoft startup credits?

Yes, across clouds, because each program sets its own eligibility. Within a program the credits stay with you: Google says they may only be used by the original applicant and cannot be shared, split or resold.

Can Google startup credits pay for the Gemini API?

Yes. Google's program credits cover its own models such as Gemini and Gemma, while third-party models are billed directly and not covered.

Do I need a VC to get AWS Activate credits?

No. Activate Founders is for self-funded startups and starts at $1,000. The $200,000 Portfolio tier needs an Org ID from an Activate Provider such as an accelerator, angel investor or VC.

Does Nodus give startup credits?

The public $30 starter credit has ended. Nodus applies any credit grant you hold, such as a promo code, before purchased credit, soonest expiry first.

title: Vercel Sandbox commands now support stdin
description:
Vercel Sandbox now lets you send input to running commands through standard input (stdin). Use it to exchange messages with stdio MCP servers such as agent-browser, or send data to other command-line programs while they run.

In the TypeScript SDK, set stdin: true and detached: true in runCommand(). Use writeStdin() to send input and closeStdin() when you’re done:

You can also set stdin to a Node.js readable stream, such as process.stdin. The SDK forwards the stream’s data and closes the command’s standard input when the stream ends.

In the Python SDK, set stdin=subprocess.PIPE and send input with server.stdin.send(). Call communicate() to close stdin, collect remaining output, and wait for the process to exit:

For commands that receive all their input at once, you can pass input directly to Python’s run_process().

Read the Sandbox documentation to get started.

title: 116 tokens: a default theme for light, dark and a phone
description:
Originally published at https://blog.galascribe.com/116-tokens-a-default-theme-for-light-dark-and-a-phone/.

Our default theme was a skin over a fixed page. When I approved a new design for it, five decisions shaped what followed. This post covers what they produced: a closed list of 116 typed tokens, a light and a dark value for each, and a way for a creator to pick their own colours without making the page unreadable.

Five decisions

I approved a working preview and asked for the production theme to be replaced with it. The decisions that went with it:

  1. No backwards compatibility. Only test users were onboarded, so we broke contracts and bumped majors, with no migration shims.
  2. The template owns layout. Themes supply design values, the tokens, plus optional skin CSS.
  3. A site script is allowed, but every page must read completely with JavaScript off. The script only enhances: search, copy buttons, the menu, the colour-mode toggle.
  4. "Most read" was dropped, because we have no visit data. The newsletter panel became a link to a sign-up address the author sets, hidden when none is set. There are no forms.
  5. The official token list grows to the preview's full set of values, each with a strict type.

116, counted

Decision 5 said "about 100 tokens". The contract list that came out of it has 116 entries and replaces a list of 35. Keys are sorted and each has a fixed type, so the list is closed. By type, counted from the list:

type          count   may differ between light and dark
color           40    yes
paint            4    yes
border           8    yes
shadow           5    yes
font-family      5    no
font-weight      5    no
length          28    no
box              3    no
number           2    no
duration         3    no
easing           2    no
keyword         11    no
total          116    57 may differ, 59 must be byte-equal

A token is a key, a type, a light value and a dark value, and nothing else. The value grammars are allow-lists. A colour is a lowercase #rrggbb or #rrggbbaa. A length is a number with px, rem, em or %. No value may contain url(, var(, calc(, attr(, expression, a semicolon, braces, a backslash or a quote, apart from a few fixed keywords.

The allow-list is partly about safety and partly about checking. Because a colour is always a literal, we can compute the contrast of any pair before a page is served. Run-time functions such as var() would make that impossible, so the grammar excludes them. To convert the preview, we resolved every var() to its literal value for each mode and turned color-mix() into its computed hex. The preview's component CSS had no theme-specific selectors, so everything a theme varies is a token, and we kept it that way.

Light and dark are both authored

Every token carries a value for each mode. The 57 whose types may differ are the colours, paints, borders and shadows. The other 59 (fonts, weights, lengths and the rest) must be byte-equal in light and dark, and the contract enforces it. Dark mode cannot quietly change your spacing or your type.

One mistake is worth owning. Look, the page where a creator styles a site, has a "Visitors see" control that saves a default colour mode. While reading code for the palette work, we found that the template never read it. The page script started from the reader's stored choice or the system setting, and without the script the page rendered light. The setting was saved and did nothing. The fix renders the author's default on the page root and, when it is light or dark, as the server-resolved mode. A reader's stored choice still wins, and when a creator allows only one mode there is no toggle.

The phone, and no script

We audited the designs in a real browser instead of trusting static checks, at 320, 360, 390, 414, 768, 820, 1024 (touch) and 1440 pixels and on a phone on its side at 844 by 390. It asserted rows, overflow, overlap and tap-target sizes, and it caught the header and the reaction bar (the row with Like and the emoji reactions) wrapping onto two lines, which the static checks had missed.

The header's mobile menu is a <details> element, which opens and closes without script. The contents list comes from the article's second-level headings when there are at least two. A card without a cover image gets a placeholder painted from tokens. Everything the script adds degrades to plain links or <details> when it is off.

Letting a creator choose colours

A theme's colours are literals in its theme.json, so a creator who wanted their own accent had nowhere to put it. There are three roles, Accent, Background and Text, each an explicit light and dark pair. A role left unpicked uses the theme's own value. Six named presets live in a list in the app, and "Theme colours" always comes first.

Three colours cannot drive 116 tokens, and they should not. A theme can bind them to at most 40: the three seeds, 24 more colours such as links, chips, header and footer, all four paints, seven of the eight borders and two shadows. The other 17 stay with the theme: code blocks and their syntax colours, the status colours, the overlay, form inputs, and the card and dialog shadows.

Each theme says which seed each of its colours follows. When a creator picks an accent, the build moves every colour that follows it by the same perceptual change that turns the theme's accent into theirs, in OKLCH, a colour space with hue, chroma and lightness as its axes. A colour whose seed has not changed keeps the theme's literal exactly, so the default palette reproduces today's colours by construction.

Two limits apply to what the creator picks. Background must be light enough in light mode and dark enough in dark mode: lightness of at least 0.90 and at most 0.30 on the OKLab scale, where our six themes measure 0.951 to 1.000 and 0.145 to 0.191. Text must reach 4.5:1 against Background in each mode. The creator's colours are used exactly as chosen. If a pick fails, Save is disabled and the reason is shown, for example "Hard to read in dark: 3.1 of 4.5".

Derived colours are different. Links, chip text and similar colours are computed from the pick, so we adjust them. We check 21 pairs in each mode on the final values: the 17 pairs already checked for every theme at 4.5:1, focus on canvas at 3:1, and the three status colours at 4.5:1. Where a pair's foreground follows the palette, the build moves its lightness by the smallest step that clears the minimum plus 0.1, aiming at 4.6 so that the browser and the build agree on a pass. A failing pair whose foreground belongs to the theme is never adjusted. It fails.

That has a visible cost: a pure yellow accent gives olive links. In our calculations on the Editorial theme in light mode, a yellow of #ffd60a gives links of #f1ca00 at 1.38:1, which the adjustment moves to #7f6900 at 4.64:1.

Where it is checked

The check runs in five places: in the app while a creator picks, where a failing role shows its ratio; in the API at save, which checks shape, lowercase hex, the background band and text on background; in the template at render, which is the authority and refuses the build with APPEARANCE_PALETTE_CONTRAST, naming the pair, the mode and the ratio; at theme release, against a stress corpus of palettes; and in a test that runs every preset and every theme's default palette through all six themes in both modes.

Every preset's pass through each theme's bindings is proved by that test, not by arithmetic, and a failing preset is retuned before it ships, with the one exception noted below.

A contrast audit found zero violations. By hand we measured one preset, Graphite, at 4.05 to 4.25:1 for muted meta text over the page glow in two themes, below our 4.5:1 aim, and it is not fixed yet.

To set up a site and try the colour choices in Look, the start flow is at https://app.galascribe.com/

title: The 7-Second Rule: What Visitors Decide About Your Website Before They Read a Word
description:
A visitor lands on your website. They do not read it. Not at first. In the first few seconds, they look at it. They take in the colours, the layout, the main image, and the first heading. Then they make a decision. Stay, or leave. Research into how people use the web has shown again and again that this decision happens fast, often within about seven seconds. Seven seconds is not much time. It is about as long as it takes to read this paragraph out loud. And yet it is enough for a visitor to decide whether your business looks trustworthy, professional, and worth their time.

The first thing a visitor judges is whether the site looks like it belongs to a real, current business. A design that looks ten years old sends a message, whether the owner means it to or not. It suggests the business may not be keeping up, or may not be paying attention. A site that looks clean and current suggests the opposite. It does not need to be flashy or expensive. It needs to look cared for. Clean spacing, readable text, photos that are in focus, and a layout that is not crowded. These are small things, but they add up to a feeling, and that feeling forms before a single word is read.

The second judgement happens just as fast. Can I find what I need here? A visitor arrives with a question in mind. They want to know what you do, how much it costs, where you are, or how to get in touch. If the answer is not obvious within seconds, they will look elsewhere. That is why the top of the homepage matters more than any other part of the site. It should say, in plain words, what the business does and who it is for. Not a clever slogan. Not a vague promise. A clear sentence. A visitor should not have to work out what the business sells. If they have to guess, they will guess wrong or give up.

Speed is part of the first impression too. A site that takes a long time to load feels broken, even if it is not. People are used to pages appearing almost instantly, and they have little patience for a spinning wheel. Large photos are the usual cause. A homepage full of huge images will look good on the designer's screen and load slowly on a customer's phone. Every second of delay loses visitors. The fix is practical rather than technical. Use smaller images, keep the homepage simple, and avoid anything that has to load before the visitor can see the page. A fast site feels professional. A slow one feels neglected.

The mobile view deserves special attention, because that is how most visitors arrive. A site that looks fine on a desktop computer can be a mess on a phone. Text too small to read, buttons too close together to tap, menus that are hard to open, and images that push the content sideways. Visitors will not pinch and zoom and struggle. They will leave. Every business owner should open their own website on a phone at least once a month and try to use it like a customer. Find the phone number. Fill in the contact form. Read the services page. If any of that is awkward, it needs fixing.

Trust signals are the next thing a visitor picks up on, even if they do not realise it. A real address, a real phone number, and a real email address make a business feel solid. Photos of real people and real work make it feel honest. Reviews from real customers, shown with names, make it feel proven. A site with no contact details, no photos, and no sign of real people behind it feels risky, even if the business is perfectly genuine. These details do not need to be fancy. They just need to be visible early, ideally on the homepage, where a visitor can see them without digging.

Clarity beats cleverness every time. A homepage that tries to be witty or artistic can be enjoyable, but it can also confuse. If a visitor has to think about what a heading means, the site has already lost a few of its precious seconds. Plain words win. Say what you do. Say who it is for. Say what to do next. A clear button that says Get a Quote or Book a Call is worth more than a clever phrase that nobody understands. Visitors are not judging your creativity. They are judging whether you can help them, and they want the answer quickly.

There is one more judgement that happens in those first seconds, and it is about focus. A homepage that tries to say everything at once says nothing. Too many messages, too many images, too many buttons, and the visitor does not know where to look. A focused homepage picks one main message and one main action, and lets everything else support them. The other services and details can live on their own pages, where interested visitors will find them. The homepage is the front door, not the whole shop.

The good news is that none of this requires a big budget or a complete rebuild. Most websites can be improved in a few hours by fixing the top of the homepage, simplifying the message, speeding up the images, and making sure the mobile view works. The best way to test it is to ask someone who has never seen the site to look at it for seven seconds, then close it and tell you what the business does and whether they would trust it. Their answer will tell you exactly what to fix.

Seven seconds is not long, but it is enough. It is enough for a visitor to feel that a business is professional, current, and worth a closer look. Or it is enough for them to leave and try the next result. The businesses that win those seven seconds are the ones that keep their homepage clear, fast, honest, and focused on the visitor. For owners who want a second pair of eyes on their own site, a design studio can review it and point out what a first-time visitor actually sees. DezignLoop (https://dezignloop.com) looks at small business websites with exactly that fresh eye, and helps owners make the first seven seconds count.

title: A small offline check for route data before making a travel animation
description:
A map animation makes movement look continuous, even when the underlying record is sparse. That visual effect can be useful for storytelling, but it can also hide missing samples, time-zone mistakes, and values that do not represent valid coordinates. Before turning an exported route into a public clip, it helps to run a few small checks and then review the map itself.

This article builds an offline Python check for a deliberately simple CSV format. It does not parse the Google Timeline export format, reconstruct a route, prove where anyone was, or determine whether a location can safely be shared. The examples and tests use synthetic values. I am associated with Timeline Visualizer, and AI assisted in drafting this article and code. Timeline Visualizer is a browser-based google timeline visualizer that turns exported location history into an animated travel video. It offers route customization and MP4 export; custom music is part of the optional Pro upgrade. This standalone code is not a feature of the product or an integration with it.

Choose a narrow input contract

The example accepts rows with three fields: lat, lon, and timestamp. Latitude and longitude are decimal degrees. The timestamp is an ISO 8601 value with an explicit UTC offset, such as 2025-05-08T09:00:00+00:00. A trailing Z is also accepted as UTC. These fields are a teaching format, not a claim about the fields present in a particular service's export.

A real conversion layer needs its own documentation and tests. If an input represents coordinates as integers scaled by a power of ten, for example, those values must be converted correctly before this checker receives them. If a timestamp is a Unix epoch, it must be converted to an offset-aware value deliberately. Guessing a format from a number's length can produce plausible but incorrect coordinates, so keep source parsing separate from validation.

The tool returns row numbers and short warning labels. It deliberately avoids printing the actual coordinates. That reduces accidental exposure in console output, although row numbers can still reveal information when combined with the original file. Treat both the input and any report as private. The function operates on data already in memory and makes no network calls; that does not make a machine or its backups automatically secure.

A small checker 

import csv
import math
from datetime import datetime


def audit(rows, gap_minutes=120):
    issues = []
    previous = None
    for number, row in enumerate(rows, 1):
        try:
            lat, lon = float(row['lat']), float(row['lon'])
            stamp = datetime.fromisoformat(
                row['timestamp'].replace('Z', '+00:00')
            )
            if stamp.utcoffset() is None:
                raise ValueError('timestamp must include offset')
            if not (math.isfinite(lat) and math.isfinite(lon)
                    and -90 <= lat <= 90 and -180 <= lon <= 180):
                raise ValueError('invalid coordinate')
        except (KeyError, TypeError, ValueError):
            issues.append((number, 'invalid row'))
            previous = None
            continue
        if previous is not None:
            delta = (stamp - previous).total_seconds() / 60
            if delta < 0:
                issues.append((number, 'out of order'))
            elif delta > gap_minutes:
                issues.append((number, 'large time gap'))
        previous = stamp
    return issues


def read_csv(path):
    with open(path, encoding='utf-8', newline='') as handle:
        return list(csv.DictReader(handle))

The bounds check rejects values outside the possible latitude and longitude ranges. math.isfinite matters because Python accepts strings such as nan and inf as floating-point values; those are not usable positions. A numeric value inside the range can still be wrong. Swapped latitude and longitude may pass, and a plausible coordinate can belong to the wrong city. This code reports basic validity, not geographic truth.

The ordering check compares each valid timestamp to the previous valid timestamp. A negative interval is flagged as out of order. An interval strictly greater than the chosen threshold is flagged as a large time gap. Two points exactly 120 minutes apart are not flagged under the default setting. A gap is a prompt to inspect the source, not proof that a device failed or that a traveler moved directly between the two points.

When a row is invalid, the code clears the previous timestamp. The next valid row begins a new comparison sequence. This avoids pretending that the checker knows how to bridge a malformed row. Depending on the application, a different policy might be appropriate, but it should be explicit and covered by tests. For example, a production pipeline may want a separate warning that a comparison was interrupted.

Exercise the boundary cases

The following small tests use fabricated coordinates and times. Save the checker as route_audit.py and run this snippet in the same directory. They test the code shown above, not the Timeline Visualizer product or any real export.

from route_audit import audit


def row(lat, lon, stamp):
    return {'lat': lat, 'lon': lon, 'timestamp': stamp}


a = '2025-05-08T09:00:00+00:00'
b = '2025-05-08T09:30:00+00:00'
c = '2025-05-08T13:00:00+00:00'

assert audit([row('48', '2', a), row('48.1', '2.1', b)]) == []
assert audit([row('48', '2', a), row('48', '2', c)]) == [(2, 'large time gap')]
assert audit([row('48', '2', b), row('48', '2', a)]) == [(2, 'out of order')]
assert audit([row('nan', '2', a)]) == [(1, 'invalid row')]
assert audit([row('91', '2', a)]) == [(1, 'invalid row')]
assert audit([row('48', '2', '2025-05-08T09:00:00')]) == [(1, 'invalid row')]
assert audit([row('48', '2', a), {}, row('48', '2', c)]) == [(2, 'invalid row')]
assert audit([
    row('48', '2', '2025-05-08T09:00:00Z'),
    row('48', '2', '2025-05-08T11:00:00+02:00'),
]) == []
print('8 synthetic assertions passed')

These eight assertions passed locally against the accompanying example. The last test uses two representations of the same instant with different offsets. Python compares aware datetimes by instant, so the interval is zero. The test is useful because sorting timestamp strings lexicographically is not generally a safe substitute for parsing offsets. Local dates are still important for a human itinerary, but that is a separate presentation decision.

Decide what a warning means

A warning should lead to a question, not an automatic correction. For a large gap, inspect the original record and any itinerary information you already have. It may correspond to a device being offline, but it may also be an intentional stop. For out-of-order rows, determine whether the file was meant to be ordered by recording time, import order, or another field. Sorting blindly can obscure an upstream issue or change the intended sequence.

Consider the threshold in context. Two hours may be reasonable for a dense city walk and unhelpful for a route sampled only a few times per day. Pass a different gap_minutes value when the sampling policy is known, and record that choice with the review. This example does not validate the threshold itself; a production implementation should reject negative, non-finite, or otherwise inappropriate settings and return structured errors suitable for its caller.

Do not use a single numeric check as a privacy guarantee. A valid point may be a home, school, workplace, or medical location. A seemingly broad map can identify a person through a distinctive combination of places and times. Review the route and audience explicitly, remove unnecessary segments, obtain consent when others are represented, and remember that a shared video can be copied beyond the initial recipients.

Turn checks into a reviewable workflow

Keep the raw export private and work on a copy. Run validation before selecting a visual style, then make a short list of warnings to inspect. Check the first and last locations, the order of major stops, missing intervals, and any labels visible at the intended playback size. If the source is uncertain, leave a gap or describe the uncertainty instead of drawing a confident line that the data does not support.

After editing, play the actual exported video from start to finish. Confirm that the map scale provides enough context without exposing more than the audience needs. If music is included, make sure the license covers the intended use. If a video will be compressed by a messaging or social platform, check the compressed copy as well as the original. A clear opening frame and a short pause at an important stop can do more for comprehension than additional motion effects.

The boundary between data quality, privacy, and presentation is important. The Python function only catches a few mechanical problems. A person still needs to decide what the journey is meant to communicate and what should remain private. A small, well-documented checker is valuable precisely because its limitations are visible: it helps organize review without replacing judgment or presenting an animation as authoritative evidence.

title: Elpis, the mother of your coding agents
description:
Elpis is an open-source desktop and terminal app for Linux where you run coding agents (GPT, Claude, Gemini). It is built on OpenAI's Codex. This post shows what Elpis does for those agents, through the picture that made it click for me: a mother and her children.

I used to call Elpis a "harness". I stopped. A harness is what you strap on a horse. What I want for my agents is closer to what a mother does: she nurtures them. She feeds them, cleans them up, keeps them safe, checks their homework and keeps them accountable.

She feeds them when they are hungry

A baby gets milk when it needs it, not the whole fridge. An agent's milk is context.

Left alone, a coding agent loads the instruction files it finds and keeps the whole conversation until the window fills. You can't see what it was told.

In Elpis, the Context Ledger lists each instruction file, chosen file and memory with its token cost. You include or exclude each one before you send the first message.

She changes the diaper when it is full

A full context window is a full diaper: the agent gets slow, confused and expensive.

/compact cleans it up now. /compact N sets a level, and Elpis compacts on its own when the remaining context drops to it. Smart Prune (experimental, off by default) goes further: it shortens a long tool result before it enters the conversation, and keeps the original in a log so you can check what was cut.

A fair warning: compaction loses detail. Check important claims against the transcript.

She puts them in a playpen

Children learn by playing, in a place where they can't get hurt.

Elpis keeps Codex's sandbox. In a workflow, each agent owns its own folder, agents/<its name>. In a Git project it works in its own worktree, and a step that changed files outside its folders fails.

The tradeoff: outside a Git project, the folders are instructions, not enforced.

She stops the siblings fighting over toys

Two agents that run side by side may not share a folder. It is Rust's rule for ownership, applied to agents:

Rust Elpis workflow
A value has one owner Each agent owns its folder
Shared borrows only read A check reads the writer's work and writes only its own notes
No two mutable borrows at once Two agents working alongside may not share a folder
The owner decides what lives The Mother agent decides what reaches your project

She checks their homework and keeps them accountable

A check follows each agent that writes. It reads the work and passes or fails it.

At the end, the Mother agent reviews the combined commit. She must pass it with evidence before Elpis fast-forwards your project. That is where this post's picture comes from: in Elpis, the agent that designs and runs a team is called the Mother agent.

She watches over them

In the desktop app, the Observability page puts each request, tool call, token and cache hit of a chat on one timeline. In the terminal, the Agent command center shows each helper under its parent chat.

She remembers

Elpis can resume a chat exactly where it stopped, and you can switch models without losing the thread. Memory saving is opt-in per workspace, and the Context Ledger decides whether a saved memory reaches later requests.

What it is not yet

Elpis is alpha (v0.5.3), Linux x86_64 only, and in daily use by me. Its release checks show it installs and runs; they do not prove it writes better code.

Try it 

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MasihMoafi/Elpis/main/scripts/install.sh | bash

Then run elpis-app for the desktop app or elpis for the terminal app.

Code: https://github.com/MasihMoafi/Elpis

What else does a mother do that an agent app should? Tell me in the comments. The best answer may become the next feature.
