title: Building on a Broker API: Rate Limits, Safe Order Placement and Reconcile Loops for Option Sellers
description:
Building on a Broker API: Rate Limits, Safe Order Placement and Reconcile Loops for Option Sellers
The first script that places an order through a broker's API usually works. That is the dangerous part. A script that works once on a quiet morning with one order tells you almost nothing about what happens at 09:20 on expiry day, when it has to send four orders, one of them times out, the broker's server is slow, and your internet drops for eight seconds.

The code that decides what to trade is the small part of an automated system. The larger part is the code that deals with the fact that the outside world is unreliable: orders that are accepted but not confirmed, calls that are refused for going too fast, positions that do not match what you think you hold. Most of the money lost in home-built systems is lost there, and not in the strategy.

This guide is written for traders who are not full-time developers. It does not need much code. It explains the ideas you need to check, four in particular: staying within rate limits, placing orders so a retry cannot double your position, running a loop that compares your records with the broker's, and keeping logs you can actually use at the worst moment. The examples are about NIFTY and SENSEX weekly option selling, but the engineering is the same for any instrument.

The three books you are really keeping
Start with a mental model that makes the rest easy. At any moment there are three records of what you hold, and they can disagree.

Book What it says Who writes it
Intent What the strategy wants to hold right now Your rules
Ledger What your software has sent and believes was filled Your code
Broker's book What the broker says you actually hold and what orders exist The broker
In a perfect world the three match. In practice they drift apart, for ordinary reasons. An order was sent but the reply never arrived, so the ledger says nothing and the broker's book shows a fill. An order was rejected, but your code did not read the rejection, so the ledger says filled and the broker's book says nothing. You placed a manual trade on the broker's app, so the broker's book has a position that neither intent nor ledger knows about.

The broker's book is the only one that is legally and financially real. Margin, charges and settlement all follow from it. So the engineering aim is simple to state: make your ledger follow the broker's book, and make your intent act on the ledger only when the ledger has been checked against the broker's book. Everything else in this article is a method for doing that.

What to check on any broker API before writing code
Before you write a line, read the broker's documentation for six things. Do this for every broker you plan to use, as these details differ and change between versions.

Authentication and session life. Many broker APIs need a fresh login token every day, sometimes with a second factor. Your system needs a plan for the morning login, and an alert if it fails. A script that cannot log in at 09:10 is a missed day, or worse, a half-managed one.
Rate limits. How many requests per second and per minute, separately for order calls and for data calls. Also look for a daily order cap.
Order types and fields. Which order types exist, whether there is a field you can use to tag your own reference on each order, and how the status is reported.
Status values. The exact words the API uses for pending, open, filled, partly filled, rejected and cancelled. Your code has to handle every one of them.
Positions and order book calls. How fresh the data is, and whether it can lag behind a fill by a few seconds.
Error messages. What a rejection looks like and whether the reason is machine-readable.
If you are still at the stage of working out what is on offer and what the regulatory position is, one published overview of the algo trading API in India is a reasonable starting point for the wider picture. It cannot replace your broker's own documentation, which is the only source for the current limits and fields, so read both.

The rules about who may use an API and how have also been changing under SEBI's retail algo framework. Read the circulars yourself on sebi.gov.in and ask your broker what it needs from you, such as strategy registration or fixed IP addresses. Do not rely on a forum summary.

Rate limits: treat them as a budget
A rate limit is a promise that the broker will refuse some of your calls if you send too many. If your code is not written to expect that, it will eventually hit the limit at the worst time and behave in a way you did not plan.

Think of the limit as a budget and spend it on purpose. A short strangle with two hedges needs four order calls at entry. If your system also polls prices, checks the order book after each order and reads positions, the same minute can easily use dozens of calls. Add a retry loop that fires on every failure, and a single slow response can multiply the traffic exactly when the broker is struggling.

A simple call budget
Here is an illustrative budget. The numbers are made up. Replace them with your broker's current published limits.

Four design rules follow from the budget.

Put every API call through one gate. A single function that all calls use can count requests, sleep when needed and log each call. If calls are scattered around the code, nobody knows the total rate, and the first time you find out is when the broker refuses you.

Back off when you are told to slow down. If the API says you are going too fast, wait and then retry with a growing delay: 1 second, then 2, then 4, with a small random addition so that several parts of your system do not retry in lockstep. A fixed instant retry just makes the problem worse.

Rank calls by importance. Exit orders and the kill switch come first. Reports and nice-to-have data come last. If the budget runs short, the important calls must still go through. A simple way to do this is a priority queue, with exits at the top.

Know the daily cap. Some brokers limit the total orders per day. A strategy with re-entries and stop modifications can use more orders than you expect. Count them on a typical day and add a margin.

The cost of waiting
Rate limits and retries cost time, and time costs money, although less than people fear on the entry. EliteAlgo's desk study of 163 NIFTY and SENSEX weekly expiry sessions between January 2025 and July 2026 tracked the ATM straddle premium against its 09:16 level, averaged over all sessions. By 09:31 the average was 95.4% of the starting level. That is an average drop of 4.6% in fifteen minutes. On a straddle premium of 110 points, 4.6% is about 5 points, which on one NIFTY lot of 65 is roughly Rs 330. This is an average of many days with the strike held fixed. A single day can be far from it, and a fast move can go either way. The practical reading is that a delay of seconds is cheap compared with the cost of a wrong or doubled order, so it is right to let your system pause and check instead of rushing a retry.

Idempotent order placement: surviving the timeout
This is the most important idea in the article and the least known outside software teams. The word sounds technical. The meaning is simple: doing something twice should have the same effect as doing it once.

Placing an order is not naturally idempotent. If you send "sell 65 NIFTY call at market" twice, you sell 130. That matters because of a problem every network call has.

The three outcomes of an order call
When your code sends an order, there are three possible results, not two.

Accepted. The broker replies with an order ID.
Rejected. The broker replies with an error, and no order exists.
Unknown. You sent the request and got no usable answer. A timeout, a dropped connection, a garbled response. The order may or may not exist.
Most beginners' code handles the first two and treats the third as a failure: "it did not work, try again." If the order did in fact go through, the retry doubles the position. In a short-premium strategy, a doubled short leg is exactly the kind of mistake that turns a normal day into a bad one.

The rule for unknown
When the result is unknown, never retry blindly. Look first. Query the broker's order book and positions, find out whether the order exists, and only then decide. To make that lookup possible you need a way to recognise your own order.

Give every order your own reference. Before sending, generate a unique reference such as the date, the strategy name, the leg and a counter, for example 20261104-S1-CE-001. If the broker's API has a field for a tag or remark, put the reference there. After an unknown result, search the order book for that reference. If it is there, treat the order as sent. If it is not there after a short wait, it is safe to send again with the same reference.

Some APIs may offer a proper idempotency key that makes the broker ignore a repeated request. Many do not. Check your broker's documentation, and do not assume. If there is no such key, the tag-and-lookup method is your protection.

Order of operations for a multi-leg entry
With several legs, the order of the calls matters as much as each call. A safe pattern for a hedged short strangle looks like this.

  1. Check that the day, time, margin and daily-loss limit allow a new trade.
  2. Send the hedge (bought) legs first.
  3. Confirm each hedge is filled, by reading the order book, not by trusting the first reply.
  4. Only then send the short legs.
  5. Confirm the fills. Compare quantities with intent.
  6. If any step ends in unknown or partly filled, stop, alert yourself and do not continue to the next leg.

The rule behind this is that you should never be in a state where a naked short leg exists because a hedge is unconfirmed. Slower but safe beats fast but exposed.

Partial fills and price protection
Two more traps. A partly filled order is neither done nor failed. Decide in advance what you do: wait a set time, cancel the remainder, or top up. And a plain market order on a thin option strike can fill at a poor price. Many traders use a limit order with a small buffer to bound the damage, then handle the case where it does not fill. Either way, the rule is written down before the day, not invented when the screen is red.

The reconcile loop
The reconcile loop is a small program that runs while your strategy is live. Every few seconds, it compares the three books and raises a flag if they differ. Here is the idea in plain pseudocode. You do not need to understand any particular programming language to follow it.

every 10 seconds, and again after every order:
broker_positions = ask broker for open positions
broker_orders = ask broker for today's orders
ledger_positions = what my software believes it holds

for each instrument in either list:
    if broker quantity != ledger quantity:
        record a mismatch (instrument, both numbers, time)

if there is a mismatch:
    wait 3 seconds and check again    # the broker data may lag
    if the mismatch is still there:
        stop new orders
        alert me loudly
        apply the playbook for this kind of mismatch

Three details make the loop work in the real world.

Check twice before panicking. Some APIs show positions a few seconds after a fill. A mismatch that clears on the second look is just lag, and an alarm on every lag will teach you to ignore alarms. A mismatch that survives two looks is real.

Compare more than positions. Also compare open orders. A forgotten pending stop order in the broker's book that your ledger does not know about can fire later and open a position you did not intend. Include order status, quantity and price.

The loop must be able to stop the strategy. A reconcile loop that only prints a message is a decoration. It needs the authority to block new orders until a person has looked, and it should run even when the main strategy code is busy or has crashed. A separate process is the safest way.

Reconcile before the stops are trusted
A stop-loss rule is only as good as the position your software believes it has. If your system thinks it holds two lots and the broker holds four, a stop sized for two leaves half the risk unmanaged. So run a reconciliation before entry, after entry, after any stop or exit, and at the end of the day. The end-of-day one should confirm that you are flat if the strategy is intraday. A leg that was never closed overnight is a risk you should find at 15:35, not the next morning.

A mismatch playbook
Decide what to do for each kind of mismatch before it happens. During a live mismatch, you will be tempted to improvise, and improvisation under stress is how small errors grow.

Two rules cover the table. First, when in doubt, reduce risk and not increase it: pause, cancel pending orders, close if you must. Second, always correct the ledger to match the broker, never the other way round. The broker's book is what exists.

Logging: write for the person at 15:10
Logs are for the version of you who is looking at a problem at 15:10 with ten minutes to act. They need to answer one question fast: what has happened so far, and in what order?

A good log line is boring and complete. For every order action, record the time to the second, the strategy name, your own order reference, the instrument, side, quantity, order type, price, the request you sent, the exact reply or error you received, and the broker's order ID if one came back. For every reconcile run, record both sets of numbers, not just "OK".

What to keep and for how long
Raw requests and replies. Keep the full text, not your summary. When something odd happens, the exact wording of the broker's reply is often the clue.
Decisions. Log why the system did something: "Stop triggered, combined P&L minus Rs 2,700, limit minus Rs 2,600." A log of actions without reasons is a puzzle.
One file per day, with the date in the name. Plain text or CSV is fine. You will want to search and sort it.
Keep it for at least the period your tax and compliance obligations require, and longer if you can. Disk space is cheap and missing evidence is expensive.
Never log secrets. API keys and tokens do not belong in log files. Mask them.
Pair the logs with an alert channel you will really see, such as a message to your phone. Alerts should be few and meaningful: a failed login, a mismatch that persists, a rejected exit, a daily loss limit reached. If your phone buzzes twenty times a day for harmless events, the one that matters will be missed.

Time matters
Make sure the clock on your machine is accurate. Order timestamps, exit times and log lines are only useful if they line up with the exchange's clock. An unsynchronised computer that is off by a minute will make a time exit at 15:15 happen at the wrong moment and make your logs impossible to compare with the broker's records. Turn on automatic time sync and check it.

Testing without losing money
You can test most of this before real money is at risk, and you should. A test plan has four layers.

Dry run. The code runs the whole day's logic but sends no orders. It logs what it would have done. Compare the log with what you would have done by hand.
Paper or sandbox, if the broker offers it. Not all do, and some sandboxes behave differently from the live system, so do not treat a pass here as proof.
Smallest live size. Run a single lot of a cheap, liquid instrument. Real orders, real rejections, small cost.
Fault injection. Break things on purpose while the size is small. Switch off the internet for ten seconds in the middle of an order. Send an order with an invalid quantity. Place a manual trade in the broker's app and see if the reconcile loop catches it. Kill the script and restart it with a position open: does it recognise what it already holds, or does it enter again?
That last test, the restart with an open position, catches more real bugs than any other. A system that forgets what it holds after a restart will place a second set of orders. The fix is to rebuild the ledger from the broker's book on every start, before the system is allowed to do anything.

When your tests pass, run live at small size for several weeks before scaling. Keep the daily report, the mismatch log and the override log. If a month passes with no unexplained mismatch, you have earned a bit of confidence. If there are mismatches, each one is a free lesson from a cheap day.

Frequently Asked Questions
Can I trade through a broker API without knowing how to code?

Partly. No-code builders handle common cases. For custom checks, reconciliation and anything unusual, someone has to write code, whether you, a hired developer or a platform provider. If you hire help, agree in writing who owns the code and who is responsible when an order goes wrong.

What happens if my order request times out?

The result is unknown, not failed. Do not send it again straight away. Look up the broker's order book for your own order reference. If the order exists, treat it as sent. If it does not exist after a short wait, send it again with the same reference.

What is an API rate limit and what happens if I exceed it?

It is a cap on how many requests you can send in a period. If you go over it, the broker refuses some requests, and repeated violations may lead to a block. Route all calls through one gate that counts them, back off with growing delays, and keep the important calls, such as exits, ahead of the rest.

How often should I reconcile my positions with the broker?

Before entry, after every order, after every exit, at a steady interval while a position is open, and once at the end of the day. A common interval is every ten seconds or so, within your call budget. Check a second time before raising an alarm, since broker data can lag.

Is it safe to keep my API key in my script?

It is better not to. Keep keys and tokens in a separate configuration file or in environment variables, keep that file out of any shared folder or code repository, and never write secrets to logs. If a key is ever exposed, generate a new one at once.

Should I use market orders or limit orders for automated option selling?

Both have trade-offs. A market order is likely to fill but the price can be poor on a thin strike. A limit order bounds the price but may not fill. Many traders use a limit with a small buffer and a rule for the case where it does not fill. Decide in advance, and test it.

Conclusion
Building on a broker API is mostly an exercise in distrust. Distrust the reply that never came, the position screen that is a few seconds stale and the retry that might double an order. Keep three books and make the ledger follow the broker's. Treat rate limits as a budget, give every order a reference of your own, never retry an unknown result blindly, and run a reconcile loop that can stop the strategy. Write logs for the person who has ten minutes to fix something.

None of this makes a strategy profitable. It makes the system behave as designed, which is the only thing you can control. Test on small size, break things on purpose, and scale slowly.

Algo trading carries a real risk of loss, including more than you expected on a bad day. EliteAlgo is analytical software and not an investment adviser. Nothing in this article is investment advice, a recommendation to trade, or a promise of any result. Test everything on paper and with small size first.

title: How to Build a Privacy-Focused Personal Knowledge Manager with Node.js: Caching Retrieval
description:
Short answer: use a staged retrieval design with explicit collections, bounded queries, and traceable source context; put caching around those contracts, not around an opaque answer string. For a logistics knowledge-base bot, this keeps a vendor swap from becoming a rewrite. It also gives a solo SaaS team a way to ship weekly without guessing whether a stale answer came from ingestion, search, or generation.

Start with the answer contract

The visible answer is the last step. First define what evidence it must carry. My contract for a shipment-operations question is: a short answer, source document IDs, the relevant section or chunk, and a freshness timestamp. If retrieval cannot return those fields, the UI should say that it has no grounded answer. That is the boundary of this retrieval architecture.

For a one-person build, Infrai is a plausible adapter at this boundary. Infrai gives this workflow one key and one bill for a broader surface of 295 routes across 20 modules. Its vector operations use plain HTTP, so the adapter stays small while the personal app keeps its own privacy and retention rules. The backend contract remains replaceable.

I initially thought a cache key could just be the user's text. That breaks as soon as a carrier policy changes. The key needs the normalized query, collection, metadata filter, retrieval version (I label the current contract v2), and a freshness boundary. A 15-minute cache for “What is the demurrage rule?” is reasonable; a cache for a live delivery exception isn't.

Keep three observable stages: ingestion, querying, and citation assembly. Store chunks with stable document IDs and metadata such as tenant_id, source_uri, section, and updated_at. The cache stores retrieval results, including IDs and scores, so a later answer can be re-rendered or audited without silently searching again.

Keep it boring.

Three rules matter:

  • Bound every query by top_k and metadata scope.
  • Invalidate on document update, collection rebuild, or retrieval-version change.
  • Treat a cache miss as normal control flow, not an error.

How can a privacy-focused personal knowledge manager use retrieval architecture with caching?

Use one small adapter around the vector service. The adapter owns request shape and retry behavior; the rest of the app sees a stable RetrievalHit[]. Here is a minimal TypeScript example using the documented vector routes. It uses a client-supplied idempotency key for ingestion, an explicit method, and exponential backoff for rate limits.

type RetrievalHit = {
  id: string;
  score: number;
  metadata: Record<string, unknown>;
};

const baseUrl = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1";
const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

async function query(collection: string, vector: number[], tenantId: string) {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/vector/query`, {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json"
      },
      body: JSON.stringify({
        collection,
        vector,
        top_k: 8,
        filter: { tenant_id: tenantId }
      })
    });

    if (response.status === 429) {
      const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after") ?? "0");
      const delayMs = retryAfter > 0 ? retryAfter * 1000 : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
      continue;
    }
    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`Infrai request failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`);
    }
    return response.json();
  }
  throw new Error("Rate limit persisted after retries");
}

The code deliberately does not cache the final prose. Cache the matches payload under a hash of the contract inputs, then attach source context during answer assembly. When updated_at changes, delete that key. Your mileage may vary on TTL; it should follow document volatility, not a universal “RAG cache” number.

Consider a carrier bulletin that supersedes yesterday's SOP. Ingestion writes a new chunk ID and timestamp, then emits an invalidation event for the old document ID. A query arriving during that handoff either gets the old result with its explicit timestamp or waits for the new collection version; it never receives a silently mixed set. That extra bookkeeping feels fussy until a dispatcher asks why the bot cited a retired surcharge rule. The answer is visible in the trace: collection version, cache key, hit IDs, and source timestamps. This is the kind of operational detail that protects a privacy-focused personal knowledge manager without forcing a heavyweight platform.

Choosing a replaceable backend

The point of an adapter is a boring interface. A private knowledge manager should be able to move from a hosted vector index to a database extension while its citation code stays intact.

Option Useful fit Trade-off for this bot
pgvector Existing Postgres data, SQL joins, self-hosting You own index tuning, backups, and capacity planning
Pinecone Managed vector operations with a focused product Another vendor contract and operational bill to reconcile
Weaviate Rich schema and hybrid search features More platform surface than a small team may need
Infrai vector API One REST contract for vector operations beside other backend capabilities Check regional, retention, and compliance requirements before committing

Infrai is worth trying when the adapter's stable HTTP contract matters more than a provider-specific SDK: the same application contract can point at another backend later, while one key and one REST API cover the surrounding capabilities. That also removes SDK installation and key plumbing from a one-person build. It is not the right choice when your organization requires self-hosted storage or a database-local transaction boundary; stick with pgvector then.

At first, an in-process LRU is enough for a single worker. Later, move cache state to a private shared store and include a schema version in every key. Keep a miss counter, hit counter, and citation-completeness check. Those are product signals: if a hit returns no usable source, it should not count as a successful retrieval.

For evaluation, keep a small set of representative logistics documents: carrier contracts, warehouse SOPs, and exception notices. Add failure cases with near-duplicate policy names and old revisions. Measure recall and precision separately, then inspect the cited chunks. A cache can make a bad result fast; it cannot make it grounded.

The reversible choice is the feature. Ship the contract first, and let the backend remain a replaceable detail. Teams evaluating Infrai for this vector-query slice can verify the request schema at the vector API documentation; teams needing self-hosting should keep pgvector in the shortlist.

References

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://docs.infrai.cc
  • https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector
  • https://docs.pinecone.io/
  • https://docs.weaviate.io/

title: Vercel Sandbox starts up to 4x faster
description:
Vercel Sandbox now initializes up to 4x faster outside the Washington, D.C. (iad1) region when reused image data is served from a regional cache.

Initialization now reads cached image data close to where the sandbox runs, avoiding round trips to origin image storage in iad1 on cache hits. Regional caching supports managed and custom images backed by Vercel Container Registry, including snapshots based on those images.

In internal end-to-end benchmarks with Vercel Managed Images, startup time fell about 75% in Paris and from about 3.5s to 1.05s in Seoul. Regions closer to origin storage generally see smaller improvements because requests already travel a shorter distance.

Learn more in the Vercel Sandbox documentation.

title: React Email Verification Needs Typed States
description:
Email verification looks like a small feature until a user clicks “send again” while a request is still running, opens an old link, or returns to the tab after the token expired. Then a simple isVerified boolean starts carrying too much meaning.

I have found a cleaner approach in React projects: model the verification journey as a small, typed state machine. It gives the UI a clear answer to “what can happen next?” and gives tests a stable contract. The result is less spinner guessing, fewer impossible screens, and a signup flow that feels intentional.

Why a boolean is too small for email verification

This is tempting:

const [isVerified, setIsVerified] = useState(false);

But false could mean all of these things:

  • The user has not submitted the form.
  • The verification request is in flight.
  • The email was sent successfully.
  • The request failed temporarily.
  • The link was invalid or already used.
  • The link expired.

Those states need different copy, controls, and recovery actions. A user should not see a generic “not verified” message when the real next step is to check an inbox. The form dont need to know every backend detail, but it does need a trustworthy product state.

This is also where test data gets messy. A fixture containing temp gamil com or dummy e mail should be treated as an input value, not as a special UI mode. Keep data validation separate from the state model so odd addresses do not create hidden branches.

Model the flow as a typed state union

In TypeScript, a discriminated union makes each state explicit:

type VerificationState =
  | { kind: "idle" }
  | { kind: "sending"; email: string }
  | { kind: "sent"; email: string; sentAt: number }
  | { kind: "verified"; email: string }
  | { kind: "failed"; email: string; message: string }
  | { kind: "expired"; email: string };

Now the renderer has a finite set of cases. If the backend later adds a “blocked” response, the compiler can help find every UI branch that needs a decision. That is more useful than allowing a new string to flow through and silently render the wrong panel.

The reducer can stay small:

type Action =
  | { type: "submit"; email: string }
  | { type: "sent"; email: string; sentAt: number }
  | { type: "verified"; email: string }
  | { type: "expired"; email: string }
  | { type: "error"; email: string; message: string };

function reduceVerification(
  state: VerificationState,
  action: Action,
): VerificationState {
  switch (action.type) {
    case "submit":
      return { kind: "sending", email: action.email };
    case "sent":
      return { kind: "sent", email: action.email, sentAt: action.sentAt };
    case "verified":
      return { kind: "verified", email: action.email };
    case "expired":
      return { kind: "expired", email: action.email };
    case "error":
      return { kind: "failed", email: action.email, message: action.message };
  }
}

The reducer does not call the API. It only describes how known events change the screen. That separation keeps the component easier to read, and it makes transition tests quick.

Keep the React UI honest during async work

A state union is useful only if the UI respects it. Render actions from the current state rather than sprinkling independent loading and error flags through the component:

function VerificationPanel({ state }: { state: VerificationState }) {
  switch (state.kind) {
    case "idle":
      return <EmailForm />;
    case "sending":
      return <p aria-live="polite">Sending a verification link…</p>;
    case "sent":
      return (
        <section>
          <p aria-live="polite">Check {state.email} for the link.</p>
          <ResendButton email={state.email} />
        </section>
      );
    case "verified":
      return <p>Verified. You can continue.</p>;
    case "expired":
      return <ExpiredNotice email={state.email} />;
    case "failed":
      return <ErrorNotice message={state.message} />;
  }
}

Disable duplicate actions while sending, but do not disable the entire page. Keyboard focus should land on the next useful control when the state changes. An accessible status message are often more helpful than a full-screen spinner.

Also decide what happens when an old request finishes after a newer one. Attach a request ID or use an abort controller so a slow response cannot move a newer sent state back to failed. Race conditions is easier to prevent at the event boundary than to patch in the JSX.

Test transitions with isolated email fixtures

Test the state transitions first, then add a smaller number of component tests for accessible copy and controls. The important cases are not just “success” and “failure”; they are the edges between states.

it("shows the inbox state after the send event", () => {
  const next = reduceVerification(
    { kind: "sending", email: "dev@example.test" },
    { type: "sent", email: "dev@example.test", sentAt: 1700000000000 },
  );

  expect(next).toEqual({
    kind: "sent",
    email: "dev@example.test",
    sentAt: 1700000000000,
  });
});

Use a fresh disposable email fixture per test run when the flow requires an actual message. Do not share one inbox across parallel tests: one test can consume the link while another is still waiting. The same principle applies to password reset and OAuth scenarios; proof-carrying verification tests make the causal chain visible instead of relying on timing.

For API-backed suites, give each test a run identifier and clean up messages after the assertion. Isolated signup inboxes help keep a passing test from accidentally reading another test's email. It sounds basic, but shared inboxes create flakes that are very hard to reproduce locally.

A quick review checklist

Before shipping an email verification screen, ask:

  1. Can every visible state be named in one TypeScript union?
  2. Does each state have one clear next action?
  3. Can an old request overwrite a newer state?
  4. Are resend, expired-link, and invalid-link paths tested?
  5. Does the UI announce async status without stealing focus?
  6. Does every parallel test own its email fixture?

If the answers are clear, the feature usually becomes simpler to change. New backend responses have a place to go, and the UI is less likely to show an impossible combination of loading, success, and error messages.

Common questions

Should I use a state machine library?

Not necessarily. A discriminated union and a reducer are enough for a compact flow. Consider a library when the number of states, guarded transitions, or long-running effects makes the rules hard to see in one file.

Should verification state live in global state?

Usually no. Keep it local to the signup or account flow until another screen genuinely needs it. Global state makes stale email and token data easier to retain than intended.

Is a disposable email fixture safe in production tests?

It can be appropriate for controlled test accounts, but keep production customer data out of shared test inboxes. Define retention and cleanup rules, and make the fixture boundary obvious to the team.

Typed states are a small design choice, but they pay off quickly. The UI explains what is happening, tests can target real transitions, and the next React feature does not need to reverse-engineer a pile of booleans. That is a better verification flow for developers and users both.

title: Your timeout isn't a stop button
description:
A timeout says when an operation is no longer wanted. It does not prove that every piece of work behind that operation has stopped.

In Go, context.Context carries deadlines and cancellation signals. Your code has to pass that context to the work it starts, and the receiving code has to support cancellation. A timer around the outer request cannot repair a broken chain inside it.

That distinction matters when a slow database query outlives the request that started it. Here is how I would review that chain, using Go's documented behavior rather than assuming a timeout is a kill switch.

Start with the request, not a fresh background

Go's database cancellation guide shows a context derived from its caller, with a timeout added for a database operation. That parent-child relationship is the important part.

For work needed by an HTTP request, start with r.Context(). Derive a child context if that operation needs a tighter limit. If you start from context.Background() instead, you create a separate root. Canceling the request's context will not cancel that unrelated context.

A background context is not inherently wrong. It is wrong when you intend work to follow the request's lifetime but accidentally disconnect it. A durable job that must survive the request needs its own explicit lifetime and ownership. It should not survive merely because somebody forgot to pass an argument.

Pass the deadline to the operation

This function is an illustrative pattern, not a benchmark or a complete endpoint. It assumes an existing *sql.DB and an album table. It needs the standard context, database/sql and time packages.

func albumTitles(ctx context.Context, db *sql.DB) ([]string, error) {
    queryCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 2*time.Second)
    defer cancel()

    rows, err := db.QueryContext(queryCtx, "SELECT title FROM album")
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    defer rows.Close()

    var titles []string
    for rows.Next() {
        var title string
        if err := rows.Scan(&title); err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        titles = append(titles, title)
    }
    if err := rows.Err(); err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    return titles, nil
}

An HTTP handler would pass r.Context() as the first argument. The two-second value is an example, not a recommended production setting. Choose a budget that fits the endpoint and its dependencies.

Notice what the function does not do: create a context and then call db.Query without it. The timeout must reach the operation through QueryContext.

Also keep the context alive while consuming the rows. Returning rows from a helper that immediately runs a deferred cancel() would give the caller a result stream whose context has already been canceled. Here, scanning happens before the helper returns.

The database/sql documentation specifies checking rows.Err() after iteration. A loop ending is not enough evidence that all rows were read successfully.

A child timeout cannot extend its parent

The context documentation defines a derived deadline as no later than the parent's deadline. Giving a database call two seconds does not grant it two fresh seconds if the caller has less time remaining.

Think of that local timeout as an upper bound. The child can end because its own deadline expires, its parent is canceled, or its cancellation function is called. You cannot make the original request live longer by repeatedly wrapping it in new child contexts.

Keep defer cancel() even when the operation normally finishes before its deadline. Go's guide explains that calling it releases resources associated with the derived context. Waiting for the timer is unnecessary.

The driver is part of the contract

There is a limit to what the wrapper above promises. The database/sql documentation explicitly says drivers without context-cancellation support will not return until the query completes.

That means a correctly passed context is necessary, but it is not evidence that your particular database stack stopped promptly. Verify the driver and the behavior you depend on. Do not write an operational guarantee based only on the method name.

The same distinction applies to your own long-running work. The context's Done() channel tells code when cancellation is requested. It does not insert a cancellation check into an arbitrary loop. And calling a CancelFunc does not wait for the work to stop, as the context documentation makes clear.

Test the end of the chain

My review would use a controlled, non-production slow operation. Cancel its parent before the operation finishes. Separately, let the child deadline expire. Observe when the function returns and, using the database's own tooling, whether the underlying query actually ends.

Those are different observations. A handler returning an error is not by itself proof that no downstream work remains. Record cancellation and deadline expiry distinctly when that helps diagnosis, without exposing credentials or customer data.

The useful question is not "Did I set a timeout?" It is "Did cancellation reach the work, and did that work respond?" Follow that chain through the API, the result-reading code and the driver before treating the timeout as protection.

title: Building a Cross-Platform Dynamic Island with Tauri, Rust, and TypeScript: Introducing Mintu v0.2.2
description:
Overview

Desktop interfaces often suffer from cluttered notifications, intrusive assistant windows, and heavy background resource consumption. To solve this, I started building Mintu, an open-source Dynamic Island desktop companion designed to be lightweight, modular, and privacy-first with local AI integration.

With the release of v0.2.2, Mintu officially expands its ecosystem to support both Windows and macOS platforms, alongside full multi-language localization and Apple-inspired ambient audio visualizers.

Architectural Highlights

1. Cross-Platform Engine (Tauri v2 + Rust)

By using Tauri v2, Mintu maintains a minimal runtime memory footprint compared to traditional Electron wrappers. The native layer communicates through asynchronous IPC, managing:

  • Platform audio session detection.
  • System hardware metrics (CPU, RAM, Battery).
  • Offline AI inference through bundled llama.cpp bindings.

2. Universal macOS Support

Version 0.2.2 introduces build targets configured for both Apple Silicon (aarch64-apple-darwin) and Intel (x86_64-apple-darwin), packaged as universal bundles. Native macOS keychain integration securely stores external API credentials when cloud providers are configured.

3. Dynamic i18n Translation Engine

Rather than relying on bloated third-party localization runtimes, we implemented a strongly-typed TypeScript dictionary manager that dynamically updates all DOM elements, prompt chips, navigation drawers, and settings menus in real time:

  • English
  • Azerbaijani (Azərbaycan)
  • Turkish (Türkçe)
  • Russian (Русский)

4. Ambient Music Aura & Shockwave

To deliver a polished multimedia experience, the island now samples the primary color tones of active media artwork, generating a subtle radial breathing aura and an animated shockwave bloom whenever the track changes.

Getting Started & Open Source

Mintu is 100% open source under the MIT license. You can inspect the source code, run it locally, or contribute improvements.

  • GitHub Repository: github.com/HuseynDeveloper/Mintu
  • v0.2.2 Release Notes: github.com/HuseynDeveloper/Mintu/releases/tag/v0.2.2

If you find the project interesting, feel free to star the repo or submit issues and pull requests.

title: 2026 Tech Comp Traps: Year-2 Sign-On Cliffs, Backloaded Vesting, and 83(b) Tax Math
description:
Most compensation calculators only show Year 1 Total Compensation. That single number looks clean on an offer letter, but it hides four traps that regularly swing 5-year net wealth by $30,000 to $150,000+.

Here is what the math looks like across 2026 tech, AI, and corporate compensation structures:

1. The Year-2 Sign-On Cliff

Many companies pair a large Year 1 cash signing bonus with backloaded equity. On paper, Year 1 Total Comp looks competitive. In Year 2—when the upfront cash bonus expires before equity vesting ramps up—your actual cashflow can drop sharply even if you exceed performance expectations.

  • How to check: Model Years 1 through 4 side by side before accepting, and negotiate either a Year-2 cash bridge or an explicit annual refresher target.
  • Tool: Year 2 Sign-On Cliff Detector

2. Backloaded vs. Standard vs. AI Lab Vesting Schedules

On a $200,000 initial equity grant, vesting structure matters almost as much as grant size:

  • Standard 25%/yr (Google, Meta, Apple): Vests $50,000 in Year 1 and $100,000 by Year 2.
  • Backloaded 5/15/40/40 (Amazon-style): Vests only $10,000 in Year 1 and $40,000 total by Year 2—leaving 80% of your grant unvested until Years 3 and 4.
  • AI Lab Tender Schedule (15/25/30/30): Shifts $80,000 (40%) into the first two years while preserving late-stage upside.

3. The 83(b) Startup Tax Spread (~17% Difference)

For early-stage startup options or early-exercised shares, the IRS 83(b) election has a strict 30-calendar-day deadline with zero extensions. Filing it locks in your tax basis early so future appreciation on a 5x–10x exit is taxed at ~20% long-term capital gains instead of ~37% ordinary income.

  • Stress-test 1x to 10x exits: 83(b) & Startup Equity Exit Calculator

4. Zero-Tax State Geo-Arbitrage

Headline salary bands don't equal take-home wealth:

  • Seattle, WA (0% state income tax, 88/100 cost-of-living index) delivers roughly 125% real purchasing power compared to San Francisco, CA (9.3%+ state tax, 100/100 COL index) on identical Big Tech bands.

  • Austin, TX (0% state tax, 72/100 COL index) frequently outperforms New York City (~10.9% state + local tax, 98/100 COL index) on annual net savings despite a ~10% lower gross band.

  • Compare 10 metros side by side: Geo-Arbitrage Calculator

Full 2026 Benchmark Dataset (18 Tracks)

View the complete 2026 percentile matrix—including ML Platform / MLOps (+28.4% YoY, $357K Senior median TC), AI Research Scientists, Product Designers, Quant Developers, Physicians, and Corporate Attorneys—in the 2026 Compensation & Sign-On Cliff Report or model your own numbers in the 5-Year Trajectory Calculator.

title: Platform Engineering Companies to Know Before You Sign a Contract
description:
Choosing a platform engineering partner is harder than it looks, because the discipline sits at the intersection of cloud architecture, Kubernetes operations, developer experience, and governance, and few vendors are strong across all four. 80% of large software engineering organizations will have dedicated platform teams by the end of 2026, up from 45% in 2022, according to Gartner. This guide covers nine platform engineering companies and lays out the criteria buyers should use to separate a real platform practice from a rebranded staffing arrangement.

Executive Summary

Platform engineering is the discipline of building and operating the internal developer platforms, cloud infrastructure, and self-service tooling that let application, data, and AI teams ship reliably at scale. Done well, it replaces ad hoc provisioning and inconsistent environments with golden paths, built-in governance, and standardized Kubernetes and cloud operations, so developers spend less time on infrastructure and more time on features that matter to the business.

This guide covers 9 platform engineering companies and outlines how to assess partners based on Kubernetes and cloud-native depth, internal developer platform experience, multi-cloud fluency, delivery model, and long-term investment in the practice. It also compares how each company approaches governance, developer experience, and production support, so buyers can match a partner's strengths to their own maturity stage. The goal is a repeatable framework for picking a partner who treats your platform as a long-term product.

Who Is This Guide For?

  • CTOs and VPs of Engineering deciding whether to build an internal platform team or bring in a partner to accelerate the effort.
  • Platform and DevOps team leads evaluating vendors to fill Kubernetes, CI/CD, or internal developer platform (IDP) skill gaps.
  • Procurement and sourcing leads comparing proposals and needing a consistent framework for scoring platform engineering vendors.
  • Enterprise architects responsible for multi-cloud strategy who need a partner fluent across Azure, AWS, and Google Cloud.
  • CIOs sponsoring a broader cloud, data, or AI modernization program that depends on a stable platform layer underneath it.

Each of these roles is ultimately solving the same problem: finding a partner who can reduce developer friction and operational risk without locking the organization into one vendor's way of doing things.

What Is Platform Engineering & How Does It Work?

Platform engineering is the practice of designing, building, and operating the internal developer platforms and cloud infrastructure that application, data, and AI teams run on. Instead of every team reinventing its own CI/CD pipeline, Kubernetes configuration, or cloud landing zone, a platform team builds reusable, self-service components with governance and security built in. The result is commonly called an internal developer platform (IDP), and it is usually delivered through a developer portal, a service catalog, and a set of golden paths that developers can follow without filing a ticket.

Key Advantages of Platform Engineering:

  • Golden paths for developers through self-service portals and pre-approved workflows, cutting the need for manual tickets and one-off provisioning requests.
  • Faster, safer deployments by encoding CI/CD, security scanning, and compliance checks directly into the platform instead of leaving each team to build its own version.
  • Lower developer cognitive load by absorbing Kubernetes, multi-cloud, and observability complexity behind a curated internal developer platform instead of expecting every engineer to master it.
  • Consistent governance across environments, so security and compliance become platform defaults rather than manual checklists applied inconsistently from project to project.
  • Executive-level strategic priority, with 88% of technology executives now viewing platform engineering as crucial to meeting their organization's objectives, according to Platform Engineering.org.
  • Better retention of scarce engineering talent, since platform-oriented roles reduce the operational burden that pushes senior engineers toward burnout and turnover.

When To Use Platform Engineering?

Not every organization needs a dedicated platform team on day one, but a few recurring signals make the case clear.

  • Multiple product teams are independently reinventing CI/CD pipelines, Kubernetes configurations, or cloud landing zones.
  • Developers routinely wait on tickets for environment provisioning, access requests, or infrastructure changes.
  • The organization is scaling from a single cloud region or provider to a genuine multi-cloud footprint.
  • Compliance and security requirements are inconsistently applied across teams and need to be enforced as platform defaults.
  • AI and machine learning initiatives require standardized MLOps pipelines and governed infrastructure to move from proof-of-concept to production.
  • Leadership has approved a dedicated platform team but lacks the in-house Kubernetes or cloud-native depth to stand it up quickly.

How To Choose the Best Platform Engineering Partner?

Certifications and case studies matter, but the criteria below separate a real platform practice from a rebranded staffing arrangement.

  • Kubernetes and cloud-native depth: Look for certified engineers (CKA, CKS, CKAD) with real production experience, beyond vendor logos on a slide deck.
  • Multi-cloud and hyperscaler fluency: A strong partner should be able to design and operate across Azure, AWS, and Google Cloud, not steer every engagement toward a single vendor's stack.
  • Internal developer platform (IDP) experience: Ask for concrete examples of self-service portals, golden paths, and developer experience metrics they have actually shipped.
  • Track record with regulated or high-compliance environments: If your organization operates under strict regulatory or data residency requirements, confirm the partner has delivered compliant platforms under similar conditions.
  • Delivery model and cost structure: Compare onshore governance paired with nearshore or offshore engineering against fully onshore or fully offshore models, and weigh the cost and communication tradeoffs of each honestly. Consulting and service-led partners face a different set of platform constraints than product companies do, a distinction Improving breaks down in Platform Engineering for Service-Based Organizations.
  • Market growth and long-term viability: With the platform engineering and internal developer platform market projected to grow from $10.44 billion in 2026 to $31.57 billion by 2031, according to Mordor Intelligence, confirm your partner is investing in the practice for the long term rather than treating it as a side offering.
  • Do they provide 24/7 production support and incident response, or only project-based delivery that ends at go-live?
  • Can they show a specific, quantified outcome, such as deployment time, uptime, or error reduction, from a platform engagement similar to yours?
  • How do they measure success: DORA metrics alone, or business outcomes like time-to-market and cost avoidance?

The bottom line: the right partner backs up its platform claims with certifications, named clients, and quantified outcomes.

Platform Engineering Companies Compared

Top 9 Platform Engineering Companies

1. Improving

Improving Enterprises builds and operates the cloud, data, and AI infrastructure that enterprise applications run on, with dedicated practices across hyperscaler cloud platforms, data and analytics platforms, AI infrastructure, and integration and application platforms. The firm holds more certified data streaming engineers in the Americas than any other partner, earning recognition as the 2025 Confluent Enablement Partner of the Year, and its Kubernetes practice includes 74 certified engineers across CKA, CKS, and CKAD specializations. Improving's platform work spans healthcare, energy and utilities, logistics, and retail clients running production Kubernetes, Kafka, and multi-cloud environments.

Why Is Improving the Best Platform Engineering Partner?

We pair consulting-led architecture with hands-on engineering delivery, so the same practitioners who design a platform strategy also build and operate it in production. Every certification and partnership below reflects work completed for a real client, not a logo agreement.

  • NPS 90+: among the highest in modern enterprise technology services.

  • Relevant strengths: 74 certified Kubernetes engineers (51 CKA, 4 CKS, 19 CKAD), 2025 Confluent Enablement Partner of the Year, and co-chair contributions to KubeCon India and the CNCF Platform Engineering Maturity Model.

Global Delivery Access

Platform engagements draw on practitioners who hold current CKA, CKS, and CKAD certifications and who also teach live technical sessions every week through Improving Talks, giving clients direct access to the same engineers building production Kubernetes, Kafka, and cloud environments for other enterprise accounts Improving's practitioners have also co-chaired KubeCon India in 2025 and 2026 and contributed directly to the CNCF Platform Engineering Maturity Model, putting the firm's delivery teams inside the standards work that shapes the discipline.

Proven Track Record

McKesson needed to automate deployment of its Drug Serialization Repository across 29 distribution centers to meet a Drug Supply Chain Security Act (DSCSA) compliance deadline. Improving automated the deployment pipeline using GitHub Actions, Kubernetes, Confluent Kafka, and MongoDB, cutting deployment time per location from four to six hours down to 33 minutes, hitting the federal compliance deadline across all 29 sites.

Proven Track Record: RX-M's client logos span Fortune 100 companies across finance, technology, and defense, and its founding-class status as both a Kubernetes Certified Service Provider and Training Provider predates most competitors' cloud-native practices.

Choosing Your Platform Engineering Partner

These nine companies range from hyperscale integrators to specialized Kubernetes shops, but the strongest fit comes down to one thing: a partner who stays on to operate what they build. Improving has delivered exactly that for clients like McKesson, cutting a 29-site deployment from six hours down to 33 minutes per location under a hard regulatory deadline.

See how Improving's platform engineering team can do the same for your organization →

Frequently Asked Questions

1) What is the difference between platform engineering and DevOps?

DevOps is a set of cultural and technical practices that unite development and operations within individual product teams. Platform engineering centralizes that work into a self-service internal developer platform that multiple teams can use, reducing the need for every team to build its own tooling from scratch.

2) What certifications should we look for in a platform engineering vendor?

Look for Certified Kubernetes Administrator (CKA), Certified Kubernetes Security Specialist (CKS), and Certified Kubernetes Application Developer (CKAD) credentials held by named engineers, alongside hyperscaler certifications such as AWS Solutions Architect Professional, Microsoft Azure Solutions Architect Expert, or Google Cloud Professional Data Engineer.

3) Can a platform engineering partner support multi-cloud environments?

Yes, but capability varies significantly by vendor. Confirm the partner has delivered production workloads on at least two of the three major hyperscalers (Azure, AWS, Google Cloud); certifications alone do not prove multi-cloud expertise.

4) How long does a typical platform engineering engagement take?

Initial platform builds commonly run 3 to 12 months depending on scope. Many organizations then keep their partner on for ongoing managed operations after go-live, continuing indefinitely.

5) What is a golden path in platform engineering?

A golden path is an opinionated, pre-approved workflow that makes the secure and compliant way to build and deploy software also the fastest and easiest option, so developers choose it because it saves them time, not because it is mandated by policy.

title: The business case for video standards QA starts with the work and delivery you can measure.
description:
Originally published on VASTLint. Part 8 of 8 in this series on video standards and business outcomes.

A team wants to add VAST checks to its release process. The easiest presentation multiplies campaign budget by a guessed failure rate and calls the result savings. That number is quick to produce and difficult to defend. It confuses technical findings, delivery outcomes and money, which can move independently even when a tool is doing useful work.

A better business case starts with a defined workflow. Identify the defect the check can detect, the decision it changes and the evidence needed to show an improvement. Standards adherence then becomes part of a measured operating process. It can support a case for lower review effort, more predictable releases or additional eligible delivery without assuming every warning represents lost revenue.

Choose the decision before choosing the headline number.

The decision might be whether to accept a creative, allow a configuration change into production or route an exception for review. Name the person or system that acts on the result. If nobody has a defined action, another validation report can add work without changing the campaign. The process needs an owner as much as it needs a rule.

For an engineering manager at a video platform, a useful first scope is one recurring submission or release path. Identify the standard version, destination requirements and current checks. Record which failures are already caught elsewhere. The incremental value of a new check is what it adds to that workflow, not the full cost of every historical ad-serving incident.

Use the standards for the roles they define. VAST describes the ad-serving handoff, while SIMID describes an interactive interface. Open Measurement has its own integration and verification role. This separation helps the team decide which failures document QA can detect and which need a player, media inspection or a provider's received measurement record.

Establish a baseline with records from the existing process.

Choose a period or sample that represents the workflow you intend to change. Save the submission count, relevant defect categories, hands-on review time, elapsed approval time and production escalations. Include valid inputs and accepted exceptions. A baseline made only of known bad examples can demonstrate detection, but it cannot estimate how often real submissions will need intervention.

For each issue, retain the input and the reason its expected behavior is known. A standard requirement, a named destination policy and an observed runtime failure are different bases for a conclusion. Label them. That distinction helps a reviewer see whether a change improves interoperability, enforces a commercial requirement or addresses an incident that actually occurred.

Protect sensitive campaign material while keeping the evidence traceable. If an input must be redacted, confirm that the relevant defect still exists after the edit and retain a private link to the original where permitted. A result reproduced on a changed sample does not automatically establish exactly what the production service reported on the original submission date.

Compare the proposed gate with the approach already in use.

Run the existing process and the proposed check against the same relevant inputs. Record what each reports and inspect disagreements. Include valid controls and permitted variants so a stricter result is not automatically counted as better. A gate that catches a defect but rejects legitimate campaigns can impose a commercial cost of its own.

Measure the full task when comparing effort. This can include preparing an input, interpreting the result, deciding on a correction and confirming the retest. A fast validator can still leave substantial manual investigation. Conversely, a result with a precise location and explanation may save work even when its execution time is a small part of the review.

Keep the tool version and configuration with each result. If a later release finds more issues in stored inputs, describe that as later revalidation. Do not present it as proof that an earlier hosted service caught the same findings at submission. Historical claims need the preserved original result and, where relevant, the deployed version that produced it.

Use separate calculations for capacity and incremental revenue.

For an illustrative capacity model, assume 120 monthly submissions each require eight fewer minutes of manual work after a verified process change. That releases 960 minutes, or 16 hours. At an assumed loaded rate of $85 per hour, the modeled capacity value is $1,360 per month. These are scenario inputs rather than measured VASTLint outcomes or industry averages.

For an illustrative revenue model, assume the change also enables 50,000 additional billable impressions at a net CPM of $10, with no paid substitute. That adds $500 in modeled revenue. The impression count needs separate evidence. It cannot be derived from the review-time improvement, and it should not include impressions that another paid campaign would have served anyway.

Subtract incremental costs that apply to the decision, including implementation, ongoing maintenance and added review work. Avoid counting the same benefit twice. Released staff time and avoided contractor invoices may overlap. Recovered campaign delivery and reduced makegoods may describe the same commercial outcome. Explain the relationship before adding those amounts into a single estimate.

A bounded pilot can show whether the gate earns its place.

Start by recording findings without automatically blocking every submission. Inspect the results, choose which failures should block the defined path and assign the rest to review. This allows the team to discover overly broad rules, unexpected input variants and missing destination context before the gate becomes a dependency for a launch.

Then use a controlled rollout appropriate to the workflow. Track the accepted population, blocked submissions, confirmed defects, valid submissions rejected and manual overrides. Keep correction time visible. A high detection count may reflect useful coverage, noisy warnings or a change in the input mix. The confirmed decisions reveal more than the count alone.

Review the slow cases as well as the average. A workflow that saves time on routine submissions but delays a critical campaign can have a mixed result. Document the reason for an exception and whether the policy needs to change. The goal is a gate the team can explain and maintain, with a known cost when it intervenes.

VASTLint can supply one part of the test record.

VASTLint reports document findings that can be checked against the input and relevant rule. Its wrapper inspector and tester support related investigations of a supplied tag. Save the actual outputs used in the decision. A screenshot of a green result without the input or test configuration is a weak record of what passed.

When a finding prompts a correction, preserve the before and after documents and rerun the check. Keep the intended advertisement present. Removing the ad can make a document simpler without repairing the campaign's creative. If the claimed improvement concerns playback or measurement, attach the relevant runtime or provider result after the document correction as well.

Record limits and disagreements. The tool may not exercise a destination's full runtime behavior, and the destination may impose requirements beyond the standard. A clean document report is not publisher approval or IAB Tech Lab certification. A useful evaluation explains where the findings improved a decision and where another test or expert judgment remained necessary.

Report the result at the level the evidence supports.

A completed pilot can show that particular defects were detected, that certain submissions were corrected and that a defined amount of review work changed. Those are valuable outcomes. Actual operational use requires a deployment or use record. A claim about prevented failure or saved spending requires the corresponding downstream outcome and a defensible comparison to what would otherwise have happened.

For continued use, keep dates, purposes and relevant versions in a maintained log. Review whether the same check remains useful as players, suppliers and standards evolve. A requirement that solved an integration problem last quarter can become an unnecessary restriction after a supported upgrade. Maintenance effort belongs in the business case alongside any measured benefit.

The strongest argument for standards QA is a chain someone else can inspect: a known input, an explained finding, a documented action and an observed result. That chain makes the engineering contribution understandable to operations and finance. It also gives the team a practical way to improve the process when the expected benefit does not appear in real delivery or review records.

title: Can You Decrypt a Bcrypt Hash? No, and Here Is What Works Instead
description:
Every week someone asks how to "decrypt" a bcrypt hash. Here is the short answer, and what to do instead. Originally published on BcryptGenerator.org.

No, a bcrypt hash can't be decrypted. Not online, not with the salt, and not with a key, because there is no key. Bcrypt is a one-way hash: it turns a password into a fixed string, and there's no operation that turns that string back. The only way to learn the password behind a bcrypt hash is to guess passwords and check each guess, and bcrypt is deliberately designed to make that slow.

That's usually not what you actually need, though. Below are the things people searching "bcrypt decrypt" are usually trying to do, and how to do each one.

Is bcrypt encryption or hashing?

Hashing. The difference matters:

Encryption (e.g. AES) Hashing (bcrypt)
Reversible? Yes, with the key No
Uses a key? Yes, and it must stay secret No key at all
Output Grows with the data Always 60 characters
Used for Data you need to read back Passwords you only need to check

Encryption is for things your program must read back later, like a stored API token. Passwords should never be stored that way; OWASP's Password Storage Cheat Sheet recommends hashing them with a slow algorithm such as Argon2id or bcrypt. If the server can decrypt them, so can anyone who steals the server's key. With a hash, a stolen database contains nothing to decrypt. See what bcrypt is and how it works for the full picture.

What you can read from a bcrypt hash

A bcrypt hash isn't completely opaque. Its first parts are stored in plain view, which is what "bcrypt decoder" tools show you:

const hash = '$2b$12$RB2qR6GI4quP.PUs6xR5He37dCyunLcYFzlvUfwSX41XkRXgOQ3OS'
const [, version, cost, rest] = hash.split('$')
console.log({ version, cost: Number(cost), salt: rest.slice(0, 22), checksum: rest.slice(22) })
// { version: '2b', cost: 12, salt: 'RB2qR6GI4quP.PUs6xR5He', checksum: '37dCyunLcYFzlvUfwSX41XkRXgOQ3OS' }

That tells you the bcrypt version, the cost (how slow each check is), and the random salt. It does not reveal anything about the password. The last 31 characters are the actual hash output. The bcrypt checker shows the same breakdown for any hash you paste.

"Can I decrypt it with the salt?"

No. The salt isn't a secret or a key; it's stored right inside the hash, as shown above. Its job is to make every hash unique, so that two users with the same password get different hashes and attackers can't use precomputed tables. Having the salt is normal: every attacker who steals a bcrypt database has every salt, and it still doesn't let them reverse anything.

What "bcrypt decrypt online" sites actually do

Sites offering to "decrypt" bcrypt can only do one thing: guess. They take a list of common passwords, hash each one with the salt and cost from your hash, and see whether any result matches. It works only if the password was weak or common, like password123 or qwerty.

Bcrypt makes even that slow on purpose. In the PHP project's measurements for its 2023 RFC, a single cost-12 bcrypt hash took about 160–330 milliseconds on ordinary CPUs. Every guess costs that much again, so trying even a modest list of common passwords takes real time, and a long, random password is out of reach. That's the whole point of bcrypt.

Two warnings:

  • Don't paste real users' hashes into third-party sites. You're handing someone else material they can try to crack, and possibly the user's email next to it.
  • "Decrypted" results only mean the password was guessable. If a site "decrypts" your hash, treat that password as compromised.

What you probably need instead

Check whether a password matches a hash

You don't need to decrypt anything. Hash the candidate password with the same salt and compare, which is exactly what every bcrypt library's compare function does:

const bcrypt = require('bcryptjs')
console.log(await bcrypt.compare('correct horse battery staple', hash)) // true
console.log(await bcrypt.compare('password123', hash))                  // false

Or paste the hash and password into the bcrypt checker, which does this in your browser. In PHP use password_verify(), and in Python bcrypt.checkpw(). If a check fails for a password you're sure is right, see why bcrypt.compare() returns false.

Reset a forgotten password (including your own admin account)

If you've lost the password to an account you control, you can't recover it, and you don't need to. Set a new one: generate a fresh hash and write it over the old one. Generate the hash with any of these one-liners (each produced a working cost-12 hash in our tests):

node -e "require('bcryptjs').hash('NewPassword!2026', 12).then(console.log)"

php -r "echo password_hash('NewPassword!2026', PASSWORD_BCRYPT, ['cost' => 12]), PHP_EOL;"

python -c "import bcrypt; print(bcrypt.hashpw(b'NewPassword!2026', bcrypt.gensalt(12)).decode())"

Or use the bcrypt generator in your browser. Then save it to the user's row:

UPDATE users SET password_hash = '$2b$12$...your new hash...' WHERE email = 'admin@example.com';

Use a real new password rather than the example, and clear it from your shell history afterwards. For other people's accounts, use your app's normal password-reset email flow instead of editing the database.

Laravel: Laravel rejects hashes that start with $2b$ (the Node and Python output) unless you change the first four characters to $2y$. The PHP one-liner already produces $2y$. Our PHP and Laravel guide explains why.

Move users to a new system

Migrating to a new app or framework doesn't require decrypting passwords either. Bcrypt hashes are portable. In our tests, hashes created by PHP, Node.js and Python verified in each other's libraries, so you copy the hashes as they are, and users keep their passwords. The one exception was Node's native bcrypt package, which rejected PHP's $2y$ hashes until the prefix was changed to $2b$ (details). Just make sure the new database column is long enough: a bcrypt hash is 60 characters, and too-short columns break logins.

Quick answers

Is bcrypt reversible? No. There's no reverse function; you can only check guesses.

Can bcrypt be decrypted with a key? No. Bcrypt doesn't use a key. If someone gives you a "key" to decrypt bcrypt, they're mistaken or scamming you.

Can a bcrypt hash be decoded? Partly. The version, cost and salt are readable (see above), but the password isn't.

Is bcrypt still secure if attackers get the database? It holds up well for strong passwords, which is why it's used. Weak passwords can still be guessed, just slowly. See how many bcrypt rounds to use for choosing a cost that keeps guessing expensive.

What about files ending in .bfe? That's a different, older tool that's also called bcrypt: a command-line file encrypter built on Blowfish. Those files can be decrypted, with the passphrase used to create them. It has nothing to do with password hashes.

Drafted with AI assistance; reviewed and tested by Shahzeb Zafar.

This article first appeared on BcryptGenerator.org, where you can also generate and check bcrypt hashes in your browser.
