title: Automatización y despliegue de TechInventory con persistencia en CouchDB
description:
Autora: Gabriela Cohaila
Una aplicación puede funcionar en la computadora y aun así fallar al publicarse. En TechInventory, el requisito de usar Apache CouchDB añade una condición: los documentos deben sobrevivir al reinicio y al reemplazo de los contenedores. Por eso la elección del alojamiento depende de la persistencia, además del precio.
El proyecto combina React/Vite, Node/Express y CouchDB. Este artículo se concentra en cómo construir, verificar y preparar su publicación automatizada, y en distinguir una configuración disponible de un despliegue realmente observado.
Una sola aplicación dos servicios principales
El Dockerfile utiliza dos etapas. La primera instala las dependencias y compila React. La segunda incorpora la API, las dependencias de ejecución y los archivos compilados. Express entrega tanto la interfaz como /api, lo que evita configurar dos orígenes para esta demostración.
Compose inicia CouchDB y espera a que responda su comprobación de salud antes de iniciar la aplicación. El directorio de datos de CouchDB se monta en un volumen. Reconstruir la imagen de Express no reemplaza ese volumen.
Las credenciales se generan localmente con valores aleatorios y se guardan en .env, excluido de Git. Una imagen reutilizable no debe contener las claves del entorno donde terminará ejecutándose.
La validación forma parte del recorrido
El workflow CI instala con npm ci, ejecuta pruebas de API, compila el frontend y comprueba dependencias. Luego levanta los contenedores y ejecuta la prueba de integración contra CouchDB real.
La primera ejecución falló al iniciar CouchDB. El contenedor ajusta permisos de sus archivos y el montaje de configuración de solo lectura interfería con ese arranque. La solución fue copiar la configuración con el propietario correcto durante la construcción de una imagen derivada de couchdb:3.5.0. La ejecución CI #3 completó las seis pruebas de API y la integración real. Esta diferencia entre una prueba aislada y una prueba con el servidor real fue una evidencia concreta del proyecto.
El workflow de despliegue está preparado para iniciarse después de un CI exitoso en main. Utiliza el commit que pasó la validación, envía sus archivos al servidor por SSH y ejecuta Compose. Su activación requiere configurar el destino y secretos; no se publica un supuesto resultado mientras esos requisitos falten.
HTTPS y una base fuera de Internet
La configuración de producción agrega Caddy delante de Express. Caddy recibe tráfico en 80 y 443 y obtiene el certificado para el nombre DNS configurado. Express queda disponible solo en loopback del host y dentro de la red de contenedores. CouchDB no necesita un puerto público.
En producción la sesión usa una cookie Secure y HttpOnly. Las escrituras también requieren un token CSRF y el origen esperado. Usar HTTPS protege el transporte, pero no sustituye la autorización ni la validación de entradas.
Qué significa realmente gratuito
La documentación de Render indica que sus servicios web gratuitos tienen un sistema de archivos efímero y no admiten disco persistente. Hospedar CouchDB allí como si fuera una base duradera incumpliría el requisito del proyecto. Tener una URL accesible no compensaría perder los documentos al reiniciar.
Azure for Students ofrece crédito académico sin tarjeta. Antes de crear recursos hay que verificar elegibilidad, saldo, vencimiento, cuotas y límite de gasto en la cuenta concreta. Los créditos no convierten una VM en gratuita para siempre: la máquina, el disco y la IP consumen saldo mientras existan según sus tarifas aplicables.
La comparación y la decisión operativa se registran en docs/hosting.md. No se habilita pago por uso ni se retira la protección de gasto para completar esta tarea.
Cómo demostrar la automatización
La evidencia más clara sigue una secuencia pequeña: cambiar un texto visible, subir el commit, observar CI, observar CD y comprobar el cambio en la URL HTTPS. Conviene mostrar el identificador del commit y la ejecución correspondiente para conectar el resultado con el código.
Después se registra un equipo, se reinicia el servicio y se consulta de nuevo. Esa segunda secuencia demuestra persistencia, una propiedad diferente del despliegue automático. Las capturas deben excluir .env, claves SSH, cookies y pantallas con datos privados.
El proyecto incluye un guion de menos de cinco minutos. El video debe mostrar resultados reales; las pantallas pendientes se graban después de resolverlas, sin sustituirlas por imágenes ilustrativas.
Límites y siguientes pasos
La propuesta usa un solo servidor y no ofrece alta disponibilidad. El workflow preparado tampoco aplica una reversión automática si falla una versión nueva. Antes de usar el sistema con información importante se necesitan respaldos con restauración probada, monitorización y una operación de administración de cuentas más completa.
Automatizar no elimina la necesidad de revisar el resultado. Reduce pasos repetitivos y hace visible qué versión se probó y qué versión se intentó publicar. Esa trazabilidad es el principal aprendizaje de TechInventory.
Código y referencias
• Repositorio TechInventory
• GitHub Actions
• Limitaciones del alojamiento gratuito de Render
• Azure for Students
• Límite de gasto de Azure
• Volúmenes Docker
• HTTPS automático de Caddy
Resultado verificado de la demostración
El 12/11/2026 se publicó TechInventory con HTTPS en una VM Ubuntu de Azure for Students. El despliegue automático #4 terminó correctamente. También se ejecutó CRUD real desde la URL HTTPS y se comprobó que asset:LT-DEMO conservaba su identificador y revisión después de reiniciar Express y CouchDB. Los registros y capturas están en evidence.

Inventario real publicado por HTTPS

Despliegue automático exitoso
La URL utilizada fue https://techinventory-codexvex-20261112.eastus.cloudapp.azure.com. El alojamiento es temporal: se retira después de recopilar las evidencias para evitar consumo continuo de créditos. Esa dirección no debe considerarse un servicio permanente. El repositorio y los registros de Actions permiten revisar la construcción y el despliegue aunque el servidor se haya retirado.

title: Chatbots for E-commerce: Boosting Sales and Support
description:
Online shoppers expect immediate answers. When a customer has a question about sizing, delivery or returns and cannot get a reply, the most likely outcome is an abandoned cart. For e-commerce businesses, chatbots have become one of the most practical ways to close that gap, improving both conversions and the quality of customer service.

This article explains how chatbots support sales and customer care, what separates an effective implementation from a poor one, and how to get started.

Why response time matters in online retail

Pre-purchase questions are usually simple: delivery timelines, available sizes, payment options, return policies and coupon eligibility. However, they are time-sensitive. A customer who is ready to buy will rarely wait several hours for an email response, particularly when a competitor is one click away.

A chatbot provides instant answers around the clock. It also maintains the same response quality during peak periods such as festive sales, when support teams are typically at full capacity.

How chatbots drive sales

Guided product discovery. By asking a few targeted questions about budget, occasion or preferences, a chatbot can narrow a large catalogue down to a short list of relevant products. This shortens the path to purchase and reduces decision fatigue.

Cart recovery. Many carts are abandoned because of a minor concern, such as shipping charges or a failed payment. A well-timed message that resolves the concern, or offers a small incentive, can recover revenue that would otherwise be lost.

Relevant upselling and cross-selling. Suggesting accessories or complementary items at the right point in the journey increases average order value. The key is relevance: recommendations should be based on what the customer is actually buying.

Customer insight. Chat transcripts reveal which products generate the most questions, where the website lacks clarity and what customers are looking for. These insights can inform merchandising, content and pricing decisions.

How chatbots improve customer support

A large proportion of support tickets in e-commerce fall into a few repetitive categories: order status, returns and refunds, and changes to delivery details. A chatbot integrated with the order management system can resolve these queries instantly and without agent involvement.

This allows the support team to concentrate on complex or sensitive issues, such as damaged goods, payment disputes and escalated complaints. The main advantages include:

• Availability: support is accessible 24 hours a day, every day of the year.

• Consistency: policies are communicated accurately and uniformly.

• Language support: customers can interact in their preferred language, which is particularly valuable in a multilingual market like India.

• Seamless escalation: when needed, the conversation is passed to a human agent along with the full chat history.

Businesses looking for a solution trained on their own catalogue, policies and brand voice should consider a dedicated AI chatbot for customer service rather than a generic, off-the-shelf tool.

What makes a chatbot effective

Poorly designed chatbots frustrate customers by misunderstanding questions, repeating the same options or blocking access to a human agent. Effective implementations share four characteristics:

  1. Integration with store data. The chatbot should access live inventory, pricing and order information to give accurate answers.

  2. Clear escalation paths. When it cannot resolve a query, it should transfer the customer to an agent rather than guess.

  3. Natural, concise communication. Short, clear and friendly responses work better than long scripted messages.

  4. Ongoing maintenance. Conversation logs should be reviewed regularly, and responses updated as products and policies change.

The underlying platform matters as well. A chatbot cannot compensate for a slow or difficult-to-navigate store. Businesses planning a new launch or a redesign will benefit from working with a team that specialises in e-commerce website and app development, so that chat support is built into the customer journey from the start.

Getting started

A phased approach reduces risk and delivers faster results:

  • Identify the 10 to 15 questions your support team handles most often.

  • Configure the chatbot to answer those questions accurately.

  • Make the option to speak with a human agent easy to find.

  • Review performance weekly, then expand coverage gradually.

Because most online purchases are now made on mobile devices, the chat experience should also be tested thoroughly on smaller screens.

Conclusion

Chatbots help e-commerce businesses respond faster, sell more and reduce the load on their support teams. When they are integrated with store data, designed with clear escalation paths and maintained over time, they become a reliable part of the customer experience rather than a gimmick.

For online retailers aiming to improve conversions and customer satisfaction at the same time, a well-implemented chatbot is among the most effective investments available today.

title: How to Find Slow Queries in SQL Server (DMVs and Query Store)
description:
Originally published at SQL & Cloud Lab.

This post was drafted with AI assistance.

Find the slow queries in SQL Server fast: ready-to-run DMV scripts for running queries, top CPU and reads, wait stats, plus Query Store reports.    Before you can tune anything, you need to know which queries are the problem. Users report "the system is slow", but the cause is usually a handful of queries. SQL Server already tracks everything you need to find them. This guide gives you the scripts I use first, in the order I use them.

1. What is running right now?

When the system is slow at this moment, start with live requests. This shows each running query, how long it has run, what it is waiting on and whether it is blocked:

SELECT
    r.session_id,
    r.status,
    r.start_time,
    DATEDIFF(SECOND, r.start_time, SYSDATETIME()) AS running_seconds,
    r.wait_type,
    r.wait_time,
    r.blocking_session_id,
    r.cpu_time,
    r.logical_reads,
    DB_NAME(r.database_id) AS database_name,
    t.text AS query_text
FROM sys.dm_exec_requests r
CROSS APPLY sys.dm_exec_sql_text(r.sql_handle) t
WHERE r.session_id <> @@SPID
  AND r.session_id > 50
ORDER BY r.start_time;
  • A non-zero blocking_session_id means the query is waiting for another session's locks.
  • wait_type tells you what it is waiting for, such as locks (LCK_M_*), disk (PAGEIOLATCH_*) or parallelism (CXPACKET/CXCONSUMER).

2. Which queries cost the most overall?

For general slowness, the most useful view is total cost across all executions. A 50 ms query that runs 100,000 times an hour usually matters more than one 30-second report that runs once a day.

-- Top 10 queries by total CPU since they were cached
SELECT TOP (10)
    qs.execution_count,
    qs.total_worker_time / 1000                        AS total_cpu_ms,
    qs.total_worker_time / qs.execution_count / 1000   AS avg_cpu_ms,
    qs.total_logical_reads / qs.execution_count        AS avg_reads,
    qs.total_elapsed_time / qs.execution_count / 1000  AS avg_duration_ms,
    SUBSTRING(t.text, (qs.statement_start_offset / 2) + 1,
        ((CASE qs.statement_end_offset WHEN -1 THEN DATALENGTH(t.text)
          ELSE qs.statement_end_offset END - qs.statement_start_offset) / 2) + 1) AS statement_text
FROM sys.dm_exec_query_stats qs
CROSS APPLY sys.dm_exec_sql_text(qs.sql_handle) t
ORDER BY qs.total_worker_time DESC;

Change the ORDER BY to qs.total_logical_reads DESC to find the queries that read the most data, which are often the ones missing an index.

Keep in mind that this view only covers plans still in cache. It resets on restart and loses queries whose plans were evicted, which is why Query Store is better for history.

3. Use Query Store for history and regressions

Query Store records query performance and plans over time inside the database. It is on by default in Azure SQL Database and for new databases in SQL Server 2022. In SSMS, open the database, expand Query Store, and use:

  • Top Resource Consuming Queries: the heaviest queries over any time window you pick.
  • Regressed Queries: queries that got slower, usually because their plan changed.
  • Queries With High Variation: queries whose duration swings a lot, a common sign of parameter sniffing.

The big advantage is history: you can compare "today, when it was slow" with "last week, when it was fine".

4. Check what the whole server waits on

Wait statistics show where SQL Server spends its waiting time overall, which points you to the type of problem:

SELECT TOP (10)
    wait_type,
    wait_time_ms / 1000.0 AS wait_seconds,
    waiting_tasks_count
FROM sys.dm_os_wait_stats
WHERE wait_type NOT LIKE 'SLEEP%'
  AND wait_type NOT LIKE '%QUEUE%'
  AND wait_type NOT IN ('BROKER_TASK_STOP','CHECKPOINT_QUEUE','WAITFOR',
                        'XE_TIMER_EVENT','DIRTY_PAGE_POLL','HADR_FILESTREAM_IOMGR_IOCOMPLETION')
ORDER BY wait_time_ms DESC;
  • PAGEIOLATCH_*: reading data from disk. Often too many reads, so look for missing indexes or scans.
  • LCK_M_*: blocking. Look at long transactions and locking patterns.
  • SOS_SCHEDULER_YIELD with high CPU: CPU-heavy queries.
  • WRITELOG: transaction log writes. Look at many tiny commits or slow log storage.

Wait stats accumulate since the last restart, so compare snapshots taken a few minutes apart for a picture of current load. This filter list is a starting point; there are more harmless background waits you may want to exclude.

5. Pick one query and fix it

Once you have a shortlist, take the query with the biggest total impact, get its actual execution plan, and look for scans on large tables, key lookups, bad row estimates and warnings. Fix one thing at a time, and compare logical reads and CPU before and after.

Quick routine

  1. Slow right now? Check sys.dm_exec_requests for blocking and waits.
  2. Slow in general? Rank queries by total CPU and reads.
  3. Slower than last week? Use Query Store's Regressed Queries.
  4. Check wait stats to understand the type of bottleneck.
  5. Tune the top query, then measure again.

Related reading:

  • SQL Server Query Store: A Practical Beginner's Guide
  • How to Read a SQL Server Execution Plan
  • SQL Server Index Tuning for Beginners

More SQL Server guides on my blog, SQL & Cloud Lab.

title: What to learn free before you pay for MERN stack training in Nepal
description:
You can learn the first part of the MERN stack for free: JavaScript, how HTTP works, a small Node.js server and basic SQL. Pay for MERN stack training only when you can do those four things, so the paid hours go to the parts that need a mentor.

MERN means MongoDB, Express, React and Node.js. Three of the four are JavaScript, and the free material for them is good. Here is the order we would follow, and how to tell when you are ready.

What does MERN stack training in Nepal teach?

A MERN course teaches you to build a whole web app in JavaScript. React draws the screen in the browser. Node.js and Express run the server and the API. MongoDB stores the data.

The only difference from PERN is the database. PERN swaps MongoDB for PostgreSQL. We compare the two in MERN stack vs PERN stack for web development training in Nepal.

Step 1: JavaScript, until you can read your own errors

Start with plain JavaScript, not React. Every later step is JavaScript, so a weak start makes everything after it slow.

The Odin Project is free and open source. Its Full Stack JavaScript path has a JavaScript course with 29 lessons and 12 projects. Do the projects, not only the lessons.

You are done with this step when an error message no longer scares you. Read the stack trace, find the line, fix it. That skill matters more than any framework.

Step 2: How HTTP works, in one evening

Every backend job is about requests and responses. The browser sends a request. The server sends back a status code, headers and a body.

Read MDN's "Overview of HTTP" guide once. Then open a terminal and run curl -i https://example.com. The -i shows the status line and headers above the page. Now 200, 404 and Content-Type stop being words and become things you have seen.

Step 3: A Node.js server with no framework

Before Express, write a server with Node.js alone. The official Introduction to Node.js page has one that is about ten lines long. It uses the built-in node:http module.

Save it as server.js and run node server.js. Open http://127.0.0.1:3000 and you see "Hello World". Then change res.statusCode to 404 and run curl -i against it again.

This shows you what Express does for you later. Express is a layer on top of this same idea. Our own course writes this kind of server in Week 3, before it touches Express in Week 4.

Step 4: Learn SQL, even though the M is MongoDB

This is the step most MERN learners skip, and we think that is a mistake. Learn basic SQL next to MongoDB.

Nepal job posts show why. A merojob post for an intern MERN stack developer, from July 2024, listed "Relational Database" in its required skills. A full stack React and Node.js post from July 2025 asked for "PostgreSQL (or MongoDB experience)" and the "ability to design and query relational schemas".

Mid-sized companies in Nepal often start with a written test at their office. It asks SQL questions on joins and normalisation, which means splitting data into clean tables.

The free PostgreSQL tutorial is the official one. Work through "Joins Between Tables" and "Aggregate Functions" in chapter 2. That is enough for a start.

How do you know you are ready to pay for MERN training?

You are ready when you can do all of these without a video open:

  • Write a function that uses map and filter on an array of objects.
  • Explain the difference between a 404 and a 500 response.
  • Run the Node.js server above and change what it sends back.
  • Write a SQL query that joins two tables and counts rows with GROUP BY.

If you can do these, a course will move faster for you. If you cannot yet, keep going free for a few more weeks. Paying early means paying for lessons you could have done free.

What is worth paying for?

Pay for the parts that are hard to check alone. The first is API design, with checks on every input. Then login, passwords and tokens done safely. Then database design, indexes and transactions. Last, putting an app online and keeping it running.

Free courses cover these too. What they cannot give is a person who reads your code and tells you what is wrong with it.

Saarathi Academy in Old Baneshwor, Kathmandu teaches the server half of this in its Backend Engineering course. It is 10 weeks of Node.js, TypeScript, Express, NestJS, PostgreSQL and MongoDB. It does not teach React. Batches have up to 10 students in the classroom, and the mentors still do the job they teach. Your first deploy is in Week 5, on your own subdomain of the academy's batch server.

What to do tonight

Copy the ten-line server from the Node.js page, run it, and break it on purpose. Change the port, change the status code, and read every error you get.

When you want to see the full week-by-week plan, read the Backend Engineering course page and the syllabus.

title: How to Build a Multi-Page Quiz App in React Using Context API and React Router
description:
Project Architecture

Our application consists of four main parts:

  1. main.jsx: Wraps the app in BrowserRouter to enable URL routing.
  2. App.jsx: Holds the global state (name and score) inside a Context Provider and defines the routes.
  3. User.jsx: Captures the player's name and navigates to the quiz.
  4. Quiz.jsx: Displays questions from a JSON file, tracks selected answers, and updates the score.
  5. Result.jsx: Displays the player's final score and allows them to restart the game.

Building a quiz application is one of the best ways to practice core React concepts. When users enter their name on a welcome screen, answer questions on a second screen, and view their final score on a third screen, your app needs two essential features: client-side routing and global state management.
In this guide, we will walk through how to build a complete, three-page React quiz app using react-router-dom and React's built-in createContext hook—and cover common pitfalls to avoid along the way.

title: How to run a 5-person usability test on your app for about $30
description:
You built the onboarding, so you can't really see it anymore. You know which button matters, what the icon means, and why step three asks for a phone number. Someone opening the app for the first time knows none of that. Most of them won't tell you where they got lost, either. They just close it.

A small usability test gets that view back. It doesn't take a research team or a sales call. It takes five strangers and an afternoon of watching. This is how I'd run one. I run a testing marketplace, so there's a disclosure near the end, but every step before it works the same however you find your five people.

Why five people

Jakob Nielsen's well-known argument is that five users find about 85% of the usability problems in a design, and each extra user mostly repeats problems you've already seen. His advice is to split the budget into several small rounds: test with five, fix, test with five more.

The same article has two caveats. The math assumes your users are roughly one group. If you have two very different audiences, say teachers and students, test three or four from each. And five people find problems; they don't measure anything. If you want a conversion rate, that's analytics.

Step 1: pick one flow

Not "the app". Pick one path with a clear end that every new user has to get through:

  • Sign-up to the first useful screen
  • Creating the first thing your app makes (a habit, a budget, a playlist)
  • The paywall, from the moment it appears to a decision
  • Checkout

If you can't choose, take the flow right after install. Every user sees it, and you've looked at it so often you no longer notice it.

Step 2: write tasks as goals, not instructions

Most first tests go wrong here. If the task says "Tap the + button and add a habit", you've told the tester where the button is, which is the exact thing you wanted to find out.

Write what the person wants to get done, in their words, and leave the how to them:

Leads the user Lets you learn something
Tap "Create budget" and set a monthly limit You want to spend less than $400 on food this month. Set that up.
Go to Settings > Notifications and turn on reminders You keep forgetting to log your workouts. See if the app can help.
Use the search bar to find a vegetarian recipe Find something you could cook tonight without meat.

Three to five tasks fill 10 to 15 minutes. Put them in the order a real user would meet them.

Step 3: the script

This is the whole thing I'd send. Copy it and swap in your tasks.

Thanks for doing this. Please record your screen and talk out loud the whole time: what you're looking at, what you expect to happen, anything that confuses you. There are no wrong answers. We're testing the app, not you.

  1. Install the app from [link] and open it. Before you tap anything, tell us what you think it does.
  2. [Goal task 1]
  3. [Goal task 2]
  4. [Goal task 3]
  5. If you could change one thing about what you just used, what would it be?
  6. Would you keep this app after today? Why or why not?

The first task does more work than it looks like. "What do you think this does?" tells you whether your first screen explains the app. If three of five people guess wrong, that's your first finding, and nobody has reached the flow yet.

Don't tell them how long anything should take, and don't explain the app beforehand. Your real users won't get a briefing.

Step 4: find five people who have never seen it

They need to be new to the app and reasonably close to your audience. Roughly from cheapest to most expensive:

  • Friends of friends, not friends. Friends are polite, and they already know what you were going for. Someone one step removed is a better stand-in for a stranger.
  • Communities your users already spend time in: a subreddit, a Discord, a Facebook group. Read the rules first. Many don't allow test requests, and the ones that do usually expect something back.
  • Your waitlist. People who signed up but haven't opened the app yet are close to your audience by definition. Offer a small thank-you.
  • A paid testing service. You pay per person and skip the scheduling. Prices vary a lot: some of the big platforms sell by quote or annual contract, and smaller marketplaces charge per tester.

Whichever route you take, ask for a screen recording with their voice, not a written summary. People describe what they think they did, and it often isn't what they did. A recording shows the four seconds of hesitation before they tap the wrong tab.

Step 5: watch with a sheet open

Watch each recording once all the way through, then again with a sheet:

Tester Time What happened Task Severity
2 01:40 Tapped the logo, expecting to go home 1 Low
2 03:15 Looked for "save" for 20 seconds, gave up 2 High

What I write down:

  • Hesitation. A pause of several seconds before a tap usually means the screen didn't make the next step obvious.
  • Backtracking: into a screen, back out, back in again.
  • Saying one thing and doing another, like "OK, that's easy" followed by the wrong tap.
  • Workarounds: finishing the task by a route you didn't design, like closing the app to get "back".
  • Their words. If everyone calls it "my list" and your tab says "Collections", the tab is wrong.

Severity doesn't need to be scientific. High means the task failed or nearly did. Medium means they got there but struggled. Low is a moment of friction.

Step 6: fix three things, then test again

After five recordings you'll usually see the same two or three problems again and again. Fix those first. It's tempting to redesign everything after one round, and I'd resist it. The point of small tests is that the next round tells you whether the fix worked.

Then run five new people through the same tasks. They have to be new, because the first five have learned your app by now.

What it costs and how long it takes

Recruiting yourself is free, and you pay in time. Expect a day or two of messages before five people actually send a recording.

On the marketplace I run, a screen recording costs $5.99 per tester, so five people come to $29.95. Some numbers from our side: 54 recorded campaigns went live after 1 June and got at least five recordings. For half of them, the fifth recording arrived within 15.4 hours, and 44 of the 54 had it within three days. Across all 825 recordings since March, the median session lasted just under 14 minutes.

Disclosure

I run TestFi. Testers there record their screen and talk through your tasks on their own phones, and each recording comes with a transcript and timestamps for the moments they got stuck. If you'd rather not recruit, it's here. Everything above works the same with five people you found yourself.

If you try the first-screen question ("what do you think this does?"), I'd like to hear in the comments what people guessed.

title: A practical portrait review workflow and crop-boundary check
description:
A profile photo has a small job: help another person recognize you and get a sense of how you present yourself. That can be harder than it sounds. A picture that looks appealing at full size may be unreadable on a phone, while a technically sharp image may feel too formal for the setting. Instead of searching for one perfect portrait, build a small set of honest, varied images and review them together.

AI Dating Photo Generator is a browser-based tool that creates dating profile portraits from your own photos, lets you choose a scene, and offers a way to review or refine results. If you decide to explore the ai dating profile photo generator, treat generated images as options to evaluate rather than as proof of what you look like in every situation. I am associated with the project, and this guide was drafted with AI assistance. Examples are hypothetical, and it does not claim independent product testing or guaranteed results.

Start with recognition, not decoration

Before changing a background or choosing an outfit, decide what a viewer should be able to recognize. A clear view of your face, an expression that feels natural, and a recent appearance are more important than a dramatic location. A useful first image should still make sense at the small size at which most people will encounter it.

Compare a candidate with a recent, unedited photograph. Check features that matter for recognition, including the shape of your face, hairstyle, facial hair, and any distinctive marks you normally show. Lighting and a different camera angle can change how someone looks, but a generated image should not make a meeting in person feel like a surprise. If you would need to explain that the picture represents an old hairstyle or a substantially different appearance, choose a more current alternative.

Gather a useful source set

When selecting input images, use photographs you have permission to upload and share. Prefer images of yourself over pictures containing other people. A varied source set can include a straight-on portrait, a gentle three-quarter angle, and a picture in even daylight. Avoid relying entirely on images with heavy filters, deep shadows, face coverings, or very low resolution.

More files are not automatically better. Review each photo for focus, current appearance, and whether your face is large enough to distinguish. Set aside any image whose ownership or consent is uncertain. If a group photograph is your only option, consider taking a fresh individual picture instead of uploading other people’s faces unnecessarily.

Keep the original files in a private location. Before using any external service, read its current terms and privacy information, including what it says about uploads, retention, deletion, and permitted uses. Do not assume that a file disappears immediately after you close a browser tab. If the available information does not meet your comfort level, use an offline photo or another method instead.

Choose a setting that supports the subject

A background should add context without competing with your face. A simple outdoor scene, an uncluttered room, or a neutral wall can be easier to read than a busy street full of signs and strangers. Think about the mood you want to convey: relaxed, approachable, creative, or active. A setting can suggest a mood without making a factual claim about your occupation or lifestyle.

Review the boundaries where hair, clothing, and shoulders meet the background. Generated portraits may contain odd edges, inconsistent shadows, or details that look plausible at a glance but not on inspection. Look at hands, jewelry, glasses, fabric patterns, and objects close to the body. If a feature looks wrong, refine or discard the image rather than hoping nobody notices.

A convincing scene is not necessarily an accurate one. Avoid selecting a location that implies you visited a place or participated in an activity if you did not. A neutral illustrative setting is easier to interpret honestly than a picture that appears to document a specific trip or event. When in doubt, pair a generated portrait with real, recent photographs that show your everyday appearance.

Check light, color, and framing

Good lighting reveals the face without flattening every detail. Look for a balance between visible eyes, natural skin tones, and enough contrast to separate the subject from the background. Very bright highlights can erase detail, while strong backlighting can turn a face into a silhouette. Color should feel consistent across the image; a warm face against an implausibly cool shadow may be distracting.

Test the crop before deciding. Leave some space around the head and shoulders so the image can survive different app layouts. A square preview may crop differently from a tall profile card. Keep important facial features away from the extreme edges, and verify that hair or the top of the head is not unintentionally cut off.

Look at the image on both a larger display and a phone. At a large size, inspect artifacts. At a small size, ask whether the expression is readable and whether the subject stands out from the background. A photo can pass one test and fail the other. Keep only images that work in the context in which they will be seen.

Build variety across a set

A profile usually benefits from more than several nearly identical close-ups. Consider a clear primary portrait, a different angle or setting, and a candid or activity image that reflects something you actually enjoy. Each picture should contribute information rather than repeat the same expression in a slightly different crop.

Variety does not mean presenting incompatible versions of yourself. A collection that switches dramatically between ages, hair colors, body shapes, or styles can undermine recognition. Place images side by side and ask whether someone meeting you would reasonably identify the same person in all of them. Keep your real appearance as the reference point.

If an activity photo includes friends, ask for their permission before publishing it. Avoid showing documents, address details, workplace identifiers, vehicle plates, or other information you do not intend to disclose. You can crop a photograph to reduce incidental exposure, but check that the resulting image still makes sense and does not misleadingly change the context.

Use a short review checklist

A repeatable checklist is more useful than endlessly comparing minor differences. For each candidate, answer the following questions:

  1. Is the picture recent enough to represent my current appearance?
  2. Can a viewer see my face clearly at the expected display size?
  3. Are the eyes, hands, accessories, and background free of distracting artifacts?
  4. Does the image avoid implying an experience, place, or identity that is not mine?
  5. Do I have permission to use every visible person’s image and the underlying photograph?
  6. Does this picture add something distinct to the rest of the set?
  7. Am I comfortable with the platform receiving and displaying the image?

If an answer is no, decide whether a simple crop or a different candidate addresses the problem. If not, leave it out. This process is not a score for attractiveness; it is a way to reduce confusion, privacy risks, and avoidable visual distractions.

Get feedback without outsourcing the decision

A trusted friend can notice a misleading crop or an expression that does not look like you. Give them a narrow question, such as whether they would recognize you from the first image or which of two crops is clearer on a phone. Broad requests for a rating can produce conflicting opinions without helping you make a practical choice.

Remember that friends may have different preferences from the people you hope to meet. Treat their feedback as information, not a rule. You remain responsible for selecting pictures that feel comfortable, accurate, and consistent with the expectations of the app you use. Check that app’s rules on altered or generated images before uploading.

A small crop-metadata check

A developer building an internal review workflow can start by validating declared crop coordinates before recording a review. The function below only checks integer bounds against supplied dimensions. It does not open a file, identify a person, verify consent, inspect image metadata, or detect manipulated content. Coordinates use a top-left origin and a half-open rectangle: a crop ending exactly at the right or bottom edge is allowed. This is a standalone teaching example, not a feature of the product mentioned above.

def check_crop(width, height, left, top, crop_width, crop_height):
    values = (width, height, left, top, crop_width, crop_height)
    if any(type(value) is not int for value in values):
        return False
    if width <= 0 or height <= 0 or left < 0 or top < 0:
        return False
    if crop_width <= 0 or crop_height <= 0:
        return False
    return left + crop_width <= width and top + crop_height <= height

I ran six local synthetic cases for full-frame and edge-aligned crops, overflow, negative offsets, zero size, and a Boolean argument. Those cases establish only that this function returns the expected Boolean for the supplied values; they are not tests of an image editor or service. A production pipeline would also need to define orientation, units, metadata provenance, error handling, and data retention before using such a check. Keep consent records separate and do not log private photographs just to test a rectangle.

For example, (800, 600, 10, 20, 790, 580) is within bounds, while increasing the crop width to 791 extends one pixel beyond the declared right edge. The function deliberately rejects Boolean values even though Python treats bool as a subclass of int; this is a policy choice for this example rather than a universal validation rule. If an application accepts other numeric types or rotated coordinates, specify those rules explicitly and test them separately.

Maintain the profile over time

Revisit your pictures when your appearance or circumstances change. A new haircut, glasses, or a different everyday style may make an older image less useful as a primary portrait. You do not need to replace every picture at once; review the set periodically and swap out anything that no longer feels representative.

Keep a small private shortlist of approved images and their original sources. This makes it easier to update a profile without repeating the entire selection process. Remove files you no longer want to retain, and use any available deletion controls on services where you uploaded them. The result should be a profile that is easy to recognize, considerate of other people’s privacy, and comfortable for you to maintain.

title: Make an agent skill update reproducible
description:
An agent skill can change upstream while the task you ask it to do stays the same. Keep a small run record so you can tell what changed before using the new version on real work.

  1. Record the source URL, commit or release, and the tool versions used for the run. If you cannot recover the exact skill version, record that gap.
  2. Keep one synthetic input and the expected result alongside the record. For a report-writing skill, that could be a short mock brief and a checklist of required headings.
  3. Run the old and new versions on the same input in separate scratch folders. Compare the generated files, paths, and any new network calls. Investigate unexplained changes before using the update on live files.

If the new run passes, update the version in your record and keep the sample for the next upgrade. Explore the Skillπ AI skill marketplace for skills to evaluate.

title: Introducing hikyaku: A Message Relay That Routes with AI and Never Drops a Message
description:
Introduction

Every backend has that one small service. It receives a webhook and forwards it to three other systems. It started as 40 lines. Then one target went down for an hour, and messages were lost. So it got a retry loop. Then a queue. Then a second target needed a different payload. Then someone asked: "can it send billing questions to billing and bugs to support?"

That service is glue, and every team writes it again.

hikyaku (飛脚) is that service, written once. The name comes from the relay couriers of Edo-period Japan. They carried letters from station to station, and they found another way when a road was closed.

hikyaku is a message relay in a single Go binary:

  • It reads messages from one or more endpoints: a webhook, a WebSocket, a Kafka topic, an SQS queue and more.
  • It delivers them to one or more others.
  • One YAML file describes the whole relay.
  • Every step retries and falls back, so a message is never dropped without a trace.
  • An AI router can pick the destination of each message, and it tells you how sure it is.

Why Glue Code Breaks

Hand-written glue hikyaku
A target is down The message is lost, or a retry loop you wrote at 2 a.m. Timeout, retry with backoff, circuit breaker, fallback chain
Every target is down Gone A dead-letter queue, and one command to replay it
"Where should this go?" A growing if chain Rules, or an AI router with a confidence threshold
A new protocol A new service A new type: in the YAML
Testing a routing change Deploy and hope hikyaku test and hikyaku route --dry-run
The sender's answer 200 OK, always 200 when delivered, 202 when the message is safe in the dead-letter queue

How a Message Travels

Four words cover the whole spec:

  • A source is where messages come from.
  • A destination is where they go. Each one has its own timeout, retry policy and fallback (the destination to try when this one gives up).
  • A route connects sources to destinations through a router. A router can be static, a list of rules, or AI.
  • The dead-letter queue (DLQ) is where a message goes when every delivery attempt failed. It is a parking place, not a bin.

A source tells the sender that a message is done only when it is delivered or stored in the DLQ.

What You Will Build

You will build a support intake relay for a SaaS company:

  1. A signed webhook receives customer events.
  2. An AI router sends each one to the billing team, the support team, the on-call engineer, or more than one of them.
  3. Billing has a backup endpoint. What still fails goes to the DLQ, and you replay it.
  4. A test file checks the routing without sending anything.

At the end, you will reuse hikyaku as an LLM proxy that picks a model for each chat request.

What You Need

  • hikyaku 1.6.1 or newer.
  • curl and openssl.
  • For the AI router: a TypeSafe API key in TYPESAFE_API_KEY. It gives access to jev, a decision model.
  • For the LLM proxy in step 8: a Gemini key and an Anthropic key.

Step 1: Install hikyaku and Fan Out a Webhook

Install 

brew install xavidop/tap/hikyaku                              # macOS
go install github.com/xavidop/hikyaku/cmd/hikyaku@latest      # Go 1.27 or newer
docker run --rm ghcr.io/xavidop/hikyaku:latest version        # Docker

Linux packages, a Scoop bucket and a Helm chart are on the install page.

Scaffold and run 

mkdir relay && cd relay
hikyaku init --template webhook-fanout
hikyaku validate
hikyaku run

✓ hikyaku.yaml: valid (1 sources, 2 destinations, 1 routes)

The template is one source, two destinations and one route:

sources:
  - name: webhooks
    type: http
    mode: listen
    listen: ":8080"
    path: /ingest

destinations:
  - name: console
    type: stdout
    format: body
  - name: archive
    type: file
    path: ./out/archive.ndjson

routes:
  - name: fanout
    from: [webhooks]
    to: [console, archive]

Send a webhook

In a second terminal:

curl -i http://localhost:8080/ingest \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"type":"invoice.paid","customer_id":"c-42","amount":129}'

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Date: Fri, 13 Nov 2026 09:48:10 GMT
Content-Length: 57

{"id":"01M7A4XCXDA6GB265DAMC01RB8","status":"delivered"}

The 200 arrives only after both destinations have the message. The first terminal prints the body. The file out/archive.ndjson gets the whole envelope: the message with its ID, source, headers and attributes.

{"id":"01M7A4XCXDA6GB265DAMC01RB8","source":"webhooks","protocol":"http","subject":"/ingest","headers":{"Accept":["*/*"],"Content-Length":["57"],"Content-Type":["application/json"],"Idempotency-Key":["01M7A4XCXDA6GB265DAMC01RB8"],"User-Agent":["curl/8.7.1"]},"content_type":"application/json","body":{"type":"invoice.paid","customer_id":"c-42","amount":129},"attributes":{"delivery.attempt":1,"http.method":"POST","http.path":"/ingest","remote_addr":"[::1]:61095"},"received_at":"2026-11-13T09:48:10.029716Z"}

Note the Idempotency-Key header. Every delivery carries the message ID, so a destination can drop a duplicate.

That is a working relay. Stop it with Ctrl-C. Now make it real.

Step 2: Write the Support Intake Relay

Replace hikyaku.yaml with this spec:

# yaml-language-server: $schema=https://xavidop.github.io/hikyaku/schema/hikyaku.schema.json
version: 1
name: support-intake

secrets:
  WEBHOOK_SECRET: env:WEBHOOK_SECRET          # a mamori ref, never a value
  TYPESAFE_API_KEY: env:TYPESAFE_API_KEY

genkit:
  systemone:
    servers: [typesafe]

models:
  decision: typesafe/jev-1.13.0               # pin a version: thresholds are tuned per release

sources:
  - name: webhooks
    type: http
    listen: ":8080"
    path: /events
    auth:
      hmac: { header: X-Signature-256, secret: "{{secrets.WEBHOOK_SECRET}}" }

destinations:
  - name: billing
    type: http
    url: http://localhost:9001/billing
    retry: { attempts: 3, backoff: 200ms }
    fallback: [billing-dr]
  - name: billing-dr
    type: http
    url: http://localhost:9002/billing
  - name: support
    type: http
    url: http://localhost:9001/support
    retry: { attempts: 3, backoff: 200ms }
  - name: oncall
    type: http
    url: http://localhost:9001/oncall
    required: false                           # best effort: a failure loses nothing

dead_letter:
  type: file
  path: ./out/dlq.ndjson
  fallback: [stderr]

routes:
  - name: triage
    from: [webhooks]
    router:
      type: ai
      when: has(msg.json.text)                # only free text costs a model call
      instructions: |
        You route customer events for a SaaS company. Pick the team(s) that must see it.
      state: "{{ .bodyText }}"
      state_json: true
      candidates:
        - { name: billing, description: "Money: payments, invoices, charges, refunds, plans and subscription changes" }
        - { name: support, description: "The product misbehaves or the customer needs help: bugs, errors, crashes, how-to questions" }
        - { name: oncall, description: "A live incident: the service is down or failing for many customers right now" }
      multi: true
      min_confidence: 0.9
      input: { redact: ["$.email"] }
      on_low_confidence: [support]
      fallback:
        - type: rules
          rules:
            - { when: 'has(msg.json.type) && msg.json.type.startsWith("invoice.")', to: [billing] }
        - type: static
          to: [support]

server:
  admin: { listen: ":9090" }

Read it from top to bottom:

  • secrets are references, never values. env:WEBHOOK_SECRET says where the secret lives. A reference can also point to Vault, AWS Secrets Manager and others, through mamori.
  • The source checks an HMAC signature on every request. HMAC is a hash of the body made with a shared secret. A request without a valid signature gets a 401.
  • billing retries three times, then falls back to billing-dr, its backup endpoint.
  • oncall is required: false. It is best effort: when it fails, the message still counts as delivered.
  • The route uses an AI router with three candidates. Each candidate is a destination with a description.

Stand-in endpoints for the teams

You need something that answers on ports 9001 and 9002. A second relay does that. It listens on the team URLs and prints what each team receives. Create teams/hikyaku.yaml:

# The three team endpoints, played by a second relay: it prints what each team receives.
version: 1
name: teams

sources:
  - { name: billing, type: http, listen: ":9001", path: /billing }
  - { name: support, type: http, listen: ":9001", path: /support }
  - { name: oncall, type: http, listen: ":9001", path: /oncall }
  - { name: billing-dr, type: http, listen: ":9002", path: /billing }

destinations:
  - { name: console, type: stdout, format: body }

routes:
  - name: print
    from: [billing, support, oncall, billing-dr]
    transforms:
      - template: '[{{ .source }}] {{ .bodyText }}'
    to: [console]

server:
  admin: { listen: ":9091" }

Start it in its own terminal:

cd teams && hikyaku run

Check the spec 

export WEBHOOK_SECRET=s3cr3t-for-the-demo
export TYPESAFE_API_KEY=...
hikyaku validate
hikyaku doctor

✓ spec hikyaku.yaml: 1 sources, 4 destinations, 1 routes
✓ secrets 2 resolved
✓ plugins
✓ destination billing
✓ destination billing-dr
✓ destination oncall
✓ destination support
✓ dead_letter
✓ dead_letter fallback stderr
✓ store default (default)
✓ model typesafe/jev-1.13.0

validate checks references, fallback cycles and every expression, without starting anything. doctor goes further: it resolves the secrets, builds the destinations and checks that the model answers.

Step 3: Route with a Decision Model

What a decision model is

A chat model writes text. A decision model does not. It answers typed questions about a piece of data, and it gives each answer a calibrated probability. Calibrated means the number is honest: when the model says 0.9, it is right about nine times in ten.

That is exactly what routing needs. hikyaku asks one yes/no question per candidate: "should billing receive this?" A candidate is chosen when its probability reaches min_confidence. With multi: true, more than one team can get the message.

The model here is jev, served by TypeSafe through the System One plugin of Genkit Go. I used the same model to route work in Genkit Flows on Kubernetes with senro and jev.

Ask the router, without delivering

Save a message as msg.json:

{"type":"ticket.created","customer_id":"cus_42","email":"ada@example.com","text":"I was charged twice for my invoice this month and want a refund."}

Then ask the router where it would send it:

hikyaku route --dry-run --source webhooks --data @msg.json

route triage: ai (typesafe/jev-1.13.0) → billing, support
    * billing              p=0.99
    * support              p=0.90
      oncall               p=0.06
    reason: chosen: billing, support
    plan: billing → billing-dr
    plan: support

The output shows the probability of every candidate, the destinations chosen, and the fallback plan of each one. Nothing was sent.

The model is sure about billing (0.99). It is also at 0.90 for support, right on the threshold. A double charge is a billing matter, so this message should not reach support. The next step fixes that with data, not with a guess.

Good to know:

  • input.redact removes the e-mail address before the model sees the message. The destinations still get the full message.
  • The message is data for the model, never instructions. The router can only choose among the candidates in the spec.

Step 4: Tune the Threshold with Labeled Cases

Write down what you expect. Create cases.yaml:

cases:
  - name: double charge
    data: { text: "I was charged twice for my invoice and want a refund." }
    expect: [billing]
  - name: plan change
    data: { text: "Please change my subscription to the yearly plan and send the invoice." }
    expect: [billing]
  - name: crash
    data: { text: "The app crashes with an error every time I open the dashboard." }
    expect: [support]
  - name: how-to
    data: { text: "How do I invite a teammate? Is there a how-to guide?" }
    expect: [support]
  - name: outage
    data: { text: "Total outage: every request fails with 503 errors since 10:00." }
    expect: [support, oncall]
  - name: double charge, longer
    data: { text: "I was charged twice for my invoice this month and want a refund." }
    expect: [billing]

Then score the router on those cases:

hikyaku ai test --route triage --cases cases.yaml

route triage: 6 cases
accuracy  83.3% (5/6)
latency   p50 193ms  p95 260ms  max 260ms

per destination   precision  recall
  billing              1.00    1.00
  oncall               1.00    1.00
  support              0.75    1.00

confusion (rows: expected, columns: got)
                      billing billing+s… oncall+su…    support
  billing                   2          1          0          0
  oncall+support            0          0          1          0
  support                   0          0          0          2

calibration (confidence → accuracy) ECE 0.122
  0.9-1.0  n=6   confidence 0.96  accuracy 0.83

misses
  ✗ double charge: expected billing, got billing, support (ai, p=0.90)

The report names the problem. Recall is perfect: every team gets what it must see. But precision for support is 0.75, because one double charge also went there, at exactly 0.90.

Raise the threshold in hikyaku.yaml:

      min_confidence: 0.95

And run the same command again:

route triage: 6 cases
accuracy  100.0% (6/6)
latency   p50 167ms  p95 240ms  max 240ms

per destination   precision  recall
  billing              1.00    1.00
  oncall               1.00    1.00
  support              1.00    1.00

confusion (rows: expected, columns: got)
                      billing oncall+su…    support
  billing                   3          0          0
  oncall+support            0          1          0
  support                   0          0          2

calibration (confidence → accuracy) ECE 0.028
  0.9-1.0  n=6   confidence 0.97  accuracy 1.00

Six of six, and a decision takes about 170 ms. The outage still reaches both support and on-call, as it should.

Good to know:

  • ECE is the expected calibration error: the gap between how sure the model is and how often it is right. Lower is better.
  • Pin the model version (jev-1.13.0). Calibration changes between releases, so a threshold belongs to one version. hikyaku lint warns about an unpinned model.
  • --min-accuracy 0.9 makes the command exit with 1 below that accuracy. Put it in CI.
  • Six cases are a start. Add a case every time the router surprises you.

Step 5: Run It and Send Real Messages

Start the relay:

hikyaku run

The webhook wants a signature, so write a small helper, send.sh:

#!/bin/sh
# send.sh '<json>': sign the body with WEBHOOK_SECRET and post it to the relay
sig=$(printf '%s' "$1" | openssl dgst -sha256 -hmac "$WEBHOOK_SECRET" -hex | awk '{print $NF}')
curl -s -m 60 -w ' (HTTP %{http_code})\n' localhost:8080/events \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -H "X-Signature-256: $sig" -d "$1"

A free-text message 

./send.sh '{"customer_id":"cus_7","text":"Total outage: every request fails with 503 errors since 10:00."}'
./send.sh '{"customer_id":"cus_9","text":"How do I invite a teammate? Is there a how-to guide?"}'

{"id":"01M7A6GEHCS0EDBNYCTDZN0K1S","status":"delivered"}
 (HTTP 200)
{"id":"01M7A6GEXXP0XD62FZRKVEJZ6T","status":"delivered"}
 (HTTP 200)

The teams terminal shows who got what:

[oncall] {"customer_id":"cus_7","text":"Total outage: every request fails with 503 errors since 10:00."}
[support] {"customer_id":"cus_7","text":"Total outage: every request fails with 503 errors since 10:00."}
[support] {"customer_id":"cus_9","text":"How do I invite a teammate? Is there a how-to guide?"}

The outage went to two teams. The how-to question went to one.

A typed event costs no model call 

./send.sh '{"type":"invoice.paid","customer_id":"cus_42","amount":129}'

{"id":"01M7A6GF4ENM3FDPZB1SHD3G9S","status":"delivered"}
 (HTTP 200)

The teams terminal:

[billing] {"type":"invoice.paid","customer_id":"cus_42","amount":129}

This event has no text field, so the router's when: has(msg.json.text) is false. The AI step is skipped, and the next router in the chain, the rules, sends it to billing. A dry run of the same event says so:

route triage: rules → billing
    fell back from ai: skipped (when is false)
    plan: billing → billing-dr

The router chain is AI, then rules, then static. The same chain protects you when the model is down or over its budget: the rules take over, and the static route catches the rest.

An unsigned request is refused

HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
Content-Type: application/json
Www-Authenticate: Bearer
Date: Fri, 13 Nov 2026 10:16:03 GMT
Content-Length: 34

{"id":"","status":"unauthorized"}

Watch the numbers

The admin API on :9090 serves Prometheus metrics:

curl -s localhost:9090/metrics | grep -E "^hikyaku_(router|ai_decisions)"

hikyaku_ai_decisions_total{outcome="chosen",route="triage"} 2
hikyaku_router_fallback_total{route="triage",to="rules"} 1
hikyaku_router_skipped_total{route="triage",router="ai"} 1

Two messages needed a decision. One skipped the model and went through the rules.

Step 6: Break It on Purpose

A relay earns its place on the bad days. Make one.

Every billing endpoint is down

Stop the teams relay with Ctrl-C. Both billing and billing-dr are now unreachable. Send a billing message:

./send.sh '{"customer_id":"cus_42","text":"I was charged twice for my invoice and want a refund."}'

{"id":"01M7A6GG95TT62N5XR4RDETANW","status":"dead_lettered"}
 (HTTP 202)

The answer came after 2.1 seconds, and it is honest. It is not a 200, because the message was not delivered. It is a 202: the message is safe in the dead-letter queue. The relay's log tells the story:

{"time":"2026-11-13T11:16:05.144194+01:00","level":"INFO","msg":"destination fallback","from":"billing","to":"billing-dr","reason":"exhausted"}
{"time":"2026-11-13T11:16:06.719256+01:00","level":"WARN","msg":"dead-lettered","id":"01M7A6GG95TT62N5XR4RDETANW","route":"triage","destination":"billing","reason":"delivery","hop":"dead_letter","err":"destination billing-dr: Post \"http://localhost:9002/billing\": dial tcp [::1]:9002: connect: connection refused"}

Read the dead letter 

hikyaku dlq list

01M7A6GG95TT62N5XR4RDETANW  2026-11-13 11:16:06  billing          delivery   ×8  destination billing-dr: Post "http://localhost:9002/billing": dial tcp [::1]:900…
1 dead letter(s)

Eight attempts in total. hikyaku dlq inspect <id> prints the whole story of the message. This is part of it:

{
  "ai.decision": {
    "answers": [
      { "candidate": "billing", "chosen": true, "p": 0.99 },
      { "candidate": "support", "p": 0.87 },
      { "candidate": "oncall", "p": 0.07 }
    ],
    "model": "typesafe/jev-1.13.0",
    "reason": "chosen: billing"
  },
  "dlq": {
    "attempts": 8,
    "destination": "billing",
    "hops": [
      { "destination": "billing", "attempts": 3, "outcome": "exhausted",
        "error": "Post \"http://localhost:9001/billing\": dial tcp [::1]:9001: connect: connection refused" },
      { "destination": "billing-dr", "attempts": 5, "outcome": "exhausted",
        "error": "Post \"http://localhost:9002/billing\": dial tcp [::1]:9002: connect: connection refused" }
    ],
    "reason": "delivery",
    "route": "triage"
  }
}

The dead letter keeps the AI decision and every hop: three attempts on billing, five on billing-dr. Six months from now, you can still answer "why did this message go there, and why did it fail?"

Replay it

Start the teams relay again. Then:

hikyaku dlq replay --dry-run
hikyaku dlq replay

would deliver 01M7A6GG95TT62N5XR4RDETANW to billing
✓ billing: delivered after 1 attempt(s) (status 200)
    · billing ×1 ok

The teams terminal prints the message, one outage later:

[billing] {"customer_id":"cus_42","text":"I was charged twice for my invoice and want a refund."}

Good to know:

  • A replay keeps the original message ID as its idempotency key, so a destination that already has the message can drop the duplicate.
  • hikyaku dlq reads the DLQ file directly. It works without a running relay.
  • The entry stays in the DLQ file after a replay. Use --since 1h or --id to choose what to replay.

Inject faults before production does

You do not have to wait for an outage. hikyaku chaos wraps a destination with a fault injector and pushes messages through its real retry and fallback path:

hikyaku chaos --destination billing --fail 50% --count 100 --data @msg.json

chaos 100 messages to billing, 117 attempts (1.2 per message)
  delivered by billing     17
  delivered by fallback billing-dr  83
  dead-lettered          0
  lost                   0
  latency p50 0s  p95 188ms

Half of the attempts on billing failed. No message was lost, and none was dead-lettered. Most of them went to the backup, with only 1.2 attempts per message. That is the circuit breaker at work. After 20 requests with half of them failing, hikyaku stops calling the sick endpoint for 30 seconds and sends traffic straight to the fallback. The command exits with 1 if a message is lost.

Step 7: Test the Relay in CI

A routing change is a code change. hikyaku test checks what the spec does with the messages you give it. Nothing is sent: every destination is replaced by a stand-in. The filters, the routers, the retries and the fallbacks are the real ones.

Create hikyaku.test.yaml:

# hikyaku test: nothing is sent, every destination is a stand-in.
tests:
  - name: a typed invoice event goes to billing without a model call
    source: webhooks
    body: { type: invoice.paid, customer_id: cus_42, amount: 129 }
    expect:
      status: delivered
      to: [billing]
      routes:
        triage: { router: rules }

  - name: billing down fails over to its DR endpoint
    source: webhooks
    body: { type: invoice.paid, id: evt_2 }
    down: [billing]
    expect:
      status: delivered
      delivered:
        billing: { via: billing-dr, contains: { id: evt_2 } }

  - name: billing and its DR both down dead-letters the event
    source: webhooks
    body: { type: invoice.paid, id: evt_3 }
    down: [billing, billing-dr]
    expect:
      status: dead_lettered
      failed: [billing]

  - name: an outage reaches support even when on-call is down
    source: webhooks
    body: { text: "Total outage: every request fails with 503 errors." }
    decide: { triage: [support, oncall] }      # answer for the router: no model call
    down: [oncall]
    expect:
      status: delivered
      to: [support, oncall]
      failed: [oncall]

hikyaku test

✓ a typed invoice event goes to billing without a model call (1ms)
✓ billing down fails over to its DR endpoint (0s)
✓ billing and its DR both down dead-letters the event (0s)
✓ an outage reaches support even when on-call is down (0s)
✓ 4 test(s) passed

down: makes a destination unreachable for one test. decide: answers in place of the route's router, so the last test checks delivery without calling the model.

Good to know:

  • decide replaces the whole router chain of the route, rules included. A test with decide checks delivery. A test without it checks routing.
  • A test without decide builds the real router, so the job needs the secrets that the spec declares, even when no model call is made.
  • Score the model's own answers with hikyaku ai test, as in step 4.

Two more commands belong in the same pipeline. hikyaku lint warns about risky specs:

! route "triage".router.fallback_models: a single model: when it is down the router fallback serves every message; add a fallback model (such as a local ollama-decisions/clef)
! destination "billing-dr".fallback: required and without a fallback: when it fails, its messages go to the DLQ
! destination "support".fallback: required and without a fallback: when it fails, its messages go to the DLQ
! server.admin.token: unset: /reload, /debug, /v1/tail, /v1/feedback and /v1/history answer loopback clients only
4 warning(s)

Step 8: Bonus, an LLM Proxy with the Same Tool

A chat request is also a message. A model is also a destination. So the same relay, with a different spec, is an LLM proxy: one OpenAI-compatible endpoint in front of several model providers.

Clients ask for fast, smart or auto. With auto, the decision model picks the model by how hard the request is. Create a new folder with this hikyaku.yaml:

# yaml-language-server: $schema=https://xavidop.github.io/hikyaku/schema/hikyaku.schema.json
version: 1
name: llm-proxy

secrets:
  PROXY_KEY: env:PROXY_KEY
  GEMINI_API_KEY: env:GEMINI_API_KEY
  ANTHROPIC_API_KEY: env:ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
  TYPESAFE_API_KEY: env:TYPESAFE_API_KEY

genkit:
  plugins: [systemone, googlegenai, anthropic]

sources:
  - name: api
    type: openai
    listen: ":8080"
    models: [auto, fast, smart]
    auth: { bearer: { tokens: ["{{secrets.PROXY_KEY}}"] } }

defaults:
  timeout: 60s
  retry: { attempts: 2, backoff: 500ms }

destinations:
  - { name: fast, type: model, model: googleai/gemini-3.8-flash }
  - { name: smart, type: model, model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5, fallback: [fast] }

routes:
  - name: chat
    from: [api]
    router:
      type: rules
      rules:
        - { when: 'msg.json.model == "fast"', to: [fast] }
        - { when: 'msg.json.model == "smart"', to: [smart] }
      fallback:
        - type: ai
          when: msg.json.model == "auto"       # only "auto" pays for a decision
          model: typesafe/jev-1.13.0
          instructions: Pick the model for this chat request.
          state: "{{ .json.messages }}"
          candidates:
            - { name: fast, description: "A short or simple request: a lookup, a rewrite, small talk." }
            - { name: smart, description: "A hard request: multi-step reasoning, code, analysis." }
          min_confidence: 0.6
          on_low_confidence: [smart]
          fallback:
            - { type: static, to: [fast] }

server:
  admin: { listen: ":9090" }

export PROXY_KEY=local-dev-key GEMINI_API_KEY=... ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=... TYPESAFE_API_KEY=...
hikyaku doctor && hikyaku run

Call it like the OpenAI API:

curl -s localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer local-dev-key' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"fast","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Say hi in five words."}]}'

{"id":"chatcmpl-01M7A5NPX91XMA3QE3HANMVQTD","object":"chat.completion","created":1794564086,"model":"googleai/gemini-3.8-flash","choices":[{"index":0,"message":{"role":"assistant","content":"Hi there, how are you?"},"finish_reason":"stop"}],"usage":{"prompt_tokens":7,"completion_tokens":7,"total_tokens":466}}

Now let the proxy choose. The model field of each answer shows who served it:

Request with "model": "auto" Answered by
"What is the capital of France?" googleai/gemini-3.8-flash
"Write a Go function that merges two sorted linked lists and prove its time complexity step by step." anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5

The easy question went to the cheap, fast model. The hard one went to the stronger model. A request without the bearer key gets a 401.

Everything from the first seven steps still applies. smart has fallback: [fast], so when Anthropic has a bad day, Gemini answers. Retries, the circuit breaker and the metrics work the same way. Any OpenAI SDK can use the proxy: set its base URL to http://localhost:8080/v1.

The gateway has its own guide, with streaming, function calling, labeled cases for the model choice and a failover test: Build an LLM Gateway with hikyaku.

What Else Is in the Box

This guide used HTTP on both sides. The relay speaks many more protocols, and each one is a type: in the same spec:

Protocol As a source As a destination
http / https listen, poll yes
ws / wss, sse, grpc listen, subscribe yes
tcp / udp listen yes
kafka, nats / jetstream, mqtt, amqp (RabbitMQ) subscribe yes
redis (Streams, Pub/Sub) subscribe yes
sqs / sns / eventbridge, pubsub, servicebus / eventhubs subscribe yes
s3 / gcs poll yes
stdin / stdout / stderr / file yes yes

The documentation also covers:

  • Transforms: filter with CEL, reshape with jq, render a template, validate against a JSON Schema.
  • History-aware routing: a follow-up from the same customer goes where the last message went.
  • Deploys: a Docker image and a Helm chart, a disk buffer that survives a crash, hot reload, and OpenTelemetry traces.
  • Your own types: add a source or a destination in Go, in your own build or as a plugin.

Conclusion

Glue code looks small, and it hides the hard parts of distributed systems: retries, backpressure, failover, and the question "where did that message go?" hikyaku puts those parts in one binary and one YAML file. The relay answers 200 only when the message arrived, and 202 only when it is safe.

The AI router is the new piece. It is not a chat model guessing in free text. It is a decision model that answers one question per destination with a probability you can measure. You tune it with labeled cases, and you keep rules behind it for the day the model is down.

Start with the boring part. Put hikyaku in front of one webhook, with one fallback and a dead-letter queue. Add the AI router later, in shadow mode, next to the rules you already trust.

Further reading

  • hikyaku on GitHub and the documentation
  • Quick start and concepts
  • Routing and the AI router: engines, thresholds, shadow mode, cache and budget
  • Retries and fallbacks and the LLM proxy
  • The examples: webhook fan-out, AI triage, a Kafka bridge, an LLM proxy and two plugins
  • Build an LLM Gateway with hikyaku, the second hikyaku article
  • Genkit Flows on Kubernetes with senro and jev, another use of the jev decision model

title: We spent months building a database client, then decided to turn it into a VS Code extension
description:
Hey everyone!

We're a small team of developers from the Czech Republic, and we've been working on DataLoam, a database client with built-in AI for VS Code and Cursor.

The idea came from working with databases ourselves. Writing SQL usually isn't the hardest part. The hard part is figuring out how everything fits together, especially in a database you don't know that well.

AI can help with that, but if it doesn't know your schema or what the data actually means, it tends to make things up. You paste a few table definitions into a chat, and you get back a query with a column that doesn't exist.

So we started building a database client where the AI has that context automatically.

From desktop app to extension

We originally built DataLoam as a standalone desktop app. After a while we realized we didn't want another window to switch to. We wanted everything right in our editor, next to the code that uses the database. So we changed direction and rebuilt it as a VS Code extension.

It wasn't a small change, but it's the version we actually wanted to use ourselves.

What it does so far

  • PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, SQLite and MongoDB support
  • A database explorer, query consoles, autocomplete and result tables
  • An AI chat that understands your schema and can help write and fix queries
  • Vim motions in result tables (hjkl, v, y, gg/G, etc.)
  • Export to CSV, JSON or Excel

The AI writes the query, you run it

This was a deliberate decision. The AI can look up your tables and relationships, write the SQL, check it and put it in your console. It can't execute anything. We wanted developers to stay in control of what actually happens to their data.

To make its answers more accurate, DataLoam keeps an index of your schema on your machine. You can add descriptions to tables and columns, or point it at an existing docs file and let it write them for you. It also detects columns that hold a fixed set of values (like an order status), so it knows which values are valid instead of guessing.

Our own SQL language server

We also built our own SQL language server for autocomplete and diagnostics. It warns you about tables and columns that don't exist before you run anything. That turned out to be quite a project on its own, and probably deserves its own post.

Try it

The core client is free, and the AI features are optional and paid, with a free trial.

  • Website: https://dataloam.io/
  • Install: VSCode Marketplace / OpenVSX
  • Discord: https://discord.gg/2skjWP88af
  • Issues and feature requests: https://github.com/VPALGO-s-r-o/DataLoam/issues

We're still early and figuring out what works best, so we'd love some feedback.

If you work with databases regularly, what's the most annoying part of your current workflow?

title: Introducing Vercel Security Review
description:
Today, we are launching Vercel Security Review in public beta.

Security Review is a new capability in Vercel Agent, alongside Code Review and Investigation. Once enabled, it scans for vulnerabilities on every push to a team's connected GitHub repositories.

Findings appear as comments on pull requests, are listed in the Security dashboard, and are available via CLI. With your permission, Vercel Agent can also validate and push fixes for findings.

How it works

Security reviews are triggered by GitHub push events, including direct pushes to your production branch. In monorepos, reviews are scoped to the project's root directory. Here is how it works:

  1. You push code to a GitHub repository connected to a Vercel project.

  2. As soon as the push lands, Security Review scans the changed code for vulnerabilities like missing authorization checks or exposed secrets.

  3. Findings are posted to the Security dashboard. On private and internal repositories, Security Review also adds a GitHub check to the commit and comments on the pull request.

  4. You can fix findings by clicking Fix with Vercel Agent in the dashboard, or use the CLI to pull findings and have your own coding agent implement changes.

  5. When subsequent security reviews no longer detect a finding, it is marked as no longer detected in the dashboard, and the GitHub comment is closed.

Each review compares the push against a base and covers only what changed. For deployments, the base is the branch’s previous deployment, so the agent reviews the change against what’s already running. Because it only scans the diff, Security Review finishes in seconds and can run on every preview and production deployment.

What the agent checks

The agent reads the diff along with the surrounding code, traces how the changed code can be reached, checks for existing protections, and rechecks each finding before reporting it. That process is how it catches logic flaws like missing authorization checks, which pattern-matching scanners miss.

Each review also applies your team’s security policies, which you can write in plain language and apply to specific projects or across your team. For example, a policy can require any endpoint that returns customer data to check that the requester owns it. You can also manage policies with the Vercel CLI, using vercel security policy.

How findings are tracked

Each new finding is checked against ones that have already been reported, so the same issue isn’t flagged twice. Every finding is tied to the deployment where it first appeared and changes are followed from there. That means that when a vulnerable change from a pull request is merged into your production branch, the finding is flagged in production as well.

When a later review no longer detects the issue in an environment, the agent marks the finding as no longer detected there.

Acting on findings

Every finding explains the vulnerability and how to fix it, with links to the commit and deployment where it first appeared.

Findings are listed in the Vulnerability view in the Security dashboard, where you can ask Vercel Agent to validate and commit fixes. Findings are also available via CLI, so you can fix vulnerabilities with your own coding agent.

Each new finding generates an audit log event, which Enterprise teams can send to their SIEM through Audit Log Drains.

Here is a demo of sample findings in the dashboard:

Fixing vulnerabilities with Vercel Agent

When Vercel Agent can fix a finding, you will see the option to click Fix with Vercel Agent on the finding page in the dashboard. After you click, the agent confirms the vulnerability still exists, then makes the smallest change that fixes it and updates the tests.

Say a developer pushes a change to an invoice download endpoint, and the lookup doesn't check which organization the invoice belongs to. Within seconds, Security Review flags that any signed-in user could download another organization's invoice by changing its ID. Vercel Agent's fix scopes the lookup to the user's organization:

Fixing vulnerabilities with your own coding agent

You can point your coding agent or other systems at the Vercel CLI to pull and fix vulnerabilities:

Findings in the dashboard also give you the ability to copy details as Markdown or JSON, making it easy to paste them into an agent conversation.

Every code change needs security review

Frontier AI models are making vulnerabilities far easier to find and exploit. Last month, researchers turned two decade-old flaws in PHP core into working remote code execution exploits with relatively little effort.

At the same time, agents are writing more of the code teams ship, and each handles security review its own way, or in many cases, not at all.

With Vercel Security Review, you can scan every push on every project for vulnerabilities by default, using the security policies you set.

What's next

Security Review starts with code pushed to GitHub. Next, we're bringing it to deployments from the Vercel CLI and v0, and to repositories that don't deploy on Vercel. We're also working on suggested fixes you can apply directly from the pull request.

Get started

Vercel Security Review is available today in public beta for Pro and Enterprise teams.

To get started, enable Security Review in Vercel Agent Settings. You can choose to run Security Review on all projects, or only the ones you choose. To learn more, read the Changelog entry and the Security Review documentation.

Security Review is billed at the Vercel Agent rate, with model tokens at the provider's rate and no markup, plus $0.25 per million tokens.

Security reviews are free until November 10, 2026. Fixes made with Vercel Agent are billed at the rate above.
