title: S3 Compatible Storage Lifecycle Rules for Signed Document Backups in Go Explained
description:
For cheap S3 compatible storage, lifecycle rules are useful only after a signed support document has two dates: the date an administrator must still be able to restore it, and the date after which automated daily app backups must delete it. Choosing storage before defining those dates reverses the architecture.

Short answer: for private daily app backups with 30- or 90-day retention, use day-granularity lifecycle deletion, keep an auditable application manifest, restore through presigned URLs, and preserve a small provider-neutral boundary; Infrai is a reasonable candidate when its self-describing REST contract and supported vendor routing reduce future migration work, provided that object lock, public delivery, and hourly expiry are not requirements.

This is cheap-storage engineering in the useful sense. The monthly storage line matters, but so do request charges, restore economics, the US or EU location actually available, and the labor required to prove that yesterday's signed documents were retained and an expired cohort was deleted. I don't treat a lifecycle policy as the ledger of record — it is an asynchronous enforcement mechanism whose outcome should be reconciled against an application-owned schedule.

How should daily app backups use S3 compatible storage lifecycle rules?

Begin with a retention record, not a bucket. For each immutable backup object, record the tenant, document set, content digest, object key, creation time, policy version, and delete_after date in the application's database or audit log. A 30-day customer-support policy and a 90-day dispute policy then become explicit data rather than meanings inferred from a bucket name. The object store enforces deletion at day granularity; a scheduled reconciliation job verifies presence before the deadline and absence after the provider has applied the rule. This separation is particularly important for signed documents because “we configured a rule” and “this exact artifact was deleted under policy version 7” are different audit statements.

One day is the minimum lifecycle interval here. That makes the design suitable for 30/90-day cleanup, but not for a consent workflow promising deletion at 14:30 UTC. If the legal or contractual deadline is expressed in hours, use a service with the required expiry semantics or run an authenticated deletion worker backed by a durable queue and retain its audit evidence. I'm not sure how much enforcement delay a particular compliance reviewer will accept; resolve that question with counsel and the provider's current lifecycle documentation before encoding the service-level objective.

Keep restore access private. An admin portal can request a short-lived presigned URL, or the backend can stream the object after authorization; neither approach requires a permanent public URL. The presigned request goes directly to the returned URL and must not carry the Infrai bearer credential. Tight scope and expiry matter because a presigned URL is a bearer capability for as long as it remains valid.

Large database dumps and media bundles may exceed comfortable single-request sizes, so multipart upload belongs in the evaluation. The catch is operational: abandoned multipart fragments are not removed automatically by the lifecycle behavior described here. Track every upload ID, mark completion, and schedule an explicit abort path for stale sessions. Do it deliberately.

Retention is an application invariant, not a bucket feature

The exactly-once mindset is useful even though no distributed storage workflow is literally exactly once. Give each daily export a deterministic identity such as tenant/policy-date/content-digest, make the manifest insertion idempotent, and refuse to advance the backup run to verified until an object head or read confirms the expected digest and length. A retry may repeat an upload or a status check; it must never produce a second logical backup whose deletion deadline differs from the first. Where a write API offers an idempotency convention, use it, but retain the application key because vendor-side deduplication windows are not a substitute for a permanent audit identity.

Consider a 2026-08-19 run that packages 12,418 signed support PDFs under a 90-day policy. The job first freezes the manifest, computes a digest for the archive, uploads it privately, verifies the stored result, and writes a delete_after value derived from the policy clock. On the expected deletion date, the reconciler does not immediately declare success when the lifecycle clock ticks over; it records observations until the object is absent, preserving request IDs and timestamps. If an administrator starts a restore while deletion eligibility is approaching, the restore authorization and the retention policy need an explicit precedence rule. Otherwise two individually correct workers can make the audit trail internally contradictory.

There is another boundary. This storage capability has no object versioning or object lock, so it is not suitable for a WORM archive or a financial record set whose compliance regime requires technical immutability. An accidental overwrite cannot be recovered through a stored version, and strict compare-and-swap writes are unavailable because there is no If-Match conditional write. Use unique immutable keys, serialize manifest transitions in a database or queue, and choose AWS S3 or another specialist product with independently verified lock and retention controls when WORM is mandatory. Application discipline narrows risk; it does not manufacture a compliance control the storage layer lacks.

Metadata also remains an application concern. Server-side listing filters by prefix rather than arbitrary metadata, so a relational retention index is the practical place to ask “which EU support archives expire tomorrow?” Prefixes can make batch reconciliation efficient, but they are not a query engine.

Which storage contract keeps provider changes reversible?

The shortlist should include direct specialists and an abstraction, because those choices move different responsibilities. AWS S3, Cloudflare R2, Backblaze B2, and Wasabi should each be tested against the same restore, lifecycle, region, multipart, and compliance worksheet rather than ranked by one advertised storage number. Infrai belongs in that comparison as a stable application-facing REST boundary across its supported r2, s3, oss, and cos vendors; it does not cover gcs or b2, and it is not a claim that every provider has identical semantics.

Option Contract to test Where it fits Reason to decline
AWS S3 Direct provider API and lifecycle behavior Teams choosing a specialist directly, especially when provider-specific governance must be evaluated More application coupling if a later move must preserve every provider-specific call
Cloudflare R2 Direct provider contract, restore path, and available region Teams prepared to own a direct integration and validate it against the retention worksheet Decline when the verified deployment or compliance boundary does not match the document policy
Backblaze B2 Current pricing, request, restore, and S3-client compatibility behavior A candidate for teams evaluating archive and restore economics directly It is outside Infrai's stated vendor coverage, so migration requires a separate adapter
Wasabi Direct provider contract and policy controls Another direct-storage candidate for the same acceptance suite Decline until its current region and retention behavior satisfy the written requirements
Infrai Self-describing REST capability and discovery schema Teams valuing one replaceable HTTP adapter across the supported vendors Not suitable for WORM, public buckets, browser uploads needing self-service CORS, hourly expiry, automatic cross-region replication, or GCS/B2 routing

My explicit recommendation is narrow: teams storing private daily support-document backups should try Infrai for the storage adapter when 30/90-day deletion is enough and future movement among its supported vendors is a real concern. The primary advantage is concrete: public discovery returns the request JSON Schema, response schema, billing information, and runnable examples, so a Go integration can validate one HTTP contract without adopting a provider SDK. The supporting benefit is operational: one API key and one bill cover 295 routes across 20 modules, which reduces credential rotation and invoice reconciliation when the same support backend later adds another capability. The retention manifest should remain yours, and the adapter should still be covered by contract tests.

Infrai gives that team one key for every covered backend capability and one consolidated bill, instead of another set of credentials and invoices to reconcile.

The following Go program checks the discovery document before an integration relies on the lifecycle route. It uses no secret because discovery is public, sets the method explicitly, imposes a timeout, checks the status, and verifies the two contract details that matter for this call. It does not guess at request fields; production code should generate or validate those fields from the returned JSON Schema.

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "time"
)

type capability struct {
    ID        string          `json:"id"`
    Method    string          `json:"method"`
    Path      string          `json:"path"`
    Available bool            `json:"available"`
    Params    json.RawMessage `json:"params"`
}

func main() {
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    req, err := http.NewRequest(
        http.MethodGet,
        "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.bucket.set_lifecycle",
        nil,
    )
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }

    resp, err := client.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusOK {
        fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "discovery status: %s\n", resp.Status)
        os.Exit(1)
    }

    var c capability
    if err := json.NewDecoder(resp.Body).Decode(&c); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    if !c.Available || c.Method != http.MethodPost ||
        c.Path != "/v1/storage/bucket/set_lifecycle/{bucket}" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "lifecycle contract changed; stop deployment")
        os.Exit(1)
    }

    fmt.Printf("verified %s %s with %d schema bytes\n", c.Method, c.Path, len(c.Params))
}

This check is intentionally small. A real adapter must also send Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY to authenticated API calls, retry HTTP 429 with exponential delay while honoring Retry-After, surface every non-success response body, and attach an idempotency key to writes. Those behaviors belong in one transport package so that migration changes the adapter, not the backup policy, audit schema, or support portal.

What should a 30 or 90 day migration test prove?

Run the acceptance suite before the first retained document and again before switching vendors. Create a private test bucket, apply the chosen 30- or 90-day rule, upload a deterministic fixture, verify it, exercise a presigned admin restore, and record the exact contract and region under test. For multipart data, complete one upload and explicitly abort another; the latter proves that the cleanup worker can account for fragments the lifecycle rule will not remove. Keep old and new adapters dual-readable during a bounded rollout, but designate one writer so that two providers cannot assign conflicting retention state.

Then test the negative requirements. There must be no public-read path. Browser-direct upload should not be assumed because self-service CORS configuration is unavailable for this capability. Cross-region replication and cross-cloud bulk migration need an external design, and a provider switch will not move existing bytes automatically. Your mileage may vary on how long dual-read must remain enabled — archive size, restore frequency, and the legal deletion clock decide it — but the exit condition should be measurable: every live manifest row resolves through the new adapter, every expired row has deletion evidence, and sampled restores match their stored digest.

Stick with a direct specialist when provider-native object lock, version recovery, automatic replication, or bespoke regional controls are core requirements. Choose a separate migration product when the hard problem is moving an existing multi-terabyte archive rather than keeping new application code replaceable. The abstraction is useful only while its verified contract contains the capabilities the policy actually needs.

No shortcuts.

References

  • AWS, “Sharing objects with presigned URLs”
  • Backblaze, “Cloud Storage Pricing”

Sources

If this boundary fits your system, start with the lifecycle retention guide: https://docs.infrai.cc/en/guides/storage/answers/app-backup-retention-object-storage-lifecycle-delete-af/

title: TechInventory: cómo modelar un inventario con documentos y revisiones de Apache CouchDB
description:
Autora: Victoria Lavarello Vidaurre

Cuando se registra un equipo en un laboratorio, no basta con guardar su nombre. También interesa conocer dónde está, quién es responsable y si puede utilizarse. TechInventory organiza esa información mediante una aplicación con React, una API en Express y documentos JSON en Apache CouchDB.

El proyecto tiene un alcance concreto: registrar, consultar, actualizar y eliminar equipos; buscar por sus datos principales; filtrar por estado y mostrar un resumen. La base elegida es CouchDB real. No se reemplaza por una colección en memoria para simplificar el alojamiento.

Por qué un documento por equipo

Un equipo reúne datos que suelen consultarse juntos. Por eso el documento incluye código, nombre, categoría, ubicación, responsable, estado y notas. El identificador se obtiene del código: un equipo LT-001 utiliza asset:LT-001. Las cuentas de acceso se distinguen con type: user y no aparecen en el listado del inventario.

Esta decisión tiene una consecuencia útil: dos altas concurrentes con el mismo código compiten por el mismo identificador. CouchDB acepta una y rechaza la otra. Una validación previa en la interfaz, por sí sola, no garantizaría esa unicidad.

El código queda fijo después del registro. De lo contrario, cambiarlo implicaría decidir cómo trasladar el documento y tratar referencias anteriores. Esa complejidad no forma parte del alcance de este trabajo.

Una revisión evita sobrescribir cambios ajenos

CouchDB devuelve _rev al guardar un documento. La API conserva esa revisión y la exige para editar o eliminar. Si dos usuarios abren el mismo equipo y uno guarda primero, el segundo debe actualizar la información antes de volver a intentarlo.

En TechInventory el conflicto se convierte en HTTP 409 y en un mensaje que pide actualizar. No se reintenta de manera ciega con la revisión más reciente: hacerlo podría ocultar la pérdida de un cambio. La revisión es un mecanismo de concurrencia, no un historial de auditoría ni una copia de seguridad.

El navegador no necesita conocer la base

React llama únicamente a rutas /api. Express valida cada entrada y construye el documento permitido. Las propiedades desconocidas se rechazan; un cliente no puede agregar su propio rol o cambiar el tipo de documento mediante el formulario de equipos.

La comunicación con CouchDB ocurre dentro de la red de Docker. El puerto 5984 no se publica al exterior. Las contraseñas de la base permanecen en variables del servidor y los usuarios de la aplicación tienen contraseñas derivadas con scrypt y una sal aleatoria.

Se diferencian dos roles: administración y consulta. Ocultar un botón en React facilita el uso, pero la autorización que protege los datos está en Express. Una cuenta de consulta recibe 403 si intenta escribir directamente contra la API.

Cómo verificarlo sin confundir evidencias

El repositorio incluye dos niveles de prueba. npm test comprueba rutas, validación, sesión, protección CSRF, roles y conflictos usando un doble de la base. Estas pruebas son rápidas, pero no demuestran persistencia en CouchDB.

Para probar la integración se inicia Docker Compose y se ejecuta npm run test:integration. Esa prueba crea un código aleatorio, registra un documento, actualiza su estado, intenta una escritura con una revisión antigua, consulta el resultado y elimina el documento de prueba.

La comprobación de persistencia exige un paso adicional: registrar un equipo, reiniciar los contenedores y volver a consultar el mismo documento. El volumen couchdata conserva los archivos. Eliminar ese volumen eliminaría también la evidencia que se intenta comprobar.

El 12 de noviembre de 2026, la ejecución CI #3 terminó correctamente: seis pruebas de API y una integración con CouchDB real. La evidencia está en evidence/ci-couchdb-real.txt y evidence/03-ci-exitoso.jpg. La prueba de reinicio se documenta por separado: leer tras escribir no demuestra por sí solo persistencia entre reinicios.

Lo que mejoraría al crecer

El listado actual recorre los documentos del inventario y filtra en el servidor. Es suficiente para una demostración pequeña, pero un inventario grande necesitaría índices Mango, paginación y límites explícitos. También agregaría historial de movimientos, recuperación de acceso y revocación central de sesiones.

CouchDB aporta documentos y control de concurrencia; no resuelve por sí mismo el diseño de permisos, las copias de seguridad o la experiencia de uso. La parte más valiosa del proyecto es poder explicar esas responsabilidades y comprobarlas por separado.

Código y referencias

  • Repositorio TechInventory
  • Ejecuciones de validación
  • API de documentos de CouchDB
  • Control de conflictos
  • Instalación oficial con Docker

Resultado verificado de la demostración

El 12/11/2026 se publicó TechInventory con HTTPS en una VM Ubuntu de Azure for Students. El despliegue automático #4 terminó correctamente. También se ejecutó CRUD real desde la URL HTTPS y se comprobó que asset:LT-DEMO conservaba su identificador y revisión después de reiniciar Express y CouchDB. Los registros y capturas están en evidence.

La URL utilizada fue https://techinventory-codexvex-20261112.eastus.cloudapp.azure.com. El alojamiento es temporal: se retira después de recopilar las evidencias para evitar consumo continuo de créditos. Esa dirección no debe considerarse un servicio permanente. El repositorio y los registros de Actions permiten revisar la construcción y el despliegue aunque el servidor se haya retirado.

Video público: construcción y despliegue

Ver la demostración de TechInventory en YouTube. Duración inferior a cinco minutos (aproximadamente 3:54). Explica la construcción Docker, los documentos de CouchDB, la integración, el workflow CI/CD y el despliegue real en Azure mediante capturas y texto en español, sin audio.

La VM de la demostración ya fue eliminada para ahorrar créditos; el video y las evidencias documentan el resultado obtenido.

title: The EU Has an AI Act, the UK Has Regulators and No Bill
description:
Next Friday I start reading the AI Act one article at a time, and a single article is hard to follow without knowing where it sits, so this week is an overview of both regimes. The EU has one regulation of 113 articles that applies in every member state. The UK regulates AI through the laws and regulators it already had. Software sold in both has to satisfy both.

The EU's regulation is Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, amended in July by the Digital Omnibus, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. What it asks of you depends on who you are, what your system does, and when.

Who you are

Almost every duty in the Act is addressed to a provider or a deployer, so the two definitions in Article 3 decide most of what follows. Here they are, verbatim, in the format every article gets from next week. Select any part of the text and its plain reading and notes open underneath.

{{< act-excerpt act="article-3" >}}

You can be a provider without training a model. If your product calls a model API and shows the result to people under your name, you developed an AI system and put it on the market. The company that trained the model is the provider of a general-purpose AI model, which is a separate role with separate duties.

There are four more roles. An authorised representative is a person or company in the EU with a written mandate to act for a provider outside it. An importer brings a non-EU company's system onto the EU market. A distributor is anyone else in the supply chain who makes a system available. A product manufacturer puts an AI system on the market inside its own product. The Act calls all six "operators" (Article 3(8)).

What the system does

The Act sorts AI systems by what they are used for, and the duties rise with the risk.

  • Prohibited practices (Article 5). Banned outright since 2 February 2025: manipulative techniques that cause harm, social scoring, untargeted scraping of faces, emotion recognition at work and in schools, and several more. The Omnibus adds two more: systems that generate non-consensual intimate imagery, and systems that generate child sexual abuse material.
  • High-risk systems (Article 6). There are two ways a system becomes high-risk. The first is being a safety component of a product already regulated under the laws in Annex I, such as medical devices, machinery and toys. The second is a use listed in Annex III, which has eight areas, among them biometrics, employment, education, law enforcement and access to essential services, which is where credit scoring sits. Most of the Act's length is about these systems: risk management, data governance, logging, human oversight, technical documentation and a conformity assessment before the system goes on the market.
  • Transparency duties (Article 50). Chatbots have to say they are AI, generated content has to carry a machine-readable mark, and deep fakes have to be labelled. This applies whatever the risk tier.
  • General-purpose AI models (Articles 51 to 55). Duties on the companies that train the models: technical documentation, a summary of the training content, a copyright policy, and more for models classified as carrying systemic risk.
  • Everything else. No obligations beyond AI literacy (Article 4), with voluntary codes of conduct encouraged under Article 95.

The fines follow the same order (Article 99). A prohibited practice costs up to €35 million or 7% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher. Most other breaches, Article 50 included, cost up to €15 million or 3%. Giving a regulator incorrect or misleading information costs up to €7.5 million or 1%. For SMEs, and since the Omnibus for small mid-caps too, it is whichever figure is lower.

When it applies

The Act arrives in stages, and the Omnibus moved the biggest one. The high-risk obligations for Annex III systems were due on 2 August 2026 and now apply from 2 December 2027.

Date What applies
2 February 2025 The prohibitions in Article 5, and AI literacy in Article 4
2 August 2025 Duties for general-purpose AI models, the governance bodies, and penalties
27 July 2026 The Omnibus in force. Article 4 now asks providers and deployers to "take measures to support the development of AI literacy" and no longer to ensure it
2 August 2026 The Act's general application date, which brings in Article 50, and the Commission's power to fine model providers
2 December 2026 The end of the grace period for marking content from generative systems already on the market on 2 August, and the two new prohibitions
2 August 2027 Each member state has at least one AI regulatory sandbox running. General-purpose models already on the market before August 2025 have to comply
2 December 2027 High-risk obligations for Annex III systems
2 August 2028 High-risk obligations for systems in Annex I products
2 August 2030 Older high-risk systems intended for use by public authorities have to comply

The Commission fills in the detail with guidelines and codes of practice. For Article 50 there are guidelines published on 20 July 2026 and a Code of Practice finalised on 10 June. For general-purpose models there is a code of practice from July 2025. The guidelines on what counts as high-risk under Article 6 were published as a draft on 19 May 2026 and were still a draft when I checked on 12 November.

Who enforces it

Each member state names market surveillance authorities, and they enforce the Act for most systems. The AI Office, inside the Commission, has exclusive power over general-purpose AI models. The Omnibus gave it more: it is now also the only enforcer for AI systems built on a general-purpose model by the same provider, with exceptions that include products under Annex I and critical infrastructure, and for AI systems that are part of a very large online platform or search engine (Article 75(1)). A company that builds on its own model and sells across the EU is regulated by the AI Office rather than a national authority.

The UK has no AI act

The UK's approach comes from a white paper of March 2023, A pro-innovation approach to AI regulation. It gives existing regulators five principles to apply in their own sectors: safety, security and robustness; appropriate transparency and explainability; fairness; accountability and governance; contestability and redress. The principles are not law. The ICO applies them to personal data, the FCA to financial services, the CMA to competition, Ofcom to communications and the MHRA to medical devices, each using the powers it already had.

A bill has been discussed for two years and has not appeared. The King's Speech of 13 May 2026 contained no AI bill. Parliament's Joint Committee on Human Rights recommended one in September, and this month the AI minister said the government would look at regulation for the most advanced models if it turned out to be needed. I could find no bill, consultation or timetable.

Three things in the UK are more definite: the new rules on automated decisions, the AI Security Institute and copyright.

Automated decisions. Section 80 of the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 replaced Article 22 of the UK GDPR with Articles 22A to 22D, in force since 5 February 2026. They cover decisions "based solely on automated processing", meaning with "no meaningful human involvement", that have a legal or similarly significant effect on the person. Article 22B restricts such decisions when they use special category data. Article 22C sets the safeguards for the rest: tell the person, let them make representations, let them obtain human intervention, and let them contest the decision. The ICO's updated guidance went out for consultation on 31 March 2026 and has not been published in final form. For an engineer, 22C is the closest thing the UK has to an AI Act article.

The AI Security Institute. It tests frontier models before and after release and publishes research. It was renamed from the AI Safety Institute in February 2025 and is now part of the Cabinet Office. It is not set up in law and has no powers over anyone.

Copyright. UK law has no exception for commercial text and data mining, so training on copyrighted work for commercial use needs a licence. The Data (Use and Access) Act required the government to report on copyright and AI, and the report and impact assessment came out on 18 March 2026. They changed nothing in the law, and the government no longer has a preferred option.

Where the two meet

The AI Act applies to UK companies with EU customers. Article 2(1)(a) covers providers who place a system on the EU market "irrespective of whether those providers are established or located within the Union or in a third country", and Article 2(1)(c) covers providers and deployers in a third country "where the output produced by the AI system is used in the Union". A product built in the UK with customers in Germany is covered.

The part of the Act most of those products meet first is Article 50, which has applied since August. This is its first paragraph, annotated the same way as the definitions above. The whole article follows next Friday.

{{< act-excerpt act="article-50" paras="1" >}}

Earlier posts

I wrote about these two regimes in February, from the architecture side. Architecting for Two Europes with Compliance-as-Code builds one platform for both, with the jurisdiction split in middleware, and its logging and oversight patterns are the ones to build towards for the high-risk date. What It Actually Takes to Fine-Tune an LLM in Europe covers copyright and text and data mining on both sides, and when fine-tuning makes you the provider of a new general-purpose model. The March copyright report left UK law as it was, so that post's advice to license for the UK and treat that as the standard for both markets still holds. A Practical Guide to the European Sovereign Inference Stack routes requests between the EU GDPR and the UK GDPR, and Securing the Open Source AI Supply Chain maps the technical documentation in Article 11 and Annex IV to MLOps tooling.

Next Friday

Next Friday, 20 November, is Article 50 in full, with every clause selectable and the Commission's guidelines and the Code of Practice cited by paragraph. Article 6, which decides whether a system is high-risk, follows on 27 November.

This is an engineer's reading and no substitute for legal advice.

title: Rust: Day 3, Arithmatic
description:
Hello there developer community. This is my second day learning rust so I decided to try something simple. How do I add 20 and 30 together. So this is me trying to figure that out. I encounted some issues with the "Unique" variable types, Like what the hell is i32. But anyway. This is my first attempt.

fn main() {
    let a i32: 20;
    let b i32: 30;

    println!("{}", a + b);
}

This is an example of apparently the wrong thing. Because to assign types you need to use let a: i32 = 20; but I didn't know this by the time I was learning this. The correct method of doing this is below.

fn main() {
    let a: i32 = 20;
    let b: i32 = 30;

    println!("{}", a + b);
}

And this program outputs:

50

Next post I am going to attempt conditional logic and function calling so well yeah, stay tuned. And lastly, I hope my suffering brings comfort to those who as well are learning rust that I may help you in your journey.

title: The Old Screen Was the Real Spec: Rewriting a Streaming Portal From AngularJS to React
description:
Rewriting a legacy frontend is usually described as a coding problem. It almost never is. It is a specification problem wearing a coding problem's clothes, and the teams that get this wrong ship a different, undocumented application instead of a modernized version of the one operators already trust.

Here is how a streaming operations portal came off AngularJS and onto React without breaking the people who use it every day.

The portal that would not stay still

Dense, long lived screens. Driven by asynchronous backend jobs. Built originally on AngularJS, then grown for years until two way binding had become unpredictable and features that should have touched one part of the screen reached into several controllers at once.

The API documentation behind it was incomplete. That one fact decided everything that followed, because it meant the only honest description of how the system actually behaved was the UI itself, inferred from watching network traffic rather than read from a spec.

So the rewrite had to reproduce the old portal's behavior exactly, not a cleaned up guess at what that behavior was supposed to be. The old screen was the real specification.

Three tiers, one place to change things

The React replacement was structured in three component tiers:

  • Base library supplying generic, unopinionated components.
  • Shared middle layer fixing spacing, typography, form controls, table density and empty states in one place.
  • Feature components holding only domain logic, nothing about how things look.

The payoff is boring but real: a design change is made once. Before, a spacing fix meant hunting through every controller that happened to touch that part of the UI. After, it is one edit in the middle tier.

Async state needs more than a reducer

Redux-Saga sits between actions and reducers, and on this project it earned its place doing two specific jobs a plain reducer does not do cleanly:

  1. Sequencing requests that depend on each other.
  2. Cancelling work still in flight when an operator navigates away from a screen mid load.

Without that second one, a slow response from a screen the user already left lands late and overwrites newer state with stale data.

Every entity in the store was normalized, so the same underlying record could not drift into two different shapes in two different parts of the state tree. That is the classic source of bugs where two views of the same object quietly disagree with each other.

The rule that was actually about trust, not architecture

The single decision that mattered most was not a pattern name. It was a rule about when the UI is allowed to guess.

Live telemetry and device health data got their own state slice, entirely separate from form state. An incoming status update could refresh on screen without ever interrupting someone mid edit on a form elsewhere on the same page. Two different data lifecycles, kept from colliding.

Optimistic updates were allowed for ordinary metadata changes. They were banned outright for hardware commands.

A screen that shows a device as on before the device has confirmed it turned on is not a faster screen. It is a screen that lies, and the cost of that lie is paid in operator trust the first time the device does not actually respond. Confirmed state only, no exceptions, for anything connected to physical hardware.

If you take one thing from this write up, take that line and draw it in your own app.

Building and shipping without a finished backend

The API contract was settled before a line of UI code was written. Mock requests and responses generated from that contract did double duty: they were the data the frontend team built against before the real backend existed, and later they became contract tests that caught any drift once it was live.

Cutover ran route by route rather than as a single flag flip. The legacy AngularJS layer and the new React layer lived side by side under one authenticated session, so operators moved one screen at a time and nothing was ever stood up that the old portal could not fall back to.

What actually changed

No benchmark numbers here, and the outcomes that mattered were not benchmarks anyway:

  • Behavior stayed consistent with what operators already expected, right through the migration.
  • Race conditions on quickly navigated screens stopped happening.
  • Live health data kept refreshing without disrupting whatever someone was in the middle of editing.
  • A single design change finally propagated everywhere instead of being re-applied controller by controller.

None of that required new business logic. It required treating the existing screen as ground truth, drawing one hard line around physical hardware state, and shipping the migration in pieces small enough that nothing operators depended on broke along the way.

Full case study: https://innerluxes.dev/case-studies/netherlands-client-updates-streaming-software?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=article

Curious where other people draw the optimistic update line. Do you allow it anywhere near physical state, or is it metadata only for you too?

title: From Prompt to Production: Why I Built Code Ghost for Instant Component Prototyping
description:
How I Vibe Coded a Mobile-First Frontend Studio Entirely From My Phone
What happens when you decide to throw out the traditional desktop setup, ditch the cramped local repository terminals, and build a full production web app entirely from a mobile device? You get Code Ghost—a lightning-fast, mobile-first component workbench and live prototyping studio built by pure intuition, AI prompting, and absolute freedom.
Check out the live application at www.codeghost.site.
The Vibe Coding Experiment
Most developer tools assume you are chained to a multi-monitor workstation with a heavy mechanical keyboard. But what if inspiration strikes while you are away from your desk? What if you want to draft a glassmorphic component, tweak design tokens, and test responsive viewports while lounging on the couch using only a smartphone?
I decided to lean completely into vibe coding. No complex backend configurations or over-engineered setups—just pure front-end momentum, natural language AI iteration, and complete code control right in the palm of my hand.
What Makes Code Ghost Different?
Traditional browser sandboxes give you raw code tabs without visual controls, while proprietary AI UI builders lock your code behind bloated frameworks and cloud-gated accounts. Code Ghost bridges that exact gap:
Mobile-First PWA: Engineered from the ground up for touchscreens, with full installable offline support so your workflow never breaks.
AI + Full Code Control: Generate components via prompt, choose whether to remix or replace your canvas, and edit the underlying HTML, CSS, and JavaScript directly. No black-box limitations.
Live Design Token Sliders: Instantly parses CSS variables and Tailwind classes into tactile visual sliders, letting you tweak colors, spacing, and border radius in real time.
Zero Lock-In: Every project saves locally via browser storage with instant export options to standalone HTML or a clean .zip archive.
Built For Speed and Flow
Under the hood, Code Ghost packs a responsive live preview stage with sandboxed iframe execution, adjustable viewport sizing presets, and dark, light, or checkerboard backdrops for testing transparent layers. Combined with a multi-tab code editor, built-in preprocessor support, and resilient AI routing defaulting to Claude with automatic free-model fallbacks, it keeps the creative momentum uninterrupted.

title: Optimizing Document Lookup: Making Atlas Search and Vector Search Up to 5x Faster
description:
Sometimes the biggest performance gains come not from making core operations faster, but from eliminating unnecessary work surrounding them. That is exactly what we discovered while optimizing document lookup in MongoDB Atlas Search and Vector Search. By removing redundant query planning and execution overhead, we made search queries up to 5x faster without changing the underlying search algorithms.

When you run a $search or $vectorSearch query in MongoDB, two key stages work together to deliver the results. First, mongot, MongoDB's search process powered by Apache Lucene, executes the search query to identify and rank the most relevant documents. Then, mongod joins the search results with the corresponding BSON documents from the underlying collection using their _ids. The resulting documents can be further processed by additional aggregation pipeline stages before being returned to the application. Figure 1 illustrates this two-stage process:

Figure 1. Search execution in mongot and document materialization in mongod.

This second stage, known as document materialization, is handled by an internal aggregation stage called $_internalSearchIdLookup. While search execution has been extensively optimized, we discovered that document lookup had become a significant performance bottleneck. For every matching document, the stage repeatedly constructed a new query plan and acquired collection resources, introducing substantial overhead for queries returning hundreds or thousands of results. In our profiling, approximately 30% of mongod CPU time was spent on query planning and collection acquisition, rather than retrieving documents.

To address this, we redesigned the document lookup execution path to eliminate redundant query planning, reuse execution plans, and amortize resource acquisition across multiple lookups. The result: up to 4.9x faster $search queries, 5.5x faster $vectorSearch queries, and approximately 2.75x higher throughput under concurrency.

These optimizations shipped in MongoDB 9.0, are enabled by default, and require no application changes. In this post, we'll explore how we identified the bottleneck, redesigned the execution path, and achieved these performance improvements.

The hidden cost of repeated query planning

Looking up a document by its _id is typically a fast operation in MongoDB, thanks to its efficient _id index. However, the original $_internalSearchIdLookup implementation constructed and executed a new aggregation sub-pipeline for every document returned by mongot, even though only the _id value changed:

For each document, MongoDB parsed the query, optimized the pipeline, constructed an execution plan, acquired collection resources, attached a cursor, executed the lookup, and released resources.

The problem was not the indexed document retrieval, but the repeated preparation work surrounding it. Even though the query structure was identical across lookups, MongoDB rebuilt the execution plan and reacquired collection resources for every document instead of reusing them. This overhead accumulated linearly with the number of results. For example, a search query returning 1,000 documents could trigger 1,000 separate cycles of query planning, collection acquisition, and resource cleanup. As result sets grew, the repeated preparation work became a substantial contributor to end-to-end search latency. Figure 2 illustrates this repeated execution overhead.

Figure 2. Repeated query planning and resource acquisition for each document lookup.

To quantify this overhead, we profiled representative Vector Search workloads. The results revealed that approximately 30% of mongod CPU time was spent on query plan construction and collection acquisition, rather than retrieving documents. This confirmed that the bottleneck was not primarily the underlying document reads, but the redundant work surrounding them.

Redesigning the document lookup execution path

To eliminate redundant lookup overhead, we redesigned $_internalSearchIdLookup around two key optimizations: reusing parameterized execution plans and batching document lookups to minimize resource acquisition overhead. Together, these changes allow MongoDB to retrieve thousands of documents without repeatedly rebuilding query plans or acquiring collection resources.

1. Reusing a parameterized SBE execution plan

The first major optimization was introducing SbeSingleDocumentLookupExecutor, built on MongoDB's Slot-Based Execution (SBE) engine. The key observation was simple: every document lookup follows the same query structure, and only the _id value changes. Instead of constructing a new execution plan for each document, the optimized executor builds the lookup plan once, caches it, and reuses it by rebinding the _id parameter for subsequent lookups.

For example, when retrieving 1,000 documents, the original implementation could construct 1,000 separate query plans. With the optimized executor, all 1,000 lookups can reuse a single parameterized plan.

This eliminates redundant query parsing, optimization, and plan construction, significantly reducing per-document execution overhead.

2. Batching document lookups to reuse collection resources

While plan reuse eliminates repeated query planning, acquiring and releasing collection resources for every document can still introduce substantial overhead. To address this, we introduced a reusable BatchedEnrichmentStage that buffers incoming search results and processes them within a shared resource scope. Instead of independently acquiring and releasing collection resources for every document, the optimized execution path reuses collection resources across multiple lookups within a batch, amortizing the acquisition and cleanup costs. For example, with 1,000 documents and a batch size of 100, collection resources can be acquired just 10 times instead of 1,000 times, i.e., once per batch rather than once per document. Although the number of document lookups still grows linearly with the result set size, batching significantly reduces the repeated resource management overhead.

Combined with SBE plan caching, this allows thousands of document lookups to share both an execution plan and collection resources, substantially reducing CPU overhead. The result is a more efficient document lookup architecture: build the execution plan once, reuse it across documents, and minimize repeated resource acquisition.

Figure 3 illustrates how the optimized approach eliminates redundant work by reusing execution plans and collection resources across document lookups.

Figure 3. Original per-document lookup vs. optimized batched lookup with shared execution plans.

Performance results: End-to-end latency and throughput

As shown in Figure 4, both Atlas Search ($search) and Atlas Vector Search ($vectorSearch) achieved substantial reductions in end-to-end query latency across all evaluated result-set sizes (100, 1,000, and 10,000 documents). At 10,000 results, median latency dropped from approximately 2.6 seconds to 527 milliseconds for Atlas Search (4.9× faster) and from 3.1 seconds to 561 milliseconds for Atlas Vector Search (5.5× faster).

An important pattern emerges: the larger the result set, the greater the speedup. This is consistent with the underlying optimization. While search execution still incurs its own costs, eliminating repeated query planning and resource acquisition overhead becomes increasingly valuable as more documents are materialized.

Figure 4. End-to-end query latency improvements for Atlas Search and Atlas Vector Search in MongoDB 9.0.

Higher throughput under concurrency

Lower latency is only part of the story. We also evaluated performance under concurrent query execution. With 16 concurrent clients running a $search workload, the optimized implementation delivered:

  • Approximately 2.75x higher throughput

  • Approximately 3x lower median latency

These results demonstrate that the optimization does more than accelerate individual queries. By eliminating repeated query planning and resource acquisition, it reduces unnecessary CPU work per document lookup, allowing mongod to process more concurrent search requests with the same execution resources. The approximately 30% CPU overhead identified in our earlier profiling and the nearly 80% latency reduction observed in our benchmarks represent different measurements and workloads, rather than directly proportional improvements.

Real-world customer impact

To understand the potential impact on real-world workloads, we analyzed 163.8 million Atlas Vector Search executions across 610 customer clusters over 90 days. The analysis shows that larger result-set limits are used across a meaningful portion of the customer fleet. At least 40% of clusters execute queries with limits between 21 and 50, and at least 17% execute queries with limits above 100.

These workloads are particularly well-positioned to benefit from the document lookup optimizations, as eliminating repeated query planning and resource acquisition becomes increasingly valuable when more documents are retrieved.

Importantly, these improvements require no application changes. The optimized document lookup path is enabled by default in MongoDB 9.0.7. Applications do not need to rewrite queries, rebuild search indexes, or adopt new syntax. Existing $search and $vectorSearch pipelines can automatically benefit when running on supported configurations.

Faster search, without the extra work

This optimization began with a surprising observation: a simple _id lookup was spending a significant portion of its CPU budget preparing to execute rather than retrieving data. By replacing repeated aggregation planning with lightweight execution, introducing reusable batching infrastructure, and caching parameterized SBE plans, we removed a major source of overhead from Atlas Search and Vector Search. The result is up to 5.5× faster end-to-end queries in our benchmarks, along with substantial throughput improvements under concurrency.

More broadly, this work illustrates an important database engineering principle: sometimes the biggest performance gains come not from making the core operation faster, but from eliminating the unnecessary work surrounding it. This effort was made possible through collaboration across MongoDB’s Atlas Search Query, Query Execution, Query Integration, Database Integration and Observability, and Server Triage & Release teams. Special thanks to Denis Grebennicov from the Database Integration and Observability team for his significant contributions to this optimization effort.

title: Architecting Offline-First Invoicing Without a Backend Black Box
description:
Every freelancer has experienced the 'airplane mode panic.' You’re sitting in a coffee shop with spotty Wi-Fi, the client is ready to sign, and your SaaS-based invoicing tool is stuck on a spinning loading wheel, failing to authenticate against a remote server. It’s a failure of architectural philosophy: why should your ability to generate a PDF depend on a server halfway across the world?

When we started building Vanza Invoices, we decided to stop treating the browser and mobile device as thin clients. We inverted the model. The device is the source of truth; the cloud is optional, or completely irrelevant.

The Death of the 'Sync-Everything' Middleware

Most modern apps rely on a 'sync-everything' middleware that pipes data to a central database before reflecting it back to the UI. This introduces latency, subscription overhead, and catastrophic failure points when the connection drops.

We moved to a local-first storage architecture utilizing IndexedDB, wrapped in a reactive persistence layer. By treating the local storage as the primary database, the app achieves sub-10ms read/write operations. When a user creates an invoice, the data lives exactly where it was typed—on the device.

Here is the stack logic we implemented:

  • Persistence Layer: We leverage Dexie.js for a robust IndexedDB wrapper, allowing for complex queries without hitting a network request.
  • State Synchronization: Instead of REST/GraphQL calls, the UI binds directly to the local database change listeners. If an invoice is updated, the view refreshes automatically.
  • Asset Generation: PDFs are generated on-device using a worker thread to ensure the main UI thread remains buttery smooth during signature rendering and complex document assembly.

Solving the 'Zero-Middleman' PDF Problem

Generating a professional invoice typically happens on the server. You send JSON to an API, a server-side process (like Puppeteer or a specialized library) renders the PDF, and it’s piped back to you.

At Vanza, we stripped the middleman. By bringing the document engine to the client, we eliminated the need for a monthly SaaS subscription. There is no server cost to pass on to the user. We utilized specialized PDF generation primitives that execute natively in the browser/Capacitor environment. This allows for:

  • Privacy by Default: Your financial data never leaves your device unless you explicitly export it.
  • Instant Previews: Since we aren't waiting for a server round-trip, the document updates in real-time as you type.
  • Offline Signature Capture: Using a canvas-based touch handler, we capture high-fidelity vector signatures that are embedded directly into the final PDF buffer via the browser’s internal file system API.

The Capacitor Advantage

We chose React and Capacitor to bridge the gap between web speed and native reliability. By shipping the application as a bundled binary, we bypass the browser's aggressive cache-clearing policies. Your invoices are stored in the app’s private container on your OS, effectively making them as durable as any native file.

For developers considering this route, the biggest hurdle isn't writing the code—it's managing the data schema migrations locally. Since you don't have a backend to migrate, your local database schema must be versioned within the app binary itself. We rely on a strict migration strategy triggered on initial app startup, ensuring that as we add new invoice fields, older data structures are upgraded seamlessly without loss.

Why We Built This

We built Vanza Invoices because the freelance economy is tired of paying rent for the privilege of creating a simple invoice. By leveraging local-first storage and offloading the computation to the hardware you already own, we’ve created a tool that lasts as long as your phone does, with zero dependency on our servers.

If you are a developer or a freelancer looking for a tool that respects your privacy and works without a signal, check out our implementation on the Google Play Store. It is a testament to what is possible when you stop building for the cloud and start building for the machine in your pocket.

title: Places Text Search Stops at 60 Results: Split the City Into Tiles (Python)
description:
You search "dentist in Pune" with the Google Places API, page through the results, and the list ends. Not because Pune ran out of dentists, but because the API did.

Google's docs say it plainly: "Text Search (New) returns a maximum of 60 results across all pages, although this limit is subject to change." Each page holds at most 20 (pageSize is "between 1 and 20"), so you get three pages and then nothing.

If you need every business of one type in a city, one query will never get you there. The workaround is geometry: ask the same question many times, each time for a smaller piece of the map, and merge the answers.

The idea

  1. Draw a rectangle around the city.
  2. Run the text query restricted to that rectangle.
  3. If the rectangle came back full (60 results), assume it was truncated: split it into four smaller rectangles and query each.
  4. Keep splitting until a tile returns fewer than 60, or the tile gets too small to matter.
  5. Deduplicate by place ID, because tiles touch at the edges.

The API supports this directly. locationRestriction takes a rectangle, "represented as two diagonally opposite low and high points", where low is the south-west corner and high is the north-east corner.

The request

Text Search (New) is a POST to https://places.googleapis.com/v1/places:searchText. You must send a field mask; "If you omit the field mask, the method returns an error.". Ask only for the fields you need, since fields map to SKUs (places.id is in the ID Only SKU, places.displayName in Pro).

import json, os, urllib.request

URL = "https://places.googleapis.com/v1/places:searchText"
KEY = os.environ["PLACES_API_KEY"]
FIELDS = "places.id,places.displayName,places.formattedAddress,nextPageToken"

def search_tile(query, low, high):
    """Return all places for one rectangle (max 60) and whether it looked full."""
    body = {
        "textQuery": query,
        "pageSize": 20,
        "locationRestriction": {"rectangle": {
            "low":  {"latitude": low[0],  "longitude": low[1]},
            "high": {"latitude": high[0], "longitude": high[1]},
        }},
    }
    found = []
    while True:
        req = urllib.request.Request(URL, data=json.dumps(body).encode(), method="POST",
            headers={"Content-Type": "application/json",
                     "X-Goog-Api-Key": KEY,
                     "X-Goog-FieldMask": FIELDS})
        with urllib.request.urlopen(req) as r:
            data = json.load(r)
        found += data.get("places", [])
        token = data.get("nextPageToken")
        if not token:
            break
        body["pageToken"] = token
    return found, len(found) >= 60

pageToken is "the nextPageToken from the response body of the previous page", so the loop just feeds it back until it disappears.

Split full tiles 

def split(low, high):
    mid = ((low[0] + high[0]) / 2, (low[1] + high[1]) / 2)
    return [
        (low, mid),
        ((low[0], mid[1]), (mid[0], high[1])),
        ((mid[0], low[1]), (high[0], mid[1])),
        (mid, high),
    ]

def crawl(query, low, high, min_deg=0.01):
    seen = {}
    stack = [(low, high)]
    while stack:
        lo, hi = stack.pop()
        places, full = search_tile(query, lo, hi)
        for p in places:
            seen[p["id"]] = p
        if full and (hi[0] - lo[0]) > min_deg:
            stack.extend(split(lo, hi))
    return list(seen.values())

min_deg stops the recursion in a dense block where even a tiny tile stays full. If you hit it, you have found a spot worth a narrower query (a neighbourhood name or a sub-category), not a smaller tile.

Run it 

# Rough bounding box: replace with your own city's south-west and north-east corners.
low, high = (18.40, 73.70), (18.65, 74.00)
rows = crawl("dentist", low, high)
print(len(rows), "unique places")
for p in rows[:5]:
    print(p["displayName"]["text"], "|", p.get("formattedAddress", ""))

Why not just vary the query?

A common first fix is to run "dentist", "dental clinic", "orthodontist" and "dental hospital" and merge the results. That helps with recall for synonyms, but every one of those queries still hits the same per-query ceiling. In a large city, four capped queries give you four overlapping slices of the same busy centre, and the outskirts never show up at all.

Tiling attacks the right problem. The cap is per query, so the fix is more queries over less ground. You can still combine both: run the tile crawl once per synonym and deduplicate on id across all of them.

A useful habit is to log every tile that came back full, with its corners. That log tells you where the density is, and it is also the first thing to check when a client asks why one neighbourhood looks thin.

Things to watch

  • Cost scales with tiles. Every split is up to three more paid requests. Start with a box that hugs the city, not the whole district.
  • Edges overlap. Deduplicating on id is not optional.
  • The cap may change. Google says the 60 limit "is subject to change". Read the count instead of hard-coding three pages, as the loop above does.
  • A name and address is not a lead yet. You still need to check which places have a website, a phone number, or an email before outreach.

That last step is the part we automate at Mantis. If you would rather describe the list in plain words than run the crawler, the full comparison of five ways to build a city list, including this one, is in our guide.

I work on Mantis. This post was drafted with AI assistance and checked against Google's Text Search (New) documentation.

title: Your API Call Doesn't Need a Save Point
description:
Open a banking app and the home screen loads in a blink. Behind it, one request quietly asks three systems for your account balance, your recent transactions, and the offers you qualify for.

Now think about a loan application. It takes two days. It waits on documents, a credit check and a person's approval, and it must never lose its place if a server restarts.

Both are workflows. They need opposite things.

What "remembering every step" costs

A loan application needs a save point after every step. If something breaks, it resumes right where it stopped. That's the job of a durable workflow engine, and it's worth the price. Saving state takes time, and for a two-day process, nobody notices.

A home screen is different. Nobody is going to resume it tomorrow. The user is staring at a spinner right now, so every millisecond spent writing down "step two finished" is a millisecond they wait for nothing. If the request fails, the app just asks again.

The point isn't that saving state is bad. It's that it should match the job.

What a fast API workflow needs

For the short, user-facing kind, the list is different from a back-office process:

Answers in milliseconds. The person is waiting.
Partial results. Send the balance as soon as it arrives instead of holding everything until the slowest call returns.
Parallel calls. Ask all three systems at once, not one after another.
Security built in. API key authentication and rate limiting, since these calls face the outside world.
Fan-out in practice

Take that home screen. One incoming request fans out: account data from one system, recent transactions from another, current offers from a third. The workflow gathers the three answers, reshapes them into the format the app expects, and returns one response.

Total wait is roughly the slowest of the three calls, not the sum of all three. That's the whole reason to fan out.

So which kind do you have?

Ask two questions. If this fails halfway, does someone need it to resume where it stopped, or can the caller just retry? And how long is a human waiting?

If a failure means money in limbo or a process that has to finish, keep the state. If it's a quick read that someone is watching load, keep it light. Most systems have both kinds, and the mistake is using one setup for everything.

Unmeshed says it's built to handle both: short API-driven flows and long-running backend processes on the same platform.

title: Your AI agent reused the wrong kind of screen. Name the experience purpose.
description:
Say you ask your AI agent for a staff check-in screen at example.com. It returns a wide editorial layout, a large heading, and a single "Get started" button. You ask for a member briefing instead, and the next result is a dense table with bulk actions.

The agent reused a familiar pattern from a different kind of work.

Design Decision Method's agent procedure asks the agent to identify the experience purpose before it decides how a screen should look and behave. The live docs already use that idea in an illustration: a short request is not operational monitoring. The procedure is more specific. It names six purposes: operational work, reading and storytelling, exploration, evaluation and purchase, creation and editing, and participation and collaboration. Mixed-purpose products can use a different approach per flow.

What follows are four short, fictional illustrations on example.com. They are not case studies, and they do not report measured results.

Operational work

A staff tool for checking people into today's workshop. The job is to find a name, mark attendance, and undo a mistake.

The procedure's purpose reference treats operational work as a heuristic, not a mandatory template. It points to stable placement, visible state, fast entry, and reversible actions. A magazine-style page that hides the current list is the wrong import. So is a decorative metric row that does not help someone complete the check-in.

Reading and storytelling

A monthly member briefing: a short article with a clear reading order, headings, and a path into a longer report.

Here the priorities shift. The reference talks about reading order, pacing, and routes into deeper content. The procedure also says that reading or exploration need not end in a transaction or a single primary button. A checkout-shaped page, or a dashboard of tiles, imports another domain's conventions. The briefing can simply be readable on a phone.

Evaluation and purchase

A flow to buy a workshop ticket, with a date, a concession option, the total cost, and the cancellation terms.

For evaluation and purchase, the reference asks for suitability, variations, availability, total cost, terms, and an informed commitment — plus a way to correct the order. A dense admin table that buries the price is not that job. Neither is a long story page that never states what the buyer is committing to. Acceptance in this flow is about an informed choice, not about finishing a staff task.

AI as a capability, not a new purpose

example.com also has a small helper that drafts a workshop description. Because that AI feature already exists, the procedure says to apply AI checks only there: say what the helper can do and where it is limited, separate generating a draft from publishing it, and do not show fabricated confidence figures.

If the product had no AI feature, the rule is simpler: do not add AI controls. The purpose reference is just as plain: treat AI as a capability within a purpose, not a reason to replace every interface with chat. The ticket flow should stay a ticket flow.

Why this matters

Agents are good at completing a pattern they have seen. They are less good at noticing that the pattern belongs to another job. The procedure warns against importing one domain's conventions into another — an operations dashboard for a site that needed a readable page, for example.

Establish context is where purpose belongs, alongside audience, frequency, mistake cost, and device. Later, deliver and validate asks for acceptance criteria matched to that purpose: task execution in the check-in tool, comprehension in the briefing, informed purchase in the ticket flow.

The method does not claim this saves time. That has not been measured. It also does not guarantee a good result. What it gives you is a place to catch a borrowed layout before it hardens.

Try it

Design Decision Method is a lightweight design decision workflow for developers building interfaces with AI agents. It follows the open Agent Skills format and is MIT licensed. Install paths for Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI, and Codex are in the README.

title: The trust boundary pattern, the architectural decision you are already making, whether you know it or not
description:
§ 01 · The definition

A trust boundary is the line between what your agent is permitted to decide autonomously and what requires a human decision, an external approval, or an explicit override.

Every production agent has one. Most teams never wrote it down. Instead, they have a collection of implicit decisions, tools that weren't added, permissions that weren't granted, escalation paths that were wired in "to be safe", that together constitute an accidental trust boundary.

Accidental trust boundaries cause two failure modes. They are either too permissive (the agent does things the team didn't realize it could do) or too restrictive (the agent constantly escalates decisions that were safe to make autonomously, eroding the value of having an agent at all).

The pattern here is how to make the decision explicit.

── Four boundary placements ──

§ 02 · Four boundary placements

Placement I, Model boundary. The trust boundary is at the model layer. The agent can reason about anything, but takes no action. Every output is a recommendation; every action is performed by a human after review. Use case: high-stakes domains where the cost of an incorrect autonomous action exceeds the cost of human review latency. Legal drafting, medical records, financial transactions above a threshold.

Placement II, Read boundary. The agent can read any data it has access to, but cannot write, modify, or trigger external actions. It can retrieve, summarize, analyze, and recommend. It cannot execute. Use case: research and analysis agents in regulated environments. Intelligence is inside the boundary; action is outside it.

Placement III, Scoped write boundary. The agent can read and write, but only within a defined domain. It can modify records in a specific table, send messages in a specific channel, update files in a specific directory. Writes outside the scope require explicit approval. Use case: the majority of production operational agents. This is the correct default placement for most teams.

Placement IV, Supervised autonomy. The agent can read, write, and take actions across a broad scope, but with circuit breakers, rate limits, kill switches, and audit trails that allow intervention. The boundary is not about what the agent can do; it is about how quickly a human can undo it. Use case: high-trust, high-volume workflows where the cost of manual approval per action exceeds the cost of occasional cleanup.

── The four questions ──

§ 03 · The four questions that define the boundary

For any agent in production, answer these four questions before deploying:

◆ What is the worst irreversible action this agent could take? If the answer is "delete production records" or "send a customer communication I can't unsend," that action must sit outside the boundary or require an explicit approval gate.

◆ What is the blast radius of a misfire? If the agent writes to one record per run, the blast radius is one. If it writes to a table, the blast radius is the table. Size your recovery cost before you set your boundary.

◆ What does escalation look like? Every agent needs a clear, tested escalation path. "The agent flags uncertain decisions" is not an escalation path. "The agent posts to #agent-review-queue with a 2-hour resolution SLA" is an escalation path.

◆ Can the boundary drift? Scope creep in agent permissions is real. The agent that started with read access to one database now has write access, now has access to three databases. Define the boundary in a version-controlled document, not just in your tool configuration, and review it quarterly.

── Boundary drift ──

§ 04 · Boundary drift, the failure mode

The most common trust boundary failure is not a single wrong decision. It is gradual drift, a sequence of small permission expansions, each of which seemed reasonable at the time, that collectively move the agent into a scope no one intended to authorize.

The pattern: initial deployment is conservative. The agent proves reliable. A new use case emerges that requires slightly broader access. The permission is added. Six months later, the agent has access to systems that weren't in the original design, and no one has a complete map of what it can now do.

The fix is not technical. It is procedural. Treat agent permission changes with the same review process as production code changes. Require a written justification for every boundary expansion. Review the complete permission set quarterly, not just the delta.

── The file that holds the boundary ──

§ 05 · The file that holds the boundary

Create a TRUST.md in every agent repository. It is a single document, version-controlled, that contains: the four boundary placement answers, the complete tool list with read/write scope for each, the escalation path with SLA, the last boundary review date, and the name of the human who approved the current configuration.

This is not bureaucracy. This is the document your team will need the day something goes wrong, and the day an auditor asks what your agent was permitted to do.

── End of pattern ──

◆ Every agent has a trust boundary. The question is whether you defined it or inherited it.

◆ Scoped write (Placement III) is the correct default for most production agents.

◆ If you do not have a TRUST.md, your boundary is drifting. You just haven't noticed yet.

ORBIRESEARCH

Originally published on the OrbiResearch Lab. We build production AI agents at orbiresearch.com.

title: 175 MB of Substrings to Read One Column
description:
I had a boring little job: a pile of CSV-shaped lines in memory, and I needed one number out of each — the amount column, third field, that's it. The rest of the row was along for the ride. I wrote the obvious loop, it gave the right total, and I moved on. Then the allocation profiler lit up on that exact loop and I went back to look. A million rows in, and I'd minted somewhere north of a hundred megabytes of garbage to read a single integer per line. Every other field I split out, I threw straight away.

Here's the loop that did it:

long total = 0;
foreach (string line in lines)
{
    string[] fields = line.Split(',');
    total += long.Parse(fields[2], CultureInfo.InvariantCulture);
}

line.Split(',') is doing precisely what I asked and nothing I wanted. For each row it allocates a string[] to hold the pieces, then allocates a fresh string for every field it finds, four of them on my data, copying the characters out of the original line into each one. I read fields[2] and let the array and the other three strings fall on the floor. Four columns, five allocations a row, one of them actually used.

The split that doesn't cut anything out

The span-based Split has been around for a couple of versions now and it works on a different idea. Instead of handing you new strings, it tells you where the pieces are. You give it a destination buffer of Range values, it fills in the start and end of each field, and you slice the original line yourself when you want to look at one. Nothing gets copied. Nothing gets allocated.

long total = 0;
Span<Range> ranges = stackalloc Range[8];
foreach (string line in lines)
{
    ReadOnlySpan<char> span = line;
    int count = span.Split(ranges, ',');
    ReadOnlySpan<char> amount = span[ranges[2]];
    total += long.Parse(amount, CultureInfo.InvariantCulture);
}

The stackalloc Range[8] buffer sits on the stack and gets reused on every iteration — one buffer for the whole loop, not one per row. span.Split writes the field boundaries into it and returns how many it found. span[ranges[2]] is a view over the amount field, still pointing into the original line's characters, and long.Parse has had a ReadOnlySpan<char> overload for ages, so it parses that slice straight without a substring in between. The row never becomes an array, the fields never become strings, and the only thing that leaves the loop is the running total.

The numbers

A million rows, built in memory, parsed best-of-7 in a container. Not a lab — I care about the ratio between the two, not the absolute milliseconds on whatever box this ran on.

rows                 : 1,000,000
string.Split sum     : 4,998,543,546
Span<Range> sum      : 4,998,543,546
sums match           : True

string.Split  best   :     75.7 ms   alloc   174.7 MB
Span<Range>   best   :     32.1 ms   alloc     0.0 MB

The sums matching is the part I care about most. Same answer, so this is a fair fight and not a trick where I quietly dropped work. On that footing the span path ran in a bit under half the time and allocated essentially nothing. The 174.7 MB the naive loop burned is all throwaway: arrays and substrings created and collected inside a single pass. Dropping it doesn't just save memory, it saves the GC the job of walking all that back out later, which is a chunk of where the time goes too.

I'll admit I expected the allocation win and only hoped for the speed one. Getting both was the nice surprise.

When I'd leave Split alone

I would not reach for this everywhere, and I'd push back on anyone who tried. If you actually need the fields as strings — you're stashing them in a list, returning them, putting them in a dictionary — then the span version just means you call .ToString() on each slice and you've bought back every allocation you saved, plus more awkward code. The ranges approach pays off exactly when you read the fields, use them, and let them go without keeping them around. Parsing to a number, comparing, summing: yes. Collecting rows into objects you hold onto: no, Split into strings is honest about what you need.

The other caveat is size. At a few hundred rows none of this registers; the naive loop allocates a rounding error and you'd never see it in a profile. This only became worth touching because the row count had three commas and a half-decent chance of growing. Reaching for stackalloc Range[] on a cold path nobody runs in a loop is effort spent making code harder to read for zero measured gain, and I think that trade is a bad one often enough to say it out loud.

One real gotcha: size the Range buffer for the most fields you expect, because Split stops once the destination is full and folds the rest of the line into the last range. Eight slots for four columns gives me headroom; a buffer that's too small turns into a silent correctness bug, not an exception.

Here's the whole thing if you want to run it yourself. It's a plain net10.0 console app — one Program.cs, nothing else, build and run with dotnet run -c Release.

using System.Diagnostics;
using System.Globalization;

const int Rows = 1_000_000;
var lines = new string[Rows];
var rng = new Random(42);
string[] regions = ["emea", "apac", "amer", "latam"];
for (int i = 0; i < Rows; i++)
{
    int amount = rng.Next(1, 10_000);
    lines[i] = $"{i},{regions[i & 3]},{amount},{(i % 2 == 0 ? 1 : 0)}";
}

_ = SumWithSplit(lines);   // warm up both paths before timing
_ = SumWithRanges(lines);

const int Trials = 7;
var (splitSum, splitMs, splitBytes) = Measure(() => SumWithSplit(lines), Trials);
var (rangeSum, rangeMs, rangeBytes) = Measure(() => SumWithRanges(lines), Trials);

Console.WriteLine($"sums match        : {splitSum == rangeSum}");
Console.WriteLine($"string.Split  best: {splitMs,8:F1} ms   alloc {splitBytes / (1024.0 * 1024.0),7:F1} MB");
Console.WriteLine($"Span<Range>   best: {rangeMs,8:F1} ms   alloc {rangeBytes / (1024.0 * 1024.0),7:F1} MB");

static long SumWithSplit(string[] lines)
{
    long total = 0;
    foreach (string line in lines)
    {
        string[] fields = line.Split(',');
        total += long.Parse(fields[2], CultureInfo.InvariantCulture);
    }
    return total;
}

static long SumWithRanges(string[] lines)
{
    long total = 0;
    Span<Range> ranges = stackalloc Range[8];
    foreach (string line in lines)
    {
        ReadOnlySpan<char> span = line;
        span.Split(ranges, ',');
        total += long.Parse(span[ranges[2]], CultureInfo.InvariantCulture);
    }
    return total;
}

static (long sum, double bestMs, long bytes) Measure(Func<long> work, int trials)
{
    long sum = 0;
    double best = double.MaxValue;
    long bytesForBest = 0;
    for (int t = 0; t < trials; t++)
    {
        GC.Collect();
        GC.WaitForPendingFinalizers();
        GC.Collect();
        long before = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();
        var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
        sum = work();
        sw.Stop();
        long after = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();
        if (sw.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds < best)
        {
            best = sw.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds;
            bytesForBest = after - before;
        }
    }
    return (sum, best, bytesForBest);
}

Have you swapped a hot Split over to ranges, or found a spot where it wasn't worth the trouble? I'd like to hear where the line fell for you.

— still benchmarking the boring loops nobody asked me to touch
