title: How AIClaw 3.10.1 Stops File Names from Becoming Controls Inside Sentences
description:
A file name in an agent answer can mean two different things: an output the user should open, or a detail the answer is discussing. Turning both into file controls makes prose harder to read. It is especially distracting in a heading, where a directory path can become a short filename with a dropdown arrow.

AIClaw 3.10.1 narrows automatic file-card rendering to standalone references. The release is published; the code and tests linked here are pinned to that version.

The earlier article about opening generated documents described file rows and their opening menu. This update addresses a different decision: when that control should appear at all.

Mentioning a file is different from delivering it

Consider this illustrative Markdown:

The results are in `report.md`; compare them with yesterday's run.

`report.md`

In the first paragraph, the filename stays inline code. In the second, the standalone reference becomes a file card. A heading containing ~/Library/Caches/go-build also retains its complete code text instead of becoming an opening control labeled only go-build.

The distinction applies to local Markdown links too. A link embedded in a sentence keeps its visible label without a file-opening action. A standalone local file link can still produce a card. Titles and table cells do not become attachment rows just because they contain a path.

This does change how an answer should deliver several files: each intended attachment needs its own standalone paragraph, or a list item containing only that reference. Putting two links in one sentence does not make an attachment list.

Use Markdown structure before path recognition

The Markdown renderer already has a path-shape check. It recognizes plausible extensions and explicit path prefixes while excluding command lines, URLs, and several ambiguous forms. That check remains useful, but path shape alone cannot tell whether the surrounding text is a title, explanation, or delivery.

The new core rule runs after Markdown inline parsing. It checks whether the inline token belongs to a paragraph and whether, after ignoring whitespace-only text, it contains exactly one inline-code token. Only that candidate receives the standalone-file marker. The inline-code renderer requires both that marker and a recognized path before producing a card.

Local Markdown links follow a similar context check. When a link has surrounding content, or belongs to a heading or table cell, the rule removes its opening and closing link tokens while retaining its label tokens. An eligible standalone link instead goes through the shared card generator.

This is a deliberately narrow structural rule. It does not scan every bare word for filenames or classify every visually separate line as an attachment. The code works with parsed paragraphs, so blank lines matter.

Preserve actual deliveries and explicit images

The change does not remove the existing open and preview actions for standalone cards. Their visible names can remain compact while the exact path is retained for the existing action route.

Explicit Markdown image syntax still follows the image renderer. A supported local image can therefore remain visible inline even though an ordinary filename mentioned in prose no longer becomes a file control. This update does not add an extra generated-image gallery.

The renderer also does not check whether a recognized file exists. Card eligibility is a presentation decision. Actual file access still goes through the application's existing host validation; recognizing a path is not permission to open arbitrary content.

What the regression evidence covers

For this article, I verified the renderer and rendering-test files against GitHub's public 3.10.1 source and ran the renderer test suite from a clean checkout at the release commit. 412 tests passed, one was skipped, and none failed.

The rendering tests cover complete paths in headings, filenames inside sentences and parentheses, local links in prose, table references, standalone references and list items, multiple inline filenames, command recognition, and explicit image handling. They also retain checks for escaped filenames and exact paths in generated cards.

The release notes separately report successful desktop build and type checks and 376 passing work-interface checks. I did not rerun that Electron suite for this article. Its public smoke script uses controlled host responses to check that sentence references remain code while standalone cards still open and preview through the expected route. That is not a claim of real application launches on every platform.

The practical result is less surprising prose: discussing a file leaves the sentence intact, while presenting a file on its own still gives the user an explicit next action.

title: Google Open Sources Ambient Quality Agent (AQuA) to Diagnose Production AI Agent Failures
description:

title: The agent is a user without a license
description:
The agent without an ID

United Airlines will restrict third-party AI agents from its website, its app, and also when they arrive through agencies and aggregators (cnbc.com).

The reason they give is that those agents share credentials and can break FAA and DOT rules.

Only a human can declare that the luggage carries no explosives.

An agent cannot sign that declaration, and not because it cannot read it. It cannot sign because there is no identity behind it to answer when the signature is wrong.

Amazon already blocked Muse, Meta's agent, and Walmart integrated it into its workflow (cnbc.com).

Two companies of the same size, two opposite decisions, and neither one is a whim. One closed the door and the other opened it with conditions.

The question left in the air is the same in both cases.

What identity does the agent act with? Who answers when it gets it wrong?

I will leave it there...

The pattern

An agent wants to act in a system that was not designed for it.

The FAA requires a human declaration and the agent cannot give one.

The agent walks in with someone's keys and the system cannot tell whether it is that person or an automated process.

There is no standard for agent authentication and every company improvises.

Integrate the agent or close the door on it?

Those are the two options available today.

The other side

An OpenAI agent accessed the Medicare statistics portal without authorization in June (apnews.com).

Australia has reacted with an AI safety regulator with penalties and an obligation to report incidents and misalignments (apnews.com).

The same month, a public PoC called worse_query lets an app read data from other apps on iOS 26.0-27.2 without jailbreak or kernel exploit (thehackernews.com).

Apple does not confirm a patch and there is no CVE assigned.

Binance warns about exposed seed phrases in the same period.

The agent is not only a user without a license when it acts for you. It is also a user without a license when it acts against you, and in both cases the system does not know who to hold accountable, though I understand the owner is traced and the weight of the law falls on them... right?

Identity or patching?

On Friday Forescout published a data point that changes the scale of the problem.

Vedere Labs cut vulnerability analysis from 9 months to 90 hours using commercial AI (forescout.com).

They validated 99 flaws across 10 TCP/IP stacks

  • 66 unknown
  • 52% high or critical severity.

If discovery compresses from months to days, patching stops being the defensive advantage.

The advantage moves to who holds the session, with what scope, and who can revoke it.

The SCKit campaign against ScreenConnect illustrates it.

It exploits CVE-2026-84869, already patched, hijacks operator sessions, and its RelayTrap module pivots back against the technician investigating the incident (thehackernews.com).

The patch closes the known hole but it does not close the stolen session, I think I have said that already.

What to look at on Monday

  • Trim the agent's scope. If an agent enters with a person's credentials, ask for them to be delegated, with permissions limited to the task and with an expiry date. Without that, the agent inherits everything its owner can do.
  • Turn on per-session tracing. Every agent action has to be tied to an identity and a moment. If you cannot reconstruct what it did and when, you cannot revoke it or audit the incident.
  • Separate the session from the patch. Review which support sessions are still open after you apply the patch. ScreenConnect shows that a closed hole does not close the session that was already inside.

How would I test it?

I would set up a local agent with read-only permissions on a test folder and give it a concrete task, like summarizing a file.

Then I would try to make it write to that folder. If it succeeds, the permission is not properly scoped and the problem is mine, not the model's.

I would repeat the test with a delegated credential and an expiry date, and what I would look at is whether the system rejects the action and whether it leaves a trace of who tried it.

With that I would have a cheap answer to the question of the week.

If my agent cannot do more than I asked, identity is solved.
If it can, I have a user without a license inside my house.

The close

The debate of the week is not whether an AI can book a flight but with what identity it does it and who answers if it gets it wrong.

Until there is a standard for agent authentication, every company has only two options.

Integrate the agent or close the door on it.

Originally published at https://sammideblas.com/notas/the-agent-is-a-user-without-a-license

title: Yabanin Core: an open-source gateway with own keys and budgets for AI agents
description:
A month ago during vacation I wrote that I finally had time to think through AI-SDLC and maybe go to open source if it is useful for other people. This is the first part of it: Yabanin Core, the gateway I use between my coding agents and the models they call. It is on GitHub now under Apache-2.0.

Coming from data platforms I find this part of the agent conversation familiar. Everybody talks about the model, and then it turns out the rest of the system needs a lot of attention too. In one of my pet-project repositories I counted 68 worktree checkouts after one day of development (some were retained from earlier tasks, so it is an accumulated inventory and not 68 agents running at once). Agents create a lot of parallel work, all of it spends tokens, and in the evening I could not answer simple questions:

  • which models was each agent allowed to use?
  • how much could it spend before somebody noticed?
  • what did a task or a PR actually cost?

With one shared provider key there is no way to answer them, and this is why I put a gateway in between.

What Yabanin Core is

Yabanin Core is a self-hosted gateway. Agents and apps connect to it through OpenAI- or Anthropic-compatible endpoints (for most clients it is just a base URL change), and it sends requests to hosted providers, your own servers or local models. It routes requests, retries and falls back to other models, caches responses and logs every request. There is also a dashboard, an admin API and a yb CLI.

Most of this you can find in other gateways too. What I wanted in addition is that an agent is a separate identity with its own limits, and below are three decisions I made around it.

yabaninai / yabanin-core

Quickstart

You do not need a provider account because a mock provider answers the requests, so nothing costs money. You need Docker with Compose v2, Git, Bash, OpenSSL, curl and Python 3.

git clone https://github.com/yabaninai/yabanin-core.git
cd yabanin-core
bash scripts/quickstart/demo.sh

The script builds and starts the gateway, Postgres, Redis, the mock provider and the dashboard, and at the end prints an API key and an admin password. They are shown only once, so save them. Put the key into YABANIN_API_KEY and send a request:

curl http://127.0.0.1:8082/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $YABANIN_API_KEY" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{"model":"mock-model","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Hello from Yabanin"}]}'

The dashboard is on http://127.0.0.1:3000 (user admin@localhost), and everything listens only on 127.0.0.1. The first build takes a few minutes, after that the stack starts in about ten seconds.

Budgets for agent keys

When a person sends prompts by hand, a key without a limit is usually fine. An agent can loop all night, so for agent keys I made it the other way around, and an agent without a configured budget cannot spend at all.

Situation Response Error code
No budget configured for this agent 403 agent_budget_not_configured
Daily limit reached 429 agent_budget_exceeded
Budget store unreachable 503 agent_budget_check_unavailable

For me the most important case is the last one. If the budget store is not available, the gateway refuses the request instead of letting it through. Simplified from pkg/gateway/admission.go:

switch {
case errors.Is(err, budget.ErrNoAgentBudget):
    // 403 agent_budget_not_configured
case errors.Is(err, budget.ErrAgentBudgetExceeded):
    // 429 agent_budget_exceeded
default:
    // 503 agent_budget_check_unavailable: never "allow" when we can't check
}

To give an agent a key and a budget you need two calls to the admin API:

POST /api/agent-keys              {"name": "nightly-etl", "org_id": "<org>"}
PUT  /api/agent-keys/<id>/budget  {"daily_limit_cents": 500}

There is one limitation you should know about. By default the budget is checked before each request against the spend that is already recorded, and spend is recorded after the response, so a request that is already running can finish over the limit. If you need a hard cap, there is an opt-in reservation mode which books the estimated cost before the call.

This is less comfortable on the first day. For myself it is the same story as with CI/CD and linters: the parts that are checkable should be enforced, otherwise people end up supervising every agent step manually.

Child keys for sub-agents

Agents hand work to other agents, and if a sub-agent gets the parent's key it also gets the whole budget and all the tools. Instead an operator can mint a child key for the sub-task:

POST /api/agent-keys/delegate
{"parent_agent": "<agent-key id>", "org_id": "<org>", "name": "subtask-render",
 "ttl": 86400, "budget_caps": 500, "mcp_grants": ["knowledge"]}

When the key is minted, the TTL is required and can be at most 90 days. The child's cap has to fit into what the parent has left today, which is its daily limit minus its own spend minus the caps of its other active children. This check runs under a lock, so two delegations at the same time cannot both pass. MCP grants are intersected with the parent's grants, so a child never gets access to a server the parent does not have, and a child cannot delegate further.

After that, on every request the parent's limit is checked against its own spend plus the spend of its children. So several sub-agents spend from one parent budget and do not get a separate budget each.

Cost per task and per PR

Some time ago I wrote about what it costs an AI agent to finish the job [link to the earlier article]. Tokens are only one part of that cost, but this part can be measured if requests are tagged. In agentic development one task usually ends up as one PR, so I put the same tag on both sides. Commits get a trailer:

git commit -m "feat: add login" -m "Yabanin-Task: a142-add-login"

Model requests get the same value in the X-Yabanin-Task header (or as a label on the key). After that spend is grouped by task in the dashboard and in GET /api/analytics/tasks, with CSV export, and you can also group it by session or by agent.

Every response also carries the routing decision in a header:

X-Yabanin-Decision: {"source":"tier_router","class":"easy","confidence":0.92,"threshold":0.7,"from":"gpt-4o","to":"gpt-4o-mini","reason":"time_window_downgrade"}

So when a request goes to a model you did not expect, you can see the reason.

Where it runs

Setup How Good for
Laptop Docker Compose, ports on 127.0.0.1 only Trying it, local models
Your cloud or servers Kubernetes with Helm, routes to the providers you configure Teams
Air-gapped Offline bundle: verify checksums, the cosign signature, the SBOM and image digests, then docker load or Helm Regulated or offline environments

Self-hosting the gateway does not make inference local. If you route to a hosted provider your prompts still go there, and for a fully local setup you need a local model (for example llama.cpp) behind the gateway.

Limitations

It is a Developer Preview, so a few limitations:

  • the release kit is Linux amd64 only for now
  • budgets are only as good as your prices. The bundled reference prices cover a limited set of models and may be out of date, so set your own before you trust the cost numbers
  • the guard hooks for secrets, PII and prompt injection are regex and checksum detectors. They will catch obvious cases, but this is not a DLP system
  • the release notes list two open findings from the dependency vulnerability scan, details are in SECURITY.md

Next steps

Today the gateway covers boundaries and visibility. In the next versions I want to add richer policy rules and detection of agent behaviour that looks wrong and not only expensive (this is a plan, it is not in the code yet).

If you try it, please open an issue when something breaks, it is much better to find problems now than in six months. As I wrote before, when you saved 80 hours of coding you still have to spend 1000 hours of support. I would also like to hear if deny-by-default is the right call or just annoying, I am not sure yet where the line should be. PRs are welcome, details are in CONTRIBUTING.md.

Own your AI, even if you depend on cloud models right now :)

title: Reconcile Money at the Same Point in Time
description:
Why provider balances, local ledgers, pending withdrawals, and snapshot timestamps must be compared together.

Reconciliation is often described as comparing two balances. In practice, two correct systems can report different balances because they are describing different points in time or different stages of settlement.

Suppose the local ledger shows 50,000. A withdrawal of 2,000 is held locally but has not reached the provider. The provider balance still shows 50,000. Comparing the raw balances suggests everything matches, even though 2,000 is already unavailable to customers.

Now suppose the provider accepts the withdrawal and immediately reduces its balance, while the local ledger waits for final settlement. A raw comparison reports a 2,000 discrepancy even though both systems are behaving correctly.

Reconciliation needs an adjusted expectation:

expected provider balance
= last reconciled provider balance
+ externally settled inflows
- provider-accepted outflows
- provider-posted fees

The exact formula depends on the provider contract, but every term needs an explicit settlement state.

Store two timestamps

Every provider snapshot should store:

  1. the provider's as_of time, when the balance was true; and
  2. the local retrieval time, when the system received it.

Without the first timestamp, a delayed response can overwrite a newer observation. Without the second, operators cannot distinguish stale provider data from a delayed polling job.

Accept snapshots in provider-time order. If an older snapshot arrives after a newer one, preserve it for audit but do not make it the current balance.

Separate observation from movement

A balance snapshot is an observation. A ledger entry is a movement. Treating them as interchangeable makes it difficult to explain a change.

Store snapshots only when the balance changes, while always updating the latest successful check time. This creates a compact history showing opening balance, closing balance, and the change from the previous observation without writing identical rows every hour.

Daily money movement should come from transaction records, grouped by settlement date, direction, provider, and currency. It should not be inferred only from balance differences because prefunding, fees, reversals, and manual adjustments can produce the same change.

Use tolerance deliberately

Currency precision, provider rounding, and delayed fees can create small differences. Define tolerances by currency and reconciliation stage rather than applying one global threshold.

A mismatch should carry context: expected value, observed value, difference, snapshot age, unsettled items, and the last matching point. This gives operations a useful investigation record instead of a generic red alert.

Reconcile progressively

Start with reference-level matching. Then compare transaction totals for a time window. Finally compare adjusted balances. A balance mismatch with fully matched transactions points toward fees, timing, or missing adjustments. Unmatched transactions indicate a different class of problem.

Good reconciliation preserves uncertainty. It does not force two numbers to agree; it explains why they do or do not agree at a specific moment.

Implementation checklist

For each provider, document when its balance changes: request acceptance, processing, settlement, or fee posting. Store snapshot source, currency, account identifier, provider time, retrieval time, and request outcome. Reject older observations from the current-balance projection while retaining them for audit.

Build reconciliation output that shows matched transactions, unmatched local entries, unmatched provider entries, timing adjustments, fee adjustments, and the final unexplained difference. Alert only on the unexplained remainder and include the snapshot age so operators can judge whether another sync should occur before escalation.

title: Testing Cloud Backup and SHA-256 Restore on Ubuntu 24.04 & Windows Without Upfront Billing
description:
Most teams treat backup setup as a checkbox and never run a restore test until something breaks. When testing a new cloud backup tool requires handing over a card upfront or signing a monthly contract first, engineers tend to put off the restore check even longer.

Today we updated Tornova Backup (disclosure: I work on marketing and QA at Tornova Software Technologies) with two changes aimed at lowering that barrier:

  1. A 12-hour Free Trial (100 MB, No Payment Required): Activate it directly at tornovabackup.com/trials, install the agent, push test files, and run a real restore to verify integrity before paying anything.
  2. Reduced Personal & Team Monthly Pricing: Personal plans now start at $1.35/month (5 GB backup + 5 GB restore allowance included), $1.75/month (10 GB), $2.99/month (50 GB), and $4.99/month (100 GB), with no auto-renewal lock-in.

A quick 4-step restore verification workflow

If you are evaluating any scheduled backup tool on a workstation or Ubuntu server, here is the minimal sanity check worth running during a short trial window:

  1. Pick a small mixed test directory (10–50 MB): Include a binary file, text configs, and nested subdirectories with timestamps you care about.
  2. Confirm the background service runs cleanly: On Ubuntu 24.04 x64, Tornova's .deb CLI client runs via systemd, and on Windows 10 (1809+) / Windows 11 64-bit, the signed client runs as a Windows service (Tornova Backup Service).
  3. Record a local checksum before modifying or deleting your test copy: 
sha256sum ~/backup-test/important.tar.gz
  1. Restore to an alternate path and compare hashes: Checking the restored copy against the original SHA-256 digest confirms the round-trip worked end-to-end before you rely on it for real data.

Current platform support and caveats

  • Windows 10 (1809+) & Windows 11 (64-bit): Stable client (EXE/MSI/ZIP, digitally signed).
  • Linux: Stable .deb CLI client for Ubuntu 24.04 x64 (systemd required).
  • macOS 15+ (Apple Silicon & Intel): Currently in Beta.
  • Hosting & Security: Hosted in the US on Microsoft Azure with encryption in transit and at rest, SHA-256 file integrity checks, optional MFA, and optional client-side double-layer encryption on Windows and macOS.
  • Important notes: Restores stay within the same OS (Windows restores to Windows, Ubuntu to Ubuntu). Alongside the free 12-hour trial, one-time paid trials ($0.27 for 500 MB / 3 days, $1.10 for 1 GB / 5 days) carry over trial data when upgrading.

For multi-machine teams, organization plans scale with tiered volume discounts (3% for 11–20 users up to 18% for 101+ users) on tornovabackup.com/pricing?for=organization.

How do you quickly verify a new backup tool before trusting production or dev machines to it?

title: Scope WebMCP Tools to the Open React Workflow
description:
On the Events list, the browser discovered zero WebMCP tools. Opening an event draft exposed four. Switching to a trip draft replaced them with five trip tools.

That route sequence is the behavior I wanted when Trip Workbench gained a second workflow. Registering every operation at startup would have exposed two unrelated domains even when only one editor was visible.

Page-scoped tools make the current context clearer. They also create a design question: how does an agent enter a workflow whose tools exist only after the right page is open?

Keep domain identity in the contract

The event editor has a title, date range, time zone, location mode, location label, and notes. The trip editor has airports, travel dates, cabin, traveler count, and purpose.

Both workflows reuse authorization, revision, and command-receipt patterns, but they keep separate coordinators, services, tables, validation rules, policy versions, and identifiers. Event tools accept eventId; trip tools accept draftId.

The event editor exposes:

Tool Purpose
get_event_draft Read saved fields, revision, status, and unsaved-change state
update_event_draft Apply an allowed patch to an expected revision
validate_event_draft Return field issues and policy findings
prepare_event_review Show findings while the event remains a draft

This synthetic example does not send invitations, connect to calendars, or book venues.

Register when the editor has context

The React editor registers tools only after it has a draft identity and status. A condensed lifecycle looks like this:

useEffect(() => {
  if (!eventId || draftStatus !== "draft") return;

  const registration = new AbortController();

  registerEventDraftTools({
    eventId,
    canMutate: Boolean(canMutate),
    coordinator: eventCoordinator,
    signal: registration.signal,
    onStatus: setRegistration,
  });

  return () => registration.abort();
}, [eventId, draftStatus, canMutate, eventCoordinator]);

Chrome’s current imperative API documents this signal-based lifecycle. As of Chrome 153, aborting the registration removes the tool without cancelling an already-running execution. That is helpful for component cleanup, but it means route cleanup and in-flight operation safety are separate responsibilities.

The draft identity belongs in the dependency list. React may retain the same component type while moving from one event to another; the old tools must disappear and the new handlers must bind to the new event.

Test the exact route sequence

The native browser run signed in normally, used visible navigation, created a synthetic event draft, and inspected the browser’s real tool collection. It did not call the coordinator directly.

Context Discovered interface
Traveler on Trips list none
Traveler on Events list none
Traveler editing an event four event tools
Traveler editing a trip five trip tools
Traveler back on Events list none
Traveler reopening the event four event tools
Observer editing the event read, validate, prepare
Observer back on Events list none

An exact-name assertion catches stale registrations:

const expected = [
  "get_event_draft",
  "prepare_event_review",
  "update_event_draft",
  "validate_event_draft",
];

const actual = page.webmcp.tools()
  .map((tool) => tool.name)
  .sort();

assert.deepEqual(actual, expected);

The observer result is useful but limited. Omitting a mutation tool reduces accidental exposure; it does not authorize anything. The server must still reject writes from an actor without permission.

Execute a useful operation, not just discovery

Tool names alone do not prove that the page contract works. The run updated a synthetic workshop, validated it, and prepared an inline review.

{
  "title": "Customer engineering workshop",
  "startDate": "2026-11-25",
  "endDate": "2026-11-26",
  "timeZone": "America/Los_Angeles",
  "locationMode": "manual",
  "locationLabel": "Demo workshop room",
  "notes": "Synthetic example; no invitations"
}

The accepted update moved the draft from revision 1 to 2. prepare_event_review displayed a MANUAL_LOCATION requirement with canSubmit: true and submitted: false. The visible title matched an independent database query, and the event remained a draft with zero submissions.

The injected test clock was October 14, 2026, so the dates were still in the future. Pinning time matters when validation depends on dates.

A narrow interface needs a way in

The Events list intentionally exposes no editor tools, so those tools cannot open their own workflow.

The recorded run used the normal Events link and “New event draft” button. A browser agent with navigation and actuation can take a similar path. A client limited to WebMCP calls cannot.

There are two defensible designs:

  1. Treat browser navigation as part of the client contract.
  2. Add a bounded list-level tool to open an authorized draft or create a new one.

I would avoid a generic “call any API” or “run arbitrary JavaScript” escape hatch. It destroys the narrow schemas and server checks that make the editor tools reviewable.

Do not turn tool count into a performance claim

This run proves that the discovered interface changes with route and role. It does not prove that a model completes tasks faster with four tools than with nine.

That requires a separate evaluation: keep the task and executable behavior fixed, vary the visible tool set, and measure wrong-target updates, workflow-entry failures, correct persisted outcomes, recovery steps, and final-answer accuracy.

The current evidence supports a narrower conclusion: expose editing tools where the relevant object is visible, remove them when the context ends, preserve server authorization, and design an explicit entry path for the clients you actually support.

title: How to Test a $10 Bank Reconciliation Gap in SQLite
description:
The September 28 bank statement closes at $40. The books have a $350 deposit and a $300 payment, both cleared. Starting from zero, that leaves $50. The last line on the statement is a $10 service charge. That one is missing from the books.

A test with just those amounts is easy to fool. Forget the date filter and it still passes. Run the fee import once and you’ll never find out what a retry does. Give the fixture a $25 payment that cleared the next morning. Then deliver the September fee a second time.

The number to assert

For this test, the gap is the statement closing balance minus the cleared book balance at the cutoff. For this statement that starts at 4000 - (35000 - 30000) = -1000 cents. A negative result means the cleared books are higher than the bank. The statement line is what tells us why.

Save this block as reconcile.sql and run sqlite3 -bail :memory: < reconcile.sql. Each entry belongs to one checking account. Amounts are signed integer cents, dates are ISO dates, and cleared_on is the day the entry cleared the bank.

CREATE TEMP TABLE book_entry (
    bank_ref   TEXT PRIMARY KEY NOT NULL,
    cleared_on TEXT NOT NULL,
    cents      INTEGER NOT NULL
) STRICT;

INSERT INTO book_entry VALUES
    ('deposit-17', '2026-09-27',  35000),
    ('payment-18', '2026-09-28', -30000),
    ('payment-19', '2026-09-29',  -2500);

CREATE TEMP VIEW at_cutoff AS
SELECT 4000 - COALESCE(SUM(cents), 0) AS gap_cents,
       COUNT(*) AS cleared_rows
FROM book_entry
WHERE cleared_on <= '2026-09-28';

CREATE TEMP TABLE checks (
    step          TEXT NOT NULL,
    gap_cents     INTEGER NOT NULL,
    cleared_rows  INTEGER NOT NULL,
    expected_gap  INTEGER NOT NULL,
    expected_rows INTEGER NOT NULL,
    CHECK (gap_cents = expected_gap AND cleared_rows = expected_rows)
) STRICT;

INSERT INTO checks
SELECT 'fee missing', gap_cents, cleared_rows, -1000, 2 FROM at_cutoff;

INSERT INTO book_entry VALUES ('fee-20', '2026-09-28', -1000)
ON CONFLICT (bank_ref) DO NOTHING;
INSERT INTO checks
SELECT 'fee recorded', gap_cents, cleared_rows, 0, 3 FROM at_cutoff;

-- The importer delivers the same bank line again.
INSERT INTO book_entry VALUES ('fee-20', '2026-09-28', -1000)
ON CONFLICT (bank_ref) DO NOTHING;
INSERT INTO checks
SELECT 'fee replayed', gap_cents, cleared_rows, 0, 3 FROM at_cutoff;

SELECT step, gap_cents, cleared_rows FROM checks ORDER BY rowid;

fee missing|-1000|2
fee recorded|0|3
fee replayed|0|3

The last two rows are deliberately identical apart from the label. After the fee posts, $310 has gone out against $350 in. Replaying the same bank line should leave both the $40 balance and the count of three cleared entries alone.

Two ways to break it

Remove the WHERE line (keeping the statement’s final semicolon). The next morning’s $25 payment slips into September 28. The first gap flips from −$10 to +$15 and the first CHECK fails. On a fresh run, change only the replay’s reference from fee-20 to fee-21. The database accepts a fourth entry, the gap becomes +$10, and the last CHECK fails.

That second failure says something about the import contract. Two genuine fees can have the same date and amount. This example relies on a stable reference for a bank line. If references are unique only within an account, include the account in the unique key. If a bank later corrects the amount under an existing reference, that needs a correction path of its own.

ChatGPT drafted this article and its SQL. The example and both failure cases were tested with SQLite 3.43.2.

title: Updates to Hobby and Pro Terms of Service
description:
We are updating the Terms of Service for Hobby and Pro customers, effective October 19, 2026. The updates clarify some existing Vercel practices, expand terms on topics such as managed accounts and credits, and reflect applicable legal requirements, including certain cancellation and service-change rights for eligible consumers in the UK and EU.

Credits and billing

A new section sets out how credits work: plan-included credits expire at the end of the subscription term and purchased credits expire one year after purchase unless stated otherwise in the relevant credit purchase terms. Credits can only be used to pay Vercel fees, have no cash value, and are nontransferable. Credits are generally nonrefundable, but unused purchased credits are refunded if Vercel terminates your account without cause.

The Terms also clarify that credit purchases are billed in advance, subscriptions auto-renew unless you turn off renewal, and third-party pass-through rates may change when provider rates change. ⁠⁠

Managed accounts

The Terms now have a dedicated section for accounts that use a company email domain (e.g., work email), clarifying that the company can manage only the Projects you create inside its Team. We also clarified that if your company wishes to manage your account using your company work email, Vercel will now notify you first and give you a reasonable amount of time to move your personal content to an account with a different email address

Renewal and cancellation

You can turn off auto-renewal and cancel or downgrade through account settings or Support. Cancellation or downgrade generally takes effect at the start of the next renewal period. The Terms also explain statutory withdrawal and refund rights for eligible consumers.

Service changes

Eligible consumers in the UK and EU may cancel the affected subscription free of charge if a change has more than a minor negative impact on their access to or use of the Services. They have 30 days from notice or the change, whichever is later, and may receive a prorated refund of prepaid amounts for the remaining period.

Other updates

The service-specific provisions have been moved to a dedicated Service Terms page. The Terms also clarify sanctions-related obligations, including that use of the Services must not be in connection with or for the benefit of a sanctioned person under applicable laws.

Read the full Terms of Service and Service Terms for details.

title: FunkyMEDIA pokazuje, jak przygotować mały zestaw testowy RAG do kontroli informacji o marce
description:
Jak przygotować mały zestaw testowy RAG dla informacji o marce? Zbierz ustalone wersje dokumentów, pytania użytkowników i fragmenty, które powinny wspierać odpowiedź. W przykładzie FunkyMEDIA każde pytanie ma oczekiwane fakty oraz regułę oceny. Osobno sprawdzamy odnalezione materiały i poprawność odpowiedzi.

Zespół buduje asystenta odpowiadającego na pytania o ofertę. Demonstracja wygląda dobrze, ale po zmianie dokumentów pojawia się błędny termin wykonania usługi. Żeby ustalić, co się zmieniło, potrzebny jest zapis materiałów i oczekiwanego zachowania.

Poniżej przedstawiamy propozycję małego zestawu do testów własnego systemu RAG. Przykłady dotyczą fikcyjnej oferty. Nie opisują warunków handlowych FunkyMEDIA.

Wybierz jeden zakres

Zacznij od jednej usługi lub kategorii pytań. Przykładowo można sprawdzać zakres audytu, materiały wejściowe i sposób przekazania raportu.

Mały zestaw ułatwia ręczne przeczytanie każdego dowodu. Liczba pytań powinna wynikać z potrzeb, które chcesz sprawdzić. Zapisz również, jakie obszary pozostają poza testem.

W roboczym projekcie FunkyMEDIA można zacząć od kilku scenariuszy i rozbudować je po analizie błędów. Wynik dotyczy wtedy tego zestawu, a nie wszystkich możliwych rozmów.

Zachowaj wersję dokumentów

Każdy materiał powinien mieć identyfikator, datę i właściciela informacji. Zachowaj kopię używaną w teście. Sam link do zmieniającej się strony nie wystarczy do odtworzenia wcześniejszego wyniku.

Jeżeli zmieniasz ofertę, utwórz nową wersję zestawu. Porównanie wyników wymaga wiedzy, czy zmienił się system, dokumenty czy oba elementy.

W przykładzie FunkyMEDIA dokument „oferta-v1” zawiera fikcyjny zakres audytu, a „proces-v1” opisuje jego odbiór. Nazwy są roboczymi identyfikatorami.

Przygotuj pytania i reguły oceny

Scenariusz

Pytanie ilustracyjne

Oczekiwane zachowanie

Fakt w jednym źródle

Co obejmuje audyt?

Wskazanie zakresu z dokumentu

Dwa źródła

Co trzeba dostarczyć i co otrzymamy?

Połączenie informacji z obu materiałów

Brak danych

Ile trwa realizacja?

Wskazanie braku terminu w źródłach

Sprzeczność

Który zakres obowiązuje?

Obsługa zgodnie z zapisaną regułą wersji

Podobne nazwy

Czy oferta dotyczy firmy A czy B?

Rozróżnienie właściwego podmiotu

Regułę dla sprzecznych dokumentów ustal przed testem. Jeśli system nie ma danych pozwalających wybrać aktualny materiał, oczekiwanym zachowaniem może być prośba o doprecyzowanie.

Oddziel wyszukanie dowodu od wygenerowania odpowiedzi

Microsoft rozróżnia ocenę wyszukanych dokumentów od oceny odpowiedzi, w tym jej zgodności z dostarczonym kontekstem i dopasowania do pytania. Dokumentacja ewaluacji RAG.

W proponowanej karcie FunkyMEDIA pierwsze pole pyta, czy odnaleziono potrzebny fragment. Drugie sprawdza, czy odpowiedź poprawnie wykorzystała ten fragment. Trzecie dotyczy kompletności wymaganych faktów.

Jeśli dowód nie dotarł do kontekstu, zacznij diagnostykę od wyszukiwania i przygotowania dokumentów. Jeśli dowód był dostępny, przeczytaj odpowiedź oraz instrukcje generowania. To kierunki sprawdzenia, które trzeba potwierdzić w danej próbie.

Przykład rekordu

Poniższy zapis przedstawia fikcyjną ofertę do ćwiczenia.

{
  "case_id": "audit-scope-01",
  "question": "Czy audyt obejmuje wdrożenie poprawek?",
  "evidence_id": "oferta-v1-fragment-3",
  "evidence": "Audyt obejmuje raport i listę zaleceń. Wdrożenie wymaga osobnego zlecenia.",
  "required_facts": [
    "raport i zalecenia",
    "osobne zlecenie na wdrożenie"
  ],
  "unsupported_claim": "wdrożenie jest w cenie audytu"
}

Ocena powinna uwzględniać znaczenie odpowiedzi. Poprawna parafraza może przekazać oba fakty bez użycia identycznych słów. Proste wyszukiwanie frazy sprawdzi obecność tekstu, ale nie rozstrzygnie samodzielnie zgodności całej odpowiedzi.

Co oznacza test offline

W tym ćwiczeniu offline oznacza pracę na zamrożonym zbiorze dokumentów i zapisanych przypadkach testowych. Jeżeli model jest wywoływany przez zewnętrzne API, sam test nadal wymaga połączenia z usługą.

Nie mieszaj wyników wyszukiwania w aktualnym internecie z oceną stałego korpusu. W rejestrze FunkyMEDIA zapisz źródło kontekstu, wersję dokumentów i dostępną konfigurację. Dzięki temu wiadomo, co porównujesz.

Przeczytaj przypadki negatywne

Pytania o informacje nieobecne w dokumentach pozwalają sprawdzić reakcję na brak danych. Oczekiwaną odpowiedź określ wcześniej, na przykład wskazanie brakującej informacji i pytanie do użytkownika.

W scenariuszu z podobnymi nazwami sprawdź identyfikację firmy. Materiał dotyczący innego podmiotu może zawierać znajome słowa, ale nie wspierać odpowiedzi o właściwej marce.

Dla FunkyMEDIA takie scenariusze są propozycją kontroli jakości opisu informacji, a nie dowodem działania konkretnego wdrożenia.

Raportuj wynik razem z błędami

Zachowaj pytanie, odnalezione fragmenty, pełną odpowiedź i uzasadnienie oceny. Wynik zbiorczy powinien mieć licznik i mianownik.

Jeżeli ilustracyjnie 7 z 10 odpowiedzi spełniło ustalone kryteria, zapisz również trzy niespełnione przypadki. Mogą dotyczyć różnych usterek i wymagać innych poprawek.

Nie zmieniaj oczekiwanych faktów tylko po to, żeby wynik poprawił się po uruchomieniu testu. Korekta błędnego przypadku jest możliwa, ale wymaga nowej wersji i zapisu przyczyny.

FAQ

Czy mały zestaw wystarczy do oceny całego systemu? Pokazuje zachowanie w wybranych scenariuszach. Zakres testu należy opisać razem z wynikiem.

Czy AI może oceniać odpowiedzi? Może wspierać ocenę, ale reguły i przykłady wymagają kontroli. Zachowaj możliwość ręcznego odtworzenia werdyktu.

Czy sam poprawny link wystarcza? Sprawdź fragment źródła oraz to, czy wspiera fakty podane w odpowiedzi.

Materiały FunkyMEDIA rozwijają pracę nad informacją o marce i jej weryfikacją. AI Search · Brand Mentions · Metodologia · Kontakt.

LinkedIn FunkyMEDIA · Facebook · Instagram · YouTube.

Artykuł przygotowano z użyciem AI. Oferta, rekord i liczby w przykładach są fikcyjne.

title: Postgres to Redshift: A CDC Walkthrough That Ends in One External Schema
description:
Redshift will answer almost any question about your data, as long as the data is already there. Getting it from Postgres to Redshift is your job, and the first version is usually a nightly dump to Amazon S3 followed by COPY. That holds until an order is cancelled at noon and the evening dashboard still counts it.

The common ways to move Postgres data into Redshift:

  • COPY from S3 exports on a schedule. A script, a scheduler and a staging bucket. Freshness is hours to daily, and updates and deletes need full reloads or your own merge.
  • AWS Database Migration Service (DMS). Change data capture (CDC) through logical replication into native Redshift tables, updates and deletes included. You run a replication instance and a task, plus an S3 staging bucket.
  • Aurora PostgreSQL zero-ETL integration. ETL is extract, transform, load, and here there is none to run: changes reach native Redshift tables within seconds. The source is Aurora PostgreSQL, and Redshift is the only reader.
  • Managed extract, load, transform (ELT) tools such as Fivetran, Estuary or Airbyte Cloud. Nothing to host, and freshness in minutes by plan. You pay per row, per GB or per connector for a second copy inside Redshift.

This tutorial takes a fifth route. OLake Go, an open source (Apache 2.0) replication tool, reads the Postgres write-ahead log (WAL) and commits the changes as Apache Iceberg tables into the AWS Glue Data Catalog. The files stay in an S3 bucket you own.

Redshift maps that Glue database onto an external schema with one statement and queries the tables in place. Athena and DuckDB read the same tables through the same catalog.

I ran this against Postgres 16 and a Redshift Serverless workgroup in ap-southeast-1, with OLake Go v1.1.0. The first sync copied 48 records in 19 seconds, and a second sync replayed 12 changes in 18 seconds. Every number below is from that run.

What you need

Postgres 12 or later, Docker, an AWS account, Redshift Serverless or an RA3 cluster, and about 40 minutes. My workgroup ran at 8 Redshift Processing Units (RPU).

The pipeline is OLake UI from its Docker Compose install, with one job that copies two tables, customers and orders, and then replays the WAL.

Step 1: Prepare Postgres

Skip the container if you already have a database. For a local test, this starts Postgres 16 with logical replication switched on:

docker run -d --name pg_cdc -p 5432:5432 \
  -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=postgres -e POSTGRES_DB=shop \
  postgres:16 \
  -c wal_level=logical -c max_replication_slots=10 \
  -c max_wal_senders=10 -c wal_sender_timeout=0

On a server you manage, those four settings are ALTER SYSTEM SET statements, and wal_level needs a restart. On Amazon Relational Database Service (RDS), Aurora, Cloud SQL, Azure, Neon or Supabase, the same settings sit behind a parameter group or a dashboard toggle.

Connect with psql -h localhost -U postgres -d shop, then create the tables and the starting rows:

CREATE TABLE customers (
  id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  name VARCHAR(100), email VARCHAR(200), city VARCHAR(100), tier VARCHAR(20),
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW(),
  updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW());

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id INT REFERENCES customers(id), product VARCHAR(100), amount NUMERIC(10,2), status VARCHAR(20),
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW(),
  updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW());

-- 8 customers and 40 orders
INSERT INTO customers (name, email, city, tier) VALUES
  ('Aarav Mehta','aarav@example.com','Mumbai','gold'),   ('Priya Sharma','priya@example.com','Bengaluru','silver'),
  ('Liam Carter','liam@example.com','Austin','bronze'),  ('Sofia Rossi','sofia@example.com','Milan','gold'),
  ('Kenji Tanaka','kenji@example.com','Tokyo','silver'), ('Emma Schulz','emma@example.com','Berlin','bronze'),
  ('Noah Kim','noah@example.com','Seoul','gold'),        ('Zara Ali','zara@example.com','Dubai','silver');

INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, product, amount, status)
SELECT 1 + (n % 8), (ARRAY['Laptop','Headphones','Monitor','Keyboard','Mouse','Webcam'])[1 + n % 6],
       ROUND(20 + ((n * 7919) % 120000) / 100.0, 2), (ARRAY['placed','shipped','delivered'])[1 + n % 3]
FROM generate_series(1, 40) AS n;

OLake Go connects as its own role and reads changes through a publication and a pgoutput replication slot:

CREATE ROLE olake WITH LOGIN REPLICATION PASSWORD '<password>';
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA public TO olake;
GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA public TO olake;
ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES IN SCHEMA public GRANT SELECT ON TABLES TO olake;

CREATE PUBLICATION olake_pub FOR TABLE customers, orders;
SELECT pg_create_logical_replication_slot('olake_slot', 'pgoutput');

-- check
SHOW wal_level;                                        -- logical
SELECT slot_name, plugin, active FROM pg_replication_slots;
SELECT pubname, puballtables FROM pg_publication;

💡 Give every job its own slot and publication. Two jobs on one slot read each other's changes, and both lose data.

Two notes for a production database:

  • Primary keys. A table without one needs ALTER TABLE <table> REPLICA IDENTITY FULL; so that its updates and deletes carry the old row.
  • The slot pins WAL. Postgres keeps the log until OLake Go has read it. Keep the job on a schedule, alert on pg_replication_slots lag, and drop the slot when you retire a job.

Step 2: A bucket, a writer and a role for Redshift

Three things have to exist in AWS before OLake Go writes anything.

  1. An S3 bucket for the table files, in the region where your engines run. Mine was in ap-southeast-1.
  2. An Identity and Access Management (IAM) user for OLake Go with Glue and S3 permissions. I used a scoped user with the inline policy below and created an access key pair for it.
  3. An IAM role for Redshift, attached to the Serverless namespace or the cluster, that can read Glue and the bucket. Mine had AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess plus read access to Glue. 
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["s3:ListBucket", "s3:GetBucketLocation"], "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::<bucket>" },
    { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["s3:GetObject", "s3:PutObject", "s3:DeleteObject", "s3:AbortMultipartUpload", "s3:ListMultipartUploadParts"], "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::<bucket>/*" },
    { "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["glue:GetDatabase", "glue:GetDatabases", "glue:CreateDatabase", "glue:GetTable", "glue:GetTables", "glue:CreateTable", "glue:UpdateTable", "glue:DeleteTable"],
      "Resource": ["arn:aws:glue:<region>:<account>:catalog", "arn:aws:glue:<region>:<account>:database/*", "arn:aws:glue:<region>:<account>:table/*/*"] }
  ]
}

You do not create a Glue database. OLake Go makes one per job on the first sync and registers each table in it.

Step 3: Start OLake UI and connect Postgres 

curl -sSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/datazip-inc/olake-ui/master/docker-compose-v1.yml | docker compose -f - up -d

Open http://localhost:8000 and sign in with admin / password.

Go to Sources, click Create Source and pick Postgres as the connector. Under Change data capture (CDC), leave Enable CDC on and enter olake_slot as the Replication Slot and olake_pub as the Publication. Under Connection details I used host host.docker.internal, because Postgres ran in another container, with database shop and user olake.

Click Set up source. OLake Go tests the connection and then checks wal_level, the replication privilege, the slot and the publication before anything is saved. When one of them fails, the dialog names the setting and its recommended value.

Step 4: Add the Glue destination

Go to Destinations and click Create Destination. Pick Apache Iceberg as the connector and AWS Glue as the catalog type, then fill in the form:

Field Value
S3 Path s3://<bucket>/lakehouse/, the path OLake Go writes under
AWS Region the region of the bucket and the Glue catalog, ap-southeast-1 in my run
AWS Access Key and AWS Secret Key the key pair of the IAM user from step 2

Click Create. If OLake Go runs on an instance that has a role, leave the two key fields empty and it uses the instance role.

Step 5: Create the job and run the first sync

One detail is specific to Redshift. It is not in OLake Go's target engine picker yet, so on this job you set the delete format yourself.

  1. Open Jobs and click Create Job. Name it postgres_to_redshift and give it a schedule.
  2. Select the source and the destination from steps 3 and 4.
  3. Under Advanced Settings, set Target Query Engines to AWS Athena and DuckDB.
  4. Click Next. On the Streams page, tick customers and orders.
  5. For each table, set the sync mode to Full Refresh + CDC, the ingestion mode to Upsert and the Upsert Type to Positional Deletes.
  6. Click Create Job, then open the job's menu and choose Sync Now.

Positional deletes are the format Redshift reads, and the two listed engines read it too.

In my run the first sync copied 8 customers and 40 orders (48 records, 2.23 KB) and finished in 19 seconds, container start included. It records the WAL position through the slot first and then reads each table in parallel chunks, so nothing written during the copy is lost.

OLake Go names the Glue database after the job, the source database and the schema. Mine became postgres_to_redshift_shop_public, and the Iceberg DB field at the top of the Streams page changes that name before the first sync.

Step 6: Query the tables in Redshift

Open Redshift query editor v2 and connect to the workgroup or cluster. The first statement maps the Glue database onto a schema, and you run it once:

CREATE EXTERNAL SCHEMA lakehouse
FROM DATA CATALOG
DATABASE 'postgres_to_redshift_shop_public'
IAM_ROLE default;

SELECT id, name, city, tier FROM lakehouse.customers ORDER BY id;
SELECT status, count(*) AS n, round(sum(amount), 2) AS total
FROM lakehouse.orders GROUP BY status ORDER BY status;

IAM_ROLE default uses the default role of the namespace or cluster. The schema is read-only: OLake Go is the writer, and an INSERT or DELETE on these tables fails.

⚠️ Create the external schema after the first sync, in the workgroup's region. Before that the Glue database is not there, and Redshift answers ERROR: Database 'postgres_to_redshift_shop_public' does not exist in the Glue Data Catalog.

Step 7: Change rows and sync again

A nightly COPY would miss everything in this step until its next full reload. Back in psql, make 12 changes, 7 inserts and 5 updates:

INSERT INTO customers (name, email, city, tier) VALUES
  ('Maya Patel', 'maya@example.com', 'Pune', 'silver'),
  ('Lucas Silva', 'lucas@example.com', 'São Paulo', 'bronze');
INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, product, amount, status) VALUES
  (9, 'Laptop', 1299.00, 'placed'), (9, 'Mouse', 25.50, 'placed'),
  (10, 'Monitor', 349.99, 'placed'), (3, 'Keyboard', 89.00, 'placed'), (7, 'Webcam', 79.90, 'placed');
UPDATE customers SET tier = 'gold', updated_at = NOW()      WHERE name = 'Liam Carter';
UPDATE customers SET city = 'Abu Dhabi', updated_at = NOW() WHERE name = 'Zara Ali';
UPDATE orders    SET status = 'delivered', updated_at = NOW() WHERE id IN (1, 4, 7);

Choose Sync Now again. The second sync read 12 records (594 bytes) from the slot and finished in 18 seconds end to end.

For customers it wrote one new data file with 4 rows: the 2 inserts plus the new versions of the 2 updated rows. One small positional delete file retires the 2 old versions, and orders has the same shape with 8 rows and 3 deletes.

Now re-run the first SELECT in Redshift, with no refresh and no ALTER TABLE before it. Liam Carter is gold, Zara Ali has moved to Abu Dhabi, and the two new customers are there.

Redshift returns 10 rows, one per key, because it applies the positional deletes while reading. The orders roll-up matched Postgres to the cent: 16 delivered orders for 8659.68, 18 placed for 10522.26 and 11 shipped for 6397.25.

OLake Go adds an _op_type column to every table. It is r for a row from the first snapshot, c for an insert, u for an update and d for a delete.

Read the same tables from Athena and DuckDB

Both engines open the files OLake Go already wrote, so no export job runs.

Athena. The Glue database appears in the query editor's database list with no registration. Pick a workgroup that has a query result location in S3, select the database and run:

SELECT id, name, city, tier FROM postgres_to_redshift_shop_public.customers ORDER BY id;
SELECT status, count(*) AS n, round(sum(amount), 2) AS total
FROM postgres_to_redshift_shop_public.orders GROUP BY status ORDER BY status;

DuckDB. It reads a table from its current metadata file, which Glue stores as the table's metadata_location. Ask Glue for the location, then scan it:

aws glue get-table --database-name <glue database> --name customers \
  --query 'Table.Parameters.metadata_location' --output text

INSTALL iceberg; LOAD iceberg;
INSTALL httpfs;  LOAD httpfs;

CREATE SECRET lake (TYPE s3, KEY_ID '<access key>', SECRET '<secret key>', REGION '<region>');

SELECT id, name, city, tier
FROM iceberg_scan('s3://<bucket>/lakehouse/postgres_to_redshift_shop_public.db/customers/metadata/<latest>.metadata.json')
ORDER BY id;

DuckDB 1.5.5 returned the same 10 customers and the same roll-up as Redshift and Athena. Each sync writes a new metadata file, so fetch the location again before a fresh read.

Tips from the run

  • Three type changes to expect. numeric arrives as DOUBLE PRECISION, so round at query time when you need exact decimal arithmetic. timestamptz becomes TIMESTAMP in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), and json and jsonb arrive as VARCHAR for JSON_PARSE.
  • A stale probe table can fail the destination test. The test opens a table called test_olake.test_olake in Glue. Mine failed with is not authorized to perform: s3:GetObject because an earlier run in that account and region had left the table pointing at another bucket. Delete the stale table, or use a region whose catalog does not have it, which is what I did.
  • Give Athena its own workgroup. Athena needs a query result location in S3 before it runs anything. I used a workgroup that writes to s3://<bucket>/athena-results/ and left the shared primary one alone.
  • Plan for compaction. Each sync adds a small data file and a delete file per table, and Glue has no built-in compaction for tables written by external engines. Spark on Amazon Elastic MapReduce (EMR) can run rewrite_data_files through the same catalog.

How this compares with other Postgres to Redshift methods

Method Freshness Updates and deletes Where the data lands What you run
COPY from S3 exports hours to daily no; full reloads or your own merge native Redshift tables a script, a scheduler and a staging bucket
AWS DMS CDC through logical replication yes native Redshift tables a replication instance and task, plus a staging bucket
Aurora PostgreSQL zero-ETL seconds yes native Redshift tables; Redshift is the only reader nothing; the source is Aurora PostgreSQL
Fivetran, Estuary, Airbyte Cloud minutes, by plan varies by tool Redshift tables, a second copy nothing; per-row, per-GB or per-connector pricing
OLake Go to Glue (this post) CDC on a schedule down to one minute yes, as Iceberg row-level deletes Iceberg tables that Redshift, Athena, EMR, Spark and DuckDB all read one Docker Compose stack, open source

If your source is Aurora PostgreSQL and Redshift is the only reader, the zero-ETL integration is the simpler choice. The route in this post earns its setup when Athena, EMR or a notebook needs the same rows, or when you want to own the files.

Its limits, stated plainly:

  • It is not native Redshift speed. An external schema is read through Redshift Spectrum, which scans Parquet in S3 on every query. For a hot dashboard, load a slice into a native table on a schedule.
  • Tables need a primary key. Without one, inserts replicate but updates and deletes are not applied, unless you set REPLICA IDENTITY FULL.
  • Stay on positional deletes. Redshift reads deletion vectors only on Serverless above 4 RPU or on RG-type clusters, and Athena cannot read Iceberg v3 tables at all.

FAQ

What happens when I add a column in Postgres?

OLake Go adds it to the Iceberg table on the next sync and updates the Glue table definition in the same commit. Redshift shows the new column on the next query of the external schema.

How often can the sync run?

The job runs on a schedule, and the interval goes down to one minute. Each run replays only what changed since the previous one, and my 12-change sync took 18 seconds.

Does this work on a provisioned Redshift cluster?

Yes. Redshift Serverless and RA3 clusters both read the Glue Data Catalog through an external schema. Attach the IAM role to the cluster instead of the namespace, and IAM_ROLE default then uses the cluster's default role.

What does this pipeline cost to run?

Storage is your own bucket at S3 rates, and Glue adds only its per-object pricing for the table entries. Redshift Serverless bills RPU-hours only while queries run, and Athena bills per terabyte scanned. OLake Go is open source and runs wherever you run Docker.

Where to go from here

  • Point the source at your real database. Managed Postgres sets wal_level through a parameter group or a server setting, not ALTER SYSTEM.
  • Once the change volume grows, put compaction on a schedule, with Spark's rewrite_data_files on EMR or with OLake Fusion.
  • The full guide, with the command line configuration, the data type table, schema change rules and troubleshooting, is on olake.io.

If your Redshift or Glue setup returns something different at one of these steps, post the exact message in the comments and I'll look into it.

title: Crediting MT5 trading accounts from Indonesian QRIS and virtual account deposits, exactly once
description:
By William Beaumont, Head of Operations at PAYJN

A client in Jakarta opens your broker's cashier, picks "Bank transfer (VA)", pays IDR 5,000,000 from their mobile banking app and switches back to MetaTrader. Somewhere between the bank, the payment provider, your webhook endpoint and your back office, that payment has to become a balance operation on exactly one trading account, once.

Many deposit problems in a broker cashier are not payment failures. The money arrived, but the system credited it twice, credited the wrong account, or never credited it at all because one step assumed another had already done its job. This article walks through a deposit design for Indonesian QRIS and virtual account (VA) payments that avoids those three outcomes. The code is illustrative Node.js with invented field names. It is not any provider's API, and mt5.balance / mt5.findBalanceDeal stand for your own wrapper around the MT5 Manager or server API.

The three things that go wrong

  1. Double credit. The provider retries a webhook because your acknowledgement timed out, or two workers process the same event at once, and both post a balance operation to MT5.
  2. Wrong account. A client has two trading accounts, or a VA was reused, and the deposit lands on the account that happened to be "current" in the session.
  3. Silent miss. The webhook never arrives (or arrives while your endpoint is deploying), nobody reconciles, and the client opens a ticket three hours later with a screenshot.

Each one has a structural fix. None of them is "add more logging".

Choose the binding between payment and trading account first

Before writing any handler, decide what links a payment to a trading account.

Method Binding What to watch
VA, one per trading account The VA number itself Never reassign a VA to another account; amounts can differ from what the client typed in your cashier
VA, one per deposit Your deposit reference created before the VA is shown Expired VAs that still receive transfers
QRIS, dynamic per deposit Your deposit reference and the QR amount Payments attempted after the QR expired

A fixed VA per trading account is convenient for clients who top up often, but it means you must accept "any amount at any time" and decide how to handle it. A per-deposit VA or dynamic QRIS gives you an expected amount and an expiry, which makes mismatches easier to detect. Many brokers offer both: a fixed VA for regular clients and dynamic QRIS for quick deposits.

Whatever you pick, store the binding before you show payment instructions. If your system cannot tell which trading account a payment belongs to without looking at the client's session, the design is not finished.

A deposit table that refuses to credit twice

The core idea: the database, not the handler code, enforces "one provider payment, one credit".

CREATE TABLE deposits (
  id               BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  deposit_ref      TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL,      -- your reference, created first
  trading_login    BIGINT NOT NULL,           -- MT5 account
  method           TEXT NOT NULL,             -- 'va' | 'qris'
  expected_idr     BIGINT,                    -- null for open-amount VA
  provider_txn_id  TEXT UNIQUE,               -- set once, from the verified event
  received_idr     BIGINT,
  status           TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'awaiting_payment',
  mt5_deal_id      TEXT UNIQUE,               -- set once, after the balance operation
  review_reason    TEXT,
  created_at       TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  expires_at       TIMESTAMPTZ
);

Two unique constraints do most of the work. provider_txn_id stops the same payment from being attached to two deposits. mt5_deal_id records that the balance operation already happened, so a retry of the crediting step can check before acting.

The webhook handler: verify, record, acknowledge, then credit 

// Illustrative only. Field names are invented.
app.post('/webhooks/payments', async (req, res) => {
  if (!verifySignature(req)) return res.status(401).end();

  const evt = req.body;
  if (evt.status !== 'paid') return res.status(200).end(); // record, but never credit

  const result = await db.tx(async (t) => {
    const dep = await t.oneOrNone(
      'SELECT * FROM deposits WHERE deposit_ref = $1 FOR UPDATE', [evt.merchant_ref]);
    if (!dep) return { action: 'unknown_ref' };
    if (dep.provider_txn_id === evt.txn_id) return { action: 'duplicate' };
    if (dep.provider_txn_id) return { action: 'second_payment' };

    const late = dep.expires_at && new Date(evt.paid_at) > dep.expires_at;
    const mismatch = dep.expected_idr !== null && dep.expected_idr !== evt.amount_idr;
    const status = late || mismatch ? 'needs_review' : 'paid';

    await t.none(
      `UPDATE deposits SET provider_txn_id = $1, received_idr = $2,
         status = $3, review_reason = $4 WHERE id = $5`,
      [evt.txn_id, evt.amount_idr, status,
       late ? 'paid_after_expiry' : mismatch ? 'amount_mismatch' : null, dep.id]);
    return { action: status, id: dep.id };
  });

  res.status(200).end();                       // acknowledge fast
  if (result.action === 'paid') queue.add('credit-mt5', { depositId: result.id });
  if (['unknown_ref', 'second_payment'].includes(result.action)) alertOps(evt, result);
});

Three decisions are deliberate here:

  • The handler never calls MT5 directly. It records the verified payment and acknowledges. Crediting happens in a worker, so a slow trading server cannot make the provider retry the webhook.
  • A repeated event is a no-op, not an error. Return 200 so the provider stops retrying.
  • Mismatches go to people, not to code. An underpayment, an overpayment or a payment after expiry is moved to needs_review. Auto-crediting the received amount sounds helpful until a client pays an expired VA twice.

The crediting worker: check before you post 

worker.process('credit-mt5', async ({ depositId }) => {
  const dep = await db.one('SELECT * FROM deposits WHERE id = $1', [depositId]);
  if (dep.status !== 'paid' || dep.mt5_deal_id) return; // already done or not creditable

  // Use the deposit reference as the comment so the deal can be found again.
  const existing = await mt5.findBalanceDeal(dep.trading_login, `DEP:${dep.deposit_ref}`);
  const deal = existing ?? await mt5.balance(dep.trading_login, toAccountCurrency(dep.received_idr),
                                             `DEP:${dep.deposit_ref}`);

  await db.none(
    `UPDATE deposits SET mt5_deal_id = $1, status = 'credited'
       WHERE id = $2 AND mt5_deal_id IS NULL`, [deal.id, dep.id]);
});

The lookup before posting matters. If the worker crashes after MT5 accepted the balance operation but before your database update, a naive retry posts the deposit again. Searching for a deal with the same reference first turns the retry into a recovery.

Record the IDR amount received and the exchange rate you used to convert it into the account currency. Clients will ask why IDR 5,000,000 became a particular USD figure, and support needs the answer without recalculating it.

Reconciliation catches the silent misses

Webhooks are a notification, not a ledger. Run a job every few minutes that asks the provider for recent paid transactions and compares them with your deposits table:

  • paid at the provider, awaiting_payment locally → the webhook was lost; process it through the same handler logic;
  • paid locally for longer than a few minutes, no mt5_deal_id → the crediting worker is stuck;
  • paid at the provider with an unknown reference → a payment you cannot place; route to operations.

Run a full daily reconciliation against the provider's settlement report as well. That is where fees and returned transfers show up.

Withdrawals need the opposite instinct

Deposits fail safe by waiting for evidence. Withdrawals fail safe by not acting twice.

  • Pay only to a bank account or e-wallet in the client's own verified name, and review a newly added destination before the first payout to it.
  • Debit the trading account (or place a hold) before you send the payout request, with one withdrawal reference per request.
  • If the payout request times out, query its status with the original reference. A timeout does not prove that the transfer failed, and a blind retry can pay the client twice.

Test the ugly paths

Before production, replay the same verified webhook ten times. Deliver two events concurrently. Kill the worker after the MT5 call and before the database update. Pay an expired QRIS. Underpay a VA. Each test should end with exactly one credit, or an item in the review queue, never two.

Disclosure

I work at PAYJN, which provides IDR deposits and withdrawals for licensed forex brokers in Indonesia. The patterns above apply whichever provider you use. If you are planning an Indonesian cashier, our page on payments for forex brokers in Indonesia lists what we review before onboarding a broker.

title: Zero-Overhead Kubernetes Cost Anomaly Detection with eBPF & Golang (< 0.3% CPU)
description:
If you are running high-density Kubernetes clusters in production, you’ve likely felt the hidden CPU/memory tax of traditional sidecar proxies and Prometheus metric scrapers. Constantly scraping network telemetry and container metrics at the application layer can quietly consume 4.5% to 9%+ CPU overhead per node—while your cloud billing dashboards still lag 24–48 hours behind actual traffic spikes.

In this guide, we explore how to build a zero-overhead FinOps anomaly detection engine using eBPF (Extended Berkeley Packet Filter) and a lightweight Golang userspace controller, completely bypassing userspace bloat.

  1. The Architectural Shift: Moving Telemetry to the Kernel Instead of injecting heavy sidecar containers into every pod, we attach a low-overhead eBPF program directly to Linux kernel tracepoints (kprobe/sys_enter_sendto).

Zero App Modification: No code changes or sidecar proxy overhead required.

Kernel-Level Aggregation: Tracks socket I/O bytes directly per cgroup_id (which maps seamlessly to Kubernetes pod lifecycles).

Instant Detection: Triggers threshold alerts in under 100ms.

  1. The eBPF Kernel Component (C) Here is the core eBPF map and kprobe code (finops_egress.bpf.c) that tracks egress socket traffic at the kernel level: // SPDX-License-Identifier: GPL-2.0 #include #include #include

struct {
__uint(type, BPF_MAP_TYPE_HASH);
__uint(max_entries, 10240);
__type(key, __u64); // cgroup_id (maps to K8s Pod)
__type(value, __u64); // Total egress bytes transmitted
} cgroup_egress_bytes SEC(".maps");

SEC("kprobe/sys_enter_sendto")
int trace_egress_sendto(struct pt_regs *ctx) {
u64 cgroup_id = bpf_get_current_cgroup_id();
__u64 bytes = (u64)PT_REGS_PARM3(ctx);

if (bytes == 0) return 0;

__u64 *total_bytes = bpf_map_lookup_elem(&cgroup_egress_bytes, &cgroup_id);
if (total_bytes) {
    __sync_fetch_and_add(total_bytes, bytes);
} else {
    bpf_map_update_elem(&cgroup_egress_bytes, &cgroup_id, &bytes, BPF_ANY);
}

return 0;

}

char LICENSE[] SEC("license") = "GPL";

  1. The Golang Userspace Controller Using the cilium/ebpf Go library, our userspace daemon loads the compiled eBPF object, attaches the probe, and polls kernel hash maps to catch cost/egress anomalies instantly (finops_controller.go): package main

import (
"fmt"
"log"
"time"

"github.com/cilium/ebpf"
"github.com/cilium/ebpf/link"

)

const (
AnomalyThresholdBytes uint64 = 500 * 1024 * 1024 // 500MB window threshold
PollInterval = 5 * time.Second
)

func main() {
spec, err := ebpf.LoadCollectionSpec("finops_egress.bpf.o")
if err != nil {
log.Fatalf("Failed to load eBPF spec: %v", err)
}

coll, err := ebpf.NewCollection(spec)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatalf("Failed to create eBPF collection: %v", err)
}
defer coll.Close()

kp, err := link.Kprobe("sys_enter_sendto", coll.Programs["trace_egress_sendto"], nil)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatalf("Failed to attach kprobe: %v", err)
}
defer kp.Close()

egressMap := coll.Maps["cgroup_egress_bytes"]
ticker := time.NewTicker(PollInterval)
defer ticker.Stop()

log.Println("Zero-Overhead eBPF FinOps Anomaly Detector running (< 0.3% CPU)...")

for range ticker.C {
    var cgroupID, totalBytes uint64
    iter := egressMap.Iterate()

    for iter.Next(&cgroupID, &totalBytes) {
        if totalBytes > AnomalyThresholdBytes {
            fmt.Printf("[FINOPS ALERT] Cost Anomaly Detected! CgroupID: %d | Egress Spike: %.2f MB\n",
                cgroupID, float64(totalBytes)/(1024*1024))
        }
        _ = egressMap.Delete(&cgroupID)
    }
}

}

  1. Production Benchmarks & Summary By shifting socket tracking down to the Linux kernel via eBPF:

Node CPU Overhead: Dropped from ~7% (sidecar scraping) down to < 0.3%.

Billing Visibility: Moved from 24-hour batch report delays to real-time sub-100ms anomaly detection.

Read the full comprehensive walkthrough and architecture breakdown here:
👉 Zero-Overhead Cloud FinOps Guide

title: Inside DOMINION: a Rust runtime for local-first AI agents
description:
DOMINION is my Apache-2.0 open-source, local-first AI agent workspace. The idea is to connect models you already use to a workspace that can execute tools, retain context, coordinate agents, and show what actually happened.

This post explains the current architecture and its boundaries. It is an active developer preview, and the source is public: https://github.com/hushmind3/dominion-rust

The model is one part of the system

A model proposes an action. The runtime still has to execute it, apply permissions, store the result, handle interruption, and decide what evidence supports completion.

DOMINION separates those responsibilities:

React interface
      |
Rust HTTP API (Axum)
      |
Native Rust agent loop ---- user-configured cloud or local model
      |
Tools, approvals, workflow jobs, and SQLite state

The agent runtime is Rust. Node.js builds the React frontend rather than hosting the execution loop. Local inference integrations include llama.cpp/GGUF and Ollama; a macOS MLX path uses LM Studio. Integrations may still require their own runtime processes.

A task needs durable state

A chat transcript alone cannot tell you whether a shell command finished, whether an approval was granted, or whether an interrupted operation is safe to repeat.

DOMINION stores jobs and execution operations in SQLite, alongside messages and memory. The implementation includes cancellation and recovery checkpoints. Where the result of an external side effect is uncertain, recovery should not turn uncertainty into an automatic repeat.

The practical benefit is inspectability: you can look at the tool call, arguments, result, and job status instead of relying solely on the model saying “done.” The source paths include src/engine/jobs.rs and src/engine/tools.rs.

Shared rooms need shared context

Multi-agent chat introduces another state problem: participants can appear to be in one conversation while receiving different fragments of it.

DOMINION has a common room conversation, separate participant roles and model choices, and discussion, round-robin, and mention-driven modes. Memory has visibility boundaries and source references; superseded corrections should not silently become current facts again.

These mechanisms are implemented, but their presence does not establish perfect recall or cheap long-running conversations. Coherent room context and context cost remain areas where real-model feedback is especially useful. A Rust runtime does not make model inference free.

Source improvement needs a separate acceptance step

The experimental RSI path can propose source changes inside an isolated Git worktree, run candidate evaluation, and rebuild accepted implementations for later generations.

That gives the system an executable source-improvement path. It does not establish general recursive intelligence gains. Model-written claims, successful tool calls, passing protocol tests, and improved results on independent tasks are different kinds of evidence.

The project documents these distinctions in docs/RSI-MAIN-INTEGRATION-2026-11-12.md. Git worktrees isolate source changes; they are not an OS or network security sandbox. This is system-level research, not model-weight training.

Trying the workspace

The repository includes screenshots, a source-build quick start, Rust unit/integration tests, and public CI. There is currently no prebuilt release download to assume is ready. You'll need the documented Rust, Node.js, and OS build prerequisites.

The same workspace includes MCP integrations and video workflows. Generative video uses a configured backend such as ComfyUI, with its own models and hardware requirements. Cloud-model usage is billed by your provider; local inference uses your hardware.

A useful first trial is small: connect a model, ask it to complete a bounded file task, and inspect the resulting execution record. If you try shared rooms, check whether participants can accurately refer to the same earlier message.

I would welcome reproducible setup and model-compatibility reports, especially anything that makes the first-run experience confusing. Please leave credentials and private conversations out of reports.

Disclosure: This article was drafted with AI assistance from the public repository and implementation documentation. The project is a developer preview; no fixed token savings or general intelligence improvement is claimed.
