title: Who Should Modernize Your Legacy Systems? A Field Guide to Cloud Replatforming Partners
description:
What happens when the system running your core operations was built for a business that no longer exists? For a lot of enterprises, that is not a hypothetical question. It is the reservation platform, the claims system, or the pricing engine that nobody wants to touch because everyone has quietly built their workflows around its limitations. Legacy modernization and cloud replatforming exists to answer that question on the enterprise's own timeline, before a vendor's end-of-life notice, a failed compliance audit, or a competitor's faster release cycle forces the issue. This guide walks through eight companies that do this work, from global integrators to nearshore specialists, and what actually separates a partner who can be trusted with a mission-critical migration from one who cannot.

Executive Summary

Legacy modernization and cloud replatforming moves outdated, high-maintenance applications onto scalable, cloud-native architectures, replacing brittle monoliths and unsupported platforms with systems that can integrate with modern tooling, scale on demand, and support AI-driven initiatives. The core benefit to the buyer's organization is a direct reduction in the cost, risk, and talent dependency that legacy systems otherwise impose on the broader technology roadmap.

Ahead, you will find eight legacy modernization and cloud replatforming companies assessed on migration methodology, platform certifications, delivery governance, and proven, quantified outcomes, along with a look at how delivery models differ between large-scale systems integrators and specialized engineering providers, and how regional delivery choices affect the outcome. The goal is a framework buyers can use to match a partner to their specific legacy environment and risk tolerance.

Who Is This Guide For?

  • CTOs and VPs of Engineering deciding whether to replatform a legacy system in place, rebuild it entirely, or continue funding its maintenance.
  • Enterprise Architects evaluating which cloud target (Azure, AWS, or Google Cloud) and which modernization pattern (rehost, replatform, refactor) fit an existing legacy estate.
  • CIOs and IT Directors accountable for the operational risk and licensing costs tied to unsupported or end-of-life systems.
  • Procurement and Sourcing Leads comparing vendor delivery models, pricing structures, and contract risk across global and boutique providers.

Each of these roles shares the same goal: retiring the risk and cost of a legacy system without disrupting the business that depends on it.

What Is Legacy Modernization & Cloud Replatforming & How Does It Work?

Legacy modernization and cloud replatforming is the process of moving outdated applications, often running on unsupported languages, on-premises infrastructure, or end-of-life licensing agreements, onto modern, cloud-native architectures. It typically combines an architecture assessment, a phased migration or rebuild, and a change in how the application is deployed, monitored, and scaled. It rarely looks like a single one-time migration event.

Common models and approaches:

  • Rehosting (lift-and-shift): moving an existing application to cloud infrastructure with minimal code changes, prioritizing speed and lower up-front risk over long-term optimization.
  • Replatforming: migrating to cloud-native services (containers, managed databases, serverless compute) while making targeted code changes to fit the new environment's cost and performance model.
  • Refactoring and re-architecting: restructuring a monolithic application into microservices or event-driven components, typically the highest-effort, highest-payoff approach for systems central to the business.
  • Full rebuild: replacing the legacy application entirely with a new system built on current technology, reserved for applications too brittle or undocumented to migrate incrementally.

Legacy Modernization vs. Full Rebuild vs. Maintaining the Status Quo

Not every legacy system needs the same treatment, and the wrong choice among these three paths can cost far more than the modernization project itself.

Bottom line: modernization is almost always the lower-risk path for systems the business still depends on, while a full rebuild should be reserved for applications too broken to migrate incrementally.

When To Use Legacy Modernization & Cloud Replatforming

A handful of signals reliably indicate it is time to start a modernization conversation instead of scheduling another maintenance sprint:

  • The application runs on hardware, an operating system, or a database version that has reached, or is approaching, end-of-life support.
  • Licensing costs for the underlying platform (for example, an on-premises Oracle or mainframe environment) are rising faster than the business value the system delivers.
  • The system cannot integrate with newer platforms, APIs, or AI tooling without significant custom middleware.
  • Deployment cycles are measured in weeks or months rather than days, slowing the business's ability to respond to market changes.
  • The engineering talent that understands the legacy codebase is retiring or leaving faster than it can be replaced.
  • A recent security or compliance audit flagged the system as a liability due to unpatched vulnerabilities or an unsupported platform.

How To Choose the Best Legacy Modernization & Cloud Replatforming Partner?

The following criteria separate partners who can be trusted with a production-critical migration from those who cannot:

  • Proven migration methodology: the partner should be able to walk through a phased assessment, migration, and validation approach for a system as complex as the buyer's, not a generic "lift-and-shift for everything" pitch.
  • Platform-specific certifications: verify hands-on delivery credentials on the buyer's target cloud (Microsoft Azure, AWS, or Google Cloud), not just a reseller or sales partnership badge.
  • Legacy-language and platform bench depth: ask whether the partner has verified staffing for the legacy language or platform the current system runs on (COBOL, Java Swing, VB6, and similar), instead of a generalist team learning the platform on the buyer's engagement.
  • Cost governance during migration: consumption-based compute can spike well past the initial estimate once a migration is underway. Ask how the partner controls spend as the work progresses and after cutover, not only at the proposal stage.
  • Zero-downtime or minimal-downtime track record: for systems the business cannot take offline, ask for a specific example of a production cutover completed with a defined, and met, downtime window.
  • Transparent, outcome-based case studies: ask for named clients and specific, quantified metrics, such as an exact deployment-speed improvement or downtime reduction, rather than general claims of being "faster" or "more efficient."
  • Post-migration support model: confirm whether the partner remains engaged for optimization and incident response after go-live, or hands off the system once the migration is complete.
  • Buyers should also ask: Can this partner show a reference client that modernized a system of comparable scale and criticality? What is the rollback plan if a migration phase fails validation? How is knowledge transferred to our internal team after the engagement ends?

Bottom line: the right legacy modernization partner is judged less by size and more by whether its migration methodology, platform certifications, and case studies match the buyer's specific legacy environment and risk tolerance.

Legacy Modernization & Cloud Replatforming Companies Compared

Accenture is one of the largest professional services firms running legacy modernization work worldwide, anchored by application engineering practices spanning mainframe transformation, cloud migration, and AI-assisted code remediation. Accenture routinely coordinates multi-region modernization programs for the largest global enterprises, running concurrent workstreams across geographies without losing a single point of accountability.

Building a Legacy Modernization Partnership Built to Last

Legacy modernization and cloud replatforming is no longer a project a business can defer indefinitely. Every year a critical system stays on unsupported infrastructure, the licensing costs, security exposure, and talent risk compound, while the AI and automation initiatives the business wants to pursue stay blocked behind a data and application layer that cannot support them. The right partner depends less on brand size than on migration methodology, platform certifications, and a track record of specific, quantified outcomes rather than general claims. Global integrators bring scale and cross-industry breadth. Boutique and nearshore specialists bring focused delivery and faster team assembly. The right fit depends on the buyer's system complexity, industry, and risk tolerance.

From COTS Dependency to Cloud-Native, Without Stopping Operations

We have seen this play out firsthand. NCLH was locked into a rigid commercial booking system that took months to update and could not operate reliably at sea. Improving rebuilt the platform using Domain-Driven Design and Reactive Architecture, a cloud-native, microservices system that ships features in days and keeps running when connectivity is gone, with 40+ Improving engineers on the engagement and a multi-year active partnership still delivering today.

If your organization is evaluating a legacy modernization partner, explore Improving's legacy modernization and cloud replatforming services to discuss your specific environment.

Frequently Asked Questions

1) What is the difference between legacy modernization and a simple cloud migration?

A cloud migration typically moves an existing application to cloud infrastructure with minimal changes, often called a lift-and-shift. Legacy modernization goes further, restructuring the application's architecture, code, and deployment model to take advantage of cloud-native scalability, resilience, and integration capabilities rather than simply relocating the existing system.

2) How long does a typical legacy modernization project take?

Timelines vary widely by scope and system complexity, from a few months for a single application to over a year for enterprise-wide programs involving multiple interdependent systems. Buyers should ask each prospective partner for a realistic timeline to the first production cutover rather than the full program end date.

3) Should we rehost, replatform, refactor, or rebuild?

The right approach depends on how well-documented and business-critical the system is. Rehosting suits systems needing a fast, low-risk move to the cloud. Replatforming and refactoring suit systems central to the business that need real architectural improvement. A full rebuild is reserved for systems too undocumented or brittle to migrate incrementally.

4) What certifications should a legacy modernization partner have?

Look for certifications specific to the buyer's target cloud platform, such as Microsoft Solutions Partner designations, AWS Advanced Tier Partner status, or Google Cloud Partner status, rather than general cloud experience claims alone.

5) Is nearshore or offshore delivery a good fit for legacy modernization work?

Nearshore delivery can reduce time-zone and cultural-alignment friction compared to fully offshore delivery, while offshore delivery typically offers the deepest bench at scale. The right choice depends on how much real-time collaboration the migration planning phase requires.

title: A Full Table Scan Isn’t Always a Mistake
description:
The orders dashboard is slow, so you pull up the Oracle execution plan. There it is: TABLE ACCESS FULL on a million-row table. The query filters on status, and there’s already an index on that column. You run the same query with a different status and see an index range scan. It’s tempting to conclude that Oracle missed an obvious optimization on the first run.

Now look at what the two queries ask for. One totals nearly every order the system has ever shipped. The other totals a small set of orders held for review. Both have the same SQL shape and use the same filter column, but they ask Oracle to retrieve very different amounts of data. We’ll follow both access paths, see where the work goes, and use the executed plan to check whether the full scan makes sense.

An index finds the rows. Oracle may still need the table.

An access path is how the database retrieves rows. With a B-tree index on status, Oracle can navigate to the first matching entry and walk the matching leaf entries. That operation appears as INDEX RANGE SCAN. Each entry carries a rowid, which identifies where a row lives in the table.

If the query also needs amount and the index contains only status, Oracle uses those rowids to fetch amount from the table. In the plan, look for TABLE ACCESS BY INDEX ROWID above the range scan. Oracle can also batch rowids and try to visit rows in block order. That variant appears as TABLE ACCESS BY INDEX ROWID BATCHED. A block is the unit in which Oracle stores and accesses table data. One block can hold many rows.

The trade-off depends on how many blocks you touch

With a full scan, Oracle reads the table’s data blocks and applies the filter as it scans. It can read multiple adjacent blocks in a single I/O request. With a range scan that fetches table rows, Oracle reads the matching index entries and then visits the blocks those entries point to.

Imagine a table with 10,000 blocks. If a query’s matching rows occupy 20 of them, the index can help Oracle skip most of the table. If the matching rows are spread across almost all 10,000 blocks, the index path can visit almost the whole table anyway, on top of reading the index. Batching can improve the order of those visits. It still has to retrieve the rows.

Oracle’s clustering factor describes how closely table row placement follows a particular index’s key order. A value near the table’s block count suggests that rows encountered close together in index order tend to share blocks. A value near the row count suggests more scattered visits. That’s one reason the same percentage of matching rows can favor different plans on different tables.

Skew can give the same query two sensible plans

Selectivity is the fraction of rows that satisfy a predicate. When values occur at very different frequencies, the data is skewed. For an orders table where SHIPPED is common and HELD is rare, an average across all statuses can hide the difference between these two queries. A histogram, a statistic that describes the distribution of values in a column, can help Oracle estimate their cardinalities, meaning the numbers of rows expected from each operation.

The columns you request matter too. An index on (status, amount) could supply both columns needed by the example below and avoid table rowid fetches. That changes the cost comparison. The worked example uses an index on status alone so you can see the cost of going back to the table.

Worked example in Oracle

Run this in a scratch schema. The table has one million rows. Every thousandth row is HELD, so those rows are spread across the load. SHIPPED accounts for 900,000 rows. The padding keeps the rows closer in size to a wider application table.


CREATE TABLE scan_demo_orders AS
SELECT LEVEL AS order_id,
       CASE
         WHEN MOD(LEVEL, 1000) = 0 THEN 'HELD'
         WHEN MOD(LEVEL, 1000) <= 900 THEN 'SHIPPED'
         ELSE 'PENDING'
       END AS status,
       MOD(LEVEL, 10000) / 100 AS amount,
       RPAD('x', 100, 'x') AS padding
FROM dual
CONNECT BY LEVEL <= 1000000;

CREATE INDEX scan_demo_orders_status_ix
    ON scan_demo_orders (status);

BEGIN
  DBMS_STATS.GATHER_TABLE_STATS(
    ownname          => USER,
    tabname          => 'SCAN_DEMO_ORDERS',
    estimate_percent => 100,
    method_opt       => 'FOR ALL COLUMNS SIZE 1 FOR COLUMNS SIZE 3 STATUS',
    cascade          => TRUE
  );
END;
/

Run each aggregate and display its cursor plan immediately afterward in the same session. The GATHER_PLAN_STATISTICS hint collects execution statistics for the statement.

SELECT /*+ GATHER_PLAN_STATISTICS */ SUM(amount)
FROM scan_demo_orders
WHERE status = 'HELD';

SELECT * FROM TABLE(DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY_CURSOR(NULL, NULL, 'ALLSTATS LAST'));

SELECT /*+ GATHER_PLAN_STATISTICS */ SUM(amount)
FROM scan_demo_orders
WHERE status = 'SHIPPED';

SELECT * FROM TABLE(DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY_CURSOR(NULL, NULL, 'ALLSTATS LAST'));

Illustrative cursor-plan excerpts. These show possible plans and example row counts. Actual plans depend on the optimizer environment.
Predicate: STATUS = 'HELD'

Predicate: STATUS = 'HELD'
| Id | Operation                             | Name                       | E-Rows | A-Rows |
|----|---------------------------------------|----------------------------|--------|--------|
|  1 |  SORT AGGREGATE                       |                            |      1 |      1 |
|  2 |   TABLE ACCESS BY INDEX ROWID BATCHED | SCAN_DEMO_ORDERS           |   1000 |   1000 |
|  3 |    INDEX RANGE SCAN                   | SCAN_DEMO_ORDERS_STATUS_IX |   1000 |   1000 |

Predicate: STATUS = 'SHIPPED'
| Id | Operation                             | Name                       | E-Rows | A-Rows |
|----|---------------------------------------|----------------------------|--------|--------|
|  1 |  SORT AGGREGATE                       |                            |      1 |      1 |
|  2 |   TABLE ACCESS FULL                   | SCAN_DEMO_ORDERS           | 900000 | 900000 |

Both aggregates return one row. The difference is in the work beneath them. The HELD query can use the index to identify 1,000 rowids and fetch their amounts. The SHIPPED scan emits 900,000 rows after applying the filter. To check how much work that took, look at Buffers in your own cursor plan. It counts logical block accesses. E-Rows and A-Rows show estimated and actual output rows, respectively. For these single-start access operations, you can compare them directly.

Further reading

  • Oracle Database 19c SQL Tuning Guide · Optimizer Access Paths
  • Oracle Database 19c SQL Tuning Guide · Optimizer Statistics Concepts
  • Oracle Database 19c PL/SQL Packages and Types Reference · DBMS_XPLAN

title: Why High-Frequency Trading (HFT) Firms Still Rely on Bare Metal Over Cloud Servers
description:
In High-Frequency Trading (HFT), speed is the actual product. A single millisecond delay dictates whether a strategy captures a profit or absorbs a loss.

While streaming platforms, social networks, and retail banks have migrated heavily to AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud, the HFT sector stubbornly anchors its execution systems to physical hardware. They rely on bare metal.

Understanding why well-funded quantitative firms reject infinite cloud scalability requires looking at physics, predictable execution, and absolute architectural control.

What Is High-Frequency Trading (HFT)?

High-Frequency Trading is an algorithmic trading method that utilizes powerful computers to process massive volumes of orders in microseconds or nanoseconds. These strategies capitalize on fleeting market inefficiencies. Because multiple firms often target the same micro-opportunity simultaneously, the firm with the fastest execution architecture captures the trade.

4 Core Architectural Advantages of Bare Metal in HFT

1. Eliminating Hypervisor Jitter

Cloud environments rely on hypervisors to divide physical servers among multiple virtual instances. This virtualization layer introduces overhead and, crucially, jitter—microscopic, unpredictable spikes in network response times.

Bare metal servers eliminate this virtualization layer entirely. Trading algorithms interface directly with physical CPUs and network interface cards (NICs). By utilizing kernel-bypass networking protocols like DPDK, firms route data past the standard operating system stack.

The result is consistently flat, sub-microsecond latency. In HFT, consistent execution predictability matters just as much as raw speed. A highly tuned strategy simply cannot survive random processing delays.

2. The Physics of Co-location

Physical distance equates to latency. Light traveling through a fiber-optic cable takes roughly five microseconds to cover one kilometer. To eliminate this transit delay, HFT firms utilize co-location. They lease rack space directly inside, or immediately adjacent to, the stock exchange's primary data center.

Public cloud regions are strategically built in locations optimized for cheap power and vast physical space, placing them geographically distant from financial matching engines. For latency-arbitrage strategies, that physical distance renders public cloud architecture non-viable.

3. Eradicating Resource Contention

Public clouds operate as multi-tenant environments. If a neighboring virtual machine suddenly spikes in workload, it competes for shared physical resources like memory bandwidth, CPU cache, and network capacity. This creates the "noisy neighbor" problem.

Average cloud performance may appear sufficient, but a microsecond lag caused by another tenant during high market volatility is catastrophic for an active trading algorithm. Bare metal provides a 100% single-tenant environment. Resource availability remains completely static, guaranteed, and predictable around the clock.

4. Bespoke Hardware Engineering

HFT infrastructure requires hyper-specialized hardware modifications. Firms extensively deploy FPGAs (Field Programmable Gate Arrays) to execute tasks like parsing market data and generating orders directly at the silicon level.

Engineers strip down BIOS settings, install proprietary network cards, and frequently deploy heavily overclocked processors. While public cloud vendors offer standard FPGA instances and compute-optimized hardware, they restrict low-level firmware tuning. Bare metal allows trading firms to engineer and optimize their hardware stacks down to the individual component level with absolute autonomy.

Bare Metal vs. Cloud in HFT Infrastructure

Feature Bare Metal (HFT Standard) Public Cloud Servers
Latency & Speed Lowest achievable; sub-microsecond routing via customized networking stacks. Higher baseline latency; susceptible to hypervisor jitter.
Physical Location Co-located directly at or adjacent to the stock exchange. Remote data centers prioritized for scale and power costs.
Resource Allocation 100% dedicated hardware; zero risk of external resource contention. Shared multi-tenant hardware; vulnerable to noisy neighbors.
Hardware Autonomy Total control over BIOS, customized NICs, and tailored FPGA logic. Standardized commercial offerings with locked firmware.
Scaling Dynamics Manual provisioning requires physical hardware acquisition. Instant, elastic scaling on a pay-as-you-go model.

The Hybrid Model: Where HFT Firms Actually Use the Cloud

Trading firms do not ignore cloud technology entirely; they simply segment their workloads.

Latency-critical execution systems remain strictly on co-located bare metal. However, asynchronous operations run in the cloud. Firms heavily leverage cloud infrastructure for backtesting trading strategies, running intensive historical risk analytics, and storing petabytes of market tick data where microseconds do not impact the bottom line.

The cloud remains unmatched for enterprise flexibility, global scalability, and dynamic cost control. Yet, the high-frequency trading sector plays by a different set of physical rules. When trading profits are won and lost in microseconds, financial firms require zero virtualization overhead, physical proximity to the exchange, entirely dedicated processing resources, and silicon-level hardware customization. Until cloud platforms can engineer solutions that bypass the laws of physics and virtualization limits, bare metal will remain the absolute standard for latency-critical market operations.

title: Packaging my own design as a template: the unglamorous parts
description:
I turned my portfolio design into a template. The code was done. The real work was removing myself from it.

This post is about the unglamorous parts of packaging software for other people: what had to change, what I almost forgot, and what's still unfinished. If you're thinking about selling a starter kit or template, this is the checklist I wish I'd had.

Why a template

As I wrote on Day 4, I weighed several ways to earn online and chose the one that needed the least new work: packaging a design system I'd already built. A portfolio template is something other students genuinely need, and it was a better fit than starting a product from scratch.

The principle: separate the owner from the engine

My live site is full of me: my name, links, location, project list, certificates, even phrases in the chat assistant's persona. A template can't have any of that hard-coded. Everything owner-specific has to live in one clearly marked place, and the rest has to read from it.

I worked on a separate copy, so the live site stayed untouched. (That's the "copy, don't rewrite" approach from Day 22.)

What had to change

1. One config file for every owner-specific fact

All the personal facts moved into a single site object: name, tagline, links, location, and values derived from them (full name, site URL, and so on).

// src/data/site.ts  (simplified)
export const site = {
  name: 'Avery Quill',
  tagline: 'Designer-developer',
  url: 'https://your-site.example',
  location: 'City, Country',
  github: 'https://github.com/your-username',
};

export const FULL_NAME = site.name;
export const SITE_URL  = site.url;

Then I hunted for hard-coded copies. This is the tedious part: search for the old name, old URLs and old city across HTML, scripts, metadata and generated files. Every miss would have shipped a stranger's details to a buyer.

2. A template-driven index.html

The HTML head contains the title, description and social tags, which must also come from the config. A small build plugin fills the HTML from the same data, so the page's metadata can't disagree with the site.

3. Build scripts that read the same config

Anything that runs at build time (sitemaps, feeds, prerender, share images) had to read from the config too, through one loader, instead of having their own copies of the facts.

4. A section list that controls the page

A sections array decides which home sections render and in what order. A buyer who doesn't want a blog section removes one line.

5. Parameterised APIs

Some small stats endpoints took a hard-coded username. They now accept a query parameter, so a buyer's data shows up instead of mine.

6. The assistant persona

The chat assistant's knowledge and persona are generated from an OWNER object, so a buyer gets an assistant that talks about them.

A sample persona, not my life

The template ships with a fictional owner ("Avery Quill", The Quill Review) and placeholder links (your-username, your-site.example). Sample PDFs and images are generated by a script, so no personal photos or real certificates are included.

The licence question

This one almost slipped past. The live site has a little pixel mascot. I wasn't certain I could legally redistribute those sprites, so I removed them from the template and made a mascot an optional config feature instead.

The rule I took: if I can't verify the licence of an asset, it doesn't ship. Fonts, images, icons, sounds, sprites. Check each one. Selling something that includes someone else's work without permission is a serious problem, and "I found it online" isn't a licence.

I also wrote a draft licence for the template itself. It's a draft, not legal advice, and anyone selling software should get proper advice for their situation.

Test like a buyer

The most valuable check: do what a buyer will do, from scratch.

unzip press-template.zip -d /tmp/buyer-test
cd /tmp/buyer-test/press-template
npm ci
npm run typecheck
npm run build

Do it in a clean directory, not your working copy. Things that work on your machine because of leftover files or cached installs will fail here. I also made a customised copy (changing the name, links and sections) to confirm that the config really controls everything.

What I found along the way

Packaging forced me to look at the code with fresh eyes, and I found real bugs in the live portfolio:

  • The command palette ignored the Escape key.
  • A certificate modal's animated children lacked React keys.
  • Certificates without a URL crashed the modal and the featured row.

All three were fixed in the live site too. Preparing something for strangers is a great forcing function for quality.

What I haven't finished

The honest status, as on Day 4: the template is built and verified, the listing copy and screenshots are ready, and a demo is deployed. But the Gumroad listing is a draft that's not published, because payouts need bank details I haven't connected.

So: built, tested, not shipped. Naming that publicly is partly to make it harder to leave it that way.

A checklist you can reuse

  • [ ] Every personal fact lives in one config file
  • [ ] Search for your name, handles, URLs, city across all files
  • [ ] Sample content uses a fictional persona
  • [ ] No personal images, documents or certificates
  • [ ] Every asset's licence is verified, or the asset is removed
  • [ ] A README with setup steps a stranger can follow
  • [ ] A clean install and build from the final zip
  • [ ] A customised copy to prove the config works
  • [ ] A licence file (get advice)
  • [ ] Listing text that says exactly what's included, and what isn't

Lesson

"It works for me" and "someone else can use it" are different levels of finished. The second one took longer than the first.

Writing the listing page

A template listing has to answer a buyer's questions fast. Mine follows this outline:

# Name: one-line promise

## What you get
- A complete React + TypeScript site (list the main sections)
- Design system with tokens and primitives
- Sample content you can replace
- Documentation: setup, customising, deploying

## Who it's for / not for
For: students and developers who want a distinctive portfolio.
Not for: people who want a no-code builder.

## Requirements
Node version, package manager, hosting suggestions.

## What's *not* included
Domain, hosting, your content, support beyond [stated scope].

## Preview
Screenshots, a live demo link.

## Licence
Plain-language summary + link to the full text.

## Changelog
Version history.

The "what's not included" section prevents refunds and disappointment.

README for the buyer

The README should get a stranger from zip to running site:

  1. Requirements.
  2. Install and run commands.
  3. Where to put your information (the one config file).
  4. How to add a project, a post and a certificate.
  5. How to change colours and fonts (the tokens).
  6. How to deploy.
  7. Troubleshooting for the three most common problems.
  8. Licence and credits.

A README that a first-time buyer can follow without asking you anything is a product feature.

Support and refunds: think before you sell

I'm not a lawyer and rules differ by country and platform, so treat this as a prompt, not advice:

  • Decide in advance what support you'll offer (for example, installation questions for 30 days) and say it plainly.
  • Read the platform's terms about refunds, taxes and payouts.
  • Check whether you need to register for tax in your country once you earn.
  • Keep a record of what you sold, to whom and when.

Handling this before the first sale is much less stressful than after.

A pre-launch dry run

Do this on a machine that has never seen your project:

  1. Download the zip from the listing, as a buyer would.
  2. Follow the README to the letter. Note every place you hesitate.
  3. Change the name, links and colours. Does everything update?
  4. Build and deploy somewhere.
  5. Fix what confused you, then repeat with a friend.

Every point of friction you fix is a support email you won't answer later.

Versioning and updates

If people buy it, it needs maintenance. A lightweight plan:

  • Semantic version numbers (1.0.0, 1.0.1…).
  • A changelog.
  • A promise about how long you'll support a major version.
  • A note on dependencies: they age, and security updates matter.

Be honest about what you can maintain. An abandoned template with promises is worse than a small one that's kept updated.

What I'd tell my past self

  1. Set up payouts on day one, not last.
  2. Write the README before the last feature.
  3. Check licences as you add each asset, not at the end.
  4. Test from a clean zip early. Many problems only show there.
  5. Price low, and treat it as an experiment you learn from.

If you've sold a template or starter kit, what surprised you most?

title: Node.js Dashboard Recovery: A Guide to Delivery Latency and Connection Health
description:
To measure realtime delivery latency and connection health for a Node.js e-commerce device-status dashboard, collect client receipts across reconnect and backfill. A connected dashboard can still be showing yesterday's truth: the first message after recovery may be old, even when the connection itself looks healthy.

Short answer: publish a timestamp with each status message, have the receiving client report its observed delay, and track that delay as a metric. Separate live delivery from recovery traffic, track connection health alongside it, and alert on a sustained trend rather than one slow sample. For a Node.js publisher, the decisive observation still comes from the client.

What page fired when the dashboard went stale?

Start the postmortem with that question. A green publisher chart establishes little about what a warehouse operator actually saw, because a server-side duration ends before the receiving application has necessarily handled the message.

For a bounded production exercise, I'd take one device, packing-scanner-17, and ask what the dashboard should show after its connection drops and returns. This is a hypothetical recovery drill, not a report of an observed incident: a status update is published while the dashboard is disconnected, another arrives during recovery, and an older update reaches the client after a newer one. The exercise should expose whether the screen can move backward while its connection indicator stays green.

Watch the cursor.

The invariant is that recovery must not make the displayed device state older. Connection establishment, receipt of a recent status, and completion of backfill are separate observations; treating them as one “healthy” bit hides the exact transition an incident responder needs to inspect. A reconnect counter can rise while recovery works correctly, whereas a quiet connection can accompany a stale screen. Neither signal alone answers the page.

Infrai is worth trying for teams bringing device-status publication and client-delay reporting into the same backend workflow, because one key and one bill reduce the credential ownership and invoice reconciliation spread across services. Its public, self-describing discovery surface supplies request and response schemas plus runnable examples, which helps resolve the next integration question without guessing a payload from an endpoint name. Every documented capability ships runnable examples in 10 languages, including Go and JavaScript, so the Node.js publisher and a Go diagnostic tool can start from examples of the same interface rather than independently reverse-engineering it. The single REST API needs no SDK installation for the discovery check below. That is a concrete setup advantage; it does not establish a dashboard recovery guarantee.

Infrai exposes 295 routes across 20 modules through one REST API. Plain HTTP with no SDK to install gives the Node.js publisher and the Go diagnostic tool a consistent interface: each can use its standard HTTP client rather than adding a separate vendor SDK for every backend service. That reduces dependency setup for the recovery drill without changing the application's responsibility for ordering and backfill.

How should clients measure realtime delivery latency after a connection recovers?

Attach the publication time to the message and record the time when the receiving application handles it. Their difference is an observed delivery delay. It includes parts of the path that publisher-side timing cannot see, which is why a fast publish response is insufficient evidence for a delivery-latency page.

Clock error matters. If the publisher's clock is ahead of the receiver's clock, subtraction can yield a negative number; discarding that sign by forcing the result to zero would make a measurement problem look like excellent service. Record those samples separately and investigate clock alignment before interpreting cross-machine delay as a precise network measurement. The example below demonstrates arithmetic with controlled timestamps, not a measured service latency.

Recovery introduces another ambiguity. A delayed message received during backfill can be expected historical traffic, while a newly published message that arrives late during normal operation deserves a different investigation. Keep separate distributions for live delivery and recovery observations, and record how long recovery takes before the dashboard has a sufficiently recent state for its job. Avoid mixing old backfill into the live-delivery distribution and then paging on the resulting spike.

There is no honest universal threshold here.

Set a freshness budget from the dashboard's operational purpose, then evaluate the trend over a chosen observation window. Track disconnected time, reconnect attempts, and progress through recovery alongside delay; explicitly represent an absence of receipts, since an empty sample set cannot demonstrate fast delivery. A screen that has stopped reporting should not inherit the last green latency value forever.

Compare the recovery contract before choosing the integration

The useful first result is a status that survives the disconnect drill with understandable measurements. An animated dashboard is a much weaker milestone, even if the initial SDK setup takes only a few minutes.

The following comparison describes selection criteria, not a benchmark or a claim that any named service meets a particular retention or recovery limit. Check each candidate's documentation for the contract your application needs.

Option Setup and SDK decision Recovery question that should decide the trial
Ably Evaluate its client integration as a specialist messaging candidate; include the work of managing its credentials beside your existing backend credentials. Can its documented recovery contract satisfy the dashboard's disconnect duration and ordering requirements?
Pusher Channels Evaluate the channel and client integration against your existing application, including the separate receipt-reporting path you need to build. What must the application do to reconstruct a current device state after reconnection?
Socket.IO Evaluate the application integration and the operational responsibility your team is prepared to take on around its deployment. Which recovery assumptions hold in the deployment you intend to run, and what happens outside them?
Infrai A shared REST surface reduces separate backend keys; public schemas and examples reduce payload discovery work. Can the verified capabilities support your application-owned recovery design, with its required semantics checked explicitly?

These are three real alternatives worth evaluating, rather than interchangeable names in a feature checklist. For Ably, prioritize evidence about recovery behavior; for Pusher Channels, make state reconstruction the acceptance test; for Socket.IO, include deployment responsibility in the integration estimate. Those are trial priorities, not asserted product limitations.

Prefer a specialist when its documented recovery behavior meets a requirement that would otherwise require substantial application logic. Prefer the shared backend surface when credential and integration friction are the immediate problem and the application already owns the state-reconstruction contract. Neither choice excuses missing client receipts.

The W3C WebRTC specification is useful background when evaluating WebRTC-based systems, but it does not establish the delivery or backfill behavior of an unrelated messaging service. Keep evidence attached to the system it describes.

A small preventative path, with an explicit boundary

The Go program below first calls Infrai's public discovery surface, then runs a recovery-check fixture for a Node.js-backed dashboard. It consumes illustrative receipt data, reports observed delay, separates recovery samples, and prevents an older sequence from replacing the selected device state. The field names belong to this example's application contract; they are not a vendor request schema.

There are three receipts for one device. The second represents a newer state and the third represents an older state arriving afterward. All timestamps are synthetic. The program uses only the standard library and can run as a single Go file. The discovery request is read-only, sets an explicit method, checks errors, and retries rate limits with bounded exponential backoff while honoring Retry-After. Discovery requires no key; if INFRAI_API_KEY is set, the example reads it from the environment and sends it as a Bearer token.

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "log"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

type Receipt struct {
    DeviceID    string `json:"device_id"`
    Sequence    int64  `json:"sequence"`
    PublishedMS int64  `json:"published_ms"`
    ReceivedMS  int64  `json:"received_ms"`
    Recovery    bool   `json:"recovery"`
}

func inspectDiscovery() error {
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet,
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        if key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"); key != "" {
            req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        }
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            wait := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            value := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(value); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                delay := time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
                if delay > wait {
                    wait = delay
                }
            } else if until, err := http.ParseTime(value); err == nil {
                if delay := time.Until(until); delay > wait {
                    wait = delay
                }
            }
            resp.Body.Close()
            if attempt == 3 {
                return fmt.Errorf("discovery rate limited after four attempts")
            }
            time.Sleep(wait)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 8192))
            resp.Body.Close()
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery status=%d body=%s read_error=%v",
                resp.StatusCode, body, readErr)
        }
        var result json.RawMessage
        err = json.NewDecoder(resp.Body).Decode(&result)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        fmt.Printf("discovery=%s\n", result)
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("discovery attempts exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if err := inspectDiscovery(); err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    const fixture = `[
        {"device_id":"packing-scanner-17","sequence":41,
         "published_ms":1000,"received_ms":4000,"recovery":true},
        {"device_id":"packing-scanner-17","sequence":43,
         "published_ms":4100,"received_ms":4180,"recovery":false},
        {"device_id":"packing-scanner-17","sequence":42,
         "published_ms":3000,"received_ms":4200,"recovery":true}
    ]`

    var receipts []Receipt
    if err := json.Unmarshal([]byte(fixture), &receipts); err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }

    last := make(map[string]int64)
    for _, receipt := range receipts {
        delay := receipt.ReceivedMS - receipt.PublishedMS
        if delay < 0 {
            fmt.Printf("device=%s clock_sample_invalid=true\n",
                receipt.DeviceID)
        } else {
            fmt.Printf("device=%s recovery=%t observed_delay_ms=%d\n",
                receipt.DeviceID, receipt.Recovery, delay)
        }

        previous, exists := last[receipt.DeviceID]
        if exists && receipt.Sequence <= previous {
            fmt.Printf("device=%s sequence=%d applied=false\n",
                receipt.DeviceID, receipt.Sequence)
            continue
        }

        last[receipt.DeviceID] = receipt.Sequence
        fmt.Printf("device=%s sequence=%d applied=true\n",
            receipt.DeviceID, receipt.Sequence)
    }
}

The fixture deliberately reports receipt delay before checking whether the state should advance. An old message remains evidence about recovery even when the dashboard correctly refuses to apply it. That distinction prevents the UI's ordering guard from silently deleting the very observations needed to explain a reconnect.

This guard assumes the application can assign a meaningful increasing sequence per device. It demonstrates selecting a newer state, not proving that every intermediate event arrived. If every transition must trigger an action, keeping only the latest state is insufficient; the application needs a gap-handling and processing contract appropriate to that requirement. A device restart also needs a defined sequence policy before this guard belongs in production.

Keep device identifiers in diagnostic records rather than automatically turning each one into a metric dimension. Aggregate live and recovery observations deliberately, and preserve enough context to investigate the device that triggered an alert.

Where this advice stops

The discovery call verifies a read-only integration path; the receipt fixture does not connect a dashboard client, implement persistent backfill, or send a metric to a service. Its useful result is narrower: a reproducible check of the application rule that recovery must not move a displayed device state backward, while preserving evidence about delayed receipts.

For an actual integration, obtain the capability's schema and runnable example from discovery before implementing publication or reporting. A verified route name alone is insufficient to establish its request fields, client subscription behavior, or recovery guarantees. Keep backend credentials on the backend and define the receipt-reporting boundary explicitly.

Finally, rehearse silence as well as delayed delivery. Ask what page fires when the client stops reporting entirely, what evidence distinguishes a disconnected dashboard from a stale device, and what tells an operator that recovery has completed. If those answers depend on staring at a green connection chart, the recovery contract still needs work.

Sources

References for checking candidate integrations and the relevant protocol scope:

  • Ably documentation
  • Pusher Channels documentation
  • Socket.IO documentation
  • W3C WebRTC 1.0

If the shared backend boundary fits your dashboard, start with the schemas and runnable examples in the Infrai documentation.

title: Zoho CRM subforms vs related modules: which should you use?
description:
Disclosure: Skyfall Labs is an official Zoho Partner. This is a cross-post of our guide; the original, with sources, is at https://www.skyfallhq.net/resources/zoho-crm-subforms-vs-related-modules

Short answer: a subform is a table of line items inside one record. It suits small, fixed-shape lists such as order lines. If the child data needs its own searching, filtering, workflows or ownership, Zoho's help suggests it will not work well in a subform, because several features do not reach subform fields. Zoho's pages also disagree on which editions allow custom subforms, so check your own account first.

What a subform is, per Zoho

Zoho describes a subform as a secondary form or table that lets you add multiple line items to a primary record, creating a one-to-many relationship. There are two types, Standard and Static, so choose the type carefully when adding the subform. Standard lets users add rows with predefined fields as columns, with the maximum rows set between 1 and 100. Static has a fixed number of rows with predefined values for some fields, capped at 25 per subform per layout.

Source: Zoho Help: Subforms

Limits worth knowing before you build

  • Columns: Zoho's help says a subform allows a maximum of 25 fields per layout; the Kaizen FAQ says up to 25 columns per subform.
  • Rows: up to 100 per subform outside inventory modules. Inventory modules (Quotes, Invoices, Sales Orders, Purchase Orders) allow up to 200 rows, and that 200 is a combined cap across all subforms in the module, custom and system-defined.
  • Subforms are not available for Tasks, Calls, Meetings or Pricebooks.
  • Subforms and their fields are specific to each layout.
  • Fields from a lookup module can be shown in a subform but are not synced with the source module, and are not populated during lead conversion, quote conversion, API updates, data migration or import.

Source: Zoho Help: Subforms, Zoho Community: Kaizen #155 - Frequently Asked Questions on Subforms

Where Zoho says subform fields do not work

This is the list that usually decides the question. Per Zoho's subform help page, subform fields do not appear in custom view columns, advanced filters, layout rules, Blueprint validation, web forms, import, global search, template merge fields, validation rules, or workflow field update and criteria. The Kaizen FAQ adds that triggering workflows on subform field changes was not supported as of September 2024 and may have changed since.

What does work: Zoho says subforms can be selected as related modules in reports, so you can build summary reports and dashboards from them, and subforms can be added to mail merge templates. Aggregate fields (SUM, AVG, MAX, MIN or formula-based) can total the rows on the parent record.

Source: Zoho Help: Subforms, Zoho Community: Kaizen #155 - Frequently Asked Questions on Subforms

Which editions allow custom subforms (Zoho's pages conflict)

Zoho's subform help page says subforms are available in Professional and above, with 1 subform per module in Professional, 2 in Enterprise and 5 in Ultimate. Zoho's Kaizen FAQ says Professional has no custom subforms (only system-defined ones in inventory modules), Enterprise and Zoho One get 2, and CRM Plus and Ultimate get 5, and that custom subforms need Enterprise or higher.

We cannot tell you which is current. Advice: check the Feature Availability page and your own Setup before designing around a subform, because the answer changes whether a Professional account can use this approach at all.

Source: Zoho Help: Subforms, Zoho Community: Kaizen #155 - Frequently Asked Questions on Subforms

A practical decision guide (advice, not vendor documentation)

  • Use a subform when the rows only make sense inside one parent record, are few, and mostly need totals: order lines, a list of attendees, simple specification rows.
  • Use a related or custom module when you need to filter or search the rows, put them in custom views, trigger workflows on them, validate them with validation rules, import them, or give them their own owner and permissions. Our custom modules guide covers that choice.
  • If you are unsure, list the five questions people will ask of that data. If most start with "show me all the rows where...", a subform will frustrate you given the exclusions above.

Existing setup that does not behave? Typical causes

Per Zoho, if a subform is required it must have values in at least one row before the record saves, and if a row contains any data, all mandatory fields in that row must be filled. Users who describe a record that "will not save" with no visible error often hit this. Bulk addition of rows via lookup is, per Zoho, being released in phases, so what you see may differ from a colleague's account.

Skyfall Labs reviews Zoho CRM data models and can restructure a subform into a related module, or the reverse, with data migration. Because we are a Zoho Partner, treat our view with the interest we have disclosed.

Source: Zoho Help: Subforms, Zoho Community: Kaizen #155 - Frequently Asked Questions on Subforms

Frequently asked questions

What is the difference between a subform and a related module in Zoho CRM?

Per Zoho, a subform is a table of line items inside a primary record. Zoho's help lists many features that do not reach subform fields, including custom views, advanced filters, global search, import and workflow criteria, so child data that needs those usually belongs in its own module.

How many rows can a Zoho CRM subform have?

Per Zoho's Kaizen FAQ, up to 100 rows per subform outside inventory modules, and up to 200 in inventory modules as a combined cap across all subforms. Static subforms are capped at 25 rows per layout.

Can I use workflows on subform fields?

Zoho's help lists workflow field update and criteria among the places subform fields do not appear, and its Kaizen FAQ said triggering workflows on subform changes was unsupported as of September 2024. Check current behaviour in your account.

Which Zoho CRM editions include custom subforms?

Zoho's pages conflict. One says Professional and above with 1 subform in Professional; another says custom subforms need Enterprise or higher. Confirm on Zoho's feature availability page.

Can I import subform data?

Zoho's subform help page lists import among the places subform fields do not appear. The Kaizen FAQ says the Bulk Write API can insert subform records together with their parent record.

Can I report on subform data?

Yes. Per Zoho, subforms can be selected as related modules in reports, and you can build summary reports and dashboards from them.

Sources

  • Zoho Help: Subforms
  • Zoho Community: Kaizen #155 - Frequently Asked Questions on Subforms

Need hands-on help? Skyfall Labs offers Zoho consulting, implementation and customization. Original guide: https://www.skyfallhq.net/resources/zoho-crm-subforms-vs-related-modules

title: PostgreSQL fixes 52 security issues, including a 22-year-old vulnerability
description:
PostgreSQL released updates fixing 52 security issues, notably addressing a 22-year-old type confusion flaw tracked as CVE-2026-6460.

The updates impact versions prior to 18.7, 17.12, 16.16, 15.20, and 14.25.

Full mitigation requires server updates, rebuilding C extensions, and updating client utilities.

How the problem works

The vulnerability concerns the way the server handles complex data types, where a field type could change while older values ​​were still stored. Security researchers were able to show how the issue could cause the server to crash or read portions of its memory. According to available evidence, no real attacks have been recorded so far that exploit this issue.

Researchers had notified major cloud service providers that offer databases, such as Amazon, Microsoft, Google and others, since August. The issue affects all older versions before 18.7, 17.12, 16.16, 15.20 and 14.25. It is noted that the 14 series has now completed its lifecycle and version 14.25 is the last one released for it.

What should administrators do?

In addition to the core server, the update also includes fixes for tools used for backup and management. To fully protect systems, administrators are advised to update the software, rebuild or update all C-based add-ons installed on the server, refresh indexes, and take new backups.

title: When stdout is nil: stopping a WinRM panic in GitLab Fleeting
description:
A nil writer is one of those values that looks like "I don't care about this output" and behaves like "please crash." In GitLab Fleeting's WinRM connector, that's exactly what happened. The library always copied command output to stdout. When stdout was nil, the process panicked.

This is the story of gitlab-org/fleeting/fleeting!151, my fix for that panic, opened during the October 2026 Hackathon. I'll cover the issue, the test that reproduced it before the fix existed, the one-guard change, and the fake WinRM transport that made the tests possible.

The issue: a panic on a path that meant "no stdout"

The issue was gitlab-org/fleeting/fleeting#66, opened by Brandon Bruce. It came from GitLab Runner's instance_ready_command path for Windows autoscaling (support case 759678).

Fleeting is the library GitLab Runner uses to provision and connect to autoscaled instances. The WinRM connector is how it talks to Windows. winRMClient.Run took opts.Stdout and handed it to the winrm library. The library copies command output to that writer unconditionally. When Stdout was nil, the copy was a nil pointer dereference.

Nil Stderr was already handled. Nil Stdout was not. An earlier MR, !117, had tightened stderr-writer handling and concurrent writes, and had left this hole.

The plan: reproduce it first

I wanted this issue for the October 2026 Hackathon, and I didn't want to guess about the panic. I commented with a plan that started from a failing test:

I would like to work on this for the October 2026 Hackathon. I reproduced the panic on main with a unit test that drives winRMClient.Run through a fake winrm.Transporter with Stdout: nil (it crashes in io.Copy inside RunWithContextWithInput). Planned fix: default a nil opts.Stdout to io.Discard in Run, plus that regression test.

The contributor platform assigned me, and I opened the MR the same day.

The guard

The production change is a nil check at the top of Run, before anything is passed to the library:

func (c *winRMClient) Run(ctx context.Context, opts RunOptions) error {
    // winrm copies the command output to stdout unconditionally, so a nil
    // writer would panic.
    if opts.Stdout == nil {
        opts.Stdout = io.Discard
    }

    var stderrWriter *stderrOmitWriter
    if opts.Stderr == nil {
        stderrWriter = newStderrOmitWriter()

io.Discard is the right default here: the caller asked to run a command and didn't provide a place for stdout, so the output should be thrown away, not written into a nil interface. Stderr already had its own guard, a stderrOmitWriter. I didn't try to unify the two. I made stdout safe in the same place — at the start of Run — with the simplest writer that cannot panic.

A fake SOAP transport, so the test doesn't need Windows

A unit test for this can't talk to a real WinRM endpoint. The winrm client speaks SOAP: it creates a shell, starts a command, and receives streams. I added connector/winrm_test.go with a fake transport that answers those three requests and ignores the rest:

// fakeWinRMTransport answers WinRM SOAP requests with canned responses for a
// single command that writes "hello" to stdout and exits with exitCode.
type fakeWinRMTransport struct{}

func (fakeWinRMTransport) Transport(*winrm.Endpoint) error { return nil }

func (fakeWinRMTransport) Post(_ *winrm.Client, msg *soap.SoapMessage) (string, error) {
    body := msg.String()

    switch {
    case strings.Contains(body, "transfer/Create"):
        return fakeWinRMCreateShellResponse, nil
    case strings.Contains(body, "shell/Command"):
        return fakeWinRMCommandResponse, nil
    case strings.Contains(body, "shell/Receive"):
        return fakeWinRMReceiveResponse, nil
    default:
        // Signal and Delete responses are not parsed by the client.
        return "", nil
    }
}

The receive response carries a base64 stdout stream of hello (aGVsbG8=) and an exit code of 0. The client is built with TransportDecorator so it uses the fake instead of the network:

params := winrm.NewParameters("PT60S", "en-US", 153600)
params.TransportDecorator = func() winrm.Transporter { return fakeWinRMTransport{} }

Two examples sit on top of that:

func TestWinRMRunNilWriters(t *testing.T) {
    client := newFakeWinRMClient(t)

    require.NotPanics(t, func() {
        err := client.Run(context.Background(), RunOptions{Command: "echo hello"})
        require.NoError(t, err)
    })
}

func TestWinRMRunWritesStdout(t *testing.T) {
    client := newFakeWinRMClient(t)

    var stdout strings.Builder
    err := client.Run(context.Background(), RunOptions{Command: "echo hello", Stdout: &stdout})
    require.NoError(t, err)
    require.Equal(t, "hello", stdout.String())
}

The first one is the regression test. Without the guard it panics with invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference. With the guard it passes. The second one is there so the discard path can't accidentally swallow output when a writer is provided.

I ran go test ./... -count=1 and golangci-lint run ./connector/ locally, and both were clean.

Review and merge

GitLab Duo reviewed the MR and had no change requests. It checked that a nil Stdout is replaced with io.Discard before it reaches runWinRMCmd, that other callers of runWinRMCmd (DialWinRM, DialRun, deployTunnelBinary) already pass non-nil writers, that the fake transport's substring routing doesn't overlap, and that TestWinRMRunWritesStdout writes to a strings.Builder from a single goroutine.

I marked the MR ready for a maintainer. Arran Walker reviewed it, thanked me, and merged it on 14 October 2026, two days after I opened it.

What I took away

1. Reproduce a panic with a test before you write the fix. The issue comment already said where it crashed (io.Copy inside RunWithContextWithInput). A NotPanics example on main turns that into something you can watch go from red to green.

2. Guard nil writers at the boundary you own. The panic was inside a library that always writes to stdout. Fleeting can't change that library's contract, but it can stop passing nil in.

3. io.Discard is the nil stdout. If the caller didn't provide a writer, throwing the bytes away is the behavior they asked for. Don't invent a more clever sink.

4. Fake the protocol at the transport boundary. A WinRM unit test doesn't need a Windows host if you can answer Create, Command, and Receive with canned SOAP. Keep the routing strings tight so they don't overlap.

5. Keep a positive example next to the panic example. TestWinRMRunNilWriters proves we don't crash. TestWinRMRunWritesStdout proves we still write when we should.

Links

  • Issue: gitlab-org/fleeting/fleeting#66
  • Merge request: gitlab-org/fleeting/fleeting!151
  • The earlier stderr-handling work: gitlab-org/fleeting/fleeting!117

Thanks to Brandon Bruce for the issue, and to Arran Walker for the review and the merge.

If you've been thinking about contributing to GitLab, the community issues are a great place to start: contributors.gitlab.com.

title: Keep a RAG index in sync with a docs site by re-embedding only the chunks that changed
description:
A support bot or internal assistant built on a documentation site goes stale the week after launch. The docs change, the vector index doesn't, and the bot keeps quoting the old pricing page. The usual fix is a nightly full re-crawl and re-embed, which pays to embed thousands of unchanged chunks to pick up a handful of edits, and still leaves deleted pages in the index unless you diff the URL lists yourself.

What the index actually needs from each sync is three lists: chunks to add, chunks to replace, chunk IDs to delete. This post gets exactly that from a scheduled run and applies it to a vector store in Python.

Disclosure: I'm Aurelix, and I built the Website Change Tracker. It's a paid tool (prices below).

How it decides what changed

You give it start URLs (or sitemap URLs) and a corpusId. The first run with that ID is the baseline: every page comes back as added, split into Markdown chunks. Every later run re-checks the site and returns only pages that were added, changed or deleted.

  • Chunk IDs are anchored on content: the page's canonical URL, the heading path and a hash of the normalised text, as valid UUIDs. Chunk boundaries are cut at content-defined points, so editing one paragraph re-cuts only the chunk it sits in, and an unchanged section keeps its ID when the sections around it change.
  • Boilerplate is not a change: navigation, footers, cookie banners and lines like "Last updated" or "x min read" are dropped before comparing.
  • A broken page is not a deletion: a page is deleted only on a 404/410 or a redirect away. A known page that errors, shows a bot challenge, comes back as an empty JavaScript shell or shrinks by more than 90% is returned as extraction_failed (free), and its previous version is kept.

Each change record carries change, doc_id, url, title, upsert_chunks (each with chunk_id, heading_path, text and a ready citation), delete_chunk_ids, and counts of upserted, deleted and unchanged chunks.

A nightly sync into a vector store

This uses Chroma, which embeds documents itself; the same three steps work with Qdrant, Pinecone, Weaviate or pgvector, since the chunk IDs are UUIDs.

pip install apify-client chromadb

import os

import chromadb
from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient(os.environ["APIFY_TOKEN"])
run = client.actor("aurelix/website-change-monitor").call(
    run_input={
        "startUrls": ["https://docs.apify.com/academy"],
        "corpusId": "apify-academy",
        "maxPages": 500,
        "chunkSize": 1500,
    }
)
changes = list(client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items())

index = chromadb.PersistentClient(path="index").get_or_create_collection("docs")
upserts, deletes = [], []
for c in changes:
    if c["change"] == "extraction_failed":
        print(f"skipped (kept previous version): {c['url']} ({c['reason']})")
        continue
    upserts += c["upsert_chunks"] or []
    deletes += c["delete_chunk_ids"] or []

if deletes:
    index.delete(ids=deletes)
for i in range(0, len(upserts), 100):
    batch = upserts[i:i + 100]
    index.upsert(
        ids=[ch["chunk_id"] for ch in batch],
        documents=[ch["text"] for ch in batch],
        metadatas=[{"url": ch["url"], "citation": ch["citation"]} for ch in batch],
    )
print(f"{len(changes)} pages changed: {len(upserts)} chunks upserted, {len(deletes)} deleted")

Run it once to fill the index, then schedule the same input daily (save it as a task in the Apify Console and click Schedule, then run the script after it, or call it from your own scheduler). A quiet day returns nothing and embeds nothing.

A few input choices that matter:

  • Already loaded the site another way? Set "returnBaseline": false and the first run records the corpus silently, so you pay per page checked, not per page returned. The Website to Markdown API is a good way to do that first full load.
  • Help centres with orphan pages: "scope": "domain" with "useSitemaps": true tracks pages no menu links to; excludeGlobs such as ["**/search**", "**/tags/**"] keeps out listings that change on every visit.
  • No polling: set webhookUrl to an n8n, Make or Zapier webhook and the delta is POSTed in batches of 25 records; the last batch has final: true and the run's counts.
  • Chunk size is fixed per corpus so IDs stay stable. To re-chunk, use a new corpusId, which starts a new baseline.

Why this tool

  • Built for a machine reading the output: Markdown chunks to upsert and chunk IDs to delete.
  • Chunk IDs are anchored to the content, so they stay put when nothing in that section changed.
  • Blocked or empty pages are never reported as deleted.
  • The delta, chunks and delete IDs, can be pushed to a webhook.
  • What it doesn't cover: severity scores or diffs written for a person to read.

Limits

  • No JavaScript rendering. Pages that are an empty app shell are skipped, and flagged if they were already in the corpus.
  • HTML pages only. PDFs, images and other files are skipped; HTML pages over 2 MB too.
  • maxPages caps pages checked per run (up to 20,000). Known pages not reached in a run are kept, not deleted; set it above the size of the site.
  • Polite pace: at most two new requests a second per site, about 1,000 large documentation pages an hour. robots.txt is always obeyed.
  • rel=canonical is followed within the same site and scope, so a site whose canonical tags all point to one page collapses to that page.
  • No login, paywalled or bot-challenged pages.

Cost

Two parts: a small charge per page checked, and a larger one per changed page returned. A run with no changes costs only the checks and the start fee. Extraction failures, robots.txt blocks, fetch errors and duplicates are free. The current prices are on the Store page; Apify's free plan includes $5 of credit a month, enough to check a 250-page docs site every day for a month when only a few pages change.

Links

  • Website Change Tracker on the Apify Store

title: A Practical Website Accessibility Review for Small Teams
description:
Accessibility improvements are easier to make when a team turns them into repeatable checks instead of a last-minute audit. You do not need to begin with a specialist tool or a redesign. Start with the most important tasks visitors come to complete, then check whether people can complete them in different ways.

1. Try the main journey with a keyboard

Put the mouse aside and use Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Space, and the arrow keys. Follow a path such as opening the navigation, finding a service, submitting a contact form, or completing a purchase. A visible focus indicator should make it clear where you are. The order should make sense, and no control should trap the keyboard. If an element looks clickable but cannot be reached or activated from the keyboard, note its name and location for the developer.

2. Check headings and page structure

Headings should describe the section that follows and form a sensible outline. A page title should identify the page; section headings should help someone scan it. Use lists for related items and real buttons or links for actions rather than styling plain text to look interactive. This structure helps screen-reader users navigate and also makes dense pages easier for everyone to understand.

3. Make forms understandable

Every input needs a clear, persistent label. Instructions should appear before a person needs them, and required fields should be identified in text rather than by color alone. Test what happens with an empty submission and an invalid value: the error should explain the problem, point to the field, and preserve what the visitor already entered. Confirmation should be announced and easy to find.

4. Review contrast, images, and motion

Check text against its background in normal, hover, and disabled states. Give informative images concise alternative text that explains their purpose; decorative images should not create noise. Captions and transcripts can make media useful to more people. Avoid auto-playing motion, and respect reduced-motion settings where animation is not essential.

5. Recheck after every meaningful change

An automated checker can reveal missing labels or contrast issues, but it cannot judge whether instructions are clear or a workflow makes sense. Pair it with manual keyboard checks and, when possible, feedback from people who use assistive technology. Keep a short issue list with the page, steps to reproduce, expected behavior, and owner. Revisit it after updates because themes, plugins, and new content can introduce regressions.

A useful first pass is small: choose one high-value journey, document what blocks it, fix the biggest barriers, and test again. For more practical web-development reading, visit the MGTech Labs blog.
