title: You might not need a modal library: <dialog> and the popover API in React 19
description:
Most React apps pull in a dependency for modals, tooltips and dropdowns. They handle focus trapping, Escape, click outside, and rendering above everything else. In 2026 the browser does all of that for you. Here is how I used the native pieces when I rewrote my component library, and the few places where you still need some JavaScript.

A modal with <dialog> 

"use client";
import { useLayoutEffect, useRef } from "react";

export function Modal({ open, onClose, children }: {
  open: boolean;
  onClose: () => void;
  children: React.ReactNode;
}) {
  const ref = useRef<HTMLDialogElement>(null);

  useLayoutEffect(() => {
    const el = ref.current;
    if (!el) return;
    if (open && !el.open) el.showModal();
    if (!open && el.open) el.close();
  }, [open]);

  return (
    <dialog
      ref={ref}
      onClose={onClose}
      onClick={(e) => e.target === e.currentTarget && onClose()}
      className="rounded-xl p-0 backdrop:bg-black/40"
    >
      <div className="p-6">{children}</div>
    </dialog>
  );
}

showModal() puts the dialog in the top layer, so no portal and no z-index fights. Focus moves inside and returns to the trigger on close. Escape fires the close event, which we forward to onClose. A click on the dialog element itself (not its content) means the backdrop was clicked.

One extra line locks page scroll while any dialog is open:

html:has(dialog[open]) { overflow: hidden; }

Animating in and out 

dialog {
  opacity: 0;
  translate: 0 8px;
  transition: opacity .2s, translate .2s, overlay .2s allow-discrete, display .2s allow-discrete;
}
dialog[open] { opacity: 1; translate: 0 0; }
@starting-style { dialog[open] { opacity: 0; translate: 0 8px; } }

@starting-style defines where the enter animation starts, and allow-discrete keeps the dialog visible until the exit animation finishes. Wrap it in @media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) to respect user settings.

A dropdown with the popover API 

<button popoverTarget="menu">Options</button>
<div id="menu" popover="auto" role="menu">…</div>

popover="auto" closes on Escape and on a click outside, and opening one auto popover closes the others. What the browser does not do yet in every engine is anchor the popover to its button, so I listen for the toggle event and set top/left from getBoundingClientRect(), flipping to the other side when there is no room. Once CSS anchor positioning works in every browser, even that part can go.

Accordion with <details name> 

<details name="faq"><summary>Is there a refund?</summary>…</details>
<details name="faq"><summary>Can I use it for clients?</summary>…</details>

Giving several <details> the same name makes them exclusive: opening one closes the others.

What is left for JavaScript

  • Positioning popovers and tooltips.
  • Arrow-key navigation inside menus.
  • Tooltips that open on hover and focus, which use popover="manual".

That is roughly a hundred lines, compared with several dependencies.

The result

I used these pieces to rebuild my old react-bootstrap library as Bon UI: 30+ components, React 19 + Tailwind CSS 4, zero runtime dependencies, about 13 KB of JS gzipped. You can browse every component in the Storybook at https://ui.bontemplates.com.

What do you still reach for a library for? I'm curious which native APIs people already trust in production.

title: MaxRAMPercentage vs Xmx: Sizing Java Heap in Containers
description:
Your Java service runs in a Kubernetes pod with a memory limit, and you have to decide how big the heap may grow. There are two ways to say it: a fixed -Xmx, or a percentage with -XX:MaxRAMPercentage. This guide explains how MaxRAMPercentage vs Xmx behaves inside a container, which one to pick, and how to choose the number so the pod is not OOMKilled. It is written for engineers who deploy JVM services on Kubernetes and have to defend the setting in a review.

“Shipping container stacks – Port of Rotterdam – 2014 – 2” by AgainErick, CC BY-SA 4.0

What the JVM does when you set nothing

Since container support is on by default, the JVM reads the cgroup memory limit instead of the node’s RAM. The java command reference says the default for -XX:+UseContainerSupport is true, and that the VM uses the detected memory and processor count to allocate resources.

The same reference lists these heap defaults, all measured against the memory the JVM considers available (capped by -XX:MaxRAM, which defaults to the available memory or 128 GB, whichever is lower):

  • -XX:MaxRAMPercentage: 25 percent.
  • -XX:InitialRAMPercentage: 1.5625 percent.
  • -XX:MinRAMPercentage: 50 percent, applied to small heaps of roughly 125 MB.

Microsoft’s guide to containerizing Java applications turns that into a table of default maximum heap by available memory: up to 256 MB gives 50 percent, 256 MB to 512 MB gives about 127 MB, and above 512 MB gives 25 percent. The practical result is that a 2 GiB container with no flags gets a heap of only about 512 MiB. That is safe but wasteful, which is why most teams change it.

Watch the naming trap: despite its name, -XX:MinRAMPercentage does not set a minimum heap. As the Microsoft guide points out, it sets the maximum percentage for systems with up to 256 MB of RAM. To set a starting heap, use -Xms or -XX:InitialRAMPercentage.

MaxRAMPercentage vs Xmx: how they differ

-Xmx is an absolute size and is equivalent to -XX:MaxHeapSize according to the same reference. -XX:MaxRAMPercentage is relative: the JVM multiplies the percentage by the memory it detected at startup. Everything else follows from that.

Question -Xmx -XX:MaxRAMPercentage
Value depends on the pod limit No, you must keep it in sync by hand Yes, it follows the limit automatically
Same manifest for several sizes Needs per-size config Works unchanged
Predictable exact heap Yes Only after you do the arithmetic
Risk if the limit is lowered later Heap may now exceed the limit, so the pod is OOMKilled Heap shrinks with the limit

If both are set, the explicit -Xmx is what ends up as the maximum heap. Do not rely on memory for this; check it on your JDK, as shown later.

Why the heap cannot equal the container limit

Kubernetes enforces memory limits reactively: the resource management documentation says the kernel enforces them through cgroups, and a container that goes over can be OOM-killed. The JVM uses much more than the heap: metaspace (unlimited by default, per the java reference for -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize), thread stacks, the code cache, direct buffers and GC structures. The Microsoft guide states it plainly: do not set the maximum heap equal to the container memory, because that can cause container OOM errors and crashes. It suggests 75 percent of container memory for the heap as a starting point.

To see where the rest goes in your own service, use the memory-pool method from Java OOMKilled in Kubernetes: Find the Memory Pool with NMT. For a quick estimate, the JVM Container Memory Calculator adds heap, metaspace and direct memory for you.

Choosing the percentage: a worked example

The numbers below are hypothetical and computed from the limit alone. The “left for non-heap” column is limit minus heap.

Memory limit 25% (default) 50% 75% Left at 75%
512Mi 128Mi 256Mi 384Mi 128Mi
1024Mi 256Mi 512Mi 768Mi 256Mi
2048Mi 512Mi 1024Mi 1536Mi 512Mi
4096Mi 1024Mi 2048Mi 3072Mi 1024Mi

A percentage hides an important fact: non-heap memory does not grow in proportion to the limit. A service needing roughly the same metaspace, stacks and code cache will have a much larger share of a 512Mi pod taken up by them than of a 4096Mi pod. So 75 percent can be fine at 4096Mi and too high at 512Mi. A better way to choose is to work backwards from a measurement:

  1. Measure non-heap memory under load (NMT, see the link above). Suppose, hypothetically, it is 280Mi.
  2. Add a safety margin for spikes, for example 100Mi. Non-heap budget: 380Mi.
  3. Subtract from the limit: with a 1024Mi limit, the heap may use 1024 – 380 = 644Mi.
  4. Divide: 644 / 1024 = 62.9 percent. Round down to 62.

For a 512Mi limit with a measured 200Mi of non-heap plus a 64Mi margin, the result is (512 – 264) / 512 = 48.4 percent, so 48. Note that this is below the 50 percent the JVM would already use for tiny heaps, which shows why small pods need measuring rather than a blanket 75.

The Kubernetes QoS Class Checker is useful at this point to confirm how your requests and limits translate: Mi and M are different units, and a limit written as 1G is 1,000,000,000 bytes, not 1024Mi.

A ready-to-use Deployment snippet

The manifest below sets the limit and makes the heap follow it. Requests equal limits, so the memory is reserved, which is the condition under which Microsoft recommends setting the initial heap equal to the maximum.

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: orders-api
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: orders-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: orders-api
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: registry.example.com/orders-api:1.0.0
        resources:
          requests:
            memory: "1024Mi"
          limits:
            memory: "1024Mi"
        env:
        - name: JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
          value: "-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=62 -XX:InitialRAMPercentage=62"
  • requests.memory equal to limits.memory reserves the whole amount for the container.
  • JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS is read by the JVM at startup, so the same image works with any command line.
  • MaxRAMPercentage=62 gives a heap of about 635Mi on a 1024Mi limit; InitialRAMPercentage=62 starts the heap at that size so the JVM does not resize it repeatedly.

Verify what the JVM actually chose

Never trust the arithmetic alone. Run the same flags under the same limit and read the result. With Docker, you can reproduce a Kubernetes limit locally:

docker run --rm --memory=1g eclipse-temurin:21-jre \
  java -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=62 -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version \
  | grep -E 'MaxHeapSize|MaxRAMPercentage|InitialHeapSize'

Here --memory=1g sets a 1 GiB cgroup limit, -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal prints every flag after ergonomics, and grep keeps the three that matter. MaxHeapSize is in bytes, so divide by 1048576 to get MiB. To test the precedence rule for your JDK, add -Xmx256m to the same command and compare the output.

For a running pod, ask the live process:

kubectl exec deploy/orders-api -- jcmd 1 VM.flags
kubectl exec deploy/orders-api -- jcmd 1 GC.heap_info

VM.flags shows the effective MaxHeapSize, and GC.heap_info shows how much of it is in use. This assumes the JDK image includes jcmd and the Java process is PID 1; a JRE-only or distroless image will not have the tool.

When a fixed Xmx is still the better choice

  • You run one tuned service and want an exact, reviewed heap size in the manifest.
  • The same image runs with very different limits and you want the heap to stay constant while only the limit changes, for example in a load test.
  • Your measurements show non-heap memory is stable, so subtracting a fixed amount is more accurate than a percentage.

If you use -Xmx, put a comment next to the memory limit in the manifest and change them together. The usual failure is somebody lowering the limit during a cost review and leaving the old -Xmx in place.

Key takeaways

  • The default maximum heap is 25 percent of the detected memory for containers above 512 MB, so an untuned 2 GiB pod uses only about 512 MiB of heap.
  • Prefer -XX:MaxRAMPercentage when the same image runs with different limits; prefer -Xmx when you want one exact, reviewed value.
  • Never set the heap equal to the container limit; 75 percent is a reasonable start for larger pods, and small pods need a measured value.
  • Work backwards: limit minus measured non-heap memory minus a margin, divided by the limit.
  • -XX:MinRAMPercentage is not a minimum heap; use -XX:InitialRAMPercentage or -Xms.
  • Confirm the result with -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal or jcmd VM.flags instead of trusting the calculation.

Conclusion

Use a percentage when you want the heap to follow the pod limit, use -Xmx when you want a fixed number, and in both cases leave room for everything the JVM keeps outside the heap. Measure that room once, derive the percentage from it, and check the effective value on the real container.

Related reading

  • Java OOMKilled in Kubernetes: Find the Memory Pool with NMT
  • JVM Container Memory Calculator
  • Kubernetes QoS Class Checker

title: New FMCSA authority leads and DOT number lookup in Python
description:
Every working day FMCSA grants operating authority to a couple of hundred new carriers and brokers. Each one needs insurance on file before the authority goes active, and most need factoring, an ELD, fuel cards and a dispatcher in their first weeks. On the other side of the market, brokers need to check before every load that a carrier's authority is active, that insurance is on file and that there is no out-of-service order.

All of that is public, but it is spread across FMCSA's company census, operating-authority history and out-of-service orders, and since FMCSA moved registrations to its new Motus system the authority data sits in different datasets than older guides describe. The FMCSA API joins them into one record per carrier, updated daily. This post builds a new-authority lead feed and a carrier check in Python.

Disclosure: I'm Aurelix, and I built the FMCSA API tool. It's a paid tool (prices below).

What each record holds

  • dot_number, legal_name, dba_name, docket_numbers (MC/MX/FF), status, entity_types (carrier, broker, shipper...), carrier_operation.
  • Contacts as FMCSA publishes them: physical_address, mailing_address, phone, cell_phone, email, company_officer_1 and _2.
  • Fleet: power_units, trucks, tractors and trailers owned or leased, total_drivers, cdl_drivers, cargo_types, hazmat.
  • authorities: each docket's authority type and status, with BIPD insurance required and on file, and cargo insurance and bond required and on file.
  • out_of_service with date and reason, safety_rating, mcs150_date, and safer_url for the SAFER snapshot.
  • In the authority feed: event (granted, applied, suspended, reinstated...), event_date and FMCSA's event_reason.

Carriers whose authority was granted yesterday 

pip install apify-client

import csv
import os

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient(os.environ["APIFY_TOKEN"])
run = client.actor("aurelix/fmcsa-carrier-api").call(
    run_input={
        "feed": "authority_events",
        "authorityEvents": ["granted"],
        "authorityTypes": ["property"],
        "states": ["TX", "OK", "LA"],
        "daysBack": 2,
        "incremental": True,
        "stateKey": "south-granted",
    }
)
rows = list(client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items())

with open("new_authority.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    w = csv.writer(f)
    w.writerow(["event_date", "dot", "name", "phone", "email", "city", "state", "power_units", "bipd_on_file"])
    for r in rows:
        bipd = max((a["bipd_insurance_on_file_usd"] or 0 for a in r["authorities"]), default=0)
        w.writerow([r["event_date"], r["dot_number"], r["legal_name"], r["phone"], r["email"],
                    r["physical_city"], r["physical_state"], r["power_units"], bipd])
print(len(rows), "new authorities")

With incremental on, the first run returns every grant in the window (up to maxResults, 200 by default). Each later run with the same stateKey skips grants it has already returned, so a daily schedule pays only for new ones. bipd_on_file shows who already has liability cover on file, which is the first thing an insurance agent wants to know.

Other events are worth watching too:

  • Applied ("authorityEvents": ["applied"]): carriers whose application is pending, before the grant. Very new applicants may not be in FMCSA's census yet; their record then takes the name, address and phone from the authority file (in_census is false).
  • Suspended and reinstated: carriers whose insurance lapsed or came back, for compliance teams and load boards.
  • New USDOT registrations ("feed": "new_registrations"): everyone who got a USDOT number, including private fleets and shippers, with filters for cargo, power units and drivers.

Vetting a carrier before you book 

run = client.actor("aurelix/fmcsa-carrier-api").call(
    run_input={"dotNumbers": ["53467"], "mcNumbers": ["MC-133655"]}
)
for r in client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items():
    active = [a for a in r["authorities"] if a["status"] == "Active"]
    print(r["legal_name"], "| active authorities:", len(active),
          "| BIPD on file:", max((a["bipd_insurance_on_file_usd"] or 0) for a in active) if active else 0,
          "| out of service:", r["out_of_service"], "| rating:", r["safety_rating"])

USDOT numbers can carry a USDOT prefix, leading zeros or come as SAFER links, and MC numbers can be written as MC-138328 or just 138328. A number FMCSA doesn't know is named in the run's status and not charged.

One detail if you compare with SAFER: power_units is the census figure FMCSA publishes in its open data, while SAFER's snapshot shows trucks plus buses (truck_units + bus_units here). On small fleets the two can differ by one or two.

Why this tool

  • Authority events by the day they happened: grants, applications, suspensions, reinstatements and more.
  • Insurance amounts required and on file per authority.
  • New registrations by date, plus USDOT, MC and name lookup.
  • Cargo and entity-type filters, and an only-new mode.
  • $1.00 per 1,000 records ($0.80 on paid plans).
  • What it doesn't cover: insurer names, policy numbers and a lead score.

If you sell to companies outside trucking that just started, Companies House Scraper does the same for new UK companies.

Limits

  • US FMCSA data only. No inspection, crash or CSA scores, and no insurer or policy number.
  • New applicants lag. Their census fields (fleet, cargo, email) can fill in a day or two later.
  • Motus era only for authority events. Older authority history isn't in the feed.
  • Contact details are as FMCSA publishes them. Many small carriers are owner-operators; follow telemarketing and email rules when you reach out.

Cost

You pay per record returned plus a small start fee. Records outside your filters, unknown numbers and records an earlier run already returned are free. The current prices are on the Store page; Apify's free plan includes $5 of credit a month, about 4,900 records.

Links

  • FMCSA API on the Apify Store
  • Example repo

title: Normalizing U.S. Company Names Before You Match Them
description:
Company names from different sources rarely agree character for character. "The Acme Group, L.L.C.", "ACME GROUP LLC" and "Acme Group" could be one entity or three. A normalized name gives you a stable comparison key, as long as you remember what the key discards.

What usually needs cleaning

Case and spacing. Pick one case, trim the ends, and collapse repeated spaces.

Punctuation. Periods, commas, and quotes are noise. Curly and straight apostrophes should end up identical, or be removed. An ampersand is safest as the word "and."

Accents. "Peña" and "Pena" should compare equal. Unicode normalization followed by an ASCII fold handles the common cases.

Legal endings. LLC and L.L.C., Inc. and Incorporated, Corp. and Corporation, Co. and Company, Ltd. and Limited, plus LP, LLP, and PLLC. Map the spellings to one short form and move it out of the name into a field of its own. It tells you the entity type, and "Acme Inc" and "Acme LLC" can be two separate legal entities.

A leading "The". Sources disagree on whether to keep it, so the key should not depend on it.

Trade names. A string like "Acme Group LLC dba Bright Path" holds two names. Split on dba, d/b/a, aka, or fka and keep both parts, labeled. Matching on the trade name alone can attach a record to the wrong legal entity.

Same name, different state

Identical names across states are common, because each state checks name availability only against its own registry. A key that ignores the state will merge strangers. Put the state, or the registry the record came from, into the key, and treat a cross-state match as a lead to confirm with other fields.

A teaching example

This is a teaching example, not production code. It returns the state, the core name, the entity-type ending, and any trade name found after dba, aka, or fka.

import re
import unicodedata
ENDINGS = {"INCORPORATED": "INC", "CORPORATION": "CORP", "COMPANY": "CO", "LIMITED": "LTD"}
ENDINGS.update({e: e for e in ("LLC", "INC", "CORP", "CO", "LTD", "LP", "LLP", "PLLC")})
ALIAS = re.compile(r"\b(?:D[./]?B[./]?A|A[./]?K[./]?A|F[./]?K[./]?A)\b\.?", re.I)

def words(text):
    text = unicodedata.normalize("NFKD", text).encode("ascii", "ignore").decode()
    text = text.upper().replace("&", " AND ").replace(".", "").replace("'", "")
    return re.findall(r"[A-Z0-9]+", text)

def company_key(raw, state):
    legal, *alias = ALIAS.split(raw, maxsplit=1)
    core = words(legal)
    ending = ENDINGS.get(core[-1], "") if core else ""
    while core and core[-1] in ENDINGS:
        core.pop()
    core = core[1:] if core[:1] == ["THE"] else core
    return state.upper(), " ".join(core), ending, " ".join(words("".join(alias)))

Two calls show the behavior, including an edge case:

company_key("The Acme Group, L.L.C. d/b/a Bright Path", "tx")
# ('TX', 'ACME GROUP', 'LLC', 'BRIGHT PATH')
company_key("Peña & Co.", "or")
# ('OR', 'PENA AND', 'CO', '')

The second result leaves a dangling AND, because "& Co." is really part of how that firm writes its name. Rules like these are blunt, and every ruleset produces cases like this one.

Order matters as well. Split off the trade name before removing punctuation, or "d/b/a" falls apart into loose letters that look like part of the name.

To keep the rules honest, build a small table of pairs you know are the same entity and pairs you know are not, and rerun it whenever you change a rule. A fix for one case often breaks another.

What the key throws away

Normalization is lossy on purpose. Store the raw name next to the key, keep the ending and the trade name as separate fields, and never treat an equal key as proof of identity. Confirm with something the name cannot fake: a registry ID, a formation date, or a principal address.

title: Policy and Disclosure: 2026 Edition
description: Since 2021, Project Zero has followed a “90 + 30” vulnerability disclosure policy, allowing vendors up to 90 days to remediate a vulnerability plus an extra 30 days “soak time” for patch rollout. Our goal was to encourage faster patching and give vendors time to deliver patches to users. The advent of AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and exploitation has changed the threat landscape such that the vulnerability remediation timeline encouraged by our disclosure policy is clearly insufficient. LLMs have increased the speed at which attackers can find and exploit vulnerabilities, alongside the risk that multiple parties, including malicious ones, discover the same bug. A vulnerability reported today presents a much higher immediate risk to users than one reported last year. In this new environment, it is crucial that vendors move towards remediating vulnerabilities faster.

title: Designing a dashboard a 70-year-old business owner can actually use
description:
Most dashboards are built by people who love dashboards. Charts, filters, tabs, a dozen KPIs above the fold. That works if your users are analysts. It doesn't work if your user runs a bakery, a dental clinic or a family hotel and has five minutes between customers.

That's the user we design for at Reviot, a reputation intelligence tool that shows business owners what's being said about them online. Our internal test is simple: could a 70-year-old owner open it and understand what's going on in under a minute?

Here are the principles we're applying. None of them are new, but they're easy to forget once you start adding features.

1. Answer the question before showing the data

Someone opening a reputation tool has one question: "Is anything wrong?" So the first thing on screen should be the answer, in words, not a chart they have to interpret.

  • Bad: a line chart of sentiment over the last 30 days.
  • Better: "3 new mentions this week. 1 needs your attention."

The chart can still exist. It just doesn't go first.

2. Compact by default, expandable on demand

Progressive disclosure is the whole game. Every item starts as one line: what happened, where, and whether it's good or bad. If the user wants more, they tap and it expands with the full detail.

You don't need a library for this. The native <details> element gets you surprisingly far:

<details class="mention">
  <summary>
    <span class="badge badge--negative">Needs attention</span>
    New 2-star review on Google Maps
  </summary>
  <p>"Waited 40 minutes and nobody apologised..."</p>
  <p>Posted 2 hours ago on Google Maps</p>
</details>

.mention summary {
  cursor: pointer;
  padding: 12px 16px;
  font-size: 1.05rem;
}

.mention[open] summary {
  font-weight: 600;
}

.badge--negative {
  background: #fde2e1;
  color: #9b1c1c;
  border-radius: 999px;
  padding: 2px 10px;
}

It's keyboard accessible, works without JavaScript and screen readers understand it out of the box.

3. Words over numbers, plain words over jargon

"Sentiment score: -0.42" means nothing to most people. "Negative" does. Same with "SERP", "share of voice" or "mention velocity". If a term needs a tooltip to make sense, it probably shouldn't be on the main screen.

4. Colour means one thing

Use colour only for status: good, neutral, needs attention. Not for branding, not for categories. When red always means "look at this", users learn it in seconds.

5. Let AI write the summary, but make it sound human

A lot of what we show is summarised by AI. The trap is text that reads like a machine-generated report: rigid, full of headings, the same structure every time. We aim for the opposite: short, natural sentences that sound like a colleague telling you what happened, with formatting only where it actually helps.

6. Bring the information to them

The best dashboard for a busy owner is the one they don't have to open. A short briefing at a time they choose, and alerts only when something really matters, beat a beautiful dashboard nobody checks.

Wrapping up

Designing for non-technical users isn't about dumbing things down. It's about deciding what matters, saying it plainly and keeping everything else one click away. Power users will still find the detail. Everyone else will finally understand what they're looking at.

If you've designed for a similar audience, I'd love to hear what worked for you in the comments.

AWS Batch now supports additional Kubernetes security context settings in Amazon EKS job definitions, including Linux capabilities, seccomp profiles, and pod-level settings. For EKS clusters that enforce the Kubernetes Pod Security Standards restricted profile, you can now run AWS Batch jobs with only the privileges and system calls they require.

To get started, use the RegisterJobDefinition API to set capabilities and seccompProfile in a container's securityContext, or set securityContext in podProperties to define pod-wide settings such as fsGroup. Container-level settings override pod-level defaults. You can configure these settings through the AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, AWS SDKs, or AWS CloudFormation.

The additional security context settings for AWS Batch on Amazon EKS are now supported in all AWS Regions where AWS Batch is available. For more information, see the Amazon EKS properties section in the AWS Batch User Guide.

title: Want to Become a Python Developer? Indentation Matters!
description:
When learning Python, you will learn variables, conditions, loops, and functions.

But there is one important thing you should understand: Indentation.

What is indentation?

Indentation means adding spaces at the beginning of a line.

Example:

if 10 > 5:
    print("Hello Python!")

Notice the spaces before print().

These spaces tell Python that the print() statement belongs inside the if condition.

What happens if we don't use indentation? 

if 10 > 5:
print("Hello Python!")

This code gives an IndentationError.

Why? Because Python expects spaces before the code inside the if condition.

Why is indentation important?

In Java, we use curly braces {} to separate code blocks.

if (10 > 5) {
    System.out.println("Hello");
}

But Python uses indentation instead.

if 10 > 5:
    print("Hello")

Where do we use indentation?

We use indentation in:

1. If conditions

if True:
    print("Correct")

2. Loops

for i in range(5):
    print(i)

3. Functions

def greet():
    print("Welcome!")

Tips to remember

  • Use 4 spaces for each indentation level.
  • Keep statements in the same block aligned.
  • Don't mix tabs and spaces.
  • Check indentation when you get an error.

Try this challenge!

Find the mistake in this code:

if 10 > 5:
    print("Hello")
  print("Python")

Can you fix it?

title: SurrealDB 4. The database and memory for every agent
description:
Author: Tobie Morgan Hitchcock

SurrealDB 4 is generally available today. It is the database and memory for every agent. And with it, SurrealDB Earth: serverless SurrealDB, built on Cloudflare, that scales to as many agents and users as you need, wherever they are. SurrealDB 4, the engine underneath, returns vectors, graphs, documents and full text in one query, in one transaction, and speaks PostgreSQL and MySQL over their own wire protocols, so users and agents can write the SQL they already know.

What is in the release

  • SurrealDB 4 is the database engine: a rebuilt query core, PostgreSQL SQL and MySQL support over their wire protocols, mql.js 1.0 and more than 240 fixes that no 3.x release contains. It runs embedded, on a laptop, in the browser, on your own servers or in SurrealDB Cloud.
  • SurrealDB Earth is serverless SurrealDB, built on Cloudflare, that scales to as many agents and users as you need, wherever they are. Every Earth database is its own isolated instance, with dedicated storage and commit log.
  • SurrealDS is distributed storage backed by object-storage for large SurrealDB clusters, in SurrealDB Cloud multi-node clusters and self-hosted Enterprise Edition deployments.
  • Agent Memory, launched in October, is a separate, managed service built on the same engine. Memory in one query is built into the engine, and Agent Memory is the managed way to get it.

Earth is where you run it, and SurrealDB 4 is what you run.

Try it now

If you already work in Postgres and do not want to touch SurrealQL yet, this is where you can start. SurrealDB does not need PostgreSQL installed: the listener lets Postgres clients talk to SurrealDB. On your machine, start SurrealDB 4 with the PostgreSQL listener on, then connect with psql and select the PostgreSQL dialect:

surreal db start --user root --pass secret --postgres-bind 127.0.0.1:5432 memory

psql "host=127.0.0.1 port=5432 user=root password=secret dbname=main/main options='-c dialect=pgsql'" -c 'SELECT 1;'

Both wire protocol listeners are off until you pass --postgres-bind or --mysql-bind. The PostgreSQL and MySQL protocol references list the connection options.

Why do agents need a database?

Most agents today are short-lived. Their state is rebuilt from a conversation history, a vector store or a set of external systems each time they run. As agents become persistent software, they need somewhere durable to keep:

  • long-term memory
  • the entities they know about and how those entities relate
  • current and historical state
  • tasks and intermediate results
  • documents and embeddings
  • permissions and identity
  • state shared transactionally with other agents

That state has to outlive whichever model or process happens to be running the agent at the time. SurrealDB is built to hold it, and SurrealDB Agent Memory, launched in October, is the managed product built on the same engine for exactly this job.

SurrealDB Earth: serverless SurrealDB on Cloudflare

SurrealDB Earth runs SurrealDB serverless on Cloudflare's global points of presence. Instead of provisioning a server and sizing it in advance, your application or agent creates databases on demand, and Earth decides where and how they run. Every Earth database is its own isolated instance, with dedicated storage and commit log, keeping each tenant's data separate. Each one is fully transactional and spins up and down on demand. Earth is web-native, so it connects over HTTP and WebSocket.

A database starts with its first query, in ~300ms from cold, and scales to zero instantly when idle, so you pay for requests and storage, with no idle server costs. Its data stays durable in Cloudflare's storage.

That makes fine-grained isolation practical. A SaaS platform can give each customer a database, an application can give each project one, and an AI platform can give an agent a persistent database of its own when it needs one. Each one's data is isolated, and removing a customer removes their database.

Scale is one reason to choose Earth, and not the only one. At peak, Earth handles 10+ billion rows per second, fully transactional.

Start free on Earth with no card, see the full Earth pricing.

SurrealDS: compute is replaceable, data stays durable

SurrealDS is distributed storage for workloads that grow beyond a single machine and runs on object-backed storage. It separates compute from durable storage, a pattern common in analytical databases and rare in transactional ones. Query nodes keep the state and caches they need to run queries quickly, while durable database pages live in shared object storage such as Amazon S3. Compute and storage each grow on their own, with no manual sharding.

The design assumes that nodes, disks and networks will fail. A write is acknowledged only once it is on two disks in two zones, and a replacement node recovers from the surviving copy and object storage rather than from the machine that failed. The protocol is model-checked. The aim is predictable behaviour when infrastructure stops being healthy, not only availability when everything is fine.

Together with Earth, it gives SurrealDB one range:

  • One agent: one lightweight database on Earth.
  • Many agents: many isolated databases, each its own Earth instance.
  • Large agent platforms: shared SurrealDS clusters, where many agents read and write the same data transactionally.

The data model is the same at each step. SurrealDS is available in SurrealDB Cloud multi-node clusters and self-hosted Enterprise Edition deployments.

Memory in one query

Memory in one query is built into the engine. An agent's memory is several kinds of data at once: what something means, what it is connected to, and what was actually said. SurrealDB returns all three in one statement, inside one transaction:

SELECT
    text,
    ->mentions->person.name AS people,
    search::score(1) AS relevance
FROM note
WHERE embedding <|5,40|> $question
    AND text @1@ 'contract renewal'
ORDER BY relevance DESC;

The example query finds the five notes nearest in meaning to the question, keeps those that mention a contract renewal, follows the graph to the people each note mentions, and ranks the results by relevance.

SurrealDB 4 adds PostgreSQL SQL and MySQL

PostgreSQL and MySQL clients connect to SurrealDB 4 over their own wire protocols. SurrealDB 4 adds PostgreSQL SQL, selected for each connection, and the MySQL protocol with MySQL SQL. Each listener is off until you turn it on, and a connection picks its dialect. That SQL runs through the same query planner as SurrealQL and reaches the same records, so an agent can write the SQL it was trained on.

The PostgreSQL dialect (select it with SET dialect = 'pgsql', or with options=-c dialect=pgsql when you connect) supports joins, grouping, aggregates, inserts with ON CONFLICT, schema changes, transactions, non-recursive WITH, COPY in text and CSV, and pgvector columns. The MySQL dialect supports joins, grouping, aggregates, non-recursive WITH and INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE.

This is a defined subset of SQL. Window functions, recursive CTEs and FULL OUTER JOIN are refused with a named error (0A000), and a few statements, such as CREATE SCHEMA in the PostgreSQL dialect, are accepted but change nothing. The PostgreSQL and MySQL protocol references list what is supported, what is refused and where behaviour differs.

For Node.js applications written for the MongoDB driver, mql.js 1.0 brings that driver's API to SurrealDB, including aggregation pipelines and Mongoose models. mongosh, Compass and MongoDB drivers in other languages cannot connect.

Faster at every size

A database scales furthest when each query costs less, so SurrealDB 4 rebuilds the query core to do less work for every query. Our benchmarks page goes into full details on the full results and how they were measured. We'll continue to expand our benchmarks for distributed database comparisons, vector search (HNSW throughput and recall), full-text search (BM25), graph query performance benchmarks, and more.

Stability is a feature

Some reliability work is not dramatic: finding edge cases, improving error handling, tightening correctness. It is a major part of this release. SurrealDB 4 includes more than 240 fixes to the database that no 3.x release contains, including more than 90 community bug reports on GitHub.

Rebuilding a query core can quietly change years of behaviour, so the change was made behind a safety net: while the new engine was built, every query test ran on both the earlier engine and the new one, and failed if the two disagreed. Today more than 4,500 SurrealQL test files run in CI.

Also in SurrealDB 4

SurrealDB also includes many other features such as:

  • ISO GQL support, for graph pattern matching
  • Schema migrations: existing rows convert as they are read, and the table is rewritten in the background
  • Filtered, exact and permission-aware vector search
  • Python SDK 3

Upgrading from 3.x

SurrealDB 4 is recommended for new (greenfield) database deployments. For existing deployments running 3.x, we recommend upgrading to SurrealDB 4.1 once it becomes available. Our internal testing of the migration process has shown promising results, but we want to validate it further against a broader range of real-world workloads and deployment scenarios from our community before recommending it for production migrations. This additional validation will help us deliver a more robust and reliable upgrade experience in 4.1.

For those who want to test upgrading from 3.x to SurrealDB 4, we've introduced an experimental in-place upgrade process designed to make the transition as seamless as possible, without requiring an export and import of your data. This requires explicit opt-in and should only be attempted after taking and verifying a backup, ideally using a copy of your data. The upgrade is one-way, meaning migrated datastores cannot be reopened with 3.x.

Before testing the upgrade, we recommend updating to the latest 3.3 release, running the new surreal db upgrade-check command to identify compatibility issues, and updating your SDKs.

A few additional changes to be aware of:

  • RocksDB and IndexedDB have been replaced by SurrealKV. Existing RocksDB datastores are automatically converted on first use, requiring additional time and disk space. Existing SurrealKV datastores also migrate to the new storage format.
  • Some indexes need rebuilding to preserve query correctness, while others can be rebuilt to benefit from performance improvements in SurrealDB 4.
  • SurrealML has been removed. Existing models must be exported, if needed, and removed before upgrading.

For detailed instructions, including how to enable the experimental upgrade, compatibility considerations and rollback options, see our 3.x to 4.0 upgrade guide.

Get started

Start free on SurrealDB Earth or install SurrealDB 4 to run it locally. See everything in the release. For deploying SurrealDS clusters, talk to our team.

The goal is one database that grows from a single lightweight workload to the infrastructure behind millions of users, devices and agents. SurrealDB 4 is the biggest step towards it so far. Thank you to everyone who reported a bug, opened a pull request or answered a question on Discord this year: a large part of this release is yours.

title: Count Rows, Not Errors: 7 Data Bugs I Reproduced
description:
To find out whether a write path loses data, count rows in the source of truth after a forced failure or a concurrent run; the error rate will not tell you. In seven bugs I reproduced over the past week, every call that lost or duplicated data returned success, and one independent count caught each bug.

This story was written with the assistance of an AI writing program. Each case ran on the real software (PostgreSQL 16.4, Kafka 4.4.0, Elasticsearch 7.17.29, Redis 8.10.2, SQLite 3.46.1); only the external payment and webhook providers were simulated. Each section ends with the check that caught the bug.

1. A Caught Exception Rolled Back the Row It Protected

A migration dual-writes in one Spring @Transactional method: insert into the legacy table, then into the new one inside a try/catch that counts failures and queues the id for repair. I left out the new table's December partition and recorded 20 events, 10 in December.

All 20 calls returned normally, and nothing was logged at WARN or ERROR. The legacy table, the source of truth, held 10 rows: PostgreSQL aborts the whole transaction when one statement fails, so COMMIT silently rolled back (pgjdbc 42.7.8 and 42.2.5). None of the 10 queued ids existed in legacy, so repair had nothing to copy.

// as written: 20 calls OK, the legacy table keeps 10 of 20 rows
@Transactional
public void record(OrderEvent e) {
  legacyInsert(e);
  try { v2Insert(e); } catch (DataAccessException ex) { caught(e, ex); }
}
// fix: nested is a TransactionTemplate with PROPAGATION_NESTED (a savepoint)
@Transactional
public void recordNested(OrderEvent e) {
  legacyInsert(e);
  try { nested.executeWithoutResult(s -> v2Insert(e)); } catch (DataAccessException ex) { caught(e, ex); }
}

The savepoint kept all 20 legacy rows, as did autosave=always on the JDBC URL. 2,000 clean writes took 3,150/3,005 ms instead of 2,646/2,850.

Check: after a forced failure, count the legacy table, not the failure counter.

2. Exactly-Once Kafka Paid 20 of 40 Payouts Twice

One partition, 40 payouts, read_committed, one transaction per poll of 20. Nothing crashed. One provider call took 12 s, past max.poll.interval.ms (10 s), so a second consumer took the partition and restarted at offset 0. The first, still alive, paid the other 14 payouts of its batch after the handover; its CommitFailedException came about 8 s later.

With a fresh UUID as the idempotency key per attempt, 20 of 40 payouts were paid twice, in both runs and under KIP-848. Kafka looked perfect: committed offset 40, 40 output records. A key derived from the payout, "payout:" + payoutId, turned 60 provider calls into 40 transfers.

Check: count transfers per payout id at the provider.

3. A Conditional UPDATE Protected the Row, Not the Charge

Two checkouts of one order, 0 to 20 ms apart, each read pending, called the provider, then ran UPDATE ... WHERE status = 'pending'. The loser's UPDATE matched 0 rows after its charge went out: 100 of 100 orders were charged twice. Claiming before the call brought it to 0:

def claim(conn, oid):
    attempt = uuid.uuid4().hex
    cur = conn.execute("UPDATE orders SET status = 'charging', attempt_id = %s WHERE id = %s AND status = 'pending'", (attempt, oid))
    if cur.rowcount == 0:
        return 'skip'
    provider(oid)
    cur = conn.execute("UPDATE orders SET status = 'paid', updated_at = now() WHERE id = %s AND status = 'charging' AND attempt_id = %s", (oid, attempt))
    return 'paid' if cur.rowcount == 1 else 'lost'

In production, also pass attempt_id to the provider as its idempotency key; my fake took none.

Check: fire two checkouts 0 to 20 ms apart and count provider calls.

4. The Checkpoint Reached the Max and Still Skipped Events

A projector read WHERE global_seq > checkpoint on a BIGSERIAL column. The number is assigned at INSERT; the row becomes visible at COMMIT. If 101 commits before 100, the projector checkpoints 101 and never reads 100. With 8 concurrent writers the checkpoint reached max(global_seq) every run, yet 201 to 214 of 3,228 events were never projected. One writer missed 0.

Storing pg_current_xact_id() per event, reading only tx_id < pg_snapshot_xmin(pg_current_snapshot()) and checkpointing on (tx_id, global_seq) missed 0 in 8 runs. The price: any open write transaction stalls the projection.

Check: after the drain, events must equal projected rows.

5. bulk.close() Returned Before the Last Bulks Landed

An Elasticsearch reindex fed a BulkProcessor (5,000 actions, 2 concurrent requests), called close(), then swapped the alias. close() is awaitClose(0, NANOSECONDS), so two bulks, 10,000 documents, were still in flight. Counts through the alias right after the swap: 45,676, 68,830 and 70,116 of 100,000 (the 1 s refresh hid the rest). failedItems stayed 0. awaitClose(60, SECONDS) plus a refresh gave 100,000 in 3 of 3 runs.

Check: swap only after awaitClose returns true and the new count equals the source count.

6. A Webhook Got a 200 and Was Processed Zero Times

The handler claimed the delivery key in Redis with SET NX PX 30000, then processed. Processing threw, the handler returned 500, and the claim stayed. The retry at t=5 s hit the claim and got a 200 for "in progress"; most providers stop on any 2xx. At t=31 s the claim had expired with no done marker: processed 0 times. Releasing the claim in the catch (random token, Lua compare-and-delete) let the 5 s retry process it once. Answer 409 for in-progress claims.

Check: make the handler throw once, replay 5 s later, count successful runs.

7. Eight SQLite Workers Committed 2,000 Times and Kept 250

Eight Python processes each added 1 to one row 250 times: read, update, commit. All 2,000 commits succeeded; the counter ended at 250 in six of six runs. Default sqlite3 opens the transaction at the UPDATE, after the read, and the 5 s busy timeout turned contention into waiting, not errors. BEGIN IMMEDIATE before the read gave 2,000. Full write-up here.

Check: N workers add 1 M times each; assert the result is N × M.

What I Test Now

Error rates count calls that failed; all seven bugs lived in calls that succeeded. Before I trust a write path:

  • Force one failure, then count the source of truth.
  • Count external side effects per business id.
  • Test with concurrent writers: the checkpoint gap was 0 with one writer, about 200 with eight.
  • Count before switching reads: alias, checkpoint, new table.
  • Replay a delivery after a failure; claims and dedupe keys break on the second attempt.

title: ISC Stormcast For Friday, November 13th, 2026 https://isc.sans.edu/podcastdetail/10178, (Fri, Nov 13th)
Building AppTracer: a spec-driven time tracker with Angular, Spring Boot and an AI assistant
description:
Angular 22, Spring Boot 3 and PostgreSQL, ten functional specifications, and an AI coding assistant kept on a short leash

Most teams still track their time in a spreadsheet that nobody enjoys filling in. I wanted to build the opposite: a small, focused app where logging a day takes seconds and a manager sees the team's week at a glance.

The result is AppTracer, open source under the MIT license:

  • Live demo: https://apptracer-demo.onrender.com (demo accounts are listed in the README, data reset every night)
  • Code: https://github.com/SalaheddineBns/apptracer

This article is less about the features than about how it was built: an AI coding assistant wrote most of the code, and what kept it on track was a set of specifications with numbered rules and tests named after them. Along the way, a few problems turned out to be more interesting than expected.

What the app does

  • Employees log what they worked on by the hour, the whole day, or a range of days, choosing an activity type (project work, meeting, spec reading, code review…).
  • Managers get a read-only view of their team's week, member by member.
  • Administrators manage accounts, teams, job titles, activity types, projects and the length of a standard day.
  • Everyone only sees the projects of their own team.
  • The whole interface is available in French and English, works with the keyboard and screen readers, and is usable from 375 px wide.

Start from the rules, not the screens

Before writing any code for a feature, I wrote its functional specification. Each one contains two things (the prefixes come from French: RG for règle de gestion, business rule, and CA for critère d'acceptation, acceptance criterion):

Business rules, each with an ID. For example:

RG-01-06: a time entry cannot overlap another entry of the same user.

Acceptance criteria, written as Given / When / Then with real dates and values:

Given an entry on Monday 5 October from 09:00 to 10:00,
when the same user logs 09:30–10:30 that day,
then the entry is refused with an overlap message.

Ten specifications later, this gives the project a property I now find hard to live without: every rule ID is cited in the code, and every acceptance criterion has a test named after it.

@DisplayName("CA-01-04 : 09:30-10:30 sur une saisie 09:00-10:00 donne 409 RG-01-06 avec la date")

(Test names are in French in the code base: the acceptance criterion ID is what links them to the specification.)

When a rule changes, searching for its ID finds the specification, the implementation and the tests in one go. Reviewing a change becomes a question of "does this match RG-xx-yy?" rather than "does this look right?".

The stack

  • Front end: Angular 22 with standalone components and signals, PrimeNG and Tailwind CSS.
  • Back end: Spring Boot 3 on Java 21, Spring Security, Flyway migrations, PostgreSQL 16.
  • Contract first: the OpenAPI contract is exported from the back end, and the TypeScript client used by Angular is generated from it. Nobody edits the client by hand, so the front and back end cannot silently drift apart.
  • Authentication: short-lived JWT access tokens, and refresh tokens that can be used only once (each renewal invalidates the previous one).
  • Tests: 600+ back-end tests (JUnit 5, Testcontainers on a real PostgreSQL) and 500+ front-end tests (Vitest).

Three problems worth sharing

1. Overlaps under concurrency

The service checks that a new entry does not overlap an existing one. That works, until two requests arrive at the same moment: both read the database, both see no conflict, both save.

The real safety net is in the database: a PostgreSQL exclusion constraint on the entry's time range, per user. Here is the actual migration:

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS btree_gist;

ALTER TABLE time_entries
  ADD COLUMN occupied tsrange GENERATED ALWAYS AS (
    CASE WHEN granularity = 'HOUR'
      THEN tsrange(start_date + start_time, start_date + end_time, '[)')
      ELSE tsrange(start_date::timestamp, (end_date + 1)::timestamp, '[)')
    END
  ) STORED;

ALTER TABLE time_entries
  ADD CONSTRAINT ex_time_entries_no_overlap
  EXCLUDE USING gist (user_id WITH =, occupied WITH &&)
  WHERE (deleted_at IS NULL);

Two details matter here. btree_gist is needed so that a GiST index can handle the plain equality on user_id. And the '[)' bounds make the end of a range exclusive, so 09:00–10:00 followed by 10:00–11:00 is allowed.

A generated column turns every entry into a time range: an hour slot for HOUR, whole days for DAY and RANGE (weekends included). The WHERE clause means a deleted entry no longer blocks anything.

The service check gives a clear error message in the normal case; the constraint guarantees correctness in the rare one. A dedicated test, CA-01-04 : deux requêtes simultanées, la contrainte SQL donne aussi 409 RG-01-06, fires two simultaneous requests and checks that the constraint answers with the same 409 and the same rule ID as the service check.

2. Durations that must never change after the fact

A "day" is not always 8 hours: the length of a standard day is an admin setting. If an admin changes it from 8 h to 7 h, should last month's entries suddenly be shorter? Clearly not.

So the duration is computed and frozen when the entry is saved, together with the standard day in force at that moment. Changing the setting only affects new entries; history is never rewritten.

3. A test that only failed in CI

One persistence test compared a timestamp in memory with the same timestamp read back from the database. It passed on my Mac and failed on GitHub Actions.

The reason: on Linux, Instant.now() returns nanosecond precision, while on macOS it stops at microseconds. PostgreSQL stores microseconds. On Linux, the value read back was truncated, so the two were not equal.

The fix was to compare with the value as stored, not with the one in memory (truncating with truncatedTo(ChronoUnit.MICROS) before saving works too). It is a small bug, but a good reminder that "works on my machine" can hide in the last three digits of a timestamp.

Deploying for free

The demo runs on free tiers:

  • One Docker image: Spring Boot serves the built Angular app itself, so there is a single URL and no CORS setup.
  • Render runs the container, and Neon hosts PostgreSQL.
  • A GitHub Actions job resets the demo every night: it drops the schema and redeploys, and the app recreates the demo accounts, a team and two weeks of sample entries at start-up.

The only trade-off is the free tier's cold start: the first visit after a quiet period can take about a minute.

How it was built

I wrote the specifications, made the architecture decisions and reviewed every step. An AI coding assistant wrote most of the code from those specifications.

What made this work was not the assistant on its own, but the structure around it: rules with IDs, acceptance criteria with concrete dates, a generated API client, and a test suite that fails loudly when something drifts from the specification. The specifications told the assistant what to build; the tests told me whether it did.

Try it, and contribute

  • Demo: https://apptracer-demo.onrender.com
  • Code: https://github.com/SalaheddineBns/apptracer

The repository has a contributing guide, issue templates and a few good first issues (end-to-end tests, a one-command Docker setup, extra CI checks). Feedback, issues and pull requests are welcome, and if you find the project useful, a star on GitHub helps other developers find it.

title: Everyone forgets the embed
description:
People put a lot of work into making their websites look nice. They pick the fonts, tune the spacing and argue about the shade of a button. Then they forget about the embed.

By the embed I mean the small card that shows up under a link when you paste it into Discord, Messenger or Slack. It has a title, a line of description, sometimes a coloured bar down the left side and a big image. It's usually the first thing anyone sees of your website, and it's the part almost nobody remembers to design.

I forgot too. When I started writing this, I checked what my own essay "On Walking" handed to Discord when someone pasted it. The title said "Stimmie". The description said I'm a software engineer with a lifelong passion for technology, and the picture was a screenshot of my homepage. Nothing on the card mentioned walking. Two more of my older essays previewed the exact same way, because I never gave them their own tags and they fell back to my homepage's. Someone scrolling past would have had no idea the link was an essay at all. I've fixed all three now.


On Walking, pasted into Discord before the fix.

I think it's easy to forget because you never see it while you're building. The embed doesn't live on your page. You write a few meta tags in the head of the page (og:title, og:description, og:image, and theme-color if you want Discord to tint the bar). Then you hand them to an app you don't own, and it draws your card however it likes. If you skip them, nothing breaks and nothing warns you. You only find out when someone else pastes your link.

That would be fine if people clicked through, but most don't. In 2016, researchers at Columbia and Inria followed a month of tweets linking to stories from the BBC, CNN, the New York Times, Fox and the Huffington Post. They found that 59 percent of the links shared in their sample were never clicked at all. A 2024 Penn State study of more than 35 million public Facebook posts found that about 75 percent of shares happened without the sharer clicking the link first. For a lot of people, the embed is the only part of your website they'll ever see.

The fix is cheap. Before you share anything, paste it into a chat with yourself and look at the card. If it doesn't make you want to tap it, it won't make anyone else want to either.


The same link after the fix.

Further reading. Gabielkov, Ramachandran, Chaintreau and Legout, Social Clicks: What and Who Gets Read on Twitter? (SIGMETRICS 2016). Sundar and colleagues, Sharing without clicking on news in social media (Nature Human Behaviour, 2024). Discord's page on link previews, which lists every tag it reads.

Originally published at stimmie.dev. Source and images on GitHub.

title: How Shopify Killed Third-Party Cookies (And How to Build Embedded Apps with App Bridge 4.0 in 2026)
description:
If you’ve tried building an embedded Shopify app recently using older Express or cookie-based session tutorials, you probably ran into the dreaded blank white screen on Safari, iOS, or modern Chrome.

Here is why that happens—and how the modern 2026 Shopify stack completely solves it with App Bridge 4.0 and Header-Based JWTs.

The Death of Third-Party Cookies in Iframes

Historically, Shopify apps ran inside an <iframe> on admin.shopify.com. Developers set traditional HTTP cookies to maintain merchant sessions:

However:

  1. Apple Safari ITP (Intelligent Tracking Prevention) blocks all cross-site cookies inside iframes by default.
  2. Google Chrome Privacy Sandbox has systematically phased out third-party cookie access.
  3. If your app attempts to read document.cookie or expects session cookies in an embedded iframe, the request fails silently, leaving merchants with a broken spinner or white screen.

The Modern Solution: App Bridge 4.0 & Cryptographic Session Tokens

In modern Shopify architecture, we never use cookies. Instead, authentication relies on short-lived, cryptographically signed JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) generated directly by Shopify's frontend client.

Step 1: Client-Side Token Injection

With Shopify App Bridge 4.0, you don't even need bulky npm packages on the frontend. A single script tag in your root document handles everything:

<script 
  src="https://cdn.shopify.com/shopifycloud/app-bridge.js" 
  data-api-key="YOUR_SHOPIFY_API_KEY">
</script>

App Bridge automatically intercepts all native window.fetch requests and injects a 60-second signed JWT in the request headers:

Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9...

Step 2: Backend JWT Verification

On your backend (React Router / Remix or Node), you verify the token using your SHOPIFY_API_SECRET and extract the authenticated shop domain:

import crypto from "node:crypto";

export async function verifyShopifySessionToken(request: Request) {
  const authHeader = request.headers.get("Authorization");
  if (!authHeader || !authHeader.startsWith("Bearer ")) {
    throw new Response("Unauthorized: Missing Bearer Token", { status: 401 });
  }

  const token = authHeader.split(" ")[1];
  const [headerB64, payloadB64, signatureB64] = token.split(".");

  // Verify HMAC SHA-256 signature against your App Secret
  const calculatedSig = crypto
    .createHmac("sha256", process.env.SHOPIFY_API_SECRET!)
    .update(`${headerB64}.${payloadB64}`)
    .digest("base64url");

  if (calculatedSig !== signatureB64) {
    throw new Response("Forbidden: Invalid Token Signature", { status: 403 });
  }

  const payload = JSON.parse(Buffer.from(payloadB64, "base64url").toString("utf-8"));

  // Extract authenticated merchant domain
  const destUrl = new URL(payload.dest);
  return { shop: destUrl.hostname };
}

No cookies. No Safari ITP blocks. 100% reliable across every modern browser.

Want the Complete Zero-to-Production Guide?

Building a production-ready Shopify app in 2026 involves more than just auth. You need:

  • GraphQL Admin API Leaky Bucket rate-limit handling & cursor pagination
  • Webhook HMAC verification with Dead-Letter Queues (DLQ)
  • Prisma Multi-Tenant Database modeling
  • Shopify Billing API for recurring SaaS subscriptions
  • Multi-stage Docker & Fly.io zero-cost cloud deployment

I compiled everything into a comprehensive 59-page engineering handbook:

👉 Get The Modern Shopify App Development Blueprint on Gumroad

It includes complete starter code, architectural blueprints, and a 25-point App Store pre-flight checklist.

Drop any questions below about App Bridge 4.0 or GraphQL Admin API—happy to help!

title: Honest intermediate states for small web tools
description:
A spinner tells someone that the interface is busy. It does not, by itself, tell them whether a request was accepted, where work is happening, whether a usable result exists or when it is safe to try again.

Disclosure: I maintain the six projects referenced below. This article proposes interface copy and transition rules. It does not report changes shipped to these sites, user research or product acceptance tests. The linked pages supply published constraints; the example messages are design suggestions.

1. A result can be ready while copying is incomplete

Small Text Studio provides its note on what to do when Copy fails. The fallback is to select the displayed result and use the system copy command when the site's button cannot access the clipboard.

Those are two separate states: a result exists, and the clipboard operation did not complete. Replacing the result with a generic error would hide the useful part.

Suggested copy:

The result is still shown below. Try selecting it and using your system Copy command.

Do not show “copied” merely because a click handler ran. If success is unknown, keep the output available and describe the remaining action. Pasting into another application is a further handoff with its own behavior.

2. A guide date is not a checked game version

PokéSurvivor Hub provides its note separating announcement dates from the guide's update date. Both dates can be useful without identifying the game build on a particular device.

A broad “up to date” badge can collapse these different facts. Keep the date's role visible, and leave an unknown running version unknown.

Suggested copy:

Guide updated: [date]. Announcement dated: [date]. The running game version has not been checked in this view.

Fill those fields only from their respective sources. A newly edited reference page is not evidence that a player's session changed version.

3. Rejection needs an explanation, not a universal retry button

WatermarkPilot provides its note on rejected formats and keeping your originals. The photo page identifies format and provenance-related restrictions and warns that exports may not retain camera or color-profile metadata.

Suggested copy when an input is refused:

No export is available for this input. Check the format and metadata restrictions, and keep your original.

“Try again” does not explain whether the same input can succeed. Changing an extension or choosing a JPG/PNG is not a universal recovery guarantee: a supported format still has other eligibility conditions. Keep the refusal reason separate from a processing fault and retain the cautious “may not” wording about metadata.

4. A service job needs evidence for each stage

Sonify provides its note on queue load and when the file is offered. The page describes server-side work, timing that depends on the source and queue load, and a file being offered after verification finishes.

Suggested copy while there is no available result:

No download is available yet. Check the current processing stage.

Use a label such as “queued” only when the service actually reports that stage. A frontend timer cannot establish it. Do not promise cancellation of queued work from a page that makes no such promise.

Once a result is available, keep its deadline visible. The stated fifteen-minute window starts after completion, not before it or when the visitor opens the page. Access expiry and physical cleanup are different events; a disabled download alone does not prove physical erasure.

5. A local processing limit is not a server queue timeout

GifLoom provides its note that very complex jobs stop after 90 seconds. This describes a local processing limit. It is a different kind of event from waiting for a conversion service.

Suggested copy when processing has stopped and no usable result exists:

Processing stopped without a completed result. Keep the original and review the task settings before another attempt.

Only report a stop after the worker has actually stopped. Do not infer that another attempt will succeed immediately, or describe the event as a server cleanup problem. A page's local-processing declaration also does not prove the absence of every network request made by the website.

6. Clearing input and changing privacy choices can affect working state

Square Footage Calculator provides its note on what a reset or a privacy change clears. The page distinguishes entered measurements from calculated area and says withdrawing an active analytics choice refreshes the page and clears the current calculation.

Suggested copy before an action with that effect:

This action clears the current calculation. Copy or print any result you need first.

Keep the input, derived result and persistence rule separate. A displayed number is not a saved record. Likewise, unavailable controls should not look like a completed zero-area calculation. Show the actual unavailable state and a relevant next step instead of a plausible-looking result.

Use state labels as small factual claims

For each transition, ask three questions: what event has actually happened, what remains unresolved, and what action is currently available?

“Result displayed,” “copy incomplete,” “input refused,” “service still working,” “local job stopped” and “calculation cleared” describe different events. Give each one a specific message rather than routing all of them through the same success or error banner.

These remain design suggestions from the maintainer of the six linked projects. Testing an implemented transition needs its own observations and results.

title: Diagnose Vercel CLI setup problems with vercel doctor
description:
Vercel CLI now includes vercel doctor, which checks your setup and shows the command that fixes each problem it finds.

It checks the CLI version and install, your login and current team, the project link, and your project configuration in vercel.json. It also reports active incidents from the Vercel status page.

Each check reports OK, Warning, Failed, or Skipped. When vercel upgrade can't update the installed CLI, the install check shows where the CLI runs from and how to reinstall it.

Doctor runs without a login or a linked project, and it never prompts, logs in, or links a project, so coding agents can run it before guessing at a fix. Add --json to get each check's status and suggested commands as structured output.

Update to the latest CLI version and run vercel doctor to check your setup, or read the doctor command reference.
