title: I built an SSTable storage engine
description:
Hello people!

I've been working on a project called Stryx — github, for a couple of weeks. I don't really have a motivation for as to why I built it — I read about "Sorted String Tables" somewhere, found them cool, coincidentally at the same time I'd been itching to build something involving binary formats. So I thought it would be fun, and here we are.

Contents

Part I: Background

  1. What's an SSTable?
  2. Designing the Stryx Table

Part II: The File Format

  1. How Records are Stored
  2. Index
  3. Filter
  4. Footer, and How open() Works

Part III: Reading and Writing

  1. The Whole Flow: get(b"cherry")
  2. Building a Table
  3. Reading Records

Part IV: Behavior, Performance and Getting started

  1. Compression, Concurrency and Caching
  2. Benchmarks
  3. Limitations
  4. Getting Started

If you'd rather see the format before reading about it, I built an interactive explorer that walks through the exact byte layout described below —

→ Explore the Stryx table format

Part I: Background

1. What's an SSTable?

  • It's essentially a file-based storage format that stores key-value pairs in sorted order. The records are arranged lexicographically by their keys, which makes looking up records and performing range queries efficient compared to scanning an entire file.

  • SSTables are immutable, meaning that once the table has been written and finalized, its contents aren't modified (new data is written into a new table). This makes the format relatively straightforward to read concurrently and also avoids the complexity of managing in-place updates.

  • They're commonly used as building blocks in storage engines and databases, often alongside structures such as memtables. Systems like RocksDB and LevelDB use this general approach.

For Stryx, I wanted to explore this storage model at a lower level: how records are encoded, organized into blocks, indexed, fetched, their metadata, and so on.

2. Designing the Stryx Table

A Stryx table is a single file that you write once and never touch again. Records are sorted by key, grouped into blocks, and a small amount of metadata at the end of the file describes how to find everything.

The reader starts by locating the footer at the end of the file, which tells it where the other sections are (all integers are little-endian). Both the metadata section and the optional filter section are prefixed with an 8-byte little-endian length, which lets the reader seek past one to find the next.

+------------------------------------------+
| data block 0 ... data block N-1          |  Sorted records, optionally compressed
+------------------------------------------+
| index                                    |  First key, offset, and size per block
|                                          |  Entry count + CRC32C
+------------------------------------------+
| metadata (length-prefixed)               |  Record count, block count, key range,
|                                          |  compression, file size, index location
+------------------------------------------+
| filter section (optional, len-prefixed)  |  Binary Fuse filter + CRC32C
+------------------------------------------+
| footer (29 bytes)                        |  Index offset/size, filter type, version, magic
+------------------------------------------+
 ^                                          ^
 |                                          |
file start                            file end (footer starts at len - 29)

To understand how the rest of the format works, let's start with how a single record is represented.

Part II: The File Format

3. How Records are Stored

For this walkthrough let's take these three records:

Key     Value
apple   red
banana  yellow
cherry  red

First record (encoded): key apple and value red.

record = [key_len: u16][value_len: u32][key][value]
Field Value Bytes Why it exists
key_len 5 05 00 Keys are variable-length, so the reader needs to know where the key ends. A u16 allows keys up to 65,535 bytes.
value_len 3 03 00 00 00 Same idea for the value. A u32 allows values up to 4,294,967,295 bytes.
key apple 61 70 70 6c 65 The raw key bytes, which are compared lexicographically.
value red 72 65 64 The raw value bytes. Stryx doesn't interpret them.

That's 6 bytes of header plus 8 bytes of payload, so 14 bytes in total. Notice that the integers are little-endian: 5 as a u16 is 05 00, with the low byte first. Both keys and values are opaque bytes, so there is no schema and no type information in the format.

Records Inside a Block

Writing records one after another is straightforward, but there's a small problem: records are variable-length, so you can't jump straight to the second record without knowing where it starts.

That's why Stryx groups records into blocks and keeps an offset table for each block. The block also stores a record count and a checksum:

[record 0][record 1] ... [record N-1]
[offset 0: u32] ... [offset N-1: u32]
[record_count: u32][crc32c: u32]

Here is a block holding apple and banana:

Block layout

byte 0                                      byte 32
  |                                            |
  v                                            v
  +------------------+------------------------+
  | apple record     | banana record          |
  | 14 bytes         | 18 bytes               |
  +------------------+------------------------+
  | offset 0 = 0     | offset 1 = 14          |  8 bytes
  +------------------+------------------------+
  | record_count = 2                          |  4 bytes
  +-------------------------------------------+
  | CRC32C                                    |  4 bytes
  +-------------------------------------------+

  Total block size: 48 bytes

The record area is 32 bytes. The offset table takes another 8 bytes, followed by 4 bytes for the record count and 4 bytes for the CRC32C, making the entire block 48 bytes.

Each part does the following:

  • Offset table: lets the reader binary-search within the block. It jumps to the middle record, reads its key, compares, and repeats. Without it, a lookup would have to scan the block.

  • record_count: sits at a fixed position at the end, so the reader can read backwards from there and find the offset table.

  • crc32c: computed in finish() over everything before it (records, offsets and count) and appended last. It catches accidental corruption such as bit rot or a truncated write.

How Big Is a Block?

Records are packed into blocks until the next record would exceed the configured block_size target. A record is never split across blocks, so blocks are approximately the target size rather than exactly that size. A single record bigger than the target simply gets a block of its own.

Since the records are sorted, each block can be represented in the index by its first key. That brings us to the next part of the format.

4. Index

A table with a million records might have thousands of blocks, and the reader needs to know which one to read. The index answers that. It is sparse, with one entry per block rather than per record. Each entry holds:

+-----------------------------+
| key_len                 u16 |
+-----------------------------+
| first_key             bytes |
+-----------------------------+
| offset                  u64 |
+-----------------------------+
| size                    u32 |
+-----------------------------+
| uncompressed_block_size u32 |
+-----------------------------+

                  Index
+------------------------------------------------+
| Entry 0                                        |
|                                                |
| first_key:              "apple"                |
| offset:                 0                      |
| size:                   48                     |
| uncompressed_block_size: 48                    |
|                                                |
+------------------------------------------------+
| Entry 1                                        |
|                                                |
| first_key:              "cherry"               |
| offset:                 48                     |
| size:                   27                     |
| uncompressed_block_size: 27                    |
|                                                |
+------------------------------------------------+

                    |
                    | Each entry points to a block
                    v

+----------------------+----------------------+
| Block 0              | Block 1              |
| apple ...            | cherry ...           |
+----------------------+----------------------+

For our example table, assuming no compression:

Entry First key Offset Size Uncompressed size
0 apple 0 48 48
1 cherry 48 27 27

The total encoded size of an entry is 2 + key_len + 8 + 4 + 4 bytes. The index is serialized with its entry count and a CRC32C checksum. The reader uses it to find the candidate block without having to scan all the data blocks.

How the Reader Finds the Block

Each entry identifies a candidate block based on its first key. The reader finds the last index entry whose first key is less than or equal to the requested key.

Looking up cherry

  • Binary-search the index for the last first-key ≤ cherry.

  • apple ≤ cherry and cherry ≤ cherry, so entry 1 wins.

  • Read 27 bytes at offset 48. That's block 1.

  • Binary-search its offset table, and cherry is there.

For this example, only one block is read. Two other cases follow from the same rule:

  • blueberry (not in the table): the last first-key ≤ blueberry is apple, so the reader reads block 0, searches it, finds nothing, and returns None.

  • aardvark, which sorts before every first key: no entry qualifies, so there is no block to read and the answer is None straight away.

5. Filter

The index can only answer "which block would hold this key?", not "is the key present?". A missing key still costs an index search and potentially a block read. The optional filter exists to skip that work.

At finalize(), Stryx hashes every key into a u64 (xxHash3 with a fixed seed), sorts and deduplicates those hashes, then builds a Binary Fuse filter (8, 16 or 32 bits per key, from the xorf crate) over the distinct hashes. Before touching the index, the reader asks it:

  • "Definitely absent" → returns None immediately, without loading a data block.

  • "Maybe present" → carries on to the index.

A false positive only wastes an index search and potentially a block read, because the block's binary search always has the final word. A filter can never cause a wrong value to be returned. Fuse8 is the smallest, and Fuse16 and Fuse32 spend more space for fewer false positives.

Filter Variants

Variant Bits per key False-positive rate (approx.) Memory for 1M keys
BinaryFuse8 ~9 ~1 in 256 ~1.1 MB
BinaryFuse16 ~18 ~1 in 65,000 ~2.2 MB
BinaryFuse32 ~36 ~1 in 4 billion ~4.5 MB

The Guarantee

To make the guarantee concrete, consider looking up aardvark, which sorts before every key. The filter has never seen it, so it returns "definitely absent" and the reader returns None without touching the index at all. If the filter returns "maybe present" for a key that isn't actually there, the reader falls through to the normal index-and-block lookup and still correctly returns None. The filter can save work on misses, but it can never change an answer.

The Performance Trade-off

The performance trade-off is a little counterintuitive: hits get slower, because every successful lookup pays for a filter check first, while misses get faster because most of them are rejected before any index or block work happens. In my benchmarks, hits go from ~80 µs to ~97–99 µs per 1,024 lookups, and misses drop from ~12 µs to ~9.2–9.5 µs. That's roughly a 20% improvement on misses.

My guess is that on a warm, memory-mapped file a miss without a filter is already cheap, since it's only an index search and a block search with no real disk I/O. A filter should matter more when blocks have to come from disk, and I haven't measured that.

6. Footer, and How open() Works

The index and filter are useful only if the reader can find them. The footer is what makes that possible. It is a fixed 29 bytes at the very end of the file, at a known position:

Field Type Bytes
index_offset u64 8
index_size u64 8
filter_type u8 1
version u32 4
magic bytes 8

What TableReader::open() Does

  1. Read the footer. Seek to file_len - 29 and read 29 bytes.

  2. Validate the magic. If it doesn't match, this isn't a Stryx file, and the reader stops here.

  3. Validate the version. The format is versioned but not yet stable, so a file from an incompatible version is rejected cleanly rather than misread.

  4. Locate the sections. index_offset and index_size say exactly where the index is. The metadata and filter sit after the index (the order is index, metadata, filter, footer). The metadata begins with an 8-byte little-endian length, and the optional filter section (when filter_type != None) is also length-prefixed, so both can be skipped or bounded precisely.

  5. Load index, metadata and filter. These are read into memory. The index and optional filter have their CRC32C checksums verified. The metadata is validated structurally (bounds and field consistency) rather than via a checksum.

  6. Prepare for lookups. The index, filter, metadata and memory-mapped file are put behind an Arc. Cloning a reader for another thread shares the table state while each reader has its own scratch buffers.

Why Opening Is Cheap

The data blocks are not eagerly read into memory during open(). The file is memory-mapped, and blocks are accessed on demand. Compressed blocks are decompressed when needed. That's why opening doesn't require reading the entire table: about 15 µs for 10,000 records, and roughly 740 µs for a million. These are from my current benchmark run.

Now that the file layout and lookup structures are established, let's follow an actual read to see how all these pieces work together.

Part III: Reading and Writing

7. The Whole Flow: get(b"cherry") 

Requested key: cherry
        |
        v
Filter check ........ "definitely absent"? -> return None
        |  "maybe present"
        v
Index lookup ........ last first-key <= "cherry"  ->  entry 1
        |
        v
Locate data block ... offset 48, size 27
        |
        v
Load the block ...... from the block cache if present, otherwise access it through mmap
        |              decompress if needed, CRC-check on first use
        v
Binary search ....... offset table -> compare keys -> find the record
        |
        v
Decode the record ... read key_len, value_len, then the value bytes
        |
        v
Return Some(b"red")

8. Building a Table

Everything so far describes the finished file. This chapter covers how TableBuilder produces it.

let mut table = TableBuilder::create("fruit.stryx", options)?;
table.add(b"apple", b"red")?;
table.add(b"banana", b"yellow")?;
table.add(b"cherry", b"red")?;
let (metadata, stats) = table.finalize()?;

Key Ordering

The format requires sorted keys, so the builder has to get them sorted somehow. key_order picks how:

  • Presorted: you promise the input is already in order. The builder checks each key against the previous one and rejects anything out of order. This is the cheap path, and records can be streamed straight into blocks without being held in memory.

  • Lexicographic: you can hand over records in any order, and Stryx routes them through an external spill-sorter (64 MiB in-memory budget by default) before writing. This lets arbitrary input become sorted output without holding the entire dataset in memory.

Accumulating Records Into Blocks

Internally, a block builder holds two growing buffers: the encoded records, and a list of each record's offset. Each add() call:

  • Encodes the record as [key_len][value_len][key][value].

  • Notes its offset, which is the current length of the data buffer.

  • Appends it to the buffer.

  • Remembers the key if this is the block's first record, since that becomes the index entry.

Sealing a Block

When the block fills up, the builder seals it:

  • finish() appends the offset table, then record_count, then the CRC32C of everything before it.

  • The bytes are compressed if the table uses LZ4 or Zstd.

  • They are written to the file.

  • The block's first key, file offset and size are pushed onto the index.

  • The buffers are cleared and the next block starts.

This is also why the index records each block's size. Compressed blocks have different lengths, so the reader can't work out where the next block starts from the block size alone.

What finalize() Does

The last block is usually only partly full, and the file doesn't have its index, metadata or footer yet. finalize() finishes the job. Steps 1–2 build everything in memory; steps 3–6 write the file:

1. Flush the last partial block         -> data blocks done

2. Build the filter in memory           -> Binary Fuse over the sorted, deduped key hashes, plus CRC32C
   (skipped when filter_type is None)

3. Encode and write the index           -> one entry per block, then entry count + CRC32C

4. Write the metadata                   -> 8-byte length prefix + encoded metadata

5. Write the filter section (if any)    -> 8-byte length prefix + filter data + CRC32C

6. Write the footer (29 bytes)          -> index_offset, index_size, filter_type, version, magic

The footer comes last because it needs the offsets of the sections before it. The filter is built here, not earlier, because a Binary Fuse filter is constructed from the complete set of keys in one go — it can't be extended key by key. finalize() returns the table's metadata and write statistics.

9. Reading Records

Every read operation uses the index to pick candidate blocks and the offset table to search inside them.

Point Lookups

get() follows the lookup path from earlier (filter, index, block, binary search) and returns an owned Vec<u8>.

let mut reader = TableReader::open("fruit.stryx")?;

let value = reader.get(b"apple")?;   // Some(Vec<u8>)
assert_eq!(value, Some(b"red".to_vec()));

let missing = reader.get(b"durian")?;
assert_eq!(missing, None);

Note: contains_key() follows the same path through get() and therefore materializes the value before discarding it. If you only need presence, calling get() directly is no more expensive than contains_key() — but contains_key() is not a cheaper check than get().

assert!(reader.contains_key(b"banana")?);   // true
assert!(!reader.contains_key(b"durian")?);  // false

If you only need the answer as Bytes rather than a Vec<u8>, get_in_bytes() returns the same lookup result without the extra copy.

let value: Option<Bytes> = reader.get_in_bytes(b"cherry")?;

Batch Lookups

get_many() is for looking up multiple keys together. The reader sorts the requested keys, then walks them against the index in a single pass. Keys that land in the same block can be answered from one block load, and results are returned in the caller's original order.

let keys: &[&[u8]] = &[b"cherry", b"apple", b"durian"];
let results = reader.get_many(keys)?;

assert_eq!(results[0], Some(b"red".to_vec()));     // cherry
assert_eq!(results[1], Some(b"red".to_vec()));     // apple
assert_eq!(results[2], None);                      // durian

get_many_in_bytes() does the same thing but returns Vec<Option<Bytes>>.

let results: Vec<Option<Bytes>> = reader.get_many_in_bytes(keys)?;

This can avoid repeatedly traversing the index and loading the same block, although sorting the requested keys also has a cost.

Range and Prefix Queries

Sorted storage is also what makes range queries possible. For a range, the reader uses the index to find the block that could contain the start key, searches the block's offset table for the first record at or after the start, walks records forward (moving to the next block when one runs out), and stops at the exclusive end bound. Only the blocks that overlap the range need to be read, and they sit next to each other in the file, so access is mostly sequential.

for record in reader.range(b"apple", b"cherry")? {
    let record = record?;
    println!("{:?} -> {:?}", record.key, record.value);
}
// apple  -> red
// banana -> yellow
// (cherry is excluded: the end bound is exclusive)

An inverted range is rejected rather than silently returning nothing:

assert!(reader.range(b"cherry", b"apple").is_err());  // InvalidRange

prefix() provides a dedicated prefix iterator:

for record in reader.prefix(b"ban")? {
    let record = record?;
    println!("{:?}", record.key);
}
// banana

Iteration

A full scan doesn't need to search the index or the offset tables for individual keys. It decodes each block's records one after another, using key_len and value_len to move from record to record, then moves to the next block.

for record in reader.iter() {
    let record = record?;
    println!("{:?} -> {:?}", record.key, record.value);
}
// apple  -> red
// banana -> yellow
// cherry -> red

Part IV: Behavior and Performance

10. Compression, Concurrency and Caching

Compression

Compression is chosen once per table: None, LZ4 (fast) or Zstd (smaller). It's applied to each block separately rather than to the file as a whole. If the whole file were one compressed stream, reading one key could mean decompressing a much larger portion of the file; with per-block compression, the index points at a block and the reader decompresses that block alone. Smaller files cost CPU time on every uncached compressed block read; the block cache can avoid repeated decompression.

Concurrency

Opening a table doesn't read it all into memory. Only the small structures at the end of the file are loaded: the index, the metadata and the filter. The data blocks are accessed through the memory mapping when needed, and the OS manages which mapped pages are resident.

The shared state sits behind an Arc:

Shared across all readers (Arc) Private to each reader
The mapped file Scratch buffers (decompression, decoding)
Index Read statistics (readstats)
Filter
Metadata
Block cache (if enabled)

Lookups take &mut self, so one TableReader can't be used from many threads at once. You open the table once and clone() a reader per thread. A clone only needs its own scratch buffers and an increment of the Arc reference count, so it's very cheap.

let reader = TableReader::open("data.stryx")?;

std::thread::scope(|s| {
    for _ in 0..4 {
        let mut r = reader.clone();
        s.spawn(move || { let _ = r.get(b"some-key"); });
    }
});

The Block Cache

The cache is off by default. When enabled, it keeps decoded (decompressed and verified) blocks and is shared between all clones, with a size you set in bytes. A block only enters the cache on its second load, so blocks that are read once never pay for an insert. Two threads can each decode the same cold block once before it lands in the cache, and a uniform random workload over a table much bigger than the cache gets little benefit from it.

11. Benchmarks

Single-machine microbenchmarks comparing Stryx's own configurations; I make no claims about other libraries. Point-lookup times are per 1,024 lookups.

Environment:

Intel i5-12450H, Linux 6.18.38-1-lts, Rust 1.96.0, Criterion.

Point lookups:

Operation Config Time Throughput
hit no filter 79.9 µs 12.8 Melem/s
hit Fuse8 / 16 / 32 97.0 / 97.5 / 99.3 µs ~10.3–10.6 Melem/s
miss no filter 12.0 µs 85.5 Melem/s
miss Fuse8 / 16 / 32 9.5 / 9.2 / 9.4 µs ~107–111 Melem/s

Throughput, by configuration:

Workload Config Throughput
Sequential scan, 4 KiB blocks None 643 MiB/s
Sequential scan, 4 KiB blocks LZ4 461 MiB/s
Sequential scan, 4 KiB blocks Zstd level 1 306 MiB/s
Concurrent point lookups 1 thread 11.0 Melem/s
Concurrent point lookups 2 threads 24.8 Melem/s
Concurrent point lookups 4 threads 40.0 Melem/s

Full tables — including scan times for 16 KiB blocks, opening latency at 10K/100K/1M records, and block-cache results across compression settings — are in the cargo bench harness and on the crate page.

A filter adds cost to successful lookups but helps reject missing keys — the same trade-off discussed in Filter. Four threads gave roughly 3.6× single-thread throughput on this machine and workload.

12. Limitations

  • Pre-1.0 API. The format and Rust API may change between minor versions. Version is validated on open, so an incompatible file is rejected cleanly rather than misread — but expect breakage.

  • Single-writer, immutable tables. There's no in-place update or delete. New records mean a new table; merging tables is left to the caller.

  • No compression tuning per workload. Compression is chosen once per table and applied per block; there's no adaptive policy, and no measurement yet on cold-cache (disk-bound) reads.

13. Getting Started 

cargo add stryx

Or from source:

git clone https://github.com/vamsi200/stryx
cd stryx
cargo test
cargo bench

For more details:

  • docs.rs/stryx
  • crates.io/crates/stryx
  • github.com/vamsi200/stryx

And that's it — that's the whole design and inner workings of Stryx. I've omitted a few details, but this is mostly it. Thank you for reading!

title: Integrating TorchTPU into TorchTitan and Optimizing Models for TPU
description: TorchTPU integrates a native torch.device("tpu") backend directly into PyTorch, allowing developers to train large-scale models on Google Cloud TPUs without rewriting code in JAX. The TorchTitan TPU fork enhances this with production-grade scaling primitives like SimpleFSDP, Graph Trainer, and custom Pallas kernels that achieve high Model Flops Utilization (MFU) across dense and MoE architectures. Developers can leverage these battle-tested optimization playbooks, recipes, and the Hugging Face modeling backend to efficiently scale their own workloads on TPU infrastructure.

title: The other half of the software factory
description:
Software factories are back in my feed, and the argument is the one I thought we had settled twenty years ago.

Between 2000 and 2020 offshore development promised businesses cheap custom software, and what they often got was cheap software. The quality problems were real, and the answer the industry found was not to shout at the suppliers but to make coding, testing and deployment mechanical: boring, repeatable, and checked by a machine rather than by a hero.

That part is done. A linter runs on every commit, a test suite runs on every push, a pipeline builds, signs and releases, and a fleet pulls its own desired state from a repository. In our own shop a release is a tag, a deploy is a reviewed commit, and nobody logs in to a box to restart anything. None of that is clever any more, which is the highest compliment engineering can pay a practice.

That is half of the problem, and it is the half that was always going to yield to tooling, since it is about how code is handled rather than about what the code does.

The half that does not yield to tooling

The other half is the functional one: deciding what the software should do, and writing it so that the decision survives contact with a team, a successor, or now a coding agent. You cannot make that mechanical by buying a tool, but you can make it mechanical by changing the shape of the work, and three practices do it together. Some people have started calling the combination EVE, and I will use the name.

Event storming comes first. Before anyone draws a database, the people who know the work stand at a wall and name what happens, in the past tense: a member registered, a book was procured, a reading finished. The orange notes on that wall are the vocabulary of the business and nothing else, and the commands that cause them and the rules that react to them are added only once the events are agreed. Anyone who runs the club could read that wall, which is the test it has to pass, since the owner of the business will be reading it too.

Vertical slicing decides where the code lives. One capability, one folder, and everything that capability needs inside it: the command, the event it produces, the rule that decides, and the door the outside world knocks on. Not a folder of controllers and a folder of services with the feature smeared across both, but one folder called register_member that contains the whole of registering a member.

Event sourcing decides what the state is. The state of a club is not a row that gets overwritten but the list of what happened to it, in order, and any table you need for reading is built from that list afterwards, by a separate part of the system that only writes tables, and read by a third that only answers questions. Writing, recording and answering are kept apart on purpose, which is the CQRS part of the name if you like acronyms, and which means each part can be small and dull.

Put the three together and the code that comes out is boring and predictable, and I mean that as praise. The same shapes repeat. In the book club below a desk is four files, an event is one module, a projection is one event to one table, and a query is one question with one answer. That is the property that matters for a factory: when the shapes repeat, they can be produced by a template or by a language model, and checked by a machine.

What a stranger sees

Here is a book club, built this way, with the code public. There are three applications. The first holds what the club can do: initiate a club, register a member, procure a book, start and finish a reading, plan a party, archive the club. The second is organised around the events, one folder per event, each turning it into rows in the tables the third app reads. The third answers questions: a book, a member, a reading, by id.

Open the first folder and you can read the process of running a book club without opening a file. You can also read a policy as a sentence, since one folder is named after it: on member registered, maybe plan a party. And you can tell which three facts the club shares with the outside world, since those folders start with emit. That is screaming architecture: the names say what the code does, not how, and the structure is the documentation. We call it the stranger test. A stranger opens the repository and tells you what the business does, and if they cannot, the names are wrong.

Those three folders are also the whole of the club's public contract, and the only thing anyone outside the club can depend on. The nine events inside are ours to change. A fact that has left the club is not: its version is in its name, a published version never changes and never disappears, and when the club has more to say it publishes a _v2 next to the _v1, which is the open/closed principle applied to a contract. Who consumes a fact is not the club's business, and that is the point of publishing facts rather than calling consumers: the club keeps no list of them, cannot break them by accident, and does not wait for them when it ships. Who owns the club is equally short. One division, one repository, one owner, and a person's yes before anything reaches main.

Onboarding changes character when the test passes. A new colleague reads one folder and owns one capability by the afternoon, and a coding agent, which is the newest colleague in every shop now, reads the same folder and produces the next one in the same shape, because there is only one shape to produce.

The same club, walked through from the wall to the stored event, in sixteen minutes:

Five Ds, with a nod to four Cs

Simon Brown's C4 model gives architects four zoom levels for drawing a system: context, container, component and code. It is good and we use it. For the process side we name five levels of our own, all starting with D, partly as a wink to C4 and partly because the fifth one is the point.

A Domain is the whole business endeavour. A Division is one cohesive piece of software inside it, the bounded context, the thing that gets its own repository. A Department is one of three roles inside a Division: commands, projections, queries. A Desk is one capability inside a Department, the folder you saw above and the atomic unit of work. And the Dossier is the aggregate: the folder of event slips that passes from desk to desk and grows as it goes. C4 tells you where the boxes are, and the fifth D tells you what moves through them.

The desk is also why the factory idea stops being a metaphor. A desk is small enough to describe on one sticky note, strict enough to template, and complete enough to test on its own. Give one desk to one person or one agent as a work package, ask for the failing test first, have a second pair of eyes pass the change, and let a person say yes before it reaches main, and you get the same quality from the tenth desk as from the first. If a desk is a unit of work it is also a unit you can price, which is where I want to take this.

The first storm

Granted, the first storm is the hard part, and no factory removes it. Getting the right people in front of the wall, naming the events honestly and finding where one division ends and the next begins is thinking, and it stays thinking. What the method does is make everything after the wall boring, so that the thinking is the only thing a person has to spend attention on.

The book club above is our teaching repository, in Erlang, which is one language and not the one most readers write in. The rules it follows live in a public corpus, with the naming rules, the templates, and a long list of the mistakes we made and wrote down so we would not make them twice. The crew of coding agents that builds this way is called Martha, and it still needs a person to say yes before anything reaches main.

The first half of the factory is a product you can buy. The other half is a way of working, and it is the half that decides whether the code an agent writes tomorrow is something you can still read in five years.

Would you let a factory like this build your next system, and if not, which half worries you?

title: Taming Rust Compile Times in 2026: A Practical Playbook with cargo --timings, Cranelift, mold and sccache
description:
Rust 1.100 vừa ra, cộng đồng lại bàn về một dự án JIT compiler cho Rust với mục tiêu giảm build time. Điều này cho thấy compile time vẫn là nỗi đau lớn nhất của Rust, dù ngôn ngữ đã trưởng thành nhiều. Team mình có một service khoảng 80k dòng Rust, chia thành 14 crate trong workspace. Có thời điểm một lần cargo build incremental sau khi sửa đúng một dòng mất 40 giây. Khi AI agent tự sửa code rồi tự chạy test liên tục thì 40 giây đó bị nhân lên hàng trăm lần mỗi ngày. Bài này tổng hợp những gì mình đã làm để đưa con số đó xuống khoảng 6 giây. Không có phép màu nào cả, chỉ là đo đúng chỗ rồi sửa đúng chỗ.

1. Đo trước, tối ưu sau

Lỗi phổ biến nhất mình thấy là đổi linker hoặc thêm cache theo cảm tính mà không biết thời gian thực sự bị tiêu vào đâu. Cargo có sẵn công cụ đo khá tốt:

# Báo cáo HTML: crate nào build lâu, crate nào chặn song song
cargo build --timings
open target/cargo-timings/cargo-timing.html

# Xem generic nào sinh ra nhiều LLVM IR nhất
cargo install cargo-llvm-lines
cargo llvm-lines -p my-core --lib | head -20

# Thời gian từng pass của rustc (cần nightly)
cargo +nightly rustc -p my-core -- -Z time-passes

Trong báo cáo cargo-timing.html, hãy chú ý hai thứ. Thứ nhất là các thanh dài nằm trên critical path, thường là crate trung tâm mà mọi crate khác phụ thuộc vào. Thứ hai là phần màu tím (codegen) so với phần màu xanh (frontend). Nếu codegen chiếm phần lớn, vấn đề nằm ở LLVM và monomorphization. Nếu frontend chiếm phần lớn, nguyên nhân thường là macro (serde, sqlx, tokio) hoặc trait resolution phức tạp.

Để chọn đúng công cụ, cần biết mỗi giai đoạn build tương ứng với công cụ nào:

flowchart LR
    A[Source .rs] --> B[Frontend: parse, macro, typeck]
    B --> C[MIR + monomorphization]
    C --> D[Codegen: LLVM / Cranelift]
    D --> E[Linker: ld / lld / mold]
    E --> F[Binary]
    S[sccache] -.cache toàn crate.-> D
    W[Tách crate / bớt generic] -.giảm.-> C
    CL[Cranelift] -.thay LLVM.-> D
    M[mold / lld] -.tăng tốc.-> E

2. Linker và codegen backend: thắng nhanh nhất

Với incremental build, phần link thường chiếm tỷ lệ lớn đến bất ngờ, vì mỗi lần sửa một dòng là phải link lại toàn bộ binary. Từ Rust 1.90, target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu đã dùng lld làm linker mặc định, nên nếu bạn đang dùng toolchain mới trên Linux thì đã được hưởng phần lớn lợi ích này. Trên các target khác, hoặc khi muốn nhanh hơn nữa, mold (bản 2.x) vẫn là lựa chọn rất đáng thử.

Bước tiếp theo là Cranelift. Đây là codegen backend viết bằng Rust, sinh code chạy chậm hơn LLVM nhưng compile nhanh hơn đáng kể. Cranelift hợp với dev build và test, không nên dùng cho release. Hiện tại nó vẫn cần nightly:

rustup toolchain install nightly
rustup component add rustc-codegen-cranelift-preview --toolchain nightly

Sau đó cấu hình trong .cargo/config.toml và Cargo.toml:

# .cargo/config.toml
[target.x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu]
linker = "clang"
rustflags = ["-C", "link-arg=-fuse-ld=mold"]

[unstable]
codegen-backend = true

# Cargo.toml (workspace root)
[profile.dev]
codegen-backend = "cranelift"
debug = "line-tables-only"   # đủ cho backtrace, nhẹ hơn debug=2 rất nhiều

# Dependency ít thay đổi: tối ưu một lần, cache mãi
[profile.dev.package."*"]
codegen-backend = "llvm"
opt-level = 2

Có một mẹo ở đây: dependency bên ngoài vẫn dùng LLVM với opt-level = 2, vì chúng chỉ build một lần rồi được cache. Còn code của mình, phần thay đổi liên tục, thì dùng Cranelift. Kết quả là test vẫn chạy đủ nhanh mà vòng sửa-build lại ngắn. Với project của mình, riêng bước này đã giảm incremental build từ 40 giây xuống khoảng 14 giây.

Lưu ý: một số crate dùng SIMD intrinsics hoặc inline asm có thể chưa tương thích với Cranelift. Nếu gặp lỗi, hãy chuyển riêng crate đó về llvm qua [profile.dev.package.ten-crate].

3. Cấu trúc workspace: tối ưu bền vững nhất

Linker và backend chỉ giúp bạn đi nhanh hơn trên con đường sẵn có. Cấu trúc crate mới quyết định con đường đó dài bao nhiêu. Có ba nguyên tắc mình áp dụng:

  • Tách crate theo tần suất thay đổi. Domain types ít thay đổi thì để vào crate riêng ở đáy dependency graph. Business logic thay đổi liên tục thì để ở các crate lá. Sửa crate lá thì chỉ crate đó cùng binary phải build lại.
  • Không để mọi thứ phụ thuộc vào một crate common khổng lồ. Mỗi lần sửa common là cả workspace phải build lại. Đây là nguyên nhân chính khiến build của team mình chậm.
  • Giảm monomorphization. Dựa vào kết quả cargo llvm-lines, với các hàm generic lớn, hãy tách phần thân thành một hàm non-generic bên trong: 
// Trước: toàn bộ thân hàm bị nhân bản cho mỗi kiểu P
pub fn load_config<P: AsRef<Path>>(path: P) -> Result<Config> {
    // ... 80 dòng parse ...
}

// Sau: chỉ wrapper mỏng là generic
pub fn load_config<P: AsRef<Path>>(path: P) -> Result<Config> {
    fn inner(path: &Path) -> Result<Config> {
        // ... 80 dòng parse, chỉ compile một lần ...
    }
    inner(path.as_ref())
}

Thư viện chuẩn cũng dùng đúng pattern này, ví dụ std::fs::read. Ngoài ra, hãy chạy cargo machete hoặc cargo udeps để loại bỏ dependency không dùng, và rà soát feature flags. Bật tokio với features = ["full"] trong một crate chỉ cần sync là lãng phí.

4. Cache trên CI và giữa các máy

Ở local, incremental compilation đã làm khá tốt. Trên CI, mỗi job bắt đầu từ trạng thái trống, nên cache là bắt buộc. Mình kết hợp hai lớp:

sequenceDiagram
    participant CI as CI Job
    participant RC as rust-cache (target/)
    participant SC as sccache (S3/GCS)
    participant R as rustc
    CI->>RC: Restore target/ theo hash Cargo.lock
    CI->>R: cargo build
    R->>SC: Hash input của crate
    SC-->>R: Hit: trả artifact
    SC-->>R: Miss: compile rồi upload
    CI->>RC: Save target/ (chỉ trên main)

File workflow GitHub Actions rút gọn:

- uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable
- uses: Swatinem/rust-cache@v2
  with:
    save-if: ${{ github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' }}
- uses: mozilla-actions/sccache-action@v0.0.9
- run: cargo nextest run --workspace
  env:
    RUSTC_WRAPPER: sccache
    SCCACHE_GHA_ENABLED: "true"
    CARGO_INCREMENTAL: "0"

Ba chi tiết dễ bị bỏ qua:

  1. CARGO_INCREMENTAL=0 trên CI: incremental artifact rất lớn và gần như không có ích khi đã có sccache.
  2. save-if chỉ lưu cache trên main: nếu mọi PR đều ghi cache, giới hạn 10GB của GitHub sẽ bị dùng hết rất nhanh.
  3. cargo-nextest (0.9.x) chạy mỗi test trong một process riêng và song song tốt hơn cargo test. Với test suite lớn, nó thường nhanh hơn 30-50%.

Kết luận

Build time của Rust không phải là thứ bắt buộc phải chịu đựng. Nếu chỉ có một buổi chiều, mình gợi ý làm theo thứ tự sau:

  1. Chạy cargo build --timings để xác định critical path trước khi thay đổi bất cứ thứ gì.
  2. Kiểm tra linker: trên Linux x86_64 với Rust từ 1.90 trở lên, bạn đã có lld. Trên target khác, hãy thử mold.
  3. Thử Cranelift cho profile.dev, đồng thời giữ LLVM với opt-level = 2 cho dependency.
  4. Đặt debug = "line-tables-only": thay đổi một dòng nhưng giảm kích thước target/ rõ rệt.
  5. Rà soát dependency graph: tách crate common, xử lý các hàm generic lớn, cắt feature flags thừa.
  6. Trên CI, dùng rust-cache + sccache + nextest và chỉ lưu cache trên main.

Trong thời đại AI agent tự build và tự test hàng trăm lần mỗi ngày, mỗi giây tiết kiệm được ở vòng lặp build sẽ được nhân lên rất nhiều lần. Đầu tư vài giờ cho build time thường là khoản đầu tư có lợi nhất cho team Rust.

title: Terraform for Beginners: Build Cloud Infrastructure by Writing Simple Code
description:
A short story to start

Imagine you spent a whole afternoon clicking around the Azure or AWS website to set up a server, a network, a database and a few security rules. It works. Well done.

Now your manager says: "Great, can you build exactly the same thing again for testing, and another copy in Europe?" Can you remember every click? Every setting? Every small box you ticked?

Most people cannot. That is the problem Terraform solves. Instead of clicking, you write down what you want in a simple text file. Terraform reads the file and builds it for you, the same way, every time.

1. What is Terraform, in one sentence?

Terraform is a tool that turns a simple text file into real cloud infrastructure.

This idea is called Infrastructure as Code, or IaC for short. Your servers, networks and databases are described in code, just like an app.

A good way to picture it is a building plan. An architect does not build a house by shouting instructions to workers one by one. She draws a plan. Builders follow the plan. If you want ten identical houses, you use the same plan ten times. Terraform files are your plan.

Terraform is made by a company called HashiCorp. It works with almost every cloud: AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud and hundreds of other services. You may also hear about OpenTofu, a free open source version that works in almost the same way. Everything you learn here applies to both.

2. How does Terraform work?


Figure 1: You write the code, Terraform reads it, the provider talks to the cloud.

There are only a few moving parts:

  1. You write files ending in .tf that describe what you want.
  2. Terraform reads those files and works out what needs to be created, changed or deleted.
  3. A provider is a plugin that knows how to talk to one platform. There is a provider for AWS, one for Azure, one for Google Cloud, and many more. Think of it as a translator.
  4. The real cloud ends up with the servers, networks and storage you asked for.

The most important idea: you describe what you want, not how to build it step by step. Terraform works out the steps.

3. The words you will hear (made simple)

Word What it means in plain English
Provider The plugin that talks to a platform, such as aws or azurerm.
Resource One thing you want to create, such as a server, a network or a storage bucket.
Variable A value you can change without editing the main code, such as a region or a name.
Output A value Terraform prints at the end, such as a website address or a server IP.
State Terraform's memory of what it has already built.
Plan A preview of the changes Terraform is about to make.
Module A reusable bundle of Terraform code, like a Lego set you can use again and again.

4. Install Terraform

Go to the official Terraform website from HashiCorp, download the version for your computer (Windows, Mac or Linux) and follow the install steps. On a Mac you can also use Homebrew, and on Windows you can use Chocolatey or winget.

Then open a terminal and type:

terraform -version

If you see a version number, you are ready. I also recommend installing Visual Studio Code with the official HashiCorp Terraform extension. It colours your code and spots mistakes as you type.

5. Your first project (no cloud account needed)

The best way to learn Terraform without any risk of a cloud bill is to start with something local. We will ask Terraform to create a simple text file on your own computer. The steps are exactly the same as for a real server in the cloud.

Step 1: Create a folder and a file

Make a new folder called my-first-terraform and inside it create a file called main.tf with this code:

resource "local_file" "hello" {
  filename = "hello.txt"
  content  = "Hello from Terraform!"
}

Let us read it slowly:

  • resource says "I want to create something".
  • "local_file" is the type of thing: a file on this computer.
  • "hello" is the nickname we give it inside our code.
  • Inside the curly brackets are the settings: the file name and what to write in it.

Step 2: Run the four magic commands


Figure 2: init, plan, apply and destroy. You will use these every single day.

Open a terminal in your folder and run:

terraform init

init gets everything ready. It notices you used local_file and downloads the provider that knows how to create files.

terraform plan

plan shows a preview. You should see something like "Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy". Nothing has been created yet. This is your chance to check before anything happens.

terraform apply

apply does the real work. Terraform shows the plan again and asks you to type yes. Type it and press Enter. Now look in your folder: there is a new file called hello.txt with your message inside. You just used Infrastructure as Code.

Step 3: Make a change

Change the content line to say "Hello again from Terraform!" and run terraform plan. Terraform notices the difference and tells you it will replace the file. Run terraform apply, type yes, and open the file again. It has been updated. You did not tell Terraform how to update it. You only changed what you wanted.

Step 4: Clean up 

terraform destroy

destroy deletes everything Terraform created in this folder. Type yes and hello.txt disappears. In the real cloud this is your best friend: one command and everything you built for practice is gone, so you are not paying for it.

6. The state file: Terraform's memory


Figure 3: Terraform compares what you want, what it remembers and what really exists.

After you ran apply, you may have noticed a new file called terraform.tfstate. This is Terraform's memory. It records what Terraform has built, so next time it knows what already exists and what needs to change.

A few simple rules for the state file:

  • Never edit it by hand. Let Terraform manage it.
  • Never share it publicly or upload it to GitHub. It can contain passwords and private details.
  • In a team, store it in a shared, safe place such as an Azure Storage account, an AWS S3 bucket or HCP Terraform. This is called remote state, and it stops two people changing the same thing at the same time.

7. Variables and outputs: making your code flexible

Hard coding values works, but variables let you reuse the same code for different situations. Add this to your main.tf:

variable "message" {
  default = "Hello from Terraform!"
}

resource "local_file" "hello" {
  filename = "hello.txt"
  content  = var.message
}

output "file_name" {
  value = local_file.hello.filename
}
  • The variable block creates a value called message with a default.
  • var.message uses that value inside the resource.
  • The output block prints the file name when apply finishes.

Now you can change the message without touching the resource, for example: terraform apply -var="message=Good morning".

8. A small real cloud example

When you are ready for the cloud, the pattern is exactly the same. Here is how you would create a storage bucket on AWS:

provider "aws" {
  region = "eu-west-1"
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "my_bucket" {
  bucket = "my-first-terraform-bucket-12345"
}

Same commands: init, plan, apply. Same clean up: destroy. Before you try it, create a free tier account, set a budget alert, and log in with the AWS command line tool so Terraform can use your account. Bucket names must be unique across the whole world, so change the numbers at the end.

9. Good habits from day one

  1. Always read the plan before you type yes. It tells you exactly what will be created, changed or deleted.
  2. Keep your .tf files in Git, so you have a history of every change.
  3. Add a .gitignore file that keeps out terraform.tfstate, the .terraform folder and any files with secrets.
  4. Run terraform fmt to tidy your code and terraform validate to catch mistakes early.
  5. Make small changes and apply often, instead of one giant change.
  6. Destroy practice resources as soon as you finish, so you do not get a surprise bill.

10. Common beginner mistakes

  • Typing yes without reading the plan, and deleting something important.
  • Uploading the state file or secret keys to a public GitHub repository.
  • Changing things by hand in the cloud website after Terraform built them. Terraform will get confused, or undo your changes next time.
  • Forgetting to run terraform init after adding a new provider.
  • Trying to learn modules, workspaces and remote state on day one. Master the basics first.

11. A simple learning path

Stage What to do
Week 1 Install Terraform and complete the local_file project in this guide.
Week 2 Learn variables, outputs and terraform fmt and validate.
Week 3 Create one small real cloud resource, then destroy it.
Week 4 Build a small network and a virtual machine, and keep your code on GitHub.
After that Learn remote state, modules, and running Terraform inside a CI/CD pipeline.

Final words

Terraform can look scary at first, but the core idea is simple: write down what you want, check the plan, then let Terraform build it. The same file can build the same setup again tomorrow, next month or in another country.

Your challenge this week: create the hello.txt file with Terraform, change it, and destroy it. Those three commands, plan, apply and destroy, are the heart of everything you will ever do with Terraform.

Happy building!

title: Model Holds as Ledger Records, Not Balance Mutations
description:
Preventing retries, cancellations, and concurrent withdrawals from making reserved balances drift.

A payment system often needs to reserve money before the final debit occurs. A withdrawal may be awaiting provider acceptance, a bank transfer may require manual review, or a card authorization may remain unsettled for several days.

The tempting implementation is a mutable counter:

account.held_amount += requested_amount
account.save()

This looks efficient, but it hides the reason money is unavailable. It also makes correctness depend on every success, failure, cancellation, timeout, and retry updating the counter in exactly the opposite way.

A safer design treats each hold as an identifiable financial record:

hold key: withdrawal:{reference}
owner: wallet identifier
amount: 125.00
currency: USD
status: active

Available balance then has a precise definition:

available = posted balance - sum(active holds)

The important ordering is to claim the hold identity before changing any cached aggregate. Within one database transaction, insert the hold using a unique business key. If that key already exists, compare the canonical request payload. A matching retry returns the existing hold; a different amount or wallet is a hard conflict.

Only the request that successfully creates the hold may apply any associated cached balance update. This ordering prevents a retry from incrementing a counter before discovering that the hold already exists.

Treat the hold lifecycle as a state machine

A hold should move through explicit states such as active, captured, released, and expired. Terminal transitions must be idempotent. Releasing an already released hold should return the existing result instead of adding the amount back again.

Capturing a hold normally creates the final debit and marks the hold captured in the same transaction. Releasing it removes the reservation without creating a debit. Expiry should use the same release service as a manual cancellation so there is only one implementation of the financial rule.

Lock the wallet and hold together

Two withdrawals can arrive simultaneously. Both may observe enough available balance before either creates its hold. Lock the wallet row, calculate active holds inside the transaction, and create the new hold before releasing the lock.

A database uniqueness constraint on the hold key protects retries. Row locking protects competing requests for the same funds. They solve different concurrency problems.

Use aggregates as caches, not truth

For high-volume reads, summing holds repeatedly may be expensive. A cached held_amount is reasonable if the hold rows remain authoritative. Reconciliation should periodically compare the cached value with the sum of active records and repair or alert on differences.

The same rule applies to provider-side reservations. Local accounting needs to distinguish posted funds, reserved funds, pending outbound money, and externally settled money.

Test the failure boundaries

Useful tests include duplicate requests, two simultaneous withdrawals competing for the same balance, a crash after hold creation, repeated release commands, capture after expiry, and late provider success after a hold was released.

The goal is not merely to stop a negative balance. It is to retain an explainable record of why funds were unavailable and ensure every retry reaches the same result.

Implementation checklist

Give every hold an immutable owner, currency, amount, business reference, and payload fingerprint. Enforce uniqueness in the database. Define exactly which states contribute to reserved balance and which transitions create ledger entries. Lock the wallet during affordability checks, and use decimal arithmetic at the currency's supported precision.

Monitor active holds by age and reason. A growing population of old holds usually indicates a missing provider callback, failed release task, or incomplete operational workflow. Provide staff with a permission-controlled release action that records the actor and reason while still calling the standard hold service.

title: Cerebras signs Microsoft as its third hyperscaler customer
description:
📅 November 13, 2026 • Source: Data Center Dynamics

Cerebras has signed Microsoft as a customer, with the deal inked in October 2026 and confirmed on the Q3 2026 earnings call held on November 12, per Data Center Dynamics and CNBC. CEO Andrew Feldman named the buyer in a CNBC interview: the top-3 hyperscaler teased on the call is Microsoft. Per TradingKey, both WSJ and Reuters corroborated the customer identity. Microsoft joins AWS and Oracle to become the third hyperscaler customer on the Cerebras roster, per Data Center Dynamics.

Revenue from the Microsoft deal is expected to start flowing in Q1 2027, with details to follow during 2027 and terms undisclosed, per DCD and CNBC. The quarter was strong by the company's own methodology: core revenue reached $230.9 million in Q3, up 70% year over year and 10% quarter over quarter, above the LSEG consensus of $214.7 million, per CNBC citing LSEG and DCD. AI cloud revenue came in at $145 million, and the company expects it roughly flat in Q4 because data center capacity is the limiter, with new capacity deploying from December, per DCD.

Guidance moved up as well: core revenue for 2026 is now expected at $940-960 million, raised from the earlier $880-890 million view, per AI Stock Wire and TradingKey. The company expects revenue to triple in 2027, per DCD, and Feldman said the company expects to exit 2026 with roughly 10x the manufacturing capacity it held at the start of the year, per DCD.

Remaining performance obligations stood at $26.1 billion as of September 30, 2026, a figure that excludes both the Oracle and the Microsoft deals, per DCD. OpenAI accounted for 34% of Q3 revenue, per the quarterly 10-Q cited by AI Stock Wire.

Capacity is the other half of the story: the company points to 700 MW of planned data center capacity, per Feldman, with large parts of contracted capacity deploying in mid-2027. More than 75% of planned 2027 capacity sits outside the US, in Canada, France and Norway, per DCD. Contracts for Norway and Finland were signed within the quarter, and a Sao Paulo site, the first in South America, is at the final stage of contracting, per DCD.

CFO Bob Komin explained the logic of the company's own cloud, per DCD: Cerebras began deploying it in early 2025 because AI-native companies scale fast, while hyperscalers plan allocations years ahead. Customers evaluate the system inside the Cerebras private cloud and then choose between buying hardware or consuming the cloud. Feldman added that data center availability remains a constant constraint for the industry, and Cerebras is no exception — the limit comes down to land, power and data center shells, per DCD.

IMPACT: For infrastructure planners the deal is another signal that fast inference has become a standing procurement line for the largest cloud buyers. The binding constraint the company describes is capacity, not demand, so siting, power and shell availability will shape how much of the announced revenue actually lands in 2027.

title: Node.js SaaS App Weekly Support — Background Job Queue, HTTP Workers, Retries, DLQ
description:
Short answer: put each weekly customer-support digest on a background job queue, make the Node.js worker idempotent, and use cron only to enqueue the scheduled work. Choose by the cost of recovering one failed digest, not by the cost of one queue operation.

The constraint is awkward but decisive: a cron run can call only a public http_url and stops at 900 seconds. A weekly batch for active customers can outgrow that window, especially when rendering, email delivery, and webhook calls share the same run. Queueing separates the clock from the work, so retries and a dead-letter queue (DLQ) remain available after the scheduler has moved on.

For a small support SaaS, I would try Infrai for the enqueue-and-worker boundary when reducing operational glue matters: one key and one bill cover its backend capabilities, and the plain REST surface doesn't require another Node.js SDK. That's a narrow recommendation. The queue earns its place through a shorter recovery path, while the consolidated account and HTTP integration reduce the surrounding work.

Implement the tenant-week fence first

Write the recovery invariant before comparing products: one failed customer digest must be retryable without resending any completed digest. Model a Monday batch that reaches 9,999 active customers and stalls on customer 10,000. With one long cron handler, the useful question isn't how little the trigger cost. It is whether the system can identify that customer's job, retry it without resending the first 9,999 digests, and quarantine a poison message without rerunning the whole weekly batch. Those recovery actions consume engineer time, downstream email or webhook attempts, worker time, and storage. They also create support work when duplicate delivery escapes.

That's the bill I care about.

The queue design gives every customer and reporting window its own durable identity. For example, tenant-1042:2026-08-17 can identify one digest attempt across redelivery. Standard queues provide at-least-once delivery, so a worker may see that identity more than once; its first durable step must therefore check whether the digest was already committed. FIFO deduplication is useful, but its five-minute window cannot replace that durable check. An acknowledgement deletes the message, retention tops out at 30 days, and this isn't Kafka-style history. Persist the digest result in the application's own system of record before acknowledging.

Delayed delivery helps with bounded deferral, but only up to seven days. The message body is capped at 256 KB, so enqueue identifiers and a reporting window rather than a rendered digest or a ticket transcript. Keep the big data where the application already governs it.

Small payload. Sharp boundary.

Before picking a product, write down what happens to one digest at each transition. The ledger for this build has four states: scheduled, enqueued, committed, and acknowledged. scheduled belongs to cron. enqueued belongs to the queue. committed means the application has durably recorded the rendered digest and delivery outcome. Only then may the worker acknowledge the queue message. The initial implementation needs just that boundary and a compact job identity; workflow abstractions can wait.

This ordering turns duplicate delivery from a mystery into a lookup. If a worker receives the same tenant and week again, it finds the committed record and skips the external side effect. If processing fails before commit, retrying is safe. If a message repeatedly fails, the DLQ preserves a bounded recovery target rather than forcing an operator to reconstruct a giant cron run from logs. A 429 Too Many Requests is also ordinary retry work — honor Retry-After when it exists, otherwise apply exponential backoff. Don't spin.

Rollout: move the weekly job from cron to queue workers

Cron has one job here: call a public endpoint that publishes the weekly work. It shouldn't fetch tickets, render summaries, or wait for downstream delivery. Paused cron schedules don't backfill missed triggers, trigger timing may vary by seconds, and run output keeps only the first 4 KB. The application should therefore keep the expected weekly window and reconcile that window against committed digest records. That reconciliation is part of the effective operating cost, even though it never appears in a queue's per-call rate.

US and EU deployment adds another line to the ledger. Put the tenant's region in the job identity and keep regional policy in the worker; don't assume one global replay button is appropriate. I'm not sure a single queue remains the right boundary once data residency dominates the design. The deciding evidence would be the application's tenant-isolation rules and the location of its durable records.

Keep the enqueue adapter small

Publish a compact job whose identity survives retries. The following TypeScript is intentionally the smallest queue-side piece: it uses the verified publish route, sets the method explicitly, reads the key from the environment, supplies an idempotency key, checks every response, and backs off on 429. The worker behind it must apply the durable commit-before-ack rule described above.

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

type DigestJob = {
  tenantId: string;
  weekStart: string;
  region: "US" | "EU";
  idempotencyKey: string;
};

async function publishDigest(job: DigestJob): Promise<unknown> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 5; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/publish", {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": job.idempotencyKey
      },
      body: JSON.stringify({
        queue: "weekly-support-digests",
        message: job
      })
    });

    if (response.ok) return response.json();

    const errorBody = await response.text();
    if (response.status !== 429) {
      throw new Error(`Publish failed (${response.status}): ${errorBody}`);
    }

    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("Retry-After") ?? "0");
    const waitMs = retryAfter > 0 ? retryAfter * 1_000 : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
    await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, waitMs));
  }

  throw new Error("Publish retry budget exhausted");
}

await publishDigest({
  tenantId: "tenant-1042",
  weekStart: "2026-08-17",
  region: "US",
  idempotencyKey: "tenant-1042:2026-08-17"
});

The five client attempts above protect the enqueue request from throttling; they are not the job's business retry policy. Keep those budgets separate. Queue retries govern a failed digest worker, while HTTP retries govern the call used to publish work. Mixing them produces a counter nobody can explain during an incident.

Contain failures at the public webhook boundary

There is another boundary: push subscription targets must be public HTTPS endpoints, just as cron requires a public http_url. A private worker endpoint won't receive those calls. Use a pull consumer or another product when exposing an HTTPS target conflicts with the network model.

Which background job queue should own HTTP retries and the DLQ?

Time three steps before comparing products: locate one failed tenant, prove whether its external side effect happened, and retry only that unit. Then count products by the recovery responsibility they move onto your team. Infrai fits a simple HTTP-oriented backend that needs retries, delayed messages, and a DLQ without adding SDK and account sprawl; its self-describing discovery surface also publishes request schemas and runnable examples, useful when a CLI must validate a call. AWS SQS is the natural benchmark when the application already lives inside AWS and its team wants that ecosystem's dead-letter queue controls. The other options solve different-sized problems.

Option Recovery boundary Better choice when Poor fit when
Infrai queue At-least-once jobs, delayed delivery, and DLQ recovery behind plain HTTP A small SaaS values one key, one bill, and little Node.js integration glue The system needs workflow graphs, joins, replay, or private push targets
AWS SQS Queue and dead-letter queue controls inside AWS AWS is already the operating boundary Adding AWS-specific operations is the larger integration cost
Temporal Workflow orchestration rather than a simple job envelope Long-running workflows and explicit orchestration drive the design A queue plus an idempotent worker already covers the job
Airflow DAG-oriented scheduled orchestration The work is a dependency graph Per-customer HTTP job dispatch is the primary problem
Kafka Retained event history with replay and multiple consumer patterns Replay or independent consumers is a requirement The team wants a small queue with ack-and-delete semantics

This comparison isn't a universal ranking. Temporal and Airflow are better answers for DAG or workflow orchestration and fan-out joins. Kafka is better when replay and multiple consumer groups are core requirements. Infrai doesn't provide those patterns, nor native debounce, throttle, or topic fan-out; separate queues are needed when consumers require independent acknowledgement. Stick with those specialists when their missing primitive would otherwise become application code.

BullMQ can also be the pragmatic local choice when Redis is already an accepted part of the Node.js stack and the team wants job control there. I wouldn't introduce Redis solely to make a weekly HTTP digest feel local, but existing operational ownership changes that calculation. Your mileage may vary.

Recalculate the operating bill at scale

First, split queues by failure domain rather than by arbitrary service boundaries. Email rendering and a customer webhook may have different retry budgets and different poison-message owners. They shouldn't block each other just because both began from the same Monday schedule.

Then automate the ledger check. For every expected tenantId:weekStart, confirm that a committed outcome exists; alert on missing outcomes and DLQ depth, and make redrive a deliberate operator action. Cron's missed runs are not backfilled after a pause, so reconciliation must detect a week that was never enqueued as well as a job that failed after enqueueing. A delayed message can cover a short wait, never an eight-day scheduling gap.

Keep the limit visible: a cron trigger still has a 900-second cap, delayed messages still stop at seven days, and queue retention still stops at 30 days. At larger scale I would also test the recovery procedure independently in US and EU, because a runbook that assumes cross-region access can fail the policy review even when its queue mechanics are correct. The benchmark is blunt: time how long it takes an operator to find one failed tenant, prove whether an external side effect happened, and retry only that unit. Use the result to compare the full operating bill.

If this boundary matches your system, start with the current queue documentation and inspect the live schema before wiring the request into a worker.

References

  • https://docs.infrai.cc/en/guides/queue/answers/best-simple-background-job-queue-for-saas-app-nodejs-20/
  • https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/queue.create
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-dead-letter-queues.html
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/429
  • https://docs.temporal.io/
  • https://airflow.apache.org/docs/
  • https://kafka.apache.org/documentation/
  • https://docs.bullmq.io/

title: The Cloud Reliance Trap: When Convenience Becomes a Single Point of Failure
description:
Introduction

Last week we watched it happen again. Microsoft 365 and Azure services went down — not for minutes, but for hours — across nearly every region. Train tickets wouldn't open because they arrived via Outlook. NHS hospitals reached for paper records. Traders went back to phones and faxes. And thousands of businesses simply… stopped working.

It's easy to point fingers at Microsoft. But the harder question sits with us: how much of our business continuity have we outsourced to a single provider? And is the convenience worth the risk?

This isn't an anti-cloud rant. It's a cost conversation that every engineering and leadership team needs to have — because the bill for cloud isn't just the monthly invoice. Sometimes it's the outage you never see coming.

The Cost of an Outage Isn't Just "Downtime"

When services go dark, the visible number is "5 hours of outage." The real cost is much harder to calculate and much higher:

  • Lost productivity: 10 million affected workers at an average of £30/hour over 4 hours = £1.2 billion in wages paid for zero output
  • Missed revenue: Delayed transactions, lost trading opportunities, cancelled client deadlines — some losses are never recovered
  • Recovery overhead: Once systems come back, there's the backlog, the catch-up work, the rescheduled meetings. That often costs more than the outage itself
  • Reputational damage: When your customers can't work because your tools are down, trust erodes faster than any SLA can repair
  • Engineering distraction: Teams scramble to verify systems, explain delays, rebuild confidence — work that was supposed to happen gets pushed aside

The Uptime Institute found that more than 57% of organisations report their most recent major outage cost over $100,000, and one in five exceeded $1 million. And the scary part? Microsoft's subscription revenue barely dipped. You paid — and you still paid — for the service you didn't receive.

The Other Side: What Does Self-Hosting Actually Cost?

So we should all run our own email and file servers, right? Not so fast. Self-hosting has its own price tag, and it's not written on a price list.

The hidden costs of going your own way:

  • People cost: Someone has to maintain it. Updates, backups, security patches, monitoring — that's not zero labour. If your senior engineer spends 4 hours troubleshooting a mail server, that's more expensive than the £80/month license you avoided
  • Expertise gap: Most teams don't have someone whose job is running a resilient mail platform. Small configuration errors become multi-hour outages of your own making
  • Disaster recovery: When your server fails, who do you call? Restoring from backup is easy — unless you don't have a tested one
  • Scale limitations: Cloud gives you "infinite until you stop paying." Self-hosting hits a wall. You can't spin up 50 more instances during a traffic spike — you have to buy them first

But the trade-off is control. You decide your uptime. You choose your update schedule. And when something breaks, you don't sit refreshing a status page waiting for someone else to fix it. You own the problem — and the solution.

The Middle Ground Nobody Talks About

Here's where I think most teams get it wrong: it's rarely "all cloud or all self-hosted." It's about criticality and independence.

Ask yourself… Likely answer
If this goes down, can we work at all? Keep it diversified or local-first
Does it need to scale globally in seconds? Cloud is almost certainly the answer
Is our data sovereignty non-negotiable? Maybe self-host or dedicated colocation
Can we tolerate 4–8 hours of downtime once a year? Cloud with SLA credits is fine
Can we survive 1 hour without it? Redundant, multi-provider, or on-prem

The smartest move isn't abandoning cloud — it's not letting one provider become your single point of failure. That could mean:

  • Running email through one provider and your core systems on another
  • Keeping critical workflows documented offline
  • Having backup tools for when Teams or email are unreachable
  • Self-hosting internal dashboards or knowledge bases that you literally can't work without

Here's Where I'll Probably Start an Argument

I think we've drifted too far toward "someone else's computer" for things that don't actually need to be there. Productivity tools, internal documentation, basic file storage — these are well-understood, predictable workloads. They don't need elastic scaling to 10,000 nodes. They just need to be there when you arrive in the morning.

For those things, the crossover point where self-hosting becomes genuinely cheaper — not just in server costs, but in reliability and independence — is much sooner than we think. A modest server or two running Nextcloud, Mattermost, or a simple knowledge base doesn't need a team of engineers. It needs a sensible setup, good backups, and basic monitoring. And when the global cloud goes dark? Your team still works.

But here's the counterpoint I respect most: cloud outages are highly visible; self-hosted outages are silent and internal. When Microsoft goes down, everyone complains together. When your self-hosted mail server dies at 2am on a Sunday? That phone call is yours. Every. Single. Time.

Over to You

I'd love to hear your team's philosophy on this one.

Where do you draw the line? What stays in the cloud and what — if anything — do you keep under your own roof? And have you ever had that moment where you watched a status page and realised you'd handed your entire working day to someone else's infrastructure? Drop a comment — I'm genuinely curious which side of the trade-off your team sits on.

Feature

Custom organization policies for Agent Platform Workbench instances

You can now use custom organization policies to allow or deny the creation and update of Agent Platform Workbench instances based on their configuration. Custom constraints for the notebooks.googleapis.com/Instance resource are enforced when you create or update an instance, and support dry-run mode. This feature is now generally available (GA). For more information, see Create custom organization policy constraints.

Apigee X

Feature

Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool arguments are sent to the location their OpenAPI parameter declares

This change applies to Apigee X in all supported regions.

An MCP tool argument whose OpenAPI parameter declares in: header is now sent to your backend as a request header, and one that declares in: cookie is sent in the Cookie header. Previously both were appended to the query string. in: query and in: path parameters are unchanged, and every parameter still appears in the tool's inputSchema, so MCP clients supply arguments exactly as before. If a backend reads one of these values from the query string, declare the parameter in: query or read it from its declared location.

On a tool call that supplies at least one cookie argument, the Cookie header is replaced with only the declared cookie parameters, omitting any others. Any cookie your backend relies on must be declared as an in: cookie parameter.

An MCP proxy that was already deployed continues to use the previous query-string behavior until its configuration is next regenerated. To adopt the new routing on an existing MCP proxy, deploy a new revision of it.

For the full mapping, see Tool argument placement on the backend request.

Security

On October 24, 2026, we published a security bulletin for Apigee.

Two vulnerabilities in PHP core (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, "PHP2Shell") allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code remotely on a server running a vulnerable PHP version. The impact is limited to Drupal-based Apigee developer portals, which customers deploy and operate. Apigee, Apigee Hybrid, and the Apigee integrated portal don't use PHP and aren't affected.
