The same operations are available as GitRepositoryLink methods in the Developer Connect REST API.

For more information, see the Developer Connect MCP reference.

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Feature

Control user intent matching for semantic governance policies

You can now turn user intent matching on or off for semantic governance policies by setting the sgpUserIntentMatching key on the authorization extension metadata. User intent matching is on by default; set the key to DISABLED to turn it off. Turning it off reduces protection against indirect prompt injection. When the key is set, policy evaluation logs report the mode each evaluation used in the sgpUserIntentMatchingMode field.

For more information, see Control user intent matching.

Feature

Cloud Storage output support for Gemini image generation models

Direct Cloud Storage output persistence is generally available (GA) for Gemini Nano Banana 2.1 (gemini-nano-banana-2.1), Gemini 3.1 Flash Image (gemini-3.1-flash-image), Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite Image (gemini-3.1-flash-lite-image), and Gemini 3 Pro Image (gemini-3-pro-image). You can set outputConfig.outputUriPrefix and generationConfig.responseFormat[].image.delivery to "URI" in generateContent and streamGenerateContent requests to write generated and edited images directly to a Cloud Storage bucket and receive the object URI in fileData.fileUri instead of inline bytes. For more information, see Save generated images to Cloud Storage.

Feature

Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS and Gemini 3.8 Flash-Lite TTS are Generally Available (GA)

Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS and Gemini 3.8 Flash-Lite TTS are available in General Availability (GA) in the global location and the us and eu multi-regions. The models support structured speaker and style metadata, inline vocal tags, multi-speaker dialogue, and streaming. Voice design and voice replication capabilities remain available in Preview.

For more information, see Generate speech with Gemini TTS.

Feature

Semantic governance policies support more model providers

Semantic governance policies now evaluate tool calls from agents that use models from providers other than Gemini. The policy engine reads each provider's request and response format, so the same policies apply whichever model your agent uses. Supported APIs include the Gemini Developer API and Gemini models on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, the Anthropic Messages API, Claude models on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, the OpenAI Chat Completions API, the Mistral AI API, the OpenAI-compatible endpoint on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform (including Llama models), and self-hosted OpenAI-compatible servers such as vLLM. Streamed model responses aren't supported.

To govern these providers, update the when condition of your authorization policy to match each provider's request path. The updated condition also matches requests that include a query string.

For more information, see Supported model providers and Connect the policy engine to Agent Gateway.

Knowledge Catalog

Feature

Support for Looker (Google Cloud core) in Data lineage is now generally available. This support includes lineage views for LookML views and Explores, Looker dashboards, dashboard elements, Looks, LookML dashboards, and Conversational Analytics agents. You can control data lineage ingestion at the organization, folder, and project levels. You can also visualize the end-to-end flow of your data from BigQuery sources through the Looker semantic layer to downstream assets.

For more information, see Track data lineage with Knowledge Catalog, About data lineage, and About data lineage ingestion control.

Looker

Feature

Looker (Google Cloud core) data lineage is now generally available (GA). The GA launch adds end-to-end visibility for LookML dashboards and Conversational Analytics agents. Lineage enablement is now managed independently through the Data Lineage API and service-level ingestion controls, which decouples it from Looker's internal Knowledge Catalog metadata settings. For more information, see About data lineage.

Feature

The Looker-managed Model Context Protocol (MCP) server is now generally available (GA), allowing AI agents to securely interact with business data and LookML models without the need for additional middleware. This launch is supported by a new Manage OAuth Clients admin page, which provides a centralized interface for governing identity-based access for AI agents and other external applications. Administrators can now quickly enable pre-configured integrations from the Application Library or register custom OAuth clients with specific redirect URIs and group-based access controls.

Model Armor

Feature

Model Armor enforces the constraints/modelarmor.managed.requireTemplateDataResidencyCompliance managed Organization Policy Service constraint by default. When you create or update a template, this constraint prevents you from setting data_residency_compliant to false or clearing the Enforce data residency option unless an Organization Policy Administrator disables the constraint. This feature is generally available (GA). For more information, see Disable the organization policy constraint for data residency.

Oracle Database@Google Cloud

Feature

The Oracle Database@Google Cloud remote MCP server is generally available (GA) and adds tools to create and manage Database Connections and run SQL statements with database_connection_executesql. It lets you interact easily with Oracle Database@Google Cloud resources from LLMs, AI applications, and AI-enabled development platforms.

For more information, see Use the Oracle Database@Google Cloud remote MCP server.

title: Build Payment Corridors from Capabilities, Not Country Switch Statements
description:
Designing configurable international transfers without turning every new market into an application release.

International payment products often begin with country-specific code:

if country == "A":
    require_bank_code()
elif country == "B":
    require_iban()

This works for the first few corridors. It becomes fragile when one country supports several rails, a rail has different fees, funding is enabled before payout, or a provider temporarily disables a destination.

A more durable model separates four capabilities:

country availability
funding methods
payout methods
recipient requirements

A country can be active in the directory while funding remains disabled. A payout method can be available for one currency and unavailable for another. A bank rail can require an account number and routing code, while a wallet rail may require only a handle or an optional QR image.

Make recipient fields data-driven

The recipient form should come from a requirement schema attached to the selected country, currency, and payout method. Each field needs a stable key, label, type, validation rule, display order, and required flag.

This prevents a wallet recipient from being asked for an IBAN or a bank beneficiary from receiving irrelevant mobile fields. The backend must validate against the same schema. Client-side visibility alone is not a security or data-integrity boundary.

Keep provider routing behind the corridor

The customer chooses a destination and payout method, not an internal provider. Routing should resolve the configured provider after validating availability. Persist the selected route on the transaction so a later configuration change cannot reinterpret an existing payment.

Configuration changes should affect new quotes and transfers. Existing transactions should retain the provider, fee, exchange rate, destination snapshot, and requirements used when they were created.

Return capabilities through one contract

Mobile screens for send, deposit, and withdrawal should not maintain separate hard-coded country lists. A capabilities endpoint can return whether each action is enabled, supported currencies, methods, and recipient requirements.

Default selection can use the customer's location only when that country supports the requested action. Otherwise, choose an explicit product fallback and explain the selection rather than silently showing an unusable flow.

Audit operational changes

Staff should be able to activate or deactivate corridors and capabilities in bulk, but every change needs an actor, timestamp, previous value, and new value. High-impact changes should support staged activation and validation before becoming visible to customers.

Cache the directory for performance, but include a configuration version in the response and cache key. When staff switch a provider or change a bank directory, clients should receive the new version without requiring users to refresh repeatedly.

The architecture scales when adding a country is primarily a configuration and validation exercise, while the shared transaction state machine, ledger, and operational fallback remain unchanged.

Implementation checklist

Version corridor configuration and validate it before activation. Ensure every enabled payout method has a provider route, currency, fee rule, recipient schema, and fallback policy. Reject configurations that create an enabled customer path with no executable route.

Test the capabilities contract against each client version still in circulation. Add contract tests for required recipient fields and verify that old clients receive a safe unavailable response when they cannot render a newly introduced method. Operational flexibility should not create an invalid form on a previously released application.

title: Black Friday code freeze: what design can still change
description:
Black Friday is November 27 this year, and most freeze guides put the lock on theme, app and checkout changes between November 13 and 20. Today is the 13th. If your team treats "freeze" as "stop thinking about the storefront", you are about to spend the busiest two weeks of the year leaving known checkout problems in place.
This article argues that a freeze should lock code, not design. It shows which checkout and product page fixes are safe because they are content, not code, ranks them by what the research says costs you orders, and gives a plan for the 14 days left.

A freeze protects code, and that is all it protects

The reason for a freeze is simple. A new bug in browsing or checkout costs the most when traffic peaks. The Good's holiday code freeze guide says it plainly. Feature changes that need code wait until the freeze ends.

Look at how those guides define the line, though. The Shopify-focused Craftshift 2026 plan sorts work by how fast you can undo it. Theme code, app installs, checkout customizations and Shopify Functions are red, because rollback takes hours. App settings and styling are amber, with rollback in minutes. Prices, banners, product copy, images and collection membership are green, and you can undo them in seconds. Its dates are one vendor's recommendation, not Shopify policy, but the logic holds. Risk follows rollback time, not whether a designer touched it.

The same Craftshift plan locks configuration on Friday, November 13 and code on November 20. So you have a week where content and data stay open, and a few days where only critical fixes ship. Too many teams spend that week waiting.

That is a mistake, because checkout problems are mostly not exotic. They are well documented, and several of them live in copy and data.

Rank the fixes by what actually loses orders

Start from the evidence instead of the backlog. Baymard's cart abandonment research averages 50 studies at a 70.22% abandonment rate. Among shoppers who intended to buy, it lists the reasons. 40% cite extra costs such as shipping, tax and fees, 20% slow delivery, 19% distrust of the site with card details, 18% forced account creation, 17% a long or complicated checkout, 12% a total cost that was not visible up front, and 13% an unsatisfactory returns policy.

Now sort those by rollback speed. Extra costs and a hidden total are a data and copy problem for many stores. Think shipping thresholds, delivery estimates, a line on the product page. Delivery speed is partly a promise you can state more clearly. Returns policy is a page. Trust is wording, badges and payment method labels. Account creation is a setting on Shopify and most other platforms. Only a long checkout is a real code problem.

Baymard also says that fixing solvable checkout usability issues could raise conversion by 35.26% for a large site. Treat that as an upper bound for sites with many unfixed problems, not a forecast. Baymard has also said it is retesting its checkout research and expects new findings in the second quarter of 2027, so the exact percentages may move. The ranking of reasons has been stable for years, which is why I trust it for a two-week decision.

The point is that most of the top reasons for abandonment can be addressed with changes your freeze policy already calls green or amber.

Show the total cost before the cart

Since extra costs are the top reason, start there. A shopper who sees a $9 shipping fee for the first time on the payment step reads it as a trick, however fair the fee is.

The no-code fixes are boring and effective. Put the free shipping threshold in the announcement bar and on the cart drawer with a live "you are $14 away" line, which is a content block on most themes. Add estimated delivery dates by region to the product page, because for Black Friday orders the question "will it arrive by December 24?" is the one on people's minds. State your holiday returns window in one sentence near the buy button. Make guest checkout the default and hide account creation until after payment.

If you cannot show exact tax, show a range and say it is an estimate. A range that is roughly right beats a surprise that is exactly right.

Check each change against one question. Could this break a payment? Copy, banners and threshold messages do not touch the payment flow. A new fee calculator does, so it waits until December.

Test less, but do not stop looking

Many guides argue about whether to run A/B tests during the holidays. The honest answer is that most stores should not start new ones now. Convert's guide says Black Friday through Cyber Monday is a two to four day window of hyper-shopping, and that conversion rate, average order value and revenue per visitor swing sharply, with flash deals, ad spend and competitor offers all changing the conditions. A test that starts on November 24 and ends on November 30 tells you about Black Friday, not about your store in March.

The Good takes the opposite line. More traffic means faster significance, and "your biggest risk is doing nothing". Both can be right. That article is from 2021 and gives no data, so I read it as a reminder, not as proof. Traffic does speed things up, but only for questions that matter in a normal week.

My rule is this. If a test can reach a readable result by about November 20, let it finish. If not, ship the obviously better version to everyone only when you have a documented reason, not a hunch, and write it down. Baymard's reasons are such a reason. A hidden shipping cost is not a hypothesis to test during Black Friday.

What you should do is watch. Heatmaps, session recordings and customer service tickets cost nothing in risk terms. Set up your conversion tracking before traffic arrives, as The Good advises, so that you have clean data for the first week of December.

A plan for the next 14 days

Here is the sequence I would run, assuming a Shopify store and a team of one to three people.

Today and tomorrow, take a snapshot. Duplicate the live theme as a restore point, export your settings and list who can publish. The Craftshift plan recommends the same, plus one monitoring dashboard and a rollback rule agreed in advance, such as "revert if checkout completion drops by a set amount over an hour".

By Monday, audit the green list against Baymard's reasons. Open your store on a phone, add a product to the cart and go through checkout as a stranger. Write down every moment where you learned a cost, a date or a policy for the first time. Each one is a copy or data fix.

By Wednesday, ship the fixes. That means a threshold message, delivery dates, returns line, guest checkout default, and payment method icons. Log each change with a time and the person who made it, so a bad hour is easy to explain.

From November 20, touch nothing in code. Content stays open, including prices, stock, banners and emails. Keep the thaw date at December 1 or later, since Cyber Monday orders arrive until midnight.

Last, keep a list of the red items you wanted and could not ship, such as a faster checkout step, a new cart design or an app. That list is your January plan, and it will be better informed because you watched real peak traffic first. For help judging whether your conversion numbers are healthy when peak week ends, my Shopify conversion benchmarks piece explains why published figures disagree.

Originally published on kireev.us.

title: LED strip flickers only at low brightness? My 10-minute debugging order
description:
A strip that is stable at 100% but flickers at 20% is not necessarily defective. Low brightness is where dimming method, controller resolution, power supply behavior, and wiring noise all meet.

This is the order I use before replacing anything.

1. Find out what is actually doing the dimming

A PWM controller, a phase-cut wall dimmer, and an addressable controller creating dimming in software are three different systems. A lamp-rated wall dimmer feeding an ordinary LED strip supply can produce exactly this symptom, and no change to the strip will solve it.

For a low-voltage DC strip, I want a compatible constant-voltage supply and a PWM controller on the DC side. If there is a phase-cut dimmer on the AC side, every component has to be designed for that chain.

2. Check whether the flicker follows the output level

Set the controller to a fixed low level and watch for a minute. Then raise it slowly.

Regular pulsing at one brightness often points to PWM frequency or limited dimming resolution. Random flashes while the level changes can be a control or signal issue. A brief drop when another load switches on points me toward the supply and wiring instead.

A phone camera can help reveal pulsing, but I do not use it as the only test. Cameras add their own sampling artifacts.

3. Measure the DC bus at the strip

Measure at the strip terminals, not only at the supply. Compare full brightness and the problematic setting.

A loose terminal or undersized lead can sit unnoticed at low current and become unstable when the load changes. I also check that the supply is not operating below a required minimum load. Some supplies need a small stable load to regulate cleanly.

4. Separate PWM flicker from data flicker

With analog white or RGB strip, the controller switches the power rails. With WS2812 or similar pixels, the power rail stays on and the controller sends data. Those failures look similar from across the room but need different fixes.

For addressable pixels, I check the ground shared by the controller and pixels, the data resistor, and the first pixel before touching the rest of the run. For PWM strip, I check the controller's output frequency and whether it supports the frequency I need.

This comparison of PWM and pixel control is a useful reference when choosing the control method: https://suntechlite.com/pwm-vs-spi-led-lighting/

5. Bypass one component at a time

My fastest useful test is a short known-good strip on the same controller. Then the original strip on a known-good controller. One variable at a time.

If the short strip flickers too, the original run is probably innocent. If the problem stays with the original run, I inspect connectors, damaged sections, and the first powered joint.

I replace the strip only after those tests point to it. Most low-brightness flicker complaints I see are compatibility or control problems, not dead LEDs.

title: Website accessibility for small business sites: the WCAG 2.2 fixes that take under an hour
description:
Short answer: The accessibility problems on small business websites are mostly the same few, and most of them are quick to fix. WebAIM's 2026 scan of the top one million home pages found low contrast text on 83.9% of them, missing image alt text on 53.1% and missing form labels on 51%. Fixing text contrast, alt text, form labels, visible focus, tap target size and the page language takes about an hour on a typical five-page site. It removes the most common barriers, but it doesn't make a site fully WCAG conformant on its own.

This post walks through those fixes with the WCAG 2.2 success criterion behind each one, the code, and how to check your work. It also covers what the law does and doesn't say, because that's the first question most owners ask.

What is WCAG 2.2, and what level should a small business site aim for?

WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines) is the W3C's standard for accessible web content, and Level AA is the usual target. WCAG 2.2 was first published as a W3C Recommendation on 5 October 2023, with the current version dated 12 December 2024. It added nine success criteria and removed one (4.1.1 Parsing, now obsolete).

Each success criterion is a testable rule with a level: A (the minimum), AA (what laws and contracts usually reference) and AAA (enhanced). Two of the new AA criteria matter on almost every small site: 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) and 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum). Both are in the fixes below.

Is website accessibility legally required for US small businesses?

There's no federal regulation with detailed technical web standards for private businesses, but the ADA still applies to them. The Department of Justice's web guidance says the ADA's requirements apply to all the goods and services offered by businesses open to the public, that inaccessible website features can limit access to them, and that "the Department of Justice does not have a regulation setting out detailed standards." It describes WCAG as "helpful guidance."

The rule people often hear about is the 2024 Title II rule, which adopted WCAG 2.1 Level AA for state and local governments, not private businesses. An interim final rule published in April 2026 moved its compliance dates to April 26, 2027 for larger governments and April 26, 2028 for smaller ones.

What this means for you as the developer:

  • Don't sell "ADA compliance" or anything that sounds like legal protection. You're not the client's lawyer, and nobody can promise that.
  • Be wary of one-line overlay widgets that claim to fix everything. In April 2025 the FTC finalized an order requiring accessiBe to pay $1 million over claims that its plug-in could make any website WCAG compliant.
  • Sell what you actually do: fixing real barriers that stop customers from reading, calling and booking.

How do you fix low contrast text? (about 10 minutes)

Make body text at least 4.5:1 against its background, and large text at least 3:1. That's 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum), Level AA. "Large" means at least 18 point, or 14 point bold, which works out to about 24 CSS pixels regular or about 18.7 CSS pixels bold.

On small business sites the failures cluster in the same places:

  • Light grey body text on white, chosen because it "looks cleaner".
  • White text on a hero photo with no overlay. Contrast changes across the image, so part of the headline fails.
  • Placeholder text inside form fields.
  • Brand-colored buttons with white text, such as light green or yellow.

Check each color pair with a contrast checker (WebAIM's is free) or the color picker in Chrome DevTools, which shows the ratio. For hero text over photos, add an overlay rather than changing the brand color:

.hero { position: relative; }
.hero::before {               /* darken the photo under the headline */
  content: ""; position: absolute; inset: 0;
  background: linear-gradient(90deg, rgb(0 0 0 / .65), rgb(0 0 0 / .2));
}
.hero > * { position: relative; }
body { color: #333; }          /* #333 on white is well above 4.5:1 */

Icons, input borders and focus outlines fall under a separate rule, 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast (AA): at least 3:1 against adjacent colors.

How do you write alt text that actually helps? (about 15 minutes)

Give every meaningful image a short text alternative that says what it shows or does, and give decorative images an empty alt="". That's 1.1.1 Non-text Content, Level A, and missing alt text was the second most common failure in the WebAIM data.

<!-- Meaningful photo -->
<img src="deck.webp" alt="Cedar deck with built-in benches, finished in 2025">

<!-- Logo that links home: describe the destination -->
<a href="/"><img src="logo.svg" alt="Fictional Example Decks, home"></a>

<!-- Decorative divider: empty alt, so screen readers skip it -->
<img src="wave.svg" alt="">

The one we see most on local sites is worse than missing alt text: the opening hours, the menu or a price list posted only as an image or a scanned flyer. Put that information in real HTML text. It helps screen reader users, people who zoom, and search engines, and the owner can update it without opening a design app.

How do you label form fields properly? (about 10 minutes)

Every input needs a visible label tied to it with for and id. That's 3.3.2 Labels or Instructions (Level A), with 1.3.1 and 4.1.2 covering the code side. A placeholder isn't a label: it disappears when you start typing and is usually low contrast.

<label for="phone">Phone number</label>
<input id="phone" name="phone" type="tel" autocomplete="tel" required>

<label for="job">What do you need help with?</label>
<textarea id="job" name="job" rows="4"></textarea>

Page builder form widgets sometimes hide labels and rely on placeholders by default. Look for a "show label" setting before writing custom code.

How do you make keyboard focus visible and not hidden? (about 10 minutes)

Never remove the focus outline without replacing it, and make sure sticky headers and cookie banners don't cover the focused element. The first is 2.4.7 Focus Visible (AA). The second is new in WCAG 2.2: 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum), Level AA, which requires that a focused component "is not entirely hidden due to author-created content."

/* Replace "outline: none" in the theme with a clear indicator */
:focus-visible { outline: 3px solid #1a56db; outline-offset: 3px; }

/* Keep focused elements from scrolling under a 72px sticky header */
html { scroll-padding-top: 88px; }

Test it by pressing Tab from the top of the page to the footer. You should always be able to see where you are. If the cookie banner sits over the bottom of the screen, make sure focus can reach its buttons and that it doesn't cover the links behind it.

How big do tap targets need to be under WCAG 2.2? (about 10 minutes)

At least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, or spaced so that a 24 px circle around each one doesn't touch another target. That's 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum), Level AA. There are exceptions, including links inside a sentence and controls the browser draws itself. The AAA level, 2.5.5, asks for 44 by 44 pixels, and that's a sensible design target for a site people use on their phone.

The usual offenders are the row of social icons in the footer, the close "X" on a popup, and phone and email links squeezed together in a top bar.

.social a, .popup-close {
  display: inline-grid; place-items: center;
  min-width: 44px; min-height: 44px;   /* passes 2.5.8 comfortably */
}

What else fits into the hour?

Three quick ones that also show up in the WebAIM top six:

  • Set the page language. <html lang="en"> (or es, or whatever the site is in). That's 3.1.1 Language of Page, Level A, missing on 13.5% of home pages in the 2026 scan.
  • Name icon-only buttons and links. A hamburger button or a phone icon with no text is an "empty button" or "empty link" to a screen reader. Add visible text or an aria-label.
  • Make link text say where it goes. "Click here" and "Read more" tell nobody anything out of context. "See our drain cleaning prices" does. That's 2.4.4 Link Purpose (In Context), Level A.

Here are all of the fixes in one place. The times are our rough estimates for a typical five-page site, not measurements:

Fix WCAG 2.2 criterion Level Rough time
Text contrast 4.5:1 (3:1 large) 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) AA 10 min
Alt text, empty alt for decoration 1.1.1 Non-text Content A 15 min
Visible, connected form labels 3.3.2 Labels or Instructions A 10 min
Visible focus indicator 2.4.7 Focus Visible AA 5 min
Focus not hidden by sticky UI 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) AA 5 min
Tap targets 24x24 px minimum 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) AA 10 min
Page language 3.1.1 Language of Page A 1 min
Named icon buttons, clear link text 4.1.2 and 2.4.4 A 5 min

How do you check your work?

Use one automated tool and two manual checks. Automated tools catch only part of the problems, so don't stop at a green score.

  1. Run WAVE (from WebAIM) or axe DevTools on each page and fix what they flag.
  2. Tab through every page with the keyboard only. Can you reach and see everything, and open the menu?
  3. Zoom the browser to 200%. Text should still be readable without content being cut off (1.4.4 Resize Text, Level AA).

When you report back to the owner, describe barriers removed, not legal status. A fictional example:

I fixed the issues that stopped some customers from using your site: the grey text on the homepage was too faint to read for many people, the quote form fields had no labels for screen readers, and the hours were only in a picture. Those are all fixed now. This isn't a full accessibility audit, but it covers the most common problems we see on small business sites.

Finding sites that need this

The manual way: search a trade and a town, run a few home pages through WAVE, and note the ones with faint text and unlabeled forms. On most local sites you'll find something within a minute.

If you'd rather start from a list, LeadReef finds local businesses whose websites are outdated, broken on mobile or missing, shows what's wrong with each one, and helps with a first mockup and outreach message. You choose who to contact and send everything yourself. The first 10 leads are free. Full disclosure: we build LeadReef. Everything above works without it.

Frequently asked questions

What WCAG level should a small business website meet?

Level AA is the usual target and what most laws, contracts and policies reference. The current version is WCAG 2.2, which adds nine new criteria to WCAG 2.1 and drops the obsolete 4.1.1 Parsing.

Is ADA website compliance required for small businesses in the US?

The DOJ says the ADA applies to the goods and services of businesses open to the public, including what they offer online, but it has no regulation with detailed web standards for private businesses. For legal questions, the owner should talk to a lawyer; your job is fixing the barriers.

What contrast ratio does WCAG require?

4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text (at least 18 point, or 14 point bold) under 1.4.3, Level AA. Icons, input borders and focus indicators need 3:1 under 1.4.11.

What is the minimum tap target size in WCAG 2.2?

24 by 24 CSS pixels under 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum), Level AA, with exceptions for spacing, inline links and browser-drawn controls. 44 by 44 pixels is the AAA level and a good design target.

Do accessibility overlay widgets make a site compliant?

Don't count on it. The FTC finalized an order in April 2025 requiring overlay vendor accessiBe to pay $1 million over claims that its plug-in could make any website WCAG compliant. Fixing the underlying HTML and CSS is the reliable route.

Sources (checked November 2026): W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2; W3C WAI, What's New in WCAG 2.2; W3C WAI, Understanding 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum); WebAIM, The WebAIM Million (2026); U.S. Department of Justice, Guidance on Web Accessibility and the ADA; Seyfarth Shaw, ADA Title III blog, DOJ extends ADA Title II website accessibility deadlines (April 2026); Federal Trade Commission, FTC approves final order requiring accessiBe to pay $1 million (April 22, 2025).

title: Managing Compatibility Between Host Apps and Mini Apps
description:
A wallet's invoicing Mini App works on a developer's current phone. Its new document-import flow calls a host capability introduced in the latest wallet build. An earlier wallet can still support manual draft creation, but it does not implement that handoff. Meanwhile, the provider's backend is preparing to accept the imported invoice items.

The release decision concerns a set of running combinations. It cannot be reduced to whether the newest Mini App package passed its own tests.

This illustrative integration uses a document-import capability implemented by the wallet team, with its own interface contract.

Track the independently changing layers

FinClip supplies the Mini App runtime SDK, development tools and management platform. The enterprise or its implementation partner builds the host application, Mini Apps and backend connections. The business provider operates the invoicing service.

For this integration, the relevant dependencies are:

Layer What the release record should identify
Installed Host App Actual app build, platform and supported operating-system environment
Runtime SDK SDK embedded in that build
Framework or base library Framework version actually used by the runtime
Mini App package Tested artefact and package version
Host capability contract Document handoff inputs, outputs, cancellation and errors
Business backend contract Accepted invoice requests, identity context and response behaviour

The project maintains this integration record alongside its release evidence. A package approval, a runtime version and a backend deployment describe different facts.

Read the version field you actually need

FinClip's basic API documentation distinguishes appVersion, runtimeSDKVersion and frameworkVersion in system information. It describes SDKVersion separately as a compatibility value that may be fixed or declared through application configuration. Do not assume the latter identifies the native SDK embedded in the host.

A small diagnostic example using the documented fields is:

ft.getSystemInfo({
  success(info) {
    console.info({
      hostAppVersion: info.appVersion,
      runtimeVersion: info.runtimeSDKVersion,
      frameworkVersion: info.frameworkVersion
    });
  }
});

Confirm availability and returned values in the SDK and platform you support. This captures context; it does not prove that the wallet's document-import bridge exists or that a particular merchant can access an invoice.

Keep your custom bridge contract explicit. Decide how the Mini App learns that the implemented capability is available, what happens when the request is cancelled and how unsupported environments are handled. Implement and test that agreement on both sides. Avoid interpreting a familiar app version string as evidence for a capability that has never been exercised in that build.

Turn dependencies into a testable support matrix

Use named host builds and retained package artefacts to populate a matrix. The following rows describe test intentions, not real FinClip version numbers or supported combinations:

Host environment Mini App state Backend state Expected result
Supported earlier build Current package Transition-compatible backend Manual draft creation works; import is handled as unavailable
Current supported build Current package Transition-compatible backend Manual entry and import both complete correctly
Current supported build Earlier downloaded package Updated backend Previously supported request format still works
Next host candidate Current released package Current backend Existing service passes regression checks
Retired build Any observed package Current backend Unsupported task leads to clear upgrade guidance

Attach evidence to each supported row: build identifiers, package hash, relevant configuration, test date and owner. Include the business result being checked. “Mini App opens” is insufficient when document import returns to the wrong draft or an invoice request carries the wrong merchant context.

If an optional capability is absent, a reduced journey should still complete a defined task. In this example, manual entry can remain a supported way to create a draft. If the business makes import essential, it needs a different support decision and an upgrade path before entry into that task.

Exercise update transitions as well as clean starts

The FinClip development FAQ describes an existing downloaded package opening while an update is obtained, with a completed replacement used on a later opening. Poor connectivity can prolong the old-package state.

The backend should therefore be assessed against the earlier clients that the support policy still includes. In the example, adding an import field should not unintentionally make it mandatory for manual-entry requests. The provider can introduce a compatible change, migrate callers and later retire the earlier format under an explicit plan. The implementation must establish what “compatible” means for that service.

Test an existing installation, its downloaded Mini App and representative saved draft data. Exercise interrupted downloads, repeated openings and return from the host workflow. Verify that cancellation leaves a comprehensible state and that retries do not accidentally create duplicate business work. The service backend needs to implement and validate the appropriate retry behaviour.

The next native host build needs the reverse test: run the currently released Mini App against it before the host change reaches customers. A partner cannot be expected to detect a host regression using only its own package pipeline.

Diagnose the failing boundary before choosing recovery

Record enough non-sensitive technical context to reproduce a failure: host build, runtime and framework versions, Mini App package identifier and relevant contract revision. Decide separately how the project handles business identifiers and diagnostic data. Avoid collecting invoice contents merely to establish which software combination failed.

Then locate the failure. A missing native handoff requires a host or journey decision. A changed response shape requires an interface correction. A backend rejecting an earlier request format requires a backend transition decision. These causes can look similar from a merchant's screen but need different remedies.

FinClip's Mini App management documentation describes trial, review and online versions, with publication and version-recovery mechanisms. Use the controls available in the selected environment, and verify their effect. Restoring an earlier Mini App package does not restore an earlier backend or rewrite saved business records.

For the same reason, access to a host capability is separate from backend authorisation. A correctly implemented document handoff must still associate its result with the intended business and permitted task. Test that boundary when host context changes.

Make the matrix part of the release decision

The matrix should remain small enough to operate. Use actual customer environments and a declared support policy to decide which combinations matter. Retaining every historical build indefinitely is a business commitment with engineering consequences.

Host teams own their build and capability evidence. Mini App teams own package dependencies and the supported interface behaviour. Backend teams own the server-side transition. A service owner coordinates whether the tested combinations meet the promised customer experience.

An unresolved row should result in a narrower supported scope, additional validation or a postponed release. It should not disappear because each team independently marked its own component complete.

When evaluating FinClip, test one current Mini App against a supported older host build and the next host candidate. That gives the team a concrete basis for assessing the runtime, development tools and management workflow alongside its own interface contracts and compatibility policy.

title: Letting an AI assistant read SQL Server without letting it write
description:
The problem

The request sounds simple: let an AI assistant answer questions from a company's on-premises SQL Server. The hard part is what the assistant must not be able to do.

The threat model treats the assistant itself as the attacker: it can be prompt-injected, for example by text stored in a table it just read, or simply make a mistake. The goal is that three things still hold: it cannot change the database, it cannot read outside the connected database, and it cannot get data back from a call before that call is recorded.

First, what no gateway fixes: the rows the assistant reads leave the building, to the AI vendor that runs the model. Read-only does not change that. What may be sent, under which personal-data rules (KVKK in Turkey, others elsewhere), is the firm's decision.

The design

mssql-readonly-mcp is a free, open-source (MIT) MCP server in C# on .NET 10. The assistant's client starts it as a local stdio process. It offers three tools: list_tables, describe_table and run_query. Only run_query takes SQL.

Layer 1: a SELECT-only gate built on the parser

Before anything is sent, the SQL text is parsed with ScriptDom, the T-SQL parser library. It must be exactly one plain SELECT, and every node in its syntax tree must be on a hand-written allowlist of node types and function names. A refused call opens no connection.

It is an allowlist, not a keyword filter, because the publicly reported bypass classes are shapes, not words: stacked statements, GO batches, EXEC of a string, DML inside or after a CTE, nested comments. The regression table replays them (71 allowed and 247 refused rows), and a generated test makes sure a node type that a later ScriptDom version adds cannot pass silently.

The parser and the server do not always read text the same way: a GO on its own line is a batch separator to the parser, but SQL Server reads it as a column alias and runs both statements. 335 lexer cases go to a real SQL Server, and the test asserts the split exactly: 269 refused by the gate, 61 allowed and read the same by the server, 5 allowed and refused by the server.

Layer 2: the login, checked at startup

The gate is not trusted alone. At start, the server asks SQL Server what its login may do, and it will not start with a login that fails its permission check: exit code 3, no override. A setup script grants SELECT only on the tables and views the firm lists; a table without a grant is not even listed.

Every run_query call also runs in a transaction that is always rolled back, but that is not counted as a layer: a read can still leave an auto-created statistics object behind.

Limits on every call

Results are capped by rows (200 by default), characters (40,000) and time (30 s per call). Each session sets a lock timeout (5000 ms by default) and low deadlock priority, so the assistant's query loses a deadlock against a session at the default priority. A call that has not ended 0.5 s after its limit is answered as Timeout with no data; its clean-up goes on at SQL Server after the answer.

A tamper-evident audit log

No call returns data before its hash-chained audit line is written. A line is one JSON line with SHA-256 hashes and the hash of the previous line, so the file forms a chain, and it is flushed to disk before the result goes back. If the line cannot be written, the query has still run and the call returns an error and no data. verify-audit exits 0 on an intact file and 1 on a tampered copy.

How it was tested

Test suites. In the last full run before v0.1.1 (2026-11-13, on Windows) all tests passed: Gate 416 and Audit 90 unit tests, and Integration 259 of 259 on each of three SQL Server images (2019, 2022 and 2025). CI runs the suites on every push and pull request. An Extended Events trace of the reader login shows no batch, RPC or login event for refused statements. One integration test is still not stable: it failed in 4 of 19 runs on the 2022 image on earlier code, and the failures whose message was captured after v0.1.0 had a cause other than U-1R (below). It can fail in CI or locally.

Five attack-test runs. A harness spoke JSON-RPC over stdio to the built server, against SQL Server in local containers:

Run What it found What was done
1 No gate bypass, no change to database state, no password in any output. X-1 (LOW): a malformed tool call got no audit line; no SQL ran. X-1 fixed: such a call is audited before its answer.
2 584 outcome rows per engine, same counts on all three; X-1 fix retested. 18 of 19 extra logins refused at start. The one that passed owns another database: a documented limit.
3 788 rows per engine. T-1 (LOW): a timed-out call ended up to about 5 s past its limit; T-2 (LOW): a frozen connection was not bounded. Answer at the limit plus 0.5 s.
4 Every single-call Timeout at most 0.56 s past the limit. New: U-1 (MEDIUM), a session could keep a read transaction and a lock after the network recovered; U-2 (LOW). The server closes a broken connection the client library left open.
5 U-1 fixed for every frozen-link, cancel, cut and schema-tool case measured: no session 0.2 to 0.7 s after the release, where the pre-fix build still had it at 60 s. New: U-1R (MEDIUM). U-1R fixed in v0.1.1, best effort (below). U-2 unchanged.

A code security review found 1 MEDIUM, 3 LOW and 6 NOTE items; the MEDIUM one (C-1), a time limit per network read instead of per call, was changed to one limit per call. Scans on 2026-11-12, on an earlier commit than the last code changes: gitleaks no leaks, semgrep 0 findings, CodeQL 0 open alerts, no vulnerable NuGet package. The dependency scans reported three advisories, two of them HIGH, in packages under the build-time packaging tool (not in the server); since 2026-11-13 its lock file resolves versions outside their ranges.

The attack tests and the code review are my own, run apart from the writing of the code. They are not a third-party audit, not a penetration test by an outside firm and not a certification. They made no finding of severity HIGH or above. The attack tests were not run again for v0.1.1.

What v0.1.1 changes: U-1R

In attack test run 5, before v0.1.0, on a link throttled to 5 KB/s, 8 of 27 single calls and 21 of 450 calls repeated 50 in a row were answered Timeout but left the reader's session at SQL Server with an open read transaction and a lock. No data leaked, no audit line was missing.

The diagnosis found the case v0.1.0 missed: the client library broke the connection a second time, which left its parser Broken, and v0.1.0 closed only a connection whose parser was Closed. v0.1.1 also closes such a connection, best effort, under the conditions its release notes list. The fix was retested on SQL Server 2022 on Windows only, with the link throttled to 5 KB/s, a 3 s limit and the throttle released 10 s after the limit: in 100 of 100 runs the call was answered Timeout and no run left the session.

Not shown for the fix: SQL Server 2019 and 2025 in this case, the 50 calls in a row, a link throttled for 60 s, a real slow network, Linux and macOS.

Known limits

  • Data leaves the building, as said above.
  • U-2. Many calls frozen at once in the middle of a row delay every answer: with 60 or 120 such calls at a 5 s limit, the median answer came after 8.2 to 30.2 s.
  • One unstable test, above.
  • Error text can reveal that a table without a grant exists, and its column names; no row data.
  • The login check runs once, at start, and does not inspect everything.
  • Other SQL Server versions and Windows installations were not tested.
  • The audit chain does not show removal of the newest lines or a full rewrite, unless the last hash is copied somewhere the writer cannot write; the hash has no key. On Windows a second server process on the same path writes a sibling file: verify every file.

How to try it

The release has builds and MCPB bundles for Windows x64, Linux x64 and macOS arm64: https://github.com/oguzhanpisgin/mssql-readonly-mcp/releases/tag/v0.1.1

The README's "Five-minute start" has four steps: download the build and check it against SHA256SUMS; list your tables in scripts/create-readonly-login.sql, run it as an administrator, then check-login; connect your client; ask, then run verify-audit. The install page says which client blocks were run. Not shown yet: the Linux and macOS builds started on their systems, and a v0.1.1 bundle installed in any host. docs/demo.md records one Claude Code run, with a refused UPDATE.

Found a write or a call with no audit line? Please report it privately, as SECURITY.md describes.

Most of the code and the documentation of this project, and this article, were written with AI coding assistants, directed by me.

Free and MIT-licensed: https://github.com/oguzhanpisgin/mssql-readonly-mcp

title: CoReMem: Cost-Internalizing Memory for Successive Coding Tasks with Prospective Valuation
description:
Coding agents that work across successive tasks on an evolving repository face a memory problem: they must decide what to remember before they know what the next task will ask. Every memory segment costs tokens to write, tokens to retrieve, and context window space to store. The agent needs to predict which fragments will pay back those costs when the next task arrives.

CoReMem (Coding-Repository Memory) treats memory selection as a cost-benefit problem. It measures the prospective value of each trajectory segment by running the next task twice: once with the segment included, once without. The difference in resolution rate and step count becomes the segment's measured value. The agent then builds a compact memory around anchors (repository locations and executable checks) that showed positive value, and learns when to act on that memory versus waiting for more context.

The Memory Selection Problem

Most coding agents either dump everything into memory or use heuristic filters (error messages, file edits, test results). Neither approach internalizes cost. Dumping everything bloats context and slows retrieval. Heuristic filters discard segments that might be useful and keep segments that won't be.

CoReMem frames the problem explicitly:

  • Write cost: tokens spent serializing the segment
  • Read cost: tokens spent retrieving and re-parsing it
  • Storage cost: context window space occupied until the segment is used or pruned
  • Future utility: expected improvement in resolution rate and step reduction on unknown next tasks

The agent selects memory when expected utility exceeds combined costs. This requires estimating utility before the next task is revealed.

Prospective Segment Valuation

CoReMem runs a two-pass evaluation on each candidate segment from the previous task's trajectory:

  1. Baseline run: execute the next task starting from the inherited repository state, without the candidate segment in memory
  2. Memory run: execute the same next task from the same state, with the candidate segment included

The segment's value is the difference in outcome (resolved vs. unresolved) and efficiency (step count, token usage). Segments that improve resolution or reduce steps get positive value. Segments that add no benefit or slow the agent down get zero or negative value.

This approach requires access to the next task for measurement, so it works as a training signal rather than a runtime filter. The agent learns which segment types (error traces, file diffs, test outputs, dependency graphs) tend to have high prospective value across task distributions.

Anchor-Based Memory Structure

CoReMem organizes memory around two anchor types:

  • Location anchors: file paths, function names, class definitions, variable scopes
  • Executable anchors: test commands, linter invocations, build steps, runtime checks

Each anchor links to the trajectory segment that produced it. When the agent encounters a location or needs to run a check, it retrieves the linked segment. This structure keeps memory compact and makes retrieval deterministic.

The agent prunes anchors when their linked segments show low prospective value across multiple tasks. Pruning happens between tasks, not mid-task, to avoid destabilizing the current rollout.

Actor Adaptation with Provenance-Gated Credit

The agent learns when to act on memory versus when to wait for more information. CoReMem uses a reward function that prioritizes resolution and penalizes step count in successful runs:

reward = resolution_bonus - (step_count * step_penalty)

The agent runs rollout groups with and without memory access. The difference in on-policy reward estimates the memory's value. Provenance-gated credit assignment splits this value:

  • Outcome credit: every step in a successful run gets the resolution bonus
  • Memory credit: only steps that used memory-supplied anchors get the additional value term from the memory-vs-no-memory comparison

This prevents the agent from over-attributing success to memory when the task would have resolved without it. It also prevents under-attribution when memory enables a shortcut that saves steps.

Architecture and Flow 

┌─────────────────┐
│  Task N (done)  │
│  - trajectory   │
│  - repo state   │
└────────┬────────┘
         │
         ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────┐
│  Prospective Valuation          │
│  - run Task N+1 without segment │
│  - run Task N+1 with segment    │
│  - measure Δ(resolution, steps) │
└────────┬────────────────────────┘
         │
         ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────┐
│  Anchor Selection               │
│  - keep high-value segments     │
│  - prune low-value segments     │
│  - serialize anchors + links    │
└────────┬────────────────────────┘
         │
         ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────┐
│  Task N+1 (new)                 │
│  - actor retrieves anchors      │
│  - provenance tracks usage      │
│  - reward split: outcome + mem  │
└─────────────────────────────────┘

The cycle repeats for each successive task. The agent's memory grows when new anchors prove valuable and shrinks when old anchors stop paying back their cost.

Implementation Considerations

Component Trade-off Mitigation
Prospective valuation Requires running next task twice (expensive) Amortize over batch of segments; use cheaper proxy model for initial filtering
Anchor pruning Aggressive pruning loses useful context; conservative pruning bloats memory Track anchor usage frequency and recency; prune when both are low
Provenance tracking Adds instrumentation overhead to every step Use lightweight span IDs; batch provenance writes
Reward shaping Step penalty may discourage thorough exploration Tune penalty coefficient per task distribution; use separate exploration budget

The paper reports results on ChainSWE, a benchmark of successive coding tasks on evolving repositories. CoReMem raised the 27B actor's resolve rate from 21.0% to 25.7%, with 17% fewer steps and 11% fewer total cache-aware tokens (including memory module calls) relative to the untrained actor without memory.

When Memory Value Goes Negative

Memory can hurt performance in three scenarios:

  1. Stale anchors: the repository evolved and the anchor points to outdated code
  2. Misleading context: the segment describes a problem that no longer exists or a solution that no longer applies
  3. Retrieval overhead: the cost of fetching and parsing the segment exceeds the value it provides

CoReMem handles staleness by re-validating location anchors against the current repository state. If a file path or function name no longer exists, the anchor is pruned immediately. Executable anchors are re-run to confirm they still produce useful signals.

Misleading context is harder to detect. The agent relies on prospective valuation to identify segments that consistently reduce performance. If a segment type shows negative value across multiple tasks, the agent stops selecting it.

Retrieval overhead is managed by tracking token counts for each anchor retrieval. If retrieval cost exceeds the segment's measured value, the anchor is marked for pruning.

Deployment Shape

CoReMem requires three components:

  • Memory module: stores anchors, handles retrieval, tracks provenance
  • Valuation pipeline: runs paired task executions, computes segment value
  • Actor training loop: collects rollouts, assigns credit, updates policy

The memory module can be a separate service with a vector store for anchor embeddings and a key-value store for segment content. The valuation pipeline runs offline between task batches. The actor training loop runs online during task execution.

For production deployment, the valuation pipeline can be replaced with a learned value estimator that predicts segment value without running the next task. This trades measurement accuracy for speed.

Failure Modes

  • Value estimation drift: if the task distribution shifts, historical value measurements become unreliable
  • Anchor collision: multiple segments link to the same anchor, causing retrieval ambiguity
  • Credit leakage: provenance tracking misattributes memory usage when the agent uses memory indirectly (e.g., memory informs a search query that finds the answer)
  • Pruning thrash: the agent prunes an anchor, then re-discovers it in the next task, wasting write cost

The paper does not address multi-agent scenarios where memory must be shared or synchronized across actors working on the same repository.

Technical Verdict

Use CoReMem when:

  • Your agent works on successive tasks where repository state carries forward
  • Memory bloat is a bottleneck (context window exhaustion, slow retrieval)
  • You can afford offline valuation runs between task batches
  • You need explainable memory selection (anchors provide clear provenance)

Avoid CoReMem when:

  • Tasks are independent (no repository evolution)
  • You need real-time memory selection without offline training
  • Your task distribution shifts frequently (value estimates go stale)
  • You cannot instrument the actor for provenance tracking

The framework is most valuable for long-running coding agents that maintain a repository over weeks or months. For short-lived agents or one-shot tasks, the valuation overhead exceeds the memory savings.

Source Links

  • CoReMem paper on ArXiv
  • PDF

title: Toggle Switch Animation CSS: A Stretchy, Accessible Switch From a Checkbox
description:
Originally published on Crafttor.

TL;DR: A good toggle switch animation in CSS starts with a real checkbox, so it works with keyboards and screen readers for free. Slide the knob with transform, fade the track colour, and add a short stretch to the knob while it moves. Finish with role="switch", a visible focus ring and a reduced-motion fallback. Or start from the Stretch Toggle in the Capture Motion gallery.

Toggles look simple, but they are one of the most touched controls in any settings screen. A flat jump from left to right works. A knob that leans into the move and settles feels like a physical switch. The extra polish costs about ten lines of CSS.

The markup: a checkbox and a label

Start with a native input. Do not build a toggle from a div and JavaScript. You would have to rebuild focus, keyboard support and form submission by hand.

<label class="switch">
  <input type="checkbox" role="switch" class="switch__input">
  <span class="switch__track" aria-hidden="true">
    <span class="switch__knob"></span>
  </span>
  <span class="switch__label">Email notifications</span>
</label>

The role="switch" tells assistive tech this is an on and off switch, not a checkbox in a list. Screen readers then announce "on" or "off" instead of "checked". The visible track and knob are decoration, so they get aria-hidden="true".

Hide the input visually, but keep it in the page so it can take focus:

.switch__input {
  position: absolute;
  opacity: 0;
  width: 1px;
  height: 1px;
}

Avoid display: none here. It removes the input from the tab order and from the accessibility tree.

Toggle switch animation CSS: track and knob

Now style the track and the knob. Use custom properties so sizes stay in sync.

.switch {
  --w: 52px;
  --h: 30px;
  --pad: 3px;
  --knob: calc(var(--h) - var(--pad) * 2);
  display: inline-flex;
  align-items: center;
  gap: 12px;
  cursor: pointer;
}

.switch__track {
  position: relative;
  width: var(--w);
  height: var(--h);
  border-radius: 999px;
  background: #c9c9d1;
  transition: background-color 220ms ease-out;
}

.switch__knob {
  position: absolute;
  top: var(--pad);
  left: var(--pad);
  width: var(--knob);
  height: var(--knob);
  border-radius: 999px;
  background: #fff;
  box-shadow: 0 1px 3px rgb(0 0 0 / .25);
  transition: transform 260ms cubic-bezier(.22, 1, .36, 1);
}

Slide the knob

When the input is checked, move the knob across the track. The distance is the track width minus the knob and both paddings.

.switch__input:checked + .switch__track .switch__knob {
  transform: translateX(calc(var(--w) - var(--knob) - var(--pad) * 2));
}

Use transform, not left. It stays smooth because it avoids layout on every frame.

Change the track colour

The track colour is the main on and off signal. Make it clear.

.switch__input:checked + .switch__track {
  background: #17171c;
}

Check contrast between the knob and the track in both states. A pale grey off track on a white page can fail. A darker border on the track is a simple fix.

Add the stretch: the detail that makes it feel alive

A real knob does not teleport. A stretchy version widens while it travels, then snaps back to a circle when it lands. You can fake this with a short keyframe animation on the knob's width.

The trick is that the knob must stretch toward where it is going. Moving right, it grows on its right edge. Moving left, it grows on its left edge. Two keyframe sets handle that, one per direction.

@keyframes stretch-on {
  45% { width: calc(var(--knob) * 1.35); }
}
@keyframes stretch-off {
  45% {
    width: calc(var(--knob) * 1.35);
    margin-left: calc(var(--knob) * -0.35);
  }
}

.switch__knob {
  animation: stretch-off 260ms cubic-bezier(.22, 1, .36, 1);
}
.switch__input:checked + .switch__track .switch__knob {
  animation: stretch-on 260ms cubic-bezier(.22, 1, .36, 1);
}

Keyframes with only a 45% step animate from and back to the knob's normal size. The knob is pinned by left, so a wider knob grows rightward on the way on. On the way off, the negative margin-left shifts the growth to the left edge. Because the animation name changes on each flip, the browser restarts it every time.

Two trade-offs to know. Animating width and margin triggers layout, but on one small knob the cost is tiny. The off animation also plays once on page load, which most people never notice. If it bothers you, add a class to the switch after the first change and scope the animations to it.

Keep the peak stretch between 1.2 and 1.4 times the knob size. Beyond that, it reads as a bug, not a feature.

Timing guidance:

Part Duration Easing
Knob travel 220 to 300 ms Decelerating curve
Stretch peak About 40 to 50% of the travel Same curve
Track colour 180 to 240 ms ease-out

If you want a springy settle instead, CSS linear() can approximate a spring in pure CSS. Our guide on CSS linear() easing shows how to build one.

Accessibility: role, focus and reduced motion

A toggle that looks great but fails a keyboard user is a broken toggle. Cover these three points.

Role and label

You already have role="switch" and a visible text label inside the label. Clicking the text toggles the switch, and screen readers read the label. If the visible text is not enough context, add aria-describedby pointing to a helper sentence.

Focus ring

Because the input is hidden, show focus on the track instead:

.switch__input:focus-visible + .switch__track {
  outline: 2px solid #fb9f3d;
  outline-offset: 3px;
}

:focus-visible shows the ring for keyboard users without flashing it on every mouse click. Space toggles a native checkbox, so keyboard support comes for free.

Reduced motion

Respect users who ask for less motion. Drop the stretch and shorten the slide, but keep the colour change.

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .switch__knob {
    animation: none;
    transition-duration: 1ms;
  }
}

The state is still clear from the knob position and the track colour. Motion is decoration on top of that, never the only signal.

Quick accessibility checklist

  • [ ] Native input type="checkbox" with role="switch"
  • [ ] Visible text label inside the label
  • [ ] Focus ring on :focus-visible
  • [ ] On and off states differ by more than colour alone (knob position)
  • [ ] Contrast checked in both states
  • [ ] Reduced-motion fallback in place

A ready version: the Stretch Toggle in the Capture Motion gallery

Building it yourself is a good way to learn the parts. If you would rather start from a finished piece, the Capture Motion gallery has a Stretch Toggle. The knob leans toward where it is going, stretches on the way, and inverts the track as it lands.

From the gallery, you can customize it and then:

  • Send it to Figma as a Figma Motion timeline, with the keyframes and easing on tracks you can edit.
  • Copy it as code in CSS, Framer Motion or GSAP, or download it as HTML and React.

It sits next to other interactive components in the gallery. If you like the stretch idea, the liquid tabs animation uses the same leading-edge principle on a tab indicator. For a bigger gesture on a confirm action, see the slide to confirm button animation.

Seen a toggle on another site that you want to study? The Capture Motion extension can record its real keyframes, durations and easing, then export them to code or Figma. Capture or rebuild only designs you own or have permission to use.

FAQ

Should a toggle switch use a checkbox or a button?

A checkbox with role="switch" is the simplest robust choice. It works in forms, supports the Space key and reports its state. A button with aria-pressed also works, but you have to handle the state in JavaScript.

How long should a toggle switch animation be?

Around 220 to 300 ms for the knob travel. Shorter feels abrupt, longer feels sluggish on a control people flip often.

How do I make the knob stretch while it moves?

Animate scaleX or the knob width with a short keyframe that peaks near the middle of the move. Set transform-origin so the knob grows toward its direction of travel.

How do I keep the animation accessible?

Use a native checkbox with role="switch", a visible label, a :focus-visible ring and a prefers-reduced-motion fallback. Make sure the on state is clear from the knob position, not just colour.

Is there a ready-made animated toggle I can use?

Yes. The Stretch Toggle in the Capture Motion gallery can be sent to Figma as a Figma Motion timeline or copied as code.

title: Why CSS Utilities Clobber Each Other — And How @property + :where() Fixes Composition Forever
description:
If you have ever built a CSS utility library, a design system, or even a small set of helper classes, you have hit two classic CSS cascade walls:

  1. Multi-value properties overwrite each other. Applying both .transition-colors and .transition-transform to the same element means whichever rule comes later in the stylesheet wins—and silently deletes the other.
  2. Default values fight overrides. If .transition sets a default transition-duration: 200ms, then writing class="duration-500 transition" can break depending on the order those classes were defined in your CSS file, not the order you wrote them in HTML.

Most frameworks work around these issues with JavaScript class-merging utilities (tailwind-merge), bloated combinatorial classes, or !important.

Modern CSS gives us a much cleaner, zero-runtime solution. By combining CSS @property with zero-specificity :where() selectors, you can build composable, completely order-independent CSS utilities that never leak into child elements.

Here is how the architecture works in practice.

Problem 1: transition-property Is All-or-Nothing

In CSS, transition-property accepts a comma-separated list, not additive rules. Suppose you write two standard utility classes:

.transition-colors {
  transition-property: color, background-color, border-color;
  transition-duration: 200ms;
  transition-timing-function: ease-in-out;
}

.transition-transform {
  transition-property: transform;
  transition-duration: 200ms;
  transition-timing-function: ease-in-out;
}

When you put both on a button:

<button class="transition-colors transition-transform">Save</button>

Because .transition-transform appears later in the stylesheet, the browser computes transition-property: transform and completely drops your color transitions. Swapping the class order in your HTML does nothing—CSS cascade order is determined by the stylesheet, not the class attribute.

The Fix: Custom Property Slots + @property

Instead of having each utility write a different transition-property list, give every transition group its own custom property slot, and have all of them write the exact same combined transition-property list:

@property --transition-colors {
  syntax: "*";
  inherits: false;
}

@property --transition-opacity {
  syntax: "*";
  inherits: false;
}

@property --transition-shadow {
  syntax: "*";
  inherits: false;
}

@property --transition-transform {
  syntax: "*";
  inherits: false;
}

Each utility class now only toggles its own slot:

.transition-colors {
  --transition-colors: color, background-color, border-color, text-decoration-color, fill, stroke;
}

.transition-transform {
  --transition-transform: transform;
}

.transition-colors,
.transition-opacity,
.transition-shadow,
.transition-transform {
  transition-property:
    var(--transition-colors, --none),
    var(--transition-opacity, --none),
    var(--transition-shadow, --none),
    var(--transition-transform, --none);
}

Look closely at what happens when an element has class="transition-colors transition-transform":

  1. --transition-colors resolves to color, background-color, ...
  2. --transition-transform resolves to transform
  3. Unset slots fall back to --none—an unanimateable custom property name that browsers safely ignore.
  4. Both properties transition simultaneously, regardless of which class came first in CSS or HTML.

Why @property Is Mandatory Here

You might wonder why we registered those variables with @property instead of just using plain --transition-colors variables.

Inheritance leaks. Normal CSS custom properties inherit down the DOM tree. Without inherits: false, putting .transition-colors on a parent card would set --transition-colors for every child inside that card. The moment a child element used .transition-transform, it would accidentally inherit its parent's --transition-colors value too.

Registering each variable with inherits: false scopes the slot strictly to the element itself. Zero leakage into descendants.

(Bonus: This exact same pattern solves composable transform utilities—--translate-x, --scale-x, --rotate—and gap-aware flex layouts without inheritance bugs.)

Problem 2: Defaults Overriding Explicit Modifiers

Now look at the second half of those rules: default duration and easing.

If .transition-colors sets transition-duration: 200ms directly at normal class specificity (0, 1, 0), you immediately hit a source-order trap:

/* Defined early in your stylesheet */
.duration-500 {
  transition-duration: 500ms;
}

/* Defined later in your stylesheet */
.transition-colors {
  transition-duration: 200ms;
}

Even if a developer writes class="transition-colors duration-500", the duration stays stuck at 200ms because .transition-colors was declared lower in the CSS file.

The Fix: Zero-Specificity :where()

The :where() pseudo-class always has 0 specificity (0, 0, 0). By separating the property declaration from its default timing declarations, any explicit modifier wins automatically:

/* Specificity: (0, 0, 0) */
:where(.transition, .transition-colors, .transition-opacity, .transition-shadow, .transition-transform) {
  transition-duration: var(--duration-200);
  transition-timing-function: var(--ease-in-out);
}

/* Specificity: (0, 1, 0) — always beats :where() */
.duration-500 {
  transition-duration: var(--duration-500);
}

Now:

  • class="transition-colors" gets 200ms and ease-in-out out of the box.
  • class="transition-colors duration-500" gets 500ms.
  • class="duration-500 transition-colors" also gets 500ms.
  • No !important, no duplicate classes, and no JavaScript class-merging runtime required.

Scaling This Into a Sass Mixin Engine

When you generate this from Sass, you can expose the exact same architecture both as HTML utility classes and as composable mixins inside an apply() dispatcher:

.card {
  @include apply(
    transition-colors,
    transition-shadow,
    duration(300),
    ease(out),
    shadow(md) hover
  );
}

Which compiles down to clean, deterministic CSS:

.card {
  --wu-transition-colors: color, background-color, border-color, text-decoration-color, fill, stroke;
  --wu-transition-shadow: box-shadow;
  transition-property:
    var(--wu-transition-colors, --wu-none),
    var(--wu-transition-opacity, --wu-none),
    var(--wu-transition-shadow, --wu-none),
    var(--wu-transition-transform, --wu-none);
  transition-duration: var(--wu-duration-300);
  transition-timing-function: var(--wu-ease-out);
}

.card:hover {
  box-shadow: var(--wu-shadow-md);
}

Wrapping Up

Modern CSS primitives like @property, :where(), @layer, and native <dialog> / popover APIs eliminate a huge amount of the complexity we used to solve with build-time JS scanners and runtime class mergers.

We built this entire pattern into WovenUI—an open-source, CSS-first design system and 54-component UI kit powered by Dart Sass with compile-time token validation and zero-JS native HTML components.

If you want to inspect the full Sass source or try the live compiler playground, check out the repos on GitHub:

  • Core Engine: github.com/WovenUI/core
  • UI Components: github.com/WovenUI/components
  • Wovenui Playground wovenui.com/playground

(If you find the architecture useful, dropping a star on GitHub helps a ton as we push toward our first community milestones!)
